I will preface this review by saying I am truly enjoy survival and construction games.  Particlarly when they have an unforgiving bend to them.  I played wurm for several years and truly enjoyed it before its recent decline of private servers.
After 46 hours of play and managing to play my way into intermediate stages of the game.  I enjoyed my time in LiF   I would love to see the game succeed.  If you love survivor/builder games this has a good skeleton.  It needs some tuning to be excellent in my opinion.  The engine provide a beautiful setting and the visual landscape is artfully rendered.   Most objects look like they fit in the theme.  Terreforming was good.  Building and character advancement were all fun and exploration of the land enjoyable.   This is early access and I provide the following feed back in support of the game, not to spite it.
I enjoy the game but came to a fundamental conclusion that the skill tree's are fundamentally too simple and merit broadening and deepening.  There are several walls that force dependency on other trees that are too heavy handed and could be developed in other more compelling parallel tracks.  The skill dependency advancements on prior grinding, specifically, of things that are non related is not very compelling game play.  Nesting rope behind cleaning chicken coops made no thematic sense to me...  Just seems like a designed block that was poorly implemented.   A player should be able to explore skills with out so many dependencies nested so deeply in other trees.  I found it frustrating after having ground out a skill to only realize I was blocked buy another skill three layers deep into another tree.
The combat skills are also blocked by arbitrary nesting.  Please, can somebody tell me why the bow skill is nested 3 layers behind leather armor?  forcing a player on player beating to grind into it? Nothing was more frustrating to me than making my first bow and then realizing I had no way of using it...   Basic combat skills should be grindable from 0.    Hit boxes on mobs are too small in some cases.  I can swing at the♥♥♥♥♥of a moose and hit zero.  I suspect its too far forward and given the animals AI to run its a recipe in frustration not amusement.  I did desperately try to beat that moose down with a hatchet!!!  I hit him about a dozen times but could never hit him in the rump.  It would have been nice if he had turned and squashed me as a casual suggestion...
Farming mechanics around fields becoming fallow are over tooned to the over dependancy on fertilizer...  Or else you need to implement a dark age manure spreader!  Coops should be earlier in the construction skill tree and produce more manure faster.  Feeding coops is problematic in the early stages due to the crop fertilization thing.  It seemslike a broken dependency.  90 level skills seemed to make little difference on production.  I found that oddly disatisfying.  If I grind it up I expect better results.  I would prefer to see skill gains slower but more meaningful.
Building and property control, specifically around destroying things needs some work.  The builder should be able to destroy something regardless of monument status.  Making a wattle fence in the wrong spot early on is a long time to correct...
Food is hard early on and camp fires break too often.  I can understand fueling but the campfire should not need to be rebuilt so often and further if it breaks should be deconstructable so I dont have to have three broken fireplaces in my camp in the early game.  Fishing is just eye gougingly painful...  It should be broken out from hunting.
Reparing things is a problem.  I would prefer to repair my tools than have to make 10 of them knowing I will burn through the stack in the early game.  A tool should feel like an achievement and the quality of the tools should be something that can be improved post production.  It gives a better vehicle to grind than just spamming objects.
Boats would be just damn cool!
Early game storage is seriously gimped and the wagon should be able to hold ore and stone.  As it sits, that seems just very broken.  I built one and was grossly disapointed in its utility.  It should be a game changer in materials moving and is just, meh...
Random herb properties are very cool.  I think that was a brilliant idea harkening back to AC 1.  Nicely done.  Combat has great promise.
I really have such high hopes for the game and hope this feedback and its direction is recieved with the best of intentions!  Please keep developing and I look forward to frequent revisits and patches come.

Game is constantly patching as the game permits terraforming and object creation therefore there is new data to be downloaded everytime you log into  a server. Animations are stiff, UI is awkward always having to TAB between mouse function or movement function, thought it is at least customizable. Solved some graphic issue with correcting a game file that had viewdistance at 10,000 ...put that down to 2,000 and was finally able to turn around without a game stall. Search steam forums for this solution if you want step by step instructions. Lots of keyboard commands that are not documented in the keybind control settings or in the help section inside the game. Oh...if you have the game fullscreen and have to tab out of it to go searching for websites, videos or any other sort of help  the game will not return to normal when you alt tab back in, screen gets funky, goes sort of windowed but not really, losing most of the UI around the border of the screen. Have to log out and restart the game then. Otherwise if you need to switch screens then you have to go into settings and turn the game into windowed mode before attempting to deal with websites or voice applications.
The other issue is that in order to play this game you either get it running on your own computer and play it alone. Or you connect to one of many player run servers. These come and go, everyone has thier own rules, decent website listing them all, ping times, popularity and comment sections but often there is no info on the game server, who runs it or what they expect for rules.
There are some pretty solid looking servers out there, repleat with websites introducing thier concept, rules and some of them look fairly dedicated. But watch out...unless they say 'noob friendly' somewhere in the game server website or title you may be in for a shock. I found one that by day 2 expected me to know what I was doing and be good at it. Died officially 2 times. Frictional gaming are known for tellling unsetteling stories, without the need of crazy cutscenes, explosions or high-end graphics. They typically draw you into their stories with fantastic sound design, excellent maps and atmosphere, terrifying enemies and great music. Soma is on par with Frictionals usually high level of fidelity and quality. Though this time pushed to the next level, in a highly familiar genre we all got to know and love through their previous stories Penumbra and Amnesia: The Dark Descent. Even though familiar, this title feels oh so fresh and brings something new to the table.
Every part of the game feels very rooted in a reality which seem like a possible outcome of our lack of care for our home world, and it is this idea that constantly evolves as you progress. The more you play, the more it becomes clear that a future without makind is possible if we don't become more proactive and forward thinking with future consequences in mind.
Finally, the most interesting part of this game are all the thoughts it provokes. What does it really mean to be a human? What is conciousness? Where do we draw the line when it comes to being alive? How is our future on this earth going to look in 100, 200, 500 years? How will our race evolve with this continuously evolving technological and progressive world we share, which seem to speed up exponentially both in terms of expectancy and demand of where we should be as a race and technologically.
Yes, the game is not perfect, but it delivers such a joyous ride that those small inconsistencies are easily overlooked. 10/10 Will play many times...

I'll start out by saying that the game has massive potential.  The skill systems and crafting are wonderful.  But there are a few problems that have been present for extended periods and make the game nearly unplayable for extended periods.
The method the game uses for saving changes to the terrain is very inefficient, which makes it very difficult to maintain a server for extended periods of time.  And if you terraform below the elevation of the water anywhere on the entire map, it causes corruptions in the game database which results in ongoing lag.  Leaving tree stumps after cutting down trees also causes server lag, and so does having too many trees on the server.
Each of these issues don't seem to be terribly important on their own, but they have all been present for an extended period and the game developers continue to add new features and have moved on to working on the MMO version fo the game rather than addressing existing bugs.  Until the developers give the game the attention it needs, this game is not worth playing.

Im going to start off by saying, although i recommend it and i love playing this game, its still in early acces so you may not like the game right now but maybe you will later.
OK so for me, this game seemed like a very cool concept, similar to dayZ, but instead first person. Also unlike dayZ, nether has strayed from the typical zombie enemy and has come up with teleporting humans turned into aliens from a massive solar flare that ravaged the earth, so it wasnt hard for me to get into.
As soon as you start up nether you will be brought to a screen of multiplayer servers hosted by the commpany. Meaning as far as playing goes, its only going to be multiplayer so be wary about that when choosing to buy or not.
Gameplay:
Nether starts you off in a character selection screen where you have a few choices as to what look you want your character to have. After selecting one, you spawn in at a random spot on the, not too enormous, map, which i believe will eventually be expanded. the first thing you are going to want to do is search for the, almost always difficult to find, items, which can range from weapons, to ammo, to food, and also sometimes money or sell items. the only items you start off with is a knife and a backpack so finding things fast is a necessity. this searching for items is made even more difficult by the large amount of enemies scattered around the world that will sometimes even spawn in front of you. Also you have to be careful to stay away from other players at first becuase as far as i can tell, everyone wants to kill you dead. once you have a few items to work with, you have a couple of options: One, you can run to one of the four safezones in the world which keep you safe from players and nether, and also allow you to buy and sell items and store your stuff in a global inv. or Two, you can try and use the items you have found to stay out and kill nethers and players to obtain more stuff while searching for more stuff.
Leveling:
as you play the game there are a few ways to level your player.
1. fighting the different nethers will you give you xp based on the type of nether you killed
2. killing players will reward some xp aswell
3. selling items will give you small amounts of xp
4. package running, in each of the safezones there are packages laying on the ground that you can pick up and run to the corresponding safezone for which the package is meant for, the farther away the safezone you need to go to is from the one you picked the package up from determines how much money and xp you will gain from trading in the package
Using Your Levels:
In the players skill tree there are 6 different branches. Each branch contains 3 special abilites that you will be rewarded with after the 1st, 4th, and 10th point you put into the same tree.
The 6 branches are as follows:
1. GUNS: this tree allows you to do more damage with headshots and eventually all guns
2. STAMINA: this tree allows you to lower the cost of stamina a melee attack costs, jump higher, and also run for longer periods of time.
3. SURVIVAL: this tree allows you to get more from using food items, get health from overeating, and get more hp from hp items
4. STRENGTH: this tree helps with gun sway, how much hp you have and how much you can carry
5. STEALTH: this ones pretty straight forward
6. MELEE: gives you the blocking ability, and also allows you to do more damage with melee weapons

Overall this is a fun game to play by yourself and with friends. although its quite difficult alone...

This game is wonderfully well-written and presents an alternate history/steampunk vision of the traditional Around the World in 80 Days myth. This game is essentially a choose-your-own-adventure novel with good writing. The choices are diverse, and there are light inventory/money management elements that give the gameplay some diversity and agency in choice. However, the real star here is the character imbued in every word, in every scene, in every moment of foreshadowing that suggest, to use the words of the Knight in The Last Crusade, that you have chosen wisely or poorly.
If you enjoy story in games, are willing to invest in creating a world in your mind, and are interested in exploring the world and discovering mysteries and adventures, check it out! You won't regret it.

I first encountered Gabe's story back in the mid '90s, shortly after it came out, and I was hooked. Granted, Tim Curry playing a good ol' Cajun gent with the body of a 12-year old boy (in-game reference) was a little off-putting, but I've always been a fan of the 'So-bad-it's-good' school of doing things. The story was darker than most Sierra titles at the time, and I was immediately hooked. Sadly, the older that game got, the harder it was to run on progressively newer machines.
But then, there were two. This new version is appropriately advanced in form and function. There are a few new puzzles, and entirely new voice cast. Rather than reinvent the wheel, the new cast attempts with differing levels of success, to emulate the original cast. I actually found Malia's VO to be fairly weak, and the Dragon soundd kinda 'eh', but all in all, it was a splendid auditory experience. The updates make sense, and I love what Jane and Co have done to give the game a richer, more vibrant NOLA feel. Robert Holmes' remastered soundtrack is awesome as ever, though I do miss the original St. George's theme. Except for a few weird bugs, my time playing the game (two consecutive playthroughs thusfar) has been largely very enjoyable.
For fans of Sierra's old school adventure games, and/or fans of occult/horror adventure games, whether or not they are Sierra fans, this title should be a no-brainer. The puzzles are logic-based, but fairly simple, and the game will probably leave a lasting impression. It did for me. Many kudos to Jane Jensen and her team at Pinkerton Road, as well as Phoenix Studios for putting together such a delightful trip down memory lane.

80 Days is an interactive "choose your own adventure" type game with a great narrative and fantastic writing. Highly recommended, especially if you loved the original tale.
Each journey takes about 2 hours (within 80 days) to 3 hours (more than 80 days). While you can always take a break from the game at any city, the story is so engrossing that you would probably complete your playthrough in one sitting. There is high replay value as you explore different routes and choices.
The clock is always ticking so you feel a sense of urgency as you have to decide quickly between visiting the market, exploring the city, or planning your route. Add to that balancing your duties as valet and friend to Fogg without losing your eye on the prize. To win the game, you have to complete the journey within 80 days. However, the journey itself is fun even when you come across obstacles. Get robbed, thrown into jail, or crash your vehicle... There are many unexpected surprises along the way that make delays more amusing than frustrating.

The original version of Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers is one of my most favourite video games of all time and I bought the 20th Anniversary Edition expecting it to miss the very high standards I would hold it to.  I wasn't wrong.
The remake is competent enough.  Many of the visuals - which is the key thing the remake has been sold on - are very pretty and the cutscenes in particular are excellent (though I would have liked a way to disable the speech balloons).  The voice acting is solid and, once I got used to the new voices, very much enjoyed them,  The story and characters still hold up while - for the most part - the puzzles are not too obtuse.  There are some animation issues and the quality of the backgrounds is not always consistent (I really don't like Jackson Square at all) but I didn't find these things too problematic.  So if you enjoy adventure games and have never played the original, then I suspect you will find the game worth the price of entry.
But if you *have* played the original game I'd suggest caution, for at least in my case the remake does not improve upon it and, in fact, is inferior in several ways.  Critical here are the visuals.  While the original game managed to produce a mood perfect for the story through its dark backgrounds and strong use of contrast, the brightness and colour of the backgrounds in the remake fail to do the same.  An exception here must be made for the cutscenes which, in contrast, do an excellent job capturing the mood of the story.  Yet, ironically, this only serves to highlight the absence of atmosphere in the rest of the game.  This is most clearly demonstrated in the final scene (no spilers) which slips between cutscenes and regular gameplay.  Here, the cutscenes do all of the work while each shift back to regular gameplay spoils the tension that has been produced by them.
In addition to this, changes in the pacing of the game also disrupt its mood.  Access to areas of the game is more staggered than in the original, which helps spread out the content of the game more evenly but also - for me anyway - takes away from the world-building at the outset of the game.  Moreover, minor additions to the game's content (a few small puzzles and scenes) are often out of place and stand out as obvious bolt-ons with little or no necessity (the very minor scene at the Wright family tomb, for example, left me astounded by its pointlessness).  I also found the music disappointing compared with the original (though perhaps this is simply because I grew up in the '90s and have acquired an unreasonable fondness for midi tracks!).
How to conclude, then?  If you like adventure games and have never played the original, you should buy this.  If you have played the original and are interested (like me) in seeing first hand how the game was reworked, or if you would like to play Gabriel Knight again but find its old interface or graphics a deal-breaker, then you should buy the game.  But if you are wanting this game to recapture the spirit and character of the original, then I do not recommend it.  Or else, I recommend that you be braced for disappoinment.

The main problem with this game is level design. Despite being a "first-person shooter" Duke Nukem Forever doesn't actually have you doing much shooting. The short duration of most of the game's gunfighting segments makes this problem even worse.
Despite all of its other well-documented flaws, Duke Nukem Forever could have been a very fun game if it were a mindless, comical, action-packed, old-school shooter. But the overabundance of physics puzzles and platforming sections simply made it feel like a very cheap Half-Life 2 imitation. The glimpses of juvenile fun early in the game give way to a bogged-down chore. The game features a lot of cool weapons like shrink rays and freeze rays but barely gives you a chance to try them all out. Ultimately, I cannot recommend this game because it is exactly what all games strive not to be: boring.

For cost conscious people, the original version on
might be the better option.  You can argue that it looks better, sounds better because of the original Hollywood cast, and maybe even plays better.
But all that said, the 20th anniversary edition of the game is a perfectly fine version to play if you want something that is a bit more modern.  Built in hints, some light commentary on each screen of the game, and some UI overhauls make the game a bit more accessible than the original.  As a remake, it's well done.
But regardless of which version you pick up, Gabriel Knight is unequivocally one of the best adventure games in the genre.  You play as the eponymous Gabriel Knight, a novelist who gets involved with a series of murders in New Orleans.  As Gabriel learns more about the case, he also learns more about his own mysterious past, including the madness that claimed his father's life.  It's a compelling combination of a crime procedural with the supernatural world of Voodoo and Gabriel's dark and mysterious past.  It really is a great story to watch/read through, and it's the reason why Jane Jensen and this game in particular is celebrated among adventure game fans.
The adventure game part of it is fun as well, with some clever puzzles and interesting solutions.  There's nothing as frustrating as the infamous Gabriel Knight 3 mustache puzzle, so you don't have to worry about getting stuck.  And even if you do get stuck, the hint system in the game will get you moving on to the next great story beat if you just want to move on and experience the story.
This game is a classic and definitely worth playing if you have any interest in the genre.  Whether you pick up the original on
or the updated version here, I don't think you are going to be disappointed.

The original Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Father remains my favourite adventure gamel (and overall favourite game). So I was hesitant to try this remake, especially after the disappointing Moebius.
However, I greatly enjoyed this. I prefer the original, but this remake has its merits.
In short? I recommend the original game, which you can get on Good Old Games. It's a good remake, but not worth full price. It's worth getting on a sale, though.
Pros:
-Fantastic graphics and art design. The character and location remodels are drop-dead gorgeous. They're a massive improvement to the original game. Where the game especially shines is in the panelled, graphic novel style cutscenes that made the original game so memorable. All are recreated with gusto and there are many more new ones that turn previous in-game cutscenes into the graphic novel style. The updated graphics and art style alone are worth the price of admission.
-The voice work is quite good. I was worried, since Phoenix Online couldn't use the original voice work, but the new cast does a fine job. For the most part. I'll get to that.
-A small handful of puzzles have been reworked. About half a dozen. Two, in particular, are very nice changes: where Gabriel needs to change his looks, and somewhere he needs to break into.The latter is incredibly creepy.
Cons:
-Some animations are awkward. Sometimes, the characters stifly spin on the spot like "tank controls" of older 3D third person games. They're rare, fortunately. There are other moments where the 3D animation is choppy or awkward, but it's still a massive improvement from Moebius.
-While most of the voice acting is good, there are times it feels very stiff and unnatural compared to the original game. Little, intricate details in line delivery is lost at times. I loved Tim Curry's delivery of a German poem, but this voice actor's delivery is very deadpan. Some of Mark Hamil's little ways of spicing up Mosely's characters are lost, which hurts the character's presentation. I'm biased, though, given my love for the original.
-As I said, about half a dozen puzzles have been redone. Some, unfortunately, have absolutely infuriating, immersion-breaking logic puzzles like something out of Myst. One puzzle gives little indication of what to do (a tiny, barely readable guide in a the bottom corner of the screen). They feel completely out of place with the rest of the game and are only a nuisance than anything else.

So, you came here most likely wondering: "Should i buy this early access game? Is worth it?" Well, the short answer to this is: "YES". I'll review some of the game features here and, if you're in a hurry, there is a tl;dr section at the end.
You're in charge of a trading colony on Mars and you compete with other companies to gain monopoly on the planet. It fits really nice with all the talks going on about an actual manned expedition to Mars.
You have to buy stocks of the other players and gain control of their company. You win the game when you have bought all the other companies. If your own company gets bought, you instantly loose the game.
You start off with a little cash and ressources (or none, there are options to set it before starting a game). You'll then have to build some buildings (like a mine or a steel mill) to harvest some ressources, be it iron or steel, etc. You can then transform these ressources into building materials or goods which you use or sell on a global market. All the players affect that market; if someone sells a lot of a product, its price is going to go down and, on the contrary, if someone buys a lot of a ressource, its price is going up for everybody.
With the money and the ressources, you can expand your colony, buy some stocks or use the black market (i'll get back to it later). In order to build more, you'll need to spend some claims. Claims that allow you, and only you, to use a tile in the game. So, especially at the beggining of a game, the fastest to find and lay claims on ressources is most likely to have the better spots. Those claims are obtained by expending your HQ or bought on the black market. So, the twist of the game is, you'll be struggling with few claims and you'll have to prioritise what building you need. Are you going to try and be self-sufficient? Or maybe invest in a pricey ressource gathering infrastructure? That's the kind of questions you'll be dealing with most of the game.
You HQ and your ressource transforming building will need some base ressources that you can mine yourself, or buy on the market (thus making it pricier). When you're lacking a ressource it increases your debt, which affect the value of your stocks. If your stocks are cheap, it's easier for other players to buy and you might loose the game. So watch that debt carefully.
Mostly, yes. There are some researches and upgrading you can do in the game, but you'll spend those hard-earned claims mostly on harvest/producing more.
You can't directly attack other players, at least in a classic RTS way. There are no soldiers and you can't steal a nice spot claimed, but you can affect their production with the help of some saboteurs available on the blackmarket. For some money, you can dynamite one of their building or launch an EMP that will freeze their buildings for sometime. Of course, you can also be the target of such attacks and, if you're not defended (with goons also from the blackmarket), you won't know who hit you.
Of course, as it is the goal of the game, you can buy other players stocks and then win the game.
Yes. I haven't add issues with the game crashing. It's working really well on my end and all the features are there. Of course, some elements are still to be updated. As an exemple, there are no dedicated servers provided for multiplayer games, making the game quit if the host leaves the game. Like in the good old days.
But, for the rest, everything is there and you'll be able to enjoy all the mechanics.

And the price, for about 500mo of game, not that nice graphics and all, is a bit high. But, in my opinion, it is worth it.

Cons:
In the end: really great game that will get you an alternative RTS we don't see much these days. If you like strategy games, wargames and ressource management games: this is for you. I recommend it without any doubt.

SW:KOTOR 2 is an RPG game Developed by Obsidian Entertainment. The game takes place  a few years after the events of KOTOR 1 after Revan defeated Malak and saved the galaxy. But now after departed deep into the outer rim of the galaxy, a bunch of Sith Lords, have appeared and have almost completly destoryed the Jedi order and the remaining Jedi Masters are into hiding. You play as a male or female Jedi Exile which you learn later into the game about why you were exiled from the Jedi Order. After escaping a Mine Fuel facuilty (Either by blowing it up and evading a sith ship) you head to a orbiting facilty above a planet called Telos. After being imprisoned and captured by them you find out the ship you traveled in, the Ebon Hawk has been stolen. After helping a light or dark side corporation and meeting a soldier that knows your character, you travel to many places into the planet until you get your ship back after finding out a Jedi Master lives in a acdemy in a polar region of the planet. After a companion gets the data base at the academy you find out why, your charcter was exiled and leaves you between two roads: Do you gather up the rest of the Masters to help you fight the sith, or do you join the sith and hunt down and kill the Jedi Masters?
The companions you meet are all cool and deep. They all have secrets behind them which you have to get them to trust you to find out. Some of them you may not enjoy (like a stupid robot that is a jerk), but alot of them are fun to talk too, a few of them were in KOTOR 1 that make a return like T3-M4 and HK-47.
One of the highlights of this game is the Light and Dark side paths. Through multiple parts of the game you sometimes given a choice such as kill an innocent by raiding his house then kill him as he returns (Dark Side) or saving someone from mercneary thugs (Light Side).
The gameplay is a turn base or real time action (Can be chosen through menu) game. The game has powers that are ran by a 1d20 system. I'm stupid so I don't know much about the system but if you know stuff from Dungeons & Dragons you might understand it. The level cap is to belive is 30 but that doesnt mean its easy and should be taken lightly. Like how Fallout 3 and NV take a while so does this. This also means you want to spend Attributes when making a character very carefully as messing up might make it harder to clear the game. For example: putting alot of points into Constitution and Intelligence might give alot of VP and skill points to use, but at the cost of FP (force points) which might make it harder for you to use force powers.
OVerall KOTOR 2 is a fun game, with it just getting workshop, people can get the restored content mod and get the true and perhaps best parts of the game. Problem is sometimes that game can be difficult with what planets you decide to visit and there are some annoying puzzles. Wow, this game is dumb. It's a twin-sticks shooter in an admittedly good art style with good music, but the controls and gameplay make this game frustrating and pointless. You can only move along the X or Y axis at a time, no diagonal movement here. You control a ship that fires little globules across the screen as you try to take down some big blobs that are at first stationary, then turn into ghosts that chase you around and around, and then later you encounter some ships that move and fire at you. It's made awkward by the fact that you can't really control where your shots go. There's no mouse support so you're limited to WASD for moving along the X- or Y-axes at a time, and the arrow keys to fire in those general directions. You can fire diagonally but the real problem is you can't really move where you want to because you can't move diagonally. Also, I like how after a certain number of points, you get a mandatory power-up, and ONLY ONE of them is useful. The one I'm talking about is of course the multi-shot; everything else TAKES AWAY your ability to fire in exchange for a short burst that takes a long time to recharge. What kind of sense does that make? Oh, but here's the best part. If you get hit after taking the multi-shot, you can't get it back again: you're forced to lose your ability to fire. This game is really bad, and from the posts on the forum, it seems like others are in agreement. Check it out if you're interested, since it's free to play, but imo it's not worth the time or hard drive space.

Jets'n'Guns was the game I was waiting for since the days of X-Out on the C-64.
I was always hoping for a spiritual successor to this sidescrolling shooter from the 80s,
where you were able to customize ships, weapons, special equipment and even had
a grid to position them around your ship.
Jets'n'Guns was originally released in 2006. It was the first game for me in this genre,
which came close to the gameplay, atmosphere and sheer fun playing, without being
punishing, since X-Out in 1989. And it is still the only one since then. There have
been sidescrolling shooters in the last years, some lackluster, some quiet good.
But Jets'n'Guns just has the right parts, put together with a lot of heart, good design
and an overall direction that lets it stand out.
With its beautiful 2d art it even stands the test of time and manages to still look
beautiful in 2014 on a resulation of 1900x1200. I even dare say, it looks better
than some titles in the genre of the last years.
Jets'n'Guns will keep you on your toes and lets you forget the time. With all
the customization and choices you have, you won't feel grim when you don't
get it right the first time. It is one of the games, where you will try it
'Just one more time'.
The soundtrack, composed by Machinae Supremacy, is another integral
part that adds to the atmosphere and is also available free to download.

Perfect game for any car fan, regardless of age.
There's not a whole lot of fancy graphics, no lens flares, relatively simple smoke/dust effects, most foliage (except trees) are made of flat textures (which are pretty well done, you can't really tell unless you stop and zoom right in on the grass, looks fine if you're driving even at low speeds), and the shaders aren't modified to give a 'cinematic look'. So this game isn't an astonishingly pretty game. But you know what, that's okay.
Each vehicle is intricately modelled, down to the point where you can see each individual part of the engine. You can see the butterfly valves on your supercharged V8 muscle car, you can see the engine block move around in its mounts slightly as you rev the engine. The level of detail is insane. Hit a harsh bump that bottoms out your custom, lowered car? Be prepared to potentially have your entire exhaust system ripped out of your car. Hit a sharp kerb at high speed? Might wanna watch your tires, they can pop, giving your car an unnatural feel. The physical damage in this game is brutally realistic, as each car is not 'hard-coded' with performance stats, health points, etc. Each INDIVIDUAL PART of a car makes up it's whole performance, much like a real car. Pop your front-right tire, and your car will start veering slightly to the right. Fit sport tires, you might be able to handle a corner slightly faster. Lower your suspension, you'll reduce body rolls and keep all 4 tires on the road better, resulting in better grip.
It goes on and on. The soft-body physics overall are brilliant, the cars crumple, wobble, and react exactly how you'd expect a car to react.
Maps:
The maps that come with the game are very nice, and quite varied.
Gridmap: A testing map, with an assortment of jumps, surface types (from sand and dirt to mud and water), slalom cones, objects to crash into and a few high-speed race courses.
Port: A small map set on a port, a perfect map for Gymkhana or drifting fans, with all kinds of shipping containers, warehouses, and a few ramps along with it.
Industrial Site: A medium sized map set on a seaside industrial area, it features a RallyCross track with multiple configurations, an offroad racing track laced with thick mud that will bog down your average rally car, but take a big 4x4 and you'll plow straight on through, and a more traditional tarmac race course. The industrial area also features many warehouses like the Port map, and a nice little circuit that races around it, featuring a jump over a small inlet.
East Coast USA: Set in the East Coast of the USA (As the nae suggests), it has a medium-sized town, along with fairly well maintained roads, that go from the coast to snaking through the forest. Lots of dirt trails through fields and woodlands for rallying around too.
Jungle Rock Island: On a Tropical Island, this map has poorly-maintained roads that call for terrifying high-speed driving along the coastline of this island. It also has many offroad dirt trails that run through the forest, and can quite easily end up getting you lost! There's also a few little rally trails, and industrial areas, quarries, and a port. Probably my favourite map.
Cliff: Spawns you in at the top of a cliff, the only way around is down the cliff. Fun little map for just throwing stuff of cliffs and watching it arrive at the bottom as a mangled mess. Not much to the map other than that, but still fun nonetheless.
Hirochi Raceway: A race-focused map, this raceway is GP-styled, with very wide, smooth corners, along with fast straights and chicanes thrown in. This map also has a few forest routes, that can take you on a narrow road through some forests, so any mistakes can be fatal.
So, quite a few maps, with lots of variety.
Scenarios
The game has a wide variety of scenarios, too many to list here, that cover multiple fun aspects of the game.
These can range from tutorials, to shakedowns of various cars, police chases, races, delivery challenges, even a 'hyper-miling' challenge where you have to cross Jungle Rock Island with very little gas left in your car. There's even a demolition derby scenario for people to 'party play'.
Overall, I'd give this game a 8/10, I'd like to see networked multiplayer (something the BeamNG devs might implement if their engine can support it) and a campaign mode (which the devs have planned pretty much since day 1 of the project)
Lots more potential, the modding community is great, who make new maps, scenarios, vehicles, etc, etc.
Definitely worth the buy, especially for car fans, IMO.

1. I am not a Dev.
2. I own, play and enjoy DayZ.
3. I believe that Nether, in its current state, is playable fun and easily worth 20 bucks and if they keep improving the game (crafting system, player structures, traps for example) Nether might become more than just a viable choice for the MMO Survival segment.
The game has a remarkable atmosphere! The sound as well as the lookd of the sunken city are great. I'm not talking about the graphics per sé but the very style, starting with the level desing, the chose of background sound and going as far as the colors. Call me Blasphemer, but the runied cityscape of Nether gives me chilles in a way Chernarus never could.
The gameplay is not as complex as it is in DayZ - Nether is not based on a simulation, as you should notice after a few moments and it feels like a straight-line shooter. This, however, does not mean that there is a lack of stealth or tactical manoeuvering. If you run about like John Rambo you're gonna be deader as Stalones career (c'mon The Expendables does NOT count) rather quickly.
Not only the combat mechanics are less complex than in DayZ, the survival mechanics  are, too.
You've got your HUD with health, stamina, ammo and so forth. You don't need to worry about thirst AND hunger and there's no rotten kiwi that will end you like the little b*tch you are. (Rotten Kiwis are bad motherf*ckers, we all have made that experience).
But is this lack of complexity a bad thing? Not at all! It's a good thing! Nether is not DayZ and sometimes you just don't want to starve with your pockets full of canned food just because you don't happen to find a can opener. It's quicker with less mirco managment
Contrary to many reviewers I have neither experienced server stability issues nor greater bugs (10h+). There are a few graphic bugs (hovering grass and cars) and the collition is not always perfect, especially when it comes to rubble.
So what's the problem? As far as I'm concerned there is none.
Is Nether a scam like Worldwar Z? I don't know, I hope not.
Is it worth the 20 bucks? Easily!
Is it a DayZ killer? Is the apple going to kill the pear?
Nether is a rather positive surpise and I can only reccommend it to you if you are interested in the MMO Survival genre or if you 're looking for a game that is similar to DayZ without being just a copy.
One can enjoy Nether AND DayZ!

Right. So, this one is a bit conditional, i can't just say "Yes or No."
Ok, do you like rust style gameplay?
Do you like combat similar-ish to Chivalry/Mount&Blade?
Do you have a lot of free time?
Do you have at LEAST two other people to play with, or are you willing to join a random group on a server? (3 other people or more recommended)
If you answered YES to at elast three out of the four questions, you'll love it. Just like I did. Sadly my group got bored and i sort of ell off. You CAN NOT solo this game. You can not be a jack of all trades. Think of it as medieval rust, but much more serious feeling; more realistic, more time consuming, etc. Again, in rust you find a blueprint, and you can build it. In LiF, you have all the blueprints, but you need the skills to use them.
You chop trees, you become a better lumber jack. You cut wood, you become a better carpenter. You mold stone, you become a better mason. You CAN NOT be a jack of all trades. The more you specialize, the better, but you have to fill all roles to prosper. So, the beauty of other players comes in. If you have a person for each role, you can all fully excel - OR you can spread yourselves among two or three trades, lowering your specialization and skill in each, but making up for the lack of people. In other words, the main limiting factor is the number of people you need. if a few people get bored, its over for all of you unless you can replace them.
So, if you can get a group of people you trust to commit, or if you can join a server and are willing to ask in chat to join someone long term (wouldnt recommend, the early game was my favorite, watching your mud huts evolve to cabins, to outposts, to pallisades, to castles is an amazing thing and joining late game when they're fully militarized robs you of that joy... however it is useful for learning the ropes.)
But as much as the intensive human cost is a con, it is also a pro for the game. Playing with friends in it is amazing, as you're all working together for a common long term goal. the interactions are great, and there's a nice social aspect.
Speaking of such, i would love to get back into the game. If a group of people needs an extra sword at your side, feel free to message me, be you a group of friends jsut getting the game, or just people that need to replace someone or expand.

SOMA is a sci-fi, horror game where you play as Simon Jerett, a man with an unknown brain condition who lives in Toronto and is the subject of a research project to find a cure. Once the vague introductions and mini tutorial is done, things go to hell and you are suddenly dumped into an apocolyptic, underwater world with very little info and very little capabilities.
In this review I will use a 1 to 10 grading scale and provide summaries of several aspects of this game such as graphics, gameplay, sound and story.
(WARNING: May contain minor spoilers)

The gameplay revolves around a "hide and sneak" style of play where you can't confront the various entities out to get you and to find various bits and pieces of information to progress with the plot and figure everything out. There some actions such as "grabbing", "running" and interacting with online computers but there are very little options on how to go about, which aims to add to its horror element with a sense of frailty and limitation. You can't take a haphazard approach and have to go around logically and patiently which will end up making the game a lot simpler and less frustrating. There are also some "puzzles" and tasks to complete the more you progress in order to continue on, but they aren't very difficult and are just there to add to the story. The various monsters in this game tend to be scary at first, but after a few attempts and exposure it lightens the horror element and end up annoying and hindering you. Even if you end up getting caught, the game is pretty generous about giving you second chances and even provides "healing" stations in the form of a black organism you stick your hand into to help you recover from an "injured state". Overall, the difficulty isnt that high and the main object of this game is the plot and to immerse yourself in the game by putting yourself in SImon's shoes which the game does a good job of doing.

The game has little lighting a majority of the time and can get blurry, but is aesthetically pleasing when looking at the environment and some of the several monsters you will encounter as you go along. The actual people aren't as nice to look at compared to other high-end games since the level of detail you find when looking at the surroundings just isn't there when looking at other humans, even if there are very few of them hanging around and are usually disfigured beyond recognition. Overall, since the game is in first person and revolves around knowing your environment to make out the various clues and key items, the graphics are appealing to eye and gives the game more depth to its horror aspect.

The sounds in this game really compliment the graphics and surroundings which really create the game's horror theme. The background sounds leave you tense from start to finish and constantly remind you just how bad the situation your in truly is. The sounds also help with actual gameplay and can point you in the right direction by listening to subtle "foreign" sounds and random footsteps coming from enemies. The voice acting is pretty well done and goes along with the depressing theme of the game. Overall, the sounds in this game are one of its finer aspects and can play an important role in the game which helps make immersing yourself into the game easier.

As a sci-fi game, everything takes place in the future where technology is much more advanced and humanity has achieved a new form of consciousness through machines. There are a few plot twists and turns but for the most part the actual plot is linear and there isn't many actions that actually affect the story or outcome besides some personal choices based on your own morals and actions. The actual storyline is pretty interesting and keeps you intrigued enough to actually see it through to the end to see and achieve your ultimate fate as Simon. You only develop one real relationship through the hellish journey and in a way helps to add to the distraughting atmosphere that constantly surrounds PATHOS: II. Overall, the storyline felt like a mixture of other sci-fi games/movies at times but in the end still retains its own genuine plot with a unique, somewhat unexpected ending.

The game can get buggy at times and loading up new areas or from saved states can cause minor lagging and frame skips. Also, Nvidia users don't always get ideal FPS despite having high-end graphics cards, especially if using SLi. For the most part though, the game runs smoothly and isn't very taxing on the CPU or RAM. Its a modest ~11 GB install and playable for most users. Overall, the optimization isn't perfect and can be improved but not game breaking and noticeable only when going into new areas.

The first PvC I've ever played! That would be "Player vs Crafting" in this case. The crafting system is simply the best, you can gain much satisfaction from leveling up and being able to forge your first iron tools and when you see a screenshot or video of a large settlement you can be suitably impressed by the huge amount of work it took for the players to reach that level. Collaboration is the key here and this may be the first game to actually make other players consider you as an asset rather than a liability.
The graphics are fine to good, as are the annimations. They are not so bad as to diminish from the gameplay and I'm sure with future updates or modding they will improve considerably. I haven't found too many bugs, except for the occasional camera through terrain problem, but that's not uncommon in any game. I also haven't had any crashes or negative experiences with the servers. The online side of things appears very stable, which is a must for such a collaborative game.
The price may be a little steep for what is still essentially an unfinished game. So if you need to, it might be best to wait for a 50% off sale here or on a discount website like humble bundle or bundle stars. Just don't let the negative reviews worry you unless you have a slow rig or are expecting a fully finished game.

I've played ALOT of games and i never write reviews for them but this game is just.. mindblowing. The story line was amazing and disturbing all at the same time and the monsters were equally as terrifying. At one point i was scared so bad it felt like my nerves were fried for the next hour. There's a certain atmosphere present in the original game that is just... somehow lacking in this version. The character models and animations look like they were lifted straight out of the Sims, and a couple of the puzzles added in this remake just don't fit, even through "Adventure Game Logic." (For example, there's a very out-of-place sliding tile puzzle in the *spoiler redacted* library, and a completely nonsensical mechanical puzzle in *spoiler redacted*'s house). If I'd never played the original, I might think differently on that.
That said, this is like comparing steaks; even though this game's New York Strip isn't quite comparable to the original's Filet Mignon, it's still a deliciously worthwhile $20 purchase both for fans and for those who've never played the original Gabriel Knight. The remastered music is absolutely aces, and many of the cutscenes that were rendered with the original in-game engine are now rendered in a fantastic animated graphic novel style that just OOZES awesome. The voice acting is pretty amazing too, with a couple of minor exceptions. There are also a couple of really creepy sequences that weren't present in the original game that caught me as a pleasant surprise.
Overall: 8/10 (versus the original's 10/10)

Great little game !
It is a mix between a rogue-like and a "your own adventure" book, so it's mostly text based with little stories well stitched together that make an exciting global story that feels really yours ! (at least for the 2 runs I did :-) )
I was really pleasantly surprised by this game, although it has some small flaws, it is really captivating, thanks to its quality writing and originality.
If its description intrigues you, you should really give it a try, you won't be disappointed if reading triggers your imagination.
- Original gameplay : a mix of rogue-like and a "your own adventure" book
- Very stylish visuals and art direction
- There's enough stories to a do at least 3 or 4 runs without too much repetitive feeling
- The different little stories are very well stitched together as well as customized depending of your current run, which makes the whole story flow natural
- Very good writing
- It'll make you (a bit) better at geography as you'll discover many cities that aren't that famous ! :-p
- A good part of the game is in realtime, really fast realtime, which gives unnecessary pressure ; some people might get more excited from this, but it'd be nice to be able to turn it off or at least slow it down for a more relaxed and thoughtful mode :)
- gameplay wise, there's a lot of cities that makes little sense (ie: the south part of the globe) ; it'd have been nice that the wager requires to pass through at least 2 cities within a list of 5 created randomly at each game start
- A lot of choices are made without understanding clearly the consequences ; for me, it's alright and it's part of the fun (especially when the sh*it hits the fan ;-) ), but it might annoy people accustomed to more standard games

As a big fan of the original series, this game was like greeting an old friend again. Everything is faithfully recreated, but it's also extremely approachable for any fan of adventure gaming in general. The story is top-notch, comparable to a very good novel.
What I liked is that they balanced out the activities in each of the days, so that each day you have a clear set of objectives and a few side objectives. The voice acting is solid but admittedly not as exciting as the first game which featured heavyweight voice talents like Tim Curry, Mark Hamill and Leah Remini (before she was famous!).
For people who have played prior games from Pinkerton (Moebius) or Phoenix (Cognition), this game shows some progression by the development team. The animations are now done using motion-capture so they are not as offensive as the ones from those games. The engine is still not quite as good as the old Sierra engine was, and responsiveness can be a bit slow as times. But overall it is not a major distraction.
This is the best way to jump into the series at this point, and to relive a piece of gaming history. Highly recommend, can't go wrong with this game if you have any love of engaging stories, crime solving, supernatural and history - this is the game for you.

You and your partner (if you want to have a really good time) have to make your way from street to street, kicking in doors, scavenging for supplies, using ammo carefully (no spray and pray here), deciding on upgrades vs. ammo vs items vs. new weapons and stay alive doing so while mashing the crap out of the undead and seeing what they had in their wallets. Markets change from street to street and not all vendors sell items for the same price or even sell the same items.
With all of this, there really isn't much micromanagement which is amazing. It's fairly quick and you stay in the action, but you have to use your head as much as your twitchy-twitchy fingers. At times it can be pretty tense in that awesome way that we all like to pay for tense experiences that we call SUPER FUN VIDEO GAMES.
So, go buy it. Then play it.

Not sure why I bought this.
So you know how some RTS games with an economy focus let you sell off spare resources to get other stuff you need? It's basically that game, except you win by selling enough resources to buy out your opponents. There isn't any reason to build an economy beyond that goal. As a free-market capitalism tutorial I guess it's educational, but it probably would have made a better board game than a videogame.
As for the state of the alpha right now, balance is pretty wonky, such as lower-valued companies can easily and unpreventably buy out more valuable competitors off the back of a single off-world shipment plus a little commodity selling, and the framerate is both unlocked and badly optimized enough that my computer tries to melt a hole in the floor just on the main menu.
The game has ran stably for me but I don't know how they're going to bulk out the gameplay to make this an interesting thing to play. It is tuned so the commodity production and everything else can be done very quickly, so twitch plays a factor and you can't play this with anything but undivided attention, which is unfortunate since I find it quite boring. If it were slower paced and less hectic I could at least listen to a podcast or something while I played.

I usually don't write reviews, but I rarely encounter games as good as Jets'n'Guns Gold. Inspired by Tyrian 2000, Project-X, Walker, R-Type, and Darius, this old school side-scrolling shooter offers wicked difficulty as well as wicked charm.
Instead of collecting weapons akin to R-Type, this game takes a page from Tyrian where you have the option of buying weapons after you complete each level. And trust me you are going to need to upgrade as soon as possible because each level gets progressively more and more difficult. Gamers looking for a breeze need not apply because it is not easy.
The graphics to J'n'G are reminiscent of an old 2D side-scrolling shooter. Nothing to hold in high acclaim, but still very nice to look at. Has kind of computer 90s feel. J'nG Gold also offers a comic book intro and outro to each level(or at least during the first few levels, I haven't gotten too far into it), which is also very nice.
Oh and the music? Fantastic!  Machinae Supremacy and its sister production company, Hubnester Industries does a fantastic job at providing a heavy metal and chiptune atmosphere. Trust me, the music definitely adds a lot to already great game.
If you like great side-scrolling shooters, please buy this game. It's $3 right now, but even if it is $6.99 J'nG is still worth the price.

I clicked 'Yes' to recommend, but in truth, I only recommend as an introduction to the characters for the 2nd and 3rd entries in this series. Heileen 1 is short, with limited input and very brief, shallow storyline. The endings are easy to get, and it is an easy game to get 100% on with only 3 achievements. It does contradict the second novel (the ending of this one, to the start of the 2nd) - so do play with the knowledge that they don't seamlessly merge together into one story.
I've completed this on android and steam. It is the weakest in the series, but I'm glad to have played it as groundwork for the later games. The 2nd is enjoyable, with a lot more interactivity and a lot more depth as an adventure visual novel. The third is a 'proper' dating visual novel, and highly enjoyable. So only buy/play this if you you intend to play the others - try to grab on sale or in a bundle.

SOMA is a sci-fi, horror game where you play as Simon Jerett, a man with an unknown brain condition who lives in Toronto and is the subject of a research project to find a cure. Once the vague introductions and mini tutorial is done, things go to hell and you are suddenly dumped into an apocolyptic, underwater world with very little info and very little capabilities.
In this review I will use a 1 to 10 grading scale and provide summaries of several aspects of this game such as graphics, gameplay, sound and story.
(WARNING: May contain minor spoilers)

The gameplay revolves around a "hide and sneak" style of play where you can't confront the various entities out to get you and to find various bits and pieces of information to progress with the plot and figure everything out. There some actions such as "grabbing", "running" and interacting with online computers but there are very little options on how to go about, which aims to add to its horror element with a sense of frailty and limitation. You can't take a haphazard approach and have to go around logically and patiently which will end up making the game a lot simpler and less frustrating. There are also some "puzzles" and tasks to complete the more you progress in order to continue on, but they aren't very difficult and are just there to add to the story. The various monsters in this game tend to be scary at first, but after a few attempts and exposure it lightens the horror element and end up annoying and hindering you. Even if you end up getting caught, the game is pretty generous about giving you second chances and even provides "healing" stations in the form of a black organism you stick your hand into to help you recover from an "injured state". Overall, the difficulty isnt that high and the main object of this game is the plot and to immerse yourself in the game by putting yourself in SImon's shoes which the game does a good job of doing.

The game has little lighting a majority of the time and can get blurry, but is aesthetically pleasing when looking at the environment and some of the several monsters you will encounter as you go along. The actual people aren't as nice to look at compared to other high-end games since the level of detail you find when looking at the surroundings just isn't there when looking at other humans, even if there are very few of them hanging around and are usually disfigured beyond recognition. Overall, since the game is in first person and revolves around knowing your environment to make out the various clues and key items, the graphics are appealing to eye and gives the game more depth to its horror aspect.

The sounds in this game really compliment the graphics and surroundings which really create the game's horror theme. The background sounds leave you tense from start to finish and constantly remind you just how bad the situation your in truly is. The sounds also help with actual gameplay and can point you in the right direction by listening to subtle "foreign" sounds and random footsteps coming from enemies. The voice acting is pretty well done and goes along with the depressing theme of the game. Overall, the sounds in this game are one of its finer aspects and can play an important role in the game which helps make immersing yourself into the game easier.

As a sci-fi game, everything takes place in the future where technology is much more advanced and humanity has achieved a new form of consciousness through machines. There are a few plot twists and turns but for the most part the actual plot is linear and there isn't many actions that actually affect the story or outcome besides some personal choices based on your own morals and actions. The actual storyline is pretty interesting and keeps you intrigued enough to actually see it through to the end to see and achieve your ultimate fate as Simon. You only develop one real relationship through the hellish journey and in a way helps to add to the distraughting atmosphere that constantly surrounds PATHOS: II. Overall, the storyline felt like a mixture of other sci-fi games/movies at times but in the end still retains its own genuine plot with a unique, somewhat unexpected ending.

The game can get buggy at times and loading up new areas or from saved states can cause minor lagging and frame skips. Also, Nvidia users don't always get ideal FPS despite having high-end graphics cards, especially if using SLi. For the most part though, the game runs smoothly and isn't very taxing on the CPU or RAM. Its a modest ~11 GB install and playable for most users. Overall, the optimization isn't perfect and can be improved but not game breaking and noticeable only when going into new areas.

Duels 2015 represents a major step backward from its predecessors.  From the first moment of every startup of the game, the user is dragged through a sluggish, draconian UI that insists upon form way over function.  This philosophy is mirrored throughout almost every aspect of the game - from deck building to actually playing - the game's focus is exclusively on creating a flashy experience but not a tight, practical one.  I want to hit a menu and be in the game in less than ten seconds, dammit.  D15 makes its users sit through excruciatingly long fades and transitions at every corner.  The overall experience is totally unenjoyable.
Then there's the card pool.  The Duels series has always been designed to be an introduction to Magic for new players, and in my case Duels 2012 was a massive success.  I was exposed to so many exciting, flavorful cards that were just downright cool!  The next two installments in the franchise did much the same.  D15 seems to break that trend.  Its card choices reads like a list of the most boring cards from the past several blocks.  Magic is many things to many people, but to me it's a game of discovery and expression.  On both notes D15 falls flat.
It is, however, the first Duels in the series to create a strictly limited draft environment.  For you.  You're still playing against preconstructed decks.  Maybe this is just a pedantic gripe but it's a one-sided illusion of a draft experience, and not even that.  The packs aren't very reflective of paper Magic packs, and the smaller cardpool leaves a lot to be desired.
There is a major upside though.  This game is dirt cheap.  The overall quality of the Duels series has been so good at such a low price that I think the developers are afforded a miss, but hopefully they've learned from their mistakes on this game.  Compared to its predecessors, it's a tragedy.

I'm only an hour into it but am having so much fun I had to share!  The game looks simple on the surface -- travel around the world in 80 days -- but there is much more to this game.  Juggling suitcases, buying and selling goods, exploring cities, talking with people and learning things, and keeping your master happy are just some of the things you have to do.  Do you travel across Russia?  If so, does the master have cold weather gear?  Do you go south and cross North Africa and risk crossing the desert and, yes, riding a camel?
The interface is incredibly easy to use.  Managing your suitcases and inventory is a simple drag and drop process.  To buy goods, you drag them to your suitcase.  To sell, you drag them out.  Easy as can be.  All of the items have tooltips that shed some light on them -- the value, where they should be sold, and/or how they might help you during your journey.   Your market purchases can impact your travel plans too.  Certain items can be extremely valuable in certain cities.
Using the map is very intuitive.  Your mouse wheel is used to zoom in and out.  Click and drag spins the globe around.  There are also buttons for zooming in and out as well.
What really hooked me is the "choose your own adventure" aspect to the game.  As you converse with your master, train porters, and people in various cities, you are presented with a few dialog options to choose from.  Each option has pros and cons.  Some will improve your relations with your master.  Some will shed light on travel routes.  Some will tell you little facts about various cities, histories, or travel tips.   As you learn new things, little information boxes appear when you click on each city -- no need to remember stuff or write it down.
I'll update this review when I finish.  I'm in Singapore right now!

I do not understand why this game got mixed reviews. It is one of the best survival games at the moment. In most survival games after 1 week you have crafted everything and you start enhancing your PvP skills. Well in Life is Feudal this is not the case. Depending on how large your group is, after 1 week you will not have made a castle (ingame name Keep or Large Keep) up yet. You first need to do other things. What other things? Well farming, wood cutting, mining, setting up a wall, warehouse, chests, blacksmithing, setting up a snare trap to get a chicken or hare, taming a horse or cow, or both!, etc).
Setting up a decent farm already costs about a week solo play with 2 hours playing time each day. But since you also need the correct tools you also need a blacksmith. Oooh darn... you need to have a friend who learns that skill because thats another tier.
Welcome in Life is Feudal, where it takes a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of time to actually do things. Which forces players to work together and focus on 1 skill tier each (Metalworking, Woodworking, Herbology, Engineering, Argiculture). You need players from every tier to set up a good base, or trade with other towns (/ people) in the server. This sounds hard, annoying and stupid but it is actually the most social and hard working survival game I have played in months (or even years).
So now im going to chop wood for at least 3 hours to have 25% of my wall finished before the evening...
A small note: Yes there is PvP and it is overpowered which forces smaller players to forge deals with their landlords (taxes) or work together with other towns to start a rebellion. PvP works almost flawless altough I do not have much experience in that yet.

On my first playthrough, I only arrived in London after 86 days. Game Over. And I had enjoyed every second of the game, even when it became apparent I would not beat the game the first time around. I had been kidnapped by overzealous nuns, and walked on the bottom of the sea. On my second playthrough I failed to solve a murder mystery aboard a boat, but took a big gamble and blew up our airship just before arriving back home in England. But I did arrive in London within 60 days. I can’t wait to see what other adventures are in store. Taking Place in a Cyberpunk version of Jules Verne’s Around the World in Eighty Days, you play as Phileas Fogg’s valet, his personal servant Passepartout. Remarkably well balanced, 80 Days tasks you to both carefully master your master’s finances, his needs and whims, and to keep the end goal in mind. Some of the game’s best moments come from the tensions between these: the player might want to explore a city or move speedily on (all so the master wins his bet), but Phileas Fogg himself might insist on having a proper dinner made ready. Travel is ingenious and goes by airship, submarine, car, and anything in-between. Often there are multiple routes available, with widely diverging prices; you only find out which routes there are by questioning characters during your travels. Which route you take: the expensive, speedy, and experimental one or the slow, safe, and cheap one is up to the player, and their finances. Better not visit the market to sell your belongings if the next train leaves within an hour though. A typical trip round the world can be made within 2 hours. Brilliantly written, and brilliantly crafted.

I am a veteran for Frictional's games after having played Penumbra and Amnesia, this feels like a natural continuation for their storytelling and really shows off just how far this company has come. The visuals were exceptional, apart from a couple muddy textures(glitches?) it was very stunning to look at. The atmosphere really sells the game, as it progresses it gets darker and more claustrophobic, the whole world seems like it closes in around you with the pressure of the deep ocean. The sound design is also stellar in this title, and helps you navigate away from the world's enemies and can be creepy at times.
However, in comparison to the older titles of Frictional, this is less of a horror game and more psychological and story driven. Some parts could be tense but I never really felt that absolute dread like what the invisible puddle monsters in Amnesia gave me. It gives you some interesting things to think about and keeps pace pretty well, with lots of areas to explore and listen to logs or memories of crew to piece things together. I feel that the puzzles are a bit simple some times and you can get turned around in the dark quickly, but there are not too many other shortcomings. The whole game took me just over 10 hours of playing and I managed to get every achievement through the progression. There may be some points with alternatives that I had not explored.
All in all, it lends itself to be an interesting science fiction title set in a fantastic environment, and I would recommend it for seasoned Frictional fans and horror/scifi enthusiasts.

This is definitely not a "typical" FPS. There is no skill tree to unlock, you can't run and gun your way through a level and your health doesn't automatically regenerate after being shot in the face. 
What this FPS does is make you think about little things such as the weight of your equipment, the type of equipment you need for the job, the distance of the target, the layout of the environment, how to use a compass... basically it does a good job at mimicking what an actual soldier would need to think about when tackling a mission. 
Where it fails, however, it's in the delivery. The game is poorly optimized, the menus are confusing and there's a steep learning curve before you can fully appreciate the experience. 
 
Absolutely! Bohemia Interactive did a good job in creating an experience like very few other FPS out there. While not without its flaws, the game offers hours of great gameplay that can be forever extended by the strong modding community.  
If you have not done so already, give this game a try. See you on the Battlefield!

My play time so far has been split 10hrs for story and 12hrs for multiplayer. So first the story line.
Campaign: I thought the story was fantastic, and well written. It may be short, but certainly not lackluster. There are 3 parts to the story, one for each faction, and all three connect to each other seamlessly throughout the game, and converge into one at the end. I was able to make it through 2/3 the campaign on the highest difficulty, which was challenging. As for the 3 final bosses at the end of each chapter, they are extremely hard to defeat on the highest difficulty and i have not been able to master them just yet. They're are several well placed hidden items and pieces of lore spread throughout the game for an extra challenge.
Multiplayer: So there are a few multiplayer modes available which are: 1v1, 2v2, 4v4, and a 4v4 dominion match, which is your basic capture/defend the 3 zones game. the maps are well designed and genuinely balanced. There are 12 unique heroes to select from, almost all of which have their own unique weaponry and skills.(a couple classes with 2h swords and a couple with 2h axes) Classes feel exceptionally balanced for now, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. The combat in the game is very looks and feels very fluid. Every kill and every combo made or broken feels rewarding.
As for the quality of connections while playing multiplayer, I've yet to experience any dropped connections, any lag, or any abnormal wait times for a match. The worst thing I have experienced during a match is a host migration, which literally takes less than 5 seconds, and rarely happens. The longest I've waited for a match to be found is maybe 30 seconds if that. As for unlockable items. Yea, you can pay to unlock♥♥♥♥♥♥instantly. Honestly, what game doesn't have this mechanic? It's just a re-skin folks, nothing to get all bent out of shape for just because you can't have it instantly without paying for it. you can always grind it out just like every other multiplayer game on the market.
As for whether or not the season pass is worth it is yet to be seen. I'm sure they will add more maps to play on and more character customizations. More campaign would be great but that's a stretch. Check back later when new heroes unlock to catch the same trolls complaining that the new characters are op and ubisoft wants their money. Of course they want your money, that's the business folks. nobody makes a game hoping to make $0. Most triple A games will cost $100 overall with dlc(some cost more) And why not put in a mechanic to capitalize on people being impatient. it's every where in the gaming industry these days.

Alright, so before we begin, I would like to say that this IS NOT A BAD GAME.
It's actually a pretty good game, and I thoroughly enjoyed a few scenes in it.
With that being said, here are many flaws.
The main character (MC) has a wonderful backstory and first couple of chapters. However, much potential was squandered for character development. There could have been a much more exciting plot considering how strong the game started. 6.5/10
Voice acting:
No complaints. 9/10
The soundtrack:
It's not bad, but it's quite simplistic. The best song (shown after chapter 0) is rarely used and it's a real shame. Over time, the music gets really repetitive and even annoying. The music tells you what to feel, instead of guiding you to those feelings and enhancing the experience. Sometimes the music starts too early (like it'll start right after a scene change) and will ruin the scene for you by telling you what kind of scene happens next. Overall, it's boring, bland, and not immersive. 4/10
Plot: pretty predictible for the most part. There are some twists in there, but I mean, if you're familiar with this kind of literature, you basically know how this VN will generally play out by the first few chapters.
The tropes are very strong in this VN's general arc.
Rise and Chiho get sidelined a bit into comedic relief by being predominantly used as being part of a love triangle. I feel this really takes away from their potential as characters.
Motifs: This game takes place at a Christian school and thus has very strong Christian, specifically Catholic themes. Well, let's just say that that was the attempt at least. How did the writer do his research into Christianity? By watching Cartoon Network? The way that this novel tries to integrate Christian motifs is abysmal. Much of it is a blatant misrepresentation, and anyone familiar with Christian theology will see this very quickly. It's a shame that the writer(s) couldn't have put in more effort researching something that's so integral to the core of this game. 2/10
Pacing: It's pretty slow; there is a good bit of filler. The endings (after the plot's climax) weren't very long, much to my dismay. Also, you need to choose the same girl 5 times in order to get their routes and not a bad end. Which tbh makes for a bit of unnecessary skipping on replays. 5.5/10
So did I enjoy this game? In general,  yes.
Would I recommend it? Probably not. It takes a good bit of time to finish the routes, and there are much better things to do with your time. I'd recommend playing Doki Doki Literature Club and "If my Heart Had Wings" instead. Maybe once you're done reading all the good VNs out there, you can come back to this one. Or don't. Because it'll seem bland in comparison.
Final Verdict: 5/10 for experienced VN readers. 6/10 for newbies. Generally wouldn't recommend. Not because it's a bad VN per se, but because it takes a long time to read, and in the time it takes you to 100% this VN, you could have been reading much better VNs or doing other things.
