It's a "like" from me, but a *very* weak like.  TL;DR - it's fun, but has some definite flaws, and is probably overpriced.  Giving it a 'like' because I still enjoy it, warts and all, but it's definitely not for everyone, particularly at the current price point.
This is not a grand strategy game; this is a short and simple "economic RTS" that's probably closer to M.U.L.E. than anything else (but not nearly as fun).  Games are played on a small, randomized map, and finish in anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour or so.  The core gameplay is simple: claiming a limited number of resources, game the market and hobble your competition enough to buy out their stock before they buy out yours.  Some resources get consumed as upkeep, many of the rest are required for upgrades or advanced buldings, but at some point you reach a point of self-sufficiency, at which point everything surplus is for sale.
What makes it interesting is the various ways in which you can try to kneecap them by limiting resources, either by throwing one of a very small set of 'black market' attacks at them to disable buildings or resources, or by manipulating the market somehow.  Cut off their oxygen supply; don't sell surplus power; sabotage their mines; flood the market with the commodity that they rely on as a cash source.  The supply chains are long enough that there's usually a weak point in everyone's, and finding and attacking your opponents' while adapting to attacks on your own is the main challenge of the game.
What makes it not interesting is that there's a strong self-reinforcing going on; if you start out ahead, you have the resources to keep your competitors under your heel.  If you start out behind, it can be almost impossible to get ahead.  By the time you've hit the mid-game (base upgrade level 3-4 where you start becoming self-sufficient) you usually know who the winner is going to be.  The bulk of the interaction between players happens in the market at one remove, so it's sometimes hard to tell that you're competing against other players rather than an arbitrary resource cost.  It feels like more of a race than a fight.
There's also some interface issues; it's very sluggish, particularly towards the end of a game, the text is too small, and the graphics are perhaps best described as 'functional'.
So all that said, it's entertaining, but perhaps not at the price point.

The devs at Obsidian Entertainment have always been exceptional storytellers. Despite this game being 10 years old, KOTOR 2 has memorable NPC's, an epic yet personal story, and great characterization and atmosphere. The main complaint (rightly deserved) that people had with this game was that it was originally released in a buggy, obviously rushed state. But that was several years ago. Today with The Sith Lords Restored Content Mod (TSLRCM) available on the Steam Workshop, we can experience KOTOR 2 as it was meant to be played. It's amazing.
Here are some of the things that TSLRCM does:
1) It fixes 99% of the bugs that Obsidian never got around to fixing. This allows Obsidian's excellent story to really shine.
2) Cut content from quests and cutscenes have been restored. This enriches the story and makes the characters' motivations *much* clearer.
3) HD Widescreen resolution support. You will have to seek out other mods to get higher resolution textures, though.

Loosely based on Shakespeare's
and Milton's
, Eek! Games'
offers deep, introspective social commentary against the backdrop of a singular personal journey through Hell in a 50+ hour suburban social simulation RPG.  Cast as a nameless soul in the afterlife, players will find themselves in what would appear to be a normal, suburban house party of 20-somethings, but one look outside demonstrates that this is no ordinary house.
Situated in a void of nothingness and fenced in with no escape, the house stands alone in an endless night as a perversion of the modern suburban "paradise" to which the players have been unwittingly invited.  In a subtle nod to futility, the opening tutorial message encourages players to simply explore and experiment, but plants the seed that your only option is to repeat the journey over and over again.  "You cannot accomplish everything in one go," it warns you in not so many words, ensuring that players are well-prepared for the chaos to unfold before them.
At first, the house seems like a quaint slice of the suburbs.  It's a 3-bedroom, 3-bath house adorned with flatscreen televisions, framed pictures of cats and random photos of a family that doesn't appear to live there.  The house is fully-furnished with a full kitchen and even has a two-door garage.  Slowly, but surely, however, the illusion begins to unravel and you realize that you're not where you ought to be and players are left wondering what sins the nameless player-character committed to be sent here.  You'll quickly realize that nobody attending the party knows you, not even Madison, the hostess (read: the
).
Left to your own devices, you can explore and interact with the house and its guests, and that's when things begin to unfold.  The subtlety of Eek Games satire can be missed for those not paying attention - the guests at this party are 3 men - including the player - and five women, all of whom fit neatly into familiar archetypes from the idiot drunk to the shy sex bomb locked in her room; yet underpinning the surface apperance of an ordinary house party is a scathing criticism of current social justice politics -  there are no people of color or LGBT representation at this 'party' and your sole purpose, at least on the surface, is to use every trick in the book to demoralize and/or objectify the women.  It is no coincidence, then, that the inhabitants of Hell or Limbo (it's hard to determine exactly where we find ourselves in this dark comedy) are all vapid and easily-manipulated into various acts of debauchery or mischief.  Basically, everyone here deserves to be here, and each relationship between the characters can be explored and exploited for personal gain, but the trick of it is that the gain is always pyrrhic.  Even should you manage to get into bed with the woman of your dreams, you will be left completely unsatisfied and will only have to start again, as if you were Bill Murray in
, only instead of being in Punxsutawney, you're stuck in a personally-tailored exploration of the consequences of sin.
If there is an argument for games-as-art,
would be front-and-center.  There is no doubt that, like all great works of art, it will be misunderstood and unappreciated in its own time, but its biting satire and darkly-comedic look at the suburban lifestyle of the 2010s will surely serve future generations as a cautionary tale of avarice and hedonism.  While still in Early Access, there is still a lot to be discovered from Eek Games' entry into interactive literature and I look forward to the final product as it will stand as a pillar of the movement to leverage games as a tool to push for social change.

Okay, so after over 100 hours in this game I think I can finally safely review it because I'm tired of seeing all these negative reviews that are just whiny people that can't handle this type of game.
So first I would like to say that I personally have enjoyed this game a huge amount. WHen I started playing this game I did not know a single person in here. 100 hours later I have my own guild and we have a Mumble server specific to our guild with anywhere between 5 to 10+ people in it at any given time and we've formed a pretty great bond with each other.
You need other people to play this game. They don't have to be people you knew prior to starting to play. Basically everyone who plays this game is older because it simply doesn't lend itself to younger gamers so if you're looking for a game with a more mature audience then this game is for you.
Okay, time to say what this game is all about. This game is truly all about surviving and progressing, and it takes a long♥♥♥♥♥time. Don't get me wrong I'm not complaining when I say that. It is such a great feeling to spend hours working on a singular project with others who all have a different hand in it and watch it finally be done, but be aware this game takes time.
If you're wondering why you need others to play this game it's because this game, which will eventually be launching as an MMO with a 10k player cap per server, takes an MMO approach in that you only have so many skill points that you can spec in to skills. Your choices are to become a jack of all trades in the low tiers of every skill or to look at one or two skills that you really want and that your guild really needs. You do that, and suddenly you're an irreplaceable asset to a group who will always need you.
This game is so much fun with a group and I can't stress that enough, it's long, and some things can be a "grind", but if you're with others this game will never feel like a true grind it will feel like you're accomplishing something. I think that's what a lot of these negative reviews miss out on.
Now, what negatives do I have about this game? A lot. I love this game I really do. But, it's a buggy mess and I can admit that. I usually crash 4 or 5 times in a very long game session of 6 or 7 hours. Sometimes you encounter objects that you personally can't see and you get stuck on them. You can glitch through a wall in a mineshaft and fall into the endless ocean beneath the map. The list goes on. But clearly based on the people that have put over a THOUSAND hours into this game really should show you that if you enjoy slower paced survival games where you really have to work to survive then this game could be for you.
The combat is also an issue right now. It feels like a slower, clunkier version of Mount and Blade. However, in the thick of battle when you're going against 5 or 6 other people at once, swinging your sword, blocking strikes from the enemy, you forget all that and just get sucked in to what's going on because you could lose not just your items but your skill levels. So you fight and you call for help and you scream at your enemies because you're out for blood.
This game is just a lot of fun. I'm afraid I don't see where a lot of these negative comments come from because while the game has a lot of issues it also has a ton of potential. Should it be out of alpha yet? No. Do I understand why they released it straight out of alpha? Yes. Am I ready for the MMO version to release? Hell yeah!

It's very difficult to articulate my experience in SOMA. As a horror game, it has scares and creepy moments aplenty, but it won't scratch that hardcore survival-horror itch you might be feeling. As a commentary on human consciousness and existence, it excels... provided you are willing to invest and immerse yourself. This what I bought the game for, and it delivered in spades. I won't pretend that I'll be walking away from this game with my eyes opened with new knowledge about the human condition, but I *will* be pondering the choices and themes SOMA has presented for a very long time, especially the ending.
Perhaps SOMA's greatest attribute is how it makes you think. Curiosity will fuel you through this game, wanting to know what happened and what happens next. The notes and audio logs contain a rich narrative that takes some effort to piece together, but is entirely worth it in the end.
Another strong point for SOMA is the environment it lays out for you. Frictional have really honed their craft in this area, able to tell stories entirely from visual cues and details. One area in particular comes to mind, an Escher-esque tower that is home to one of the most memorable sequences in the game. Diagrams and documents prior to this area explain exactly why there are toilets on the walls and ladders descending horizontally, but I will leave that a secret for now.
The long and short of it is, if you want a good story, great environments, and a thought-provoking commentary about human life, this game is for you. If you want a survival-horror scarefest, you will leave SOMA with much less than everyone else.

One of the most innovative, interesting and exciting games that I have played in a long time. However, it is definitely not for everyone.
This game is more akin to games like Shadowbane and UO: Online of old and the more recent Darkfall. I really feel like it catches the atmosphere of living in Feudal times. One must survive in a open, dynamic world that is completely controlled by players. One can choose to live their Feudal life as they see fit.
A good deal of the game is crafting and building. Not only that but it takes a good deal of time to get anything done. For these reasons, I find that many are turned off by it. However, it is such a rewarding game for those who value creating one's own settlement and then getting involved in the world around them in whatever ways they see fit.
The combat system is quite good yet takes a bit of time to get used to. Once you get used to it, though, you will most likely really enjoy it. It takes a more realistic approach to combat, where one must learn the range of your weapon and must aim at body parts for maximum affect. It is definitely not an easy system to master and takes practice to get good at it.
The only drawback that it has is it is still developing and you will run into small bugs and issues that need resolving. I feel that it is a constant work in progress.
That being said, if you like the idea of an open, dynamic, Feudal world where you make your own way, and you don't mind having to put lots of time to accomplish it, then I can say look no further than this game!

I have encountered a bug where I will pick up the envelope from the police station, and its contents disappear, along with anything else I picked up earlier (the hair-gel and the black shirt). I had to go back and re-play picking up all of these items and keep my fingers crossed that they stay in my inventory or show up on the day that they will be needed for.
Aside from the bug and minor 3D problems (sometimes Gabriel's foot will go through the counter at St. George's Books, a minor irk) , the game is incredibly faithful to the original. I recommend this game to those who play the original, or those who would like a trip back to 1993, when Adventure games were in their glory.

It's a "like" from me, but a *very* weak like.  TL;DR - it's fun, but has some definite flaws, and is probably overpriced.  Giving it a 'like' because I still enjoy it, warts and all, but it's definitely not for everyone, particularly at the current price point.
This is not a grand strategy game; this is a short and simple "economic RTS" that's probably closer to M.U.L.E. than anything else (but not nearly as fun).  Games are played on a small, randomized map, and finish in anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour or so.  The core gameplay is simple: claiming a limited number of resources, game the market and hobble your competition enough to buy out their stock before they buy out yours.  Some resources get consumed as upkeep, many of the rest are required for upgrades or advanced buldings, but at some point you reach a point of self-sufficiency, at which point everything surplus is for sale.
What makes it interesting is the various ways in which you can try to kneecap them by limiting resources, either by throwing one of a very small set of 'black market' attacks at them to disable buildings or resources, or by manipulating the market somehow.  Cut off their oxygen supply; don't sell surplus power; sabotage their mines; flood the market with the commodity that they rely on as a cash source.  The supply chains are long enough that there's usually a weak point in everyone's, and finding and attacking your opponents' while adapting to attacks on your own is the main challenge of the game.
What makes it not interesting is that there's a strong self-reinforcing going on; if you start out ahead, you have the resources to keep your competitors under your heel.  If you start out behind, it can be almost impossible to get ahead.  By the time you've hit the mid-game (base upgrade level 3-4 where you start becoming self-sufficient) you usually know who the winner is going to be.  The bulk of the interaction between players happens in the market at one remove, so it's sometimes hard to tell that you're competing against other players rather than an arbitrary resource cost.  It feels like more of a race than a fight.
There's also some interface issues; it's very sluggish, particularly towards the end of a game, the text is too small, and the graphics are perhaps best described as 'functional'.
So all that said, it's entertaining, but perhaps not at the price point.

CPU players are far too aggressive (Think Civ 5 Ghandi meets the Red Skull) and do not seem to compete with one another.  There is a bug currently in the game that allows CPU players to purchase stock in your company even when they do not have the funds to do so.  The game also, apparently, gives stipends of cash to the AI player, resulting in an early game juggernaut.  Every game is a zerg rush - there is no long term strategic play in this game whatsoever.
Sabottage corporations in particular are incredibly frustrating to play against and their playstyle is one dimensional: to deny others the ability to play. Though billed as a point and click adventure, Tormemtum has little in common with the genre staples like Broken Sword or Monkey Island. Rarely, if ever, will the items you collect and jam into the infinite confines of your cloak have to be assembled together into some wacky contraption that conveniently bypasses the obstacle of the moment. Exit your cell and you find a shard of mirror. On the next screen over, you find a broken mirror in need of some reflective shards. Explore your cell and excavate a jeweled eye from one of the skeletons. On the same screen as the broken mirror is a statue with empty sockets for eyes.
There’s rarely a hidden motive for collecting items and everything has a clear purpose, so puzzling comes in to form of, well, puzzles. And herein starts the unwelcome comparisons to the hidden object genre. Kind of, anyway, because as a genre, it’s moved away from presenting random screen full of jumble and asking you to pick out three blue telephones and a heron yet has someone still kept its name. I mean, I don’t know what else to call it without having to start using the world casual unironically, and I’m far too sober to attempt that.
To be clear, the kinds of object searching both genres are famed for are nonexistent in Tormentum. You rarely have to junk-sort or pixel hunt as hotspots are highlighted by a flickering aura of light. Instead, the game turns to the logic puzzles that have evolved in their place, which doesn’t have to be a bad thing. You can obtain a jewel by lowering the right corpse-laden cages chronicled in a desperate sketch found outside your cell. Piecing together the broken mirror asks you to manipulate rays of light to open a passageway further into the nightmare-choked castle. Fixing a series of fuses and collecting the tattooed remains of a skeleton summons an electrified ghost you can help put to rest. It’s either that or spend more time taunting the giant needle-toothed worm who jealously guards your rat chum’s jail.

I definitely recommend Tormentum, it is certainly worth the standard price and even better if you can grab it on sale!

Princess Evangile is the sort of game that comes around every once in a while that puts me in a really uncomfortable position. What started as something I had strong expectations for ended up being bitterly disappointing. The strong opening chapters gave way to a mediocre and often irritating first half that was not wholly redeemed by the much better character-specific stories in the second half. The end result being that I come out of this game feeling uncertain about what to do now that it is time to review it.
My first experience with the game was playing the demo, which covers a few of the early chapters of the story. First impressions were good. The protagonist, Masaya, had a rather nasty start where he was screwed over by his own father in a particularly despicable way. It put in me a hope that, perhaps, he would be a developed character of his own along the lines of, say, Tomoya from Clannad, Okabe from Steins;Gate, or Yuuji from Grisaia. His unpleasant backstory was more than enough cause to produce a jaded character who, while wanting to do the right thing, would still have an eye out for suspicious activity or behavior. In other words, I had a hope that Masaya would be, in contrast to quite a lot of VN protagonists, interesting and savvy enough to see when people were trying to mess up his life rather than just being a victim to other people's actions.
Instead, I ended up seeing a faceless stupid perverted doormat character that manages to be worse than most VN protagonists I have come across. I can understand that some people might not be the sharpest tools in the shed, but Masaya's repeated walking into situations where all the signs point to "this is a bad idea" is almost impressive in its stupidity. I had hoped that the first chapter of the game would be a life-changing event for him (as it would for basically anyone else), but the rest of the game just makes it clear that Masaya is, has, and will always be a sucker falling into other people's traps.
To say that I was disappointed would be an understatement: it did very serious harm to my opinion of the game as a whole. It's a case of when you end up getting high expectations from a first impression, the fall when reality ends up failing those expectations is all the harder.
Another character I have no choice but to bring up is Misako, the headmistress of the school. I've come across quite a few despicable, spiteful, and irredeemable characters before, but even I was a bit thrown by how foul she ended up being. The trouble is that she is at the center of virtually all of the drama in the story, which means she gets quite a lot of screentime. None of it, not even the bits you get about why she is the way she is, makes anything she does acceptable.
The standout moment for me came in one of the character storylines where she not only is deeply unpleasant, she breaks the law to advance her warped agenda. I'm not talking about a "Oh, the police may scold you or lock you up for a night" kind of crime, but one that in the US would get you at least 20 years in prison. And while I (sort of) understand why charges were not pressed in that situation (collateral damage), it sealed the deal for me that Misako was completely irrational, unsympathetic, and worst of all faced no real consequences for her actions. As with Masaya, her presence in the story actively hurt Princess Evangile.
Ok... so I despise two of this game's major characters. What about the rest? Well, while there was quite a few stereotypical VN/anime moments/tropes throughout the story, things actually got more interesting once the character-focused storylines came into play. This probably reflects badly upon me, but the moment when I really started thinking "Maybe I won't throw this game into a fire after all" was when someone got stabbed. Woohoo violence. But in all seriousness, even if Masaya's role in the story is pretty much entirely stereotypical and stupid, the female leads such as Rise, Chiho, Ritsuko, and Ayaka had more than a few good moments. I'm not sure which would be my favorite storyline, but Ayaka is the clear winner when it comes to this game's characters. But really all four of them are alright, and the various side characters are ok even if they mostly are just in the background and don't do much. Not in the same league as Clannad or Grisaia, but they are acceptable.
And now the hard part... Can I recommend this game?
The game is split into 26 "chapters", with 16 onwards, depending upon your choices, being the character focused storylines. Most of those first 15 chapters were draining to get through, especially when the obnoxious headmistress got involved. But, as already stated, the character storylines are noticeably better and improved my overall opinion of the game. If I was judging this game on the first 15 chapters, I would throw this game in a dumpster and light it on fire. But because of the character storylines, which in practice ended up being more than half of the game's overall playtime since there are four character routes, I can't do that as easily.
So I find myself at the end of this review, after 30 hours of playtime and close to 2 months attempting to chew through this game, conflicted. Ultimately, it is a question of if a friend decided to ask me whether or not this game was worth playing, what would I tell them? That the first half of the game isn't very good, the protagonist and main villain grate on the nerves, but that it ends up getting better in the second half? Sadly, the improvement in quality in the character storylines is not enough to make me want to tell my friends "get Princess Evangile and play it ASAP." It makes me want to tell them "Perhaps, but there are much better VN's out there that you can play instead."
So I guess that's a "no". A "no" for a game with a 95% approval rating on Steam is certainly going to get this review flamed. That's how internet people are after all: ragey people with hair-trigger tempers that will attack anything that remotely bugs them, regardless of the strength of the arguments presented. But I can't give a game a "yes" just because I don't like having my reviews downvoted. I'm going to have to bite the bullet on this one.
Princess Evangile is, in short, a middling VN that starts promising, rapidly squanders that, but ends up being fairly good once you get into the second half. But while this game is not "bad", the fact remains there are far too many other VN's I would recommend before this one.
But most of all, I'm just disappointed. :(

I will say this, I am very much looking forward to the next Duke Nuekm game to see how it improves.

If you are a fan of old school style shmups with weapon/ship upgrades, GET THIS GAME. If you are a fan of Machinae Supremacy's music, GET THIS GAME. Even if you're not super into either of these things, GET THIS GAME. It is so, so worth it for the price because it's just that fun. I originally purchased this game back in 2006 when when the Jets'nGuns Gold edition came out.  I'm a huge fan of Machinae Supremacy's music and their metal+chiptune sound is perfect for this game. You can download the complete soundtrack for free on their website
and in fact, they did the music for the original game completely for free as well. I think it's a shame that they're not listed in the official Steam description here, so I thought it important to mention them. If you've played Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams, they contributed to that soundtrack along with Giana Sisters' original composer.
There are a ton of levels, weapons, and upgrades in the game, and a new game+ mechanic where it automatically bumps you up to the next difficulty after you finish the game. This allows you to use all the shiny stuff that you picked up and destroy things even more. There are some great mechanics in this game, like when you shoot down enemies, they will destroy things on the ground when you crash into them (and everything you destroy gives you money), and the store lets you sell things back and will refund you their full price (even after they're upgraded!) so you can feel free to switch out weapons at will. It also has a "test level" which you access from the store that has floating items with HP labels to kill, so you can approximate how much damage you're doing. Don't be afraid to experiment! The game isn't a cakewalk and can definitely be challenging, so you have to be flexible about your loadout in order to succeed.
While the game only has partial controller support, I can confirm that the 360 controller works fine for flying/regular gameplay. It'll even control the cursor in the menus, though it's quicker to use the mouse for that. You can configure the flying controls for it as well, as they're not hard-coded. The maximum resolution is pretty small, but if you set the game to fullscreen, it upscales well and doesn't change your entire desktop to its own resolution (which is handy for me, as I run dual monitors).
There are secrets and collectibles to find, as well as achievements for the game that track progress and even when you die, progress towards stuff like the number of troops you have killed will save even when you die. The game is also really funny, as there are many jokes and cultural references in the game (though they may seem a bit dated, as the original game released 10 years ago, but still). One of the reasons Rake In Grass chose to do a sidescrolling shooter was so the player could have some time to read some of the jokes they inserted into the game.
Way back in the day, I had problems with my save and posted on the RIG forums about it. The developers responded, asked that I send my save file to them, I did, and they returned it to me with the problem fixed. I was so thrilled about it and was really happy that they were so involved with their community. I didn't realize the game was on Greenlight, and if I had, I would have supported it then, but I'm so happy that this game is available on Steam now so I can give the devs more support. I heartily encourage you to give this game a chance and check it out, as there's so many hours of fun gameplay to be had for the price.

I hope everyone takes the time to read this review as much as I took to write it.
This wasn't the sequel that fans of the original Knights of the Old Republic were hoping for. I, especially, was surprised to hear that too when i heard that the sequel to the compelling game series was ruined by lazy development. Yet, here i am, typing a bad review of a game series that I loved so much.
Lots of opinions of this game start off by saying the graphics had.. become lacking in the polish the original had, leaving a lot to ask if they had recycled the game engine. I believe that the shift in development to Obsidian Entertainment had contributed to the poor resolution of graphics compared to the careful, meticulous details of the first from Bioware and Aspyr. They had defintiely improved the animations of character expression (which to be fair is difficult as it is from an animator's perspective) but Obsidian seemed more obsessed over making all the combat look "cool" and "immersive" that they had forgotten to write a story with the same qualities.
Bioware and Aspyr understood that a story has to be compelling to really convince people that they are there in the universe of Star Wars. They took a lesson from ol' Lucas himself when writing the first game's story... they had conflict in the beginning, a mission to save a damsel, a wookie, an asthmatic cyborg villain, visiting different planets, a revelation of immense proportions and finally a gigantic space battle. This was the formula, and it didn't matter if the graphics looked subpar from 2003, you just knew that when an NPC in the game talked about their homeworld of Corellia in the Outer Rim of the galaxy, that they were a part of a living world, they added to the immersion and they didn't even have to show you, they just had to say it. Somehow, saying that the Jedi Enclave on Dantooine being decimated by Malak's armada was more of an impact than showing it. That's what made KOTOR so amazing for it's time.
Obsidian Entertainment tried their best, however, they gave a story that followed the formula of how to make a Knights of the Old Republic game, not how to make an amazing Star Wars game. I liked where they were coming from when it came to writing and character development, especially the villains representing aspects of the Exile (Darth Nihilus to represent the abandonment of moral principle and belief, Darth Sion to represent the idea of pain from the past keeping yourself stronger and Darth Traya representing betrayal to the people you swore you'd fight for) however, these only served as snippets of what the developers could have done.
Then comes the infamous ending that so many fans hate about this game. Originally, your companions were supposed to serve as a compelling part of the ending on Malachor V. However, back in 2004 when the game was originally supposed to be released, Obsidian Entertainment was going through some setbacks and had to rush their deadline to release the game. Many have criticized it as being an incomplete game, especially towards the end. I feel like we've come this far as a gaming community to understand that rushing a deadline for a game is probably a good indicator that it's not going to live up to expectations.
So to wrap it up, I felt like this game was definitely more unique in some ways and lacking in others, but to condemn this game as sacrilegious to the KOTOR series would be going a little to far. I invite newer gamers to give the first game a try, however this was definitely not the sequel that i was hoping for, and unless you're a diehard Star Wars fan as well as a diehard KOTOR fan, then i wouldn't recommend this game to you, even if asked to play it.

The Sequel to the Bioware masterpiece, Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic II - The Sith Lords, is another incredible gaming experience and an important addition to the Star Wars universe. This game has a much darker undertone than its predecessor and although the plot arc isn't quite as rewarding as the first game, it still manages to stay faithful to it with an interesting plot twist. The gameplay is enhanced from the original with more feats, powers, weapons, customization options, and levels available, as well as new Jedi and sith prestige classes. The squad you recruit changes depending on your gender, and your alignment with the force, and some can be trained to use the force and become Jedi. Squad members remain interesting characters and now change based on the player's interactions with them. Several characters from the first game return (though not all are playable characters) and the Ebon Hawk is still your personal starship. Your journey takes you to a handful of worlds in the Star Wars Universe, some are new and some you may remember visiting or hearing about from the first game.
For a more enjoyable and complete experience I would recommend all players download the TSL: RCM from the workshop or internet. The Sith Lords Restored Content Modification add in many things that the original game lacked due to time constraints in development. A community project which took many years to perfect, this mod adds a whole slew of new content to the game which big or small, makes the overall experience twice as enjoyable. For those who have only played the Xbox version of the game, or did not previously have the mod installed, you will find that this mod makes it a whole new experience.
The recent update that adds achievements and workshop support is the best thing to happen to this game in the last decade. Now that everyone can add mods to this game AND earn some achievements, this game has new life breathed into it. I give it a 9/10.

Hey, remember when B-level action games were a thing? You know, stuff like Prototype, Dark Sector, and Singularity. The kind of game that probably won't win any awards or blow your mind in any way, but provides enough competent design and mindless chaos for a couple fun weekends. That's what Sniper Elite V2 is.
To start, it's worth mentioning that despite the name this is by no means a realistic sniper simulator - sometimes you have to follow targets or compensate for gravity at long distances, but there's also almost no recoil and you've got regenerating health. It's really a typical cover based shooter that focuses on sniping, and I'm fine with that.
The main problem I have with this game is that the developers really, REALLY need to get better at checkpointing. I had a few instances where I finished a tough sequence only to die immediately afterwards and be forced to do the previous section again. It really isn't fair, and gets pretty frustrating.
Having said that, this was pretty fun for a freebie, and I'm defintely curious to see how SE3 turns out (although I probably won't buy it at full price).

One of the most innovative, interesting and exciting games that I have played in a long time. However, it is definitely not for everyone.
This game is more akin to games like Shadowbane and UO: Online of old and the more recent Darkfall. I really feel like it catches the atmosphere of living in Feudal times. One must survive in a open, dynamic world that is completely controlled by players. One can choose to live their Feudal life as they see fit.
A good deal of the game is crafting and building. Not only that but it takes a good deal of time to get anything done. For these reasons, I find that many are turned off by it. However, it is such a rewarding game for those who value creating one's own settlement and then getting involved in the world around them in whatever ways they see fit.
The combat system is quite good yet takes a bit of time to get used to. Once you get used to it, though, you will most likely really enjoy it. It takes a more realistic approach to combat, where one must learn the range of your weapon and must aim at body parts for maximum affect. It is definitely not an easy system to master and takes practice to get good at it.
The only drawback that it has is it is still developing and you will run into small bugs and issues that need resolving. I feel that it is a constant work in progress.
That being said, if you like the idea of an open, dynamic, Feudal world where you make your own way, and you don't mind having to put lots of time to accomplish it, then I can say look no further than this game!

House Party is [as the video states] a raunchy, comedy, puzzle adventure where the main objective is to get laid. This is my first early access title, as I usually steer clear of early access games, but I for one am not disappointed. I completed all the story lines in about 8.5 hours, but really only because I used guides because I'm a chump.
The puzzles are actually pretty challenging, as the game doesn't give you any real hints on how to solve quests. While this may seem annoying, it makes the game that much more challenging, and gives a much greater sense of reward when you finally complete a quest. If you don't use any guides or walkthroughs, you're looking at over 10 hours. The reason it's this long, is because the puzzles are challenging, and you will restart. A lot.
The charcters you meet are all charming in their own way, yes even Frank. They each have their own personality, body language, and way the talk. Ex: Madison, the host of the party, can be a b*tch at times, and wants you to prank her sister, but is overall nice. Katherine is top of her class (as she states) and is condescending of others because of it (though she is still likeable). Ashley, Madison's sister, is fairly normal (I say normal because she has no real traits that make her stand out), and relaxed. Stephanie is an airhead (though when it comes to drugs she's a genius), and what most would consider a sl*t. Rachael, like Ashley, is real normal and laid back. And Brittany is a sweet shy girl with a cute country accent.
All the characters are really likeable, yes even Frank who, when you boil it down, really just wants what's best for everybody. The game is also beautifuly voice acted, and really helps convey the characters and their personalities.
Now, this game is not without its flaws.
For a game where the ultimate goal is to get laid, there aren't a lot of positions you can take when having intercourse. As of right now, it's only missionary and doggy style. While they are animated really well, it does get kind of boring. Hopefully they'll add more positions in future updates.
There also isn't a real variety of music in this game. There is only one song playing at all times on a constant loop. But I'm positive they'll add more music in the future.
Also the jacuzzi and the lounge by the jacuzzi are unaccessable, which is really disappointing, because in a game about getting laid, those spots would've been real interesting; though I expect them to be accessable in the future.
As of right now you can only get it on with 4 out of the 6 girls in the game. Stephanie and Brittney's quest lines are incomplete, though will more than likely updated in the future.
In a nutshell
Pros:
-Unique
-Interesting characters
-Good character design
-Female models are beautiful
-Voice Acting is great
-Challenging
-High Replay Value
-Sex
Cons:
-Lack of animations
-No variety in music
-Incomplete questlines
-Jacuzzi and Lounge inaccessible

This  game? This game is special. You don't have to  worry about end game, you don't have to worry about a gear treadmill.  All you need to do is interact with other players and make the world as lively as possible.
After seeing runescape turn into a wow clone in terms of combat, At first, I enjoyed it. Then I start to realize how boring the combat is. All I was  doing is going from one skill to another, just to maximize my dps. At that point, my mmo heart has turned hollow. Looking for a new mmo to fill that void. I tried countless other mmo that has the same uniqueness to runescape pre eoc. I can't. It's all the same. Every single one of them. The boring quest grinding, that even runecape didn't have that problem, The daunting gear treadmill. I just couldn't do it. Gw 2 was  pretty decent and it held me up for a while with it's more simpler combat system. The same with Eso. (Seriously, Voice acting during questing is a god send.) But this game? It has sparked my love for mmos in general  and embraced it wholeheartedly.

This sniping-stealth hybrid is the second in s series of games made by Rebellion, who've had some interesting ideas in the past with titles like Neverdeadbut tend to have terrible execution with titles like Alien Vs. Predator. Does this game fall into the same trap of good potential yet bad execution like so many others? We shall see.
This game revolves around an American special ops soldier (this is what must be assumed, he never interacts with another person) whose name is also never revealed. All of his mission breifings are done by himself and any other human being he ever comes across ends up horrifically dead. For all we know he could be some nut running around Germany at the end of the war.
Mr. Whitebread here has the objective of killing a series of German scientists who worked on the V2 rockets before they fall into the hands of the Russian menace. So you kill both Germans AND Russians. This is when we were still allied with them, keep in mind. You of course prevail and destroy the V2 rockets and their creators, of course.
As the title indicates, you are a sniper. And this game deosnt have simple CoD esqe sniping, no, this game has the advanced ballistics on higher difficulties. There is bullet drop (which without indication on the higher difficulties, results in the guessing game) and fairly realistic enemy reactions to bullets. You fire at somone in the head, they die, you fire at somone in the heart. they die. Same goes for the lungs, stomach, and yes, testicles. While it has realism with vital organ hits, it still takes an unrealisitc number of hits at any other part of the body. There is also a kill-cam, in which if you hit a vital are on an enemy, the camera may do a stylized folling of the kill. It follows the bulet in slow motion and shows the impact in slow motions (sometimes x-ray, even more gruesome). This mechanic is very entertaining at the beggining but starts to become flow-killing after some time. You can turn it off as well as change how much it happens, but on default settings it happens too much for a decent flow.
Graphically, the game is okay. It has decent looking effects and for a game that came out two years ago, looks good. Considering how basic the levels are though, it could certainly be better. It is also pretty well optimized, allowing for older machines to play as well.
The sniping is undoubtedly the best aspect of this game, with a fairly disastorous attempt at stealth. To impliment good stealth into a game, you MUST have good AI. AI that is fairly predictable (as to make it possible to play) and acts like a human being. The enimies in this game can hear you if you move at more than a duck-walk from hundreds of feet away, or will go back to normal patrols after seeing their friends have his brains blown out right before his eyes. In short, the AI is all over the place. Another aspect to good stealth games is level design. Giving you options upon where to go, what entrence to take, how to deal with your foes. In my opinion, the best stealth games allow you to get through a level without ever taking an enemy out or ever knowing you were there. Here, you are forced to kill every last person you come across and are forced through very linear and lifeless enviornments. All in all, much is left to be desired and some may find it simply unejoyable.
In addition to the few campaign missions, there are two other game modes. The first is a co-op gamemode in which you play through the singleplayer levels with another person. Lack of dedicated co-op maps should be the first red flag here, simply placing two people in an already prepared mission shows extreme laziness. It also results in levels being far too easy, even on full difficulty, with two players fighting where one was designed ro be. From there it feels more competative than cooperative, with the players fighting over kills and objecives. In short, co-op is very tacked on. The multiplayer on the other hand is argueable the most fun part of the game. Most of the game modes are standard, team deathmatch, free-for-all, CTF, and so on. There is however Team Distance King and Distance King, which encourage the player to make long distance and skillfull shots as to win. Multiplayer here is fun, resulting in tense sniper fights and cooperative gameplay. The maps are fairly open and well designed for sniping. It results in an enjoyable online experience that can well extend the playtime of this game.
In conclusion, I'd reccomend Sniper Elite V2 to those who much enjoy sniping and can swallow mediocre stealth, levels and standard graphics, and a very barebones story. This game had very good and big ideas of a WW2 special ops game that could allow the player to feel the tension of a lone wolf sniper operative in enemy territory. It somewhat pulls through with a moderately fun experience 5.5/10

This is an updated review.
I have always loved the concept of this game.  I did give it a negative review in the past however.  The reason for my previous bad review was due to the servers for Your Own being privately run thus servers being incredibly unstable and not lasting long.  That said, let's move onto the good.
I've sunk quite a few hours into the game now.  The hours listed, span from right after the game was listed on Steam and there were only male characters, to present day.  This game has made HUGE improvements since it first got the Greenlight on Steam.  Many bugs ironed out and countless new features as well.
My biggest issue with the game was that it was designed to be an MMO, but was not a full fledged MMO.  The new release of the MMO has finally fixed that for me.  That said, I love the sheer amount of possibilities in the game.  There are so many things to craft and build that if you like crafting, this game is difficult to get bored of.  The game CAN be a bit overwhelming if you are trying to play it solo, but there are now plenty of long time helpful players around to help new players get into the game.
Each crafting tree feels very unique to me.  There is enough variation to make each crafting tree feel like it's own thing, without feeling like everything is copy/pasted for different outcomes.  The game itself now, feels like most of the bugs have been ironed out.  I've struggled to find bugs that are game breaking, which is a nice change from initial release.
The game world is beautiful, the music is beautiful, and the craftable buildings and armor all look and feel unique.  I have not run into another game that is quite so in depth as this one.  When planting a field of vegetables, one has to take into account the weather and soil as well.  I could go into more detail on this, however this review would never end.
I am now playing the game in the MMO version, and am quite happy that I decided to keep following it's development.  Yes this is quite a niche game, but it is one that I am very happy I continued following.  The Your Own experience can be very rewarding in itself.  However when you get into the MMO, this game really shines.  It brings everything together quite nicely and you can definitely tell that Your Own was meant to be an MMO.  To anyone out here considering picking up the game, I'd highly recommend the MMO version.  Yes it is more of a grind, but it really feels like it has brought all the elements together.  Trading is now a vital thing in the MMO, with options to sell to "The Crown," if you can't find a player to buy your goods.  With the skill cap being dropped it HAS made it difficult to solo.  However, it has brought around a great chance to interact with other players via trade.  Please feel free to message me about any specific information you are looking for.  I will try to help the best I can.  Best regards, and have fun!

SOMA is yet another exceptional game released by Frictional Games. The fact that they are a small game developer studio did not hamper the quality of this latest release. While maybe not as scary as their previous game, Amnesia: The Dark Descent, (albeit this may be due to desensitization to the genre since Amensia's release), the game offers very tense environments with enemies that have you cowering in a corner whispering to yourself "Don't look at it, don't think about, go away go away..".
The scares are not the biggest highlight of the game. They seem to have been incorporated to add to the story, to make you feel isolated, and to further reinforce your personal beliefs of the human consciousness. Are these monsters corrupted, unliving, programs whose only intent is to kill, or are they confused, lost souls driven to insanity due to the complications of a conscious mind living outside of it's normal host? On that note, the biggest highlight of this game is the story in how it can put you into fear driven existential crises. When I finished SOMA, it stuck with me for a few days. I was questioning the ideas and concepts brought up within the game.
My only real problems with the game were that it was a bit easy, and my choices didn't have an apparent affect on outcomes later on (I have yet to start another playthrough to see if my choices change the ending, or just different dialogues etc). So I started this game with no real expectations. It looked lke your standard Battle for Middle Earth/Civillization knockoff game, with none of the interesting storytelling, and all of the grind. It plays well enough, with no truly devastating glitches that I know of yet, but there was one thing that made me stop playing. Before I get to that thing, let me explain some of the pros and cons of the game:
As I've said before, it's like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mix between LOTR: Battle for Middle Earth and Civilization, with both Real Time Strategy elements and that good old fashioned resource management component to give it a realistic hue. You kind of get tossed into the game with no proper training, and the beginning of the game, as a result, can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Thankfully, you get an awesome amount of Battle Protection, which keep the PVP hawks off of you until you can set up a decent and defensible foundation. There are four main resources: wood, food, stone, and gold, and a fifth pseudo-resource called Influence, or Crowns. Crowns are not important when you're getting your basics down for your town, but later on, they will become a very valuable resource that will become frustrating for you to acquire, since they mostly are acquired via quests of PVP. Luckily, however, you can convert gold to crowns, and if you're good at resource management, then it shouldn't be too much of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to handle. Getting the controls down isn't exactly a synch, but it isn't impossible to nag down, if you're experienced with RTS games.
The game's story are lore are unimaginative and yawn inducing, with the generic, Tolkien esque knockoff vibes stemming from the three main factions: The Humans, the Elves, and the Orcs/Goblins. The dialogue is badly written, with some of the texts even bleeding off the boxes they are cramped into. The way the dialogue is written, it feels like the writers are trying to copy off ye olde engrish ways of writing, where every word and sentence is a headache to put together and understand in your head. Even if you do manage to finish translating the drek, it's all this very generic lore, with the elves and their nature and magic, the orcs with their war and tribal mentality, and the humans with their... Human♥♥♥♥♥♥ I guess... There's obvious betrayals, with obvious setups for war and bloodshed, and the whole campaign is just there for filler, so the antisocial ♥♥♥♥s can feel like they're playing the game while the PVP nuts hash it out with each other.
Now I'll admit it: the gameplay is riddled with dozens of little gems that made me keep wanting to play the game. You had a versatile unit structure (at least with the humans), that allowed for different approaches to siege and warfare. You can fight to defend your stronghold, you can fight to siee someone else's stronghold, and you can just get your army out on a field and hash another army's brains out for all you care. It's a nice, versatile game structure that allows for a lot of possibility. The problems crop up when it comes to controls and the AI itself, and this is where the story of why I stopped playing begins:
I was set up as the Human faction, with a nice little stronghold on a hill in the mountains. I had set up everything I needed and didn't need, including a few mercenary workers from both the orc and dwarven lands to work in my mines when I needed them to. I had my peasants fully upgraded and able to handle and gather any resource I needed within minutes. I had an army with knights, mounted knights, cavaliers, and archers, all battle hardened and toughened up wth the scars and calluses from the many grind battles I did on account of Sir Lentoth. it's a very faithful remake of the original gabriel knight game. all the original content is there and there are some new bits and pieces added. the story - set in new orleans circles around theme of voodoo - is still as engaging as it ever was. and this should do as an overall summary - it is still the sins of the fathers that we know and love, only it looks better and works better with modern systems.
it's very nice in the art department, both being faithful to the original and enhancing on the original with added details - a lot of which seem to be from original designs but not implemented in original (mostly for technical reasons like art and display resolution).
soundtrack matches closely to what's been done to the art. it is the same yet improved. and it is really good.
voice acting quality tends to vary. occasionally it is really good, occasionally it is not good and most of the time it lingers somewhere around good. at times actors seem to be trying too hard to emulate the mannerisms of the dialogs in original game. not a bad thing in itself but a bit too obvious. acknowledging that it is very very difficult to top the voice acting of main characters from the original gabriel knight I cannot really blame the remake to fall a little short in this area. what we have in the game is still a respectable result.
technically, it's not bad. unfortunately, it does have the downsides.
large resolutions are supported and it works at 1080p (and higher) without problems. not related to resolutions but aspect ratio - some images look out of place with widescreen (16:9) aspect ratio - both studio's and game's logos in the beginning looked just a little bit off.
animation is stiff and feels unpolished. wooden gabriel walking around is not too bad but in the first day introduction seeing grace walking into the stairs and then slowly rising above it (while she was the only moving thing on the screen, grabbing attention) left a strong impression of game needing just a bit more polish.
tutorials are quick and simple but great and do give a small overview both to new and old players of how the ui works.
adding labels to the actionable items on screen when pressing onscreen button or space is a great idea and a good way to remove pixelhunting (especially as this never was the point of gabriel knight games).
unfortunately, there are issues with the ui as well. at times, after action or listening to a description, the game waits for a few seconds before allowing the next action. when skipping an action (not too uncommon with some items giving multiple descriptions on repeated views/actions) it gets more common. this also seems to depend on the area/screen, in the very beginning of the game, inside of the cabinet was a bad offender. an additional related problem - having clicked on a hotspot, the only way to continue is to select an action, there does not seem to be a way to cancel.
clicking to skip/fast forward lines is unreliable, often skipping multiple lines of dialogue. it seems that due to the way skipping is implemented cursor basically jumps around on the screen (to the skip button and back to where it was before, sometimes missing the target on the latter) and quick clicking is thus discouraged.
as a bonus, especially for fans of the original, there is extra material for each scene - concept art, artwork, comparisons of the remake and the original, interviews etc.
for an adventure fan, this is a definite recommendation. for everyone else - give it a shot and you might be pleasantly surprised.

As someone who never played much of the original (and only played the third game till a technical bug prevented any progress) I thoroughly enjoyed the 20th Anniversary Edition. Gabriel might be too much of a playboy at first, but he got better towards the end. And the other characters are insteresting enough and offer voice acting that I can't complain about. I really didn't like the narrator, though. Her voice can be turned off, however.
The story is also interesting from beginning to end, although I found Gabriels relationship to Malia highly unrealistic.
And for an adventure game, it offers a whole lot of puzzles, all of  which are logical enough to be solved without having to endlessly wreck your brain. I hated the pantomine, however. And deciphering some of the codes towards the end took me a while.
But if you're ever stuck, the game offers a hint-system with multiple levels. It doesn't offer solutions on a silver platter, but gets you far enough to proceed. Except for day 4, where I found myself wandering around aimlessly as I had no idea how to solve a specific puzzle until I decided to look at a certain book again.
These comfort-features do have a downside, though. Their implementation is lacking.
Show all hotspots - plasters terms all over the screen instead of showing subtle hints
Skip through dialogue - speeds up the game, which is very noticeable at times. Also can lead to skipping multiple lines of text
Run to a specific spot - run? Gabriel doesn't run. He teleports!
Continue - does not continue from your last save but from an autosave at the last map you visited
It does have a few good features, however. If you click on an exit, the screen fades out almost instantly. And you can get to the worldmap from almost any screen. Important dialogue is also marked. And the journal contains extra-features for every map, like interviews, artworks etc...
I'm sure I could mention more, but I've already written a whole review in German :D

I've been following this game since before it was on Steam. Such a great concept! And it does not disappoint.
The Good
* Simple game mechanic that grows to a complex interconnected system
* Easy to learn, requiring almost no tutorial, but difficult to master
* Fun and addictive gameplay
* A lot of the usual grind has been automated, leaving the player almost entirely grind-free to focus on base management (yay). The sole exception is the Saboteur system, which you can find in "The Bad" section below.
* Challenging AI
* Very satisfying victories without long drawn-out endgames
* Decent graphics (if a bit blocky)
* I am playing this in early-access, and yet the game seems full-featured and stable.
* Interesting and current topic (mars colonization)
* Well thought-out in terms of resources, resource usage, and gameplay mechanics
* Offword mining and its actually about (mostly) peaceful commerce? What an original idea!
The bad
* The core game mechanic involves getting resources first, and then combining/upgrading to extract them faster. Other than avoiding pirate raids, no thought is given to logistics. I would have liked some road or train building, or having to run power lines or pipelines, rather than everything being delivered via hover selds
* The sabotage system is annoying and feels "taped on". Its mostly ineffective, and yet pulls the player away from base management. Especially towards the end of the campaign, this can get kind of grindy... with players always having to repair or re-up their goon-squad, and keep track of attacks all over the place
* The first colony almost always wins - I suppose that's incentive to drop early, but with a pausable interface, all the level3 resources near the colony are gone by the time the second corporation touches down
* The game seems weighted towards Expansionist and Saboteur factions, with little real benefit for the robots or scientists
* Synth voices for the characters are annoying
Not sure if these are good or bad...
* I feel like there should be more of a sandbox mode, perhaps with some far-future constructions like terraformers?
* Game is also quite short. It seems like a perfect length for what this game is. However, its a lot of fun, and I kinda hope it gets more features, which (I think) would need a longer campaign
* Its cliche, but I expected at some point to find alien ruins / fossils / alien tech, but didn't. This could go either way. It adds a bit of mystery and alien-ness, and deepens a story.. but it is very typical and overdone too.
Conclusion
Loved it. I love strategy and simulation games, so this might get a touch of extra appreciation from me that might not be shared by all. Even so, I'd give Offword Trading Company a 9.5 / 10.

Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers is an adventure game classic. It was full of adult humor and powered by a dark mystery surrounding voodoo. HD Remakes are now the nature of the game, and Gabriel Knight is next to get its upgrade. It does away with the 2D visuals of the first game and takes its steps into a fully realized 3D world.
For those who don’t know about the story of Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers, it follows a charismatic novelist who gets involved in a murder case. He’s been having terrible dreams that depict him dying a specific death, and soon he’ll discover that they lead to even more problems. Gabriel will travel across the city investigating the "Voodoo Murders" for his book. He will find love and intrigue as he tries to discover the secret behind the murders in New Orleans.
The Anniversary Edition makes some major changes from the original. The visual bump from 2D to 3D is the obvious change, with many of the key areas and characters re-imagined for higher resolutions. Even the comic book scenes have been changed to include better art and speech baloons. It definitely looks much better than the classic version, but it loses all of the nostalgia factor for those that have already played it. Despite a few odd animations when moving around the title is a beautiful recreation of the classic.
Interacting with objects and moving around the city is easier than ever. Simply double tapping an area will teleport Gabriel to a certain point in the room. A new icon now allows players to quickly leave an area and head to the world map at any time. No more waiting through long animations to wait for in a game with tons of backtracking.
That's a staple of classic adventure games but this HD remake makes some changes to how the story unravels. Certain aspects of the story and puzzles are shifted around among the various days. For example, in the original game Gabriel would visit his grandmother on the first day. In the new version he doesn't visit her until the week is nearly over. It's subtle little changes like this that adds a welcome freshness to a familiar story.
Fans of the classic will notice that the voices have changed for many of their favorite characters. Anyone that has played the original would be familiar with the popping and static in the original game. Sadly, Tim Curry, Mark Hamil, and many others were not able to re-record their voices. Instead, they have been replaced by a whole new cast who try to replicate the voices as much as they can. They do a fairly great job at sounding like the original characters, and some voices actually sound better than the original. The only change I miss is Leah Remini's fiesty run as Grace Nakamura.
The upgraded animations are the best improvements to the title. You can actually tell what everyone is actually doing on-screen. It comes at a small sacrifice however, as there are zones where the world feels less alive because of ambience removal. The crime scene was hectic when Gabriel reaches the location in the first game, but it seems much calmer in the upgraded version. Also, the police station doesn’t have that lively hustle and bustle about it anymore.
It’s good that the upgraded puzzle design outweighs a few removed animations. No more randomly clicking on pixels to find a snake scale in the sand. U.I. upgrades and of course cleaner graphics improve the experience from the original. The puzzles in Gabriel Knight have always been well thought-out (besides that awful clock puzzle.) Now Gabriel has a journal to keep up with current events for the day, and if all else fails a new hint system is in place to help players push through the story.
My only real complaints come from the puzzles that allow players to clear manual input. Some of them have incredibly long strings, but the player will only be able to clear all the text instead of deleting a single character. Another problem I have is the strange speech baloons during the comic book cutscenes. Maybe it is the extensions that block the visuals on screen, but I just think it looks out of place and unnecessary.
Do any of these changes make the Anniversary Edition better than the original? That’s going to be subjective to anyone that’s played the first game. There are always going to be games that we mesh more with and don’t want touched (Chrono Trigger, I’m looking at you) but for people who don’t mind seeing games upgraded, you can’t go wrong with this remake. It's a fantastic recreation of a classic title, and it even features some behind the scenes content from the original game for the nostalgic. Geek Citadel gives Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers 20th Anniversary Edition 4 stars out of 5. A lot has changed to bring this classic to the HD world, but it's still very much a classic.

80 Days is a lovely steampunk reimagining of Jules Verne's "Around the World in Eighty Days" as a text adventure combined with a map and a minimal city UI with a few options to choose from whenever you arrive somewhere. The game is full of humour and adventure, and even if the mechanics do not vary much I am finding it quite entertaining and worth the discounted Summer sale price I paid for it.
However, I wish the developers had paid more attention to a few details: the game is never too hard and all in all I find it well balanced, but there are a few hurdles that make it more frustrating rather than adding proper challenge. For example:
- The little maps that show new routes around the world take away A LOT of space in the luggage, and they MUST stay in the luggage otherwise Passpartout and Fogg will forget them. I think they could have had their dedicated space, or take away much less since in reality they are flyers that can be folded and take away virtually no space at all.
- The passage of time isn't always clear or well stated: I lost a lot of days of travel in one city because whenever I went to the bank +2 hours would go away and I would miss my boat. While it does state "+2 hours" when you visit the bank, it doesn't state so when it says "funds available" instead. A warning message from Fogg woulda been nice, since we planned the trip, he knows about it and he is capable of warning about other stuff like the Market.
- During trips Passpartout can speak to people like the ship's captain to learn things such as new routes. It would have been great if it was possible to look at the map while asking for directions, I never remember which city I am interested in! Also it would have been nice to have a list of possible things to do during trips to go back and forth from rather than having them happen in a linear, pre-decided order. I think a hub like the city one would have been great!

I'm going to get downvoted to hell, and i'm glad.
I like this game. It's exactly what Duke Nukem Forever was going to be, being released when it was.
Let me elaborate.
Duke Nukem was always both an FPS and a meme-ridden parody. Most of the well beloved humor and quotes from D3D were quotes and references to pop culture back then, just like most of humor in DNF is quotes and references to pop culture of today (including Video Game cliches). The difference being that over time, the public opinion on such practice has shifted greatly. Mostly because now a good chunk of pop culture is related to the internet, and the internet is either very defensive or radically hateful of their "culture".
As for gameplay.
Duke 3D was born in the era of such games as Doom and Quake. And the gameplay REFLECTED this.
D.N.F. was released in the era of more "cinematic" shooters with less focus on pure running and shooting, and more focus on interaction and "Press X to do something awesome" prompts. And the gameplay REFLECTS this.
I'm convinced that if DNF was released at any other time period, it would have looked differently. It could resemble Half Life 2, or the first Half-Life. Nevertheless it would still be peppered with pop culture references relevant to the time periods of when these games were popular.
I suspect that what people wanted and expected was Duke Nukem 3D but with modern graphics, and i wouldn't mind that either, i'm with you on this one.
However if i'm right about Duke Nukem games being parodies of the games popular AT THE TIME of the game's release, then this is exactly what we were supposed to get. And personally, i love it.

The game is about 40 hours, with the chance to branch routes about 15-20 hours in (chapter 11 if you were wondering). Each chapter on auto is about 40 minutes, and there are 26 or so chapters per route (though the first 11 are the exact same). So if you get this prepare for a LONG novel. There are four routes, Rise, Chihiro, Ayaka, and Ritsuko.
So you play Masaya, a boy with a deadbeat dad whose mom had left earlier. Your dad left you in debt with mobsters, and it's all you can do to not kill him. You're going to drop out of school when the first girl you meet, Rise, manages to get you enrolled in an all-girls catholic private school. It goes about as well as you can imagine. I won't say too much more, but to me the story was super engaging.
Note that this is the All Ages version, so pictures have been changed to be less risque and some hentai scenes have been removed entirely. There is no patch to fix this, so to see them you'll have to get the game from MangaGamer ($59.99) but it does come with a steam code if you do so. There is also a fandisk coming out soon "Princess Evangile w/ Happiness" that will expand routes to most of the other ladies in the game.

It's certaintly not a bad game, but it has too many features that it doesn't properly utilize. Don't bother customizing your weapons, it takes far too long and within an hour you will have found a weapon that outperforms your current customized weapon. Don't bother dashing during combat or parrying, none of the enemies telegraph their attacks enough to properly utilize it. Don't bother using "magic", it's extremely weak compared to any normal weapon, even when fully upgraded and using boosts. Plus, some enemies are immune to it. You know what every enemy is vulnerable to? Bullets. Or melee attacks.
It's sad, really. It's a game ruined by having too much of a good thing. The game just isn't fun when one of your guns vastly outperforms every other weapon you have. There's no point in using SMGs, pistols, shotguns, or assault rifles because heavy machineguns deal more damage, and have more ammo. There's no point in having 9 weapon slots if you're only using one gun the whole time. Melee combat is fun, but there's really no point in using it unless you've run out of ammo... Especially when some melee weapons USE AMMO! The last game I played that had melee weapons with ammo in it was Shadow the Hedgehog.
Enough said.
Also, shops and quest menus don't have mouse support for some reason, which is really odd. This will probably get patched or has already been patched, but it might still be in the game, so be wary.
Final verdict, it's a... good game. Just not one I would recommend. It's definetely not worth the $40 price tag.

hey everyone,
like many of you (possibly) i was on the fence about purchasing a survival genre game. i had heard many things about many other games (Dayz,Rust,The Dead Linger) and so i did some research ( as one would normally do before purchasing a game they are not sure about). I had gone through many google searched and stumbled across the site for this game. I had looked at it before but was unsure if i wanted to purchase a game that wasn't out yet. well a few months later i foudn the site again and saw it was out. Still, i was unsure. then i read a review on Steam about how the game is "as bad♥♥♥♥♥as you want it to be", so i decided to take the plunge. I must say i have been falling ever since ( thats a good thing ).
ok now that i have said that lets get to the pros and cons.
Pros
=======
1. I am enjoying the visuals quite nicely
2. It isn't an MMO style game with thousands of players gunning at you ( i think 64-65 people is max on a server ATM)
3. When you die you lose everything you have gathered and all levels and experience.
4. looks like there is alot of feedback from the community and developers.
5. so far the world is fairly contained, a bit small but still takes a while to get places making the world seem much bigger.
Cons
=======
1. (this is my biggest gripe) often times it seems that the hotkeys will not work (I.E when i hold E to take an item it will not show up as if i am even holding the button down, or when i hit enter to chat the chat window will not pop up.
2. see number 2 above.
3. see number 3 above.
4. Community (?) supposedly people have been running into alot of jack a ninnies.. in my experience with the game( granted its quite short ATM) i have come across 1 person who has actually killed me while looting.( and i did happen to kill a person, but in my defense i had seen that he had killed like 3 people already and was a bit paranoid) and in my last game lastnight someone was camping a safe zone and sniping people as they left.
5. as i said above the map is small but it feels quite large. it seems to me that safezones are pretty far from each other. ( as this is a survival game i understand this is kind of preferred and i can adapt. its just a personal preference of mine. i would prefer them a tiny bit closer so i could complete missions a bit easier.) to expand upon: 4 times last night i had courier packages for different safe zones and was never able to complete said missions due to nethers. ( as i said it is survival, i understand this, and will adapt.)
6. Text chat is only Global, Proximity is Voice. ( i would like some type of proximity text chat at some point, but not a big CON)
7. (added due to talking about the game with a friend and realized this) as of this moment Grouping is not available but there are plans to implement grouping soon ( my undertsanding is they might be implementing a tes version in the next update)
but with all said and done. i enjoy the game very much and several times i have felt the tension and pulse racing of fearing for my life ESPECIALLY at night when it goes damn near pitch black.
9/10 for me anyways.
sidenote: oh if you have been hearing about a problem with resolution sizes and such. there is a good guide to fix this. also for a safer method read the comments with the guide ( i believe it starts with "you should NEVER" ) well TY for reading and hope to see you soon ( either through a scope/iron sights or in a friendly manner)
Tip: also if you ARE using steam to play Nether i suggest you try to add friends from the game or RL to your friends list in order to communicate with them so as not to give away position through Global chat ( which is the only Taxt chat in the game)
