I'm picky as hell about what games I want to spend my money on. As I see it, the world of gaming have become corrupt,  money oriented, hasted and sloppy and I p*ss on most triple A games coming out today, hoping things will change for the better some day. If you're anything like me, or just someone who appreciates a really great story with a lot of details and good mind bender from time to time, you ABSOLUTELY need to learn what Frictional Games is as a company. They have in my opnion created some of the best horror and story driven games I have ever experienced. Period. To put it very simple: They put most triple A game developers to complete shame. And SOMA is no exception. This game have truely been created by people who had a burning passion for their game, and it shows. Throughout and until the very end you will be left with a strange taste in your mouth, and find your self pondering, whilst sitting on the toilet, about the point SOMA as a game, is trying to make. This is an absolute MASTERPIECE and is easily one of the greatest and most intriguing games I have ever played. Only one time before in my life have I been so interested and felt so involved in a games universe that I was left in absolute awe, and the 27 euro I paid for this pearl feels like a f*cking steal compared to the ride I was in for. If you have patience, like to explore and think about what is being presented to you before continueing on, looking at all the details and really get into a game to suck it all in, then this is a game you simply can not avoid - at any cost. If you on the other hand think this is a game with numerous jumpscares and you are one to impatiently run around, only waiting for the next thing to happen and to be scared sh*tless 24/7 because you're a little endorphin addict, this is not for you. SOMA is a fine mix of a lot subjects and have a slow but extremely strong build up. Only if you take your time to really appreciate everything SOMA has to offer, will you enjoy it. And then you can be sure as hell that this game is going to stick with you long after you're done playing.

The term DayZ clone springs to mind. Okay it's not about zombies but even still the gameplay is similar and a lot of fun, even though it is a fully online game which means often your good time would be ruined by one other player who makes it his/her mission to kill other players.
Upon joining a server you realise just how cruel the game is when you check out your inventory and see you have nothing but a kitchen knife...and that is just the beginning. This game is cruel and brutal to new players and advanced players alike. Spend hours in a life gathering all the right equipment and food to survive the night when out of nowhere an insta-kill attack leaves you dead and all your weapons lost. Can you tell I'm annoyed yet? However this brutal punishment for dying is part of the game and the very nature of how it works. Without the fact you lose everything when you die and have no chance of recovering it you wouldn't feel that intense feeling when you here a scream of a monster from down the street and realise you have one round in the chamber. Guns are hard to come by and when you find them you'll see they drink ammo like a greyhound drinks water. Every enemy you come across may be your end if it doesn't kill you the horde of other enemies that just 'no-clip' across streets, from miles away to right in front of you will, which makes surviving an encounter tough even with every gun known to the game. With one objective, to survive, the game gives you a challenge, but the challenge makes it intense, something other similar games fail to grasp. The speed of your decisions on whether to fight or run or go and cry in a corner will directly impact on how much blood will still be in your body a second later in game. Its not a casual game, I'll give you that for free.
However like a sex starved midget in the bedroom this game definitely has it's shortcomings and thats excluding all the character clipping bugs. Firstly how brutal it is to new players, yeah okay it makes sense, survive by killing or running is clear but how? With no weapons to start with and no idea where weapons are it is difficult to get into the game, but when you do it's difficult to put it down. This game keeps pace up all the time through the use of requiring food to stay alive, meaning you have to go out of safe zones to find food if nothing else, but on the flip side your player gets hungry a lot to quick for my liking and by the time you've made it four blocks down the street your character is bleeding out all over the floor because his tummy was rumbling, nawww didums. Secondly other players, I suppose you cannot blame a game for how players use it but perhaps a private server option would be nice? Maybe that will be released with the full game but up until then, other people are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ That means that even if you did stumble upon a weapons stash capable of bringing down Godzilla and his 3 kids chances are someone else knows it is there too and is waiting with their rifle pointed at your face, for no reason. Its a dog eat dog world out there in this game and if you are the dog that ate the most other dogs then the monsters are gonna eat you. My final complaint in this  rant is the fact that weapons, food and ammo are so hard to find. It makes sense I suppose, not like you would find a gun or even a crowbar in every block but one in every ten blocks might be nice, but maybe it is just the way I was playing. It's a large map with most buildings accessible but weapons to me were like fairy dust and unicorns, unfortunately non-existent.
To conclude on my little rant I'm going to  call a review, the game is intense and keeps pacing well by trying to kill you every time you think you are making progress. People are not very nice and act as another challenge (or even source of supplies) that you will have to deal with accordingly. Graphics are good actually and the game runs smoothly. Story, well there isn't one, its more like a test in how long you can stay alive, I suppose there are kinda small quests or well jobs, where you run packages from outpost to outpost in the city for money and experience but experience is pointless because you lose it when you die anyway. And you will die. But you can keep the money between lives which is good. If you are not very good at the game (Like I wasnt) its a good game to tab in and out of but if you are in the mood to play for hours I think you will fall into habits and knowing where things are and get bored quickly.
In all I would buy it again, bring some friends along to help though because, well it is a lot easier that way. If I was any good at the game I think I would have enjoyed it a lot more, but I suppose you could say that about any game. It's cheap and can spend a lot of time on it, just have a go. I just wish the game had either a solo mode or a suicide button.

The main problems at this time of writing (Feb 2015) are listed below:
1) AI is extremely aggressive even on Intern and Assistant level.
2) Stock valuations for AI companies are skewed too high (perhaps due to AI aggressiveness?)
3) AI has a real tendency to buy your company shares once you're doing fine and having low debt-equity ratio, yet your company's share price doesn't go up by much?
4) The AI also likes to bid aggressively on the auction house, and takes good plots of land before you are fast enough to react!
5) Hex coverage for pirates does not make sense if the transport system makes no sense - for example, if the freighters travel in one straight line to HQ, and the HQ occupies larger than one tile, the effectiveness of using the pirates ability is rather muted.
Things that I would like to see
1) Adjustable game speed and better notifications/audio feedback on events (I mean, come on, the sound of a can being trashed is the sound for a resource surplus?)
2) Ability to "unclaim" a hex

I do not write reviews for games.  I will also say that I quit preordering PC games due to the fact that a lot are released with many bugs (SimCity) and/or are stripped of many dynamic features of its predecessor, such as recent Civilization games.  However, I took a chance with this game as it is the first early access game that I have ever purchased.  I am shocked at the stability of the game and how much fun this game is given the fact that it is early access and within two days of release.  This game is worth the cash, especially with more on the way in regards to content.  I have only crashed once in my 14+ hours of gameplay.  Yes, there are things that could be balanced or added to increase the length of each map.  Also, I believe that the maps could be bigger, but they are nearly the perfect size for the current content.  The tutorials could use some work with directing you, but I learned quickly outside of the tutorials in the actual single-player after the AI beat me a couple of times.  Regardless, this game is extremely enjoyable, especially the single-player campaign.
The single-player campaign adds a new dynamic that I find intriguing.  You are against a number of AI opponents going for different locations on a planet.  You do not face the same combination of AI opponents, usually, on the different locations.  If you win the map, then you (or the winning AI) own the map and the perks/income associated with the map are the winners to use for the next location.  Also, the remaining AI battle for some of the other locations while you are playing your map, but never more than the remaining opponents can fill up.  For instance, if there are 8 players including you, then you choose the location that you want to play.  The location can have one-three AI players (2-4, including you, of the 8 total).  This leaves 4-6 AI to battle for 2-3 of the other locations.  After every match, new locations open up.  Depending on the victory conditions (how well you win), you increase in the leaderboard of that campaign.  As you move through the campaign, you use your income to buy new engineers to enhance or unlock buildings, same for the AI winners of other maps.  Each map is different in size, terrain, rules, and some have events such as “dust storm,” which lowers the efficiency of any solar plants built on the map.
This game is definitely worth buying as is and even more so knowing that the game will have more content added due to how early in the "early access" we are.  I highly recommend this.

As many other reviewers of this game have stated, the price point of this game is simply way too high for what you get, especially considering the game is in early access and I expect them to only raise the price from here. I don't shy away from early access games and I've had more than a few that never really progressed as I hoped/expected, but most I feel I at least get my money's worth out of them, but at $35, this is one of the few I definitely regret picking up.
It's not really a bad game and it is an interesting concept, but the sacrifices the developers have made to make matches fit into 20-30 minutes have made the gameplay chaotic and often times inconsistent... not things that are typically appreciated in an economic game, competitive real-time or not. It also lacks any decent mechanisms to defend yourself from sabatoge or simply being bought out once the bulk cash transactions start coming in in the late game, so winning or losing a match can be both frustrating and unsatisfying. You can carefully manuever yourself into an advantageous position to corner a market on a resource or disrupt an opponent's supply chain but then you get 75k from one offworld shipment of a base resource like oxygen, dump all your resources on the market, and hit a + button a couple times and win without any of it mattering.
The game definitely lacks depth and each match usually hinges completely on the base materials like glass or power. Regardless of which resources are the focus on any given match, the gameplay is mostly the same every time. It can be fun and it does have potential if the developers are open to some design changes, but it is simply not worth $35 or more right now and I seriously doubt it ever will be.
I would love to be wrong and see great things happen for this game as development continues, but right now, I can not recomment it.

Princess Evangile is a romance Visual Novel game and it has a wonderful, dramatic story and funny moments. Let’s talk about this game and review it to know if this game is really worth your money.
Story:
Masaya Okonogi is a young man who has financial troubles because of his father’s actions, forcing him to take different jobs. However, his father left him behind, and also gave Masaya his debt to the loan sharks, forcing Masaya to run away from their house. In the streets, however, he saved a girl named Rise Rousenin twice that night. Because of that fateful night, Masaya was enrolled at the school Rise is attending; Vincennes Academy, an all-girls school. He was chosen by Rise as a male sample to help her promote gender integration.
Gameplay:
Princess Evangile is a visual novel game, so it consists of clicking with the mouse to scroll the text. You will play as Masaya Okonogi, the main character of this game and your main objective is to promote gender integration. Although the way you can do this is by selecting certain choices. In some part of the game, some choices will pop-up and will let you decide which path you’d like to take.
This game, however, has bland and few choices that the player can choose to affect the game. Bland because the choices are very simple that it literally says which choice determines the route’s heroine. After choosing the path you wanted, well, there are no other options. Enjoy reading through the chapters! Hey, at least the story’s interesting.
Graphic:
The game has a nice HUD interface, with a theme that suites the Filles De La Vincennes ("Maidens of Vincennes") elegance and innocence. The shortcuts are nicely arranged above the textbox, and the settings menu has a nice design to it, making it look like a monarch’s settings for his throne’s adjustable backrest.
The art style for the characters is like the style from anime and their facial expressions are well drawn and very excellent. Character models were not only fixated into one pose, but they also made two for most of the cast.
The background used in the game is very excellent. The artwork is really great, as if you’re looking into a painting in an art gallery. The backgrounds are also drawn in day and night form, as well as certain events such as school festival and Christmas.
The CGs used in this game are very amazing! There are well drawn CGs that shows the tear jerking scene, wacky and funny scenes, and many more. The way the art is drawn is really awesome, as it shows what is going on in that event and how cute/beautiful the characters are.
Music:
The music of the game fits the theme and atmosphere of the game. The character’s theme song greatly describes their personalities and characteristics, like Ayaka’s jolly and carefree attitude and Ritsuko’s refined and stoic personality. The music greatly expresses the atmosphere of the situation occurring, like a dumbfounded moment, confessing their true feelings, etc.
Most of the music has elegance in it, which completely suits the setting of the story. Classical music composed by Mozart, Bach and Strauss were remixed for this game, and I actually find it relaxing. But the most exciting music in this game is “Insanity”. This will play most of the time whenever Konomi appears. You’ll find it entertaining.
Presentation:
The game has four routes, with one of the four main heroines becoming the love interest of Masaya. The player can choose what route to take depending on which choices have been selected. The heroines are Rise Rousenin, the girl with a strong will who wanted the school to reform; Ritsuko Kitamikado, the refined girl who always stick to rules and opposes the gender integration; Ayaka Kitamikado, who is known as the “other Kitamikado” due to her making pranks on others and is always laid back; and Chiho Sagisawa, the sporty childhood friend that is also a tsundere.
The characters introduced are like living in a separate dimension: a school disconnected from the common world and is very innocent of what’s the norm to the public. They are so distant that majority of the students has no contact with the male gender except with their fathers. This setting sets the characters’ mind set and personality for the rest of the game to give the player the following thoughts: “How will I be able to turn this academy into an all-gender school?” Well, maybe that curiosity will be enough for the player to keep on playing.
Overall:
Princess Evangile is a great visual novel, with comedic scenes, dramatic and tear jerking scenes, and romantic stories. Sure, the player’s choices are very minimal compared to other visual novel, but it focused itself in the story. It’s like playing a kinetic novel but you have an option to choose which heroine you’d like to end up with. Also, there are only four heroines available, which is kind of disappointing since there are some interesting female characters such as Ruriko and Konomi. Despite that, Princess Evangile delivers a great moe story and interesting characters. I can recommend this game to gamers who wanted to relax and play something refreshing with a good story.

Duke Nukem Forever is a first person shooter, developed by Gearbox Software, and published by Take 2 Interactive. Releasing in June 2011 on PC, PS3 and 360, the title was 12 years in the making, and was a highly anticipated release given the popularity of the previous Duke Nukem games.
First of all the gameplay is your regular run of the mill slap stick run and gun action. With Duke Nukem games, you will be used to fast paced action with tons of enemies charging at you, DNF takes a slight different approach and gives you more of an adventure style game world to explore, with plenty of dreaded platforming puzzles to solve. Within the first half an hour I was already sick to death of the amount of jumping puzzles this game had - the action is also very few and far between at times. I was really expecting mayhem from this title but was so disappointed with the honestly boring game play.
DNF has voice acting right the way through, but most of it is just cringe worthy. You have barbie doll type girls with unfunny toilet humor most of the time, with some of the classic lines coming from Duke too. A lot of the time I found myself wincing with emotional pain listening to it; I think we’ve probably just all outgrown the Duke humor now. Visually DNF looks OK. It definitely looks like it was released in 2011, but then when you compare it to other games from that year like Skyrim, it still looks very basic. Not to mention some of the animation of character’s movements look weird as anything!
We do have three levels of difficulty to contend with though, which makes for veteran FPS players looking for that extra challenge can hit their spot, I couldn’t really tell a difference between the normal mode and easy mode though.  In total this game took me about eight hours to finish the story mode. The game also has a multiplayer mode, but this is virtually empty and I struggled to find a game within any sort of respectful timeframe.  Unless you are an FPS junkie, there is little need for a second playthrough, completely linear story and gameplay makes any more than one pointless.
Like I said, this game does offer us something different from the Duke franchise. We have an explorable world on a larger scale than we are used too. With a couple of easter eggs waiting to be found on each stage, and interactive items found throughout too, the level design is definitely the game’s few positive points.
Thankfully the game seems to run OK still, I was able to ramp all the graphics settings to full, and still achieve over 100+ at all times. I did need to turn V-sync off as this gave a strange graphical bug where it looked as if the frame rate was fluctuating when it wasn’t which made me feel a little motion sick, after turning it off though, it fixed the problem. The game is most certainly best played using keyboard and mouse even though a controller is supported.
Duke Nukem Forever had to live up to high expectations, but didn’t even come close to getting past the bare minimum unfortunately. The boring and uninteresting gameplay quite frankly was a laughable excuse for a Duke Nukem game, and the cringe worthy voice acting topped this off to be a pretty poor excuse for a game full stop. I think it’s quite cheeky from the developers to have this game still marked at £14.99 as it isn’t even worth half of that. I wouldn’t even want to recommend DNF even when it’s on sale to be quite honest with you. Sadly I think this will be the last we’ve seen from Duke, but we can all hope for a resurgence like we’ve seen from the likes of Doom and Tomb Raider in recent times.

Dead Pixels is side-scroller shooter, with basic rpg system, where you are killing a lot of zombies and you have to get through 20 levels to get to safety. A simple and fun game, where you don't have a ton of different mechanics, just run and gun.
It a 2D game with pixel graphics, so you wont't too many video options. But what surprise me here is the sheer number of controllers you can use – xbox 360, ps3 or whatever you have and also you can rebind all the keys. This feature have to be in every game. And also you can play with mouse and keyboard.
Next is gameplay. Basically you go from left to right, through 20 streets (levels) in the city, finding or buying new gear and blasting zombies. No complicated story, no crafting, just pure fun. I like simple games like this. You have standard weapon arsenal – pistols, shotguns, rifles,assault rifles and flamethrower. Visually they are the same, but there stas are different. The good news is, when you look up a weapon you immediately see if it's better from what you have. One stat catches the eye – Penetration. This shows if the bullet will pass through enemy and hit the standing one behind him. Larger the stat more zombies will be hit. It is awesome to gather a group of enemies and blast them.
While walking through the streets you will search abandon buildings for bullets, weapons and other usefull and useless stuff. Everything you don't need you will sell it in the shops. There also you can save your game, buy upgrades, weapons, bullets and other items (i'll be writing about them  later).
The upgrades are standard – health, melee, luck, bargain, running speed, strength and weapon damage. And money is need it in the shops. How do you acquire them? By collecting coins from dead zombies and from selling useless stuff. I mentioned other items above and they are several types of granades, flares, molotov, anti-tank mine and others. There are also some passive things like jar of ooze (zombies can't detect you, until the shooting start), adrenaline (you move fast), my favourite fireworks – use the and all zombies freeze and you have a chance to kill them. There are few other items, but you will see them yourself.
Two things to keep in mind. The first is you can overweight, you can carry everything. This mean you will be very slow and this could be disastrous. The second is zombies respawn and the ammo is never enough, so don't waste too much time in a level. And when you are out of bullets you have two options – poke the zombies to death or run past them. Sometimes when searching empty building, alarm will go off and it will attract a lot of zombies and heated up the scene. The zenemies you face are generic. Slow zombie, fast zombie, spitting zombie, some are easy to kill, others take few shots more. My biggest disappointment is the lack of boss battles. Come on, how could you not include at least final boss? Such a shame.
The sound design is good. Zombies are making zombie noises, guns sound different, but the biggest star here is the music – it's amazing and it's free !!! Outstanding metal soundtrack, that never get old during my hole time with the game.
There are two modes beside the main campain – The Last Stand: stay alive as long as you can and Solution. Here you choose between several premade characters with different stats and you can't upgrade them. You can acquire weapons, ammo and others by finding them or by calling for support on a radio. When you use the radio you are buying from the military and they drop supply crate when you are ready. But you have limited calls, so choose wisely. I played The Last Stand and Solution just to get impressions of them. All three modes have co-op, but it's local only.
Sometimes you just need light and fun game. Dead Pixels is that and it have a lot of content for the price. Even if you play only the campaign, it's still worth buying. So the game offers a lot of content, amazing music, nice variety of weapons and items, nice pixel graphics, but it's lacking of online co-op and boss battles. I definitely recommend it.

is a flavorful mix of interactive novel and adventure game, based on the famous novel by Jules Verne, but set in an alternate steampunk universe. Every game consists of an attempt to make the journey around the world in 80 days (or less!), but rather than following a fixed itinerary, you get to choose the path to take at every leg of the journey. Not all paths are immediately available to you and it'll take multiple playthroughs to unlock everything -- that's OK, though, because you're almost guaranteed to get something new and interesting on every journey. Maybe you'll get kidnapped while trekking through the jungle. Maybe you'll brave the arctic in a steam contraption and discover a hidden city. Maybe you'll spend your last funds on a rickety airship to Reykjavik, arriving barely in the nick of time to win. Maybe you'll even find love... who knows?
This is a game for people who like to read. The graphics and sound are fine, but the interesting parts happen in small bits of writing that exercise your imagination. The writing is excellent, painting a recognizable world that's nevertheless much different from our own, with a lot of winks and nudges to both the source material and actual history. Having read
isn't required, but strongly recommended, as you'll miss the chance to have your expectations subverted otherwise. Besides, it's still a really good read.
A warning for people who like their adventures/stories strictly turn based: the game is semi-real time, with time passing at various rates while you're traveling, buying inventory or planning the next leg of your journey. It never becomes a twitch game, but you may miss a connection if you dawdle too long. There's a strong impetus to keep moving forward, which is perfectly in line with the theme of the game, but it may turn some people off. There's no need to regret a missed opportunity too much, though: you can always have another playthrough. A full journey around the world takes only 1-2 hours, depending on how you play it. Most encounters have multiple outcomes, of which you'll see only one in each playthrough. There are achievements for various likely and less likely events; people who like a challenge should enjoy planning for those.
I got this as part of a bundle, but it's absolutely worth money on its own. If you're a fan of the original novel and/or interactive fiction in general, don't hesitate to pick it up on a sale. If you're looking for puzzles or long stories, though, look elsewhere.

As somebody who spent most of 1997 spamming the spacebar to ogle some pixellated breasts in Duke Nukem 3D, I truly wish I had pleasant words for this game – but I don't.
After slogging through almost 45 minutes of circuitous, underlit levels designed by a blind sadist and interminable cutscenes, I feel it is my duty to spare you a similar fate.
If you like cringing and groaning audibly every few seconds, by all means, play this game. There are hours' worth of truly horrendous one-liners written by your awful step-dad. And I didn't time it, but half of the first forty five minutes are just pauses waiting for characters to say the next line of dialog. Hate good level design? DNF features frustrating maps that ignore any semblance of logic or rationality (Press 'Space' to pry the door open for the 42nd time? How 'bout you go f–k yourself). There are ham-handed references to a 12 year old game, auto-aim that makes you wonder if Duke has developed some kind of palsy in the last few years, and terrible, horrible, no-good, very bad AI. Like "hasn't changed since 1996" bad. Textures pop in and out like you're on some kind of f–king acid flashback.
Truly an abomination.

I'm not much for horror games as I'm extremely susceptible to jump scares. I tend to scare myself before the monster gets a chance. So its safe to say this game a fair bit out my my comfort zone or so I thought.
I had heard of this game a while back but I had dismissed it completely being another traverse the scary dark hallway game and wait for the monster to get you. Until someone brought it back up and I decided to actually give it a chance. The second I saw a robot unconvincingly speaking to the player regarding his robotic body I was sold. I didn't even care if this game was going make me poop my pants or not.
I had some major snafus however, it would be better for me to just list them and get them out there to ward off would be haters of early criticism.
- This game frequently crashes, I'd say around 10 times all throughout. Which wouldn't have been a huge issue if I had not been forced to sit through the same dialogue and repeat puzzle sections. I will mention however you can save anytime yourself (down to your exact position) though it requires leaving the game and returning after a loading screen.
-The monsters are not super scary. Even for me. Hiding and waiting is not fun. There is no way to stop the creatures from.. doing whatever it is they do to you when they get too close.
- The game seems to be poorly optimized. Chugging for no apparent reason other then having a difficult time loading the next area. Texture pop in and single digit frame rate. I'm running a GTX770 and should have no problem getting 60 frames even at max settings which brings me to my next point.
- The visual, GFX, video settings leave something to be desired. The only AA option being FXAA. Which is better than none I suppose. There are still options for Bloom, V-sync and SSAO but that's about it. There are many particles floating about so its only natural to expect some frame droppage from time to time even in a dimly lit corridor but chugging to single digits and crashing, frequently, just seems like poor optimization.
The story is the main draw here. I am a self professed 'fan' of narratively driven games. I hate doing things without context and there is no shortage of that here.
The prologue introduces you to the mechanics of the analog control over things and general overview of who the player character is. Without revealing too much Simon is essentially a guinea pig for an experimental treatment for a condition causing very strenuous headaches. Being as ambiguous as possible, the treatment requires placement in a machine in which brain scans take place. A sort of new age MRI. Simon takes a seat, the machine starts and so does the adventure.
I really really like the story, its excellently told. The voice acting is excellent, The world building is great and it will make you want to explore to find another terminal or notepad to read another email or scribblings of minds gone awry. The ending is very satisfying and altogether perplexing in the aspect of what the term 'alive' actually means. I'd go as far as to say that humans of any variety lack the vocabulary necessary to convey the idea properly.
I love the art direction and level design so much, that at times I wish there were a way to stop the creatures from being around. As in, have the tense moment of fear and satisfaction from outsmarting the enemy but then allow the player to explore the environment unimpeded. Now the strange aspect of the creatures is they are very lumbering and sort of silly, almost lobotomized. As long as your flashlight is off and you're crouched you become almost completely invisible. And in the off chance you are caught. (They sense you electromagnetically, very lore friendly) They are easily outrun. I'm told it has a very Alien Isolation feeling to the tension.
Your character is able to get what are essentially audio files from dead corpses and other devices for reasons I'd rather have you explore yourself to find out. The reason I even bother to mention this is when listening to these files your character is immobile which for pacing reasons seems like an odd choice.
The story seems to pull from a number of different areas for inspiration. I don't mean to name drop as I don't believe mechanically it compares but as far as story elements go it reminded me of games such as System Shock 2, Cradle, and The Fall. As well as other sources such as Hugh Howeys Wool series, or his short story Halfway Home. Which I absolutely adore all of those and wholeheartedly recommend as well.

Singleplayer Grade 7/10 (mainly due to bugs)
Multiplayer Grade 8/10 (If you buy this game for multiplayer, remember to check if there are still active players online playing this game)
IMPORTANT:
1) TRY FREE DEMO BEFORE PURCHASING!
2) Mount & Blade Warband is much better and it has mods that bring firearms to the game.
Short review: Like mount & blade Warband, but in different setting. If you hate idea of firearms in this kind of game you shouldn't buy this game. The grade is lower than in Warband, due to some problems in gameplay and large amount of gamebraking bugs.
Full review:
The singleplayer of this game gives you the possibility to lead mercenary warband in the setting of 17th century eastern europe. Like in mount and Blade warband, the experience is generally exciting and unique. Unlike Mount & blade Warband, which is like huge sandbox, this game tries to create what many consider the the Holy Grail of gaming , which is combining story and sandbox gameplay. Unfortunately the developers failed in this in many ways.
First problem is that many players didn't care at all about the story and wanted to play sandbox game, but this was difficult due to the fact that unlike in Warband, you can't create your own kingdom. You can't get married either and there are no tournaments. Because of these and some other reasosn he RPG and sandbox elements are lacking compared to Warband.
Second problem is that if you follow the story (I played the Black Mace campaign which on my opinion unfortunately wasn't interesting) you will face problems. The first one of those are huge amount of bugs, that force you to load your saved game many times during the campaing. Many of these bugs are related to the fact that the world of the game changes usually independently comapred to the story. Even when these changes don't cause actual bugs, they can seriously hamper the players attempst to progress in the story. I was for example given task to capture certain city from hostile country Poland, but by the time I had army to capture it, neutral country Crimean Kahanate had already taken it. In order to capture the town, my country would have to start war also against them. This would have been almost certain defeat due to getting into war in two fronts.
Third problem is the setting. Some people might be scared about the strange setting, but that is not what is the main problem. The problem that the setting causes is that it affects the gameplay negatively. In mount & Blade Warband, the player can both be commander of his/her troops and also be the superhero in shining armour that kills dozens of enemies on his/her own. This is even somewhat historical because armour made medieval knights very difficult to kill. In Mount & Blade: With Fire & Sword, half of those filthy peasants :-) that you used to kill without trouble are now armed with firearms, that kill you with one or two shots on hardest difficulty. Even on lower difficulty levels it is difficult to be superhero anymore. The one shot kill firearms also make melee weapons relatively weak, which is a shame, because one of the best things in Mount & Blade series is the melee combat.
Despite the severe problems in singleplayer I gave this game grade of 7, because the basic mechanics of Mount & Blade series are still there and they are great.
Multiplayer part is good, mainly due to the uniqueness of Mount & blade combat. The reason to not to give 9/10 for multiplayer is that there are no modifications for multiplayer unlike in Warband, and because the gameplay is slightly worse due to what firearms cause to the gameplay.

You're dropped into the shoes of Karl Fairburne, a German-American soldier sent by the Office of Strategic Services to eliminate key targets associated with the V2 program.
To accomplish this, you start the game out with a Welrod Mark I(a silenced and surprisingly effective handgun) and an M1903A4 Springfield Sniper Rifle as well as an M1A1 Thompson for use in emergencies(you only carry one magazine with you for that). These three weapons can of course be exchanged for other variants, if you should find them, but they're all you really need. The Welrod is the only silenced pistol in the entire game, making it especially essential for your survival.
The selling point of Sniper Elite V2, however, is the slow motion bullet cam that'll show an "x-ray" of the enemy when you hit them, if the shot is judged well enough by the game.
But in general, the whole game feels very... Generic? There aren't too many selling points. The story isn't a blockbuster story, there aren't really any interesting characters, and as a whole the game feels very empty. Still, if you like challenges with semi-realistic bullet physics, I suppose you can't go too wrong with this.

Life is feudal is often compared to games like Rust or Ark because of the survivals elements of the games. In truth the similarities between the games stop there. LIF is more a cooperative survival/medieval simulation and I think it have more in common with old MMORPG like Ultima Online than survival games like Rust.
The cooperative aspect of the game is really important. If you work alone you are gonna get stuck really early in the game because of the way the crafting system is made. Here an example: A blacksmith gonna need a builder to build is forge and cook the coal he need, a carpenter for the wooden handle for the tools, a farmer for the leather for the armors and weapons and a herbalist for the flux to make steel. Basically, every crafting professions are going to need another profession to craft something at one point or another. Teamwork is the name of the game.
The skill system is good. You got to grind to get your skill points for your profession/weapons proficiency but usually it's pretty quick to get to a level where you can do something useful. The real challenge come between 90-100 where it rise up really slowly. But for most profiencies 100 skill point actually unlock "fluff" active or passive that doesn't really impact the game.Other than that it's a great game that can be really immersive. Many time i wanted to play "a little bit" just to realize that i had passed all evening on it.
On the downside, the game is still a bit laggy and for those used to typical survival games will find that it has a slower pace than the other game. Also, i do not recommend it for player that are "lone wolf" type of player. These player are gonna reach a wall and get bored really quickly. Other than that I recommend this game. It's one the best games a played since a long time.

Dont mind the number of hours ive put into this, ive really got to say that this is possibly one of the best shooters I have played in my life, nvm, one of the best games ive ever played. From simple things like the ambient lighting to the core gameplay mechanics the guys at Bohemia really have outdone themselves for. You can either hop into a session of Eden Editor and just make up your own scenerios and play with some of the best bots ive ever seen in a shooter or have your friends join you in fighting some bots together while the host (The Zeus) spawns stuff in and tries to make an entertaining match. Or you can go into a multiplayer session and play on one of the official gamemodes like End Game, Escape, ect and have just as much fun. This game puts the massive scale of battles in BF3 and 4 to complete shame, the veriety of tactics, vehicles and weapons just blow any other game out of water. And this is just the plain vanila version of the game, once you start getting mods you then really find out what this game is about. The Arma 3 community is filled with talented and creative modders that make hundreds of unique mods that enhance your gameplay, add massive maps, add entire story lines, ect. Then you have the awsome dlc that the devs made which are definitely worth buying. These dlcs range from adding new weapons and vehicles to the coop mode called the Apex Initiative (I think thats what they called it). Heck there even was a dlc that added karting to the game and even that was done very well, fast paced and fun driving is always welcome. Then for those who like a good story, well this game has one, but its nothing special, you still get to have loads of fun with the games mechanics, but the story itself is meh at best.
I will recomend everyone who wants to get this game to wait for the Apex version of the game to go on sale and get it then. Finally, the biggest issue that I could think of is that in servers and in zeus sessions that you are playing with your freinds, if you spawn any dlc vehicles or weapons, they simply cannot use them and the map "Tanoa" (arguably the best map made for the game, I mean, its a freaking detailed as ♥♥♥♥ rainforest) simply cannot be experienced by your freinds that dont have the dlc. Even then, the dlc isnt even that expensive, its just the Apex Initiative thing that comes with the Tanoa map that has a large price tag.
All in all, great game, worth a buy.

While limited in content (only a 406 MB download on windows atm), this is a promising little trading game with a hopefully bright future.
You get to choose from 4 different classes of corporation to play from. Standard capitalists, Robots, Scavengers and Scientists. They each have a very different play style that works for them, for example Robots don't require food or water to survive, meaning they can focus right away on resource gathering.
You can't just throw down a load of buildings to gather what you need right away, you have to 'claim' ground and resources to gather them, and you can bid against other corporations or upgrade your head-quarters to get more 'claims'.
To win a game you have to buyout your opponents corporation, this gets harder as the game goes on, and the surviving corporations get bigger and more effective, but a single campaign could last maybe a couple of hours.
rapid expansion, careful selling and buying of goods, and sometimes abit of espionage can soon become formulaic. For example I've only spent about 4 hours, and I've manage to figure out how to win every time with the Robot faction (haven't won much with the other 3 yet)
IF the dev's add more to the game then I could see a lot of re-playability in this game, but at the moment its limited, and you may wish to wait while the price tag drops a bit, I kinda regret getting this at £26 (that was with a 10% discount).
Wait a few months, see what the price is like, see how much its changed, and I'll come back and do a second review of the updated version.

is a flavorful mix of interactive novel and adventure game, based on the famous novel by Jules Verne, but set in an alternate steampunk universe. Every game consists of an attempt to make the journey around the world in 80 days (or less!), but rather than following a fixed itinerary, you get to choose the path to take at every leg of the journey. Not all paths are immediately available to you and it'll take multiple playthroughs to unlock everything -- that's OK, though, because you're almost guaranteed to get something new and interesting on every journey. Maybe you'll get kidnapped while trekking through the jungle. Maybe you'll brave the arctic in a steam contraption and discover a hidden city. Maybe you'll spend your last funds on a rickety airship to Reykjavik, arriving barely in the nick of time to win. Maybe you'll even find love... who knows?
This is a game for people who like to read. The graphics and sound are fine, but the interesting parts happen in small bits of writing that exercise your imagination. The writing is excellent, painting a recognizable world that's nevertheless much different from our own, with a lot of winks and nudges to both the source material and actual history. Having read
isn't required, but strongly recommended, as you'll miss the chance to have your expectations subverted otherwise. Besides, it's still a really good read.
A warning for people who like their adventures/stories strictly turn based: the game is semi-real time, with time passing at various rates while you're traveling, buying inventory or planning the next leg of your journey. It never becomes a twitch game, but you may miss a connection if you dawdle too long. There's a strong impetus to keep moving forward, which is perfectly in line with the theme of the game, but it may turn some people off. There's no need to regret a missed opportunity too much, though: you can always have another playthrough. A full journey around the world takes only 1-2 hours, depending on how you play it. Most encounters have multiple outcomes, of which you'll see only one in each playthrough. There are achievements for various likely and less likely events; people who like a challenge should enjoy planning for those.
I got this as part of a bundle, but it's absolutely worth money on its own. If you're a fan of the original novel and/or interactive fiction in general, don't hesitate to pick it up on a sale. If you're looking for puzzles or long stories, though, look elsewhere.

If you can overcome these issues, the game actually turns out to be... ok (I din't say great or anything similar). It really is about trading so you can afford to loose money on cheap resources that you don't produce as long as you earn more on expensive resources that you produce.
The number of tiles (aka buildings) that you can build is very limited so you should be careful about how you use them and how you place them. You can scrap a building to build another but only at the same place.

One should also note that this a rather fast paced game especially at the beginning (or maybe it is just the game lagging that prevents you from playing fast enough).

You've no doubt already heard of this game's reputation.
Allow me to confirm what has been said before.  First though, let's reminisce a little:
Duke Nukem 3D was a defining pillar in the history of PC games.  With quick action, over-the-top kills, great weapon selection, always on-tap (if a bit juvenile) humour and Duke-talk smackdowns, awesome level design with a metric butt-ton of secrets and easter eggs, and delightfully hilarious multiplayer dukematches, Duke 3D absolutely nailed the first person shooter genre, and showed the world what was possible on the PC platform at the time.
So what has fifteen years of development yieded with its sequel, Duke Nukem Forever?
Game freezes on startup, long level load times, absolutely linear levels, boring gameplay, checkpoint game-saves, player limited to carrying only 2 weapons at a time, pitiful and painfully cringe-worthy attempts at humour, and Duke now has all the personality of a limp noodle.
Everything that made the previous game great is missing here.
Bottom line:
F*** you Gearbox for putting out this absolutely terrible and blatantly obvious console port and s***ting on PC gamers who made this franchise great.
A typical example of this shoddiness is the turret level.
Whoever designed the turret level needs to be taken out back behind the barn and shot and p***ed on.  Because of no save-game feature, you WILL replay this level over and over. And over.  You'll see Duke's smashed red blood-stained sunglasses over and over too.  And be forced to wait an insulting five seconds while you stare at them before the game finally prompts you to hit Enter to reload, which takes a further ten seconds.  And then you have to start all over AT THE BEGINNING.
It's an exercise in frustration that is inexcusable given the fact I have the game installed on a Core-i7 machine with an SSD.  I keep saying this every time I buy a game with them, but if I wanted checkpoint saves I'd play this game on an XBox.  I bought the game on Steam, and I'm playing the game on a PC, so f*** off with the checkpoint saves and give me the ability to save the game anywhere I d*** well want.
Final verdict:   Not even on a Steam Sale.

First, this is hands down my favorite visual novel of all time. I found it entertaining very well put together. Though, it does get repetitive in each route from time to time, but it also adds unique elements within them too.
Basically, this visual novel is about a teenage boy (Masaya, the MC) who pretty much grew up on the streets with his deadbeat father. They accumulated a large debt over time from the local yakuza/mafia and have been on the run for years. The father one day disappears and pushes the debt onto Masaya, who has been working months and months just for some extra cash. So, now Masaya has to find a way to clear his debt... while doing so conviently running into a rich teenage girl and conviently winning the lottery, thus clearing it up. After he clears his debt, the girl invites him to be the first and only male at an all girls highschool as a sample for future integration. Here on, lives his whole year within this highschool, falling in love and getting into trouble.
So, if you like cute, slice of life, school, romance kind of stuff, then I suggest checking this out. Whether it be the Steam version or the patched 18+ version, it is still a very good visual novel.

I'm going to tell you how it is, this game is NOT a good Duke Nukem game. This game is not what the series deserves, this game did not deliver the hype because it just isn't right. This is a great FPS, just the wrong series to implement said gameplay.
With that in mind, it is a great FPS. Duke Nukem's character is usually really enjoyable, but he is mediocre in my opinion in this title. The gameplay is modern FPS mechanics, as in only two weapons may be carried and health regenerates. This is not suitable for Duke Nukem.
The lines are mediocre from Duke Nukem. I want to like Duke's character in this game, but I feel he is sorta missing the target just a little bit. His humor isn't god awful, but it just feels lack luster all the same.
The gameplay is fast paced and fun. The weapon, level, and gameplay variety isn't massive but it is a good size. There is a lot of puzzle elements which feels a bit out of placed in how they're implemented but they're not dreadfully boring. In my opinion, the puzzles would be better gone, it only slows down the action and I feel that's a mistake if it's for mediocre puzzles.
The entire campaign is alright. It's not amazing, it's enjoyable though. I feel like it had too many shrinked Duke levels, which is when you're shrinked to a Ken sized doll. I kinda wish it had more space levels, or any for that matter.
There is also online, which is actually pretty fun. Get a group of mates and you'll have a blast for a few hours.
Overall, good game. It did not deserve the hate it got, but that's what happens when you change too much of a series' formula and hype it to death. However, the $20 price tag is attorcious. I suggest wait for a sale.  7-8/10
Pros-

Enjoyable gameplay
Online is pretty fun
Cons-
Humor is not super hilarious, sorta meh
Level variety is not as good as it could be.
Puzzle moments feels like it slows down the game, despite the puzzles being super simple
It is not a true Duke Nukem game, it could have been a new game series.

I really wanted to like this game having played and liked the original. Ive had some ups and down; at the start I liked it but as time went on what I seen initially as an improvement I started to see as a bloated feature that wasnt needed. In the end Shadow Warrior 2 got boring because of the features I will detail below, but I will keep an eye on it and see if the developers resolve what I consider to be the weakest parts of the game.
For the record I havent tried the co-op, so this is from my single player experience:
Pros:
Nice graphics, most of the levels genuinely look gorgeous and I had no problems running the game at max settings
Melee combat is improved over the original and it felt easier to cast the spells
Great variety of enemies
Free DLC/update added some cool elements to the game like the challenges and the xmas update gave a useful reward
Weapon models look awesome and there is loads of variety in the weapon skins
Cons:
Procedural generation was something I liked at first but over time I noticed most of the levels, while they look great, also look too similar and there was hardly any personality to them. They are just a collection of the same map pieces slotted together in different configurations, so no environmental storytelling or personality you will find in games where a level designer has done the work. To be fair there are seveal "themes" to levels, so some will be future based, some will be fantasy based and some are a mixture etc, but the actual design feels too random.
Enemy placement and vareity makes little sense most of the time because of how the levels are procedurally generated. This meant that on some levels I was experiencing more empty space and downtime in a level than actually fighting enemies. That coupled with the open nature (which is usually a good thing) means the pacing is way off.
The loot system is bloated beyond belief and takes a lot of the fun out of collecting loot and upgrading your weapons. For example you can upgrade your weapon to be dual weilding but in doing so you will have a reload time penalty to the point where it isnt worth even upgrading. Compare this to the upgrade system in Doom, where every upgrade felt powerful and useful, basically made you feel more like a badass, the SW2 upgrade system is a joke. No "upgrades" should ever penalise the player, it just takes the fun out of it.
The many trinkets/loot you acquire will be sold at the shop. I quickly fell into a routine of collecting loot and selling most of it to buy something better at the shop. The problem is you do end up getting a ton of loot with each run and because most of it is bland/samey you end up not looking at any of it until you are in the shop and even then you may keep 1 or 2 pieces of it.
Summary:
A decent follow up that unfotunately changes the game type for me, this is more like Borderlands while the original was more like Doom. That was too much change imo, and while the procedural levels look pretty they suffer from the irony of procedural generation; it creates something technically "different" every time but what you end up with lacks personality and looks the same as the level you were on before.

Even with the game in early development, and fairly objectiveless world, there is a surprising amount to do in Nether. The survival aspects alone give playing the game a constant 'on-edge' feel. The game is true to its word when it says death is always right around the corner. That tense feeling of gameplay, and extreme punishment for dying, give the game a lot of character that isn't seen much in games these days. The game has a few 'quest-like' things to do, but I've always found it much more fun to interact with the world and other players, creating my own objectives.
Exploration is a lot of fun in this game. You can go inside almost every building, many of which have multiple levels, with attached roofs (and even a hang-glider to fly from building to building). There is also a subway system, meaning that there are essentially 3 ways to travel; rooftop to rooftop, on ground, or underground. There are several 'safezones' around the map, where you can store your items, so you don't lose them on death. These act almost like 'checkpoints', where you can restock on supplies, and deposit anything important you have, before setting off to explore and scavenge again.
One reason I would suggest this over similar games, is that the monsters are actually a threat in Nether. They are fast, and have a few different special abilities and attributes. You will be swarmed and killed fast if you are careless. The players are just as much of a threat. Often, when getting from one area to another, you will have to make a choice between going through an area that is typically more player-heavy, or more nether(monster)-heavy. These choices are what make the game fun. Usually when I die, it's because I took a gamble and lost; trying to go somewhere through a quicker less-safe route, or firing my weapons when other nethers/players were around to hear it.
Now, the game does have a few flaws. If you want to read my full thoughts on how to improve those, you can see them here
. Though, I will go into a few things here.
-PvP needs to be thought about a bit. It is too easy for players to camp 'safezones' and kill you, after hours of work.
-While there is a lot to do, most of it amounts to earning cash for cosmetic items. This is fine for me; I like cosmetics. However, I can see that becoming dull quickly for some players.
-Ammunition and weapons are just too abundant. I find them more often than food. Finding a weapon would mean a lot more if they were rarer.
-There is limited building detail. For the most part, the game looks gorgeous. Very detailed scenery; destroyed remains of civilization, crumbling buildings overgrown with flora. The main issue is INSIDE the buildings. For the most part, they are completely empty; half of the city looks like parking garages. Though, being able to go inside almost every building does add a lot to the game itself. Hopefully more inner-detail will be added later.
-The part of the map that is playable is quite small. However, the potential to expand is there, and it looks like the developers plan on making the map huge.
If you run out of steam (no pun intended) with Warband and it's DLCs, you should purchase this. If you are somehow done with the new campaign, you should move onto the original Mount & Blade.

Saw this game on sale recently for about $7, more than a lot of newer games in the same sale. Why? Because despite the aging of the game's graphics, and even if you're not a diehard Star Wars fan, it's an amazing game.
KOTOR 1 was also an amazing game, and it's hard to compare them because other than the basic combat and conversation gameplay they are so very different. KOTOR 1 is Star Wars as we know it; lowly character discovers the Force and slowly becomes the most powerful person in the galaxy, with a very clear divide between good and evil.
KOTOR 2 is a different beast; you can still choose light or dark, but in 2's story it doesn't change who you fundamentally are. Instead of a conquering hero, you're a rogue ex-soldier following your own path. 2's story is much darker; no one knows or cares who you are, and when you eventually succeed it's in a far corner of the galaxy that everyone else has forgotten.
Like the first game, the protagonist has huge baggage from before the plot, though unlike the first game the main backstory point is morally ambiguous. Where KOTOR 1 is the typical Star Wars story played straight in all it's glory, 2 is a complete deconstruction of it, going as far as to label Dark side as pragmatic and Light side as naive and stagnant.
The other aspect of the KOTOR series thats propels it to greatness is the NPC companions, and in 2 they are much more fleshed out. Not only do each have an individual influence bar, but their alignment will change to reflect or oppose yours depending on how much influence you have. In addition, the roles of your main two companions are reversed from the first game: Instead of goody-two-shoes Carth, your roguish soldier is now morally ambiguous, and instead of Light-with-Dark-shades Bastila your main mentor is hardline grey who calls you out for being pointlessly good or petty evil. This game takes binary Star Wars morality and turns it on its head, and while it doesn't hit every note it still is a much more engaging experience.
The combat is unchanged, but the new crafting and loadout system lends it more depth. The conversation trees are better than ever, with many more situations with multiple outcomes including those with your own crew. The planets on the whole are probably not as vast and interesting as the first game, though some locations are revisted after the sequel time skip which adds value for veterens.
All up, this game is a must-play for fans of good RPGs, Star Wars, the first KOTOR, or the idea of grey morality itself.

This game is a work of art in the literal sense. It is representative of the pinnacle of the point-and-click adventure genre in many ways: a sort of visual novel that uses interactivity, animation, music and sound to engage the listener in a thought-provoking story.
The criticisms, while generally accurate, in my opinion miss the point of what is being delivered. Yes, it's short, a bit too easy, and the morality of the game is controversial, but none of this really detracts from the essence of what's being presented. (In fact, the very presence of a morality that gets people fired up is a big hint that there's something noteworthy about this game.)
OhNoo has distilled the genre to its fundamentals and executed those almost flawlessly. They are a young studio with limited resources that deserves your support. The art and atmosphere of this game beg to be expanded upon. I cannot imagine what these guys might do in the world of Tormentum, given sufficient resources and ambition. Buy this game.

When Mount & Blade came out, it was an ambitious project that did not reach its full potential. The first standalone expansion  (Warband) added some key improvements to the formula, but ultimately it felt like a re-release of the first game with just short of enough new content to justify paying full price for it if you already owned Mount & Blade. With Fire & Sword is the breath of... semi-fresh air that the series needed. The essentials of the gameplay remain almost identical (except for the great addition of powerful firearms and some other additions, which force the player to come up with new tactics). However, it is the setting of this game that really sets it apart from the two previous M&B titles.
Based on Henryk Sienkiewicz's historical novel "Ogniem i mieczem", the game pushes us back to a period in real world history instead of fiction. We are taken to mid-17th century Eastern Europe, where the once great Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth is facing war with multiple of its neighbouring nations. This is where the facts end, as the player can choose to ally himself/herself with any of the real factions included in the game (the 'Polish Commonwealth', the 'Kingdom of Sweden', the 'Cossack Hetmanate', the 'Muscovite Tsardom' or the 'Crimean Khanate') and alter the course of history. Alternatively, like in Warband, you may choose to form your own kingdom or simply remain neutral throughout the duration of the game.
Ultimately, the gameplay of With Fire & Sword is refined to such an extent that it feels like the most well-designed of the first three M&B titles. However, it is still very similar to the previous games and suffers from the same main flaws at the core: lack of significant unique content in terms of story. The cold and calculated nature of the tasks and actions the player is permitted to do in the game may get tedious after a while of playing. If you didn't enjoy M&B, then perhaps you should skip this one unless you really like history. On the other hand, if you enjoyed Mount & Blade then I see no reason why you shouldn't like this game (its unique and unusual setting, which explores a period in history rarely ever mentioned in video games, makes this experience more interesting).

I'm not much for horror games as I'm extremely susceptible to jump scares. I tend to scare myself before the monster gets a chance. So its safe to say this game a fair bit out my my comfort zone or so I thought.
I had heard of this game a while back but I had dismissed it completely being another traverse the scary dark hallway game and wait for the monster to get you. Until someone brought it back up and I decided to actually give it a chance. The second I saw a robot unconvincingly speaking to the player regarding his robotic body I was sold. I didn't even care if this game was going make me poop my pants or not.
I had some major snafus however, it would be better for me to just list them and get them out there to ward off would be haters of early criticism.
- This game frequently crashes, I'd say around 10 times all throughout. Which wouldn't have been a huge issue if I had not been forced to sit through the same dialogue and repeat puzzle sections. I will mention however you can save anytime yourself (down to your exact position) though it requires leaving the game and returning after a loading screen.
-The monsters are not super scary. Even for me. Hiding and waiting is not fun. There is no way to stop the creatures from.. doing whatever it is they do to you when they get too close.
- The game seems to be poorly optimized. Chugging for no apparent reason other then having a difficult time loading the next area. Texture pop in and single digit frame rate. I'm running a GTX770 and should have no problem getting 60 frames even at max settings which brings me to my next point.
- The visual, GFX, video settings leave something to be desired. The only AA option being FXAA. Which is better than none I suppose. There are still options for Bloom, V-sync and SSAO but that's about it. There are many particles floating about so its only natural to expect some frame droppage from time to time even in a dimly lit corridor but chugging to single digits and crashing, frequently, just seems like poor optimization.
The story is the main draw here. I am a self professed 'fan' of narratively driven games. I hate doing things without context and there is no shortage of that here.
The prologue introduces you to the mechanics of the analog control over things and general overview of who the player character is. Without revealing too much Simon is essentially a guinea pig for an experimental treatment for a condition causing very strenuous headaches. Being as ambiguous as possible, the treatment requires placement in a machine in which brain scans take place. A sort of new age MRI. Simon takes a seat, the machine starts and so does the adventure.
I really really like the story, its excellently told. The voice acting is excellent, The world building is great and it will make you want to explore to find another terminal or notepad to read another email or scribblings of minds gone awry. The ending is very satisfying and altogether perplexing in the aspect of what the term 'alive' actually means. I'd go as far as to say that humans of any variety lack the vocabulary necessary to convey the idea properly.
I love the art direction and level design so much, that at times I wish there were a way to stop the creatures from being around. As in, have the tense moment of fear and satisfaction from outsmarting the enemy but then allow the player to explore the environment unimpeded. Now the strange aspect of the creatures is they are very lumbering and sort of silly, almost lobotomized. As long as your flashlight is off and you're crouched you become almost completely invisible. And in the off chance you are caught. (They sense you electromagnetically, very lore friendly) They are easily outrun. I'm told it has a very Alien Isolation feeling to the tension.
Your character is able to get what are essentially audio files from dead corpses and other devices for reasons I'd rather have you explore yourself to find out. The reason I even bother to mention this is when listening to these files your character is immobile which for pacing reasons seems like an odd choice.
The story seems to pull from a number of different areas for inspiration. I don't mean to name drop as I don't believe mechanically it compares but as far as story elements go it reminded me of games such as System Shock 2, Cradle, and The Fall. As well as other sources such as Hugh Howeys Wool series, or his short story Halfway Home. Which I absolutely adore all of those and wholeheartedly recommend as well.

From my Blog about this game:
You died. Now you have to escape your cell, traverse a wasteland filled with strange creatures, solve puzzles and make choices. Your afterlife depends on your actions, are you going to heaven or to hell? Make your choice. This is the overall story of the game Tormentum: Dark Sorrow. It’s made by Oh Noo Studios, a three man team with ambitions of grandeur. The team based the world and artwork on the paintings of famous artists H.R. Giger and Zdzislaw Beksinski. H.R. Giger was a Swiss surrealist most famous for being part of the team that won Alien their Academy Award for design.  All of his artwork is on display in his own museum in Zurich. His style of artwork usually melds man and machine in what he called biomechanical. Zdzislaw Beksinski was from Poland and worked more on dystopian surrealism in a more environmental for his earlier works. For his later works he focused more on dulling the background and unnatural lighting on the subject of the painting. In true dystopian fashion he was murdered in his home for refusing to loan his caretaker’s son $100.
While the style of H.R. Giger and Zdzislaw Beksinski are more dark fantasy and gothic, I feel like the themes and style of the puzzles is way more steampunk. The mechanics are simple, it’s a point and click. Some of the puzzles are challenging but there are notes throughout the game that will make things make a little more sense. You might get stuck, you might get frustrated, hell you might even give up once or twice, but the beauty of this game will draw you in and hold you till you lose your sanity. I mean until you finish the game. For those of you like myself there are achievements and there are different endings so there is replayability. I don’t really want to give away the game but I would like to talk about my favourite part of the game.
My favourite part of this game is the cathedral. A blind old man has been trapped in this cathedral for…well I’m not sure how long he’s been there. All this time he’s been painting. There are dozens of paintings and the old man gives you paint and a brush to fix up 30 of them. But he also has a pet, this pet is kind of a♥♥♥♥♥♥ instead of fixing up 30 painting you can destroy 3. In both my playthroughs I spent a solid hour picking and deciding which painting I would restore. The art is amazing, for a three man team I don’t know how they were able to create such an awe inspiring visuals. Everything from hanging tree’s to tortured souls you will find plenty of artwork you want to as backgrounds.

Especially considering they recommend basically poking holes into your router's firewall. Also there are countless games out there that have actually managed to establish even a peer-to-peer connection from my computer without me having to recalibrate my router. No-go from a customer service perspective.
I would have really liked to play this game, but up until now, i'll have to say "don't buy it" - unless Ubisoft releases a fix for the specific problem.
Here's to hoping I can get a refund.

Dont mind the number of hours ive put into this, ive really got to say that this is possibly one of the best shooters I have played in my life, nvm, one of the best games ive ever played. From simple things like the ambient lighting to the core gameplay mechanics the guys at Bohemia really have outdone themselves for. You can either hop into a session of Eden Editor and just make up your own scenerios and play with some of the best bots ive ever seen in a shooter or have your friends join you in fighting some bots together while the host (The Zeus) spawns stuff in and tries to make an entertaining match. Or you can go into a multiplayer session and play on one of the official gamemodes like End Game, Escape, ect and have just as much fun. This game puts the massive scale of battles in BF3 and 4 to complete shame, the veriety of tactics, vehicles and weapons just blow any other game out of water. And this is just the plain vanila version of the game, once you start getting mods you then really find out what this game is about. The Arma 3 community is filled with talented and creative modders that make hundreds of unique mods that enhance your gameplay, add massive maps, add entire story lines, ect. Then you have the awsome dlc that the devs made which are definitely worth buying. These dlcs range from adding new weapons and vehicles to the coop mode called the Apex Initiative (I think thats what they called it). Heck there even was a dlc that added karting to the game and even that was done very well, fast paced and fun driving is always welcome. Then for those who like a good story, well this game has one, but its nothing special, you still get to have loads of fun with the games mechanics, but the story itself is meh at best.
I will recomend everyone who wants to get this game to wait for the Apex version of the game to go on sale and get it then. Finally, the biggest issue that I could think of is that in servers and in zeus sessions that you are playing with your freinds, if you spawn any dlc vehicles or weapons, they simply cannot use them and the map "Tanoa" (arguably the best map made for the game, I mean, its a freaking detailed as ♥♥♥♥ rainforest) simply cannot be experienced by your freinds that dont have the dlc. Even then, the dlc isnt even that expensive, its just the Apex Initiative thing that comes with the Tanoa map that has a large price tag.
All in all, great game, worth a buy.

It’s great to see something refreshingly original. Loosely based on the book, you play the role of Fogg’s valet; planning the trip, exploring local towns, buying and selling to fund your trip. Plays a bit like an interactive novel and is a great joy to read. My only criticism is that you only know if you’re going to fail towards the end; you either make it in 80 days (4 hours) or you don’t.
Completed in 4 hours (101 days)
Extra
There are SO many different things to see in this game if you take the time. Loads of extra stories and exciting adventures to go on. I visited 25 out of 169 cities and may well come back to play it again to see different stories. I almost made it in 80 days on my first trip, but I failed because the final air trip I needed to take cost £7000 more than I had, so I had to go back the way I came to find a bank, then wait a week to get more funds (I didn’t want to faff around with the markets and more travelling by that stage), then the airship crashed in the sea just outside England. I think the general strategy is that you need to make a lot of money early on in Europe to fund the more exotic locations. Unfortunately I felt rushed throughout, but if you treat it like an exploration game instead of a race, you might actually enjoy it more.

The campaign is relatively easy but can get tricky if a viable deck is not being used which is understandable for any campaign. It can be a bit tedious to get all the cards but it adds more satisfaction when you collect every single one. Even if you get bored there is still achievments, avatars and titles which can be unlocked through gameplay. However with all of these positives I don't however recommend this for veteran players unless you enjoy a limited card pool. There are also frequent glitches that cause me to exit the game when navigating menus every 30-60 minutes. I myself thoroughly enjoy the game and like finding those combos and deck combinations that most others will miss.
