I realize the game is still in a beta phase and so I am not going to go on about obvious graphics, collision or other coding related issues as those will be fixed/improve over time.  I am more concerned with gameplay.
1. Permadeath - This annoyed me within the first 10 minutes.  My last playthrough, I actually got to level 6, and was doing fairly well, but I kept running into gangs of Nethers and I wasn't able to get anywhere near a safe zone.  Trying to sneak was useless as they seemed to home in on me from across the map.  I had a nice stockpile of equipment but when you are getting hit by 3 or 4 at a time, you have to pull out a gun.  Guess what, this attracts even more.  I died, lost all my goodies, and then when I next spawned, it was on the opposite side of the effing map so I couldn't even get over to where my stuff dropped.  This idea is new and nifty, but there has got to be something that can carry over from life to life.  Having to start out each time with a kitchen knife gets boring after the first couple of times.
2. Starting Location - Really, do you have to start me out in the middle of nowhere when I logged off I was inside a safe zone?  This is totally idiotic.  You should log in where you logged out, either in or out of a safe zone or just always start in a safe zone.
3. Healing/food - Good concept, bad implementation.  There is no way to heal except with healing items which are stupidly priced.  There is no way to sell stuff you pickup but don't need (at least not that I could find), you can only trade if you happen to have what the trader wants.  Of course you can do courier missions to earn cash, but if you are low on health, then you are screwed as even small Nethers do stupid amounts of damage.  At least have food do some healing in addition to its other uses.  Oh, and how about cutting food and healing item prices by 75%, that will make it easier to play.
4. PvP - Forced PvP will turn a lot of players off the game completely.  It can only be fixed one of 2 ways, unless they come up with a way to make it really benefical to work together.  First option, have PvP be togglable feature, either on or off and it takes 24 hours for the status to flip from one to the other.  A second (and better) option (in my opinion), is to have dedicated PvP servers so players who prefer not to join in can play just against the enviroment.

Like most of the Steamers(?) out there(here), I was really skeptical of this game when I first saw it. Intrigued by the gameplay and planned features, but hesitant because of games like Infestation. However, a part of me wanted to buy it even still, because it seemed to ooze potential.
Fast forward to this past week; the Winter Holiday Sale, when this game was $5 off. Better deals notwithstanding, I pressed "Add To Cart" on a whim. After about thirty minutes trying to get into a server, it would suffice to say that I was a little discouraged and upset. I had really wanted to play this game.
When I finally did get into a server, though, my expectations disentegrated. They were somewhat low at that point, but I have to say this game is fantastic; its potential definitely palpable. Surpsingly difficult to actually survive (you get the hang of it, though), loot is well distributed to give the map a feeling of desolation but not the player hopelessness; the combat pleasantly satisfying, the gunplay surprisingly adept. Overall, the visuals, the gameplay, the...the...everything is exactly what I would've hoped this game to be (as of this moment, of course; it'll get better), and then some. Buy it! If you're into this kind of thing, of course.
Sidenote: I love how smooth the PvP blends with PvE, considering no one pops up on the map and their names don't appear until you're close, just to add to the player's paranoia, considering I'm not a huge team player, but also not an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (I.E. don't kill everyone I see, unless necessary), so it works well.

I actually had to go back to a previous save after picking a girl, realizing when I had more info about one of them that I'd rather go that route instead. 10/10 on that part.
Overall this is the best Visual Novel I've read, giving it a solid 9/10 even a 10/10 perhaps when I finish all the routes.

I'll start by saying this game does not appeal to me, but I'm not disparaging those people who do enjoy it. With that in mind I will explain why I would not recommend this game:
1.  There is a steep learning curve with virtually no in-game help features. You must rely totally on the benevolence of your fellow players or go to YouTube and watch videos just to figure out basic functions.
2.  There is virtually no explaination of the various skill trees and how to unlock them.
3.  There is no real persistent server. You play on player-provided servers and if for some reason they feel like wiping and starting over you've lost all of the time you put in. And trust me, you're going to put in a lot of time because:
4.  EVERYTHING takes FOREVER to do. Very basic things like creating tools for you to do anything requires you to break a branch of a tree, gather some flint, and harvest flower fiber. Each attempt takes 10 seconds and you are not guaranteed success. Want to build a campfire and light it? That can take up to 10 minutes of gathering twigs so  you can have the fire reach full fuel. How exciting is harvesting branches? Think standing in front of a tree and clicking it over and over and over and getting one branch at a time.
5.  You're hungry constantly. You have to find apples, trap your food, fish (never caught a single fish btw), hunt, or otherwise scavenge food. I would rather be working on figuring out how to build a house...but I can't because I'm hungry and that's going to take hours to stock up. But don't spend too much time because...
6.  Other players can come up to your flint-using character, knock you unconscious, and steal everything you just spent hours harvesting. The combat system is clunky and you can be killed quite easily by someone who has been around a while.
Honestly, real life is easier than this game. I felt like I should be getting paid to play it. I would rather go to work on Monday than slave away in a virtual world that could be gone tomorrow. If you enjoy playing solotaire for the repetition then you may like this game. It's rote, pretty shallow, and ultimately erasable. Not for me.

SOMA takes high concept science fiction, Lovecraftian horror, and Bioshock's Rapture, layers them on top of each other and bakes them into a pretty delicious, disgusting treat. These inspirations are fairly obvious and the game can suffer from a bit of the “been there, done thats” that can take the edge and shock away from the prolific horror game player, but the overarching narrative that explores human consciousness and existence is well worth the journey. And it still managed to scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me a few times.
You play as a brain damaged car crash survivor undergoing an experimental procedure that calls for a high tech scanning of his brain. Shortly after the questionable treatment you awake roughly a hundred years later in an underwater facility built to act as a kind of last resort fallout shelter where the last of humanity is working to load an artificially intelligent facsimile of mankind into a pod, and shoot that “ARK” into space. Before you cry “spoilers”, know that the game goes out of it's way to drive home the point that it isn't a “mystery” story; there aren't any major twists that pull the rug out from under you, and looking for clues so you can feel smarter than your average gamer is pointless. This isn't an M. Night Shyamalan movie; the narrative is straightforward, and any extraneous detail is there to add flavor, not clue you in on some hard left turn the game will take later on. Are you a robot? An AI? Is the world really dead, and is this really the future? Well... yeah, dummy. It's all laid out in front of you. Accept it and focus on the larger story and bigger questions, because there's engineering problems to solve and monsters to hide from. I quite appreciate this approach, as the game's themes and effectiveness don't live or die on how grand of a twist it delivers at the end.
The moral and emotional questions explored in SOMA impressively hit home, and are rather timely if you buy into our species rapidly approaching the technological singularity. Would you give up your body to carry on living as an AI? What weight would life and death carry at that point? How would you deal with copies/clones of yourself? These complex and mature intellectual queries are handled very well in the game, and the story congeals symbiotically around them. Your AI companion/door opener, Catherine, provides most of your guidance and exposition as you make your way throughout the dead underwater habitat, fixing things or breaking things as needed to progress. Your interactions with Catherine always come off as small moments of sanity in an otherwise completely alien and hostile environment. The only drawback to these character moments are some spotty voice acting; everyone seems overly calm and unimpressed in the face of death and the complete global apocalypse. I can understand the need to throw some lighthearted moments into such a heavy experience, but the offhanded nature of the protagonist and some of the supporting cast pulled me out of the immersion at times.
If you've played Amnesia the hide-and-don't-look strategies for dealing with the malformed monstrosities that hunt you in the dark won't be a big surprise. At one point Catherine even remarks, “You know the drill...” in a moment of self-awareness. The familiarity doesn't make certain, terrifying moments any less nerve-racking as you throw any piece of debris you can find down a hallway to distract the screen-distorting, tentacled creatures. It also helps that these scenarios are used sparingly, so the tension doesn't wear out it's welcome. Only once did I feel like the game crossed a line where I was running around directionless in a maze, and the monster became more annoyance than nightmare. Otherwise the gameplay effects just being near one produces are still gleefully disorienting and freaky. Scattered around the game are organic “health stations” of a sort to heal your fragile mind, because just like in real life: if you're feeling down, fisting a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ will make you feel oh so much better.
Graphically the game is quite good. You spend a surprisingly large chunk of time exploring the vast, open ocean floor which looks fantastic. It manages to be both oppressive and agorphobic at once, with some nice lighting and particle effects that really drive home the hopelessness. The other major environments are all tight, claustrophobic interiors clearly inspired by the Alien movies... or more recently/fittingly Alien: Isolation. In fact, most of the puzzles you're tasked with solving adhere closely to the formula established by the recent Alien survival-horror game. Kind of tangentially, I think Alien: Isolation might be a better, more cohesive overall video game, but it also had the benefits of a much larger budget and the established franchise... but don't let that dissuade you from SOMA, as the themes and aspirations of either are completely different. If you did enjoy the structure of Alien, however, you're bound to appreciate SOMA if you can dig what it has to offer.
SOMA is a very good sci-fi/horror game. It will make you think about life, death, what it means to be human, then it will throw some tentacle zombies at you. It successfully blends both genres with equal measure, and weaves a tale of morality and mortality that's well worth the price of admission and damage to your psyche you'll take on the trip. Think about it.

This newest Frictional game is better than Machine for Pigs but no where near as good as The Dark Descent. SOMA brings a lot to the table as a horror game and has a remarkable library of sound effects that make the game world feel very alive and reactive. The detail in some of the enviornments in SOMA is astounding and greatly sets the mood for an unnerving sci-fi game. Sadly it suffers from terribly written character dialogue that makes the main protagonists of the game very difficult to relate to.
Frictional fans that enjoyed Amnesia: The Dark Descent for its horror elements will love the creatures in SOMA. There are quite a few new monsters that will keep you on the edge of your seat. The majority of these new monsters work well to scare the player in the environments that they are presented in. A few of the monsters seem to lack any real purpose, being far too easy to avoid or simply walk past without penalty.
Death in SOMA is hardly a consequence at all. Let the monster touch you once and you get stunned and have to find a healing station to make your screen less blurry. There is a small game over screen when you get hit too many times or if you fall off a ledge and it sends you back to your previous check point.
Although the visuals and the ambient sounds do wonders to reel you in, it's very hard to stay hooked whenever the main character of SOMA opens his mouth. Simon's dialogue and line delivery makes him sound like a very bored college student that could care less about the things going on around him at Pathos II. Occasionally the voice actor delivers a decent line that shows off the actor's tallent, but he and his female companion Catherine stumble through the majority of their out of place dialogue with many 'whatever's and 'and all that's in place of saying something intelligent. If anyone playing SOMA finds these two characters to be unbearable because of their dialouge they will tear their hair out because there are long segments of this game where nothing happens other than long exchanges of dialogue between Simon and Catherine. This problem with the writing majorly weighs down the impact SOMA has on the player - not only as a horror game but an interactive experience that is -supposed- to immerse the individual that paid $30.
Furthermore, SOMA does try to invite the player to wander around the game world but provides no rewards for exploration.  There are no such relatives to items like lamp oil, tinderboxes, or laudanum in SOMA. There are plenty of interactable objects and recorded messages but they stay where you find them. This means any recording or picture you find in world cannot be listened to or viewed again when you've progressed to the next level. You have no fixed inventory to view, and the personal data assistant that you carry around only works when you find a plot-progressing console to use it at.
There has also been quite a few forum posts about poor optimization. Personally I have also experienced framerate loss in open areas and occasionally I have noticed that when I turn my camera too quickly I can make models like locker doors dissappear. The game also crashed on me more than three times before I lowered my settings. This wasn't a big issue and when I lowered my settings nearly all of my graphical issues vanished and I stopped crashing.
The lack of scavengable items in SOMA, the bad voice acting and dialogue, and some of the poorer monster encounters provides less replayability and detracts from player immersion. If you were hoping for a game closer to The Dark Descent, this will be a dissappointment. It's a headache for players that need their horror games to contain less obnoxious character chatter. If you're easily annoyed by bad voice acting, avoid this game. It's still very much worth a buy if you love creepy sci-fi underwater settings and a few spooky monsters.

80 Days is the digital evolution of the "choose your own adventure" books, sprinkled with some nice sense of adventure, none of the frustration, and some resource management.
As Passepartout, you'll have to manage your and Mr. Fogg's journey across the globe in the alloted time (80 days, of course) with a finite set of resources, via decision-making (which city will you travel to? will you wait 2 days until the next train or rent a camel? will you follow that stranger's advice?) in a mostly text format that, rather than cumbersome, becomes like a nice book read. You´ll never have to deal with large walls of text, but instead, the dialogue is well distributed and the relationship between the protagonists keeps it engaging all throughout the journey.
It is a short game, around 2 hours to complete, but the replayability is extremely high, so it is hardly fair to judge its durability on a single run. It is also very fairly priced.
One of those rare mobile games that work just as well on PC and doesn't feel forced or shoehorned. If you want to play something fresh, it is a must-have.

As a long time fan of Duke3D, I had pretty much waited *very* patiently when it came to this game. And for the longest time, all I would have cared to get to be satisfied was essentially Duke3D's open environments, sarcastic humor, with newer graphics and a more current appeal.
For the most part, that's what we got.
Do I think the 2001 previews looked and appealed better? Yes.
Do I think the 2001 version might have made a better game? Yes, but that's not the point.
Most of those that were giving this game awful reviews were either those expecting something much, much grander in scope, or were basically kids that grew up on Call of Duty and were just expecting more of that. This is not for those people.
This is more for the Duke faithful that can still fire up and run through the episodes of Duke3D with a smile.
While I still wish for someone to finally give this franchise the love letter it truly deserves, I'm just at least relieved that Duke Forever finally got to see the light of day.

Overall, somewhat suprised and pleased with the game. I'm still not terribly happy with the price point (I think for EA something around $20 would be more fair with a possible $30-$35 point when the game is finished) but I don't think I wasted my money.
Some of my negative comments first:
- The UI can be a bit clunky and laggy at points.
- If you leave a campaign game in the middle you seem to automatically lose that round (no way to save it and return later unless I'm being oblivious).
- If you start losing rounds in the campaign it becomes extremely difficult to make up the lost ground.
- No clear indication of when a campaign is over/ability to have multiple campaigns going at once.
My biggest takeaway - no problems with the gameplay. The rounds definetly go by quicker then I thought they would as do the campaigns. I do wish there was an option in the campaign to vary the number of starting opponents (simply because once they are all eliminated you win and they can get eliminated fairly quickly) but thats fairly minor. The AI is extremely robust and even the start of the game takes some thought (eg do you drop your base quickly and move to what nodes you can see, do you spend longer scanning hoping to hit the motherload, etc). It does feel like it's really all just a race to the offworld markets (they are so lucrative that whoever gets their first is more or less going to win the game) but the gameplay itself is great. The game takes some forethought as you are limited in what you can do via a limited number of claims (it would be nice if you yourself could give up or auction off a claim). Graphics overall are simple (but clean) and make it extremely easy to see what is going on in-game.
All in all I still do have a bit of an issue recommending it at this price point but if you think you'd happen to like the genre and aren't tight with cash I would pick the game up. Hopefully this turns into a good example of Early Access but even if we never heard another word from the Devs the game is completely playable now.
Edit: After playing some more I do have to say there are some annoying balance issues (some of the "races" are clearlier to play/win with then others and some of the abilities/techs are way to strong while others are almost useless) but hopefully those will be addressed going forward.

Here are a few points of interest in this engaging title:
Atmosphere -
, unlike other recent horror titles, utilizes much more sophisticated means of psychological disturbances in comparison to the usual mirage demonstrated by jump-scares. As expected,
is quite dark, to the point that extended exposure to dimly lit rooms drains Daniel’s-the protagonist-sanity; this causes the player to expend light sources such as the portable lantern and tinderboxes to illuminate the area. Violent screams and ominous groaning aide in this title’s atmosphere, as these auricle displays may or may not contribute to the actual game experience in ways other than overall feel; whether or not such sounds are relevant can only be determined through play. There are few disruptive sequenced events since each offers context to the game’s illusive story, and Daniel has created a few “Note to Self’s” for the player to find that only add to the unsettling unknown.
Story - As stated, this title’s opening entails the protagonist awakening in a seemingly uninhabited structure with no prior memory of interactions within. From here the player must quest through the house to uncover its secrets. This title-fittingly-is very psychological, maddening even, as the tale is surfaced only by exploring the massive home to horror. Just the right amount of information is revealed through playable scripted events and texts, but the full story remains outside of the player’s reach unless portions of this illusion are pieced together; even so, some questions remain unanswered to service some ambiguity. So as to not reveal anything of major importance, I will halt this segment with these final words: search well.
Trivial Gameplay - Combat-apart from flailing chairs and other loose objects at unmentionable daemons-is nonexistent.
advocates primarily as a puzzle mystery game in which player must resolve encounters with cunning rather than physical prowess. Challenges are crafted well enough to accommodate
campaigns while retaining a similar theme to a remainder of the game. As for the controls, players maneuver with the standard W, A, S, and D key layout while also adding giving simple commands for lifting objects, illuminating wall- and table-mounted torches, accessing in-game menus, and equipping items such as the lantern; it is a simple system, but this sort of title requires no such complexity in having to remember an obscene amount of button combinations.
TL:DR - Challenges range in difficulty from moderate to complex, with an intense atmosphere throughout.
is best presented in a dark room while playing alone and utilizing a decent sound system. Uncovering journals, I realized how much I did not know, but also that this most frightening revelations could possibly be recurrent or relevant to the current protagonist’s stride; this game truly knows how to disturb the player. I highly recommend this title to anyone that enjoys explorative mystery, puzzle, or horror titles from the first-person perspective. In my honest opinion,
is a legend in the horror genre, so I would not pass on this title. Thanks for reading.

"My father dumped his mafia debt on me, so I decided to cop a feel on a total stranger before I die. That experience has changed my life forever..."
In all seriousness, the game isn't too bad with the pervy scenes. Think Hayate no Gotoku taking place at an all-girls school (even though Hayate is pretty much the only guy in that series anyway). I have both versions of the game, so I don't have much playtime on the Steam version (all ages), but I have played through one of the routes already (18+).
The game is good at getting you involved in the story, but this is certainly not a game which you play for H-scenes. That isn't to say that the artwork isn't good; it's actually quite amazing. But know that you are meant to get into the game for it's story, so don't buy it if you only want something ecchi.
I'd say the game is about 40 hours long, so it is a lot of reading. In the route I did, the first and last H-scenes were written into the story (as in, they were actually kind of crucial for the story/character development). I actually feel like the other H-scenes kind of ruined the flow. I believe this is a game in which the All Ages Version could be just as enjoyable as the 18+ one, but I would have to play through it to know for sure. It actually may lack the character development the first H-scene allowed.
There are 4 heroines total, so it's possible you won't find any of the "routes" attractive to you, but if the game sells well, then Mangagamer might localize the fandisk which has a bunch of the side characters available in it. Also, there aren't many choices in the game, and it's obvious what to choose when you get to each.
Go check out Lost Pause on youtube if you're still debating it.

So, I really needed to get this done while it's fresh in my mind. WOW! Another amazing masterpiece from Frictional Game Studios! I want to start by saying that this game has possibly the most intriguing, disturbing, scary, emotional, and existential storyline I have ever had the great pleasure of experiencing. I really feel like this game made you truly consider the value of human life, what it means to be a human, and if there's really more to existence (can there be?). The game really changes the traditional (or current) idea of meaningful choices in games by completely deconstruction the notion and reassembling it to perhaps mean something new, if you allow it to. By presenting you choices that don't necessarily have to effect the long or short to outcome of the game, you're rather faced with decisions that can change YOUR view by the end. You're given the power, and the choice, to do some pretty uncertain, perhaps questionable acts throughout the game and I felt that the effect of the choice had so much more meaning and power behind it because it was left entirely up to me, and my (or the character's) conscious. This is an excellent approach to choice in a video game that I'd really like to see more.
And the horror of course! If you loved the Dark Descent (I loved it by the way) then you will absolutely love and hate this game for giving you just enough time breathe in between its horrifyingly perfect scares. This is the same horror from Dark Descent that truly made you dread to move from the comfortably well lit spot you fashioned yourself behind some crates, or the uncertainty of if switching on your torch to light the way for fear of alerting the beast which lurks nearby. My favourite movements include times where you have no other option but to run for your life and slam the button to close the door behind you, hoping to slow your persistent stalker. The monsters were varied and their patterns were more difficult to spot which kept each encounter fresh and equally as terrifying as the last.
To close off, I just want to go back and really commend Frictional for delivering such an amazing game for us! Many, including myself, were overall disheartened by A Machine for Pigs, though it had its strengths, it did not feel like a worthy follow up to Dark Descent, which is still my favourite horror game of all time, and though the game studio didn't actually develop AMFP, the name took a bit of a hit. This work completely turned that around and set huge expectations for the future. Thank you Frictional for this memorable experience that I will likely continue to ponder for months to come. I look forward to the next project!

Nether is a post apocalyptic, survival, action, horror game. While the horror aspect of it is debatable, I found myself getting jumpscared/terrified many times. But then again I am a 17 year old guy who get's scared by horror movies so don't qoute me on it.
As of now Nether is a lot of fun, I've been playing the game for around 12 hours and one of the things I like the most is that unlike DayZ the infamous walking simulator, loot is way more accessible meaning that you can find a gun, some canned
goods and cash within 20 minutes so you actually stand a chance against the evil nation known as other players.
And while you can get all of those things in a short time you still won't have a unfair chance towards other players unless they are hardcore, where you will know that because they will most likely be wearing military uniforms.
But players aren't the only evil lurking in this post apocalyptic image of Chicago, there are also Nether. Nether's are mutated people which feast on you and other players and dear god they are terrifying at night time. There are many different Nether's and all equally scary, it rages from small crawlers to golem's which are basically a bit slower L4D tank and about same size, and they can all teleport. So the game almost forces you to scavenge gun's and ammunition before taking on the larger Nether's.
There are also a hunger factor in the game and you need to get stock of food by either collecting it in various stores or warehouses,  or buying it with in-game money. In the in-game store you can buy anything from melee weapons to armor(only cosmetic). There are however microtransactions in the game but they can only be used to purchase cosmetic stuff like outfits, helmets, armor and flashlights.
The size of the map is quite large but not as big as the DayZ map. However you never feel like you are trapped.
Now a big + for the game is the fact almost every building can be walked into, and that is very good for the immersive point of view.
But with it being a Early Access Game there are bugs, but so far for me the worst thing have been that sometimes you can walk through a table or get temporarily stuck on props. While there are fps problems for some people I have not had any so far and the game runs on a smooth 45-70fps for me. However the severity of bugs obviosuly vary from pc to pc but for me it have been nothing serious.

So imagine you're a hack games journalist in 2011. Your traditional revenue streams are hemmoraging before homoncular internet fetuses who play games in videos while making dumb faces and emitting unintelligible noises. Your editor wants clicks, but the people whose fingers you're impelling to do the clicking would have to read after they did that, and that's not what they're into. And then, like a rocket from the sky, the news emerges; Duke Nukem Forever, of all things, has been completed, and is being released. Soon.
Nobody ever actually thought this would happen, and nobody even cares anymore. Even though you weren't smart enough to get a decent job, you're smart enough to understand that it can't really live up to expectations, any more than it can recreate the experience of being 12 and seeing pixellated stripper boobs for the first time, or that feeling of power that occupying the shoes of the world's most famous narcissist can give you. That internet feminism is a thing now too, and Duke Nukem, that rascal, loves to objectify those women.
Looks like you've got a byline, and a perfect opportunity to trash the decent work of a games studio whose work, no matter how good, could never come close to recreating the time and place that was so integral to many people's experience of D3D. So pontificate about how gaming has 'moved on' from the puerile adolescent power fantasy of Duke Nukem, and watch those revenue streams divert ever so slightly from the unintelligible homonculi you despise so much.
I don't know what people were expecting of this game. I also played Duke Nukem 3D as a kid when I shouldn't have been, as well as the tangentially-related originals, although those were slightly more family friendly. This game can't recreate that. It was either going to be a slavish recreation of its predecessor or a faithful transliteration of that character into the (then) modern era of gaming. It is very much the former.
While it irks me that modern cancers seeped into it, such as regenerating health, cover-based action, Call of Duty running, and a limited weapon loadout, these things were not integrated poorly and were very much a part of First Person Shooters at the time this game came out. Duke Nukem is the polyglot ripoff we know and love, Aliens steal his babes, and he steals the alien's lives. The aliens look great, especially the creepy Master Brains, who are translated excellently from the original. The action is well-done and the mechanics change enough to keep things interesting. And the less said about the muckraking journalists who took advantage of political convenience to bash an easy target and the good work of many people, the better. If you want a decent, updated Duke Nukem game with the character you know and love, Godspeed to you. We probably won't ever get better than this.

Videogames can take you on a thousand different adventures, but few offer the thrill of travel as 80 Days does. It’s a story game adaptation of Around The World In 80 Days, and it’s accordingly full of exciting, exotic locations to visit, with capers to pull, revolutions to incite and derring-do to perform at many of them. Yet it’s in the quiet moments that it best captures the sensation of going on a journey. For me those moments were the mathematician I met, full of hope for the future of her home country, and the air pirate who kidnapped me in northern Europe but then entrusted me with delivering something personal to her. For you, they might be very different – but wherever you go, the appeal is the same. 80 Days is full of romance, and mystery, and intimacy, and a deep, abiding sense of melancholy, because it understands that what make journeys and adventures compelling isn’t only the mutinies you lead, but the people you meet along the way. It is consequently the most human game I’ve ever played.

Let's be honest here. It isn't the worst game ever made, and it isn't the worst game of 2011. It is true that it isn't as good as Duke Nukem 3d by any means, but calling it the worst game ever is a massive exageration. This is a game for Duke fans first and foremost. If you are a fan of Duke Nukem 3d you will get at least some enjoyment out of this game. If you have never played a Duke Nukem game before, go and get Duke 3D. 3D is a much better game,m and this will seem like another generic FPS to you.
Now that that's out of the way, I'm going to tell you that overall I did like and enjoy the game. It has a fair bit of problems but Duke is still a fun character like he was back in 1996. This is the same Misogynistic, Evil Dead quoting idiot who drowns in narcissism. It's a joke and it's intentionally over the top, and if you find that offensive then I don't think you would even be looking at a Duke game. You could argue that Duke is a dated character that should have remained in the 90s, and that might be true, but I still think that having a shallow character fits an action game more than giving us a pretentious character who talks about how horrible killing is before going out and murdeing an entire army.
Duke Nukem Forever is a generic modern FPS with Duke and his weapons being the only standout features. The classic arsenal is all here, we still get the Freezethrower, Devestator, and Shrink Ray . Unfortuanately you can only carry two weapons at a time, and the levels are extremely linear. Remember how in the 90s FPS you had to actually look around and find ammunition? The Developers game you the resources you needed but you had to find them.In duke forever you literally can run up to a ammo crate an infinite number of times and restock on ammo. You can't even explore the levels as much as you could in 3D.  And this is one of the biggest problems. In a Duke game we should have large complex levels, instead of the simple linear ones we got. The regenerating health is also out of place, but at least they tried to justify it with Ego.
My other biggest problem with the game is that most of the weapons feel underpowered ESPECIALLY the Devestator. The only weapons that feel like they have actual power to them would be the shotgun and the chaingun. The rest aren't much fun to use, and you probably won't be using them.
So get this only if you like Duke Nukem. You will like it. If you have never heard of Duke Nukem before go and play Duke Nukem 3D, it is a much, MUCH, better game and it is one of the must-play classic FPS game of the 90s. Duke Nukem Forever will be just a generic FPS to you.

Quite frankly, I really enjoyed the sniping mechanics, especially the parts where you're actually trying to stay hidden. That was a fantastic touch and greatly added to the immersion. And then I hate everything else.
For a game that calls itself sniper elite, you spend an awful amount of time as if you were in a cod multiplayer match.
Enemies come out of nowhere, you have no idea what's going on, and stealth does not work.
Stealth is the biggest gripe I have with this game. It doesn't exist, period. Playing on Sniper difficulty gives your enemies pixel perfect accuracy, and you just enough health to take 3 bullets. The problem is, sniper rifles are pretty much the only thing you're good at. Every other weapon in the game is rubbish to use.
For example, the silenced pistol, the only silenced weapon in the game, is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t in a firefight, Every other weapon has ridiculously bad aim, to the point where firing point blank can result in X-com like results.
These seem to point you towards a stealth playthrough, which seems reasonable. But no - enemies can detect you, randomly, I might add, from distances and scenarios where they shouldn't be able to. A ♥♥♥♥ing tank spotted me while it was going in the opposite direction. One mission where you infiltrate a museum, the enemies will detect you, no matter what, even if you employed MGS-like stealth, the moment you reach a certain point, every damn soldier in the area will point their gun at you.
I really don't understand the design decisions - your equipment, the trip mine, rocks, seemingly encourage stealthy playthroughs - actual gameplay revolve around quickscopes, which really isn't as fun as you might imagine. Blowing a guy's nuts off is not as fun when it took you a couple of hours to reach the vantage point to set up the bloody shot.

Horror Game Soma, from the creators of Amnesia and the Penumbra series successfully captured the essence of great story telling once again.
For returning fans, Horror game newcomers, and veterans, Soma is the kind of game that tells an amazing story while leaving you in the dark at the same time.
You'll instantly say "oh, I already know what's going on here." because they put into motion a series of events that seems to cliche to tolerate, but quickly pulls a 180 and messes with your judgement.
Pros:
The story is really nice.
The game is gorgeous and has a wonderful ambiance that really sells the mood of the game.
The music and sound effects work well with the enviroment, especially for those wearing headphones.
Just the right amount of suspense to keep the game tense without being overly frightening.
Cons:
I've had several crashes, audio issues and setbacks, typically in certain areas. but its launch day, so whatever.
I noticed a distinct lack of cover to hide behind which often made me run into a room, and holding the door shut manually until my persuer gave up.
The game takes a really weird turn about an hour or so in, taking a turn from Comfortably tense, to really difficult.
Trying to avoid as many spoilers as possible, There was a point where I had to get through a specific room, however, the enemy inside the room would spot me easily, despite where I tried to hide, so the only method of progress was to intentionally aggro this villain that could kill me in one hit, and lure him somewhere else before running through the room. This wouldn't be much of a problem if the enemy couldn't Teleport. I mean, literally one minute not there, the next about five feet from you.
Other than that, the game is fantastic and was worth the some 5 years I've waited for it.

Video Review:
80 Days is an interesting game and I’m not quite sure how to classify it. It’s strikingly similar to the Oregon Trail if you just take out all of the survival mechanics and add a lot more encounters and events that no player will ever experience without playing the game through a dozen times or more.

The game is played out by traveling from city to city. In each city you are greeted with an event that allows you to look around the city as you desire and have any number of things happen to you. You can visit the market to buy and sell items, the bank to withdraw cash, and plan the rest of your journey out. While travelling you also encounter similar events and the goal is to circumnavigate the world in 80 days. You have to pick your path and balance your budget while attending to your rich master of whom you play the servant. Collecting certain sets of items along the way will help make your travels easier, but there is one giant flaw to this gameplay. Time ALWAYS moves outside of events. You have no time to leisurely play this game and examine things or get up and get a drink without hitting the escape key. You’re playing a strategy game where you’re on a time crunch and to make the time crunch even worse, you’re given about a minute upon arriving to each city before it’s too late to travel out for the day and now you have to spend money to sleep at the hotel because there is no pause button for time. If you want casual relaxed gameplay this is not the game for you. The events are so long and filled with so much text too that the devs clearly want you to enjoy, but you’ll probably find yourself trying to click through them extremely quickly in-pace with the anxiety-riddled “hurry up or you’ll miss the only train for the next week” gameplay that the rest of the game forces on you. Also, the goal in the game is to spend as little money as whilst circumnavigating. That’s something they don’t actually tell you until you beat the game. So it’s good to know before going in.

It’s a very small indie game so I’ve actually already talked about all there is to talk about in it. There’s graphics but they’re just really of a world map. It’s a small game; one you’ll beat in two hours. The intention of the devs is clearly for you to play it multiple times and try different paths around the world. But for me it just wasn’t fun enough for that. I give it a 4/10. It’s below average. Imagine a featureless version of the Oregon Trail that punishes you for every second you spend not traveling. That’s 80 days.

Offworld Trading Company is an intense economic macro-oreiented RTS. But don't be fooled by the lack of military units, the game won't be easy. There's a lot to manage, other players to worry about and futures to predict (or create). Those of you who've played M.U.L.E. will find this extremely familiar, but in real-time rather than the turn-based style of the original.
The game itself is relatively simple to pick up, but there's a lot of depth and interacting complexity to master. You'll be deciding which resources to focus on, which buildings are cost inefficient, picking between the two research options, deciding whether to double short the or just to rush into Off World Markets, not to mention who to wreck with blackmarket tech and when.
Of course, it's not perfect being that it's in Early Access, the UI needs polish, and I find the game can be sluggish at times, especially in the end game (though, that's likely my fault for running it at 1440p), but overall the game is ridiculously fun, and the core mechanics are extremely solid, and the multiplayer community is really strong and friendly (though, they may still wreck you at first, no hard feelings, of course). Absolutely worth picking up.

I have always secretly had this suspicion that people who play Dark Souls just don't want to be happy. I think the same can be said for people who play Moe Mekuri. That is not to say Moe Mekuri is Dark Souls hard, just that both seem like games someone plays to punish themselves rather than to have fun.
Moe Mekuri SP is an anime-themed puzzle game, based loosely on Lights Out. Your goal is to turn all tiles on the board face down to reveal a picture of an anime girl, which is then added to your gallery. Higher difficulties of the same level show the girl in more revealing outfits. The game has its origins on the Xbox Live Indie Game store, where there are three (or four, depending on your count) versions of the game: Moe Mekuri, Moe Mekuri 2 (and 2.5), and Moe Mekuri 3. I personally only own the last game in the series, so take my words with whatever amount of salt you feel is appropriate.
Moe Mekuri SP collects the puzzles (and artwork) from the previous games in one package, along with the soundtrack for the games. That being said, if you own the previous titles on Xbox there is not much to see here. In fact, this feels like a bit of a lazy port; there are no settings of any kind. You cannot change the volume, or the resolution, or play the game in full screen. Despite its origins as an Xbox Live title, there is no controller support. There are also no achievements, which is true of the originals as well, but it feels like it would not have taken much effort to add them for the Steam release.
As one would expect from a direct port, all the annoyances of the original are still present. The difficulty curve is all over the place. There is no rhyme or reason to which puzzles will be hard to solve; puzzles on easy are often harder than those on higher difficulty levels, and later puzzles are often easier than earlier ones. There is no hint system, or way to bypass a puzzle; if you cannot solve a puzzle, you cannot proceed and are simply stuck. You also cannot play the higher difficulty of any puzzle until you have completed all puzzles on the earlier difficulty levels.
I completed all puzzles on Moe Mekuri 3 on all difficulty levels, but even I found myself frequently unable to proceed, sometimes for weeks at a time. Unless you are some kind of puzzle God, a lot of the time it will just become a game of pressing everything and praying something works.
The artwork is fine, but nothing horribly interesting. There is nothing lewd to see here. Even by simple fan service standards, this game is pretty tame. Music is a variety of upbeat songs with Japanese vocals. Some of the songs are pretty good, while others are forgettable.
Considering Moe Mekuri SP is three game's worth of content rolled into one, and it has the soundtrack, you might want to pick it up if you are really into puzzles, or really, really into anime girls. Otherwise give the game a pass, there are better puzzle and anime games on Steam.

If I could select one change off the bat, it would be more market information and more dynamic markets. Right now the only truly dynamic resources is energy. Global prices are, it seems, driven by either player stockpile purchases or running deficits, which someone else could capitalize on. I'd like to see the markets function by net contribution and less stockpile driven, so rather than attempting to accumulate valuable goods and selling them off in bulk to buyout opponents have running market contribution. There seems to be a bit too much "random invisible supply and demand we dont know" driving market function. Giving us some idea of ambient demand and supply balance or even "global stockpile" that determines pricing would be nice, and then introducing exogenous price shocks to randomly shift market prices would be cool too. Something to give the pricing a bit more depth.
Similarly, the share ownership function could also gain more depth, giving extra utility to ownership would be quite interesting. Defensive ownership blocks provide no real benefit if you're behind, and spending that cash on buying yourself only means you can't spend it on further expansion which I could see leading to increasingly snowbally gameplay. It seems like it would always be better to build ownership blocks in other companies.
Finally adding more depth to the debt system would be quite cool. This review may only be temporary. Here's hoping.

Always-on DRM strikes again.
So I finally downloaded the full retail version after playing the open beta and decided to play through the story mode before going back into multi. It gave me a choice of six options for how I wanted my Warden to look. I picked one with armor I didn't really like since it has a symbol that I did like, only to get in game and find that it didn't even use the symbol it had shown me. Seems simple enough, I'll just go back and pick the armor I liked the look of then.
Or not.
After looking around the ingame menus for a while I came to the conclusion that there isn't any way to change the appearance you picked at the start. Anywhere. OK, so I'll just restart story mode from the beginning.
Or not.
There's no ingame option to start a "New Game". Anywhere. OK, then I'll just go find my save data and delete it. Problem solved.
Or not.
After searching extensively through every folder I've ever seen games save to, users, steam\userdata, local, roaming, ubisoft game launcher, my documents, my saves, etc. and doing several searches across multiple hard drives, all I came up with were two ini files for graphics and control options. I even searched through my registry. So I figured I'd ask on a forum. Surely someone on the internet must have found the save location.
Or not.
After getting a few suggestions of places I already checked, someone came in and said it was probably stored in the cloud. I thought to myself, "surely not", as I have cloud saving disabled in both Steam and Uplay and always have. And I'm only looking for the single player save file, not the multiplayer one. I'll simply set both Steam and Uplay to offline mode and prove that the saves must be located somewhere on my local machine.
Or not.
The game won't even launch if Uplay is in offline mode. So it appears that random forum user was correct. I'll have to contact Ubisoft support to get this resolved. Surely they can reset my save, or failing that, it should be a simple matter to just delete it so I can start over.
Or not.
After waiting over five hours in line, I finally got to chat with a human being who could actually do something about this.
Or not.
According to my support agent, Ubisoft in incapable of changing my characters appearance, or of even deleteing my single player save game. And they have no plans to add such a feature.
So in conclusion, the unnecessary use of always-on DRM for the single player portion of the game, combined with the ridiculous omission of a simple way to change your character or even to start a new game from scratch, combined with slow and unhelpful customer support means I have to give this a negative rating for the time being. And that's without even getting into the pay-to-not-grind aspects of the multiplayer, or the connectivity issues and hassles trying to get friends to actually be able to join the same game, etc. Or the price.
Here's hoping they fix this and I'm eventually able to focus more on the gameplay and multiplayer issues rather than dealing with idiotic feature omissions, bad tech support, and always-on DRM.

The question you're probably asking is whether this game is worth $35. The answer to that is subjective of course, but I generally say that a game is worth it if I get 1 hour per dollar. I know that's a bit of a cop out answer, so here's my actual review
Is the game good?
Yes
Is the game great?
Debatable, visual novels are somewhat different from most games in that the order you do the routes in them actually does have a significant impact on your experience. I did Ayaka's route first which made the other routes suck by comparison.
The game has a good sense of humour, and made me really laugh, like laughing hard enough for my head to touch my desk funny. That humour is one of the selling points. This is a feel-good VN, there are some darker parts to it, but for the most part it's supposed to make you smile.
That is an issue in some respects though, the game was enjoyable and entertaining. It was not however terribly touching (except one part of Ayaka's route brought tears to my eyes... her route is the best by far). Of the four romances:
One was cheesy (Ritsuko's was too ridiculous to ever take seriously)
One was pure vanilla extract (Rise's route... of course hers was also the funniest because they openly made fun of how over-the top vanilla it was. The drama felt a little forced though, and the romance overall felt unrealistic.)
One was good (Chiho's route was fairly standard, but had an actually realistic romance progression, [ it took two ♥♥♥♥ing months after declaring undying love for eachother in Rise and Ritsuko's routes for the first kiss] and was fairly exciting)
One was very good (Ayaka's route had stellar character development, she seems like an interesting character and winds up being interesting in ways completely different from your expectations. All development is explained logically and I felt this was the most realistic route due to the interal conflict and difficulty they had expressing their feelings... I mean come on, it's not easy to ask someone out, let alone confess your love to them before the first date).
Do I regret buying it, since 2 routes weren't my cup of tea?
No. Rise's wasn't bad per-se, it just wasn't to my taste, some people will like it, and some people even liked Ritsuko's route, in this kind of game, there will always be some contention when ranking routes and saying what was subjectively better. The forums do seem to agree that Ayaka's route is the best though, and it is.
Ritsuko's route was kinda like Mega Pirhana, one of those cheap♥♥♥♥♥Sci-Fi channel movies that are just hilariously bad. I couldn't really tell if the dev's were taking it seriously or not, but I wound up laughing during the climax (of the plot... the game is censored, but they did a really good job of it so I'm not complaining) which makes it a failure in my book.
The fact of the matter is that I got my money's worth, and would buy the fandisc if it came to Steam (assuming it was at or under $15)
As I mentioned before, order matters, I would reccomend Chiho's route first, then Rise/Ritsuko and end with Ayaka for maximal enjoyment.
Overall I'd give it a 7.5 / 10

It's trying to emulate IRL magic by allowing you to make your own decks from scratch. That wouldn't be so bad if it was an added extra to the decks you get from the base game.
Unfortunately, at the end of the tutorial boss (which you
to play, there's no choice to skip it) you pick a deck from the list. A list which tells you nothing bar maybe the colour of what you'll be choosing. Aaaaand, that's it. That's the only deck you get.
From that point on, you earn cards through playing the game. Each time you win, you get a booster. But you'll get stuck pretty sharpish as your starter deck won't effective against certain planeswalker decks (Eg; Your deck is black zombie based, and the Planeswalker is white prot. from black), and you won't have enough boosters to make a deck sooo...... Microtransactions.
In the other two PC magic games I own, you can buy extra decks for under £1 and they give you enough flexibility to modify existing decks and do on. In this one, you pay £3.99 for a booster which has all the cards from a certain plane. So.... you get a poor amount of really average cards from which to try and build a deck to use. Inevitably ending in a terrible deck. The whole point of being able to make a deck from scratch is that you can choose what it does (milling deck, white weenie, green monsters, graveyard based....). So you just build sub-par decks from boosters with no ability to try and get specific cards like you can IRL, so the whole thing is rendered entirely pointless.
As another point, the campaign is MUCH shorter than the two previous versions. Making them too skint to play it properly.

Big thumbs down, I'm very disappointed.

I've become sort of addicted to the whole zombie/mutant survival games, ranging from the Fallout series to LFD and I must say Nether definitely has some things going on for it. I noticed some rather bad reviews for this game, but I really like the whole premise that it's not solely reliant on it's PVP aspect (although at this beta version it's pretty much mandatory). What it brings to the table already create a very eery and chaotic formula for a post-apocalypse surivival horror game, in MMO fashion; looting, running, shooting, tactics and intelligence. You don't just plan out what your going to eat for din-din, you plan out short term, mid-term and long term goals for survival. The game casts you into an unknown world with a knife, and it's your job to figure out just what the hell is going on. Sometime's you have some helpful players online that are noob-friendly and their guidance and informed knowledge of the gameplay aspects help tremendously; or you get surrounded by a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and they chop you up. It's your run of the mill MMORPG in that sense, but there's just so much more to the game than those principles alone. Runs on the Unreal Engine, which definitely brings to life more details than other games of its type, Infestation: Survivor Stories for example has a HUGE map but even in Ultra settings the tree's look like blobs up close; this game doesn't have that problem. For a beta (just like Infestation) it's fairly well polished graphic wise and leaves me actually waiting for the game to be finished (unlike Infestation). All in all, there's still a lot missing as well as a lot left to be desired, like having a reason to want to keep playing because as of right now, you lose everything when you die (including skill points) and there's really not that many randomly spawned items, besides that some of the enemies (IE: Golems) feel like they have way too much power/health and you pretty much know you're going to die if you don't have a bunch of extra ammunition. Clunky controls make it kind of annoying running out of ammo because there's really no way to quick-swap other than to your sidearm or melee weapon which offer no real comfort up against these harder oponents. Do I recommend Nether? Yes. But I think they need to really polish off the gameplay in order for this game to be worth the 21.99 I paid for the basic beta key. I look forward to the improvements as they release patches, especially when they add in the crafting ability.

Horror Game Soma, from the creators of Amnesia and the Penumbra series successfully captured the essence of great story telling once again.
For returning fans, Horror game newcomers, and veterans, Soma is the kind of game that tells an amazing story while leaving you in the dark at the same time.
You'll instantly say "oh, I already know what's going on here." because they put into motion a series of events that seems to cliche to tolerate, but quickly pulls a 180 and messes with your judgement.
Pros:
The story is really nice.
The game is gorgeous and has a wonderful ambiance that really sells the mood of the game.
The music and sound effects work well with the enviroment, especially for those wearing headphones.
Just the right amount of suspense to keep the game tense without being overly frightening.
Cons:
I've had several crashes, audio issues and setbacks, typically in certain areas. but its launch day, so whatever.
I noticed a distinct lack of cover to hide behind which often made me run into a room, and holding the door shut manually until my persuer gave up.
The game takes a really weird turn about an hour or so in, taking a turn from Comfortably tense, to really difficult.
Trying to avoid as many spoilers as possible, There was a point where I had to get through a specific room, however, the enemy inside the room would spot me easily, despite where I tried to hide, so the only method of progress was to intentionally aggro this villain that could kill me in one hit, and lure him somewhere else before running through the room. This wouldn't be much of a problem if the enemy couldn't Teleport. I mean, literally one minute not there, the next about five feet from you.
Other than that, the game is fantastic and was worth the some 5 years I've waited for it.

A game with steampunk vehicles, reimagined literature, playing the sidekick, a time limit and no killing things at all. I made a huge gamble, even with spending only 10$ on it. That is everything that I would normally hate in a video game, yet I took the chance.
It paid off. I already own a few other games about getting from point A to point B while having adventures, the Curious Expedition and Renowned Explorers, which I have both reviewed before. While unable to reach their greatness of those two games, this is still something I plan to own for years to come, despite the fact I have yet to actually finish the race in 80 days. People who only want games about doing epic things should go elsewhere, but 80 days has walking cities, uprisings to dodge, Fogg's funny social awkquardness and quite a lot of other things that add to its charm. It appeals to the content junkie in me, and the part of me who always has thought the unsung heroes are the most accpmplished. Even the look is sharp, graphic novel-like, despite the lack of animation or voice acting.
That said, it seems to be lacking in tactical depth and it needs several replays for you to realize what the game's really all about, and really capable of. If you go by first impressions, you will get bored of it quickly, but patience and replays bring out its real spirit. Another minus is that while the game does the book due justice, its seriousness and low stakes might not appeal to younger gamers, though the same traits at least keep away the kind of people who would make fun of it on principal. This game is still good despite being a shallow romp because it defies convention and shows you an indie game can spit in convention's face without resorting to making bashing its own medium its central premise.

80 Days is entertaining yet smart, funny yet moving short steampunk-esk visual novel with branching story telling and medium replay-ability.
The story is, obviously, the main focus of the game. You are Passepartout, the loyal valet of the British gentleman Phileas Fogg, who intends to travel around the world in 80 days. The story is set in a steampunk version of 1873.
As Foggs servant you have the task to pick the route and to reach the 80 days deadline, while taking care of your master and your travel funds. Since there are no routes visible in the beginning, you have to find routes by talking to characters and exploring cities.
One playthrough takes circa two to for hours, however, there are countless possibilities and decisions, meaning every play-through is unique. The game has a rich story with wholesome characters and interesting decisions and turns. Also, the strategic part is well done.Less positively, sometimes you are limited in your decisions, which do not seem to matter from time to time. The game tends to get repetitive at certain points.
Still, 80 days is lovely and entertaining adventure which is certainly worth a try.

I'm only a couple hours in - and I have to say, I'm impressed thus far.
I will be honest and say Amnesia scared me quite a bit at first, but after learning one fatal flaw I learned relating to the enemies, I lost almost all of my tension and fear. It was still an enjoyable game, but the atmosphere was hit or miss for me at points. And to be completely honest, the story did not interest me almost at all.
But this isn't a review about Amnesia. It's about SOMA. I feel like SOMA fixed a lot of issues I personally had with Amnesia. First of all, the story is clearly the main point of the game to me - I'm completely invested so far and constantly questioning things, theorizing in my head what could be possibly be happening, and questioning whether things are real, or not, or if what I'm thinking before is entirely wrong because of something new happening in the story. The story telling is very well made, and I feel entirely invested to know what exactly is happening.
The audio... man, the audio. The sound design is absolutely brilliant. There are a lot of ambient noises mixed with great ambient musical pieces, and it all fits well perfectly. I hear thumps and get nervous that something may be after me, or something is about to come after me. I hear creaks and cracks and think something may fall or break, or distance noises of computers or robots - just all of that, it fits in the world so perfectly that I feel like it's unbelievably immersive. The sound design in this game I think is the greatest part about it.
I enjoy the graphics and art style, but it may not look "the best" for everyone. For what the graphics are, I think they are beautiful and fit in with the game perfectly - they just aren't "triple A" quality, but that's not bad. It's amazing for what it is, I think. I also love the effects that happen when you look at the creatures, or something that has important audios, or whatever along those lines.
The creatures... well, so far, they're hit or miss, I would say. I like the designs of all the creatures I've encountered so far... but to an extent, none of them feel entirely threatening (minus one), but the thing is, the noises and the voices of the creatures make me feel really uneasy. They make noises that are just not welcoming to me, and it creeps me out just thinking about it. With how their audio is designed, I feel like I'm dealing with truly strange, unknown beings, and it makes me just as uncomfortable as the enemies in Amnesia and Penumbra Black Plague did.
The only real issue(?) I'm having with the game is the optimization. I don't know if it's just me or not since a friend of mine was having no issues, but the game would randomly drop FPS sometimes when look at random specific drops and cap the FPS at 30 briefly, which gets kinda annoying for me. Other than that, it runs at a smooth 60fps basically anywhere, it just dips and caps to 30 randomly for me for some reason.
So far, I'd highly recommend this game to horror lovers. It's very atmospheric with a surprisingly great narrative (thus far to where I am in the game), and feels like an upgrade entirely to Amnesia, which I think was one of the main goals of this game. The puzzles aren't way too tough, and it's a game basically about walking aaround, hiding, and solving puzzles, so keep that in mind.

SOMA is the latest first person horror themed walking simulator, developed by Frictional games, the very same guys who helped pioneer the genre with titles like Penumbra and Amnesia the Dark Descent.
You're a guy named Simon going in for a brain scan at a suspiciously abandoned research facility. During this routine scan something appears to go wrong and you wake up 100 years later, inside an underwater station overrun with robots.
This really is a well crafted and believable world, it takes a lot of cues from other games like Bioshock and System Shock. Where as in Bioshock you felt like the ocean was taking the city of Rapture back, in SOMA you get this sense of machinery taking over everything, as large robotic appendages jut out of walls and block hallways and corridors.
There's about 5 different monster types in the game, all of which you simply have to avoid. We've seen this kind of thing in dozens of first person horror games lately, the enemy patrols around an enclosed area and you have to collect something in that area or just get through it unseen.
At it's core, SOMA is a casual horror game for people who can't handle inventory and resource management and who find the idea of a health bar off putting. People looking for a hardcore horror game set underwater, avoiding murderous robots and scraping by for resources might want to look elsewhere.

[NOTE: this review assumes that the player will use the The Sith Lords Restored Content Mod (TSLRCM) from the game's workshop. This reviewer think that said mod is a necessary part of the game at this point and can't be separated from the vanilla game itself]
Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic II - The Sith Lords is a sequel to the original roleplaying game by BioWare by Obsidian Entertainment. Set once again centuries before the Star Wars' movies timeline, The Sith Lords' story picks up immediately where the story of the first game ended: the galactic Republic is now in disarray due to the Jedi civil war and Sith forces still run rampart through its planets, with the Jedi order in ruin and no Force practicioneers in sight. You take the role of a Jedi who has been exiled from his/her order before the civil war and your objective is to survive the dark forces coming after you and discover the true reasons behind your punishment and the origin of your peculiar connection to the Force.
As far the gameplay goes, the Sith Lords manages to be a better roleplaying game than its predecessor. Several gameplay elements have been overhauled or change to support different styles of play and to truly allow you to build a character following your tastes AND be able to overcome the game's challenges. While in the first Knights of the Old Republic the balance favored pure melee Jedi characters, now other specializations and characters have a chance too: enemies are less prone to resist Force powers, making them viable for pure damage or CC, and both melee weapons and blasters can now benefit from unique upgrades that really give lightsabers a run for their money. It's worth mentioning however that the Sith Lords' endgame somehow favors caster characters: by that point in the game the Force points (your mana, if you will) regen rateo has become gargantuan, allowing you to spam damaging spells or incapacitating effects ad nauseam (something that becomes really useful, since the last portion of the game are a series of straight fights against crowds of opponents).
The Sith Lords' main new gameplay gimmick is the influence system. The companions you travel with will react to your actions and choices, approving them or else following their own moral compass and objectives: therefore, your influence with them will increase or decrease accordingly. Having an high influence with a character means unlocking new conversation options and even the possibility to turn him/her into a Jedi. The main downside of the influence system is however that the parameter is increased mainly during world events, so you'll manage to get a good influence with the characters you'll use most only. Another gimmick the game likes to throw at you is the sudden playable characters changes: at many points during the game you will be forced to put aside your main character to play in the shoes of one or more companions. While these sequences are interesting in their own right and have their place in the main story, they can easily becomes frustrating if you are forced to play a character you are not familiar with or whom you neglected beforehead.
Knights of the Old Republic II is also infamous for the somehow shifting quality of its levels. There are some levels that are universally loathed by the playerbase, with the two main examples being Peragus (which is quite long for being your first proper level after the tutorial prologue, with the story going on at a snail's pace) and Nar Shaddaa (which is another planet that takes far too long as far as the main quest goes, requires a lot of backtracking and has a brutal endgame). Also, the final area of the game, Malachor V, hasn't many fans around due to having been hit the worst by the rushed development cycle and consisting in a series of straight fights against several opponents with little to none interaction or exploration involved.
Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic II - The Sith Lords remains a very divisive game in pretty much ever aspect, even the story and the setting. Some people like the deconstruction the writers wanted to pull off on the Star Wars canon as a whole and the main morality system of the series, while others find it pretentious and too much shoehorned. Some people see the game as an incomplete, rushed mess, while others can somehow get past the blatantly missing part and enjoy what they got their hands on. Personally, while the Sith Lords could had been a far stronger sequel and a Star Wars RPG in its own right, I found myself enjoying it more often than not due to the high level of the writing, the refined and more custom gameplay and its central interesting themes

Before I start, I will say that I got the game for $0.49. Even though the regular price is $0.99, 49 cents is really the highest I would pay for a game of this caliber.
Super Duper Party Pooper is a rhythm game where you must build up a certain number of points to move on to the next level. You press six different buttons for the entirety of the game: Q, A, W, S, E, and D. These buttons serve different in-game functions, such as eating a chicken wing off of a platter, destroying a cloud, and eating an ice cream cone at the perfect time. Although the rhythm mechanics were very simple, it was good and fun enough to keep me playing for about an hour.
There are six distinct levels. Each time, the location changes, but the gameplay stays the same. Each level consists of two "stages": the rhythm stage and the skill stage. These names are not mentioned in-game, but this is what I have named them. In the rhythm stage, you must use the keys mentioned above to stack up points and make huge combos. After a certain amount of time, the level transitions to what I call the skill stage. This is also where the game's potty humor kicks in. A large caucasian butt comes up from below, and it is your job to aim the butt in such a way where the feces will fly out of the butt and hit the people behind it in the face. Get it? Me neither. You really have to play the game to understand what I'm trying to say. Anyway. This stage is another opportunity to stack up points. Once you reach a certain amount of points, you will  unlock the next stage. Humorously, the final level is called "the Hood".
Another interesting element of this game is that you can add in your own music to play along to. This means you could play the game with some Slayer in the background. To match the music with the gameplay, you must also provide the BPM, or beats per minute. This was a really good option in my opinion. I had a good laugh playing one of the levels with We are Number One in the background.
Even though this game is pretty solid, I would only recommend it as a quick time-waster. It's definitely not something I could play for hours on end. In fact, I beat the game in a little less than an hour. However, it's not a bad game.

KOTOR II has been one of my favorite RPGs since the day I first played it. Many people seem to consider this game a disappointment after KOTOR I, but I played KOTOR I first and still prefer KOTOR II by orders of magnitude.
In KOTOR II, you're playing as the Exile, a (you guessed it) exiled Jedi whose connection to the force was severed when he or she chose to walk away. As you progress, you slowly regain your character's former strength, and the main plot has you hunting down your former Jedi masters to either save or destroy them, depending on how you want to handle the situation.
KOTOR II has excellent writing, first and foremost. Its moral choices are great, much better than those found in KOTOR I (which is a game I love dearly).  It has a better cast of villains that KOTOR I, which is something that can make or break a good story. The cast of party members is great, and your influence over them will affect their appearance, their demeanor, and even their skills. Many of the people who join your crew can be trained into Jedi (or Sith) if your influence over them is high enough, which is a great feature.
A big difference between KOTOR I and KOTOR II is that in KOTOR II, you begin the game as a Jedi. It takes quite some time to be able to get your first lightsaber (although you can fast track the process by making the right choices), but starting out as a Jedi lets you build your character that way from the beginning, instead of KOTOR I's awkward pre-Jedi class system. Furthermore, when you reach a high enough level, you can choose a specialization for your character which grants new and unique abilities depending on your choice.
It's true that this game has a lot of cut content, but we live in the age of The Sith Lords Restored Content mod, which takes an already great game and makes it into an undeniably better game that its predecessor. I cannot recommend that mod enough. Way back when, Obsidian was forced to rush KOTOR II out the door. As a result, a lot of planned content was cut. However, they shipped all that content with the game, hidden away and unusable, in the hopes that modders would take it and restore it. They did. Now that KOTOR II has Steam Workshop integration, installing the Restored Content mod is a breeze for anybody, and I would go so far as to say it's essential if you want the KOTOR II experience as it was meant to be.
KOTOR II is honestly one of the only games I'd go so far to call a masterpiece. If you've ever avoided this game because you heard it's not as good as KOTOR I, I would urge you to give it a try and see how great it is for yourself. INSTALL THE RESTORED CONTENT MOD THOUGH.

Think of it as a sort of competitive SimCity.  You build your "city" over terrain that offers various resources with the goal of growing your access to valuable ones while also being able to afford the industry.  A nice big patch of Iron, just ripe for mining?  Do you have the water, power, and electricity that you'll need to run that mine?  Can you buy those needs with the profits from that mine?  Up to you to figure it out.  Throw in competitors who will attempt to get there first, or sabotage you if you get there first, and you have a challenging economic game.
The interface and general gameplay information is simple enough to use (it is NOT a spreadsheet simulator at all!), very similar to the Civilization series, and you can get into the game very quickly.
A couple of things on the downside, however.  There is very, very little explanation for what you'll need to do or why you need to do it.  The first few games had me box myself into a corner because there was no explanation covering what you'll need to start a basic successful colony/company.  I still don't know how to hire specialists (required in order to build certain buildings) because the game tells me I need them, but not how to get them.   It's also very difficult to visually see what your opponents are doing; there's a scrolling bar of text that gives you updates, but it's not particularly useful while you're trying to manage 100 other things just to stay afloat.
I haven't tried multiplayer yet, so I cannot speak to that.
Overall, definitely recommended if this is your cup of tea.
