More a work of H.R. Giger inspired art than a game.
The visuals are heavily inspired by their source material, but also stand on their own with their own unique touch.  Many of the images in the game would serve well as a poster or portrait in the home of one so inclined towards the style.  The music does a great job of enhancing the somber, alien landscape and its equally alien inhabitants.
The writing is passable, serving to push the events of the story and game along, but nothing that will stick in your head when you're done playing.  The story, likewise, exists but is not worthy of remark.
It's a shame that while the art and style of the game are clearly inspired, gameplay is less so.  Puzzles in the game rely heavily on generic puzzle tropes (slider puzzles, circuit puzzles) and commonly repeat themselves.  I personally would have preferred puzzles that interacted more directly with the fascinating world this game strove so hard to create.  The game is also heavily dependent on alignment based decisions, but these choices are so black/white in nature they engender no internal discourse, save for which achievement you are aiming to unlock.
For the price, those inclined towards Giger's style will find enjoyment in this game, and I'm glad I got to experience it despite its flaws.  Those looking for a creepy game that better incorporates puzzles into its mythos may want to look towards a title like Fran Bow.

Always-on DRM strikes again.
So I finally downloaded the full retail version after playing the open beta and decided to play through the story mode before going back into multi. It gave me a choice of six options for how I wanted my Warden to look. I picked one with armor I didn't really like since it has a symbol that I did like, only to get in game and find that it didn't even use the symbol it had shown me. Seems simple enough, I'll just go back and pick the armor I liked the look of then.
Or not.
After looking around the ingame menus for a while I came to the conclusion that there isn't any way to change the appearance you picked at the start. Anywhere. OK, so I'll just restart story mode from the beginning.
Or not.
There's no ingame option to start a "New Game". Anywhere. OK, then I'll just go find my save data and delete it. Problem solved.
Or not.
After searching extensively through every folder I've ever seen games save to, users, steam\userdata, local, roaming, ubisoft game launcher, my documents, my saves, etc. and doing several searches across multiple hard drives, all I came up with were two ini files for graphics and control options. I even searched through my registry. So I figured I'd ask on a forum. Surely someone on the internet must have found the save location.
Or not.
After getting a few suggestions of places I already checked, someone came in and said it was probably stored in the cloud. I thought to myself, "surely not", as I have cloud saving disabled in both Steam and Uplay and always have. And I'm only looking for the single player save file, not the multiplayer one. I'll simply set both Steam and Uplay to offline mode and prove that the saves must be located somewhere on my local machine.
Or not.
The game won't even launch if Uplay is in offline mode. So it appears that random forum user was correct. I'll have to contact Ubisoft support to get this resolved. Surely they can reset my save, or failing that, it should be a simple matter to just delete it so I can start over.
Or not.
After waiting over five hours in line, I finally got to chat with a human being who could actually do something about this.
Or not.
According to my support agent, Ubisoft in incapable of changing my characters appearance, or of even deleteing my single player save game. And they have no plans to add such a feature.
So in conclusion, the unnecessary use of always-on DRM for the single player portion of the game, combined with the ridiculous omission of a simple way to change your character or even to start a new game from scratch, combined with slow and unhelpful customer support means I have to give this a negative rating for the time being. And that's without even getting into the pay-to-not-grind aspects of the multiplayer, or the connectivity issues and hassles trying to get friends to actually be able to join the same game, etc. Or the price.
Here's hoping they fix this and I'm eventually able to focus more on the gameplay and multiplayer issues rather than dealing with idiotic feature omissions, bad tech support, and always-on DRM.

I can whole heartedly say that this game is one of my top games of 2016. It managed to do what Doom couldn't; keep me interested. It presents a fast paced, gory, shoot and slice fest without making it feel like a chore. The story is somewhat stereotypical but with a fresh twist to it that helps keep the gameplay flowing without you knowing what will happen after every corner. Plenty of side missions are thrown around, with the ability to warp to a whole bunch of different maps to fulfill various requests.
The comedy in the game largly relies on Wang jokes, which are largely uninspired but not hard enough to swallow. Wang's actual character is that of a lovable "do I have to?" hero who just wants to make a quick buck, which leaves him relatable and understandable in a world of craziness.
The combat itself is very enjoyable. A large variety of weapons with swords, chainsaws, dual blades, baseball bats, shotguns, assault rifles, SMGs, grenade launchers, pistols, bows, nail guns and more, that allow you to pick your own gameplay on the fly but not allowing you to rely too heavily on it - as ammo can be pretty limited if you only rely on your favourite two guns. This coupled with the upgrades system that sees you collecting various gems from enemy corpses to give yourself another way to design your own play style. The upgrade system brings with it a fair downside however, in that most enemies drop a gem, with Superior enemies dropping numerous gems - as a reult you end up with a massive amount of useless gems which does nothing more than feed the need to grind for the gems you want, away from all the garbage.
I've had a few stutters and situations of frame drops, alongside somewhat long load times showing that the game certainly has its flaws technically, but as a whole it has held up with consistent textures and running.
This game is great if you're looking for a fast paced kill-athon focused on collecting loot to smash more skulls.
Deep, weighty, intuitive fighting system makes the game worth buying. Shame so many people are having network problems.

I'm only a couple hours in - and I have to say, I'm impressed thus far.
I will be honest and say Amnesia scared me quite a bit at first, but after learning one fatal flaw I learned relating to the enemies, I lost almost all of my tension and fear. It was still an enjoyable game, but the atmosphere was hit or miss for me at points. And to be completely honest, the story did not interest me almost at all.
But this isn't a review about Amnesia. It's about SOMA. I feel like SOMA fixed a lot of issues I personally had with Amnesia. First of all, the story is clearly the main point of the game to me - I'm completely invested so far and constantly questioning things, theorizing in my head what could be possibly be happening, and questioning whether things are real, or not, or if what I'm thinking before is entirely wrong because of something new happening in the story. The story telling is very well made, and I feel entirely invested to know what exactly is happening.
The audio... man, the audio. The sound design is absolutely brilliant. There are a lot of ambient noises mixed with great ambient musical pieces, and it all fits well perfectly. I hear thumps and get nervous that something may be after me, or something is about to come after me. I hear creaks and cracks and think something may fall or break, or distance noises of computers or robots - just all of that, it fits in the world so perfectly that I feel like it's unbelievably immersive. The sound design in this game I think is the greatest part about it.
I enjoy the graphics and art style, but it may not look "the best" for everyone. For what the graphics are, I think they are beautiful and fit in with the game perfectly - they just aren't "triple A" quality, but that's not bad. It's amazing for what it is, I think. I also love the effects that happen when you look at the creatures, or something that has important audios, or whatever along those lines.
The creatures... well, so far, they're hit or miss, I would say. I like the designs of all the creatures I've encountered so far... but to an extent, none of them feel entirely threatening (minus one), but the thing is, the noises and the voices of the creatures make me feel really uneasy. They make noises that are just not welcoming to me, and it creeps me out just thinking about it. With how their audio is designed, I feel like I'm dealing with truly strange, unknown beings, and it makes me just as uncomfortable as the enemies in Amnesia and Penumbra Black Plague did.
The only real issue(?) I'm having with the game is the optimization. I don't know if it's just me or not since a friend of mine was having no issues, but the game would randomly drop FPS sometimes when look at random specific drops and cap the FPS at 30 briefly, which gets kinda annoying for me. Other than that, it runs at a smooth 60fps basically anywhere, it just dips and caps to 30 randomly for me for some reason.
So far, I'd highly recommend this game to horror lovers. It's very atmospheric with a surprisingly great narrative (thus far to where I am in the game), and feels like an upgrade entirely to Amnesia, which I think was one of the main goals of this game. The puzzles aren't way too tough, and it's a game basically about walking aaround, hiding, and solving puzzles, so keep that in mind.

SOMA is the latest first person horror themed walking simulator, developed by Frictional games, the very same guys who helped pioneer the genre with titles like Penumbra and Amnesia the Dark Descent.
You're a guy named Simon going in for a brain scan at a suspiciously abandoned research facility. During this routine scan something appears to go wrong and you wake up 100 years later, inside an underwater station overrun with robots.
This really is a well crafted and believable world, it takes a lot of cues from other games like Bioshock and System Shock. Where as in Bioshock you felt like the ocean was taking the city of Rapture back, in SOMA you get this sense of machinery taking over everything, as large robotic appendages jut out of walls and block hallways and corridors.
There's about 5 different monster types in the game, all of which you simply have to avoid. We've seen this kind of thing in dozens of first person horror games lately, the enemy patrols around an enclosed area and you have to collect something in that area or just get through it unseen.
At it's core, SOMA is a casual horror game for people who can't handle inventory and resource management and who find the idea of a health bar off putting. People looking for a hardcore horror game set underwater, avoiding murderous robots and scraping by for resources might want to look elsewhere.

This game is great, in my opinion. There are pros and cons to it though, so I will list them below.
THE PROS:
A. NOT pay to win
B. Each in-game race (Orcs, Humans, or Elves,) offers a different playstyle
C. The Developers of the game seem to have put a decent amount of effort into this game, even though it is free to play
D. IT IS FREE! seriously, this is important - even really poorly done games (This one isn't poorly done though) are nice if they are free - all you need is hard drive space to play - Why not at least try it if it is free?
E. It offers many hours of play time.
F. Updates to the game are released periodically, and they are also completely free.
G. Doesn't require a super powerful PC to play
OK, there are cons too though
THE CONS
A. Not enough people play this game - I have only ever seen 200 people online at one time - not exactly MMORTS (Massive, Massive Online Real Time Strategy) more like just ORTS
B. It has some bugs - they aren't game-breaking, but they are there.
C. It is very difficult to actually gather enough army strength to sucessfully lay siege to an AI town - you need expensive and exotic units like dragons, Minotaurs, etc,  to do it reliably.
D. Most of the playerbase seems to be either Old, experienced veteran players, who have all of the best units, all the upgrades, and essentially unlimited resources. They are all but unbeatable unless they fight themselves. Most of the rest of the players are new to the game, and don't know the most basic things about playing yet. In essence, there are very few players who fall in between these two extremes.
E. If you choose to play elves, it is more difficult than Orcs and Humans to gather resources.
All in all, though, this is a great game, even more so because of the fact that is it free. I would recommend it to anyone that likes Real Time Strategy games.

This game is based on the 1998 Polish movie "Fire and Sword".  It provides a historical backdrop for 1650's warfare in central Europe, including Cossack, Tatar, Muscovite, Polish and Swedish units and cities.  Some mods extend the map and available units too.
Game is ungoddly awesome.  Something about riding a horse while shooting - it's a similar feeling to flying.  You can command units with great precision and it takes a while to master.  But what a rush to play - even though I completely suck at fighting, buidling up an army and working out the tactics is great.  The AI is is pretty good too (I'm guessing completely based on Behavior Trees).  Sometimes I play the sniper while the rest of the army is skirmishing - really hard to get in a good shot - and very satisfying when it connects.  These are ancient guns and not rifled, so they aren't very accurate from long-range.
Also playing solo (no army yet) and taking out the horse of some jerk who's tearing me up - it's a big rush of adrenhaline!
Economy is quite clever, where you can drive down market prices and then send caravans at a discount.  Can also take out loans in a pinch.
If you quit the tutorial immediately, then it's a little more challenging to start with no money, no gun and no horse - I think this is the best way to play it.

Forever is a long time. That's what it felt like with Duke Nukem Forever even though it was closer to fifteen years in reality.
This game has a distinct trait that only two other games I played share with it. Those two games are Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas. What do I mean by this? These three games are the only games that stick out in my mind as games I got about two hours into, forgot for a few years, and then completed. The thing is after completing Duke Nukem Forever I felt like it was more an obligation than entertainment.
So aliens break a treaty with Earth and capture all the women and this makes Duke go on a quest to get them back and kick alien butt. All the while you can do little things like play pool, lift weights, and admire yourself in the mirror to boost your ego so you can take more damage before your health gets affected. But don't be fooled; even on lower difficulties you still lose your Ego rather fast but it can be easily replenished by either melee killing a downed enemy or just waiting behind cover like most modern shooters which would be forgivable if this game didn't try to lampshade how "Power armor is for (synonym for cats)" obviously nodding to another FPS franchise that has the same health mechanics. You might have heard of it, it's a franchise that was about giant nuclear metal onion rings in space designed to kill absolutely everything in the universe which will probably never see any more releases on PC because a certain company has to try and justify supporting a certain console.
Driving and puzzles are to be found to try and break up the monotony of shooting things in the face because why play Mario Kart or Portal when you can play DNF? The PC version allows you to turn an option on to carry a whole FOUR weapons! You can even drink beer and take steroids to give yourself buffs if you really feel like it but such actions don't feel essential. Shooting at the pig cops until they die is a valid enough strategy.
Speaking of what you can do, let's talk about the fluff. The intro level to the game allows you to draw on a whiteboard while a soldier speaks the same two lines of dialogue! And your drawing is inconsequential! So is the autograph you sign for a young fan! Do you like to throw human waste for no reason? What about killing yourself by sticking your finger in an electrical socket?
FIFTEEN YEARS!
(I think it speaks volumes when one of the most engaging activities I had was spending almost an hour on the pinball table.)
Multiplayer itself was a fun waste of an evening or two. The most absurd sight I saw playing online was a few guys who obviously spent too much time on the game telling everyone in the match to buy the DLC during the Summer Sale. Maybe if I was even worse with my money than I actually am right now I would have, but it was a novelty and scratched that shooter itch I keep having to deal with.
I think game historians will look back on a game like Duke Nukem Forever and examine it critically, and then look at a game like the newest Doom and wonder how one company could have messed up so bad at trying to modernize an iconic franchise. When I see Duke Nukem as a whole, I can see some potential. Duke is rusty, a reflection of old 80's and 90's macho man types who fought the bad guys and always got the girl. I feel this game had to be released so he coul stretch his legs. The prospect of a new Duke Nukem game fills me with such glee in the amount of outrage he could cause in today's society.
Good luck getting that out of Gearbox though.

This is a promising unique type of Real-Time Strategy (RTS) game.  Even on its normal speed, that you could adjust even in multiplayer, things are fast paced enough to finish a match in 30mins but plenty of time to think about your actions.
You begin by scanning the map for a good starting location.  Each player does the same, but here's the catch, if you are one of the last to found you get bonus tiles (called claims) to build buildings on because you are pretty much forced away from the prime locations that the first founders took, unless your lucky and they didnt spot something.
After you found, this is the fastest part of the game, because you want to claim certain tiles first.  Now each game is going to have a different strategy.  Perhaps you want to claim that lone carbon resource so no one else can get it and force them to buy off the market.  Maybe you think that the other players are going to sell water down so the price to purchase it would be $1, so forgo water and go for more prime minerals or power sources.
As the game progresses, you can buy items off the black market or on auctions.  Some help yourself but most of the time you are buying them to stop production of your enemies or to steal one of their resources for a short time.  Each time a player buys, say a dynamite stick, the price goes up for all players the next time you want one.  There is a lot of choices in a fast matched game to choose.
End game is always the same, trying to constantly protect your Offworld Markets with shields (Goon Squads), trying your best to disrupt the enemies Offworld Markets.  It usually ends with the first one to amass a huge amount of cash to buyout the remaining shares of your competitor.  It really is no different than a military RTS how to end a game, always ends the same way with hordes of marines going time and time again.  However looking at stock prices for the end game and scanning over to your enemy base to disrupt stuff is about all there is in the end game, nothing fancy like seeing buildings get destroyed by your units.
All and all, it is a great game to try out.  They havn't really stated what will be coming in the future except for leagues and ladders like any good RTS game would do.  If they do that, they need to limit the observer mode to a delay or something, and I can see free for all getting out of whack with teams trying to join in and gang up on a player.

I've played some games in my time. And this one is remarkable. I wish we had more games like it. It's what I wish the newest Sim City had aspired to.
Offworld Trading Company is pure genius.
If you're into economy games, you'll love it.
The goal is to buyout your opponents by amassing resources as one of several differnet types of colonies. Each has there strong and weak points. This premise alone seems pretty minimal, right?
Wrong.
You're gathering your metals, making steel, etc. You start gathering water, or food. You feel safe. You're doing alright, and your money is going up.
Suddenly one of your opponents EMPs your grouping of three water generating facilities.
Now you're going into debt.
Water is $212 a unit. And you need three units a tick. That's $636 you're going into debt, each tick.
Your debt risses, you have no spare cash. The "duration" of the EMP is another THIRTY seconds.
You sell your stockpile of resources to lower your debt. It seems to be working.
But then, a competitor starts buying stock in your company. He already owned 50% and now he's at 80%
$22,000 is what it will cost for you to lose the game. Does your competitor have that much?
You're still hemoraging money from buying water, like a total noob.
The EMP wears off. You pay off your debt. You're back in the black.
You buy the last 20% of your own company with all your cash.
Then he throws pirates at you, crippling both your food and water shipments.
Your water was already low, and you start losing money.
But you have food! You'll be fine!
And then the last 20% of your stock is bought for the X2 price of $44,000 and your competitor owns you.
10/10 Would get bought out again.

Offworld Trading Company, possibly the most curious of creatures. A game that dares to break the rules, it's not quite a 4x and it's not quite an RTS, and yet it's got elements of both, as well as a very brutal and brilliant introduction into capitalism in it's most true sense.
The creator of this was the lead designer of Civ IV, still widely regarded as the pinnacle of the series and still very much fondly remembered by many to this day (and often still played by many, it's got a dedicated following, mods and glorious goodies, it's still fantastic, if you don't have Civ IV, please get it). He's brought a very unique approach to this game and has effectively talen the spirit of M.U.L.E. and brought it back, shaken it up and presented us with a entirely new set of concepts to learn and re-learn.
The game plays out over a martian map, randomly generated from various landscapes made up of craters, dried riverbeds and valleys that do a fairly solid impression of conveying the martian scene, as well as various terrain that can be covered in ice, certain areas will be marked with resource node icons indicating they are of potential exploitative value for various minerals.  Arranged on a hex grid, you'll immediately be put in mind of old strategy games, but the comparison ends there. There are no units to control, at all. You only build things.
Yes. I'll repeat that. You only build things. In this game, your structures are your units in effect. Your mines, your colony buildings, and your economy represents your "arsenal" and "weaponry". This makes for a frenetic early game as everyone jumps into the map blind, all arriving at the starport with nary but a blank map and the ability to scan in a limited range and for a limited number of times (these recharge over time, but you're effectively capped to a number of 'hops'), you'll see tantalising highlights on the horizon suggesting possible mineral nodes, but you won't KNOW what they are unless you scan right over them.
This presents the first risk/reward mechanic, because the very early stages are a gold rush, do you take your time and map out the area, performing a thorough survey and pick the best spot (and risk losing it by accident to a lucky colonist) or do you jump at the first spot that "looks good" and risk sacrificing a better opportunity later on?
During the early game, you'll be moving fairly quickly to make the optimal use of your initial claims, working out the best places to put down mines, whether you're best off setting up colony infrastructure or buying in the resources you need whilst you export minerals, again, these are all choices you have to balance, and the economics are very fluid. The game operates an exceptionally liquid supply and demand based market that fluctuates very quickly based on what is sold and what is required by the people off planet, so taking advantage of peaks in the market, and stocking up when there's a glut can make for excellent trading strategies on top of the usual manufacturing gigs.
As the game progresses you'll be offered auctions on patents, black market goods, pirates will offer their services, and the game settles into a reasonable pace, it's not too brisk that you'll be panicking over keypresses, and you'll usually have more than enough time to plan your moves, but it's juuuust fast enough that you'll not start feeling bored or that there's a lull in the action. The pace even now feels just right, and the game even at this Early Access stage feels amazingly well refined. The AI is also brutal, which makes for some excellent and tense singleplayer matches (and if you're not careful, amazingly short ones, the AI knows when to strike and buy you out, with scary precision).
The economy has a solid enough set of gears that you can work through as you expand, moving up through basic goods at first, and then you can decide to diversify, thus preventing your company from becoming exposed to the fluctuations or even possible manipulations of the market, or you can specialise in luxury goods, with the aim of striking it rich when demand is at it's highest. If, and it's a big if, you do this well, the rewards are huge, and in an RTS, would be the equivalent of nuking the base, here you win with money. Earn more than your opponent, buy them out and crush them.
This is where the true nature of the game comes to the fore, as a lesson in future capitalism, it's bold, and even at times cruel, but perhaps a very good mirror to hold up and show what can happen if the only guiding force is the market, as a game, this makes it a brilliant and unique concept, and as an Early Access product, well, it's far from "Early" in my eyes. This game feels very much close to completion, they're more talking about fleshing out the multiplayer, getting the pacing and balancing just right and layering on the polish (this game needs polish?!?! WHERE?). Truth be told, it feels very polished as it is, there's a few graphical glitches but these are -minor-.
Yes, the cost of entry is high, but for once, this is a game that actually justifies the entry fee.
This is a rare case where Early Access actually is a literal application of the term, you're paying to get Early Access to the almost complete product, and to provide feedback that helps shape it before it goes to the final version. Balancing, tweaking, and providing strategic insight to the developers, who have been listening and responding, and watching in kind.
It's a very good example of how Early Access in a "shortform" approach should work (there's plenty of longer form SEA games that have done well such as Prison Architect, but that's a seperate discussion). As a result I really have little hesitation putting the paws up for this one, it's a genuinely brilliant game and it brings something different to the table, which it should be commended for.

Early Access Review (2/12/15)
BLUF: #1 - I feel that RTS is a poor term to describe this game and #2 - from the Devs “Feedback! We want to know how players are going to break the game, suss out any degenerate strategies, and make sure we polish every rough edge off of the gameplay. Offworld Trading Company is fully funded; we are not relying on Early Access sales to finish the game.” This statement is key.
***
For those of you who have been burned by early access games before please take the note from the Devs seriously. This is a very playable and stable game right now and they already have the resources to put the finishing touches on it. So you are not really paying to make the game, you are getting an early shot at the game and a chance to drive further balance into the system. The final quality of this game will depend heavily on balancing the PVP aspects of the game so the more feedback they have now the better.
As far as this being a RTS; while it might be the closest term we have to define it, that will give many people the wrong idea. There are no units to move, no combat, and no chokepoints. You establish a base and build buildings to harvest resources (much like the Warhammer:Dawn of War series) and use those resources to develope higher teir commdities to eventually sell for cash and buy out your opponents. It is fast paced and at times will feel like a RTS, but traditional RTS tactics will fail for the most part.
The key is that the prices that determine which resource is the 'win' resource will depend on the strat adapted by the players in the game and will change from game to game. There are no Ultimate Resources that win the game each time. The higher teir products will usually have a higher price, but if everyone in that game chases them then the price will plummet and the player sitting on a pile of low teir resources can dominate. Basically the L33T strat that everyone wants to use will neuter itself before it can win.
My current concerns:
The pace of the game is very aggressive for a strategy game. The pace can be adjusted and I have only played against the AI with their GHz brains, but knowing PVP types this could quickly devolve into a 'who can spam out the first 3 correct buildings' contest.
The interface needs to do a better job of letting the player know whats going on. There are some pretty nasty things lurking on the Black Market and all you get is a chat box type readout to announce them and maybe an onscreen animation if you happen to be looking at that part of the map at the time. The trick is to find the balance where we get the info we need without getting our screen spammed out by alerts. Good luck Mohawk!

It's an okay game. Not bad, not great, but okay. It's got great artwork reminiscent of H. R. Giger, and practically every screen looks like it could be the cover of a metal album. There are a few puzzles here and there, but they're pretty simple unless you're just really bad at puzzles.
However, the things that really make this game fall flat are that it's far too short (easily beatable in under an hour), it's too linear (in that there is a set path, and there are a few puzzles that you can do in any order you choose, but you'll always wind up going to the same limited places within the game, not to mention there's no actual risk of failure), and that any choices you make are kind of pointless.
Despite having multiple choices to make throughout the game, there are only two possible endings, and if you make even one bad choice, it doesn't matter how many good choices you make, you're automatically locked into the bad ending. Based on the endings, this tells me the writer intended for the game to have a very black and white view of morality, no gray area whatsoever, no justification for why you did an action that you did, just "if you did even one bad thing, that makes you a horrible person who doesn't deserve a good ending". I believe an easy way to sum up the problem with this so-called "morality" system is to say that it's a talented art students attempt at writing a story that deals with what should be a complex and possibly complicated topic.
Overall, it has the potential to be really great, but the linearity and illusion of choice that results in one of two lackluster endings rather than having various possibilities, in addition to the incredibly short playtime and basic puzzles results in an experience that's cool at first glance, but kind of disappointing when you actually go through with it.

Tormentum: Dark Sorrow is an interactive collection of Heavy Metal magazine covers. Harkening back to the glory days of Frank Frazetta and badass Iron Maiden album covers, your main driving force for progression is to advance to the next scene and see what madness the artists have pulled from the twisted depths of their minds. There are some real simple “find the object” and logic puzzles blocking your path as well as a Lovecraftian narrative with branching paths, but the game's main draw is viewing the beautifully grotesque and unsettling.
You navigate the world of Tormentum as a cloaked, hooded figure who is taken to a castle against his will and locked in a cage. You have a dirty ratman cellmate nearby, and a knight in spiky, black armor is really keen on torturing you and the other prisoners. You make an escape by clicking around the environment until you uncover a random assortment of adventure game puzzle pieces and match Key Object A with Lock Object A. Throughout the game you'll also be presented with fairly standard puzzles to solve: slide the squares to make a picture, find the paper to decipher the symbols, memory match card games, Guess Who, etc. None of the riddles are notably difficult or obscure, but that's to the game's benefit. They feel more like brain exercises than anything. You'll get a small serotonin rush for solving them, but they're not brain twisters that will have you beating your head against a wall or rushing for a walkthrough. This keeps the momentum going and the scenery changing, which again is why you should be playing the game.
As you journey through the game's hellscape, you're presented with some binary choices that will affect your ending. Do you help a mad jester murder a caged woman in exchange for a needed key? You could enact some sweet revenge on your jailer by impaling him, but is that “right”? The best one involves busywork dusting off a blind man's paintings, which can be bypassed by siding with his cat-monster pet/thing and slashing his life's work out of their frames to get the blueprints you need. I dusted the paintings, because again the game is all about the art. On the whole the story, taken as a standard piece of fiction, is rather inconsequential and a bit nonsensical, though that's not entirely a negative as it adds to the nightmare quality of the game. Shocker: it would be right at home as a comic inside of a Heavy Metal magazine...
Viewing Tormentum as an art book with light adventure game elements, there's only a few sore points of which to be critical. Most jarring is when the art isn't good; scattered amidst the frame-worthy set pieces are mundane, functional insert shots like when you have to pick up a key or a note. These just stick out as amateurish brush strokes in comparison to the rest of the game. The pacing is off; the first area is a nice tutorial, teaching you the basics of inventory management and puzzle solving. The game then ramps up in complexity, asking you to solve puzzles that affect objects several screens away and navigating some tricky, missable areas. Then the final third basically boils down to a few simple screens and obvious objects to find and use. The game isn't about “challenge”, but the last areas feel unfinished/rushed. Finally, there's a puzzle toward the end of the game that involves reading a music sheet and playing notes on a piano. I won't spoil the puzzle or solution outright, but it makes zero logical sense when you figure it out.
I'm not a huge fan of adventure games, but I really enjoyed playing through Tormentum: Dark Sorrow. Every screen could be a month on a dark fantasy calendar, and exploring those paintings by clicking around isn't too bad, either. Throw in some simple but satisfying puzzles, and sure... it's a good game. It's good enough that at the end credits, while some cheesy metal music was playing, I made sure to hit “F12” on my keyboard and now I have a new badass desktop background.

Oozing with gore and morbidity, Tormentum - Dark Sorrow is an engrossing point and click adventure that you're sure to remember for years to come. The game itself is seething with hellish nightmarescapes, and venomously dripping with macabre dialogue; a far more tortured choice compared to many of the point and clicks available on the market today. Make no mistake, this title is not for those who may get depressed easily, as it deals with some heavy subject matter and it confronts those dark, ghastly thoughts that linger in the back of our minds; forcing us to think about our life choices, and what may be waiting for us in the afterlife.
Hands down, the main focus of Tormentum is its eerily captivating artwork. The artists did one hell of an amazing job merging the soft pastels and hazy dream-like features of Zdzislaw Beksinski's work with the harsh, alien architecture of H.R. Giger. If it weren't completely impossible, I'd go as far to say that both of these renowned surrealist artists collaborated and contributed the art straight to the game. The massive amounts of detail that has been put into the artwork alone more than makes Tormentum worth the full selling price, artists as talented as the ones who worked on this title deserve high recognition and I firmly believe that true art should never be undersold. The screenshots that you will see on the store page are just a faint few of the 70+ cadaverous hand-painted expanses that you will wander across, and there are numerous devils to encounter. The entire world that has been created for Tormentum feels overwhelmingly larger than you are.
Coupling the awe inspiring artwork is a dark, brooding soundtrack. I sincerely wish that it was for sale on Steam, as I would purchase it in a heartbeat. There was actually one part of the game, near this giant tower, that I enjoyed the music so much that I cranked my speakers, left my computer and proceeded to do housework while just listening to the audio. It's rare for me to enjoy a game soundtrack this deeply, but I would actually put Tormentum's score on a regular playlist; right along side some Bethlehem, Velvet Acid Christ and Burzum. The ominous, ambient hymns bring an entire new dimension to the art style that is displayed within the game, and they really suck the gamer in while refusing to let go.
So, what is this game actually about? Sadly, I can't delve far into the story without spoiling it completely; I will say that you are a man, wandering the huge realm of Tormentum in search of a way out. Along the way you must face tough choices, all of which will ultimately matter in the end. The character that you are playing has no more knowledge than you do, and vica versa; this is much akin to plots like that of Stasis and Sanitarium. You will learn more about the hellish world that you're traversing through by reading notes and speaking with the many interactive beings within the game. Many of these fiends are quite forlorn and profound with their dialogue, which is reminiscent of The Divine Comedy by Dante. As usual, it will all make the most sense once the game has reached completion.
Tormentum - Dark Sorrow is a completely stunning macabre point and click game that will appeal to a niche audience. Art enthusiasts will absolutely love this game for its stunning in-depth visuals, audiophiles will love it for the superbly creepy soundtrack, and fans of both will completely fall in morbid love. While the story isn't anything to rave about, it will strike a chord with fans of literature along the lines of The Divine Comedy (Dante's Inferno). The only real fault that I could possibly find with Tormentum is how short it is. I finished 3 full playthroughs in roughly 6 hours, with my initial run clocking in at about 3 and a half hours. That being said, I just can't gush and go on about this title enough. It's absolutely the best point and click experience I've ever had, but then again I love H.R. Giger, Zdzislaw Beksinski, Dante's Inferno and dark ambient music. If you're a fan of any of the aforementioned things, do not hesitate to throw your money down on this twisted nightmare.

Magic 2015 is good value for its base game. It is not suppose to replicate the real magic experience but a more arcade like version of MTG.
Duels of the Planeswalker, across its five iterations, has been created as a place where people who have never played Magic: The Gathering can learn its basic rules and strategies and make those mistakes without other people watching. Online modes are available, but in design wise Magic 2015 is at its core a single-player-focused experience.
Magic is a game where strategy evolves from additional choices. It's hard to argue against with people saying that you gain more advantage by paying more money. At the same time, I feel like that impact has been minimized to the point where people are having a fantastic Magic experience just spending the $10 on the core game.
Although the game has its problems, the positives definitely outweigh the negatives and future patches may add back features that players have enjoyed.
As long as you don't engage with the currently available DLCs, I think the game stands on its own.

Not the Duke Nukem game you are looking for.
Here's the formula for Duke Nukem Forever:
1. Put in a bunch of zero-@ssed internet jokes that any teenage intern could have gathered in an afternoon. The internet isn't funny. We've all seen every meme ever "created" i.e slapped together on imgflip or quickmeme in .9 seconds, at least 6,000 times. They were funny one time. One.
2. Slap in some obligatory attempts at crude humor like picking up poop, drawing a d1ck with a marker, or attempts at being "misogynistic" like having two girls blow Duke while he plays his own video game.
Even if you ignore the absolute lack of soul or personality that went into the humor itself,  Duke Nukem Forever was a boring, uncreative shootfest game whose best moment was aforementioned fellatio scene where you play an homage to the end of Duke Nukem 3D, which took place before the actual game even started. DNF was nothing but a Frankenstein's monster of mishmashed gaming concepts which had proven popular in the years and years the game spent in development limbo - in GOOD games. Like Counter-Strike, or Half-Life, or Halo. The vehicle segments were buggy and boring. The combat was braindead. The Duke quips were 14 years out of place. The levels were uninspired, as was the level progression, and the game's one true callback to the original was a juvenile level full of alien anuses that culminated in fighting a three titted alien who took zero effort whatsoever to kill. There weren't even strip clubs or nudey mags, or keys, and the captured human women were irrelevant (I'm not counting the mandatory, ridiculously bad strip club intermission level).
The fact that this game has 70% positive reviews would be amazing, if it weren't simply more proof that gamers have no taste. In fact, the score went up 3% since I originally wrote this. It has no replayability, and that's a stretch to say it even had playability the first time.

One of my favourite local co-op games, fantasic fun with a friend. With a cool grindhouse theme and cute pixel art, this game is a must for all couch co-op fans, especially when it can be found really cheap on sale. a fantastic retro sidescrolling take on the zombie shooter genre.
Pros:
+ Fantasic couch co-op.
+ Extra difficulty options. It definitely tests your survivability skills on hardest mode when you have to cross over 10 streets with only a single shop and a ton of zombies.
+ The Solution gives a new scenario and a relatively easy way of trying out all the funky weapons as you mow down thousands of zombies.
+ Procedurally generated maps for a different experience each time you play.
+ Cute pixel art, especially when the zombie's eyes go squinty when they notice you.
+ A large selection of cool weapons and upgrades.

+ Steam Achievements.
Cons:
- Partial controller supported only; have to use a mouse to start up the game initially.
- The Solution game mode is fairly easy, and doesn't change when difficulty increases, only more zombies to kill, which means more money to spend on a supply of infinite ammo, grenades and guns.

- May be waiting around a while if you poke a zombie off the bottom of the screen for him to come back on. Only problematic on Survival and Time Attack modes and when fighting bosses on the Original game mode. May last forever if they are also frozen. Can be easily avoided though.
My Score: 9/10

((Non-Spoiler Review))
I will rate the three primary qualities of the game (Story, Sound, and Gameplay) and include a final score below.
__________________________________________
-Story 9/10 (Great)
The player wakes from a nightmare. From that point forward, you learn of an accident prior to the game's start which resulted in the player character (Simon Jarrett) receiving a terminal brain injury. His only hope is to pursue a medical practice that is still in the early testing phases (so early that he is the first one to participate.) Upon arrive, he is asked to sit down and attach a helmet to his head. That helmet will then scan his brain. However, upon taking it off, he wakes in a retro sci-fi atmospheric room. From that point forward, the player is sent to traverse a world filled with transhumanistic ideologies paired with moral conflicts of interest.
Midway through, you find a survey which relates to your main objective. That survey seems like nothing more than world building upon first arriving to it, but at the end of the game, you realize the weight that survey held when pushing for its ultimate message. The entire game is wrapped around those questions and then finally concludes with your answers.
-Sound 10/10 (Fantastic)
Rarely will you find a game with such fantastic sound quality. Right off the bat, you're hit with the excellent effects as you fasten the helmet to your head before being scanned. If you're wearing headphones, you'd almost think you lowered a helmet on yourself as you watch the screen and listen as the sounds get caught within the closed space.
Not only that, re-occuring sounds such as foot steps, enemy encounters, machines, and underwater sequences all feel fresh and seldom will you hear a sound repeat, if ever. In fact, the only time I remember hearing the same sound more than once which effected my immersion was when I talked to a robot and it responded with the same voice line (only after engaging in conversation for a long time.)
VA work is superb. It feels oddly casual and out of place at first, but as the story progresses you understand that that's their character. There isn't any over acting, just reacting. It's all very much in character.
-Gameplay 7/10 (Good)
The multitude of Enemies within SOMA make for a new experience each location you explore. While a few will be easily manipulated by tossing an object in one direction so you can go another, some enemies react differently to hearing you, seeing you, and even where you're standing. This makes for unpredictable encounters and an incredibly memorable experience.
Some would consider this a walking simulator. While I don't disagree with that defining tag, I would like to add that each location in the game is a enjoyable and fun to explore. A lot of love was put into the level design and you can tell with each step that there's going to be something new and worthwhile to explore.
What restricts this rating to a 7 is the lack of direction. 3 times I encountered points where it felt as if I hadn't recieved enough audible or visual hints as to where to progress. I resorted to, "Okay let's check that room again and see if I can interact with anything new." If it had happened once, I would reserve it to me being clueless, but as it happened in about 3 locations, I felt that this was a detrimental aspect to a game whose majority of the gameplay is exploration and task completion.
FINAL SCORE........... 9/10 (Great)

Dead Pixels is a side-scrolling survival/shooter with some lite-RPG elements set in a zombie apocalypse.  You take control of a human survivor making their way to safety through undead filled streets of a city.  The basic aim of the game depends on the game mode.
There are three game modes; The main mode is your standard Escape the hordes.  Survival is an arena mode where by you have to survive countless waves of hordes. Timed attack is a variant of Survival where by you must last as long as you can. You need to either; get from one side of the street to the other until you reach the end or kill as many zombies as you can.  The number of streets to traverse depends on the difficulty setting.
Gameplay is representative of the standard zombie survival genre.  Find guns.  Acquire ammo.  Destroy zombies.  Dont get killed.  In addition you can loot some deserted buildings grabbing medical supplies, explosives and other useful items.  Periodically shops appear where you can sell items that are not needed or cant be used.  Shops allow you to upgrade character stats such as: Running, Weaponskill, Bargaining and Melee which to help you get past the next few stages of the game. Game progress can also be saved while inside these locations.
Gameplay consists of manoeuvring your character across streets full of zombies avoiding making contact with them or the vile bile they fling at you.  You can shoot, bash or throw explosives to destroy your opponents.   If you are low on ammo you can dodge and flee the nasty hordes, skills that become invaluable the further you progress.  There are number zombie types from slow moving zombies, to faster ones, soldier types, zombies that can attack at range by firing bile at you, and the uber-strong mutated  zombies which are hard to kill.  In addition every so often you must defeat a boss enemy with its special powers, in order to progress.
There are many weapons to choose from, the most common being shotguns, rifles and handguns. There are also a good number of equipment items to use along your adventure such as medkits, grenades (explosive, incendiary, freeze, shock) fireworks to distract, adrenaline boosters to speed your movement and though the listings are in text form it can be  particularly satisfying when you pick-up and use a chainsaw, flamethrower or minigun.
Graphics are in 2D and are basic if functional.  While the soundtrack and audio effects add to that overall retro feel.  Together they generate a wonderful ambience and give you an old skool feel providing some nice nostalgic overtones, if you played games in the eighties.
Though gameplay is repetitive in nature I found the experience to be as enjoyable as playing other zombie survival games such as State of Decay.  Real fun though be warned you need fast reflexes and nimble fingers (and luck) to complete the game on the Hardest difficulty setting.  Controls are really well coded and easy to use.
Just note that only local coop is available unfortunately.  If anything bad can be said about the game its that the inventory is text based, the graphics arent for everyone and the game can run a little too fast in some places when you could really do with slowing down the action to think your next move through.
Dead Pixels has to be one of the best made indie games Ive been fortunate to find.  Infact it could well be "the game" I would make if I could code.  I suggest you pick this one up now in the sale but if you miss it then its well worth the full price.  Note also that a sequel has already been announced for next year.

Upon loading up the game I was surprised to find that despite the early access tag, it's actually a full game with polish.
The game is sort of similar to Civ in that it is a 4x, but that's where the comparisons will end. It's closer to an economic simulator. You build infrastructure that produces resources. Resources can be used to produce new infrastructure. Infrastructure can take resources and created finished products out of them. And with all that you can sell them out to a dynamic market in which the price will fluxuate based on how much each player is selling of that commodity.
The main part of the game is surviving as a company and buying out other ones. If your company value falls low you become vulnerable to losing shares of your company to competitors. Your company value is your debt and your infrastructure value combined. So paying off debt will make it harder for people to buying you, while having a large sum will allow you to buy an opponent.
Once you have bought an opponent you gain their stuff in full and gain a significant advantage.
The game comes with a tutorial for playing the game and playing each of the four factions. Each faction comes with its own unique set of opening boosts and needs. With a few dozen maps to choose from there is tonnes of gameplay value for your dollar.
Fans of games like Port Royale, Rise of Venice, Anno 2070, and C.E.O. should definitely give this game a try. For people who are newer to economic simulators and want to give it a try, this might be the game for you.

I was excited to get this game - Civ4 was my favorite civ and so I expected a lot from Soren Johnson.
This is a much more accessible game than Civ. The complete lack of a combat system revolutionizes the RTS genre and feels alien, yet the core mechanics can be understood within 30-45 minutes of play. The interaction of the game sytems is complex, and mastery and strategy will take a lot of time to develop.
You play one of four factions, each with different bonuses and penalties. It is vital to play to your factions strengths, because you are severely resource constrained and must make difficult decisions about how to expand.
You interact with other factions in five ways: the map, auctions, the stock market, the black market, and the market.
On the map, you compete for resources and tile placement. Taking a key tile from another player can be enormously damaging by preventing adjacency bonuses.
In auctions, you bid against other players for a special bonus. This is the most "head-to-head" aspect of the game. Depending on game options, you are not constrained to bidding with cash on hand. Instead, you can go into debt to purchase the item. If you arent careful, you might win an auction to your overal detriment.
On the black market, you purchase attack powers. These seem to suck, though perhaps I just don't understand how to use them effectively yet. You are very rate limited in how quickly you can purchase these powers, they go up in price quickly, and they are usually very weak. Disabling a tile for 60 seconds is painful, but doesnt seem to be enough to cause any long term damage.
On the stock market, you buy and sell ownership stakes in each player's faction. You win by forcibly buying out the other players.
And finally the market. You buy and sell resources, and your actions affect the price of the resource. In my view, a critical weakness of the game is that the market supplies unlimited resources. Resources are not supplied by other players; instead, the market steadily raises prices. One consequence of this is that there is no resource tech race - you can buy any resources at the start of the game, which really break the idea that you are a startup colony on mars. You also get no real benefit from being the first to supply another resource.
The game also gives you very limited insight into the price elasticity of demand - how much price will change in response to a purchase or sale. This is probably because there isn't a "real" market system. In order to allow you to buy an unlimited amount of resources on the market, the game must model its own price elasticity of demand curve. This is contrived and can fall out of sync with the specifics of each game. You also have no insight into the global supply of a given resource - there is no way to answer the question "Is this resource cheap because no one needs it or because everyone is producing a surplus?" Perhaps if you had some way to view the global aggregate stockpile of each resource, this could be improved.
Because of the way the market functions and the lack of insight into its details, it doesn't quite feel like you are playing with other players. Again, maybe this is just due to my inexperience.
There are a couple UI issues:
* An easy way to see the space market price for goods.
* An easy way to find your buildings/tiles on the map.
* Graphics performance is ok, but not good.
Overall, I'm still pretty excited about this game. Its a new idea in RTS. It greatly reduces micromanagement compared to other RTS. It needs polish, but I think its going to make for some amazing multiplayer matches.

After attempting to give this game a fair try on numerous occasions there is no way I can recommend it.
Rather than list the flaws individually (which other negative reviewers have done well and quite thoroughly) I will instead share my latest gaming experience:
I’m scavenging for about 30 minutes and have yet to find a single item – no weapons, no food or drink, not even any gum – but the atmosphere of this game is great (one of its only strong suites) so I keep at it, all the while slowly starving to death.  I have to this point (luckily) not ran into any Nether since I'm only equipped with a kitchen knife. After some time of no luck on the surface I decide to head underground because there seems to always be some good loot somewhere in the subway system.
As soon as I enter – to my delight – I see an uzi sitting in an abandoned camp site. I walk up to it and I press/hold E to loot….nothing…..readjust and try again….nothing…..walk away and then come back…..nothing……try every single possible angle/direction…..nothing. So I give up and walk further down the subway tunnel, still only toting a knife with which to defend myself with. Maybe another 10 minutes go buy and I come across a room that has both a sword and a GRIMM Reaper! They’re no guns, but they’re much more effective than the knife I currently hold and at this point I am just happy to see ANYTHING.  I walk up to the Reaper and cannot pick it up….walk over to the sword and it’s the same story so that is now 3 weapons I cannot pick up.
Finally, after nearly an hour of fruitless searching, I come across another GRIMM Reaper that I am – by some miracle – able to pick up. So now I am armed at last but remember, I haven’t seen a single Nether in nearly an hour so that means I cannot level up…. I haven’t seen any other players either but I consider this a good thing because most survivors I have run into have powerful weapons and can kill you effortlessly (and usually without being seen). I’ve now been playing for an hour and am begging to run into anything I can kill….I have yet to level up at all and the atmosphere has gone from lonesome and foreboding to just plain boring.
I decide to go back above surface to keep looking for enemies to kill. As I’m running down the tunnel I hear the telltale warping of a Nether! I turn around to see what I have encountered….and it’s a Golem. I know I am outmatched so I try desperately to run away, though my efforts are useless because I continue to hear the teleporting sound and keep getting hit in the♥♥♥♥♥ It’s clear I have to stand my ground and fight this thing. I hit him a couple of times with my reaper but to no avail as he easily beats me into a pulp. That’s it - an hour of play and I end exactly where I started.
Yes, this is a beta game (though it is still functioning MUCH more like an alpha as of 1/4/2014). Yes, it was my choice to pay the ridiculous price of $30 (however to that point I will say I that I was duped by the developer pumping it up to sound like a more complete game than it is even now….the last time I checked the price had dropped to $20…still too much….).  All I am saying is that the above playthrough is a typical experience for me and others. You WANT to want to play the game, but there are just so many flaws and quirks that it just feels broken. If there ever is a final production version, I could see it being a very good game but as for now I have to strongly suggest that you avoid this title…

Offworld Trading Company is a new type of real-time strategy game, it's not a combat-war type RTS, it's a numbers-war type game, it's a player-driven, market-driven game, where money and resources is power, and power is law.
From when it was announced, I loved the simple graphics, and playing it now I'm loving how it looks, the simplicity in the design, the deep colors, the nice eye candy effects, and the quick but charming animations, all of which are splendidly made.
There isn't a story of the sense that there's a campaign with that's lengthy with a big story to tell and characters to meet, it's only where you have to be the best of the best company that should represent what the future life of the human race, in terms of the market life. But in the campaign itself, you start off with limited equipment, and as you progress through it you will start to unlock what's been locked by purchasing them, until you got everything and finish the the campaign. I haven't finished it yet, but I'm working there.
Notice: This game does not have an offline mode yet.
The gameplay itself is the same as an RTS Command & Conquer, but with a mix of a hex-based movement / placement like a Civilization game, and sort of a mix of an Anno game with how building and trading is. Combined with the new idea, one that at least I haven't seen, of power management in the market area by gathering resources, buying and sell them, advancing your buildings to produce more materials, try do some shady tactics to over power your competitors. It's new and fun, and what I like about it is that it's simple yet complicated in a way, simple enough for most to learn.
At first I was skeptical with what the game is facing the price that it has, but after playing the first 3 tutorial levels, I fell in love with it, so my skepticism went away and I was happy with the game and the price, obviously followed with playing outside of the tutorial of course, playing the single player content and multiplayer. I see my self playing this for a while, and I was kind of hungry for this type of game, so win win. Also, while the game is sufficient enough to keep it self going for some time, I wouldn't mind seeing more buildings and units to play around with, just more content.

First Impressions:
I was super-excited when I first learned about this title, as there aren't many economic RTS's out on the market right now (if any).  I finally don't have to worry about memorizing hot-keys to queue up marines or peons or whatever else I may need to reach my keystroke per second quota.  Instead, players will each get a HQ, choose a business model, and attempt to buy out their competition by buying low and selling high.  This game features both raw materials and finished goods, with the price of each being affected by supply and demand.  It reminds me of "Sid Meier's Railroads" a bit, though you are limited in your building placement by "claims"...that is, a resource that allows you to unlock one hex on the map for your personal use.  There's a bit of a learning curve and the AI can be somewhat difficult, but I found myself wanting more with each gameplay session.  The $40 price is a concern for those on a tight budget, but for those who can afford it (and love the idea of an economic RTS) should pick it up.

Its a 50/50 on like and dislike with this game. As with most Beta's it is unoptimized and graphically mediocre but it generally runs smoothly outside of the occasional freezing or frame drops. Gameplay wise, Each life is new and you do not keep levels, items(that are not stored in the Global Inventory), or anything else once you die. You have creatures which appear randomly across the map which sometimes are just absolute overkill in how they are placed(5x golems chasing you followed by 5 smaller creatures chasing you) but when in small groups are easily taking down. Money, food, ammo, and health packs are scarce and you rely on courier package runs in order to gain more but often you won't succeed in these due to either being overrun by nether or killed along the way by players just looking for easy targets. The game lacks heavy in things to do and thus the community has become reliant on camping safe zones for fun and literally spending hours sitting in safe zones waiting for people to be outside of the safe zone. In a sense, the community has turned it into Call of Duty with WoW's sit in a single spot all day style of playing which truely ruins any chance of making the game worth wild(we need limits on safe zones, as well as anti-bandit mechanics to end this type of behavior and force people to spread out in the map). Due to size of the map as well as the lack of PVE events or situations that can force groups to form, the game isn't worth playing as it stands unless you like standing in one spot camping random players all day. The game in its current state is not worth buying and you should wait and see how it turns out after it gets its final release.

I want to start by saying that I never took part in the open beta. I saw a few youtube videos, and I was interested from that point. I preordered it about two days before it released, and I am happy with my purchase...for the most part. The server glitches, even five hours into my play time at this point, are too much. Way too much. When a game mode is listed as highly populated on the third day of release, a noob player should be able to pair off with other noob players, yet it would take five minutes of slowly broadening a search to encompass all regions and all skill rankings before I could get into a match. Another time, I entered a pvp match and suddenly became the only player in a room of bots before other players trickled in and filled the spots later in the match. That being said, almost all multiplayer launches tend to hit this at some point. They still have to work out the kinks, and I am sure they will do so soon. This is fixable.
As for the gameplay, it's kind of a mixed bag. I would compare it to Dark Souls in many respects. The control scheme is also very similar on a controller, so I was able to recycle that muscle memory and feel almost at home. The only major difference is the ability to change the direction of your attack. It allows for strikes on either side and the top, which can be blocked by similar means. You can also cancel your heavy attacks if you time it right in order to mess with your opponent. That's a plus in my book. Mind games play a big part in battle, and For Honor captures that quite well. Each character has a fighting moveset similar to a more traditional fighter, and the roster is diverse enough to enhance the replayability. I'm having a lot of fun with the Warden and Orochi classes, but I'm looking forward to branching out at some point. There is a revenge mechanic that seems a little cheap on the surface, but I honestly see it as a reward for playing smart. If you defend against the enemy long enough without dying, you can gain a large boost to help level the playing field. Thus, it falls on the opposing players to play smarter and land hits around your dodging. There are guard breaks, grabs, heavy and light attacks, parries, etc. so there is enough to work with to outplay even a veteran if you take your time and think it through.
That is, unless you're in a 2v1 or even a 3 or 4 player ambush. Playing together is important, and from what I've experienced it is really hard to coordinate attacks with strangers. The fighting system works well with one on one fights, but any more than that and things get a difficult. Again, back to the dark souls example, you need to pick off enemies in the most efficient manner. The most effecient manner may not be the most honorable manner, and you may find yourself joining the winning side of a 3v1 fight just to make sure the guy stays down.
We may be fighting for honor, but we don't need to fight with honor. Victors write the history books anyway. We'll edit out the part where we unceremoniously slaughtered a lone enemy soldier who was actively running away from us.
It's not that different from real life, really. We have this grand idea of medieval combat, but a lot of times it was just an all-out brawl that favored numbers or ingenious strategies. Like knocking people off of bridges. Still, it doesn't end up feeling all that great at the end of the day. Maybe going for realism in this instance wasn't the best approach for fun.
The 4v4 modes all kind of devolve into one big mess, but there's a lot of fun to be had in the duel mode. This is what I feel like the game was meant to be. 1v1, best of five, no outside forces to destract or disrupt. It honestly reminded me of, well, a Dark Souls fight. Some are fast paced, while others are long and drawn out, and the tide can change instantly if one person makes a mistake. I was very impressed by the atmosphere, and the character differences really shine in this mode where they almost blend together in the 4v4 modes mentioned above.
It all depends on your tastes. If you like medieval warfare and are getting a little tired of the Call of Duty shooters out there, this could be a game for you to try out. Definitely check it out through other means first, because if you don't care for the combat system this game will have little to keep you occupied. You will either love it or hate it, and I found myself in the former category. If you can look beyond the flaws, there is a lot of potential in this game, and I can't wait to see where they take it from here.
I don't think I'm qualified to use numbers in my reviews, but I would give this a 7 or 8 out of ten. It's not perfect, but it's a hell of a lot of fun. ^_^

For Honor is a medieval combat game where you play as Knights, Vikings & Samurai in battles to the death.  It's also one of the most terrible uses of Microtransactions I've ever seen in a $60 game.
-Fun yet Challenging Combat System
-Single Player Campaign
-Online Multiplayer
-Currently 12 Playable Classes
-E-Sports Potential
-Tons of Microtransactions
-Single Player Campaign is lacking & fairly generic
-Connection issues
-Some people may find combat difficult
-Class Balance Issues
-P2P Connections
-Game is Glitchy
-Always Online DRM
-Denuvo DRM on Top of DRM
-Enduces Rage
-Community is Toxic
-Pay To Win/Progress Elements
-Sometimes your inputs just do not work (e.g. can't block attacks)
The game starts you off in a tutorial before you can do anything else.  Then you can choose between the Story Campaign or Multiplayer from the get go, which then also send you into more tutorials.  The Single Player is basically one giant tutorial game for some of the playable classes, but it's also a pretty decent adventure but it's fairly generic in overall quality.  There are 3 different chapters which allow you to play as Knights, Vikings & Samurai but they're all fairly similar  to eachother. You go around killing guys, dueling them, then killing some more guys, and hitting B every now and then for cutscenes.  You can hunt for "Breakables" which give a bonus to steel earned & lore objects that give a bit of story but that's about all there is to it.  Overall, the story campaign isn't too bad but not too good either.  It reminds me of Ryse a bit in level design, because it's fairly linear & basic. The single player then has AI that cheats & antisipates your every move usually forcing you to cheese your way through the game with abilities & environmental kills.
The multiplayer is probably why you bought this game, though.  The problem I have with MP is that everything in the game is locked, except for 4 starter classes.  I wasn't sure at first why they decided to go with this method, until I saw them selling Steel (the game's in game currency) and of course, it's basically a slow grind to unlock anything in the game, or buy it.  Each mission played gets you anywhere between 20 & 40 steel, but the cheapest thing you can buy costs 500 steal with the most expensive costing upwards of up to 65000 steel.  So yea, this game is a giant "♥♥♥♥ YOU!" to anyone buying it & only paying the base $60 pricetag, & probably to anyone buying the season pass as well.  It's all built up like a F2P game, that you have to pay $60 to play.  So, either Ubisoft is planning on making the game F2P in the future, or they are just trying to milk everyone for every penny they can get.  Most likely, it's both.  I honestly wouldn't be surprised if this game went F2P in a year or so, because the game is already built like a F2P game.
At least the game itself is actually pretty good.  Multiplayer is solid, when it isn't lagging, & if you have friends to play with that does make the game even better.  The downside, if you don't have people to play with you will find yourself in pugs which is never really all that fun.  The game does have several game modes available ranging from 1v1, 2v2, & 4v4 games with Deathmatch & Domination.  You also have this minigame where you can assign a point on the map to attack an enemy territory or defend one of your own.  The territory with the most points wins the round, so it's recommended to place a point whenever you have one & you usually have one after each match.
The combat is also surprisingly very fun.  It does take some getting used to at first, & I still don't like how slow you move when you lock onto a target but once you get used to it, learn your combos & the ins & outs of the game it's just a fun game to play.  You get level ups in MP as you kill minions & other players & complete objectives, & as you level up you aquire certain skills to help you win.  These range from an aoe buff, to a heal, to an extra attack, to an aoe nuke.  All of which are useful when neccessary & can turn the tide in some games.  I was in a match where my side was losing, so I called in the nukes & KO'd 2 of the enemy team & then suddenly we were in the lead & won.  These skills are no joke.  As you play & deal or take damage you build up your revenge meter, which acts differently depending on which class you are playing.  It basically turns you into a beast if used properly & can also turn the tide in battle.  Also, the meter goes up faster the more enemy players are around you so it's also meant to help balance when you are out numbered.
The biggest issue with the combat system is it's designed for 1v1 duels, but the majority of the game places you against multiple opponents whether in single player or online multiplayer.  Most game modes in multiplayer are basically derpfests where whoever outnumbers the other side at the current location will most likely win.  Occasionally you will get lucky & might be able to take down 2 opponents yourself but good luck with that.  It's easier said than done & if you're outnumbered 3 to 1 you're basically dead already.  That being said, team cooperation far outweighs skill in the 2v2 or 4v4 game modes so if you have a good team, chances are you'll win.
There's also a variety of customization options which range from colors, designs & decorations on your armor & weapons.  Some are merely cosmetic, others add or change up your stats.  You can also scrap weapons/armor you aren't using to upgrade ones you will.  You can also use steel to buy chests that hold more gear or complete daily quests to give you a chest.  Chests give you gear dependant on your prestige level. Leveling up gear is also available & can be done using steel & dismantled parts. If you buy the best chest you get at least 2 items that are of greater level than gear you currently have equipped.  Daily's also give XP & Steel bonuses, but not much steel.  The most you get is maybe 100-300 per quest, but there are several quests to do per day so get ready to grind.
The game also disconnects constantly because apparantly a multi-billion dollar company like Ubisoft can't afford decent servers.  I am actually one who prefers P2P connections but this games netcode is down right awful.  You will get disconnected frequently & you will lag in games & not be able to control your character because of it.  When you disconnect you lose all rewards & experience as well which can be frustraiting if you d/c right near the end of a match.
Another thing about this game is it makes me angry.  Like, want to break something or slam a door angry.  it's seriously frustraiting when things go wrong or when lag makes you unable to block or parry or when opponents keep throwing you off cliffs, block all of your attacks or using cheese tactics to beat you, or when the campaign glitches out & forces you to start a chapter over, or using guard break counters when for some reason you can't ever get one yourself.  It's super rage enducing, that's for sure.
The game is good, but it's not worth the full $60-100 pricetag, especially with all the microtransactions the game currently has.  You can say, "They're optional" all you want, but this game is obviously built around them.  Everything in the game costs Steel, from characters, to item upgrades, to gear, & there are even shortcuts for using steel that unlock stuff you'd normally have to grind to obtain otherwise.  The game is a big $$$ in the eyes of Ubisoft & a giant middle finger to anyone who buys it.  It is however a fun game, & sadly that means it's just another fun game ruined by greedy publishers which is also a darn shame.  If you like medieval combat with knights, vikings & samurai it might be worth it but for the average player you might be better off just waiting for a sale, or for the game to eventually go F2P because it's obviously already designed for just that.

I bought LiF:YO during EA and it was such a bore. I uninstalled and walked away within two hours. However, I decided to give it another try after it hit full release, and I've got to admit I was pleasantly surprised!
LiF:YO has come a long, long way from it's EA days. It is still a grind, but not in the "oh I have to grab 200 stones to make this" but in the "holy crap, this is a hardcore survival game!". You are not handed items, you are not handed stats, you have to earn everything you want. You want to craft an iron sword? Start prospecting, mining, and smelting. You want to plant an apple tree? Start gathering plants, sowing seeds, and tilling the land. This is a game you spend many hours on just to get started. While this may sound like a negative, it gives you a sense of accomplishment that many survival games have long forgotten.

This game and the other Mount and Blade games are very noteworthy and worth buying on a good sale.
