Oh boy, this game. Where do I even begin?
If you're someone who's looking to get into Magic: The Gathering and heard about this title as a good way of doing so, you've been fooled. This won't win you over. And that's a shame, because it does have some things going for itself. It just represents the incredibly fun game of Magic in a very slowpaced, mindnumbingly stupid way.
However, if you're someone who's already familiar to Magic: The Gathering who is just looking for a lighter version of the game to enjoy themselves with, this might be the game for you. Provided that you're the patient kind who doesn't mind overlooking the flaws and pacing of this game. And trust me, you will need that patience.
Let's look at some of the pros and cons of this game:
Pros:
-Customizable decks. A decent card pool to choose from and many fun decks that can be created from it. This is where most of the appeal will come from, if you do decide to get it. This is its best feature and one it sorely needed.
- Very fun to play with friends or even just online vs strangers. Great way to test your deck ideas and tweak them to perfection.
- It's still Magic: The Gathering. If you love the game, chances are you'll love this as well. The basic concept is still fun and the card pool is decent enough that it allows you to make several fun decks and pull of many fun tricks with it.
Cons:
- The game handles slowly and clunky. You have to sift through various menus and options to get to where you want to go. Every. Single. Time.
- No rematches. When you finish a game, the opponent disappears and you get kicked back to the opponent selection screens. If you enjoyed playing against them and would like to do so again, you can't. Unless you remember their name and try to find them that way. But who really wants to do that?
- No deck selection in the lobby. Deck selection has to be done before hand and can't be changed in the lobby. If you want to change, you have to go back to the main menu, change it and then go back to Multiplayer. Why? Who greenlighted this as a good idea? Why the step back?
- Premium cards locked unless you pay an additional fee. While the premium cards don't make or break the game, per se, this is still a horrible and incredibly greedy design.
- The first deck you choose is literally the only deck you can play with for a substantial amount of time, so you better pick something you really love. It's very limiting and frankly a gross oversight. A big part of the appeal of this game is its versatility and by forcing one deck on the players for a substantial amount of time, you basically cheat them out of that.
Final Judgment:
6.5/10. It's an improvement on the older version in some respects, and a step backwards in others. It won't win any new fans over with its current design. If you decide not to buy your way through, as I strongly recommend you do, it takes a long time and much grinding to unlock everything, but by the time you have everything, you'll be intimately familiar with the game (and its often clunky mechanics) but the endgame is where you'll have most of the fun. In short, it's like a long car ride to Disneyland. After a long, rocky, uncomfortable ride, you finally get out, itchy and sore but happy to finally be at your destination and ready to have some real fun. If you can wait that long.
I'll give it a tentative thumbs up, but that's just because I'm slightly biased and hopeful for the future of this franchise, so keep that in mind.

80 Days is a narrative focused race against time game where your choices dictate how you progress through the entire game.  You are the butler/man servant of a lord that is on a mission(as he has a bet on it) to go around the world in 80 days or less.  You decide which methods of travel and route are the best to take as well as what items you bring on the journey.  While doing all of this you are managing the clock and your own resources.
I honestly haven't seen many flaws in the gameplay, the only thing I can present is that if you don't enjoy reading then you won't enjoy this game very much.  Much of the gameplay is exploring the text and narrative the game throws in your direction.
I would give this a 4/5 or even a 4.5/5, it falls in my mind into a unique category of gameplay that is pleasant and relaxing but has the core gameplay to back it up.  I would highly recommend it at any discount to anyone, and at full price if you are someone who really enjoys narrative.

Tormentum gets a thumbs-up from me.  The art is beautifully disturbing and the mood and atmosphere are pleasantly creepy.  While the game is moderately short, it is definitely worth taking the time to find and appreciate the details, both in the art and the information about the world & characters.
The puzzles are simple and amusing (not what I would consider challenging or frustrating), but add an extra layer that tends to augment the story and world.  This is a positive aspect in my opinion since the game is a work emphasizing morality and consequence of choice.  While the choice tree is binary in nature, the end results are less so, and choices cause the story to 'ripple' in different ways as you progress.
I would certainly describe this as a casual game, and this is supported by its well-considered design that a) does not require the player to manually save the game and b) does not allow the player to get 'stuck' and have to restart.
The story was interesting and, to my surprise, actually managed to keep a few tidbits hidden from me until the very end.  Speaking of which, the ending (at least to me) was above average and included an interesting slant.
All Steam achievements are able to be obtained within two or three playthroughs, each of which get progressively faster since the player knows what choices they intend to make ahead of time.  This is why I would recommend focusing on playing the game 'naturally' on the first playthrough, instead of immediately focusing on achievement farming.  You will likely get more enjoyment out of it that way.
For some (primarily those intrigued with the art and atmosphere), the game will be worth the full price.  For others who are still interested but edgy about its short duration, pick it up during a sale.  You will still enjoy it.
Overall, Tormentum is definitely a recommended game for casual play.

The game has an interesting mechanic much like RPGs: you find new weapons and every weapons has 3 slots in it. In those slots you put gems that you find during the missions gameplay. The game features a selectable difficulty much like Diablo's, so you can replay it a lot and continue to develop your character. To those people complaining that you have to think and build weapons and skills, you can just turn down the difficulty and just pass through the levels killing the enemies like you used to in SW2013. One of the biggest pros of this game is that you can customize you difficulty, weapons, skills to fit your gameplay as you like.
Finally, it doesn't make any sense to not recommend this game just because it isn't exactly equal SW2013, you can play the game almost like the old one (except for the premade maps, which now are procedurally generated) and the game is very, very, very
by itself.

Story is interesting and explores a lot of themes about consciousness and humanity. If you're interested in the subject of transhumanism in any way the game provides a lot to think about.
If you're a horror fan it's not scary at all. The monsters aren't that intimidating and at best just present an annoying hindrance that occassionally forces you to redo an area. The explanation behind the monsters is also a little jarring and doesn't fit with the central themes - there's no real need for this game to have zombies and mutants and it felt a little forced.
I'm not quite sure why Frictional marketed this as a horror game and that's probably a decision they'll come to regret. It feels as though the developers are tired of making horrors and wanted to try something a little different, but for some reason rather than go the whole way they've reached some kind of hybrid that doesn't do either particularly well. The monster sections do nohing but impede the player from reading notes or listening to dialogue, and the story has really nothing to do with the monsters.
That said, later in the game there are several deep sea sections which are genuinely a little scary. Anyone afraid of the ocean and sea monsters will be a little freaked out, and it's difficult to see why Frictional didn't try to capitalize on this more. The game is set underwater but for the most part it's just there for a cool environment - it would be infinitely more frightening if the underwater setting was used to better effect than just adding tentacle zombies to chase the player instead of normal zombies.
Aesthetically it resembles a mixture of BioShock and Alien: Isolation. The locations are fairly interesting while being creepy but the annoying overuse of chromatic aberration can marr the experience.
Overall with a six-hour long story and no replayability this is pretty much a game you'll only play once for the story. It's a pretty good story so I'd suggest buying it on sale, but don't purchase it if you're just looking for a horror game. There's no scares to be had and all you'll find here is a pretty well done walking simulator with occassional annoying sections of running from predictable monsters.

It's been a long time since the last time we got something from Frictional Games, and so I was somewhat curious what would be different and what would stay the same, especially with this being their first game to also be released on a console. Thankfully, not much seems to have changed.
For those who haven't had the pleasure of playing Penumbra or Amnesia, all of the games from Frictional Games have a pretty unique method of control where you use the mouse to imitate actions, such as grabbing a door and sliding the mouse to open it or pulling down a lever. It's sort of counter-intuitively intuitive in that it adds a great deal of immersion by representing the inherent unintuitive nature of our bodies compared to the telepathy that's represented by most games where you just press E to open a door, and it also adds a lot of tension to the gameplay, making the difference between frantically grabbing for a lever and pulling down as fast as you physically can to seal a door off from a monster and just running in and tapping a button. Every time they make a new game I always get worried that they're going to change it, because a lot of people complain about it, and I was doubly worried that it would be removed here due to it also being on a console. Thankfully, it hasn't been altered, and hopefully never will be.
But anyone who has played a previous Frictional game already knows all about that, so how does it compare to the previous games? Gameplay-wise, it takes some somewhat unwelcome hints from A Machine for Pigs in that you have no resources to manage except health and your flashlight never runs out of energy, but despite the lack of inventory the game does still have a fair amount of puzzles to go through. But unlike AMFP, SOMA has a pretty typical Frictional Games amount of enemies to cower behind a box from, which was a welcome return. One noteworthy improvement over Amnesia is that the game no longer puts the game in slowmo to dump a narration on you every time you enter a new room, and instead spaces out the narrative in the form of logs and notes in a more traditional manner.
The biggest difference from their previous games is that the protagonist is now voiced, and has discussions with other characters throughout the game. Some people may not like this, and I personally hated the idea when I first realized that he wasn't silent, but the main character grew on me pretty quickly, and by the end of it I liked his inclusion in the game. The dialogue between the characters does a pretty good job at balancing things out so that it's present enough to let you learn to care about the characters, but not enough to diminish the atmosphere or remove the sense of loneliness that the game builds.
Overall, I thought SOMA was a pretty worthy addition to Frictional's catalogue. I don't think I could put it above Penumbra, which I still hold as one of my favorite horror games, but it surpassed Amnesia in almost every way for me. At $30 it might be a bit expensive depending on your tastes, but it's worth getting sooner or later for any horror fan.

My son loves survival games, so I decided to take a chance and buy two copies of this game for Christmas.  I was apprehensive about purchasing a Beta game with such mixed reviews but I’m glad that I did.  We really enjoy playing it together plus we’ve added four additional friends and family members to our group.  The atmosphere created by the graphics and sound give the game a very realistic feel.  You really feel like you are sneaking around a post-apocalyptic landscape with danger lurking around every corner. You have to be weary of the monsters as well as other players.  You only start out with a knife so you have to forage in abandoned buildings and subways to find weapons and supplies.  It can be very frustrating to work your way up to a high skill level, with lots of equipment and be shot by a greedy player that ambushes you as you limp into a safe zone, but that adds to the tenseness and realness of the game.  As in life, you don’t know who is friend or foe, although it would be nice if you didn’t lose all of your experience and skills when killed.  There is an option to place your surplus equipment in a global inventory so that it is not lost when you are killed but you do lose all equipment that is on you at the time of your death.  The game is best played with a buddy to watch your back.  If you enjoy a challenging game with a realistic feel then you should give it a try.

Note: I haven't had any issues with connection, so I can't comment on that. It sucks that so many people are experiencing it, but I'm reviewing the game from my own experience, not theirs.
tl;dr -- Neat combat that forces you to git gud, okay story mode with some cool lore, and multiplayer that's intense but not viable as a proper competitive game yet.
For Honor's a brawler that can be really intense and fun, if infuriating. Combat is refreshing after so many God of War and Souls clones, like a cross between Soul Calibur and Infinity Blade, with a little Souls influence. If you played Ryse and you were disappointed by the shallow mechanics, this game will satisfy you.
Story Mode is mostly a tutorial for most of the characters and mechanics, but it builds a neat alternate history and the main villain is a badass. The AI can be insanely aggressive on harder difficulties, and the game looks really good with the UI off, just seeing the combat. Also, even though most of the designs look generic, I'm a sucker for masks.
The multiplayer is fun in short bursts, but it's not esport-level competitive. Every mode besides duels has the issue of 2-4v1, and envrionmental kills and the revenge meter keep 1v1s from being entirely skill-oriented. Revenge seems like it's trying to be an analogue for meter in proper fighters, but its rules for filling keep it from being anywhere near as reliable, and there's no reason to save it rather than popping it immediately. Unless the metagame turns Dominion into a MOBA or something, there's no chance for it to be anything but a fun-with-friends mode.
You can get really good fights going if everyone agrees to not be a♥♥♥♥♥♥ like Souls PvP, but for the most part the game feels like a brawler or party fighter rather than something you'd see tournaments of. People still play Smash professionally, though, so if the community made rulesets, it might work in time.
A 7/10 game, I think. Eighty dollars is debatable, but probably definitely worth on sale.

This 17th-century counterpart to the fun-filled Mount and Blade: Warband was ill-conceived and does not even nearly measure up to its predecessor. Firearm-based warfare simply does not fit into Mount and Blade's combat system, and the result is silly, disjointed battles rife with anachronistically-accurate gunshots. In the period during which this game takes place, one would be lucky to hit a barn at 100 meters with a musket. As such, massed volleys were the order of the day. Not so in this title. Want to hit an enemy from 50 meters with a pistol while riding at full speed on your horse? No problem. And don't be surprised if you get sniped from halfway aross the map under the same circumstance. And it's not just the battles that are bad: the campaign takes a giant step backwards from Warband also, lacking numerous gameplay aspects native to that superior title. Campaign gameplay in With Fire and Sword mainly boils down to running away from bandits and endlessly playing errand boy to local lords, and is both needlessly difficult and extremely tedious.
Though this game is sold at a bargain-bin price, it is truly not worth any amount of your money or time. Avoid.

Now let me get one thing straight, this game is not for everyone.  This game is one of the very few honest to god hardcore games I have ever played (You can attribute this to a lot of the negative reviews).  Playing solo is possible on modded servers, but if you want the REAL LiF experience by playing on vanilla, you WILL need a group of people.  This is boderline non-negotionable, this is where a lot of new players make a mistake and thus ruin the experience for themselves.
Now to get on to actually reviewing it...Let me start off by critiquing it.  The game does have some honest issues.  Animations are stiff and unnatural (Which normally wouldn't be a huge issue, but this effects combat so I have to point it out), game does have some performance issues, and can be VERY tedius.
But onto why I recommend the game, even though the game has it's own set of problems and isn't exactly perfect I still have to give this game a big thumbs up on it's core design philosophy.  If you enjoy a game that punishes you, a game that is unforgiving, but pays out when you work your♥♥♥♥♥off to achieve something....This game feeds this desire better than no other in my experience.  End game isn't achieved with ease.  It takes the combined efforts of you and your group working hard to achieve your goals, which gives you a sense of satisfaction I have never felt in a game before.
So in conclusion, if you are the type of player who can't and won't dedicate all their free time to a game, a player who wants things handed to them on a silver platter, or a player who just might not have the time in their lives to play this game.....Please don't buy this game, the game wasn't made for you to begin with.  But if you are like me, someone who enjoys the feeling of putting in hours of work and grinding into a game to accomplish things other players don't have the stomach for, this game is meant for you.

As for the gameplay, it runs just like any other point and click, so there isn't much more to expect. However, each puzzle is fresh and some are unlike ones you'd see in other games. Some can be solved on the spot, some are puzzles that require a found item and some you may need a hint given to you in another location. It is sad the the game is a short one, though, but you may find yourself replaying it just to reimerse yourself in the art.
Thematically it matches the visuals: very dark. Some of the themes are quite thought provoking if you are at all philosophic.
There is a unique musical track to set the mood for each "scene". Some are beautiful, some do there job in setting a creepy background abience to better the experience. The only gripe I have is that the quality may be a bit rough on some tracks (similar to if a track was slowed down too much [a minor clipping effect]), but that is really knitpicking.
To conclude, this is a game that you definitely want to play slow and let it envelope you. Savor each scene and each thought. This is a game that was made to be experienced.

Story is interesting and explores a lot of themes about consciousness and humanity. If you're interested in the subject of transhumanism in any way the game provides a lot to think about.
If you're a horror fan it's not scary at all. The monsters aren't that intimidating and at best just present an annoying hindrance that occassionally forces you to redo an area. The explanation behind the monsters is also a little jarring and doesn't fit with the central themes - there's no real need for this game to have zombies and mutants and it felt a little forced.
I'm not quite sure why Frictional marketed this as a horror game and that's probably a decision they'll come to regret. It feels as though the developers are tired of making horrors and wanted to try something a little different, but for some reason rather than go the whole way they've reached some kind of hybrid that doesn't do either particularly well. The monster sections do nohing but impede the player from reading notes or listening to dialogue, and the story has really nothing to do with the monsters.
That said, later in the game there are several deep sea sections which are genuinely a little scary. Anyone afraid of the ocean and sea monsters will be a little freaked out, and it's difficult to see why Frictional didn't try to capitalize on this more. The game is set underwater but for the most part it's just there for a cool environment - it would be infinitely more frightening if the underwater setting was used to better effect than just adding tentacle zombies to chase the player instead of normal zombies.
Aesthetically it resembles a mixture of BioShock and Alien: Isolation. The locations are fairly interesting while being creepy but the annoying overuse of chromatic aberration can marr the experience.
Overall with a six-hour long story and no replayability this is pretty much a game you'll only play once for the story. It's a pretty good story so I'd suggest buying it on sale, but don't purchase it if you're just looking for a horror game. There's no scares to be had and all you'll find here is a pretty well done walking simulator with occassional annoying sections of running from predictable monsters.

It's been a long time since the last time we got something from Frictional Games, and so I was somewhat curious what would be different and what would stay the same, especially with this being their first game to also be released on a console. Thankfully, not much seems to have changed.
For those who haven't had the pleasure of playing Penumbra or Amnesia, all of the games from Frictional Games have a pretty unique method of control where you use the mouse to imitate actions, such as grabbing a door and sliding the mouse to open it or pulling down a lever. It's sort of counter-intuitively intuitive in that it adds a great deal of immersion by representing the inherent unintuitive nature of our bodies compared to the telepathy that's represented by most games where you just press E to open a door, and it also adds a lot of tension to the gameplay, making the difference between frantically grabbing for a lever and pulling down as fast as you physically can to seal a door off from a monster and just running in and tapping a button. Every time they make a new game I always get worried that they're going to change it, because a lot of people complain about it, and I was doubly worried that it would be removed here due to it also being on a console. Thankfully, it hasn't been altered, and hopefully never will be.
But anyone who has played a previous Frictional game already knows all about that, so how does it compare to the previous games? Gameplay-wise, it takes some somewhat unwelcome hints from A Machine for Pigs in that you have no resources to manage except health and your flashlight never runs out of energy, but despite the lack of inventory the game does still have a fair amount of puzzles to go through. But unlike AMFP, SOMA has a pretty typical Frictional Games amount of enemies to cower behind a box from, which was a welcome return. One noteworthy improvement over Amnesia is that the game no longer puts the game in slowmo to dump a narration on you every time you enter a new room, and instead spaces out the narrative in the form of logs and notes in a more traditional manner.
The biggest difference from their previous games is that the protagonist is now voiced, and has discussions with other characters throughout the game. Some people may not like this, and I personally hated the idea when I first realized that he wasn't silent, but the main character grew on me pretty quickly, and by the end of it I liked his inclusion in the game. The dialogue between the characters does a pretty good job at balancing things out so that it's present enough to let you learn to care about the characters, but not enough to diminish the atmosphere or remove the sense of loneliness that the game builds.
Overall, I thought SOMA was a pretty worthy addition to Frictional's catalogue. I don't think I could put it above Penumbra, which I still hold as one of my favorite horror games, but it surpassed Amnesia in almost every way for me. At $30 it might be a bit expensive depending on your tastes, but it's worth getting sooner or later for any horror fan.

As a fan and regular player of the developers' previous soft-body vehicular physics crashy explosion simulator, Rigs of Rods, I got to see firsthand the dramatically more complex crashy explosion physics the game presented compared to most other titles on the market.
There are surprisingly few franchises, or even titles, which come close to what RoR presents as far as vehicular collision physics are concerned: GTA IV (and later, to a somewhat different extent, GTA V) with its RAGE engine-based dynamic vehicular damage model, Burnout Paradise and Race Driver:GRID are a few examples.
None of these come close to the level of detail and accuracy Ror's successor, BeamNG:drive, provides with its real-time soft-body physics engine. On an average crash (to me, "average" means barrelling at 130+mph into a stationary environmental object head-on) in one of the game's couple-dozen vehicles, you can expect to see dynamic, direction-, mass- and velocity-based deformation similar to that expressed in GTA IV as far as dramatic appearance goes, only taken to a whole other level.
Let's say, hypothetically, that you are a hard-working, 5-year-old, half-blind muskrat which somehow miraculously has the capacity to operate a mid-90s American-market Japanese compact pickup in the pursuit of your current occupation. I know I am. (Wait, what?) You find yourself driving in a straight line at full throttle in this vehicle, which reaches 0-60 in probably 4ish seconds, traveling inexplicably straight into a collision course with a 1-cubic-meter-sized traffic bollard made out of impenetrable space concrete. Naturally, one might sensibly slow down, change course to avoid said obstacle or slam on the brakes, and all are possible here, but only one makes for an effective written anecdote.
What you will experience is a short period where the physical forces exerted on your front bumper are so great that they physically deform it in an instant, splaying body panels off the frame and out in random directions, dramatically warping the engine compartment, frame and chassis to the point where the truck's "new, trancendentally-meditated centered self" (the center of the grille, in other words, or I guess the "front face normal" for 3D graphics folks) is approximately 35 degrees to the right, 16 degrees upward with 10 degrees of counter-clockwise (from the driver's perspective) roll.
Side and rear windows will shatter instantly, parts will fly off including doors, hubcaps, wheels and light assemblies, the windscreen (or windshield, whatever floats your aerodynamic boat) will be permanently turned into a quite striking artistic glass mosaic, the ergonomics of the truck cab will be quite starkly changed from a mediocre selling feature into an OSHA violation, and depending on the breaks (and the brakes) your former work vehicle might even catch on fire, leaving you surprisingly little time to get out of the truck or even take a screenshot and post it on the Steam Community page before the gas tank ignites and causes a rather dramatic fireball a few times.
Depending on the vehicle and the circumstances of the crash, even vitally-important vehicular components like external gas tanks, the internal combustion engine and its gearbox will fly off the chassis and tumble gracefully away, leaving you figuratively (and perhaps literally, if you hit a dock or something) dead in the water.
It's such a simple yet complex experience in driving games, the crash. This game really does it justice. These physics are so dynamic and ever-changing that the concept of canned damage states isn't really in BeamNG.drive's rulebook.

It's hard to dispute most of the negative press that has accompanied this latest iteration of the Duels franchise. It seems, at least in its release form, that the desire to allow players versatility in deck design is mitigated by the lack of diversity in the card pool.
There are some frustrating inconsistences in the game (that perhaps harken back to the 'unlock cards with each win' systems of previous versions of the game), though these are mainly limited to the card pool and deck design process. Many of the cards of which you would want play-sets (especially early drops or higher rarities) have only two or three copies making for some maddenly inconsistent mana-curves. Perhaps this is so players can't create oppressively consistent decks, but it does detract from the idea that players have 'total creative control' in deck making. Duel-lands are clearly in the game - the AI utilises them in many of their decks - and yet players only have access to Guildgates for their own use. Each color can unlock singletons of two mythics, two-sets of nine rares, threes of uncommons and fours of commons; it appears Wizards have been keen to keep the power level down, overall, perhaps in an effort to preserve the newcomer friendly background that has been at the core of the Duels franchise in the past (though this version certainly appeals and rewards those with knowledge of the game). And, true, a few fan-favourite game modes are missing from the 2015 release of Duels; Wizards themselves have been quick to admit their error in this in the wake of strong player reaction.
Despite all this, the gameplay in Duels 2015 is generally terrific. Building your own deck and piloting it through the traditional challenge-based campaign is great fun, and as you unlock cards after victories the process of refining and evolving your deck/s is rewarding. Gameplay is smooth and generally fast (if you turn off some of the combat animations and hold priorities), and clear enough in its visual cues that experienced players can gauge the passing of priority and phases to weigh in on 'the stack'. The AI is definitely improved, though experienced players will quickly find it no match once the AI-weighted campaign is concluded. As each game progresses and the board-state complicates, you will find the AI turns dragging out as it 'considers' its options, though it will still make those head-scratching plays that traditionally plague CCG AIs. And, of course, the AI never concedes.
The optional in-game purchases can add some upgrades to the free-to-play card pool, but the vast majority of game content can be unlocked by completing the campaign. The menu interfaces can be annoying at times, and the need to 'equip' a deck (rather than selecting it at the pre-game screen) is cumbersome, but most players will be spending the vase majority of their time in the card-collection and deck-building screens when not in-game, and these were improved in a recent update. It's all serviceable, at the very least, and not enough to detract from the overall play experience.
Duels 2015 is to be recommended to Magic and video game enthusiasts alike. While MTG players may have been wanting a graphically improved version of Wizards' beleaguered 'MTGO', it's still a lot of fun to play and to play around in, despite lacking the total freedom of its online big brother (though, with some semblance of stability). The card collection and menu interface can be frustrating, but this doesn't necessarily detract from the overall gameplay, and at the price point there's a lot of value and fun to be had. It's safe to say that Wizards have learned from this version of Duels, and the game is likely to receive at least one content update featuring new cards, based on their past processes. So, until Duels 2016 (the franchise is becoming as inevitable as Madden), Duels 2015 is still the best looking Magic game going and offers plenty of entertainment.

is a choose-your-own-adventure game (CYOAG) based on the Jules Verne novel of the same name. You are Passepartout, French servant of an Englishman named Phileas Fogg, who made a wager to his fellow clubmembers to circumnavigate the world in, well, 80 days or less.
The game has remarkable depth for a CYOAG. Mainly your adventure unfolds based on the cities you choose to travel next, but along the way, you'll engage in interesting conversations. Some lead the story to deep, contemplative moments, while some gives you knowledge to unplanned travel routes or even access to faster, cheaper means of transport. The hundreds of cities to travel in addition to a plethora of conversational options makes it rare to experience the same story on each playthrough.
The success of your circumnavigation depends on two things: money and items. You start off with 4,000 pounds in cash, but you can buy some items in, say, Munich, and sell them for profit in, say, Istanbul. In that note, although there are some basic economic elements to it, it isn't necessarily a trading game. The items you buy makes your trip easier. For example, buying coat furs and mittens help you cope with the Siberian cold should your travel pass through there.
Although it's mainly text-based, the accompanying artwork is beautiful. You'll notice remarkably different atmosphere between cities in every continent. The excellent original soundtrack makes them even more memorable. (The music for the game's finale is my favorite!)

Nether, although still in development at the time of this writing is a really good game.  It has a great atmosphere that keeps you on the edge of your seat the entire time you play.
Nether is an online-only open world survival game.  You are tossed into a post-apocalyptic world populated by other players and monsters.  The unique thing to Nether is that once you die, that is it.  Your character is dead and your stuff spews out into the open, awaiting capture by another player.  The intesity that this delivers in the game is outstanding.  Things become more and more dangerous and tense the longer you play it.  Which can be a problem, because this is a game that you wont want to stop playing for a long time.
Although the map isn't fully finished (its less than a fourth of what its going to be when the game is finished) it is HUGE.  Walking a block in the game seems to take just about as long as walking a block in real life would be.  I like this game's attempt at realism.
This game is pretty, but not in the sense you might expect.  Although the world is mostly greys and bleak washed out colors, it still is awesome to take a minute at the top of a building to look out and enjoy the vegetated, overrun, destroyed cityscape.
Now for the gripes...  This game is buggy but that is to be expected because it is still in Beta, I believe.  There are stairs that lead to nowhere and there are some places where you SHOULD be able to get through but you cant go through.  You can go through some of the environmental sets and overall the game doesnt feel done.... But that is because it isn't done, so I can't count that against them.
But why should you play this game?  You should play this game for the intensity of the fear of death at any moment, especially when you have a lot of supplies.  This game can be fun with friends although there is no map to see where other players are (you would probably want to play in the same room and meet up at some building nearby.)  I love this game and I can't wait for them to release more content for me and my friends to enjoy.
Overall: 8.5/10

Note: I haven't had any issues with connection, so I can't comment on that. It sucks that so many people are experiencing it, but I'm reviewing the game from my own experience, not theirs.
tl;dr -- Neat combat that forces you to git gud, okay story mode with some cool lore, and multiplayer that's intense but not viable as a proper competitive game yet.
For Honor's a brawler that can be really intense and fun, if infuriating. Combat is refreshing after so many God of War and Souls clones, like a cross between Soul Calibur and Infinity Blade, with a little Souls influence. If you played Ryse and you were disappointed by the shallow mechanics, this game will satisfy you.
Story Mode is mostly a tutorial for most of the characters and mechanics, but it builds a neat alternate history and the main villain is a badass. The AI can be insanely aggressive on harder difficulties, and the game looks really good with the UI off, just seeing the combat. Also, even though most of the designs look generic, I'm a sucker for masks.
The multiplayer is fun in short bursts, but it's not esport-level competitive. Every mode besides duels has the issue of 2-4v1, and envrionmental kills and the revenge meter keep 1v1s from being entirely skill-oriented. Revenge seems like it's trying to be an analogue for meter in proper fighters, but its rules for filling keep it from being anywhere near as reliable, and there's no reason to save it rather than popping it immediately. Unless the metagame turns Dominion into a MOBA or something, there's no chance for it to be anything but a fun-with-friends mode.
You can get really good fights going if everyone agrees to not be a♥♥♥♥♥♥ like Souls PvP, but for the most part the game feels like a brawler or party fighter rather than something you'd see tournaments of. People still play Smash professionally, though, so if the community made rulesets, it might work in time.

A surprisingly nice little game.
Its based on book idea of going around the world in 80days, sadly having never read the book but seen TV/film adaptations of it, this is seems abit more crazy, with not only boats and trains but also mechanical elephants as means of transport.
Graphics are, on the one hand basic, with a top down view of the world, which you click on different cities to progress through but also, there is lovely art style to the game, showcase in the background of the cities you visit.
There isn’t really alot of gameplay except a few clicks here and there, while reading through a load of text but somehow it makes it one of those types of games where you think, just a little bit longer.
The text that you read, makes up the story of your adventure, so changes depending on what routes you take across the globe. So some stories you may find you follow all the way, some you might lose track of and your left wondering what happened to that person. But this helps add to the feel that your character is travelling the world and on a time schedule. Of course you will meet people on your travel but you will then move on, as is life.
There is also times where you can risk spending an extra couple of days to try and continue that story, say by visiting another city that’s wasn’t exactly on the route you where originally planning.
This can also happen in scripted events, where for some reason the city you where journeying to will, suddenly no longer be your destination, which can sometimes frustrate or delight.
How so, because travelling the world cost money. You start the game with plenty but unless you start doing some wheeling and dealing, you eventually find your funds running out, especially for some of the more expensive but faster journeys. So it’s up to you, to buy items in markets, and then sell them on.
The game tells you where you will receive the most money for selected items, but is it on your route? Do you head that way, just to make money, hoping that you can continue your journey from there?
And you don't have all day to decide, as part from when your reading the clock keeps ticking, and if you spend to long at the market or planning a route across the country, you may find that you've just missed your connection and the next one isn't for 5 days! Do you then choose another way? Wait the days out? Or bribe somebody to lower the amount of days until the next journey?
I've played through it three times now, not once have I stopped midway.
My first attempt, it took me 84 days and I was gutted that I just missed out! My 2nd try, it was 74 days and I was genuinely over the moon, to have made it, and exactly 10 days quicker than my first attempt. And my third attempt before writing this review, it took me 75days.
It isn’t exactly a long game but its got character and a charm about it, which somehow has you glued to your seat from the start of your journey till the end. With the feeling of plenty of time to begin with and then the increase urgency as the game progresses.
And since I got this off Humble for 80p, it was well worth the money.

I feel somewhat bad giving this game a negative review, but I feel my negative feelings about it outweigh the positive feelings, even though there are some positive things to say about it.
I'll start with the pros:
-Decent level design.  I like that, as puzzle-based games go, you're not forced to retread so much and the solutions for things are usually right there, it's just a matter of identifying them.  You have a bit of freedom sometimes in how you explore.  As linear games go, they manage to make it not feel incredibly so.
-Pretty good atmosphere.  The use of light and dark was mostly effective and the main survival-based resource, tinderboxes and lantern, was a mostly well-throught out gameplay element.  I liked that you begin to learn to be a little strategic with which torches/candles you light in order to see where you're going but not run out of inventory.
-The puzzles are mostly not too difficult and often satisfying to solve.  I was a big fan of games like Myst back in the day, and this felt at times like a horror survival version of that.
Now I'll talk about the cons:
-The story is ultimately not that interesting.  It starts out promising and that's one of the things that kept me playing.  I wanted to know what was going on.  Ultimately, though, about 2/3 of the way through the game I started to realize it wasn't really going anywhere and I feel in the end that it really doesn't go anywhere.  The ending does not give you really any reflection on what happened and I found it pretty unfulfilling.
-Another gameplay element is your overall sanity level which basically manifests in louder breathing sound effects from your character and, much more irritatingly, your vision becoming severely impaired.  I really don't like video games where your vision becomes impaired.  When I played Killing Floor, I turned off the blur effect that occurs when you get swatted by zombies.  If there were a way of turning off the visual insanity effects of this game, I probably would have.  I found it to be far more obnoxious than effective in terms of immersion.
-The game is constantly interrupting whatever you do by throwing in little flashbacks.  These aren't cut scenes, per se.  They are moments where you can still move but your vision becomes impaired, the lighting changes, and you start hearing some dialog that you recall from the events that take place before the game.  These are sometimes sparse, but in certain levels they happen every time you turn a corner or open a door.  I grew to really hate them, especially since most of them, especially in the latter part of the game, become incredibly reduntant, usually recalling yet another instant where you gruesomely tortured someone to death.
-The enemy element of the game is scary the first couple of times you encounter it.  After that, it just gets pretty silly.  You can't fight anything in this game - you simply have to hide or run.  There are essentially 2 kinds of enemy in this game:  an invisible thing that walks in water and, more ubiquitously, this lumbering zombie-like thing.  The latter appears seemingly out of nowhere at times and disappears as soon as it goes down a hallway or something. Let's get the obvious out of the way: yes, the graphics and animations are hilariously dated. Yes, some of the voice actors should probably have pursued other lines of work. Yes, it's still got glitches and bugs out the wazoo, even with the excellent Restored Content Mod. But, you know what? This is still one of the best Star Wars games, and one of the better RPGs ever made, period. If you're a Star Wars fan who hasn't played KOTOR yet, buy them both and play them through in order. You won't regret it.
Pros
The Force powers, influence, and alignment system
Companions are varied, interesting, and most of them can be trained as Jedi
Fine addition to the Star Wars mythos (not that it matters now that Disney's continuity-bombed the EU, but still)
Steam has the Restored Content Mod, which patches in a lot of the content that was altered or cut by Obsidian so they could meet their draconian release timeframe
Cons
Janky animations
Dialogue doesn't always flow naturally
Still buggy as all get-out, even with the RCM
Dat ending still kinda sucks
Overall, I definitely recommend this game, especially for only ten bucks. And, seriously, get the Restored Content Mod. I can't applaud those guys enough for their work.

This is a really fun narrative based game that can be a nice way to spend some time.  The game is based on a series of choices that the player gets to make as they step into the shoes of Passapourte, the man servant of the games "main" character, Phileas Fogg.
It does a great job capturing the magic that that the 19th century people viewed the future with, and the amount of absolutely ludicrous but at the same time simply amazing transportation methods just add to the experience.
Another huge benefit of the choice system is that you dont have to simply take an east-west course, you can travel through America first in some situations, as well as through the arctic or down through africa in the hopes that you find a faster method of travel.  All routes have pros and cons, and one of the downright coolest things is you get to see recent players on your map and guage the speed theyre going with your own.
Some of the limits placed on you really force you to play intelligently, some modes of transport only allow certain amounts of luggage meaning you must dump all that valuable junk youre carrying around, some items are of extreme value in places but on your route there is simply no way you can make the time to go there.
All things being said, I have about 50 hours in this game logged while connected to the internet, but I am sure that i have quite a bit more than that, and I still haven't really discovered everything there is.  The great thing is that a single playthrough takes about as long as you make it, you can blow through all the text, not talk to people and finish it in under an hour, or you can savor everything talk to everyone and try to find new routes and take well over an hour.

Protip: If you're going to play this game, wear old pants that you don't care about while doing so, because you will stain them.

I haven't played "Choose your own Adventure" games since I was a child so it was nice to see how much the genre has progressed since then. The world of 80 Days is interesting, the dialogues very well written and the Art style looks nice. However the game has a few aspects that can be frustratring as well. For example the clock is always ticking down and while this creates a sense of urgency there were points where I wished I could have a closer look at the map to plan my route or go through my biefcases to discard a few things I probably won't need anymore. The other thing that could cause some frustration is that (contrary to the Sorcery! games by the same dev) there is no Undo button and you only have one save which automatically gets overwritten. I'm almost certain both of those things are intentional design decisions and they fit the theme quite nicely but they also make the game more hectic than other "Choose your own Adventure" games.

Rejuvenating survival horror. Perfect, endlessly unsettling sound design. Horrifying environments. Pure chilling Lovecraftian narrative told and unearthed in a consistently engaging manner. Puzzles that are simple enough to not become frustrating and challenging enough to not feel like pointless busywork. An unshakeable feeling of being chased and even in the dingiest corners being constantly out in the open and exposed to danger. Hiding from monsters that more often than not aren't there, abusing every inch of your imagination, and when they are there delivering terrifying sequences of frantic escape slamming doors behind you and terrified hiding cowering into walls desperately trying not to be seen, having to balance attempts at avoiding them with your dwindling sanity in the dark. Leaping from box to box in a flooded room avoiding the invisible creature that waits in the water, and the panicked rush to safety when you inevitably slip and hear the splashing rapidly approaching behind you. Lighting, sanity and "flight not fight" mechanics that have impacted so much in the five years since its release, making it hard to imagine the horror landscape of the 2010s without it. The defining horror game of the decade so far.

This game is so deserving of the "overwhelmingly positive" label it has when I am writing this. It tells the story of an unknown, unseen character robed in a tattered, hooded cloak. He/she/it is captured by some militia and left in a castle to be tortured. From there you need to escape and find out who you are, all the time meeting the most bizarre characters and creatures I have seen in fantasy.
Firstly, this is a Point & Click game. I found the idea of these dull BEFORE I picked this game up during the Steam sale (whatever the price it is now it is probably worth it). It makes up for the lack of normal gameplay (i.e. moving a character around, regular animation, etc) by having some of the most macabre, horrific, gruesome yet beautiful and astounding scenes I have ever seen, accompanied each time with unique atmospheric music which at times makes me think of latter day Burzum. They are inspired by the painter Zdzisław Beksiński, H.R. Giger and I find the atmosphere remeniscent of a Lovecraftian nightmare at times.
Gameplay is somewhat typical of P&C games: each scene presents you with various things to interact with, items to collect and puzzles to solve. Solving puzzles is the key to moving from various areas and the puzzles are not too challenging or frustrating. You won't need a walkthrough if you just stop, sit back and think. Some are even remeniscent of the games you'd find on a smartphone game.
There are also a few moral choices. They are not all black and white either. Your choices decide the ending and the ending does have a twist that admittedly made me go, "wow ok, this didn't occur to me".
Replay value is not especially the highest BUT this isn't a game made for gameplay. It's for storytelling and immersion. I will play it regularly just to immerse myself again in this eldritch realm. In this respect it is perfect.
Yeah, really this game is 10/10. I see no fault at all.
If you choose to buy this game please also consider buying it directly from the developers website. They sell it but also include other options such as a high quality book of all the artwork and some other articles. The art is really beautiful and I think worthy of having in a book.
10/10, worth your time if you enjoy dark fantasy, morbid imagery and Lovecraft style fantasy.

Dead Sky is an indie action game that places you (and some friends) in a typical survival zombie apocalypse setting.  It has two modes; a single-player campaign and a coop wave survival mode.  The campaign is very short with only a handful of levels, loosely linked by a typical story and mostly played as a top-down twin stick shooter.  Other levels include; driving a car in third-person and blasting zombies in a rail-shooter played from the view of a helicopter gunner.  Objectives include; getting from A to B, defending the base and killing x zombies.
The coop wave survival mode consists of several maps, especially designed for one to four players where the goal is survive as many waves as possible.  Depending on the gamemode, gameplay consists allow picking up and using only one weapon at a time, limited ammunition and resources which can be converted to defenses, sentries or used as upgrades to the character.
+ Well made survival mode.
+ Solid customizable controls.
- Its unfinished!
- Limited map design.
- Very short uninspired singleplayer campaign.  Seems rushed and cobbled together at the last minute to provide some semblence of content.
- Sharp learning curve.  Very difficult to get into.
- Requires manual multiplayer connectivity.  Does not allow coop connection through Steam.
- Impossible to find anyone playing it for coop.
- Wave survival sometimes becomes bugged after reaching level 18.
* Coop gameplay is fun and addictive.
* Cartoony graphics are okay if nothing special.
* A mixed bag of achievements.  Some are probably not achieveable or could even be broken (unverified).
* Decent range of well-modelled weapons and character upgrades.
Overall there is very little to say about Dead Sky.  It possesses the very basic elements to make up what could have been a decent indie game if the developer had had more time or money to complete their project.  It goes to show how badly the game sold or has been played as there are only 1000 or so entries in the leaderboards.
The singleplayer campaign feels unfinished.  It amounts to six levels cobbled together that seem to represent the various modes of gameplay that the developer had in mind when they conceived the idea for this game.  The coop maps are okay for a quick run through although only one map is built to be played solo.  The others require two or three players to successfully tackle.  The characters and backgrounds are well drawn and there are a few different zombie models. Even though they remind me of Unity assets, its quite a pleasant looking, colourful game.  The controls are very solid.  While game mechanics actually quite work well given that you can only carry one useable weapon with limited ammo, you can pick more up if another dead zombie drops some.  Otherwise you can grab a different weapon.
All in all the game is playable - though just.  The thing is... I really hated this when I first played it.  I found it to be such a tragic and at times frustrating experience that its was just not worth bothering with in my opinion.  However... upon revisiting the game (to get my monies worth), I actually found that in a bizarre way the game mechanics actually work well together.  After completing what there was of the campaign which took a while to get to grips with, to my eternal surprise I found the wave survival mode to be quite fun and addictive.  However it took me over a year to find someone to actually coop with.  If the community was active, there is no doubt I would still be playing this game.  Despite its faults.
However if youre interested in the slightest in Dead Sky I would have to say quite clearly - avoid it!  I would love to recommend the game but there are better ones out there.  Nation Red being a fine example or Alien Swarm which is similar to some degree and is also free.  I guess it will remain a guilty pleasure of mine - one I will unfortunately never get to finish! :(

The trailer tells pretty much everything which is good in the game. I dont have to tell you how pretty the graphics are, and music is very atmospheric as well. If thats what you need, buy it and be very pleased!
Yet, when it comes to the game itself... The puzzles in the game are way too easy. I suppose the developers wanted every player to be able to finish the game and see all of it instead of getting stuck. The puzzles still should be a bit harder to make the gameplay more rewarding, as for now, it is pretty much picking up an object from the ground and attaching it to the obvious spot few meters away and then solving a basic gear/block/memory puzzle any 6 year old could solve. That said, the game is never boring either.
Biggest problem for me though was the dialogue. I felt that the game would be so much better with no dialogue, no text at all. There is very little dialogue to begin with and it is not very well written, so they should have just trusted more in their art and find other ways for characters to express themselves than poorishly written english. The atmosphere and art are all about unknown, -you are not even supposed to understand about where you are and what the creatures are-. So why does the dialogue have to be simple "I lost my egg, go get me my egg back!"  Some other adventure games such as called "Dropsy", "Machinarium" and "Botanicula" did this part marvellously (as well as surrealistic films made by Jan Svankmajer) , and I think that approach would have been more than suited for this game. Its a huge wasted oppurtinity that the developers didnt just put 100% on the shoulders of the art, but instead relied on old fashioned and unfitting text bubbles.
Still, for the fans of such art and atmosphere this is a must buy. Reminds me of the old  adventure game Dark Seed.

The criticism of this game has been really heavy, and much of it is deserved.  The game's menus deserve ALL of the criticism that you can muster, and then some.  However, some criticism, I feel, is misplaced or exaggerated.  I've heard a lot of criticism about grinding and microtransactions and extremely horrible starter decks.  While the starter decks are nothing amazing, if you pick a good one (I picked RG and it worked out just fine), you shouldn't have that much trouble doing the campaign and unlocking more cards.  Look for a deck list online to help you decide which starter deck to pick.  I personally find it a lot of fun to unlock packs and earn new cards to replace your horrible ones, and I think the unlocking (you could say grinding, if you wish) part of the game is very fair, all things considered.  You get a full pack of cards every time you win the duel and, like booster packs for the physical game, they guarantee a rare or mythic rare, plus 3 uncommons.  I've found it a lot MORE fun to 'grind' and unlock cards in this game, compared to older versions of DotP, because older versions of DotP only gave you 1 card (plus multiples of that same card, sometimes) every time you won, and the cards you unlocked often times weren't very good.  In this game, it truly does feel rewarding when you unlock a nice mythic rare that you can put in your deck.  Compared to Hearthstone, I would say this game is far superior at actually allowing you to acquire a good set of cards without paying extra money (my experience in Hearthstone has told me that it's a SLOW process in that game, unless you're particularly excellent at the Arena, which is why none of my friends nor myself have any interest in that game anymore).  It's also far superior at customization, since there aren't any restrictions on classes, or anything of the sort, but you must have already known that if you've played MTG before.  The customization is something that needs to be praised.  MTG has never been cheap, ever.  If you want to play on MTGO, you have to spend probably at least a couple hundred dollars to form a respectable, competitive constructed deck, or you could do draft tournaments, but those require a hefty amount of money per tournament.  It is far beyond my expectations that this version of DotP gives you completely free customization (within their more-limited, but not horribly limited card pool) for only 10 dollars, or 35 dollars if you want everything already unlocked (not counting premium cards).  But truly, it's a nice thing that when you actually do manage to acquire the cards that you want, you can actually build your own deck that feels GOOD to play.  It had always bothered me about the older versions that even when the decks were complete and you unlocked promo cards with the codes, the decks still felt really... weak.  This is just me personally, but I've never been a fan of 'weak' MTG.  I always enjoy a strong, competitive, constructed deck with a powerful and fluid strategy, so I give a hearty nod to the customization that this game offers.
That concludes the good, I would say.  It's enough good that I give this game a thumbs up and believe it's worth 10 dollars.  Now let's get to some of the... less good things.  I personally don't care in the slightest that they removed two headed giant and archenemy and sealed format, because I never liked them, but you might care, so beware.  It's a bit of a bummer that they removed the fun little challenges, but those never took much more than 10-20 minutes to finish all of them, anyway, so oh well.  The worst part of the game, though, by far in fact, is the horrible engine that it runs on.  It was OBVIOUSLY designed for phones, complete with a swipe menu that is really clunky and horrible feeling on a PC, and the menu even lags a bit and isn't as entirely responsive as you would like it to be.  The fancy animations can get really annoying when you have to wait 5 seconds every time you go to a menu screen.  I've also experienced a bit of slowness when actually playing the game, like a card would lag and not play right away when I click it, or something.  The menu is really horribly organized, too, so it can be hard to navigate through it, and unlike previous editions of DotP, the menu this time isn't just a horrizontal swipe (which is not ideal on PCs, but at least STOMACHABLE), but for some reason, it trails off diagonally, which makes it even more difficult to use and buggy with a PC.  If this game's engine was at least as smooth as previous games, and the menus were, shall we say, NORMAL, then I would consider it to be a fine game.  As is, it's a bit annoying, but I'm having my fun.  My dear hopes are that Wizards of the Coast takes a lot of the criticism that they're getting to heart and improve the game for next year's version.

EDIT: I have now completed the game and would like to revise my review a bit--no spoilers.  Leaving the original below the cut.
SOMA is definitely a horror game, but SOMA is not a horror game in what has become the conventional sense.  It's not so much about being scared as about examining the nature of both dread and hope and how they interact within the human psyche. I'm still very satisfied with the game. Frictional has done two things with this title:  they've produced an intellectual, existensial horror story and they've produced a bathypelagic, sci-fi horror story. Both of these are sufficiently rarely done well as to be of note. They have also done some brilliant design work, visually, certainly, but especially in the audio area.  The sound in this game will give you involuntary chills and raise the hair on your neck.
I can't promise you'll like this game, or that it will scare you.  Frankly, it rarely wound up really scaring me.  What it will do instead, if you let it, is push you into an uncomfortable emotional space where your own existensial crisis becomes more real to you and make you wonder about whether or not there is any meaning to hope.  It puts on offer a place of dread and a taste of hope to heighten it.  If that appeals to you, carry on.
--cut--
TL;DR - Terrifying, beautiful horror game, not recommended for those with short attention spans. Play in dark with headphones at own risk.
I've played about 8hrs of SOMA at this point and while I haven't finished the game yet, I feel like I can review it fairly accurately.  If you've played the games in the Amnesia or Penumbra series, you have a pretty good idea what it is you're getting into here. If you haven't, fair warning, everything you learned playing FPS games is pretty much working directly against you here. Unlearn it and enjoy.
Frictional have taken their horror formula and updated their engine and their setting for SOMA.  This is creepypasta science fiction (with a weird, Lovecraftian touch that feels like it's going on sub rosa the whole time). The game looks amazing and the sound design is good enough that people should probably study it to learn how to create suspense out of thin air with nothing but music and ambient sound. The game runs smoothly (I have hit a couple of segfaults, but such is the price I pay for playing a LInux game the day it's released) and the controls are sufficiently intuitive that your choice of mouse and keyboard or controller is pretty much irrelevant.
Other reviewers have criticized this game as being less scary than Amnesia.  I would actually posit that SOMA is scarier than Amnesia, but takes longer to build up the scare.  The early parts of the game are not particularly frightening, merely unsettling--and that's a key to good horror. The unsettling, constant shifting of the state of the world, the gradual decay of your initially fairly clear ideas about who you are and what is going on serve to set up the player for the payoff beautifully. By the time I quit playing I had actually had to make myself unclench my jaw and rub down the goosebumps on my arms.  This game has absolutely terrifying underpinnings and is willing to take the time and do the hard work necessary to deliver that terror to the player in full measure. This is not Doom. There are no jump scares here. There is Horror, and that is something very different.

Wherever you never played Tangram before or you did, you will love this cute puzzle game to relax. If you are looking for a real challenge, move on because most of the puzzles can easily be solved under or around a minute and only several will take some more minutes.
Very nice graphics, effects and animations. The game is really colorful so it's good for your eyes.
Only one cons is that all solved puzzles come in yellow and it would have been better to stay in that colorful theme. Despite being yellow the solved tangram let you see a nice yellow shape highlighted with some cute ink artwork.
A few sounds make this game relaxing as well as one ambiant music (menu) and a relaxing music (puzzles).
Wherever you never played Tangram before or you did, the game will have a tutorial. A nice feature that the game introduces is that overlapped pieces are highlighted in grey.
So in short Tangram is a Chinese puzzle invented some decades ago. Ta	ngram mean literally "Seven Boards of Cunning", each piece wasn't randomly selected. Each with their own size and shape. So with only 7 pieces you can make hundreds of different shapes.
Most of the shapes you need to make (outlines) have a larger scale, meaning that you don't need to worry about saving space between adjacent pieces. A few times even if you have solved the puzzle, you need to find which piece is not correctly placed : you just need to move a bit each piece until you finally beat the level.
And sometimes the shapes you need to make (outlines) have a smaller scale and that time you really need to save every bit of space available to solved the puzzle.
When you've solved puzzles you get a nice showcase at the end.
Nothing to say, you just have to solve all the puzzles.

In The God’s Chain, we have the nonsensical description about what the game is about, and our goal involves much exploration, but via foot only. The main mission is to destroy stations on an unknown land, and which we may be approached by alien hostiles. This is probably the only half-decent constituent of the story. The rest was, simply, a nightmare.
We’ll start with the controls in the game. You move as a character using AWSD keys and can shoot with the mouse. X key puts you into 3rd person, and a reload option that doesn’t even work. Shooting was difficult in my end due to the high, and unchangeable mouse sensitivity. There’s no tutorial or guide in the game either on what your controls are, or how to reload, so you have a parlous start.
The graphics and effects were also ick. Don’t expect any AAA graphics in this game. Expect to see ships with transparent to flimsy walls, aliens that can only shoot in one direction and no ammo supplies. A lot of bugs and glitches are featured in this game, such as; running and falling off the map, which is literally a cut-off part of the land; not dying at times when being shot continuously by an alien; nonexistent hit boxes, and more. You will already be attacked by two aliens by spawn on land. What’s worse, is there not being any gameover screen, or the game restarting at all, once you’ve died. You’ll need to exit the game and jump back in manually, thus resetting your progress. The only part that was close to consistent was the beginning, where you can explore the inside of the ship.
The effects and animations are as detailed as a satellite disappearing into thin air when you shoot it.
The audio and background music was generic and forgotten on my end. There was also voice acting, which was, to put it bluntly, bad. The voice actor sounded more like a high school student in a class, forced to read a script by the teacher. They were nowhere near professional, or had any tone or emotion with the dialect itself.
From falling off the map, horrendous controls and questionable effects … Even I am having a hard time explaining how much of a train-wreck of a game this is. I have not touched the other game modes, since its story mode already establishes much of how the game play will be. I’ve had my fair share of playing The God’s Chain, and never again. It gets a thumbs down from me.

Playfully skipping through your subconscience to give you a horror experience to remember. What else, the Story. The Story for me is great! After you leave your house and stuff (Im intentionally giving little context to avoid Spoilers) you go to the hospital, after trapsing about for a few minutes i found out what i had to do then i got stuff injected into my brain and BOOM you end up on Upsilon Station. After you wake up in the Station, you are immediately met with this overbearing sense of Dread and Despair. You see a very Dark area before you as you stand from the chair. The atmosphere, as expected from Frictional, is stellar. Dark shades, blurry surroundings, mix that with the ambience where you can hear the entire station creaking and moaning. For the uninitiated, the Station if you cant tell from the screen shots is underwater. Well, under the ocean. On the seafloor. To go further i will have to spoil some of the plot. STARTING NOW!!!
Okay. Upsilon is a Geothermal plant at the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean. After slowly emerging from the room you awoke in, you hear the moaning. The entire station wailing in agony. Of course all Metaphorical. So you go into this corridor, and you look to your right and left. A hallway. To your left is a locked room. To your right is a bigger open area. So you slowly peek out of each side then begin to go into the room. then you are struck by the brooding dark atmosphere. This is a HUGE buildup for the game. And its so effective! After a while of exploring and a few jumpscares, well "Jumpscares" i use the term lightly. You eventually get, The Omnitool! You can now go unlock that door you saw before. So you make your way back and open the door. Again after waltzing about the station for a while you come across a Robot. Well more of a Machine. She doesnt speak but shes hooked up to the power supply, sapping its power. When you unplug one of the two tubes connected to it, she says something and you unplug the other one. She dies. But when she spoke to you after taking out one she said something in a VERY human voice. As if its a human within a machine. So you continue after she dies and you come across a terminal. You speak to a woman named Catherine who is at the station Lambda. Communication breaks down and you continue along. A Classic Horror trope, the communication being broken suddenly. But oddly enough Catherine is extremely calm. As if she doesnt know whats going on. So she reccomends you go to the Comm tower before she cuts out which btw is really close by So you go into the next room where you see a Well going down to the earths core. Again Upsilon is a geothermal Plant. So after passing that you are met with the classic sequence where you avoid the sight of a monster. But its a machine with this weird growth on it. It stamps around loudly so dont worry about losing it. You pass by it, pull a lever near the stairs, and you go upstairs and close the mechanical hatch behind you. Thats important BTW you should close the hatch behind you. As you ascend the next set of stairs, The machine bangs against the hatch and you continue along. Well he only bangs if he saw you walk up there. Anyways. You find out your in a brand new area and you must get to the Comm tower, of which is directly above you and accessable through a staircase right next to the one you just ascended. So an Assembly line, being expendable in this intense situation youd go for, Unfortunately you have to manually shut it down. So you go into the room adjacent to you where the line is and when you go inside...you find another robot. When you speak to him, he speaks to you as if hes human. In a human body. After SOMA's credits rolled, I had to take a moment to reflect on the emotional rollarcoaster ride that was Frictional Games's new horrror title. Although this game's technical issues, lack of scares, and redundant puzzles make it far from perfect, the 11 hour campaign tells one of the most insightful, engaging, and well crafted stories I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing. Unlike Amnesia, it's not an incredibly gruesome or disturbing tale, but it's abillty to force the player ask themselves questions about concepts that humans are often too afraid explore, helps create a tremendous sense of unease that only grows throughout the course of the game. This title also brings back mod support, which was an astounding success in Amnesia The Dark Descent, and with many more assets to work with, expect that there will be many mods worth playing.
Pros:
+ Incredible story, one of the best I've ever experienced
+ Amazing sound desgin, and use of ambiance
+ Acompletely unique environment for a horror title
+ Multiple frightening  enemies
+ Descisions that will test your morals
+ 11 hours of playtime
+ Intense, stressful situations
+ Immersive, tense atmosphere throughout
+ Return of mod support
Cons:
- Technical issues including bugs, crashing, low framerates and frame drops
- Most puzzles are annoying, and serve little purpose other than increasing playtime
- Lacks scary moments
- Some enemies can be avoided simply by sprinting past them
- Speech in recordings is unclear and distorted, forcing me to turn subtitles on
Verdict:  Amazing. It's flaws do weight it down a bit, but in the grand scheme of things  the story, and the numerous other elements that are  well done, easily overshadow some of the minor frustrations you willl encounter while playing this. This is the best horror game of 2015 by a significant margin. 9.0/10

If I had to describe this game in three words, they would be:  generic, childish, and tedious.
Generic because:  There is absolutely no innovation here.  The first puzzle plays the same as the last puzzle because no new rules (e.g. no two pieces of the same color can touch) or mechanics are ever introduced.
Childish because:  The difficulty barely ever moves beyond easy, which is unsurprising because
Many of the puzzles, in order to create the shape of the thing that they are supposed to represent, feature empty slots where only one piece can possibly go, which makes them even more trivial.  I completed the average puzzle in under 20 seconds.  I have done harder tangram puzzles in hidden object games and even in free-to-play games.
Tedious because:  Since no new mechanics are introduced, the difficulty does not increase, and the shapes do not change, it simply feels like a chore to continue playing.
As for the art and music, there isn't much to say.  The simplistic art that you see in the store page's video is all you will ever see and the two songs (an ambient one for the selection menu and a standard one during gameplay to which whistles are introduced upon completion of a level) are all you will ever hear.
I only encountered one minor bug:  sometimes a puzzle would complete itself before I finished dragging over the last piece.
This is an all-around low-effort attempt unworthy of $5, especially with much better games out there for the same price or less.  It
