Dead Pixels is a 2D shooter survival horror game. Your main goal in the game is to make your way across a number of streets, shooting and smacking through zombies to survive. Dead zombies will drop cash. Along the way you'll find buildings to raid for useful items like guns, ammo, and valuables. There are also some traders stationed along the otherwise abandoned streets, looking for some good profit from the dire situation I suppose. You can buy all sort of items, weapons, ammo, and upgrades from traders, as well as sell some of your own things for cash. Basically, that's the entire game in a nutshell. Kill zombies, raid buildings, deal with traders, and try to make it to the end without dying. Pretty simple and fun.
There IS strategy involved, though. You see, you have a weight limit on what you can carry, and everything outside of ammo will weigh you down. If you go over that capacity, you will become over encumbered, which will result in your movement being reduced. And what's really neat about this is that, the more extra weight you carry, the slower you become. You can even get completely immobilized if you have too much. But you never are forced to strickly carry only what will fit in your capacity, which give you some freedom in what you value: items or your speed. Some items may not be too useful, such as valuables and weaker or duplicate guns, but they can be sold later. So do you hold on to your money makers, or try to just carry the essentials? Also, when at the traders, what skills do you want to upgrade? What will benefit you the most? Do you want to have more powerful shots to use less ammo, or maybe you should work on bargaining so other things will be cheaper in the long run. Should you sell your item here or bring it back to the trader a few streets back that was offering a good sum for it? Is backtracking worth risking possible ammo and health supplies to get more money? There are a lot of tough calls to make and replayability allows you to experiment with different strategies.
And let's not forget co op. In co op you have two people working together to survive, which can be helpful and harmful. You get twice the carrying capacity, twice the melee action, and you can do some distraction and splitting tactics with the clumps of zombies. However, you are forced to share all resources, as the shops only have limited amounts in stock. You also have to be careful not to trap another player on the edge of the screen from moving forward of backward. On the bright side, if one of you dies, the other can revive them at a trader... if they can make it there alone. Working together requires planning. You have to share resources. Who needs what more? What upgrades will compliment each other well? How will your playstyles affect each other's? Again, it's a lot to think about.
This game does SEEM like each playthrough would be a unique experence. However, I don't think that's quite the case. There ARE a good number of different things as far as guns, valuables, throwable weapons, and items go I suppose. And with the randomization of traders, prices, drops, buildings, guns, ammo... and well... almost everything that's important... the thing is... this randomization hardly changes the gameplay. You still shoot zombies, raid buildings, and visit traders the same way basically every time. The only difference is what they have to offer, what you randomly find, and the exact locations of places. That's about it. There's a case for it being different each time with how you choose to upgrade your character, but since each skill only has a few levels of upgrades, you can easily get close to if not actually max all of your stats in a single playthrough. This all makes the variety a little lacking.
Another complain I have is that, while there are a lot of different weapons, they all fit into categories based on their ammo type. This means that, at any given time, you'll probably only carry one gun of each type with you for the sake of convenience and weight management. It makes the game easier to navigate with less guns at a time, but really lacks in giving good variety. Although, there IS some variety in the extra couple of modes and different difficulty settings. So that's nice for slight change ups on essentially the same gameplay.
My smallest complaint is that this is one of those games that doesn't really commit to the retro style. Sure, the graphics and some of the sound effects are 8 bit, but the music, other sound effects, and some visual effects are much more modern. Not to mention the controls. The aesthetic is neat, but I guess it feels a little more like a reference to old games rather than reflecting the style. Maybe I'm looking too far into it.
I do like some of the music in the game. There's some decent humor in it too. A lot of people might complain about the co op only being local, but I can't blame the game for something it didn't do. The local co op is a blast and honestly, online co op would most likely be laggy and not as fun anyway. This game is a great sleepover game. You and a buddy can just play it over and over for a night and it's tons of simple fun. The controls are a bit awkward at first, not being very retro styled at all. After a bit a play you'll start to get the hand of it and realize how helpful they are. I was assuming there'd be one fire button and one button for grenades, and that they would be used in the direction I was facing. However, instead you use the left and right shoulder buttons to attack left and right. Sounds confusing at first, but it becomes very helpful. Sometmes you'll be running away from zombies but you'll still want to shoot them. Well you can't do both if you have to turn around to face them. This setup let's you more efficiently run and gun. Be careful though, as your melee attack only goes the way you are facing. Overall, I think the controls are pretty intuitive for this kind of game.
So, what's the verdict? Well, this game is a lot of simple, good fun. I'd say it's easily worth $5 on here. However, the asking price is only $3. That's a pretty sweet deal already. But if you're still not sure, wait for a sale. I got it on sale for $1 and look how much playtime I got out of it already? Plus, I've seen it go as low as 74 cents. It's definitely a great title to keep in mind when you have leftover Steam wallet funds from card sales or after you bought some other game you really wanted. It's a nice way to not let that extra cash go to waste just sitting there in your Steam wallet. I'd recommend this is you like simple shooters, 8 bit graphics, or zombie survival games. The world of 80 Days is interesting, the dialogues very well written and the Art style looks nice. However the game has a few aspects that can be frustratring as well. The other thing that could cause some frustration is that (contrary to the Sorcery! games by the same dev) there is no Undo button and you only have one save which automatically gets overwritten. I'm almost certain both of those things are intentional design decisions and they fit the theme quite nicely but they also make the game more hectic than other "Choose your own Adventure" games.

Advantages:
- you can finally build your own deck, freely without any limitations (other than cards available in game)
Disadvantages:
- slow and unresponsive menu - you have to click the same button multiple times or wait 5 seconds for stupid animation to finish
- interface bugs - sometimes when asked to make a choice you are unable to do this (e.g. you are asked to choose a card from graveyard but you cannot look into the graveyard) - the only solution is to concede a duel
- game play bugs such as AI taping one swamp to pay "one black mana + X any mana" with X = 1
- AI is taking a lot of time to make the choice (as in the previous editions)
- the game gets boring after you unlock all the cards by playing campaign
- only standard games - no archenemy, no planechase, no two headed giant
- no challenge puzzles
- some cards cannot be unlocked in the campaign, but have to be bought via micro transactions
- a lot of cards implemented in the game are not available to the player, but are used by AI
Overall the game is very disappointing and unless you are huge MTG fan you shouldn't waste your money on it. It's based on the same engine as previous editions, so the only work they have actually done was adding a deck building tool and implemented new cards.

EDIT: I have now completed the game and would like to revise my review a bit--no spoilers.  Leaving the original below the cut.
SOMA is definitely a horror game, but SOMA is not a horror game in what has become the conventional sense.  It's not so much about being scared as about examining the nature of both dread and hope and how they interact within the human psyche. I'm still very satisfied with the game. Frictional has done two things with this title:  they've produced an intellectual, existensial horror story and they've produced a bathypelagic, sci-fi horror story. Both of these are sufficiently rarely done well as to be of note. They have also done some brilliant design work, visually, certainly, but especially in the audio area.  The sound in this game will give you involuntary chills and raise the hair on your neck.
I can't promise you'll like this game, or that it will scare you.  Frankly, it rarely wound up really scaring me.  What it will do instead, if you let it, is push you into an uncomfortable emotional space where your own existensial crisis becomes more real to you and make you wonder about whether or not there is any meaning to hope.  It puts on offer a place of dread and a taste of hope to heighten it.  If that appeals to you, carry on.
--cut--
TL;DR - Terrifying, beautiful horror game, not recommended for those with short attention spans. Play in dark with headphones at own risk.
I've played about 8hrs of SOMA at this point and while I haven't finished the game yet, I feel like I can review it fairly accurately.  If you've played the games in the Amnesia or Penumbra series, you have a pretty good idea what it is you're getting into here. If you haven't, fair warning, everything you learned playing FPS games is pretty much working directly against you here. Unlearn it and enjoy.
Frictional have taken their horror formula and updated their engine and their setting for SOMA.  This is creepypasta science fiction (with a weird, Lovecraftian touch that feels like it's going on sub rosa the whole time). The game looks amazing and the sound design is good enough that people should probably study it to learn how to create suspense out of thin air with nothing but music and ambient sound. The game runs smoothly (I have hit a couple of segfaults, but such is the price I pay for playing a LInux game the day it's released) and the controls are sufficiently intuitive that your choice of mouse and keyboard or controller is pretty much irrelevant.
Other reviewers have criticized this game as being less scary than Amnesia.  I would actually posit that SOMA is scarier than Amnesia, but takes longer to build up the scare.  The early parts of the game are not particularly frightening, merely unsettling--and that's a key to good horror. The unsettling, constant shifting of the state of the world, the gradual decay of your initially fairly clear ideas about who you are and what is going on serve to set up the player for the payoff beautifully. By the time I quit playing I had actually had to make myself unclench my jaw and rub down the goosebumps on my arms.  This game has absolutely terrifying underpinnings and is willing to take the time and do the hard work necessary to deliver that terror to the player in full measure. This is not Doom. There are no jump scares here. There is Horror, and that is something very different.

First off let me say something about me. Im absolutely terrified of the depths. True Depths. Like bottom of the goddamn ocean depths. I have a keen fear of Underwater Horror. That sounds weird to say, purely because it shows no context of the fear, but its like this. The game is ♥♥♥♥ING AMAZING!! The Graphics may not be "Next-Gen" but that is such a disgusting and overused and pointless term so we arent even going to touch that. But the Graphics are VERY servicable. It seems to be extrordinarily familiar to the graphics of Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs. Next up, the sound quality. Oh my GOD the sounds you hear in this game are foggy but thats stylistic, obviously. I may have only played 2 hours of this game but i can say im terrified to continue. Thus far the Sound has been absolutely goreous. When your inside, the sounds are crystal clear and eerie, perfect atmosphere, and ambience to match. The sounds and environment hold each other hand in hand. Playfully skipping through your subconscience to give you a horror experience to remember. What else, the Story. The Story for me is great! Not exactly top of the line but its rare you come across a game like that. But the story is really really good. Amazing in my opinion. It gets you going almost right off the bat with a beautifully done opening sequence, a false sence of Security. Something Frictional is quite adept at performing. After you leave your house and stuff (Im intentionally giving little context to avoid Spoilers) you go to the hospital, after trapsing about for a few minutes i found out what i had to do then i got stuff injected into my brain and BOOM you end up on Upsilon Station. After you wake up in the Station, you are immediately met with this overbearing sense of Dread and Despair. You see a very Dark area before you as you stand from the chair. The atmosphere, as expected from Frictional, is stellar. Dark shades, blurry surroundings, mix that with the ambience where you can hear the entire station creaking and moaning. For the uninitiated, the Station if you cant tell from the screen shots is underwater. Well, under the ocean. On the seafloor. To go further i will have to spoil some of the plot. So ill end it with this for those who dont want spoilers, THIS GAME IS AMAZING! if you LOVE horror buy this game NOW. Expect a little bit of a slow start but an ultimately amazing experience. AGAIN WARNING!! SPOILERS!!!
STARTING NOW!!!
Okay. Upsilon is a Geothermal plant at the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean. After slowly emerging from the room you awoke in, you hear the moaning. The entire station wailing in agony. Of course all Metaphorical. So you go into this corridor, and you look to your right and left. A hallway. To your left is a locked room. To your right is a bigger open area. So you slowly peek out of each side then begin to go into the room. then you are struck by the brooding dark atmosphere. This is a HUGE buildup for the game. And its so effective! After a while of exploring and a few jumpscares, well "Jumpscares" i use the term lightly. You eventually get, The Omnitool! You can now go unlock that door you saw before. So you make your way back and open the door. Again after waltzing about the station for a while you come across a Robot. Well more of a Machine. She doesnt speak but shes hooked up to the power supply, sapping its power. When you unplug one of the two tubes connected to it, she says something and you unplug the other one. She dies. But when she spoke to you after taking out one she said something in a VERY human voice. As if its a human within a machine. So you continue after she dies and you come across a terminal. You speak to a woman named Catherine who is at the station Lambda. Communication breaks down and you continue along. A Classic Horror trope, the communication being broken suddenly. But oddly enough Catherine is extremely calm. As if she doesnt know whats going on. So she reccomends you go to the Comm tower before she cuts out which btw is really close by So you go into the next room where you see a Well going down to the earths core. Again Upsilon is a geothermal Plant. So after passing that you are met with the classic sequence where you avoid the sight of a monster. But its a machine with this weird growth on it. It stamps around loudly so dont worry about losing it. You pass by it, pull a lever near the stairs, and you go upstairs and close the mechanical hatch behind you. Thats important BTW you should close the hatch behind you. As you ascend the next set of stairs, The machine bangs against the hatch and you continue along. Well he only bangs if he saw you walk up there. Anyways. You find out your in a brand new area and you must get to the Comm tower, of which is directly above you and accessable through a staircase right next to the one you just ascended. Unfortunately to give it power you must chose between flow control and an Assembly line. Obviously you would go with the assembly line right? Its easily sacrificial but when you at the bottom of the goddamn ocean you kinda dont want to comprimise anything that could be contributing to the Pressurization or to the overall integrity of the station. So an Assembly line, being expendable in this intense situation youd go for, Unfortunately you have to manually shut it down. So you go into the room adjacent to you where the line is and when you go inside...you find another robot. When you speak to him, he speaks to you as if hes human. In a human body. As you speak to him he explain who he is and when you ask if hes human he says "is it the body that gave it away?" And clanks his clamper hand to his head. Gesturing that he believes he is still within a human body. Personally i like him. He was a cool dude. Emphasis on was. This is where the difficulty in the decision come in. After you and him argue,  due to his existental crisis of believing he is human despite being a hunk of assorted parts he stops chatting and tells you to go get a doctor. Hes injured. Really he is missing legs. So you go to the left and you find a switch. Finally the ♥♥♥♥ing power. And here is the most brutal moment ive encountered thus far. This one moment actually made me feel bad. After you turn off the power. For some reason, hes still on, and hes sparking, and Screaming. Loudly. The most human screams of pain you can hear. I didnt really want to hear it for too long so i turned the power back on, which stopped his agony. You talk to him and he begs you to find a Doctor. But there is none you can access currently. So i turned off the power again, only to hear his wails. I turned it off again because i felt bad and he stops talking to you. Hes alive but he stops talking to you. I turned the power off finally and he screams and screams and screams. I attempt to ignore this and be on my merry way, but as you turn on the Comm Tower hatch, as you climb the stairs you can still hear him screeching. It has an effect on the player that your leaving him in perpetual agony rather than leaving him there indefinately. After the hatch to the Comm Tower closes you then stop hearing his screaming. Ill leave off here. This game is absolutley amazing. The part im at im a little frustrated with because it involves something im not at all familiar with. But of course it could also be just my fault. If you love horror games this game is FOR YOU!! If you like Gore Horror, Underwater Horror, Atmospheric Horror, Horror Horror, This game is without a doubt up your alley. Buy it NOW!

After SOMA's credits rolled, I had to take a moment to reflect on the emotional rollarcoaster ride that was Frictional Games's new horrror title. Although this game's technical issues, lack of scares, and redundant puzzles make it far from perfect, the 11 hour campaign tells one of the most insightful, engaging, and well crafted stories I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing. Unlike Amnesia, it's not an incredibly gruesome or disturbing tale, but it's abillty to force the player ask themselves questions about concepts that humans are often too afraid explore, helps create a tremendous sense of unease that only grows throughout the course of the game. This title also brings back mod support, which was an astounding success in Amnesia The Dark Descent, and with many more assets to work with, expect that there will be many mods worth playing.
Pros:
+ Incredible story, one of the best I've ever experienced
+ Amazing sound desgin, and use of ambiance
+ Acompletely unique environment for a horror title
+ Multiple frightening  enemies
+ Descisions that will test your morals
+ 11 hours of playtime
+ Intense, stressful situations
+ Immersive, tense atmosphere throughout
+ Return of mod support
Cons:
- Technical issues including bugs, crashing, low framerates and frame drops
- Most puzzles are annoying, and serve little purpose other than increasing playtime
- Lacks scary moments
- Some enemies can be avoided simply by sprinting past them
- Speech in recordings is unclear and distorted, forcing me to turn subtitles on
Verdict:  Amazing. It's flaws do weight it down a bit, but in the grand scheme of things  the story, and the numerous other elements that are  well done, easily overshadow some of the minor frustrations you willl encounter while playing this. This is the best horror game of 2015 by a significant margin. 9.0/10

The main reason I'm giving this game a positive review is because of the low price. Otherwise, I would probably give it a neutral review. I will dive into that in a bit. Basically this is a fun game where you eat and poop! Your goal is to hit food with awesome fun music in the background, and then use that poop fuel to poop! I love the idea, the fun behind it, and the play. But there are a lot of cons that really need to be fixed before I can give it a solid positive review.
Cons:
The game is super laggy. I would like to say its my comptuer but this is a game that isn't high on graphics, and I've had less problems with higher quality games. Lagginess can cause you to lose a beat which is extremely frustrating.
The point system doesn't make sense after awhile. I could get an absolutely perfect score and still get 3rd place. Doesn't make sense. It seems to be based on the fact of how much food they choose to give you during that song, and if you get a lot of bombs you can't utilize you get a lower score by chance. Also, wiping out all the people with your poop doesn't give you any kind of bonus other than the regular multiplier. I strongly suggest they implement a better scoring system.
The music beat is off according ot hitting the food, which it mentioned it was supposed to be on beat. I used to play Elite Beat Agents on the DS that used beats to music and that was extremely fun. I wish they would more closely implement that idea. Also, I read you can upload your music but its so frustrating to do that it can be pointless.
This last part isn't so much a con as a suggestion, after hardcore it would be nice to have an even more difficult level for greater replay value.

The game is awesome, but the story is meh, I mean it's not bad and all but it is sad (and yes what i said does rhyme unintentionally) but back to the point.
The game itself while not being the best, is a good game, the graphics aren't bad and while I'll admit all of the maps aren't the best it's alright.
While some people argue the point that it's like "Call of Duty" because you have to go from point A to B, the game has puzzles, it has more difficult situations, it has a variety of ayylmao's you can kill with different powerups and furthermore it has mini activities you can do and random objects in the world that you can interract with like a casino machine or a pinball machine.
Now you're probably wondering "Wait why does this game have bad ratings?" well even if you aren't thinking that, shut up and keep reading.
The main reason why people didn't recommend it was simply because it wasn't like its previous predecessor "Duke Nukem 3D" which released on January 29th 1996.
While the game itself isn't at all "bad" or anything people had high expectations and the game didn't follow through on those certain expectations of course though if you haven't played any of the Duke Nukem titles then this one won't be a problem for you.
If you're expecting a game like Duke Nukem 3D with revamped graphics then you're not on the right game, while this game is fun in my opinion it doesn't have that fast pace to it, or that nostalgia so don't expect that nostalgia hard on because it's not here trust me.
Here are the basic Pros and Cons (Of course all these pros and cons are based on opinion as well as what it actually is, results may vary)
Pros
+Good graphics for it's time
+Has an alright array of weaponary
+Has some funny cheesy moments here and there
+Duke talk
+Epic boss battles
+Long story (atleast 5-15 hours gameplay max)
+Awesome soundtracks (though what the hell do soundtracks have to do with the story or anything?)
Cons
-Multiplayer is sort of empty(because everyone hates this game for no reason)
-Can be slighty boring at times
-Most boss battles do give you unlimited ammo, which sort of crushes the concept of a boss battle
-Doesn't feel as fast paced as Duke Nukem 3D
So in the end all I can really say is, you should put it on your wishlist and wait until it's on sale as Steam will notify you if it does go on sale, because even if you hate it I'm sure spending $4 is better than spending $20 anyway happy gaming!

Disclaimer: I own Siege on Uplay, not through Steam.
Siege is my go to game currently, and as someone who used to play a lot of CS:GO, I'm happy I found Siege. It keeps the 5 v 5 competitive design, but other than that, it plays pretty different from Counter Strike. Players choose from different offense and defense operators and attempt to plant a defuser, capture an area, or secure the hostage. Each operator's ability is unique and fun, though some are more popular than others. Shooting is closer to Battlefield or CoD than Counter Strike, and isn't that hard to learn (rumor is that learnable recoil patterns are coming in the distant future - yes please). The real learning curve is learning the operators and the maps, which can take a while as the maps are quite complex.
Unfortunately, this game has its fair share of bugs, and while things are much better now than they were, say, a year ago, it can still be an issue. It's always good to remember that it took a couple years for CS:GO to become the game it is today. However, it really looks like Ubisoft is going to keep up support for years, so right now is a great time to get into this fresh shooter.

but the plot is simple enough to understand: rich man makes a bet he can travel around the world in 80 days. Adventure ensues. The plot of this game is the same. You play as this rich guy's valet, which means you do all the work. He has the money. This is life kids, get used to it.
4. On your journey, you have a few basic tasks: find routs to new destinations, book travel, buy and sell equipment and accessories, manage money and attend to the needs of your rich guy master.
5. Circumnavigating the globe in 80 days is not terribly difficult. You are graded on how well you did in certain areas but mostly you have to find your own challenge if challenge is what you want.
6. You can chose to try to go around the world as fast as possible. You can try to visit the most cities. You can find the cheapest routs. You can try to keep your rich guy master as comfortable as possible if you want to do that for some reason. Esp. if you don't care about actually finishing in 80 days, you can do whatever it is you damn well please.
7. Each playthrough of this builds from a different seed but the variations are not that great. If you chose to take the Trans-Siberian express across Asia every time, you are going to run into about the same situations each time. If you want something truly different, you have to take it upon yourself to find it. I think ultimately this is a good thing because, really, if you want to make it your goal to get through as fast as possible, you need some consistency.
8.  Really, the joy here is in finding on how your journey plays out depending on what choices you made. Each city you visit has a bit of a story which you will discover both before, during and after your visit. The people you meet have stories you can learn about or chose to ignore. Things you do early on affect how your journey transpires later. This game is about making a story out of a few simple choices.
9. You can totally make out w/ both dudes and chicks in this if you got the swagger to pull it off.
10. The writing in this is a pretty impressive feat. Almost every few sentences, there is an opportunity for player input and the writing always goes along seamlessly w/o seeming award or computer generated. I think they must have had a writer or team of writers actually go through and compose these hundreds or thousands of conversations trees.
11. There are lots of little annoyances while playing but nothing really gamebreaking. It drives me nuts that the clock keeps running at hyper-fast in-game time while you are shopping or reviewing travel options. I get that it takes in-game time to do these things but you can basically lose a day if you get distracted in real life for two minutes.
12. Rich your guy master in this is kind of a♥♥♥♥♥♥ OK, really a♥♥♥♥♥♥ If I could offer the developers one improvement on gameplay, you should allow players to kill him and pay off officials to look the other way.
13. Honestly, during my first playthrough, I got kind of bored by the end of the game which makes it a bit hard to wholeheartedly recommend this . But as I was thinking about it afterward, something happned: I decided that I wanted to play it again. And it was worth it! So, yeah, pick this up if you like stories and also like videogames.

This games environment and ambience in general is very beautiful. I obtained this game just recently and i have to say that the game came a long way since it was first released. Everything is designed to give the person playing a "life like" experience. You literally feel as if youre in the game yourself as there is so much to do, hunt, build, and etc. Making or joining a community can be great and very interesting for the most part , as this game is completely community based as your gameplay goes on. For these reasons and a perhaps a few others, i say that this is a really great game to check out.
There is a negative side to things though, but in this review im going to focus on the character creation. The game does not really follow the aspects of its own title...well the "YOUR OWN" part. I believe the idea of the game was to in a sense, self insert yourself into the game; put yourself in the open world to fend and make the most of yourself. But i see that really difficult when there's only 3 races you can possibly pick in the game. Knowing the intention for their game, why did they decide to give the player no variety on races? It beats me. But i think this is something that should be thought of in the near future.
Everyone who plays this game will not be white or asian (hence the 3 races are basically White, white, and asian). So from my perspective and probably others, the lack of variety makes it somewhat hard to have that "self insert" vibe when playing. I see it as a major factor  that if took into consideration (as in adding races that resemble the african american, spanish, or indian race and so on) this will enhance a persons enjoyment and experience in the game when they can make a character  that represents themselves and possibly their culture in RP.
Other than that, as i said, i would highly consider to try this game, because overall, you will not be dissappointed. Just know there's A LOT TO LEARN. But it will all be understood in due time.

An interesting game, it's similar to Amnesia in a lot of ways (enemy mechanics, puzzles, the "screen sanity meter" etc.) but with a few gameplay changes, such as no inventory/HUD of any kind (except for when you take damage).
Like Amnesia, the gameplay revolves around exploring areas, solving puzzles and evading monsters. Unfortunately I found SOMA's puzzles to be a bit dull, most of them involve flipping various switches, and none of them really give you any feedback on whether or not you're doing it right. I also found the seafloor sections could drag on a bit with nothing to do except run towards your objective, and some of the areas could get repetitive in terms of their design.
However, it compensated for this with its great atmosphere and story. Granted the story is quite far-fetched, but I found it to be more interesting and thought-provoking than Amnesia's. There were a few loose ends that didn't really get tied up, and the ending was left kind of open, but maybe I just didn't find all the audio logs or something. There's lots of attention to detail in the level design, not all of which may be necessary as most of the levels are "industrial interior" or "seafloor". I'm not sure about it's replayability, you do make some choices throughout the game but none of them seem to have any effect on the overall outcome other than changing some dialogue.
I also didn't find it particularly "scary", it was more of a psychological, tense experience. But it definitely kept me interested to see where the story would end up, and what impact, if any, my choices would have. It took me about 8 hours for my first playthrough, that was with me exploring and listening to audio logs, reading things on computer terminals etc. You could probably do it in less or more time depending on your playstyle, so I'd say it can range anywhere from 6-10 hours. Frictional had the decency not to make it a full price game for this reason, I think.
Even if you don't like horror games, you can enjoy this for its sci-fi tension and story. Check it out.

This game is fantastic. It feels like a return to the roots of Amnesia: The Dark Descent, but in a modern sci-fi setting and with a richer story.
One can definitely see the results of the increased budget for this game; the graphics are better, optimisation is good and the attention to details are amazing. All the little things you can find an interact with, crabs on the seafloor and whatnot. It all helps create an immersive experience.
This game isn't just all cheap jumpscares, far from it, it's a very psychologically challenging game. The world around you feels alien and deserted. You feel alone.
And even though there isn't a constant threat around you throughout the whole game, as it has its quiet sequences with puzzles and all that, it's a design that works pretty well for the game. I like that there are intermittent quiet sequences in the game where I can take the time to read all the notes, look at all the journals and pictures, and listen to the recordings. Some of the quiet sequences are a bit too long though and could do with some additional threats.
Pros:
+ Great story that has you on the edge all the way throughout the game.
+ Very gritty and immersive atmosphere that makes the scarier parts of the game even more scary.
+ No handholding. There are nice puzzles and don't expect big signs to always point you in the right direction.
+ Decent graphics and believable world.
Cons:
- The voice acting is a tad bland... I suppose. I might be intentional considering the nature of the people in the game, but some lines sounded quite bad.
- The game could do with a slightly more persistent threat. Some of the quiet sequences are too long.

Dead Sky is an overhead dual stick shooter with a zombie theme and a cell shaded aesthetic that you'll never notice, because you're above the action. In short, the game has a lot of good mechanics I do enjoy, but the whole game is just marred by dull, uninspired level design and poor choices that make what could be an awesome game far too dull and needlessly difficult to enjoy. The game has a single player campaign, but boasts online multiplayer through a server connection, so you'll need friends and someone to host.
I'll start with the good. The game plays well enough and a controller is recommended. You have a trigger to shoot enemies, a left stick to walk and a right stick to aim. You have a flashlight that you can turn on or off, but since it never runs low on power, why turn it off? Then there's one button to reload and another to interact with things. The interactions are limited and most of the time you're picking up a weapon with the button. Other times you can pull a wall switch using the button.
To make the game more interesting, you can use the interact button to pick up and place objects that you'll find or forge using scrap. I say forge, but its just paying to have it made. There are gun sentries, flame sentries, barbed wire barricades, bear traps and so on. It turns the game into a tower defense that I rather enjoy, even if the levels are just too dull and simple to get much out of them. The companion, and weapons do their job with the only catch being that you still need to collect things from the corpses. As well as it does its job, i question the choice of targets that the sentries make. When something is closer to them, they chose to shoot a further target. Perhaps that's just closer to their view cone. Whatever the reason, I'd shoot the enemy beating me up than the one further away.
You'll find a wide array of foes, most of which are inspired or taken from Resident Evil. If you're going to take something, borrow from the best. There are arm stretching mutants, zombie attack dogs, swat zombies, electric zombies and bosses with sack heads wielding chainsaws. Other than that, there are acid sputters, exploding foes, typical zombies and a giant worm of a boss that burrows out of the ground.
There's a diverse array of things to do with good simple mechanics to do them, such as driving sections, shooting sections, on the fly tower defense and boring turret sections. Shooting zombies from a helicopter the size of ants with a mini gun designed to shoot from the side rather than top down is a needless chore. Having a cool down mechanic only prolongs the experience.
None of it is all that fun. Shooting feels weak. You can get shotguns, flame throwers and machine guns, but it never affects the zombies in a satisfying way. They all feel equally ineffective and the zombies have the same animation cycle, so if you can get a group of them together, watch as they conga line in sync with one another. The rail gun feels effective, it goes straight through a lot of zombies and everything off screen too. To balance it out, you need to reload after each shot. Chainsaws put you in harms way, because when you get close to a zombie, they can still hit you.
You start with a trusty pistol that has unlimited ammunition, but a limited clip. Shooting feels sluggish, like its slow to empty an entire magazine. I would say that's your character taking aim. Each of the weapons has a laser sight to ensure that you'll hit a target if your aim is correct. Of course weapons like the rocket launcher fire projectiles, so they have a chance to miss.
There are alternate weapons that get dropped at random by zombies. You can carry one at a time and there is no way to switch between them. If you get a new weapon, you need to drop your old one. There's limited ammunition and reloading takes quite a while. Of course, in a zombie apocalypse I'd probably take just as long to switch out a magazine. When your alternate weapon runs out of ammo its back to the pistol
Dead Sky has a few glaring issues. Nothing game breaking, but they could be improved. The first is its awful voice acting. I'd rather have bad voice acting than no voice acting, but this was a step above abysmal.There's even an announcer to tell you pick ups like "Flame thrower," and "Shotgun."
The second is the lack of checkpoints for a game with no health. To some people this is a feature, until you feel just how dull the game is with its basic level design such as a cabin in the woods with a square lawn and an underground sewer that's just a single passage with a slimy center to walk through. Having to do these over if you fail becomes a chore. If its too much, there's always a different level of difficulty.
One of the biggest sins is the camera distance. The game keeps the screen centered on you with only about 35 - 40% to the north, which becomes an issue. I'd rather see more of where I'm going, but I suppose that's a personal preference. This way you can see zombies creep up behind you long before they get to you.
Speaking of getting to you, sometimes the zombies are a distance away when they hit you. This is demonstrated with the game over screen that freezes the game as is so you can clearly see the distance. For a game that has no health at least early on, this is a big issue. You'll have to compensate and just stay away from zombies, but some of these creatures will chase you faster than you can walk.
With all the negatives out there, the single player campaign ends with a cliffhanger of what looks to be a level aboard a train followed with "to be continued." While its best to leave an audience wanting more, it feels so short and bland that its an insult to anyone that would get that far. I'd rather have a remix of areas with previously used assets than just have it cut off after six quick chapters; one of which is just a turret section. Its all just to drive you into the multiplayer.
Multiplayer is relegated to a horde mode with waves of zombies. There's no way to select from games and that hurts the fun. You need to know a server IP to join, so you need a friend, but at least you can purchase a four pack for less than the price of three.
When you do play the game online, its a simple survival that borders on tower defense and the best mode it can be. You select from four different uninspiring and small maps that are a mere square of land and you stay alive by purchasing upgrades like health and defense. You lay down traps and turrets. Then you strive to survive. It feels just as tacked on as the entire single player campaign.
Dead Sky is a budget game that manages to feel cheap rather than a good game. It has all the right mechanics, but none of the fun. With the extensive diversity it has, its never fleshed out. You use it once then destroy and that sums up the entire experience.

After 10.5 hours of playing through the whole game on stream I am in awe and somewhat in shock what I just experienced.
To my mind, you can not simply compare SOMA to Amnesia, as each game has a different kind of way to entertain the player. SOMA comes up with a deep and rich story about ethics, humanity and the purpose of life itself. If you allow yourself to immerse into this though experiment you are able to get a lot out of the plot. The player is constantly caught between two stools to either conserve his innocence or to interfere with the events and therefore lose a portion of his sanity and reason. The game hints at ethical questions that may come up within the next 20-25 years. Better make up your mind now!
Gameplay-wise SOMA is similar to Amnesia with additional and more demanding mini-puzzles. The player is able to interact with the world around him on a large scale, because the developers had a fable for detailed surroundings.
This game is tagged as a horror adventure, which is fine, but do not expect the same atmosphere like in Amnesia. The focus is clearly not on experiencing horror (for the most part), but disturbance in terms of ethical integrity and cruelty.
I would strongly recommend this game.

I think Duke Nukem 3D was for "hardcore" gamers back in the day.  My cousin Doug introduced me to Duke Nukem a long time ago, back when dial-up was a thing.  I loved the game, but I was terrible at it.  FPS was never my thing.  I played a re-release on the XBox360 and beat the original campaign.  I felt the waves of nostalgia and still remember a late-night conversation with a friend about "What if there was another Duke Nukem game?"  I was never very good at it, but I wanted to see Duke at least have a last ride.
This is it.  When I first heard about it, I pre-ordered.  When I heard Gearbox was involved, I was excited.  When I played, it was fantastic!  I don't care about the hate.  Duke Nukem was a spoof from the beginning, looking hardcore.  Some of us as kids didn't know that he was the poster child of the 80's and early 90's.  We were just excited about the graphics being the best we'd ever seen, and having blood in a game!  He still makes comments like he used to, though by now it's not so much a gimmick as it used to be.  He still has a sweet weapon set, and he's saving the day.  I am not bothered by a linear level layout or a regenerating health bar.  Gearbox made this game playable for CASUAL gamers like me.  For what little story there was, I loved it.  The DLC was a blast.  The pinball was fun.  And as far as PC is concerned, it was a blast beating the game on its hardest difficulty by setting the in-game speed to 50%.  I've never had so much fun racing and beating bosses in Slow Motion.  ^_^
There are better shooting games out there if you're into that.  If you want one with a character that couldn't keep up with the times and looks like a relic of an earlier era, here it is.  Duke Nukem fans need to realize he was a parody then, and he still is...it's just more clear now.  He's not a character that grows or matures, and maybe that's sad for some of us who have young memories of him.  Don't forget what Duke Nukem was BEFORE Duke Nukem 3D.  I played that one too, on my grandma's computer.  So, who cares about "traditional scoring?"  Not me.  I'd say "Play this game!"

What have you done to this game???
I simply loved the previous incarnations of it, and enjoyed them thoroughly, despite some minor game design issues, but this... this... this half-arsed version is making me weep.
I bought the game after being undecided for some time, and eventually gave in to my desire to play a current version, despite some reviews that yelled "don't!". Boy, was I sorry.
The bad:
- Cars are totally unreliable, they handle unpredictably. hit a huge wooden crate or even a house, no problem, you wreck it easily. Drive over a tiny (or even invisible) obstacle and you're thrown out the road just like that.
- The game sometimes "cheats" by boosting cars behind you, something I've seen time and again in racing games. You're cruising comfortably ahead, top speed, driving well, and suddenly a wild racer appears from behind with impossible speed and drives by you like a rocket out of Hell. Screw that. It's not the fact that I didn't come in first, it's the fact that the game developers resort to changing AI cars' parameters in such a way that it's blazing obvious you're cheated out of your victory.
- Races become thus an exercise in frustration, having you restart countless times or constantly praying you don't drive over something that decides to throw you off like a rodeo horse would do. I found myself looking forward for the race to finish, rather than being excited to participate in it.
- Car upgrades are totally meh. Improvements are displayed in absolute values rather than relative to the car type, and when you see an increase of 1% or so in maximum speed, it's rather underwhelming. After 12 upgrade levels, my first car didn't feel different from stock in any way.
The good?
- ...sorry but I couldn't keep playing for long enough to see it. I'm sure there is some, but it's dwarfed by the glaring issues of this game.
I say, buy it only if you ran out of other games to buy, and that includes games you don't want to buy anyway.

There are a lot of problems with this game and many reviewers have already pointed them out. I did have a positive review and I thought people were overtly whiny about the game for a while, but now, after a few months, I can definitely say this game is not going to reach its potential. Thanks ubisoft.
It's not the stability, optimisation, or connection quality that earns my downvote. It's their utter contempt for their own game mechanics.
This game is just street fighter with a skin. Because defense is so powerful they have to have cheesy unblockable moves for some while also having guard breaks and a stamina system. Once people learned how to break the mechanics there were no longer any interesting fights, because all you have to do is: defense, cheesy unblockable attack when possible, wear out their stamina then guard break/cheesy unblockable move -> throw them to the ground (when you're out of stamina you get auto knocked down from any attack that moves you), heavy attack, repeat. The combination of overly-plentiful environment cheese (cliffs, fire, spikes, and even more sadly) with the overly-rewarding nature of guard breaks just makes only one playstyle valid: the one where you do everything you can to open them up to guard breaks and use that as your means to deal damage.
What looked like a beautifully balanced combat system has shown its ugly underbelly that doesn't reward different fighting styles, just spamming whatever attacks tend to hit the most constantly, which granted can mean different things for different characters but the lack of suspense/sense of action is real when >90% players you see are only familiar with 3 moves (and they have tons of levels/gear to help em out too). This game was extremely fun and interesting in the betas and on release, but only has the hardcore spammathon demographic left, that is the people that only care about winning and exploit the game mechanics as efficiently as possible to achieve that. What makes it worse is that ubi's vision of balance is slowly shifting every character to have no particular advantages over any other, and without the prominent asymetries that should accompany such diverse fighting styles you get this very flat gameplay effect that leaves only one method of fighting valid. such a shame.

This game is definitely one I've never seen before.
The concept of it is basically to travel around the world in 80 days or less with a colleague in order to win a bet. It is in fact a
game but does a very good job with it's wording. You will start at one point and be given the freedom to traverse wherever the current location you're at can take you, assuming you can afford it. There are many different places you can visit and they're all different. You can't visit every stop in one sitting so the replay value is extremely high.
This is the kind of game where you travel point to point managing relationships, money as well as time. Again, you travel with a colleague so you aren't alone and is actually the one person you need to maintain a stable relationship with since you are with him for the entire trip. You will however run into other people in different countries and cities that can either help you or hurt you. Some will give you helpful information such as which route is cheaper, which countries/cities to avoid, or which items sell more in what countries/cities. Where as some will hold you hostage delaying your progress, steal money from you, or even backstab you. Thus, based on the events that happen, you must be able to strategize at any given moment so your trip isn't handicapped anymore than it is. 80 Days is also a game where choices do matter and affect the way the game plays out. You will run into problems no matter where you go and most if not all areas of the world you visit will contain some form of conflict you must address that will affect how you're character is perceived, how your financial status ends up as, as well as how tight your time constraint becomes. Again, time is also passing no matter what you do so time management is a really important asset to consider when playing the game.
In terms of difficulty, despite what's been said, it definitely is more lenient when you aren't able to make it around in 80 or less days. In that sense I found it quite difficult to circle the planet in 80 days or less but if you were to reach the deadline unsuccessfully, you can still play on. All that happens is that your colleague will just notify you that you and him have failed to reach the 80 day goal and have lost the bet but then says that it isn't a big deal. He then continues to say that the journey is
and you will still be able to complete the game, regardless of failing to reach the goal.
80 Days is definitely a game for both hardcore and casual gamers, although not very action packed, it is very tense. It is recommended for those who like reading and making decisions that affect the storyline, as well as managing important real life problems such as time, money and relationships. This is a summary of my review video, which I encourage you to watch if you are looking for a more in-depth review.
Tormentum-Dark Sorrow is a 2d point and click adventure with a dark and malevolent theme. The interface is clean and streamlined, and the game itself is fairly simplistic. You start off as a prisoner that goes on a journey of discovery through wastelands, purgatory, and redemption. It is evident that you have some sort of amnesia, but I found overall that the progression or motivation was hampered by too much missing story, information/lore along the way. It felt as if half the game went by when I blinked, as you are left not really knowing the deeper meanings of what was going on. Some of these questions in the end were answered, but not all. There was little if any lore or backstory, and it felt empty and slightly frustrating to want to know more about the world or my character, but was unable to.
The unique art style and atmosphere made this game enjoyable. It was original and intriguing, but didn't overdo the sense of horror or the bizarre. The atmosphere of the world synergized very well together.
One unique element to the game was that choices you make throughout the game will impact how it ends. Nothing huge or game changing,  but it was spread out and implemented well. Some of the choices might not have the impact you expected, which was misleading to say the least. You are presented with a truly evil man, for example, and your choice to kill him or let him live might not be judged as guilty or innocent as you think it would.
The gameplay is heavy on puzzles, with some scavenging quests thrown in. I would say about 75% of the items needed for scavenging come from previous quests. I find this refreshing, as it relies more on puzzles and mini-games, instead of "find the safety deposit box in a room of 500 safety deposit boxes". The puzzles were smooth and continuous, with a good sense of fluidity that kept me enthralled in the gameplay.
The artistic beauty, fluid game play, and overall synergy of the game make this an easy recommend. The story leaves a bit to be desired, but overall an enjoyable game.

I'll start off by saying I really don't want to give this a thumbs down, but unfortunately Steam doesn't have a "On the fence" button. So instead I'll just cut to the chase.
VISUALS:
-If you enjoy dark fantasy and surreal art- the gothic, the baroque, the grotesque- GET THIS GAME.
- If you like art in games, hope to make art for games, or just like creativity in games and want inspiration- GET THIS.
- If you're a fan of Giger or Beksinski, DEFINITELY GET THIS GAME.
I don't really have to go into detail on this. The screenshots speak for themselves.
LENGTH:
The game is very short. This is a 3 to 4 hour game, sans any mucking about in confusion. Not really a detriment in its own right, but definitely a factor to consider.
GAMEPLAY/PUZZLES:
The game isn't challenging. I can't remember the last time I played a point and click game, but I still breezed through this. This could be seen as a blessing for casual players just looking to experience the art firsthand, but I'm certain it would be underwhelming for any seasoned point-and-click fan.
WRITING:
It's lackluster. It's not awful, but considering what the game was trying to do it needed to do much better here. I'll avoid spoilers but it’s important to know that the writing in the game is inseparable from moral choice. The story, the theme and the visuals of the game ultimately revolve around death, sins, punishment and things not being what they seem. This could have been incredible, but for a game so trenched in morality, it is portrayed as very black and white.
There are two endings to this game and around 7 moral choices you must make. They're fairly rudimentary , and even doing two perceived 'bad' choices will give you the bad ending. Morality is very complicated and needs to be handled as such if your whole story hinges on exploring these themes. Games like Silent Hill 2, Spec Ops: The Line and The Walking Dead all accomplished this with flying colors, and had that quality of writing gone into a game like this the end result would have been haunting. Of this I have no doubt.
As it stands however, the end result is this world of beautiful visuals and unsettling atmosphere that winds up being in the service of a lot of nothing. If you're looking for a great story, interesting characters or strong worldbuilding (particularly revolving around morality and the darkness in the human heart), you will be disappointed.
OVERALL:
I bought the game on impulse and my choice to buy it was exclusively rooted in the artwork. I didn't go in with any other expectations so personally, I'm happy with what I got out of it and do no regret anything. But I cannot say with confidence that this would be the case with somebody else so I leave it at this:
If you came here for the art- go for it. An art book or ticket to a gallery show or museum often cost way more than 12$, and here the art is interactive. That's just awesome. You can't do much better than that.
Just don't expect much else from it.

I literally just sit and wait or play other games so that I can have enough resources to build a single building, and even that takes hours. Your direct commands as player are just ignored by a batshit crazy AI that makes tactics or planning impossible.
And to top it off, the animations of the units are ugly and repetative and the graphics look a good deal worse than Spellforce 1.

This game is about what one would expect from a Magic the Gathering video game.  Tap mana to play spells, bring your opponent to zero life or have their deck run out before yours does.  Standard fare for what one might expect.  The story even has some moderate relevance to the game at large, especially in the form of the new Ob Nixilis.
Building your own personal deck(s) is a new feature and one that I rather like a lot.  But there are a few things that restrict this quality.  First off, this game does not have quite as many cards as I had expected.  While, yes, it does take cards from M15, Innistrad, Theros, Return to Ravnica, and Zendikar blocks, along with a few odds and ends cards to improve the pool, you still only have access to about as many cards as you did in the previous installment, if that.  Only Evolve and Bloodrush are present from Ravnica as far as guild mechanics go for playable cards, for example, and Bestow is conspicuously absent.  This is made worse by the fact that almost 100 of the cards are additional purchases on top of the game. Secondly, this game has a few bugs and issues with the interface.  One of the primary complaints that I have had about it is that the option to choose the order of damage is not automatically on, and the interface for doing so is a bit unusual.   There are also bugs in receiving a few titles and avatars. Third, and perhaps one of the most obnoxious things out there, is the existance of decks that are illegal.  The game refuses to tell you why this deck can't be used, only that it can't be used.  I myself experienced this while trying to build a RWU deck.
Matchmaking will also frequently become an issue, as games will occasionally be joined when two players are already in the lobby, or the connections will outright fail.
Overall then, I would say that this game has a number of things to like about it, but it was heavily hyped for  being able to customize your own deck as much as you want.  What the hype did not include was how much was traded off for this functionality.  While I do not dislike this game by any stretch, nor do I dislike Wizards and their affiliates for it, I could not recommend this to a friend in good conscience.  I feel this game is underpolished and could have used a bit more time on the refining steps.

Duke Nukem Forever ist probably best know for its development history: after numerous changes of engines, faked trailers, a long silence and a lawsuite, Gearbox Software (today probably best known for the Borderlands games), finished the game. It was probably not the best for their reputation as the game is average through and through. Die graphics is roughly on the same level as Half-Life 2, without the great systems for animations and facial expressions. It follows the blueprint of a classic first person shooter, which includes puzzles in the levels whch are all well done. The rest ist mostly standard fps level design, only in very few instances the genius level design which made Duke3D a masterpiece shines through. I noticed that quite a lot of arenas are in the game, where the player is trapped and has to defend multiple waves of enemies. The weapons are part standards like a pistol and a shotgun and part crazy weapons like the ice- and shrinkray, but nothing that veterans of Duke3D aren't familar with. But they are not as effective (or should I say: overpowered?) as their counterparts in the predessesor. Since only four weapons can be equipped at the same time (two if the option is deactivated), I decided not go for the exotic weapons but more for the standards to be prepared for most situations. The number of emeny types is quite low, also mostly well known foes. But their behaviour has change quite a bit, making them a new challenge. But some more different ones would have been good. The driving stages are no highlight as especially the buggy with its huge tires is a agile as a rubber boat. The game has though bossfights, which range from very good like the one against the alien queen (which does not only require fast fingers but a bit of thought) to average like the one against the Octaking.
But that can be the summary for the whole game: nothing is really bad, but the highlights are far and few, making the whole game quite average. For fans of classic fps games it is worth picking up in a sale.

Shadow Warrior 2 is the Looter Shooter sequel to Shadow Warrior 2013 which I already reviewed here:
Played on a i5 4460, GTX 1060 (3GB VRAM) and 16GB RAM using keyboard & mouse. Looked great and ran smooth on Ultra settings HOWEVER I recommend turning off Bloom. it is pretty outrageous in certain areas of the game. So much so that you can barely see whats in front of you. If you have a monitor/tv with HDR, this game supports it.
You play once again as Lo Wang in a now post-apocalyptic, demon-filled world. After the events of Shadow Warrior the earthly world and the shadow realm collided and merged into one. Think collision of the spheres if you're familiar with the Witcher series. For Wang's first mission he's sent to retrieve an artifact for an important client. Wang is then sent to rescue Kamiko, a girl who worked undercover in one of Orochi Zilla's research labs only to be discovered and experimented on. Things go horribly wrong and her body becomes possesed by a demon. However the only way to save her soul is to put it in Wang's body (giggity) until her body can be purified.
When it comes to gameplay, there are major differences from the first game. Wang now has an expanded intventory menu that includes different weapons, skills, encyclopedia entries (Wanglopedia) as well as gems that are used for the new weapon upgrade system. You now have 8 different weapon slots and can put whatever weapons you want in them. Each weapon has 3 gem slots for further customization. Gems are found in loot containers or dropped from monsters and what gems do, exactly, is add different elemental effects or stats such as damage increase, rate of fire, life on hit, etc. Other changes I liked that are different from Shadow Warrior 1 include no fall damage and infinite stamina. Sword techniques work the same as SW1, hold down the RMB while walking in a direction decides on what tech you use. They can be charged if you hold the RMB down longer. Skill Points are earned from leveling up and can be put into different categories of skills such as sword techniques, healing, etc.
Progression works like this, there is a HUB town with a couple of shops and quest-giving NPCs. Quests and side-quests are contained in a single
area so you're only going to do one at a time. Side quests will earn you some decent rewards such as money to use in shops, skills, skill points & weapons. There are also Trials you can complete later to get the ability to further craft & upgrade your weapons using special orbs gained from killing boss monsters and quest rewards.
The monster variety is really diverse this time around, too many to get into, in fact. The game does fall victim to the old cliche enemy palette swap though. Same enemy with a different skin depending on your location.  With the introduction to elements some monsters have weakeness/resistance to certain elements. And sometimes champion enemies will summon more monsters that have to be killed before you can hurt them again.
And here's where I want to get a little passionate and ramble. As a Shadow Warrior fan I really hate to see the game go in the direction of a looter shooter when I enjoyed the first one and Classic so much. Lo Wang's personality has also changed from a snarky badass in the first game, to a snarky dumbass in this one. The supporting cast is also pretty bland IMHO. The gameplay mechanics are solid enough to make the game stand alone as a looter shooter title but in no freaking way do I consider this a true Shadow Warrior game and I hope fans of the series see that as well. Games like Borderlands do the looter shooter genre so much better and all this game makes me think about is how much I'd rather be playing Borderlands than a Shadow Warrior game. And Just like Borderlands 2, Shadow Warrior 2 was also turned into an immersion breaking memefest. I do have fun with the game because the looter shooter aspect ticks off all my OCD boxes but this is not the direction I want to see the series go. I can't in good conscience recommend this game if it meant Shadow Warrior 3 was going to be another Shoot & Loot. I'd rather see the game expand on its roots without the full-on RPG elements.
I really do have a love/hate relationship with the game because if it didn't have the Shadow Warrior name and was called like..."Ninja: Demon Slayer" (rockin 80's movie title right there) then I would have absolutely no problem with it. Don't let my biased ramblings or lack of recommendation stop you from buying it if you want to play the best shoot & loot game to come along since Borderlands 2 though.

Well, this was an interesting experience for sure.
I loved Shadow Warrior 2013, infact, it's one of my favourite singleplayer games of all time. Shadow Warrior 2 however? eeeeeeeeh, I feel like the developers played Borderlands a bit too much while developing this game. I won't go into a full review of the game and instead first say- YES I RECOMMEND THIS GAME, IT ISN'T AS GOOD AS SW2013 BUT IT IS STILL FUN- that being said,
Comparison to SW2013:
+ SW2 has more content, more filler prehaps, but the game still has more to it. Mostly in the form of side-objective mini-bosses and alike.
+ SW2 has co-op. I didn't play it but it's an addition nonetheless
+ The map visuals are MUCH better. SW2013's maps became extremely stale around halfway, all being warehouses and docks etc.
+ Replayability, due to there not -really- being a structure to the game, you can endlessly replay it and constantly try to get better loot or do the DLCs and sidequests you missed, along with trying to 100% the Skill Trees (+acheivements but they were also in SW2013)
- The story is worse. 100% not as good. There are alot of plotholes, failed attempts at character arcs and a terrible ending.
- The game is non-linear, so the pacing of the story is off and the level design (to work with being non-linear and the new co-op gameplay) is really badly done. You can skip entire segments of a level by using the invisibility cloak.
- THERE IS NO CLEAR WEAPON PROGRESSION. The devs instead opted for a Borderlands style loot system, where you can combine the upgrades with weapons to make them better. However, this means you spend 10 minutes every half an hour filing through your inventory to sort out junk and reassign weapon buffs, and if you don't your weapons end up becoming much weaker. This is in contrast to the very clear and well balanced progression in SW2013.
- The demons have weird sub-tiers, which negates using your abilities entirely as 20% of them are immune and 99% of the time they don't seem to work anyway. Using abilities also uses chi, which should be saved for health regen anyway.
- Too easy. I played on the hardest difficulty (same in SW2013) and it felt waaaaaay too easy.
- Tying in with the above point, there were no hard barriers to pass, in SW2013 I can remember atleast 3, the bottom of a staircase, a small room with 2 beserkers, and the huge final demon fight. Possibly because of the non-linear design.
- Remember the Beserkers, Warlords, and Shamen from SW2013? And how they were basically mini-bosses you had to fight for 10 minutes? Yeah, they are absolutely laughable here. They all have ALMOST NO HEALTH and they don't have their abilities anymore, except for the Shaman (who barely uses it). They added a few more `God` tier enemies but they are all equally pathetic. Again, I blame the non-linear progression here, there is no way the game can lock you in a room to fight a mini-boss or know what level you are when you fight them. pretty sad really. This is also because there are sub-tiers of enemies eg. superior and elite (pretty much `badass` etc from Borderlands) so there can be a standard Shaman and a Superior Crawler and they feel equally as hard to beat. The Shaman/ Warlord also only appeared like 3 times for me the entire game, which is quite sad considering they are some of the most interesting enemies in the series.
- Despite the map visuals being better, the actual maps seem to get reused alot. But you always spawn in different areas and the enemy spawns are changed so it feels quite strange.
- There are no clear acts. The story is really wishy-washy tbh.
- The story doesn't tie up. In SW2013 there was the final demon battle, the final human boss battle, the final god boss battle and then the final cutscene. In SW2 you have the final boss thing that was never really a boss as they were stupidly easy and then a really weird un-dramatic cutscene that tries too hard and uh it ends? It was a bit weird TBH
And this concludes my review of SW2. Purchase SW2013 if you can't decide, but if you have some money to blow, sure, get this game. I would recommend getting it on a sale though.

Super Duper Party Pooper is a rhythm game with a silly sense of humor.
I wish I could give this a neutral review instead of a negative one, but Steam doesn't give me the option, and I can't bring myself to give it a positive recommendation.
I want to start by saying I actually loved the previous game made by the same developer. "There's poop in my soup" was also equally as silly, but the gameplay gripped me more.
Super Duper Party Pooper is meant to be a rhythm game, yet it doesn't seem to reward me properly for going with the beat. I've played the drums for years, and have played tonnes of rhythm games throughout my life, so I'm not new to the genre, and have a very good sense of rhythm, but the games notes just don't seem to match the music's beat. I even tried playing on another monitor to make sure it wasn't mind causing the problem, but it was still slightly off. That's the biggest problem. It's like if you play a shooter and the bullets don't go straight to where you're aiming. Who knows, maybe it's because I have a very good sense of rhythm that I might notice it more than most people, or my computer is messing it up somehow, or perhaps I'm just terrible at this particular game.
I still unlocked 5 out of 6 levels despite that because the game gives you visual queues for when you're meant to press  the button.
Each level is set in a new location, which looks relatively different to the previous one. The music more or less fits the theme of the environment. In my opinion, the music is the best part about the game. Unfortunately, I don't even think it was made for the game.
The game does a good job at keeping levels fresh by adding new obstacles constantly. You'll need to focus on multiple places at once, or avoid bombs. When you successfully press a button at the right time, your character will eat and fill up their stomach. Depending on how well you do throughout the level, you will have a certain amount of poo to fling at the backup dancers behind you, for a few extra points at the end.
The game also allows you to import your own music, but it's way too frustrating to use. You'll need to copy paste the exact file path to tell it which song to use, and it only allows for mp3s. The game would benefit from a file browser. Not only that, but you then need to enter the Beats per minute for the song on your own so the game knows at what speed you should be matching the notes at. It's not like in games like Audiosurf where the game detects all that on its own. The game recommends using a certain site to find the BPM, but there's only a set amount of songs there from what I can tell. The chances of finding your song are very slim.
Eventually I figured out a song that I wanted to use, inputted the BPM, but I encountered a problem. Because it was quite a slow song, some of the objects I needed to press were going off the screen before their time came.
In other words, there are some food items that have lights on them. They slowly pass by your screen in the rhythm of the music, and when their lights turn green you are allowed to eat them. But because my music was slow, the lights only became green when they were off screen. It made playing that song very hard.
Overall, I can't recommend the game. Yes, it's very cheap so you can give it a go without losing much, and it isn't awful. It's just that I can't enjoy a rhythm-based game that doesn't work properly. Again, I think the dev is capable since I 100%ed their previous game, but with broken mechanics in this, it just isn't fun. And I don't think I would enjoy it too much even if the rhythm-timing was fixed.
Dont Buy

This is among the best RPGs ever made; perhaps only surpased by Fallout 1 (IMHO).
The gameplay is excellent and so is the story. It uses the a modified d20 (also known as D&D) system 3 system and it does so excellently -- it's the best d20 implementation (though not the most accurate) in any game I've tried.
There are a few bad points though -- the controls are clunky and in particular I find it strange that, when I activate mouselook using the right button, the turning keys on the keyboard are disabled. Sometimes controller input isn't registered at all -- this is particularly a problem with the scrollwheel.
The performance of the game is poor. Despite modern(ish) hardware, which is far better than what the game was designed for, enabling antialiasing and/or anisotropic filtering does degrade framerate considerably -- I find it particularly strange that whenever smoke or similar effects are visible performance is pitiful.
The main menu also has it's problems -- some times when I go back to the main menu the graphics will be skewed to the left and the right side will have the clipped part of the left screen. This is likely due to the game originally being designed for a 4/3 ratio rather than the 1.6 ratio (1920x1200) I play the game at.
Sometimes, when entering an area, the scene textures won't load -- this leads to a largely black screen, with only characters and placables being visible (doors, containers and that sort of thing). The only way I've been able to fix this is to quit the game entirely.
So, despite all these problems why do I recommend the game? Because it's awesome!
