This game is a lot of fun. A beautiful and engaging "what if" war between three factions of varying historical accuracy. The knights (who seem to have forgotten half of their plate armor) the Samurai (who can't decide what time period they got their armor from at all) and the Vikings (who have nearly completely given up on the mail hauberks they were fond of wearing and just threw a bit of fur over their shoulder).
The combat has the ability to feel fair and very rewarding when you manage to beat somebody 1v1, and gives you more than adequate tools to destroy people if someone happens to be watching from the sidelines as well. And that's just part of the very sad problems holding this game back.
The core of this game is a very good base for a 3D medieval skinned fighting game, but Ubisoft both doesn't grasp the concept of and is VERY slow to act upon when it finally discovers balance issues. They also seem to be dragging their feet on many glitches and exploits that are currently plaguing the game. Granted, it's easy to assume part of it could be trying to get as much fixed as they can per patch, as having to deal with the two console version needing to go through cert every time they want to fix their game is a time consuming process as well.
I really enjoy this game, and I will likely continue to keep playing until I am among the last of the remaining playerbase. This is something I sadly see coming far too soon if Ubisoft can't manage to fix these massive issues plaguing their game and leaving matches with more salt thrown on the chat than your average MOBA match. Granted this happens in every online game, but For Honor is one of the few games I have played where someone screaming in chat about someone doing cheesy OP BS tactics is fairly justified as that's about the only way for anyone to try and fight back anymore. If you don't, someone else will and they will beat you.
But at the end of the day, losing isn't so bad either. Just wait for someone to rage quit and likely the entire P2P network will crash and boot everyone to menu and it's like the match never even happened. Now granted with such precise frame timing needed in this game, which functions far more like a fighting game akin to Street Fighter and the like in it's play mechanics, P2P really is the way to go. Where this falls flat is in 4v4 matches where keeping a group of 8 people connected properly together in a crazy P2P web makes a VERY unstable house of cards, and when someone gets fed up with how the game is going it's very easy to "kick the table" in a sense by rage quitting and making sure the people who beat him don't get any credit for the victory. And don't forget: they get away with this with zero punishment because of course Ubisoft hasn't implemented anything yet for what has been likely the most complained about aspect of this game since launch.
TL;DR - Great game, looks beatufiul, and has the potential to be extremely fun to play. Just good luck getting into a match and staying in a match, and if you do prepare to learn how to deal with extremely cheesey and turtle based play due to lack of balancing and unfixed glitches/exploits. I really hope they get around to fixing these issues before it's too late, but what needs to be done compared to what actually has been done so far is not very promising. Keep an eye on it, but I don't reccomend buying it unless they fix the game and patch up the rapidly hemorhaging player base.

"80 Days" is a game based Jules Verne's novel, you play as Passepartout, Phileas Fogg's valet At first it may look like logic game - you have to find a route around the world while managing your "resources": time, money, inventory and Fogg's health. But after a few moments of playing you can see that it's not only moving on the world map. It's also an adventure. Each city gives you a possibility to explore and discover new routes, sometimes you'll end in different place than you planned, some things will happen during your travel. What really amazes me in this game is the sense of adventure. Your car may be captured by air-pirates, you can find that Transsiberian Railway is more than meets the eye, you may walk the oceans bottom, solve murder cases, travel with world's greatest thief and much more.
The graphics are rather simple, but it's enough for this game. The plot is given through text - so there's a lot of reading and sometimes the game may seem slow. When traveling, you see only a black silhouette of your vehicle, and those are really inventive: steam cars, hovercrafts, mechanical elephants, walking cities, flying cities, submarines, rockets. One moment you are moving with the slow horse-caravan, next moment you are flying in a bird-like airship.
While one gameplay may be completed in about two hours, the number of adventures and places to see is enough many laps around the world. The game gets better with each playthrough.

They don't make games like this anymore.  Actually, they never did, as this was forced out the door before it was ready all those years ago. But now the unfinished masterpiece has been finished, and it's better than ever, and almost any RPG released in the last few years.
The graphics are crude by today's FPS standards, but work adequately for an RPG, especially with the resolution set to max.
The characters are superb, and the game's strongest feature. Obsidian knows the best way of telling a story is via characters. The player character is not amnestic, but the surprises and story evolve via your opponents, those who travel with you, and those you pass on the way. They are portrayed in a believable fashion, and they respond to both events, and the action and conversation options you make.
The story is good, and it has the added joys of being both Star Wars and high quality Star Wars. It's pace starts off a bit more methodical than some may like. But it starts good, and gets a lot better as it unfolds.
If you play RPG's and enjoy sci-fiction, you owe it to yourself to give this game a try one afternoon. Superb value for money.

Got this game because of the interesting sounding story and the artwork in the screenshots. Due to the dark theme I can say that it's not for everyone, but personally, I highly recommend this game.
+

Bugs (although every game has them).
Seriously, I can't think of anything negative about this game except in cases where it hurts certain people's sensitivities. ;)
Had this game for the longest time, but put off playing it because of the dark themes.
True, the implied and graphical torment in this game was disturbing, but the story and concept were great and intriguing.
Story:
Not sure what to say without spoiling the story, but it's not standard fare "random hero saves random world from random threat". Consider it a story about one man's road to redemption. Whether or not he succeeds is entirely up to the player.
I really like how choices really do matter in this game. What you decide now changes who appears later in the story, and definitely affects the end as well.
Game length short - about 2-3 hours from start to finish, but definitely has replayability value.
Artwork:
Not sure how to classify the graphics in my opinion, but I'd say that they're unique, gorgeous, grotesque, well-detailed, imaginative and basically amazing all rolled into one.
I like how they separated the foreground and background in a lot of scenes and has a "slide" effect when you move your mouse towards the left or right.
Music:
Most of the game's background music is made up of atmospheric tracks and sound effects.
The ending song is really good. Got distracted while listening the song for both endings, so I can't say for sure if they are different songs.
Puzzles:
Every single puzzle is solvable without needing to refer anywhere out of the game.
Unlike most Daedalic point and click games, there is no guesswork needed as clues are provided appropriately where there's no way you can figure out a puzzle with simply logic (although clues are still provided for logic puzzles as well since there is no skip button). Never had to look for a walkthrough at any time at all.
Random non-gamebreaking bugs:
-> the "x" move sign/option disappearing if you go through the zoomed-in scenes too quickly. Easily fixed by exiting to the main menu or game and then continuing the game.
-> the matching mini-game becomes unresponsive if you happened to match the last pair at the same time the timer resets. Easily fixed by exiting the mini-game, although you'll end up having to restart the mini-game.
Overall a fantastic, well-made game. I feel it's worth every penny the developers ask for it.

First off, I've been playing this game absolutely non-stop since Feb 14th. I first started with the solo Campaign as a lot of reviewers were giving the game a thumbs down and talking about how bad the peer to peer connection was.
The campaign has a beautiful story and lets you try out most classes incase you don't want to blow all your steel on characters you've never used yet. Not to mention completing the campaign gives you a very generous amount of money, close to 2,500 - 3,000 I believe. So it's definitely worth finishing campaign first, as you should with any game really.
My experience with 1v1 multiplayer matches have just been nothing but great. The connections are rock solid, never have any wait time over 30 seconds, I honestly don't know what people are complaining so much about peer to peer. Out of the many matches that I've done including 4v4's, I've literally never come by a single lagged incident. Improve your internet maybe reviewers? Lol
The combat system is extremely satisfying and extremely difficult at the same time. The learning curve is very steep, but put some time and effort into it and you can apply similar battle theories to each class type.
I've seen some people complain that you can't block strikes even if you're blocking the correct direction while getting hit.
Here's something to clarify that, in a sense it's similar to tekken. If you're pressing attack keys while you're trying to block, it's not going to work because your block state is cancelled and you're spamming an attack state which is attackable. Common sense really.
For people complaining about the game being a money vacuum, it really isn't. It's not really pay to win either. You literally get an option to spend money on the game, but don't have to as you can earn everything benificial through play time and luck. Luck being end match loots. Of course for the cosmetic packs that cost like 45,000 it's gonna cost some $$$ but that's just cosmetics. As for the pay to win issue, I have not clashed blades with a single player whos gear is absolutely over powering due to money dumping. Even if you spend to buy scavanger crates, upgrades will only take your gears so far.
Environmental kills;
Get over it, you probably set yourself up anyway without knowing.
It's your duty and responsibility to know where you're positioning yourself at all times.
Yes I understand some classes can throw very far and can be very abusive with throws, but in the end who's the one letting those throws happen?
Yes I've come across players who only throw you off cliffsides and bridges, but just by playing smarter you can avoid being grabbed. It really isn't all that difficult once you've gotten used to the game and anticipating your opponents next move, it isn't impossible. They're all humans except the AI, everybody can crack under pressure and use telegraphed strikes because of it.
Players who complain about characters being overpowered just haven't spent enough time into learning the character that they're using. I've seen Mercy decimate Shugoki, the beefiest and tankiest character. I've seen regular wardens obliterate Nobushi. Once you've played long enough against certain classes you'll see the classes limits on what it can do, then you begin to see how other players use those same abilities. People will either all do similar things, or will be unique overall. One thing players will always do, is move in for a guard break after they've blocked a light strike.

True survival horror games are rare these days, as recent horror Games tend to be just as much focused on action as they are on atmosphere.
In Frictional Games' Amnesia: The Dark Descent, you are powerless to stop the ever looming threat of death. When a horrifically gruesome shambling creature rounds a corner on wobbly knees and its yawning rictus comes into focus, you can only succumb to its onslaught or flee in terror to hide in a corner and cry, hoping the shadows will provide safe haven in your time of need.
Amnesia plays more like a first-person adventure game than anything else, and borrows many of the environmental manipulation mechanics of Frictional's previous Penumbra series. It's a fairly short game, but one that's near impossible to forget.
If you've ever read an H.P. Lovecraft horror story, you'll find a lot that's familiar here.  Much of the horror and structure of the plot is inspired by the 20th century author, as sanity plays a big part, even showing Daniel things he'd probably never see otherwise.
During the length of the story, you play as Daniel, who awakes with a convenient case of amnesia on the floor of the huge and hauntingly empty Castle Brennenburg.
Soon after coming to, you discover a note written by your past self, instructing you to find and kill Alexander, the master of house and the main villain of the overarching story.
Unraveling the history of the place is part of what lures you forward, discovering how exactly you got to this point, what Alexander did to deserve an early death, and who is responsible for the grisly acts committed in the castle's depths.
What follows is a tale told mostly in flashback as you' re beset by ghostly visions and uncover journal entries on dimly lit desks that tell of scientific expeditions that lead to the discovery of ancient terrors. By itself the story is strong enough, and is told effectively assuming you take the time to explore and pick up a majority of the notes. Yet what really adds a quality of unsettling authenticity to the tale is the unshakeable feeling of pursuit and inevitability of some kind of horrific climax.
On the soundtrack, scratches, clicking and footsteps from unseen spaces imply an expanse of unknown rippling just beyond the limits of your perception.
Sound is very important, as it not only draws you into the world but also serves as a warning for what may lie ahead in the darkness.
Monsters groan, maidens shriek, and ghostly prisoners wail, giving a feeling of dread in later levels.
Visual cues are also crucial to reinforcing the sense of terror, as Daniel's vision is affected by ghastly sights and revelations of gruesome acts to which his previous life was connected. Sanity degrades while in the dark, causing the scene to shift like in a fashion similar to a nightmare.
When your sanity drops too far, controls are muddied, and eventually insects crawl across your field of vision. It contributes to a feeling of isolation and helplessness that adds to the sense of terror.
Staying in the light is the preferred course for those who prefer to maintain mental focus.
A lantern is always available to light up corridors, provided you've enough fuel to keep it lit...
Tinderboxes are source of light, however, they are scattered around amidst ancient books and in dusty cabinets and used to spark torches to illuminate passageways and candles within kitchens and torture chambers to make it less psychologically taxing as you explore.
You can still see in the darkness if you've run out of both oil and tinderboxes since Daniel's eyes will eventually adjust to the deep-blue murk of darkness.
Daniel is vunerable as he stumbles into blackness, it's entirely possible a shambling monster could round a corner and slash him down. It's not something that happens often, but the lingering threat is enough to make you tread carefully even if the way forward seems clear. It also sets up a gameplay dynamic between dark and light.
Do you stay in the shadows to hide from an enemy you can not see yet and risk your sanity?
Or do you light up everything you can to keep your wits?
[ih1]  Puzzles:  [/h1]
Puzzle solving is the heart of the gameplay, and like in Frictional's Penumbra games, manipulation of objects is handled in a way that gives you a greater sense of connection to the character.
To open a door, you must hold the object with the left mouse button, then draw the mouse back or push it forward depending on which way the door swings. To open a drawer it's the same mechanic, requiring you to pull back on the mouse once the handle is grabbed to open it.
The way players can manipulate the environment keeps them firmly rooted within the game world and add a touch of realism, strengthening the horror aspect.
Actually solving the puzzles shouldn't be too difficult for anyone who's played adventure games before. Despite the bizarre and often disturbing states of the sewers, morgues, and downright revolting torture chambers later on, the solutions often require you to collect a few objects and combine and apply them in interesting ways.
Frictional's done a good job of pacing the game as well, gradually expanding the area and complexity of the puzzles and mixing in jaw-clenching pursuit sequences as you plunge deeper into the mystery.


This is one of the scariest games in recent memory.

Any fan of horror and any with even a hint of curiosity should give Amnesia a shot. Few games are able to conjure up an atmosphere this genuinely frightening.

This game tries to be surreal, disturbing and deep, and fails at all of them. It's an unoriginal adventure game (pick up everything, put the button in the button-shaped slot, repeat fifty times.) There are no developed characters or story; in the last ten seconds of the game you finally learn something about the guy you were playing, which is totally unrelated to anything else you have seen, discussed, or built out of cart wheels and dead horses. (If the dead horses bit sounds fun, play Fran Bow instead.)
Easy but tedious puzzles, anything simple for the developers to code - think tile-sliding and card matching. I repeatedly got stuck and had to check a walkthrough, but only because it's hard to figure out which way you're allowed to walk. I kept having no clue rooms existed, because I'd have to hover my mouse over a certain one of the identical doorways to give me a faint arrow.
The one non-standard addition for an adventure game, the "moral choices", are terrible. It's the worst implementation of a moral system I've ever seen in a game. Half the time you don't even know the outcome of the vaguely labeled options - I was clearly evil because I pushed the wrong button once.
Oh well. Guess my soul is doomed, because there's no way I'm replaying this.

My Experience thus far:
Thrown into a space station. Okay then let's see. No Health or ammo indicators, no on screen instuctions or key prompts. Well there's a map, and it has 2 colored dots on it. Let's go there and maybe I'll get some information.
Large FPS drops. That's fine, this is something to expect from these kind of indie games anyways.
Walks to the first quest marker. A very bright room with a picnic table in it. I head inside then I suddenly have a handgun with no ammo, an assualt rifle with ammo, and a shotgun with ammo. That's a very strange inconsistency but moving on. The Guns have no texture and this is where I find out that the room with the picnic table is supposed to be an armory.
... I see... I thought this was the break room at first but whatever.
Didn't see the guns on the picnic table because the non-textured guns blended in so well with the bright room.  Anyways I decide to run around like an idiot and when I jumped, I notice the ceiling was lacking collision detection. So I wanted to see if I can glitch myself out by trying to jump through the ceiling and out of bounds. Turns out the game was kind enough to save me the trouble of working for my glitches so when I jumped on a railing to get some height, It catapulted me 100 feet in the air and I died. So yeah, great times so far.
Anyways, I restarted, went to the picnic table to pick up my weapons again, I finally get to the next objective and I am greeted with a very half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥pre-recorded ingame cutscene of two people talking about... something. Then suddenly the cutscene cuts to a decently made video of an alien on the surface of the moon, and considering how well this was made compared to... whatever the hell I was watching a second ago, I am convinced this alien footage was clearly not made by anyone who made this... thing I'm playing. Anyways cutscene ends and now I finally get onto a mission.
And as I watch a awkward cutscene of the slowest landing spaceship ever, not even a second passes by when the level starts and suddenly I am being shot at by green aliens with Tommy guns. Points for originality I guess.
So after I grasped the situation I quickly shoot and kill one of the aliens and then my gun stops working. Did I run out of bullets? Nope because my UI tells my I have 100+ bullets in reserve. I even ran around the alien (which by the way must be near sighted because it refused to fire at me unless I was 6 feet close to it) to grab more ammo and nope, gun refused to work. Oh by the way, the UI works now. Sorry for mentioning that so late but this whole situation litterally happened with in time span of 4 seconds. That was then I noticed was that there was an empty gauge on the corner of my screen. Is this... or was this my health? At this point, my expectations of this thing was pretty damn low so I run back to the near sighted alien to see if I can die. I stood there for a minute of this alien unloading bullets into me and yeah my suspicions were correct; that was supposed my health and it glitched out so I can't die.
So I eventually got bored getting shot at and started looking around for my objective. And it was here that I made a fatal mistake; My expectations wern't low enough. It's a simple fix, a VERY simple fix and it was the very fact that since it was a very simple fix that it made me rage because what that tells me if they can't be bothered to fix something THAT simple, then they don't give a flying ****.
But before I decided to do my final judgement on this thing, I thought to myself; maybe this is a Early Access. I mean it has to be. (Please note I did receive this thing as part of a random game promotion from a website so I knew nothing about it coming in.) The Political system is great there are 14 forms of governments however I find that this is the most annoying mechanic due to the little things you are always doing. With this being said I would recommended this game to newcomers to paradox games, if you have played other paradox games this game would be a waste of time and money in my opinion ( UNLESS ON STEAM SALES ) or if you are just bored out of you mind.

Despite what you may have heard about this game being unfinished or maybe not good, with the restoration mod this fixes 99% of of those problems and you find yourself a star wars RPG that is really deep and actually branches out a really meaningful story.
Some side history incase your not familiar why parts of the game were cutout in the first place. After the release of KOTOR 1 Lucasarts wanted to get the sequel pumped out around some tight scheuduales. Obsidian entertianment wanted to make a really deep and different game with lots of ideas that unfotunatly were constrained by time. To make for a holiday release, lucas arts rushed obsidian and that's why A LOT was cut out from the game and why certian aspects of the game weren't fully integrated as obsidian would have wanted. In short, lucas art's fualt, not obsidian.
Now thanks to the kind folks on the kotor 2 restoration team, we now have the really great complete experience that it was intended to be. Graphically its a little better than the first one and thanks to the recent updates you can now play with a controller, unlock achievements and play in HD resolutions. The voice acting, plot elements and of course the music hold up really damn well. There are plenty of mods for this game, though I should warn that the filefront site that hosted them shut down recently, however it seems steam workshop will be filling up soon with them. This game doesn't take you down a similiar theme like the movies, but instead does its own thing almost. I wont spoil anything, but if your looking for a fun game with good voice acting, a good story and a good amount of mystery this game is for you.

To be fair, if
delivers very little in the way of gameplay, it at least had the good grace not to promise very much, either.
The game allows you to do what you'd expect: assemble pictures of kittens from individual puzzle pieces.  It just doesn't do so very well.  It lacks novelty; jigsaw puzzles and kittens are both well-known concepts.  It lacks challenge; the puzzles have few pieces, and they cannot even be rotated.  It lacks replayability; who wants to do the same puzzle over again?  It lacks polish; every aspect of the game is minimalistic and purely functional, without extras, down to the bare-bones menu system.
Can you solve puzzles? Yes.
Are there kittens?  Lots.
Are the kittens cute? Adorable.
Is that enough to make the game good?  No.
The latest update bringing Linux support is well worth it. Aspyr did a competent job (as always) porting this to Linux.

To Preface this: I was gifted a copy by a friend.
I've only played this particular version for 17 hours, but I put in over 30 in the betas.
I enjoy the game. It's not like Mount and Blade, but it does have directional blocking and attacking.
It's not like Dark Souls, but it does have stamina management.
It's not like LoL, but it does have laning aspects.
All in all, an interesting combination of ideas. The story mode is useful in that it basically operates as a tutorial, in addition to the already existing tutorial. That being said, if you ever relished in finding a special move or combination that wasn't listed in the instruction manual, you'll find plenty to like here. There's plenty of moves on the move lists, but there's a few special techniques that aren't exclusively listed, which is interesting.
My experiences with the game waffle between elating and frustrating. There are instances when I felt robbed of victory, but there are also instances when I absolutely clutched after a long battle. For what it's worth, the experience I've had is that the AI is crazy OP at level 3, so I prefer to fighting players.
There's a difficulty curve to learning the controls, but you get used to it fairly quickly. All in all, I enjoy my time with it. Would I spend $60 on it? Maybe, maybe not. If you're the kind of person to enjoy tactical action games with a heavy duel aspect, I would say so. If you're the type of person who's looking for a quick hack and slash action, this probably isn't for you.
The kind of person that strikes me that might like this at full price is a combination of someone who would buy Battlefield on release day, and then turn around and play Mount and Blade.
But yes, I enjoy it.

A truly marvelous entertainment for distinguished gentlemen.
The game is all about options. Not only do you have to select your route from a number of onward trips, but each leg of your journey offers a narrative with dozens of choices - while sometimes it's just idle talk, often these choices linger with you on your adventure. You meet people who later help (or hold you back), you receive items that become important later etc. Thus each of your journeys becomes a unique one, and at first the game overwhelms you with this abundance of options. You replay it just to see what could have happened if you made a different choice in some place... and then make a different choice much, much earlier, derailing the adventure to a completely different route.
The narrative itself is excellent in form and content. Lots of micro-plots you encounter in your journeys have unexpected turns and sometimes you find yourself not in the place you intended to reach. The steampunk atmosphere is wonderful, it hits all the tropes of the genre, yet still feeling both genuine and creative. The amount of different contraptions, vehicles and mechanisms you see on your travels is surprising. Also, as you replay the game, you begin to value the political picture of the game's world. The nations are making wars and alliances, different organisations dabble into political affairs, and you start feeling to be a part of this grand scheme.
The main 80-day objective is relatively easy, you will most certainly hit it on your second playthrough. The real challenge, though, is the 40-day achievement, which seems impossible at first. It is much harder to nail and requires familiarising with the game, noting the fast routes and ways to make shortcuts or earn fast money.
I highly recommend this game, it is full of surprises and is quite entertaining at least for a dozen of playthroughs. I've made, like, forty playthroughs and still keep finding fun trips with narrative I haven't seen before.

So i am very disappointed to see all the negative reviews for For Honor, and before i adress what it seems people are criticing about the game i will speak where it excells
first off, by now  you probably know what for honor is, a competite multiplayer game in a medieval setting. this is probably for honors greatest appeal since very few games like this exist, chivalry is the most comparable one. in my opinion for honor is far better than chivalry is. the combat is very deep and complex; a mix of dark souls and mount and blade ( stamina control / direction blocking and attacking ) add in the great customization options and the seasonal persistant faction based pvp you end up with, in my opinion one very addicting game
now the issues. all in all this game doesnt deserve the hate and is a god send for someone like me who loves medieval settings and competetive online play which is a pairing rarely found in games. So come join me and the other vikings or die otherwise!

Rating: 4/10
Summary:  Forget-able.  One of the few games I've ever regretted having in my steam library.
Game play:
The overall game concept isn't terrible.  However, it's nothing new.  Pixelated style combined with a side scrolling shooter in a zombie apocalypse.  The resources are relatively scarce and the replayability seems to largely come from the fact that the odds are VERY stacked against you.  Completing this game would be an accomplishment both on Steam and as a testament to your patience.
Setting:
If you saw the store page you're more than aware that the game setting is not novel.  However,  I was hoping for the game to take itself less seriously as the game play implied that this would be a pixelated grindhouse film.  I don't know about you, but I can't take a pixelated grindhouse game seriously.
The style:
The grindhouse style "cinematography" takes about 10 minutes to get old.  The wandering line on the screen in the cut scenes is also in the game play along with some other fabricated anomalies meant to reflect the grindhouse film references.
The inclusion of an obscure copy of "Romanza" in EVERY shop seeks to destroy an otherwise elegant piece of music by placing it in a completely non-sensical setting.  At the exact same time, anyone without a knowledge of this classical piece of music will question the inclusion of a heavily Spanish-themed song in a zombie apocalypse.  The overworld music is redundant and aggressive but that's expected and honestly, it's about the only thing that refreshingly reflected the generic nostalgia that the imagery promises.
This game is buggy beyond belief. Unless you are really proficient in editing program files, I do not suggest getting it.

While the morality system tied to the ending has a few issues, Tormentum is an intriguing, if relatively basic hidden object and puzzle-centric adventure game. The main draw is the Giger and Beksinski-inspired dark art and the atmosphere of the decaying, corrupted world, but there's a competent enough game underneath it, if a relatively simple one. For what it is, it's a fairly interesting, non-stressful experience; there are a few points at which your progress might be delayed by a puzzle or a hidden item, but otherwise, it's a fairly straightforward affair.
Don't expect this to compare in any capacity to the juggernauts of the genre, and don't expect a large, expansive title. You'll get 2-3 hours out of an initial run, maybe more if you do any extra runs to get both endings and all the choices. If you've ever wanted to play a decent hidden object game and one with a darker atmosphere, this will work for you. However, if you want a proper adventure game with some actually meat to it, I'd recommend that you look elsewhere; this is more a twisted, Eldritch piece of candy that excites the tastebuds, but ultimately leaves you with empty calories.

Perfect game for any car fan, regardless of age.
There's not a whole lot of fancy graphics, no lens flares, relatively simple smoke/dust effects, most foliage (except trees) are made of flat textures (which are pretty well done, you can't really tell unless you stop and zoom right in on the grass, looks fine if you're driving even at low speeds), and the shaders aren't modified to give a 'cinematic look'. So this game isn't an astonishingly pretty game. But you know what, that's okay.
Each vehicle is intricately modelled, down to the point where you can see each individual part of the engine. You can see the butterfly valves on your supercharged V8 muscle car, you can see the engine block move around in its mounts slightly as you rev the engine. The level of detail is insane. Hit a harsh bump that bottoms out your custom, lowered car? Be prepared to potentially have your entire exhaust system ripped out of your car. Hit a sharp kerb at high speed? Might wanna watch your tires, they can pop, giving your car an unnatural feel. The physical damage in this game is brutally realistic, as each car is not 'hard-coded' with performance stats, health points, etc. Each INDIVIDUAL PART of a car makes up it's whole performance, much like a real car. Pop your front-right tire, and your car will start veering slightly to the right. Fit sport tires, you might be able to handle a corner slightly faster. Lower your suspension, you'll reduce body rolls and keep all 4 tires on the road better, resulting in better grip.
It goes on and on. The soft-body physics overall are brilliant, the cars crumple, wobble, and react exactly how you'd expect a car to react.
The maps that come with the game are very nice, and quite varied.
So, quite a few maps, with lots of variety.
The game has a wide variety of scenarios, too many to list here, that cover multiple fun aspects of the game.
These can range from tutorials, to shakedowns of various cars, police chases, races, delivery challenges, even a 'hyper-miling' challenge where you have to cross Jungle Rock Island with very little gas left in your car. There's even a demolition derby scenario for people to 'party play'.
Overall, I'd give this game a 8/10, I'd like to see networked multiplayer (something the BeamNG devs might implement if their engine can support it) and a campaign mode (which the devs have planned pretty much since day 1 of the project)
Lots more potential, the modding community is great, who make new maps, scenarios, vehicles, etc, etc.
Definitely worth the buy, especially for car fans, IMO.

Another ongoing review...
So far I found EU: Rome to be a lot simpler than more recent iterations. Even if compared with CK and CK2 it feels like it's been stripped off of many features. Still, the game holds on pretty well, and it might be a great entry point for anyone interested in this series, or any other grand strategy game from paradox.
Graphics are obviously dated, but they do not detract from the experience. Sound is great, and interface... well, it's a paradox game. You be mauled by text and tons of info most of the time, but you'll learn to work with it. The setting is great, and despite not being entirely faithful to historical data (generals, citizens and kings are rolled before the game begins, for example), there's a fair amount of historical background holding the scene together. Just don't try using it in history class or on your homework, if you're still at that stage of life.
Mechanics hold up quite well. There's more waiting than in, say, EU IV, but it's manageable. Kingdoms and empires are a riot to play. AI is good (better then most strategy games out there, by the way) and pacing is great. Many interesting and unique moments are bound to arise. I'm preparing a story compilation from a few playthroughs for the youtube channel, so as to exemplify it.
Solid recommendation!
P.S.: as with all paradox grand strategy games, READ THE DAMN MANUAL!

Europa Universalis: Rome is a game that uses EUIII engine with some changes to make it stand out as a true simulator of the Roman rule. You will have the ability to expand the most powerful empire of the Ancient Times, while keeping your domestic enemies and rivals at bay. The graphics of this game are definitely outdated, but if that isn't an issue for you, then EU:R deserves your attention. Even those, who played EUIII before, will find something new to learn here, such as the loyalty system of the Roman army. But be prepared to the challenging mechanics and sometimes quite-not-so-obvious rules and peculiarities of the gameplay. Also, it's cheap and the DLC is included.
+ Excellent music
+ Excellent historical correctness
+ Many starting options from different historical periods
+ Huge amount of strategy options to approach your empire management
- The resolution is pretty terrible.
- The tutorial of the game clearly overestimates the game's simplicity.
That's, I think, about it. I hope you enjoy the game.

New to the Duels series, so I have only read about comparisons to previous versions (which sound like the 2015 game removed a lot from). Starting from the top, the UI is pretty poor as it forces you to scroll through and suffer long fades. Moving on to the deck builder, while I'm very glad to have the option for complete deck customization, the interface wastes a lot of valuable space and organization options. Additionally, it is rather infuriating (and DEFINITELY WORTH NOTING) that almost every card in the Campaign and AI's decks are not available to add to your own decks - this drives me crazy since the game clearly has the mechanics of the cards built in. However, hearing that the deck builder was not available in previous Duels games is both confusing (since it's so integral to Magic for me) and reassuring - and hopefully being the first game to feature the deck builder can only mean that it will improve with later iterations.
Multiplayer is fun, however hearing that they removed options like Puzzles, Two-Headed Giant, and Challenges doesn't make sense to me and seems like a strange choice to simply trade features rather than improve them.
All-in-All, if you enjoy building decks almost as much as playing the game, then this game is worth picking up. However if you're looking for long term playability and multiplayer (I've enjoyed multiplayer but mainly because I have a group I play with regularly), then I would suggest researching previous versions of the game to determine whether it's worth it for you.

Aside from having his long-awaited sequel turning out like this, the events of this game would've been Duke's darkest hour had DNF been any other game.
The aliens came back hungry for revenge, destroyed everything the protagonist built for the past 12 years in a matter of hours (Lady Killer, Duke Dome, Duke Burger), killed everyone he cared about (the Holsom twins, at least), being unable to save almost everyone he encounters ("Not even I can save you now" in The Hive, among many others) even though they all depended on him to protect them and believed he could do anything, getting knocked out all the damn time, and the President blaming him for the alien attack so logically speaking, the people who lost their family members to Pregnators/Pigcops would be angry at him for letting all this happen.
But since this is Duke Nukem, everyone is happy that he kicked the aliens' asses again and cheered for Duke(inator) to be President. I know he's a badass and all and these things don't bother him, but his adventures turned from happy-family-friendly to bloody-ultra-violent real fast between DN2 and DN3D. Now I wonder if he steals one-liners and has women between his arms and legs every night is because he wants to hide his pain (of that, as well as not getting any good games since Manhattan Project).
Terms of gameplay, single player is fun. The four weapon system is fine with me, since borderlands also had four weapons. But playing the game with two weapon can be just as thrilling. It had me running out of ammo and struggling to find another weapon on the floor, which brings some excitment to the game. Most bosses have to be taken down by explosives and turrets, yet you can take out a regular sized enemy when you're a little Duke with a normal weapon. No mighty boot, but you can smack your enemies with your gun. The handgun, shotgun and railgun are my favorite weapons. The single player alternates between in "survive the ambush", puzzles/platforming, driving, and boss fights.
DNF's multiplater is an arena shooter. Guns spawn at spefic areas in a map and you pick it up and kick♥♥♥♥♥with it. There are four modes: Duke Match, Team Duke Match, Capture the babe, and Hail to the King. DLC includes the free-for-all versions of CTB and HTTK, and four maps.
Multiplayer is corrupted with toxic people, that point at people of being hackers just because they got killed many♥♥♥♥♥times and won't stop badgering you until you act like a newb, but in fact THEY are the god damn newbs. Even some decent players call people out for being hackers. Maybe I'm naive, this probably happens in all other competitive games. Living in North America, the servers are mostly laggy (~200 ping) because most of the players are from Sweden or Austrailia, but there are some NA servers running 24/7.
You can level up in multiplayer which upgrades your dig, do challenges and unlock wearable items. You unlock ladies in your dig which you could talk to, and have an amusing conversation. Based on the novel
by Jules Verne,
takes place in the year 1872. You play as Frenchman Jean Passepartout, valet to the Englishman Phileas Fogg. Fogg has just made a wager of £20,000 that he can make a journey around the world in eighty days or less, beginning and ending in London. It is up to Passepartout as his valet to plan out this journey and try to win the bet.
This game is a combination of interactive fiction and some strategic management. The planning of the journey itself requires the most strategy in the game. You begin the journey with a set amount of funds and you have to figure out how to use that money for the best purposes. This means deciding what types of transportation to take as different types cost different amounts of money. There is also the aspect of inventory as you can buy items that might be useful to you on your trip or you can engage in some buying and selling to help fund the journey. All along the way, you have to keep an eye on the calendar if you hope to make it back to London on time and pay attention to Fogg's health.
Aside from management, the other major aspect of the game is the storytelling. All along the way, you have the opportunity to meet and talk to many different people from all over the globe and find yourself in different situations. Talking with people comes off as important aspect to your journey as well. Perhaps a stranger knows of certain routes that will make your trip shorter or offer tips on where the best places to sell items are. Although taking place in 1872, the game's story and design contains many steampunk-themed elements. Thus, you have talk of various types of warfare and civil unrest. The steampunk theme is also prevalent in the world such as some rather unconventional types of transportation available. There is the more standard things such as trains and ships, but you also have things like hovercraft and walking cities, all with that steampunk theme. If you like storytelling, there is a lot to enjoy in this game.
I also thought the game's graphics looked pretty good even with its minimalist design. You spend most of the game looking at a simplified map of the globe, but there are stylistic graphics depicting the various forms of transportation you use and destinations you visit.
Each journey you take can probably be completed in around three hours, though I imagine a single journey can take much more time depending on the decisions the player makes. I have only played around four trips so far, so my review is based on that experience.
For me, there are only a couple of negatives. The first is a complete lack of multiple saves. The game autosaves where you left off when you quit, but there is no option to have multiple games. I really fail to see why there is such an annoyance. The other major negative aspect that I came across is that it is possible for your journey to hit a dead-end with no possible way to continue and yet there is no indication in the game that this might happen. It is quite frustrating to play for two or more hours only to have to end the game in such a way.
Overall, while a couple of flaws might be annoying, I generally enjoyed the adventurous nature of this game. If you like interactive fiction with an adventure theme, you will probably enjoy this game.

This game. This frakkin game. This scares the crap out of me. It's hard to find anything wrong with it (except that the monsters can be very moronic). The environments are so well done, the music perfectly compliments the environments and serves to reflect and also amplify whatever it is the game is making you feel; intrigue, lingering tension, or sheer terror and panic. (That weird shrieking sound when a monster spots you and gives chase? It's actually called"Terror Meter" in the soundtrack.) The distinct lack of stock sound effects was nice. The design of the monsters is.... scarily amazing. They are so well-designed and are terrifying to look at. The story is done brilliantly, pulling you in right from the start and not releasing you as you slowly unlock more of Daniel's story, until all the pieces finally fall into place and it makes you sick to think about, just like Daniel. Also the voice acting for Daniel and Alexander is incredible. The gameplay itself (oh yea that exists) is very smooth, taking the same concepts that Frictional Games started with in the Penumbra series and ironing out the issues in the physics. Thank god they took out that atrocious melee combat system from Penumbra Overture. The puzzles are well-designed and although not particularly hard, they are definitely creative, and sometimes it's downright disturbing what they expect you to do. All in all, I think it's safe to say this is one of my favorite PC games I've ever played.

My friend sent me this game while he was over seas to play with him during his downtime at night. Given I didn't play it long, it still managed to be one of the wost survival games I have ever played. My first experience with the game was spending 2 hours actually trying to connect to him. After some work on his end, we managed to but the server software kept crashing. Sometime during that 2 hour stretch we managed to finally play and stay connected. Because we were just playing with two of us for now he set it to gather and build faster since neither of us had a ton of time to spend. Even with it set to gather quickly, it still took almost 2 hours to build a 8 foot mine shaft. So, deciding to take a break, I returned to the main land (we met up on the small island to start with) for some clay. I finally found some after searching forever and returned to the island. Perhaps because i was overburdened, i couldnt swim on the surface, so I was forced to basically jump in the water, find i couldnt swim, and crawl out of it. Now as I stood there on the beach scratching my head, thinking WTF, I suddenly got to experience random death. It could have been a game mechanic from something, though if it was I am not sure what. So upon respawn, I had none of my items (not a big surprise though), my skills downgraded significantly and I was spawned clear across the main continent. So after spending ~10 minutes walking all the way back to the eastern shore, I found my stuff gone. I get survival games are supposed to be somewhat difficult, but I have played other survival games like Ark and Rust with much less fustration. The over all time it took to straighten out the multiplayer (which really just should work on a multiplayer game), how far resources are spread out over the map, the amount of time it takes to craft and dig when settings are maxxed out, among other things really made this one of the must fustrating and dissapointing experiences of my life. The concept seemed really cool, especially after watching the combat tutorial, however in execution, the game is one of the worst I have played.

Took a chance on this game, not really knowing what to expect. I was pleasantly suprised.
What normally dulls my enthusiasm for adventure games is the lack of real player agency. Most hold you by the hand, tell you a story, and then after a few hours the credits roll. 80 Days avoids this problem with playthroughs that are comparatively short (1-2 hours, depending on how you play), but have plenty of paths to take and choices to make. Some of the routes are more linear, while others will take you in all sorts of unexpected directions, and all of them are impeccably narrated. I've done maybe 10 full playthroughs or so, and while I've seen plenty, there are still cities and stories I haven't discovered yet.
Though even the most open-ended adventure game eventually becomes repetitive. Some of the early and late game events have started to wear on me, so I may not turn over every stone, but by now I definitely feel like the game has given me my money's worth in excitement and entertainment.
The only complaint I have is a bug I have encountered a few times where the game clock would get stuck and I would be forced to restart. I haven't identified a cause or a fix, so it's rather vexing when it strikes while I'm having a good run. Not a dealbreaker, but still a glaring flaw in an otherwise perfect game.

Perfect game for any car fan, regardless of age.
There's not a whole lot of fancy graphics, no lens flares, relatively simple smoke/dust effects, most foliage (except trees) are made of flat textures (which are pretty well done, you can't really tell unless you stop and zoom right in on the grass, looks fine if you're driving even at low speeds), and the shaders aren't modified to give a 'cinematic look'. So this game isn't an astonishingly pretty game. But you know what, that's okay.
Each vehicle is intricately modelled, down to the point where you can see each individual part of the engine. You can see the butterfly valves on your supercharged V8 muscle car, you can see the engine block move around in its mounts slightly as you rev the engine. The level of detail is insane. Hit a harsh bump that bottoms out your custom, lowered car? Be prepared to potentially have your entire exhaust system ripped out of your car. Hit a sharp kerb at high speed? Might wanna watch your tires, they can pop, giving your car an unnatural feel. The physical damage in this game is brutally realistic, as each car is not 'hard-coded' with performance stats, health points, etc. Each INDIVIDUAL PART of a car makes up it's whole performance, much like a real car. Pop your front-right tire, and your car will start veering slightly to the right. Fit sport tires, you might be able to handle a corner slightly faster. Lower your suspension, you'll reduce body rolls and keep all 4 tires on the road better, resulting in better grip.
It goes on and on. The soft-body physics overall are brilliant, the cars crumple, wobble, and react exactly how you'd expect a car to react.
The maps that come with the game are very nice, and quite varied.
So, quite a few maps, with lots of variety.
The game has a wide variety of scenarios, too many to list here, that cover multiple fun aspects of the game.
These can range from tutorials, to shakedowns of various cars, police chases, races, delivery challenges, even a 'hyper-miling' challenge where you have to cross Jungle Rock Island with very little gas left in your car. There's even a demolition derby scenario for people to 'party play'.
Overall, I'd give this game a 8/10, I'd like to see networked multiplayer (something the BeamNG devs might implement if their engine can support it) and a campaign mode (which the devs have planned pretty much since day 1 of the project)
Lots more potential, the modding community is great, who make new maps, scenarios, vehicles, etc, etc.
Definitely worth the buy, especially for car fans, IMO.

This game is dark, despondent, despairing and depending on how one defines horror, it could be that too.  A point and click not so adventurous "adventure" game.  (Adventure because it does fall into any other catergory, not really, other then maybe supernatural.  But even that would be a stretch.)  Has a moralistic tone of more right vs wrong, then good vs evil.
Story: The condemned arrives with a fellow prisoner at a castle specifically designed for torture, torment, and purging souls of their evil through pain, suffering, and grief.  (Dark, very dark, in tone.)  The condemned man is told this in his jail cell by the horned guard, who also informs the condemned man he (the guard) will back to torture him.  Of course, the condemned man does not wait around for that.  This begins the journey through the Hell-bound castle, and meeting its various denizans.  After that it is a trip though the wastelands, dealing with the inhabitants, and eventually to the condemned man's goal, a structure of uprised arms with a shrouded female statue inside.  Ethical choices are made throughout, in the simply question kill or not kill.
I could get into a huge philosophical discussion right about now (especially after reading other reviews, in particular the negative ones) but I will spare everyone this.  But the game and that simple life-death question does have a thought poking quality that can not be denied.  (Oh by the way I considered every entity in this game to be "evil", some just less "evil" then others, even before I finished reading the Immanuel Kant introduction.)
The game is short (I suppose).  Some say they finished in about 2 hours.  I took much longer enjoying the amazing, stunning, awe-inspiring artwork.  I am not one to talk much artwork or graphics but words like astonishing, stupefying, shocking and startling could all be used to describe this game's artwork.  This game brings to mind the paintings of Hell and Judgement done by Hieronymus Bosch (Netherland).  Now add to that the H.R. Giger (Switzerland) influence (best known for the creature 'Alien') and the Zdzislaw Beksinski (Polish) influence the developers and designers used as inspiration and Dante's Inferno (many reviewers refer to) seems like Heaven.  The art work alone is worth the game price.  (Art museum admissions cost more for this much art viewing, and one can keep this.)
Gameplay: This is a point and click game with puzzles, and plays in a linear fashion with goals that need to be accomplished.  It is played in 3D so the scene moves back and forth, and along the edges arrows appear if the gamer can go in that direction.  There are basically 4 segments to this game, castle, wastelands, town, conclusion.  The castle, wastelands, and town can also be broken in 2 subsections each.
Puzzles: Many think the puzzles are too easy.  I think hard puzzles would simply distract from the overall ambience of the entire game.  For me, this is a story about the journey, the encounters that occur on that journey, and the decisions made on that journey, not the puzzles.  Though I must say for me the highlight puzzle was a 'slider/make the gears spin' puzzle.  I could almost hear groans and sighs from those who simply detest both types of those puzzles because they were in the same puzzle. Puzzle types include logic, sliders, and codes in various forms.
Overall I think the game is worth the price and the play.  It is a journey game, not an adventure game, however, so that should be kept in mind in the gamer's decision making.

I am typically a fan of all things Rome.  This game had great potential, however it was ultimately brought down by a lack of committment to turn it into a polished product with a truly Roman feel.  It is based off of the EU III engine with a few minor tweaks which actually add a level of confusion to gameplay.  The character system seems arbitrary and is not well explained at all. Even with several traits and families competing for Roman senate dominance it is difficult to get a sense of attachment or feeling with any of them.   Finding suitable generals is a huge task, and requires a character to hold several government positions before taking command of a Legion.  The whole feel of the game feels like a forced integration between CKII and the EU series.  With all of that said, you will spend most of your time waiting for something interesting to happen so that you may expand your Roman Empire.  Do yourself a favor, and pick up EU IV instead, which contains a great deal of Rome mods in the Steam workshop.

It's very futuristic, and brings up a lot of philosophical questions about the soul.  Throw in a splash of Bioshock (haha puns) and this is what you get.
The gameplay is essentially the same as the Penumbra and Amensia series.  Part "Walking Simulator" and part "hide from the scary monsters".  You go around interracting with things, picking up items, hiding from psuedo-zombies that screw up your vision, and keep progressing.  An interesting addition is a 3 strikes system with the enemies.  If you meet one face to face you essentially black out and wake up in the same spot you were attacked, with the enemy that found you some ways off, allowing you to hide again.  Each time you're attacked your vision gets a little more blurry and your movement lopsided, but you're still able to continue.
The story is absolutly delicious, but it's hard to tell too much about it with giving major spoilers.  Essentially, you're a Canadian you got into a nasty car accident, has pretty bad brain damage, and decides to go through some experimental treatment.  Within the blink of an eye, you're suddenly in another world with no idea of what's going on.
All in all, a solid game from Frictional, and I look forward to see what they come up with next.

Everyone seems to hate this game. But as a total rookie to magic, I quite enjoyed it. This game is ment for players who want to appreciate the mechanics of Magic, without pumping in hundreds or even thousands of dollars to deck build. While it is limited to only a percentage of the official 2015 Magic card line up, it is still a really cool way to appreciate one of the best modern game franchises ever created.
PROS
-This game makes you appreciate Magic. Stunning Graphics, with great visuals and easy to view card art. The controls are simple and easy to use. Plus the tutorial lets you jump right into the action.
- Super smooth gameplay that actually works. You will have to make some setting adjustments from time to time, but once you uncheck the noob only settings, the game works great.
- No issues playing people or AI. There's a stop timer when someone plays a crazy card that you'll want to read and the game gives you ample time to make decisions, without making you go nuts if someone is taking too long.
- Great card collection, with 100% customizable decks. I read that in Magic 2014 you had to pay money to make more decks!?!?! That's just crazy. Making decks is the fun part, and you can have fun for just $10 up front costs, for sure.
- All DLC is actually obtainable without any purchases. Just pay the $10 and you can grind your way to a 90% completed card collection. DON’T BUY THE DLC!
- AI seems pretty smart, for the most part. If you don't play right, they will beat you.
CONS
- If you want to get a 100% card collection you will have to fork over an extra $28. A lot of people hate this, but I had plenty of fun for just the $10 up front. I decided to buy in after completing the game and wanting to compete online against other players for the long term. It's lame, but completely optional and only necessary if you want to compete more hardcore online.
- Some AI opponents get pretty challenging and seem impossible to beat. They definitely cheat and get cards they need in their first few hands. You can combat this with “Exile from ratgets Library” cards a little, but it gets pretty frustrating at times.
- The menu system is really dumb. It takes forever to switch to a different deck (too many clicks) and while it’s beautiful, I’d rather is just be efficient.
- There are no instructions on how you get more cards. I completed the entire game not knowing that I could “Explore” planes to get additional boosters. They need to make this more clear IMO.
- The Profile menu system is awkward too. You can click your icon to see messages, but it’s mostly full of stuff the game already told you, like and achievement you unlocked. One important note, is that if you DO win a multiplayer match, you get a booster full of random cards from all the planes, but you have to check on your profile, sift through all the unimportant messages to find the important booster pack one. Awkward to the max yo!

As someone who has played Magic off and on for the past five years or so, I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a fun, semi-casual Magic experience.  While DotP 2015 has its technical faults, it more than makes up for them by offering a package that is fun, educational and has a sharp looking user interface.
My favorite things about DotP 2015 so far are the in-match suggestion and the in-game card info features.  If I'm not sure about my next move, I can ask for a suggestion and the game will offer advice, like enchant a creature, or attack with a certain number of creatures while still having other creatures for defense.  The card info feature lets you zoom in on a card and will offer more info on a certain ability or term if you are unfamiliar with it.  I imagine more experienced players would be turned off by these, but I assure you, they are totally optional and can be disabled if you wish.
Another thing I like about DotP 2015 is the sense of progression.  You get to test drive several different decks of various colors and playstyles in the tutorial and once you beat the first boss, that's your starting deck.  After that, you begin a journey that will send you to several different planes, each with around six unique fights.  I will admit, it is a little frightening being locked in at this point with practically no way to change, but you have to press on.  You can augment your current deck or build new ones by winning campaign battles or random duels and earning booster packs.  Booster packs contain about 7~10 cards or so.  Yeah, it's grindy, but that's the point.
To the more experienced players, the tutorials are optional and many of these features can be turned off.  If you're still not sure, I would say try cranking up the difficulty if you still need a challenge.  To the newer players and people like me, looking for a fun Magic experience without embarassing yourself in public like I do at booster drafts, this is pretty cool and well worth the $10.
One more thing regarding the microtransactions/DLC:  I hate microtransactions and in-app purchases in general, so before I tried DotP 2015, I was extremely wary of the idea of subjecting myself to a scam.  I don't plan on purchasing anything beyond the base game and at five hours in, I don't feel pressured into buying anything.  There is nothing "in your face" about it.  There is an unobtrusive button in one of the menus that says 'shop' where you can choose to buy special booster packs or foil stickers if you want.  I'm a very cynical person when it comes to monetization strategies like this and so far, I don't agree with a lot of criticism of this game.

I had thought that all the reviews bashing this game were just hype.  I could not have been more wrong.  This game suffers from
balance issues.  Your starting decks, quite frankly, really do suck, and do not work as advertised (blue spells do not "bounce" in the blue/green deck, for example, and the green creatures do not have the "when entering the battlefield" effects promised.  The only exception to this is the black/white deck, but only barely, as it does indeed have a whopping three cards with lifelink)  In fact, no matter what color combination you choose, the cards you get for your color are always the same.  (you get the same blue cards for a blue/black as you do for a blue/green or blue/red).  Also, your starting decks do not have a "base" card:  that one powerful card that you build your deck around.  To compound matters, the greatest strength of this game is also its greatest weakness:  the emulation of booster packs.  the cards you get are entirely random, meaning you can (as I have twice now) wind up with no new cards to add to your deck before fighting the stage one boss, something that is absolutely critical.  Do NOT make the same mistake I made.  DO NOT BUY THIS GAME.  Buy Dream Pinball 3D or Air Control instead.

Took a chance on this game, not really knowing what to expect. I was pleasantly suprised.
What normally dulls my enthusiasm for adventure games is the lack of real player agency. Most hold you by the hand, tell you a story, and then after a few hours the credits roll. 80 Days avoids this problem with playthroughs that are comparatively short (1-2 hours, depending on how you play), but have plenty of paths to take and choices to make. Some of the routes are more linear, while others will take you in all sorts of unexpected directions, and all of them are impeccably narrated. I've done maybe 10 full playthroughs or so, and while I've seen plenty, there are still cities and stories I haven't discovered yet.
Though even the most open-ended adventure game eventually becomes repetitive. Some of the early and late game events have started to wear on me, so I may not turn over every stone, but by now I definitely feel like the game has given me my money's worth in excitement and entertainment.
The only complaint I have is a bug I have encountered a few times where the game clock would get stuck and I would be forced to restart. I haven't identified a cause or a fix, so it's rather vexing when it strikes while I'm having a good run. Not a dealbreaker, but still a glaring flaw in an otherwise perfect game.

This game has the distinct feel of a "choose your own adventure" book, but with much more fluidity and variation from playthrough to playthrough. The differences from game to game can be subtle or glaring, ranging between your starting supplies, which cities the Orient Express happens to run through, or whether or not you are granted the opportunity to go on an expidition to the moon! After the 5th or 6th time playing through, I realized that there's an option to go through the North Pole! How's that for a shortcut? (Also, if you can, do that. Some of the game's best writing lies down that path.)
The feel of the game is perfect. Since the clock is always ticking, you feel like you have to weigh careful planning with expediency, which can end up forcing you down paths you might not expect! The differing routes and methods of travel from game to game keep this feeling fresh after multiple runs.
The game captures the feel of 19th century penny dreadfuls perfectly, with swashbuckling adventure and outlandish (if somewhat campy) secrets in pretty much every run. Plus the writing is immensely good. If you like "choose your own adventure" style games at all, this game should be at the top of your wish list.

Tormentum - Dark Sorrow is a 2D point and click dark fantasy adventure game with visuals inspired by Geiger and Beksinski. It's short - ca. 3hrs for the first playthrough - but worth a buy.
It's creepy, disturbing, twisted and dark. Quite a logical game where you are allright just with common sense, I never had to use everything on something to find a way to move forward. Apart from basic pont and clicking there are several puzzles, slide some pieces to make a picture, connect pipes to make the stream flow, etc. Nothing fancy.
VISUALS
This game is all about visuals and they are most creepy and disturbing. Not for the squeamish. Look at the screenshots, if you don't like them just pass. If you like what you see then buy it as there is more. Basically, if you like that dark fantasy setting, the game is a treat. Additionally at the game's completion you also get to see some additional full screen pictures, not related to the game. And they are very very wow.
AUDIO
There is some background music. It's not bad. It's there. Note that if you want to put anything on youtube, you'll get claimed.
GAMEPLAY
Simple puzzles, simple point and clicking, a story which is not horrible. Yes, the game is short - 3hrs for the first playthrough, ca. 1-1.5hrs for subsequent ones. Yes, the game is quite simple. Still, it's a game for enjoying the beautifully drawn graphics while doing some basic puzzling. Nothing fancy or demanding. There are two endings and it takes 2-3 playthroughs to 100%.
All in all if you like your fantasy dark and Geigerish and are into point and clicking, or just watching nice pictures go for it. If you are on the squemish side and prefer your fantasy all dungeonsy dragony, or expect more challenge, you might give it a pass.

Bottom Line: Tormentum is an enjoyable, albeit short, point-and-click adventure game with an outstandingly disturbing art style. Fans of gothic and demonic art/themes will surely find much to like. However, it's lack of story throughout may make the game feel like little more than an art exhibition, for some. Expectation management is necessary with this one.
PROS:
-AMAZING & DISTURBING artwork inspired by H.R. Giger (Swiss surrealist, best known for visual design of the first Alien film)
-Puzzles are not too easy or too challenging.
-Writing is effective, although sparse.
-Offers two endings small branching paths to encourage multiple playthroughs.
-Steam Trading Cards are actually more art by the designers, even higher quality than what's found in-game.
-Music is of high quality (atmospheric, dark, and gothic).
CONS:
-Story is sparse at best. The game's conclusion ties everything together somewhat, regardless of what ending you receive, but does not provide meaningful explanations for the game's imagery.
-Game is short, expect to finish in less than four hours. Buy on sale to justify the length.

I played through Tormentum in three short sessions spread out over a couple of evenings and I really enjoying the game. All the puzzles are logical and probably won't tax people's grey matter too much, but it all comes together so well - and it's a pleasure to explore the world. I think the difficulty is perfect for an enjoyable, frustration free, experience that requires just enough thought to keep you engaged. Everything is very well designed and readable.
The art is great with big nods to Giger and Beksiński. But the artwork mostly avoids simply being derivative of the inspiration and manages to stand on its own. The sound design is also quite good, with atmospheric music that never outstays its welcome.
This game is the school example of short game length not necessarily being bad. I enjoyed every second of it and by the end it felt like a complete experience (and there's reason to play it again). There's no unnecessary filler and the game is paced almost perfectly. I respect a game that respects my time.

This happens very seldom in games, but here I feel that the creators had a vision and made it from the depths of their, to a relative extent wicked, hearts. They pay no attention to what a general public of gamers prefer. This game is dark, sometimes utterly depressing, if you care to delve into surroundings, atmosphere, and what you see and read. But it is done in a purposeful fashion, and I enjoyed every single minute of this game.
The game has a great artistic style that alone sets the mood. On top of that there is a fantastic dark ambient soundtrack that fits the setting very well. It may sound strange, but this game made me think and dwell on things in life I wouldn't have otherwise. It has a certain amount of philosphy and psychology in it, and is to some extent intellectually challenging.
And a few words about the gameplay itself: it is a standard point and click game with puzzles on easy/medium difficulty. It takes around 5 hours to complete, but is interesting to replay to see what consequences different choices have. Second playthrough also takes much much shorter time. The story is great. Go play.
You'll play this game for ten minutes and then wish you hadn't.

My most played game on Steam, and it deserves a review.
Its very indeph with loads of micromanagement, and if you happen to like the timeline, you are welcome to buy it.
You can tune it to play it with unlimited time, if that bothers you.
What sets it apart from normal EU games, is the barbarian mechanic.
There are lots of uncivilized lands where barbarians are uprising all the time, and it takes near the end of the game, to civilize them all. If you play a nation that borders to them, it makes the game very "fun" and unpredictible.
Also, you can have children and start very long dynasties. Its fun to watch.
Combat is very much EU-like and simple. A good general is the most important thing.
There is lots to know about the game, you can read on it for a very long time to understand everything indeph.
Casus belli, how to play wars, the differences of the political systems and how they work, diplomacy, techtrees, jadda jadda.
I enjoyed this good micro/macro strategy for a very long time.
Its really hard to beat it with something like a little gallic state that battles the roman empire.
But if you make it, it was an experience thats worth it. If not, you want to try again. ;)
The only bad thing i have to say about the game, is that it has a nasty bug with soldier loyalty.
It randomly applies it to characters that never led an army.
But this bug is so nasty, it really dampens the experience.
You can play around it, but it simply sux a-s-s, and its a shame Paradox never fixed it, because this is one of their very best games.

Europa Universalis: Rome is a Pausable Real-Time Grand Strategy Game (woah that was a mouthful) developed by the ♥♥♥♥ing awesome Paradox Development Studio. Released in 2008, the game is what would be considered a "budget game", basically a side project to vary from the big projects they were working on.
But just because this is a budget game doesn't mean it's not good!!
You can play as any major (and some minor) faction ranging from 280 BC to 33 BC, and guide the nation through all aspects like religion, politics, economy, military, etc... It has a small learning curve but by the time you learn you will be HOOKED!!
Sure the graphics are outdated, but what self respecting PC strategy gamer cares about graphics?? The gameplay is a wonderful blend of high level empire management made famous by the main Europa Universalis series, and the character system of Crusader Kings II. It's an overall great game that still gets attention (PDS is the greatest game company ever, and they have a wonderful practice where they go back and update their old games out of nowhere!).
So buy this game (2.49 USD on sale, so why the hell not!!) and lose yourself in the world of Rome and it's politics!!

The reload minigame is a nice feature but not in a game where millions of zombies running towards you.

The screen is too small. The charging type enemies are nearly impossible to avoid as you don't have that small reaction. The poison bomb fatty's poison area is annoyingly high and unavoidable.
The best thing that there are two enemies that can and will ATTACK FROM OUTSIDE THE SCREEN (at least on 16: 9 resolution) giving you no chance to do anything. The spitters and the megaannoying pullers are just terrible. The best happens when 2 pullers come, one pulls you out and the second pulls from the first, than the first pulls from the second and they start ping-ponging with me and i cannot do a f@@@@ing thing.
Sure it's an MP game but they were nice enough to put in an SP campaign THAT HAS 6 LEVELS! These: 1 is a training defense mission, easy / 2 you are invincible and must drive a car and kill zombies / 3 you must defense a cabin (!) that you abandon when a helicopter comes. If you wait enough and don't take the copter, you can see the bosses too and dies very fast. 4 The only mission that is good, must go through a sewer. 5 Again invincible in the copter shooting helpless zombies down there. 6 Defense mission so hard had to try it 6 times on easy difficulty. The winning screen is just an offense. Seems like a new level but it's not, it's the end.
For a real MP top-down shooter choose Nation Red, for SP choose Nation Red (yes, that's SP is very good though there is no real campaign) or Dead Horde.

TL;DR - If you enjoyed Penumbra: Black Plague and BOTH Amnesia games, you'll enjoy this one.
But as a caveat, this one has more "A Machine for Pigs" than "Dark Descent" to it, but the added story elements give you a good reason to want to see it through to the end (I just got out of Lambda, the second station of around 8, to give an idea for length), and they get the expected twist out of the way early on - whether there's another one later remains to be seen.
And the increased budget REALLY shows, as one of the monsters is able to make my framerate drop even on High settings, and it's nice to see that they took the proceeds from Amnesia to make a graphically more-impressive game, even including little touches like scuttlings crab on the sea floor
Also, be prepared for a number of gut punches due to the nature of the "what measure is a man" debate that's held within the game.  Just got to Theta station, and it's been pretty depressing so far.
And as one final caveat, if you're waffling on whether or not you want to buy this, I'd advise waiting for an optimization patch, as even with my rig I've gotten drops to 1 FPS.
