I think this game didn't stand on its own.
Overall, Shadow Warrior 1 was better in every way, and I find it hard to believe that anyone could even be moderately interested in this game if they didn't play the first one.
The good:
Such unique visuals, excellent art quality, truly a one of a kind game visually
Super awesome performance for the quality of the visuals and particles
Meaty, brutal, and visceral combat (mostly the melee)
Again, visually amazing - can't get that across enough
The bad:
Sorry guys, there was a lot this time
Story - flat and stupid, and not in a Lo Wang funny way
Inventory - Minimum 10% of the time playing this game is inventory management, and basically none of it is done well at all. So much busy work, redundant actions, nothing smart about how it is put together.
Scale - The weapons and upgrades seem to come at a completely random pace. 1/2 way through the game I had 9/10 weapons that I used ever. The idea of the drawbacks on the upper level gems completely ruined the scaling, and for the most part upgrades found very late in the game would almost never be much better than very early ones.
Level design (outside of visuals) - completely terrible. No concept of curated content, just random big rooms randomly connected, there was no thought put in to the designs at all.
Conclusion:
PLAY THE FIRST ONE BEFORE YOU EVEN LOOK AT THIS GAME. If you loved the first one and are willing to put a lot of monotonus time in to inventory management to get some more amazing sword and magic based brawling - knock yourself out. If you are in to visual design, character or level (visual) design, you might have to buy the game just for that.

I don't usually write reviews of any type for games, as I simply do not have the time.  But today, I simply must.  As for the game, it was fun the first 24hrs of game play, but then it became rather tedious.  As any gamer looking to rapidly advance, I purchased through their micro transaction store, the available boosters (which by the way, are only available once per City, so don't count on going very far without help).  And then today, I was sieged.  Before I begin with this, let me tell you about the good and bad.
The good:
Animations are good as far as details.
provides a pve based scenario for you to have a sense of achievement and as well to grant you advancement in progression.
The bad:
Random Crashes while entering scenarios.
The community is not inviting and at no time while attempting to communicate did they ever respond.
Hackers are definitely prevalent and ruin a possibly good game.  I do not believe that they have any preventative measures against this.
During siege it will state that you have the upper hand, all the while you are over run by armies of undertrained hoardes, rendering all your hard work, gone.
Graphics freezes, glitches like npc's and hero's randomly walking through or on water, or other impassable objects.
And at Last, siege battle is more of a grab by overpowered players, or by hacks (which by the way we cannot tell but it is so very obvious when your games framerate drops to nearly zero and all the sudden you have a hundred troops at your door) so why bother?
So with that being said, if you enjoy
Glitch Glitch Glitch, restart restart restart, and being hacked to death by a uncaring community, then by all means, buy the game.

Summary: One step forward, two steps back. Veterans will be upset, beginners are better off with 2014.
This is Magic the Gathering, but unfortunately kneecapped for reasons unknown. First, the interface is clearly not designed for PC use. It is very, very obvious that it was meant for swipping motions on a tablet or smartphone. 2014 had a similar problem, though not nearly as bad. The UI is also clunky. It takes way longer than necessary to perform mundane tasks.
The problems in gameplay start off with the starter deck. You get a vague description of the deck style, then you get a bunch of crappy cards. Compare to 2014, where the decks started off good and only got better. While being able to fully customize your deck is good, you're again kneecapped by the slow and random progression of acquiring cards. Add to that that the best cards are locked behind micro-transactions and it's a fairly miserable experience. The fact that you have the option to purchase sets for real money that you can fully unlock through gameplay is also a kick in the balls.
The story mode is a big crapshoot. You generally don't have a good enough deck to beat the main bosses right off the bat, and some of them use cards that you can't even get, like scry lands. You end up having to grind exploration zones to get more cards until you either get lucky or can hard counter the boss's deck. The exploration itself is random too. My very first experience was an opponent that used Pyxis of Pandemonium. Only Pyxis of Pandemonium, a card that isn't even usable. until turn 7 (assuming no land drops are missed). Others can kick your♥♥♥♥♥repeatedly.
I don't really know who this was made for. Veterans will be disappointed with the card pool and overal gameplay, while beginners will learn better with 2014.

One of my mottos when starting Steamified was that I never wanted to be just another negative review. This is because I understood that every developer (or studio) make an honest effort to provide gamers with something enjoyable. However, in saying that I also believe that if you don’t have a good game that it’s better to be awful than to be mediocre. Therefore, it saddens me to claim that The God’s Chain is easily one of the worst games that I have played this year.
The God’s Chain is a switchable first person shooter and third person shooter.
Practically everywhere. Unfortunately, there is not a single component of the game that is at a satisfactory level for gaming in 2016.
The game lacks Steam achievements. However, the developers have added it to the Steam trading card program. This makes the game partially Steamified.
Firstly, never give up. Although I am not a fan of your game and it has received an overwhelming amount of criticism on Steam never give up. If you have a passion for developing video games and that is what you want to continue then keep at it.
Secondly, keep your eyes and ears open. Take in as much advice and constructive criticism as possible. If you are able to do this then years from now, you’ll look back at this game as being a positive part of your learning process rather than as an embarrassment.
Obviously, The God’s Chain cannot get a recommendation. It is one of the worst games I have played this year and ranks among the worst I have ever played. But I do want the developers to persist with their game development efforts. Good things have come from far worse beginnings than this.

Puzzles! with pictures of cute kittens! How could you go wrong with that?!
Well...
a) The score you get on each puzzle depends on the number of "moves" you have, and the time you take. Unfortunately when a puzzle starts, it dumps a load of the pieces over the edges of the board, so you need to use time and "moves" in moving them out of the way before you start. Seems like a massive oversight. It increments the number of moves just from clicking the pieces, not specifically whether you're placing them within the puzzle area.
b) Pieces don't rotate. They are always the right way up when you pick them up.
c) For the first five puzzles in every level, it shows you where to put the pieces. There's an outline of where every piece goes! You don't even need to look at what's on the pieces to solve this jigsaw!
So every puzzle is artificially easy, some of them made super-easy by showing outlines of the pieces, marred by the loss of "moves" and time because of where it places the puzzle pieces at the start of each puzzle.
The "four difficulty levels" in the game are the number of pieces; the puzzles in the first set contain 20 - 30 pieces, and the puzzles in the last set contain 72 - 90 pieces, but still on this "hardest difficulty" it's showing you where to place the non-rotatable pieces for the first 5 puzzles on hardest difficulty.
Combine this with - if you were thinking you'd use the menu as a pause button.... the menu is actually a level select, and there's no way to go back to the puzzle you were doing without restarting it. So it's deeply annoying, if you want to "do well" at these jigsaw puzzles but suddenly get called off to do something.
Pushing Esc while on the level select takes you back to the main menu (if that's how you thought you might unpause it rather than re-selecting the level and restarting it), and pressing Esc again from the main menu exits the game entirely.
Oh and btw there's no music *at all* in the game.
Though if it was using the music that's in the trailer - "Barroom Ballet by Kevin MacLeod" - which they are perfectly allowed to do since it's royalty free music - I'd just spend every cat puzzle thinking about Okosan from Hatoful Boyfriend, and pudding, which would be entirely inappropriate. :P

A fun little jigsaw game with adorable cat pictures. It's a simple concept and the game does a decent job of providing entertainment.
There's no music and little sounds to speak of in general, but nothing's stopping you from listening to your own stuff in the meantime, so it's not a big deal.

Difficulty-wise, it starts out simple, but gradually increases the challenge by removing things like the piece grid and increasing the amount of pieces. The game has a star rating that depends on your time spent on a puzzle, but it is an optional challenge, so there's no rush to finish a puzzle for people who just want to relax.
I like this game, it's the kind of casual puzzle game you could play for a while to unwind. It's not too expensive either.
Give it a shot if you want something simple and cute to play.

Pretty unique game (or at least I haven't played too many this type of games). There is something very cool and charming about this games but there's also few issues.
Pros:
-The journey: It's pretty epic and there's always things waiting to happen you probably can't expect and it keeps you kinda on your toes the whole game. The first playthrough is pretty much for you to understand the purpose of the game and various mechanics and after that you are probably smarter to try again this time actually managing to go from London to London in 80 days.
-Replay Value: Even though the 1 trip from London to London takes maybe 3 to 4 hours depending on how many days it'll  last and how much time you do on planning and thinking the next possible route it still has a lot of replay value. There's 160 (if I remember correctly) cities to visit and (I assume) thousands of options to go across the globe so I can imagine this game to be at least worth of 20 hours of playtime (or 5 to 6 playthroughs).
-Intelligent: This game challenges you to take calculated risks and think few steps forward. It's pretty uncommon these days and I found myself enjoying in this aspect in the first playthrough (even if it took +120 days to get to London). There's always challenges waiting for you that you didn't confront the first playthrough and it even challenges you to do the around the world trip faster than 40 days (steam achievement).
-Jules Verne References: There's many references to Jules Verne's books maybe because "Around the World in 80 Days" is one of those books. I don't want to spoil anything more but all those who are familiar with Verne's novels there will be lots of "fan service".
-Something Fresh and Different: This game truly is something fresh and different and maybe that is the biggest thing I enjoyed it the most.
Cons:
- You need to read a lot: There is lots of reading you need to do through the game. Because there is no voice acting you need to read♥♥♥♥♥♥loads of text... I don't know if it's a bad thing or not (though for some it might be). For me it's not a bad thing but I don't like it that much either. I mean it can be a bit exhausting because the pacing of the game is kinda fast.
-It's a mobile game: To be honest that's what it is. I can imagine it's a bit more enjoyable to play with PC but it's still pretty much just a port of a "mobile game". Though this could be pretty good way to spend time on a plane playing this game!
-There's luck (or is there): Sometimes it feels that somethings (specially when playing blind playthrough) are happening because of luck.. 'cause no matter how much you made yourself think your next route it just might♥♥♥♥♥♥on your face and the "non logical route choice" were probably better one. And that's sometimes pretty demoralizing. But if you think of it it's the late 1800's so anything could happen in your journey around the world.
I paid 4,99€ on this and I'm pretty happy that I did. It's pretty fresh experience and maybe it's NOT something new but at least it's something different. If you think you might enjoy this I recommend of buying it. Then it surely should be at least worth the 5$/€

Another amazing game by Inkle - same guys who did the awesome Sorcery! remake for mobile, and quite possibly the best choose-your-own-adventure style game company out there (and deservedly so).
As a fan of steampunk, history, Jules Verne, Fallen London / Sunless Sea, and text-based adventures this one hit all the right buttons for me. :)
Basically, a re-imagining of the famous 80 Days Around The World classic by Mr. Verne and set in an alternative Steampunk inspired age. You are Passepartout, and your job is to guide the indefatigable Mr. Fogg around the world so that he can win his bet within 80 days.
+ The writing is SUPERB and absolutely on point (enough to rival Failbetter Games imho), and the lore is detailed and well done.
+ Good replayability, there are a lot of various routes to take all with their own stories to tell. That, and new events and storylines can unlock/appear in future playthroughs.
+ There are a lot of hidden secrets and stories which add a lot of depth to the story and lore.
+ Achievements are well done here as a lot of them are actually based on discovering and completing storylines - and there are quite a lot of them!
+ Interesting take on the travel mechanics, and yet simple enough to learn - adds a good dose of simple (but tricky) strategy as you need to plan your routes and timing.
+ Simple but gorgeous art and sound.
- After quite a few playthroughs most of the main locations can become somewhat monotonous. That said, this would only be after you played it several times - and some alternatives do appear to break it up.
All in all, i enjoyed myself immensely. :)

First off, my credentials:
I first played Duke Nukem in the form of Duke Nukem 2 Shareware on my AST Advantage 386mhz computer running on MS-DOS and Windows 3.1, shortly after, I went to spend the night at a friends house - he had "Duke Nukem 3D", It was a shooting game he said, like Wolfenstein 3D or Blake Stone, but better. With♥♥♥♥♥♥and explosions.
Well being that was just reaching puberty this sounded wonderful. I was hooked, like everyone who played DN3D I was a fan for life. To this day I can go back and enjoy it the same as I did on day one. But this isn't about DN3D, this is about Duke Nukem Forever. And the introduction is the base problem.
I just drowned in nostalgia over Duke, and expected a game in development hell for over a ♥♥♥♥ing decade was going to be anything similar. I didn't just buy Duke Nukem Forever, I pre-ordered. I spent a whopping amount of money on the initial release on console, (Xbox 360), only to be greeted with a two weapon limit, dodgy graphics and horrible load times that made Gen 1 PS1 games look fast. It was awful.
I sold Duke Nukem Forever soon after reaching the "Octaking" boss, but was gifted the game and DLC by a long time friend who wanted to make sure "I gave it a fair shot"
He was right.
The PC version of DNF is substantially better. Does this mean it's a great game? No. It's not. But it's something many games fail to be these days. Fun. It's a good game. Not great. Good. It's like 7 dollar 4 hour porno DVDs you buy from the gas station with a pack of jerky and a six pack. You know it's not going to be the prettiest or cleanest thing, but you get your fun out of it and you didn't have to spend a lot.
If Duke Nukem Forever had been released in it's current form with DLC for a lower price point no one would be complaining as much as they are. But first impressions are everything. And I can honestly say - yeah. I hated it when it came out. I hated the turret sections (Though, I like the monster truck, Gearbox driving is never a bad time) I hated the attempts to out-edge the original Duke Humor (The twins are just outright cringe worthy). Shadow Warrior is a much better example of how to update a classic FPS to the modern day. Same with Rise of the Triad. I just feel like Duke Nukem got too big for it's britches.
If I were to rate the original game, no DLC, no patches. It's a 1/10. Easily. It's up there with♥♥♥♥♥♥games like Cosmic Race or Bubsy 3D.
But the PC version, with improved textures and lighting, better weapon capacity, and overall a more pleasant experience? It's a 6/10.
I recommend Duke Nukem Forever for the sheer fact that it's a lesson in how not to develop a game. Passing it off to a bunch of people like a Thai ladyboy at a bachelor party to whoever wants to take a shot at it next. In the end we're all left a little dirtier and devoid a few bucks. But we had a good time in the process.

The game creates an amazing atmosphere with just some text, a globe, and an ever ticking clock on the top of the screen. Since I have only played one playthrough I cannot be sure of the replayability, but I only visited 19 cities out of over a hundred. I really believe this game captures the soul of the novel in a striking way.

I literally could not be happier with this development, and especially now that the game is rightly regarded as a brilliant classic. See, I got it on release and remember the sheer, unfiltered hate that this game recieved.  This was pretty much all because it wasn't KOTOR 1 - a by-the-numbers RPG with a hot jedi lady and redeemed by a masterful plot twist.   Reading the hate was like visiting the COD forum, bland idiocy about how Atton wasn't Carth (Thank God for that, he's one of the most boring characters ever) - or how there wasn't an easy surrogate for Bastilla in this game (OMFG NO WAIFU?!?! what am I gonna dooooooO!)
In fact this pretty mucy sums up Kotor2 in a nutshell.  It has a far darker, more complex story than the first with fewer cliches and cop outs - and of course Kreia, one of the best characters ever in a game.
Although the cut content in the original did give the second half of the game a very appropriate feeling of desolate emptiness, the restoration patch greatly improves the overall quality of the game and, though the barren finale somehow made sense to me in vanilla (how appropriate, given what we know about the exile?), it's far superior with the restored content.
Maybe finally people will wake up and realize that this game is better than the original.

This is a re-review of this game. I upgraded my computer and some devs or moderators helped me fix my problems so kudos to them.
This game when I played a long time ago on the Xbox was confusing and felt incomplete. With the Cut Content mod it fixed about 90% of the old problems and honestly this game is better than the original Knights of the Old Republic. It improves everything from combat, party memebers, and items. I like the new combat system and different lightsaber and force forms it really adds something to combat. I also like that ranged or blaster wielding NPCs when they verse lightsaber opponents are not helpless and can do some damage. The fact as well that Jedi and Sith aren't as numerous until the end of the game feels right in the game, you just fight many blaster wielding foes which fits with the lore and background of the game. But the biggest complement I give to this game is the lack of a romance in the game, but the focus on your party members interacting with you. With no romance you can really spread your attention and not just focus on one or two members. I remember not talking to many of the crew from the first game and just reallly focusing on Bastila. Now I talk to almost all of the crew and learn more about them and their ways. And the game rewards you with stat boosts or bonuses when you do this.
I gave a negative review about this game about this game and in hindsight it was unjust. Now I say if you like the KOTOR and you felt like it needed an update KOTOR:TSL is the answer.

A simply marvellous experience.
Glimpsing the screenshots and hearing from others about the art styles hardly does it justice; its atmosphere is fantastically creepy and I cannot count how many times it made me shudder from images or music (usually the two together).
Definite plus points:
-The art and music, wonderful together
-Characters and story
-Weight of consequence to actions you take
Could have been better:
-Strong as the ending is, it perhaps needed more winding down as it felt a bit abrupt
-If you get stuck on a puzzle or can't work out how to proceed, wandering around for a half hour can start to dampen the mystery and atmosphere of the environments
Things that worked for me (but I can see counterarguments against):
-The puzzle sections were well-spaced out and were unobstrusive. They also weren't too difficult so that made me feel smart at cracking them, and the feeling of progress and reward was great.
-Not a terribly long game, and can be completed in one sitting if you stick at it, but as it's one that focuses so much on atmosphere it would definitely wear thin before long.
In short:
Fantastic experience! Can we have a sequel?

Not a great game!
It is similar to Europa Universalis IV, but somehow quite lacking in everything!
The good:
- Same as Europa Universalis IV, but with roman country and army name of the time
- The sound and music were ok
- The family tree and traits of the leaders of Rome are interesting and bring more color to the game. You can have children, friends and rivals! Some of your leaders are completely useless just like in real life! Internal political bickering from time to time is fun.
The bad:
- The game doesn't even work after you install it via steam. You have to fetch the latest beta patch 2.36C from the Paradox forums to make it work (hassle)
- Research seems to take forever. So you got nothing to build most of the time (i tried only the earliest campaign. Maybe you have already unlocked research in the later ones). Still its far too slow compared to EU4. Also the 5 leaders you assign to research don't seem to change anything at all.
- The concept of claiming a territory is still present in this game, except you cannot claim new territories like in EU4. This concept is that when you invade a territory, you cannot annex it and add it to your empire unless you have (or forged) a claim on it. Most of my diplomats time were spent doing that in EU4. In this game, it seems you can't annex a territory unless you conquer the whole ennemy territories. That's pretty bad! Some of the ennemy has 15 or more territories and becomes an almost impossible task to do!
- You can colonise unclaimed territories from barbarians, but not if the strength of the barbarians is too high! So you need to wait forever for them to do an uprising and crush it to lower their strength and then colonise (Never happened after years(in game) of play). That is a very bad concept right there.
- For some reason, a 2 territory empire can witstand the mighty rome empire consisting of 8 territories plus the super lucrative Rome territory(which is equalt to 4-5 territories on its own)! I swear the freakin...g Epirus had an army of 20 troops when i could barely foot 36 troops in the field. They also had an 11 trireme navy! And they managed to attack me 2-3 times with 11 troops? WTF! How could they make that much money to support their troops? How could they even build that many troops in the first place? You can only build one troop at a time on one territory and it takes 90 days for the cheapest troops, the other takes longer if you have the ressources for it. The guy had horses which even rome didn't have for god sake and elephants!!!
- The game feel pretty flat compared to EU4. I don't know it's like its empty somehow.
Now i didn't play the xpansion vae victus. Not sure i will play either.
Verdict: Don't waste your money on this game. Play the much better Europa Universalis 4 which this game is based on.
Or go play Distant Worlds, a faaaaaaaar better game than EU4 in my experience as a strategy game and its in spaaaaaace!

Kitty Cat: Jigsaw Puzzles is exactly what it sounds like. It is a jigsaw puzzle video game where all of the puzzles are photos of felines. The game is very simple to play and is accessible to anyone who can control a mouse.
There are 84 jigsaw puzzles in the package. If you're quick at solving jigsaws then you're looking at a couple of hours of entertainment. Personally, I think I am rather slow at solving them and I averaged about 7 to 8 minutes per puzzle. If I am an average consumer you are looking at approximately eleven hours worth of content. Considering the price that's a bargain. Of course, the likelihood of you completing each of them is rather minimal.
If that's not enough content for you then you are graded on each puzzle using the popular three star system. I am not completely certain as to whether or not the system is just time related or whether or not it factors in the amount of moves you make. At the end of each level you are told how long you took to complete the puzzle as well as the number of moves you took. A move is considered a movement of a puzzle piece. If you lose stars for moving pieces then I would advise against doing what I did. I moved some pieces around to empty spaces - on and off of the board - in order to see as many pieces as clearly as possible.
The game has four different levels.
No. Unfortunately as is the case with all of EnsenaSoft's games they do not come with Steam achievements or trading cards. I'd like to encourage them to include them in a future update. It would make more people give their cheap casual games an opportunity. As a result this would increase the developer's revenue. It really is win-win.
If you are a fan of cats and enjoy completing jigsaw puzzles then Kitty Cat: Jigsaw Puzzles is an easy purchase. It is affordably priced and fun for all ages.

Puzzle games... What to say about them? Mechanically, they're dead simple. Figure out a way to carve up a picture so that the pieces interlock, scatter them around the outside of the board, and let the player go to town. If you've seen one, you've seen them all.
Until Cute Overload Simulator 2016. Don't bother with the "official" title of this game-- this game ( and the canine version elsewhere on Steam), have such a plethora of cute critters on board that the game is like to give you diabetes-- The instantly lethal kind.
As for this particular puzze game, it has that sort of quality that keeps my mother going down to the shop to get more: The puzzles in the first area are easy, and they get harder as you progress through the levels. Not just the number of pieces, but also the quality of the pictures for this purpose. Four levels of 21 images each give you 84 images overall for the main game, with stars awarded, Angry Birds-style based on the time you take to complete that image.
If I had to give the Devs suggestions, I would recommend that they ditch the lock-in when a particular piece is in the correct location, and add rotation to the individual pieces as an option to make things a bit more difficult for the Players. it would add much, I think, to the replayability of the game and make it worth another couple of bucks.
Speaking of, I'm of the impression that the devs could easily charge a bit more for this game on the PC market, which is usually receptive to a bit more in terms of price than the mobile market, assuming that the game isn't buggy on launch.
For $1.99 USD, cat fanciers and purveyors of cuteness everywhere could do far, far worse.
Although I did wonder if it would kill the devs to get some music in-- a soundtrack tailored to each individual image by activity/mischief level would go over very well.

It's really hard to recommend this game over Magic 2014.
The graphics are prettier, but the navigation is much slower, as all the straightforward point-and-click menus have been replaced with menus where you MUST scroll through each option one at a time.
To make sure this isn't as much of a hassle as it could be, Wizards and Stainless have removed a lot of game modes, so you don't have to scroll through them. Unfortunately, that means that every mode except Campaign, Online Duel, and Multiplayer has been eliminated.
There is custom deck building which works sort of like the Sealed Campaign in Magic 2014, but with less card variety and 140 cards locked away unless you pay more cash to unlock them, it isn't as interesting an experience.
Here's hoping Magic 2016 does things better.

From a pure gameplay perspective, you have a hybrid first/third person shooter with certain elements of exploration. The AI has some issues but that pales in comparison to the many bugs and glitches which forced me to stop playing, until some of them got fixed. It seems like it has become a norm for triple A and indie games alike, to be distributed long before they are fully functional. The game’s SP campaign however, is not the main attraction here. The God's Chain features enough MP options, to satisfy most avid players, provided you find others to share this experience with. This has also been a problem which could be immediately solved through a small price readjustment.

Sadly the technical issues are far from the only problems for this title. The graphics are decent, though nothing special. But the sounds are quite generic and do not sustain the game’s atmosphere at all.

+ Interesting story concept
+ Comprehensive Multiplayer modes
+ Steam Trading Cards

- No Achievements
- Glitches & bugs
- Currently overpriced

In spite of all its current technical shortcomings, The God's Chain shows promise and the dev team has been working hard on polishing the game for the past week since it was released. Almost all the game-breaking bugs are gone and I’m certain that with future updates and when sold in a bundle or during a seasonal Sale, God’s Chain shall no longer be perceived as an unfinished or expensive game for what it offers. Do not let the mixed reviews it has been receiving, be the sole reason to avoid it. Show some support for an indie developer that created more than just a run-of-the-mill 2D platformer which would have been a more safe but ultimately boring choice.

Exploring feels immersive and always interesting. The level up system is also solid. My only complaints are the night lighting is too dimm, i already have dimm vision from a neurological issue, so this makes night unplayable for me, it also affects outdoors lights, so they are also dimmed, which is severely unrealistic. --- The loot system, also feels like it could be deeper. Finding some weapons and gear is nice, but that gear would be a lot more satisfying if it had weapon mods, or random stats, or something to keep it fresh. A bit of diablo in a survival game, can keep it relevant while all the other games die off. --- It's a smart longterm goal. Anyway, great game, I hope it improves in the ways I want, but even now, it's a solid 8/10 game. And I am harsh.

As Steam requires that we either recommend, or not recommend a game, I will have to say that Nether is not recommended in its current state. Having said that, by no means am I implying that this is a bad game. The graphics are good. The controls are fine. The monsters are cool, and the environment is very well made. The problem with this game is that the only available game type is PVP, or player versus player, for those who don't know.
This means that friendly fire is on in an open world sandbox, and it is the most frustrating aspect of this game. Nether features permanent death, so if you die you lose all of your experience, money, and whatever guns and health items you happen to find. You have to make a new character to play again, and it's terribly annoying when you've spent a long time trying to level a character, or maybe just found some good gear, and some random jerk snipes you from a building. And believe me, snipe you they will. There are far too many people who do nothing more than sit around the safe zones, and shoot people coming or going. Sometimes they do this for your loot. Sometimes out of boredom. And sometimes they do it out of sheer meanness.
The notion of permanent death is the same as in games like DayZ, or Infestation Stories, but to be fair, Nether is vastly better than either of those games. As I mentioned earlier, the controls are fast, and responsive. Item management is a little buggy, but will likely be fixed, soon. I was surprised to find that the combat is actually quite good. Melee strikes, while slower than in games like Killing Floor, or Left 4 Dead 2, are still performed quickly enough to prove useful in killing enemies. The guns all have decent power, and perform like you'd expect them to.
I have a feeling that the problems with this game will soon be resolved, but I can't guarantee that as I've learned never to trust in developer promises. Better to err on the side of caution and wait to see if change is implemented. If you are the sort who can overlook the aggravating aspects of a PVP only style survival game, where the threat of getting killed by another player is much greater than dying from monsters, then I say go for it.  For everyone else, I say wait and see if the game gets better.  In either case, I recommend you watch some gameplay videos before you buy.
P.S.
The majority of people who play this game have requested servers with no friendly fire (PVE), because they want to play a cooperative survival horror style of game. There are some people on the forums, who are very obviously player killers, and they oppose this idea. This is for the simple reason that it's because they know that most people would prefer to play without friendly fire, and they fear that their PVP servers will be empty. It's obnoxiously selfish behaviour, but what do you expect from those who get their kicks from killing people who are just trying to enjoy the game?

Based upon the Jules Verne novel "Around the World in Eighty Days", 80 Days reimagines the journey made by Monsieur Fogg and his trusty valet Passepartout in a steampunk world. This twist adds a great level of depth to be explored due to the intriguing cultures and conflicts that derive from it.
A great example of this would be when I was making an airship trek across the Pacific and before the ship landed I was struck with a string of choices in order to find out why there was gunfire below. This resulted in the airship to change course and caused a complete detour to my trip that spawned a path that almost broke the bank. Had I chosen a different path, I probably wouldn't have had to spend a night in the streets of Havana. This more than proves the dynamic nature of choices in this game which result in an great level of replayability.
One aspect that leaves slightly more to be desired is the difficulty of the game. In my experience, missteps can be swiftly resolved with a couple of quick fixes such as getting a loan. While there is an acheivement tied to not drawing from the banks, it would be nice to have a harder difficulty where the blows to you and Monsieur Fogg's well-being are even more impactful. Though this is only a minor gripe in other wise wonderfully executed gameplay.
The artstyle of this game also does it good. With the black and white aesthetic across a colorful background, it provides a good contrast that really makes the images pop. Top notch work there.
80 Days is a great title to pick up if you enjoy choose your own adventure style games. It mixes decision making with an interesting world and gives you plenty of reason to come back for more. I could easily see this consuming more hours in my future due to it's branching path narrative that leaves you wondering "what if".

This game is absolutely phenomenal. Unlike most survival horror games, you have no weapon or any means of defending yourself except to run away like a scared little child any time you see something that freaks you out. You have a health meter and a sanity meter (hi there, Call of Cthulu!). Your sanity will frequently bounce between "Crystal Clear" and the walls-wobbling-world-shaking terror your character, Daniel, will experience any time a floorboard creaks. The game stays dark and creepy the entire way through.
My only real complaints about Amnesia are a slight problem with story flow (as in it's kind of hard to follow sometimes and I'll probably have to play through it again before I get it all) and not enough variation in environment puzzles. Most of the puzzles consist of unlocking doors, whether that's by finding a key, cranking them open, fixing a machine to crank them open, or other variations. I enjoyed the few puzzles that had me combining items, finding ways to escape from rooms, or (SPOILER...who am I kidding, how do you review a survival horror game without the whole thing being a big spoiler alert) reenacting torture scenes in order to progress in a side quest. I would have liked to see more variation and interaction with the environment beyond fixing machines and opening doors.
Overall, a very excellent game, and an *actually scary* horror game.

: OhNoo Studio
: OhNoo Studio
: A key for this game was provided by the developer for the purpose of writing an unbiased, informative review. No other compensation was given.
==========
Inspired by HR Giger's unique biomechanical style and games such as Dark Souls and Dark Seed, Tormentum: Dark Sorrow is an extremely dark point and click adventure, diving deep into themes such as damnation, sin, and redemption. While somewhat short, Tormentum is a nearly unforgettable adventure spanning across 3 different realms. Fans of this genre may find something here that rivals other titles' quality! Let's take a closer look at what Tormentum has to offer.
==========
As a point and click adventure, the game plays out entirely at your pace. Progression is limited by your ability to find hidden secrets and solve puzzles. This is done by clicking objects and areas on-screen to uncover them. Hidden objects are able to be picked up, stored on your bag, and used in other areas, typically assisting in solving puzzles presented to the player.
As you solve puzzles, you slowly gain access to more areas of the dark castle your character is being held prisoner in. Each area is it's own puzzle, so to speak, and by carefully examining each area will you piece together each puzzle. Some rooms have NPCs, which will help or hinder you, depending on certain factors. Usually they will give you an item needed to progress, in exchange for solving another, smaller puzzle or task. One NPC is a guard who gives you a shovel to dug up a piece of gold, and rewards you with a necklace that is actually a key to a door nearby--just as an example. There are many areas to explore, and many puzzles to solve!
An important aspect of the game is the Journal. It automatically keep notes on important bits of imformation you find, such as a diagram of a point of interest you find somewhere, or a crude drawing providing a clue left behind by another prisoner of the castle. This can be checked at anytime, as well as your bag where your items are kept.
Lastly, at certain points of the game you are presented with some moral choices, literally good or evil. Depending on your choices, you may get the good or bad ending...which is basically how your character is judged at the very end of the story. If you are aiming for a particular ending, make sure you hit all the right choices, a single mistake can change your ending entirely.
==========
As mentioned before, Tormentum's unique art style is heavily inspired by games such as Dark Souls and Dark Deeds, and by famous painter and sculptor HR Giger.  Giger is credited with designing the monster simply known as the 'Alien' or Xenomorph from the classic 1979 film of the same name. Giger has a very unique style, blending biological and mechanical components together to create a unique blend of flesh and machine. This is prominently seen and featured in nearly every scene of Tormentum, and in most NPC designs. This style works very well for the setting.
Hand-painted stages help to blend everything together, and are a wonder to behold. Half the fun of the game is pushing onwards just to see the next area and it's art. Everything is incredibly dark and very detailed.
==========
Featuring over 40 spine-tingling tracks, Tormentum has quite the soundtrack to help immerse you into the story and setting. Slow, yet hopeful tunes for the more docile scenes, with darker more evil tracks for the hellish scenes you will encounter. Nothing is amiss here, and it all comes together to create a memorable experience.
==========
For this type of game, a high framerate isn't needed, which is good because Tormentum ran at an acceptable 30FPS at all times. I did not run into any bugs, random crashes, or stuttering at any point. There are very few video/audio options, but honestly they are hardly needed.
==========
Tormentum: Dark Sorrow is an excellent point and click adventure, one you are bound to remember long after you finish it. Although short, it's filled with clever puzzles and hidden secrets. It's dark style, artwork, and soundtrack are the best features. Fans of the genre will find a very enjoyable experience with Tormentum, and anyone who isn't a fan may just be converted into one!

I have been waiting out for this game, because it had received (when looking at the Steam reviews) a bunch of backlash ranging from inept game mechanics, poor optimisation and bugs.
Now yesterday we wanted to play Flat Out 2, our number 1 party game on the lan party we are at and found the current networking setup do not support the features needed for lan play and because Game Spy is dead for a long time, there is no way here for us to play it.
I was pleasantly surprised to see Flat Out 4 (or Fl4t Out as they try to brand it) costs only a ~11 euro. So I dived in, and was pleasantly surprised.
Personally I do NOT bare a deep rooted hatred toward the other Flat Out games that “are not from Bugbear”, I simply did not like them. I was hoping to find some more variation by adding those games to my scope of racing party games, but they just felt lacking.
THIS GAME. On this machine has everything I enjoy about a race game and darn well delivers on what I need from a party game (install, join and have fun).  Graphics look nice and smooth, run at +100 fps on my Ryzen 7, 1700X and MSI GTX 1070. I perceive no annoying stuttering and although things in the distance do not look as nice as near, I think it just looks just as good as or even better then Dirt 3 (which I will use as my drop-in-drop-out race game at the moment).
Cars physics keep the cars on the road, steering feels direct, surfaces have a direct impact on car handling, but never it feel so slippery that I totally lose control. Which what I expect from an arcade racer. Smashing through things feels satisfying and keeps me finding a balance between the slowdowns caused by some destructible and nitro they yield or just going flat out (literally full throttle to the finish ignoring most or all obstacles).
Soundtrack is descent, it’s the kind of punk bands you would expect in this time of game and are nice. My only grippe is that the same song starts after finishing every race when returning back to the menu.
However THE MAIN SELLING POINT for me, is if it can satisfy the fun factor. Simply, is this game fun?
Absolutely a full mouthed YES. We only played for 2 hours with some race and derby games and have been laughing and smiling teeth to teeth constantly. The ice cream truck specifically has literally burned its impression on us as the new sound of death. The ramping of a jet engine combined with the tune of the horn (playing a jolly ‘everybody sings this song’), closely followed by a power hit, an explosion, lots of smoke and wondering just what the hell happened. As they guy next to you continues their ice glazed path of destruction. We recorded the tune to induce PTSD among each other, by playing it on our phones when we walk by :-)
Yes, YES, YES this is A, maybe not THE, but A worthy successor to one of our most favourite party games. It is different and not without some scrutiny. But overall, this game is worth at least twice its 11 euro price tag it has now. For it to be worth they full ~40 euro. I would expect: more crazy stunt levels, a bunch more colours for all the cars and in time a DLC for more tracks.
A word for the developers: I feel sorry the community has burned your game to the ground. Because for us, this game a whole lot of fun and well worth our time and money.
Take care, game on.

Kingdom Wars is not a game uniquely focused to multiplayer gameplay. You can play the singleplayer and by your own explore the world map the game's lore. Know that thing EA will not put in the new Stars Wars game? Kingdom War have it, and an immensely good one. And you have a lot of time to play without any multiplayer concern the singleplayer aspect of the game, because the battle protection only counts out when you’re logged in the game, so if you play two hours a day you have twelve days to enjoy the singleplayer and more important, prepare yourself for when the battle protection time expires.
Nevertheless, if you want you can play the singleplayer campaign in coop with a friend you will lose this protection, and will need to be concern with multiplayer aspects, because co-op is only possible if you both cancel the battle protection. If you just want to enjoy with a friend the lore and world map you cannot do it undisturbedly, because if you cancel the battle protection you will open the game’s multiplayer section.
Continuing, the have a large world map, if many cities to explore. Different races to interact with, and tons of others things. Definitely worth. You want to make diplomacy with the NPC cities close to you? You can. Want to conquer then all? Also can. Travel half world have interact you dwarfs and their cities, ruins and mines? Also in the game. And better, you can play as three different civilizations, humans, elves and orcs. And each one plays different and feels different Kingdom Wars is easily on of my favorite strategy games currently, the only thing that keeps this game to enter my favorite strategy games of all time is that you cannot play with a dwarven civilization. Moreover, the developers’ team is great, one of the best on steam; they are constructing a path that only makes me likes this game even more, with new huge patches and free expansions (please would you consider adding the option to play as dwarves?). At least you can have dwarven units in your army, and I loved it. Inasmuch as is not from an AAA company Kingdom Wars nails every except one aspect that a game of this genre needs. Will address this one major problem next paragraph.
There is but one thing that bugs me. The troop’s management. When you will position your troops you only see and blue arrow that indicates the direction, and gets larger or thinner. It is a hideous system, seriously.
(do not need to explain how it is, everyone knows). In the new announcement concerning the new free expansion (learn from KW’s devs CA) and patches, they said they will implement the KW 2 battle system to this game, but I yet did not played KW 2 Battles, so I do not knows how it is. Maybe will fix this that is my major problem with the game, but that is yet to be seen.
Besides this last critic, I love the game. Will play for more forty hours. Easily deserves a 6/10. Considering the new announcements, I am almost sure Kingdom Wars can advance to an 7/10.

First of all, I'd like to say that I'm an experienced but not expert player of the Paradox Games. That means that I've played Hearts of Iron III a few years ago (and enjoyed a Communist Greece, amongst my other "achievements") and also love Europa Universalis IV. I saw EU: Rome on Steam and, basically, bought it to give it a try.
CONS
1) For a 2008 Game, Graphics should've been better.
2) Not the variety of factions that HoI3 or EUIV have.
3) Steam version forces you to search for the manual here. Also, the tutorial could've been better.
4) Surely, not as worth as EUIV but I'd love to try something until HoI4 goes public.
5) There are no mods is Steam for this game. Maybe the CD version (regular installation) supports them, but I couldn't find anything here.
PROS
1) Cheap. 10 euros for a Grand Strategy Game by Paradox. It's God's will!
2) The "Vae Victis" expansion and all patches are included.
3) Historical accuracy and interesting gameplay. It starts with the Invasion of Pyrrhus in Italy and the wars between Romans and Greeks.
4) Variety of historical starts. From an early Roman Republic to the Civil Wars and the foundation of the Roman Empire. Yeah!
5) Awesome music. That may sound stupid, but have a look at YouTube... Yeah, you're welcome.
6) Don't know if it's the way the AI works, but a huge advantage of the game is that factions like Rome, Carthage, Seleucids, Egypt, Macedon and Pontus actually grow up. So, a player gets to experience the "anxiety" of fighting Rome in Magna Graecia or Carthage in Africa. If you're a TWR2 player, you'll see a huge difference. Factions like the Illyrians don't consume Empires in no time, like in Rome 2. You hear that CA?
I don't guarantee that it'll be an unforgetable experience, but it's a nice, fun game to play, balanced enough for its kind.
Have fun! God keep you all safe.

If you've ever played an economy focused RTS like Age of Empires, built up a flourishing and efficient town over the course of a match, and then felt a twinge of sadness on the statistics screen at the loss of said town, then Kingdom Wars is a good bet. (Especially for the low low price of completely free.)
Early game you'll spend most of your time optimizing your economy. Training more peasants, setting them to mine gold or stone, gather lumber or farm the fields, meanwhile using your small starting militia to complete the basic quests.
After a day or two however that part of the game virtually disappears, with you making only a few adjustments now and then. The economy does everything it needs to, but not a lot more. The main meat of the game is BATTLE. :D
PVP works like so:
1: Put together an army that you built in your town, and bring it onto the world map.
2: Click the "Search pvp" button and choose between attacking a city or fighting an army head on.
3: If you're fighting an army you'll find yourself on a small open map with some mountains and a few camps of neutral forces.
4: If you're in a siege the layout of the land can differ greatly depending on the homeland of the player. Siege weapons are required of course.
5: Rewards for winning is gold that you loot of the bodies and Crowns just for winning.
The actual combat is squad based, similar to Total War.
You can switch between different formations to optimize various types of defence, movement speed and damage. Troops will level up as they participate in battle, allowing you to spend ability points to increase their stats.
It's very worth bringing up the F2P platform, as many people shy away from games like this based on the fear of a Pay to Win barrier popping up in their way every time they were just starting to enjoy the game.
Cutting to the chase, you don't ever need to spend money in this game. There is a currency called Crowns which you can gain through the following means:
1: Winning any ingame fight - either against the AI or players
2: Finishing quests
3: Paying for it through microtransactions
Thing is though, in the case of this game you don't really pay to gain an advantage as much as you do to skip large sections of the game. Sure, you can buy a ton of Crowns in the store and get loads of endgame units and be matched with the best players, but then you lose out on all of the Battles and Sieges that, assumedly, are the reason you are there in the first place.
It is currently not possible to actually take control of AI castles, but this will be changed in an upcoming free expansion.
PS: Don't pick the human female hero. The voice acting will drill it's way into your skull.

As a fan of Day Z, I felt that this game did everything much better. The tension is still there thanks to threatening enemies that are sometimes better to avoid than kill, and of course because of the constant threat of other survivors. What this game has that Day Z doesn't is direction. With occasional world events and delivery missions, there is a purpose in the game beyond surviving. In Day Z, the fun immediately stopped once you had a few pieces of critical survival gear. Not the case in this game. In addition to having things to do in the world and reasons to drive you to different parts of the map, the leveling system also adds a much needed element of progression. Though you may lose these levels when you die, they are not altogether that difficult to get back, but allow for a sense of accomplishment as you survive longer and longer. A market and bank system also contribute to this. Perhaps the best aspect of this game that sets it apart from Day Z though is the tighter controls and movement. The game is so much easier to control, and results in a game that is flat out more fun to actually play.
As it stands at the time of this review, the game is very fun and perhaps the best I have seen in the rapidly growing and popular multiplayer survival genre, but is still quite limited. The game is not finished, and the map is quite small (compared to the vast map of Day Z) but promises to more than double in size. A few other features are missing as well, and many good ideas could be implemented to vary up the gameplay, but the developers seem to take a deep interest in rolling out updates, so the missing aspects are not only expected (seeing as it is early access) but forgiven as well. I cant wait to see all the cool places this game seems to be heading in, and I would easily recommend this to someone, even in its current state, since it will provide hours of fun.

, and he's brought quite the massive arsenal with him. Forget whatever you remember from the previous Shadow Warrior, because SW2 does not give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about any of that. This game is absolutely bonkers, in every way imaginable – From the amount of weaponry you can wield, to the insane story the game is trying to tell. In fact, I am not sure what the story is about, and I ran through the game twice. In Lo Wang's total domination of the demons from the previous game, he somehow unleashed hell onto Earth, and now demon and man live together, side by side, in this procedurally generated world... somehow.
Is 2016 the year of "procedurally generated levels", or was that last year? Or the year before that? I can't remember, and either way, I wouldn't hate something new to take its place. What happened to the hand-crafted levels of past shooters, where every corridor and enemy encounter was designed with a challenge in mind? Who decided that level designers can be replaced by number generators? Why does every game need pseudo-RPG elements forced into it? These are questions a better reviewer would ask, but I honestly found myself not too bothered. I've played far too many ARPGs with randomized levels to be bothered at this point.
, this game is a slimmed down version of Borderlands. The basics are the same, you have a hub world from where you retrieve your quests (or missions if you prefer), then you make your way to bigger (emptier) levels where you complete your quest and get your reward. There's plenty of loot to go around, though as you level up you'll realize it's just vendor trash. Unlike Borderlands however, and unlike everything else in this game, the weapons were actually created by humans. So there are only a limited amount, most of which you get as quest rewards, or drops from map bosses. Maybe two dozen or so, and a lot of them are just slightly upgraded versions of others, but some are actually quite fun and unique.
Unfortunately the Borderlands parallel doesn't end just there. There's also the enemies, which are a mirror image of their Borderlands counterpart – massive health pools and status immunities define their difficulty. An enemy that's resistant to Ice, but immune to Fire? Better equip my Shotgun with a Fire Elemental bonus attack. Long gone are the days of learning an enemy's weakness, where to shoot them, when to attack them, which enemy to prioritize, and so on, because it matters not in this game. Just click it until it's dead. Being overwhelmed by tougher enemies? Just press Z to enable God Mode for 12 seconds.
But the combat is fun, even though it is executed poorly, especially the sword-swinging. My favourite weapon was a chainsaw-sword. Yes, a chainsaw-sword. That's a sword, that's also a chainsaw. So when you're swinging your sword around, you're not just cleaving enemies in half, you're sawing through them, and it is so bloody, so brutal, and so fun. Sure, I wish there was more to it, but you have to understand, I played loads of Borderlands too. I don't hate these kinds of games, I just prefer a challenge that these kinds of games don't present.
, I say this game is a good one. A recommendation, a thumbs up. It's fun, it's quirky, and Lo Wang is still Lo Wang. So what if the rest of the game doesn't make any sense – It's not like we're in it for the riveting story-telling either way. Still, I'd recommend the first game (from 2013) over this one, any day of the week, but here's hoping you've already played that one if you're considering this.

Though in it's infancy, it is clear Nether has the potential to be a big contender to DayZ. I played DayZ back in the mod days, and after playing Nether, I actually found Nether to be comparable, and even a little bit better, than DayZ.
I do miss the sim-ness of DayZ, but the trade off is well worth it. The game has friendlier controls, and the city setting fixes one of the things that I hated most about DayZ: Traveling. Although there is a lot of walking involved, there is usually always something to see, something to find, and something to fight. Anyone who has played DayZ, I'm sure is familiar with the hour long treks through the forest looking for a town or city, only to be shot in the face as soon as you got there. In nether, you're always a corner away from either♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off some sort of creature or getting shot in the face (and making new friends). It's both annoying and welcome. As slow as the game is, it is very exciting.
It's not perfect. I don't like that you can spend real world money on Gold, which you can use to purchase items in the game. Thankfully, most of the items you can spend Gold on are cosmetics like masks, although there are a few in game items like a white light flashlight and a glider. Thankfully, the game has it's own in game currency found through the city and through doing missions, and everything can also be purchased with that as well. Also a good thing, is that you CANNOT BUY GUNS. Guns can only be found, thankfully.
The controls and game world are also wonky. You can and will get stuck in the world. Not every object has a mesh, so you'll find yourself walking through chairs and tables sometimes. There are weird lag issues even though lag is generally kept to a minimum.
On the whole, I've found myself enjoying the hell out of this game. It's a great second choice (and currently cheaper option) to DayZ, and if the developers keep things in line and try to keep themselves clean, they can become real competiton.

inkle took their in-house storytelling engine, found a well known early Sci-Fi novel in the public domain and built a branching, highly replayable and engagingly written adventure around the world driven by choice and circumstance. There's a surprising degree of gameplay depth as management of money, time, trade goods and key character items plays an integral role in how each trip takes shape, along with your input as Passepartout influencing everything from inner monologues to personality traits and unforseen story threads to pursue.
Passing through new destinations, discovering new means of travel and taking in the local flavor text reveals intricate, well researched and fantastical world building that isn't tied to the page yet remains true to the voice of the author. The game has a clean visual look that uses color and static silhouettes effectively but it's a mobile port so set expectations accordingly. A new UI for the PC release would have been nice but the story scope has been expanded over time, and while some repetition is unavoidable after dozens of hours on multiple platforms there's still plenty to uncover.
An exciting approach to literary adaptation for the medium. If Carmen Sandiego and Choose Your Own Adventure books were your jam, this is where it's at.

Ahhh, Duke Nukem Forever. The mythical game that was never to be released.
Sadly, it shouldn't of been. Duke Nukem had his time in the 90's; when his particular brand of macho humor was well appreicated and seen for the comedy it was. These days, however, Duke's practically trademark sense of humor is as outdated as it is offensive.
The game itself plays host to a variety of other mechanics seemingly lifted from other games; mechanics that have since been refined in others, but kept in a very raw form in this game. The overall impression being that the developers ran through a list of potentional game mechanics in a pick'n'mix fashion. That said, the developers have done a wonderful job of keeping the game stable, with no crashes or other problems noted.
But, if you can look past the seemingly poor gameplay mechanics, and the humor that is so awful it's actually insulting everyone rather than trying to make them laugh...you wind up with a liner first person shooter filled with the reanimated enemies of games long since past and very large amounts of womenfolk who really, REALLY need to put on some damn clothes. It feels like I've been sucked into a 14 year old's wet dream, to be frank.
This, it seems, is Duke's swan song. He needs to go back into retirement alongside his troupe of scantiliy clad women (that may or may not be aliens) as the gaming community wishes him well.

I found the puzzles to be fairly easy, pretty straight forward if you take a realistic approach but they're still interesting nonetheless. There are two monsters in the game and sadly only one of them is scary. The other one just looks like a zombie with broken jaw. There were also quite a bit of overuse of the monster spawns, a notable example being when you pickup an item, and the monsters themselves only seem to growl with no footsteps sound or anything that thickens the atmosphere. So many custom stories also adds to replayability. The Great Work is by far the best one I have ever played, literally Amnesia 2.0 and I'd hate to say this, but I enjoyed that one more than the main game.

You will probably want more than one standing army, each tailored for various tasks and so you will need to generate gold to train the troops, though they will slowly train by winning battles.  It is more likely you will pay for their training as it is by far the quicker and economical option.
You will probably also need help fulfilling the battles that unfold as your story progresses which apart from chat is your only avenue of co-operative play with others.   You can make friends and ask them along which, if they have an army of similar strength, they have the option to do.   Added to this, attacking others happens on a random basis so far as army matches go. If you like, you can scour the area and maek battle with innate cities/armies.
People will attack you, and if you don't have the time, or don't want to take losses you can pay them off instead, rather than fight.  So I find when I need to off load goods that my industry is generating and recruit or train more troops, I log in every few hours.   If I want to battle I log in with expectation of taking maybe an hour - some sieges demand an element of patience - and If I just want to sort out my armies, again Iog in for a while as necessary.
So although many of the sieges are similar, they are not tedious, and since some players have been at this game for a year  or two, it is sustainable and so far as things go, I think I might be found here in this land in a few years time too.

I've played some very bad games. Some really bad games, even AAA titles that shipped with memory leaks so bad that, after 15 min., the game would crash & the developers never released an update to address that issue, let alone any other.
This game is worse. It's controls are far from intuitive & can't be remapped; the graphics (which are "so-so"), and, though my rig isn't a powerhouse, it should've been able to push this game's graphics to the "Fantastic" setting (the highest such setting). Instead, I had to run it at "Simple" (the lowest setting). There was still a bit of a hitch in the FPS here and there.
The cutscenes were worse looking than the actual game. The dev should've just used the in-game engine for the cutscenes instead of the low-res ones (which appear to have come from circa 1995-1996—yes, I'm "old").
The voice acting was just horrible, but I'm certain the guy didn't actually speak English. It was bad enough that I would've preferred subtitles throughout sans voice acting. And, to the point of the subtitles, the words were all white and, unfortunately, oftentimes against white backgrounds (the moon, for instance).
As far as the story goes, it is unoriginal, though an interesting premise, nonetheless. I'm uncertain just how well the story may have evolved through however long the game would take; however, since there doesn't seem to be a way to save the game, I imagine not long.
As far as the "shooter" aspect of the game goes, it's bad. It works. I think. The aliens glitch out extremely bad (glitching out of existence, sliding horizontally at Warp Factor 5 & then glitching out of existence, et cetera), making the actual gameplay unenjoyable.
Lastly, your character's animations (if you want to see a third-person perspective in-game hit "V"), the gunplay, and the aliens are extremely stiff and make 1950s era Hollywood robots' movements seem fluid beyond anything humanly possible.
As you can see from my above time of ~0.2 hrs (approximately 10 minutes), I did not put much time into the game. I feel as if I don't need to explain why my time with this game is so limited. I also don't feel as if more time was really warranted. It feels as if this game was a partially finished college class project.
Another reviewer below made mention of it using Unity graphics. Don't let that, by default turn you off of Unity's engine in various games. If time is taken to refine both the models and animations (see 7 Days to Die—pull up YouTube videos of it throughout its alpha lifetime and see how much it has visually changed. It is, and always has been, a Unity Engine game).
In short, do not purchase this game. If you have already purchased this piece of [censored] excuse of a game, then I apologize for your misfortune. My best recommendation if you already own The God's Chain, just idle the cards, then uninstall the game.

Dead Pixels is a very simple game, but an enjoyable one. It's a much less polished and much more shallow zombie take on River City Ransom. You go around the city earning money from killed zombies and entering shops to buy weapons, items, and upgrades for your character. There are two different story modes, and one wave/time attack mode with Steam leaderboards. The gameplay itself is fun even though it tends to get repetitive about halfway through each of the story modes. This is not due to a lack of weapons and items. It's because once you learn how to approach the game, it becomes very easy to cheese your way through both campaigns without too much of a challenge. There is also the option of playing co-op, but it is only available locally, which is always a wasted opportunity. Overall, Dead Pixels is well done and offers a lot of content for its extremely low asking price.

Tormentum: Dark Sorrow is one of those games that makes you reflect on your own life. Or, well, at least it did for me. The premise of the game has heavy religious backstory that is based around how sin affects your life. The land that your character enters has a purgatorial concept where people who are taken there have to atone for their sins and attempt to get out by enduring suffering that cleans their soul. The choices that you make with your character ultimately lead you either to heaven or hell.
The graphics in the game is what originally lured me in. The game has amazingly detailed artwork, is easy to use, and has a lot of both easy and difficult puzzles scattered throughout. The music is fantastic as well. Between these aesthetics, and the story being played out, I felt myself getting attached to the characters in the game. Which is funny, because the game in itself doesn't take long ot beat.
If you're looking for something casual to play while relaxing, but want something that has depth and beauty, I would highly suggest this game.

80 Days is a game developed by inkle Studios (known for the Sorcery! series) and ported from the original mobile port by Cape Guy Ltd. and is based on Jules Verne's classic: Around the World in 80 Days
After travelling the world once, I literally felt as if I'd experienced an epic trip around the world and I can recall all the craziness and wild adventures as if they were real memories, the game is very immersive
The writing is masterfully done writing and the story (which is based off Jules Verne's book) is really good, and just feels incredibly immersive and a great balance of strategy and story-telling with lots of classic literature easter eggs to be found
The gameplay consists of you playing a servant in 1872 but with a steampunk twist. You are the servant of Phileas Fogg as he takes a bet that he can travel the world in 80 days or less, you make text-based decisions about how you want to interact with people and situations and where you want to go. 80 Days also has heavy strategy elements because a large part of your success depends on how you plan out your route around the world. There is also an economy element of balancing your funds through buying and selling items, among other things
However, 80 Days has ;ots of reading and is not for the impatient, thankfully you can change the text speed from slower to faster. Originally, 80 Days was built for mobile, but enough has been added/tweaked to merit the more expensive Steam purchase
80 Days takes Jules Verne's Around the World in 80 Days and makes it into an interactive wild ride!

I wanted to play this once I found it on Steam, but the screenshots didn't seem like the game was worth the $3 price tag...and it isn't, but during the Steam Summer Sale, it got marked down to $0.75, so I had to pick it up. I wasn't expecting to put as many hours into it as I have since most of the people that reviewed it didn't even play the game for more than an hour, but it has some pretty cool features. There's a variation of weapons from pistols, shotguns, bolt rifles, grenades, fireworks to distract your enemies and so on, about 10-15 different zombies, an upgrade system for your character, and a few game modes.
Dead Pixels is basically a wave based campaign mode that gets harder and longer as you raise the difficulty and ends once you reach the extraction point. The Solution gives you the choice of a few characters to choose from with already upgraded attributes and your goal is to make it to the nuclear facility to trigger an explosion that will wipe out the city. This mode was my favorite because you have to make it all the way there, without traders to buy goods from, (you get ammo and guns from looting and calling in drop boxes from your commander), and then run back before the nuclear reactor explodes. It sounds annoying, but it's the best mode in my opinion. And survival. Would it really be a zombie game without survival?
I only have a few problems with this game. The hardest difficulty mode is ridiculous. It should be called impossible mode. Yes, you can beat it, but when you switch from hard mode to hardest mode, you rarely get any weapons or ammo and traders really only appear at the beginning of the game and at the end. May as well just get rid of the traders and force the player to bash his way through. Hardest difficulty isn't bad because it's hard, it's bad because it's extremely cheap and significantly unbalanced. My other complaint is really a recommendation. Just add bosses and it will vary the feeling of the game instead of running constantly down streets shooting the same zombies. Also, the achievements seem buggy, so you could be looking at a few extra hours just to find ways of unlocking them, even when you already did what they said.
If you see this game on sale and you like zombies, pick it up. Otherwise, wait for Dead Pixels 2 or just let the game be.

Been a Star Wars fan for a long time and KOTOR II in my opinion is the best out of Star Wars video games. This new update they've implemented has been very much needed for a long time. I'm not going to list the improvements, because I think of this as a reboot of the game. That's how big this update is for this game. I mean, it no longer crashes on start up on modern computers. Just that bug fix would've made me happy so I wouldn't have to search the internet for 6 hours to figure out how to make it work. (sigh)
Now to the actual gameplay:
Much like Fallout, but in the Star Wars universe, but with less customization of the character.
Like Fallout, you can make good decisions and bad decisions, but instead of karma, it's the side of the force you're on. (Important in late game)
FANTASTIC STORYLINE: Obviously I'm not gonna put spoilers in here, but the story telling of Bethesda is 10/10 once again.
This game is both RPG, and a realtime strategy game, all in third person. Who should I attack, with whom should I attack, what do I attack with, when do I heal, when should I use the force? So many variables to think about.
Many different force powers are in this game, and when certain powers are combined with a certain character setup, (levels of strength, charisma, wisdom, etc.) they can become very powerful.

I did not wait long for this game. I have heard about it here and there on my time on the internet but I never played the original till two years ago. This game is infamous for its 10 year development cycle. The game has been scrapped many times and unfortunately this is the weakest out of all the rebirths. The 1998 trailer and the 2000s one looked much more fun than the final product. Does that mean the final product is a horrible game?
Who am I kidding it's not great but not bad.
Story:
10 years after you defeated the aliens in Duke Nukem 3D they come back to take revenge. They take the women and Duke's steady girlfriends (yes that is plural). You are placed in many interesting situations in your quest to take out the aliens. In one part you are shrunk and have to use a race car to traverse a casino, in another you have to find three items for a stripper so she can perform a lap dance, the list goes on but what I am trying to say is that the game is not a typical shooter.
Gameplay:
This is unfortunately a regenerating health linear shooter. No maze like levels or health packs. The health system is unique. You can gain more health by defeating bosses or interacting with certain world objects. Some actions that will give you health are: urinating, benching, shooting a basket, getting a highscore on a pinball game, and much more. Unfortunately you only see these in the first half of the game. As far as I know the second thirds of the game have practically no ego boosts other than the bosses. Another bummer is that while the first two halves of the game are interesting (for the situations I have stated) the final third takes place in the corridor heavy Hoover Dam. It is very dull compared to the rest of the game. Imagine if Duke Nukem 3D's third episode took place in a dull military base. People would be mad. Also in the dessert there is a minecart area and it is ridiculously short. The trailers made it out to be longer with more action. But you don't kill anyone in it.
Your enemy variety is low. Most are pigs but you will occasionally find flying teleporting aliens, shielded ones, and octabrains. It would have been nice to go after assassins hired by the corrupt president (like Bombshell in the first trailer). Instead you get the same old same old.
The weapon system got a lot of controversy because you could only carry two weapons. They have an option in this version to carry 4. The weapons are not very good mostly because of the lack of enemy variety. You use any random weapon without consequences. The rocket launcher only holds 5 rounds (Picard shame pic) and the ripper is just as weak as it was in Duke Nukem 3D. The rail gun is an interesting weapon because it kills most enemies in 2 shots. You can also quickfire pipes and tripwire mines with a bound key. A big disappointment is that the Freeze Ray is ridiculously weak. I unloaded an entire clip on an enemy and he still would not freeze.
Surprisingly some people play multiplayer and DNF supports dedicated servers. It is pretty fun and you get the cool weapons from the game and more like the Expander.
Conclusion:
The first two thirds of this game are interesting. I only played to the end after I reached the Hoover Dam because I just wanted to say "I beat a game that was in development for 10 years". Duke Nukem is still a cool character and I did play all the way through despite its flaws. It is definitely a game that most will enjoy but there are many better shooters than this like F.E.A.R. and Half Life. And if you are not satisfied just play the DNF mod for eduke32.
