For those of you that consider picking up this game:
Europa Universalis: Rome is a game I like very much at the moment, I have not played any other Europa Universalis games and some of them might be better (after I bought the game I heard from people that 3 is better) I however do not regret my purchase since I like the ancient world theme a lot more than almost anything else set in the real world and is for me a tie with the cold war.
Why did I like this game?
I think It is mechanically very sound, the combat mechanics are very limited but unlike for example civ 4 I do not find it annoying to fight wars and the combat does not distract too much from what works really well with the game.
So what does work really well in the game?  The economic gameplay in the game is solid, it is less about buildings than for example Rome total war 1, however there are various other things that have an influence on the economy such the governors of the province that you can select (very much like Rome total war 1) but also stuff like the people you have chosen to take positions in nationwide politics, the laws you have passed, religious blessings, trade and the kind of civ you have( for example dictatorship monarchy and various kinds of democracies).
That brings me to something else that works pretty well in this game, Politics. The game has 5 political factions that battle (sometimes in case of civil war literally) over political control of your nation. Each factions power can grow or diminish depending on your actions, the populist party will for example gain more political attraction if either peace or war last too long, while the religious faction can grow from invoking blessings on your nation or sacrificing to the gods, but all factions grow from having representatives in important functions for (for example the research positions) the people taking these functions are chosen by you. But on the other side the factions can also influence your decisions, if you don't have the political support in the senate you can't start wars or make use of various other mechanics in the diplomacy interface.
What doesn't work?
The game doesn't do such a good job of explaining to you what various mechanics in the game do and how they are calculated (I for example still don't know fully how diplomatic skill is calculated) most of it however isn't that annoying and can in a way even increase your enjoyment, since you get the feeling that after your first playthrough you really got to know the game, therefore also giving you an incentive to try another one. It also isn't that bad, now after some wiki reading I think diplomatic skill is the only thing I do not really understand that I would like to understand. The game could however do a better job of presenting its information, the game could for example tell you what the traits characters could gain during events do before you need to selects them. Also I think the game could have been better if the people of your nation belonged to larger but fewer families and give you a better way (for example the family tree in Rome total war 1) to look at these families and their relations to other people in your nation
In the end I sill liked this game very much but it could have been better

As is typical of Paradox Interactive's "gap" titles, EU: Rome is not very remarkable. It is a game that could have been quite good, but was ultimately left by the wayside as its developer moved on to more significant projects.
If you look at the developer's history of releases, you'll find that that it very often intersperses minor, derivative releases between its major titles. These titles are almost without exception unpolished and unimpressive, and EU: Rome fits that bill perfectly. You'll find that the gameplay is very similar to that of EU3, with necessary variations that were poorly implemented. Even the expansion pack, Vae Victis, was not enough to salvage this game, and neither were the relatively few major mods released for it. It's a shame, really, as the Roman era was an interesting time, and the foundations of this game were relatively well-conceived; had it received the necessary attention, it could have been a very entertaining title.
While it may look attractive---it appears, to the casual eye, as EU3 in the Roman period---this game  just isn't very good.

Nether is a great addition to the Survival game genre. With the greats out there at the moment such as Rust and DayZ, Nether does a really good job of being, well, different!
Some really bad stuff happened and now there are these monsters only Keiichirō Toyama could dream up skulking the desecrated city you call home sweet home. Aesthetically, Nether is very pleasing however there is lots of room for improvement. The city has a very The Last of Us and I Am Legend feel to it.
Your job, as a survivor, is to gather loot, run trading missions, whack Nether and try not to die.
Safe Havens give you respite if things get tough and even other Players can't attack you in there!
Combat is fluid and your character can level up using XP received from killing Nether/Players, completing Trading runs and selling loot procured in the city.
Once your character ascends a level you get a skill point you can use in the handy skill trees to increase your stamina, steady your aim, block with a melee weapon and acquire a skill to silence your footsteps whilst crouched! (Those Nether can hear you, you know!)
One thing with survival games, is more often than not the AI opponents are dumb, buggy and little more than a Lion that's declawed and defanged. Nether really are a scary and tough adversary with different types of Nether you can face and different strategies required for beating them.
I'd recommend picking this up and diving straight in.

Shadow Warrior 2 after completing the game I decided to write my own little review because I would like to compare this one to the 2013 reboot.
I also completed the 2013 reboot and I thoroughly enjoyed that game it was fun it was silly it was a big monster frag festival with great weapons powers and a sword funny one liners and alot of humor in the dialoge.
Shadow Warrior 2 imo tried to make itself over complicated I feel it is like the developers felt the need tp innovate from the reboot.
Question is were these changes for the better? if you ask me no , the developers added this hub where you can talk to npc's and get quests and side quests from and also buy various upgrades for weapons ammunition and power upgrades and also new weapons would you so desire.
The main hub also does some story telling but the game didnt need this main hub they could have also told the story through just cutscenes after ending a level , in fact the main hub did make me feel disconnected from the actual game which was a bit of a miss for me.
The combat in this game is good the shooting is really satisfying but the whole upgrade system attached to the weapon system should have been left out.
In the 2013 reboot there was a fixed set of weapons and the further you progressed the more weapons you would find some are single weapons and some u could dual wield which was super fun.
However in SW2 they decided to implement this upgrade system and items which allow you to enhance your weapons with fire,electric,poison,ice elements and then there is another category which enables you to change that stats of your gun more damage done to this creature or gain more chi etc etc.
I think the implementation of the upgrade system is a miss why ? because at first I didnt bother with the whole upgrade system until I realised wait now I need some upgrades or I will keep on dying.
By applying the upgrades the game suddenly became super easy I didn't really have to try all that hard to make my way through the levels even the boss fights were easy.
In SW1 you  sometimes had to rely on your other powers and your sword because you would run out of ammo sometimes because the SW1 the levels were huge and the hordes of monsters were massive SW2 I missed having to use my sword and also my special powers I did use the sword but not as often as in SW1 and the special powers in this game are totally useless because ALOT of enemies are immuun to your special powers so that element of gameplay which was so great in SW1 completely went to waste in SW2 which is a real shame.
Level design wise SW2 isn't up to par with the level design of SW1 I found the levels in SW2 to be more generic alot of open area's caves retro looking levels and you will visit the same levels again through out the game but with different objectives, in SW1 each level was different and unique no rehasing of the levels which they do in SW2.
This game doesn't take itself all to seriously so there was plenty of humor in SW1 and there still is plenty of humor in SW2 you have these funny conversations with kumiko and all the other characters you will meet so thats fun to listen to and ofcourse it is always great when you use the shotgun a Lu Wang shouts boom goes the boomstick :).
Even tho this game in my point of view wasn't as strong as SW1 I still had a great time playing it there is just something about butchering up these ugly b*****rds you meet in the game :).
Graphically the game looks nice not mindblowing but nothing to complain about the graphics or the performance it did run well on my pc , one thing I was disappointed about graphics wise were some of the npc's in cutscene and the lip syncing that was just horrible tbh.
So after 15 hours of playing I made it to the end and well the end lacks severly you beat a boss and you get a cutscene which ends rather strangly.
I immediatly thought ok with a end like this maybe they will release more DLC for this game or make a sequel because the ending in SW2 is S**T!!! no reward at all in the end and the story hasn't been told entirely for me, so Iam thinking more DLC or sequel.

So I will close my little review with my final thoughs if you are looking for a fps shooter and if you are curious about SW1 and SW2 first play SW2 because this game is weaker than the first when you beat SW2 then play SW1 that will give you a really oldschool FPS experience again :)

While I would reccomend it to my friends this game is incredibly frustrating in its current form and can be downright unenjoyable at times due to the learning curve. I have played MtG since I was 12
(28 now) and even I am finding myself at a loss of how to face some bosses. The starter decks that you begin with have some major flaws (as all starter decks should) but with no side board to speak of if you choose badly you can soon find yourself only able to pass a zone by waiting till the computer gets mana screwed. It took me 8+ hours of solid play just to get to the boss of the second zone due to the starter decks inability to adapt to certain colors. This is not MTGO, do not expect us to wade through a ton of BS as there is no monetary reward as there is in MTGO. DotPW are suppossed to be the "casual" magic, games that we can take light-heartedly to try out different decks and card to see if we want to purchase them IRL, instead we get a grindfest with little to no feeling of success/reward. Also making it so that you can "pay to win" by purchasing all the cards for $25 is a lame way to fix the issue. Here are some improvements I would like to see in future updates:
- 15 card sideboard for starter decks to help them deal with weaknesses vs bosses
- Two Headed Giant
- Sealed Draft Play
- More Multi-Color Cards

The fact that I'd never heard of this game before yesterday is proof that I'm following the wrong kinds of game news outlets. It's lavishly detailed, dripping with atmosphere, and full of the sort of weird, imaginative, borderline nightmarish imagery that I'm always on the lookout for. Mature point-and-click adventures are coming back, and I couldn't be happier.
P&Cs have a (deserved) reputation as being full of obtuse puzzles that are more about reading the designer's mind than using a realistic problem solving approach. I'm happy to report that isn't the case here. Each puzzle (and there are quite a lot of them) has a well-conveyed goal and comes together logically. For every minigame you've seen before -- slide the blocks, connect the wires, or match the tiles -- there's another that's new and interesting, and even the familiar ones often come with a twist.
For me, games are first and formost about offering the player a new world to explore, and Tormentum delivers beautifully on that end. I'll admit I groaned when my character played the amnesia card at the very beginning, but it works out surprisingly well -- this world is as alien to him as it was to me. It's a bizarre setting full of creatures and locales both otherworldly and twistedly familiar, yet everything is presented in such an unassuming, matter-of-fact way that it never stops feeling believable. It's a world you're dropped into without any explanation - because you don't need one. No lore-heavy monologues or lists of invented names to be found here. It's about as earnest and unpretentious a fantasy setting as I've ever seen.
I like the inclusion of moral choices, though they can be a little too obvious -- I don't personally subscribe to the belief that there is no right and wrong, only "shades of grey", but I do appreciate it when I'm forced to make a decision without having all the answers. With a few exceptions, the choices you'll be making are pretty clear-cut between right and wrong, and given the surreal setting, I would have hoped for a bit more ambiguity. Still, they add a nice layer of reactivity to the story and offer welcome motivation to play through more than once.
The one real complaint I have is about the controls. Moving the mouse simultaneously pans the scene in parallax while also moving the cursor, meaning that objects on screen move as you move the cursor towards them. You have to actively guide the cursor instead of allowing your muscle memory to do the heavy lifting. It also (for me) caused some amount of light motion sickness early on. Your milage may vary of course.
Ultimately I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this game. It's a refreshing surprise that ticks all the boxes I care about. Check out the demo if you're still on the fence, but personally, this is one impulse buy I don't regret in the slightest.

Honestly, I really wanted to like this game, but I can't for a few reasons.  I was able to power through a lot of the game without using any stealth and just bottlenecking all the AI into one place and mowing them down, and I was playing on the highest difficulty.  The only real problem I had with this strategy was when there was a very, very close range area, where the enemy had the PPSH-41 (You know, that gun that was basically a bullet hose), but even that type of encounter was easy to deal with with a quick grenade lob and a duck behind cover.  Speaking of the AI, the tank AI is the weirdest AI ever (if they're mobile), the one time I was actually using stealth in a mission (and I used stealth because just mowing the enemy down was boring), a tank was about 20 to 30 feet away from me, I was completely undetected by anyone yet.  But as soon as I peak a slight part of my body out while prone on the ground next to debree piles making me impossible to spot from even foot  soldiers who had passed by earlier.  The tank, facing the complete other way, spun around 180 degrees in less than half a second and shot a shell straight into my head instantly ending my stealth run, so back to just going HAM with the sniper again I guess.  That was just one thing that bothered me, something else is that the game looks unpolished.  There are so many graphical glitches, sometimes when you move about, the textures  in distant buildings flicker, making me instantly get down as low as possible and get ready to make some heads roll, but looking at the open window in the building I see nothing.  There were multiple, god damn multiple parts of the game where parts of wall models didnt even appear unless I looked at them from just the right angle, but they were mostly out of the way in places where you shouldnt go.  Unless you want to get the all of the collectables, then you get to go around the map and look at all the textures just freak the ♥♥♥♥ out as you go about picking up bars of gold and bottles (I know the gold bars are relevant historically and are actually a cool idea for collectables, but where do the bottles come from?).  The game wasnt terrible, it was fun at moments, like when I was able to see someones eyeball burst as a bullet traveled through their skull with slow motion and x-ray effects, but that thrill quickly goes away and the slow motion starts to get annoying after you see if for the hundredth time.  It just leaves me sitting, watching a bullet travel so, so, so slowly towards some poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who is about to get his testicals shot off.  The slow motion lasts for around 4-5 seconds, but when there are 4 guys clustered together and I decide take each of them out quickly one after the other, each time having to wait 5 seconds for my bullet to take its goddamn time to kill him, I wind up waiting a total of about 30 seconds just trying to deal with a few enemies in succession. Im too lazy to think of a nice segway to talk about this part of the game, but it gets very repetetive quick, just repeating the same thing over and over again.  Infiltrate some random place, kill everyone in the area, do a specific objective, then leave.  Its the same thing practically every mission with ever so slight variations. If you did not get this game during it's time when it was free to get, it's not worth the price.

I bought this game a good, 6, 7 maybe even 8 months before writing this review here. I never thought it would be much of a game, it was on sale for 99 cents and I bought it just on the off chance it would be good, and because it was so cheap.
Recently I was talking about one of my favorite old NES games, River City Ransom, and had asked a friend if he knew of anything similar that is on the PC. This is the game he mentioned.
And while I do not think this game is better than River City Ransom, or even close to as good. It definitely scratches that itch I had for a similar game.
The controls are nice and responsive, the movement is fluid, and the gameplay is challenging enough. You can loot abandoned buildings, then turn around and sell the items you find to traders that have storefronts randomly throughout the game and use those funds ot buy weapons/ammo/health kits form them. The traders also have a 'wanted' option to click when in their store, and they name an item that they want and they offer high amounts of money in exchange.
The game also has level progression and slight RPG elements, skill upgrades, a nice assortment of weapons. Weapons which have stats that you can compare.
Overall I'm pleased with the game so far, and although i havent put in a whole lot of time with it yet, i can see im going to enjoy it a lot. But i also see that it's going to get quite repetitive, which may or may not be a bad thing.
I definitely would reccomend this to anyone whos into retro gameplay. at ANY price, the $2.99 price tag when it's not on sale is nothing, it's well worth that.

Obsidian was smart and kept those audio files and some of the incomplete areas in some game files. Some modders were able to recreate and add this content over the years, and thanks to the recent Steam workshop support, it is even easier to download these two mods. With the restoration mod, the game is transformed into one of the most well written and thought provoking games that I have ever played. While the first one serves as an excellent homage to the original movies, Kotor II takes the Star Wars formula and flips it over and asks questions morality never seen in a Star Wars game, or any other meda. Absoletely timeless.

This game can pretty much be summed up as "I need to find a work bench to upgrade my lightsaber before I am bombarded with more empty dialog."
To elaborate a bit on what I said...
SWKOR 2 isn't as good as the first. The first was brilliant. Great story, great combat system, great loot progression system, great characters, great character backstory. The steam version of the first is about as buggy as the second yet it still is one of the best rpgs and one of the best games created.
The sequel is broken. I might give it another go in a month or so on a new toon now knowing what I know and see what I can milk out of the game. But it is broken. It is difficult to explain fully without spoilers. The first companion you get is broken. They make combat trivial because of their passive ability. Your main becomes a juggernaut of destruction and consequently makes combat moot because of the first companion you get. Aside from that your first companion is an eyesore. If you opt not to use your first companion because they are broken then you may get much more out of the combat system.
The games story seems generic. The protagonist is a cipher. I felt little attachment to his cause. This consequently makes dialog choices seem inconsequential. And thus the dialog choices become centered around the stuff you get rather than the story which unfolds. But since combat is broken because of your first companion even the stuff you get is inconsequential.
Now knowing what I know if I do another play through I will probably pursue the darkside on my main on hard difficulty and not use the first companion and cut everyone to bits (usually in rpgs I play the good guy that helps everyone)  and see if I can spark the magic that made the first great.
The potential of the game has been realized and I change my recommendation to yes. If you roll a darkside consular with 8str, 8dex, 14con, 14int, 16 wis, and 15 cha (which becomes 16 as soon as you get a stat point at level up) and play on difficult then most pieces of the game become relevant. To get through the mining facility you need grenades, shields, medpacks, shock. Fighting unarmed is the best way to go so your character is much like Jon Irenicus from BG2. Thus the start of the game is similar to slow starts consistent with D&D style games; the whole of the start is uniformly slow and not just the dialog(which occurs if you roll a guardian and own everything).
After completing the game I conclude that the story is the worst of any star wars game or movie. A good rpg nonetheless.

SOMA is a pretty good psychological survival-horror game. It's more like Alien: Isolation in that it builds the tension from the atmosphere of the game, rather than via cheap jump-scare tactics. There's a good story that talks about what it means to live, with talking robots that have the consciousness of their masters. Visuals are decent, while the sound design and voice acting are great.
Even when there's no immediate danger, just listening to the sound gives you the chills. Can never be too sure what lurks around. The tension by way of the audio design is particularly brilliantly done in SOMA.
You can customize your controls fully, there are some graphics options to customize and you can save at any time and exit the game.
Anyway, so far, I have two issues with the game. Both are worth mentioning but still overall my net outlook of the game is positive and that it is worth getting, especially if you like the premise of it.
The first is that the enemies can be frustrating. The first enemy I met was a "big daddy" kind of enemy. Easy to get around him, and I never saw it again so far. Then I think there's an enemy in the water but can't be too sure if that's considered an enemy or not. Anyway, the third one is kinda tricky and I had to brute force my way through. He can sense you electromagnetically, and I'm not sure how to get past. Trial and error took me past the first, and now there's another one of it that I can't seem to get past. So yeah, maybe I'm missing something, but this enemy is kinda frustrating making me try over and over again.
The second is that the graphics optimization is kinda underwhelming. Ok sure, I only have a GTX 750, but for this kind of a "corridor" based linear game, I expect 60fps on reduced settings. But often, being in a static room, my framerate would only be 45-50fps, and many times when moving around it may just be around 40fps. Can't really understand why. It doesn't look particularly amazing or demanding. I run Alien Isolation at 60fps no issues at High settings. The fact that the PS4 version only runs at 30fps (and even then not smoothly) where many other linear "corridor" games run at 60fps shows that the game could have been better optimized.
So yeah, overall it's still a very engrossing and immersive game, with an interesting theme and a good story. If you like narrative-driven games and don't mind some psychological horror elements, give this one a go!

Europa Universalis Rome is Paradox's attempt at creating a game to bridge the gameplay gap between the great but somewhat generic grand strategy of Europa Universalis and the personal management and dynastic aspects of Crusader Kings. Unfortunately this is not a marriage made in heaven and the two styles does not mix well in this game.
Rome is a grand strategy game, you pick your nation among those that were around at whatever start date you chose and then go about doing what ever you please. War, trade, diplomacy, like in other Paradox grand strategy games you can play your country however you please but the game is still geared heavily in the favor of warfare. You will simply gain more and gain it faster by taking it from others.
Introduced in this game is a myriad of characters that rule your cities and lead your armies all with their own traits, preferences and family relations. Unlike in Crusader Kings you don't have your own family tree in this game but instead simply try to manage your various powerful subjects in this manner. Although this is a great idea in principle it is fairly poorly executed. Managing the many, many characters available to you is a huge task that only grows larger as the game goes on and if you chose to ignore the micromanagement for too long you might have a revolt on your hands.
Rome is a game that brings a lot of cool aspects together from two very great game but it is also a game that has a lot of issues with implementation and execution that makes it a chore to play at times. It is still a Paradox grand strategy and that means there is quality underneath it all but it is still the weakest one in their lineup.

What were they thinking with the direction they took this game in?
I thought Shadow Warrior 2013 had a good template, but I still thought it needed serious improvements (like gunplay and level design). However, while guns are viable now and feel pretty good, pretty much every other problem remains or is made worse. For example, while the levels are more open, the randomly-generated nature of them makes them feel "aimless" and I've seen plenty of areas that seem to exist for no real reason. Also, it wasn't long until I've seen tiles start to repeat. For loot, in comparison to something like Borderlands, it's ♥♥♥♥ing lame. The only interesting things they could do is add an elemental effect to your weapon, or add on a firing mode, the rest is just marginal state bonuses that you barely notice (or don't at all).
Another thing, remember when I said that guns are now viable? Well I say that because they now have good sound and animation assests and they are about as effective as melee weapons. What I didn't mention is that, especially with the higher-tier enemies, is that damage-sponges are still rampant. Like honestly, it's probably comparable, or even worse so, to enemies in BL2 on True Vault Hunter Mode, and I just played this on normal difficulty, I can't imagine what it's like on the higher settings. Like, I remember confronting a mini-boss who looked just like any other human being, and he took a hundred ♥♥♥♥ing rounds. This would already be a massive deal-breaker for me if it was relentlessly difficult like Borderlands is on UVHM, which it isn't, not at all.
If you want to play a fun single-player shooting game, get the recent DOOM and/or Wolfenstein games.
If you want to play one that's based on loot in particular, get Borderlands 2.
If you want fun first-person sword combat, just get the previous Shadow Warrior game.
I wish they could've just made SW'13 but better, but they didn't, and they made gameplay changes that ultimately doesn't benefit it, makes it feel generic, and doesn't make it feel like a Shadow Warrior game.

I used to have a sarcastic review here detailing all the horrible things this game does incredibly wrong.  I've given up.  5 stages of grief have come and gone.  It's over.  I don't have any hope of those things being corrected, so I removed them.
Instead, imagine you're on a hill.  A very large hill, but not a mountain, a gentle but tedious incline that exhausts you but isn't dangerous.  Hour after hour you try to climb this hill, you almost always see yourself at the crest of it.  Once you get over that crest, you're golden.  It's all downhill, nice smooth ride down the other side.  It never comes.  You spend more hours and more hours and get closer, but you have to take a break and then you realize you're on a down escalator the whole time and any time you waste you just get all your progress sucked away.  You keep thinking all you need to do is reach the top then the way down will be fun, enjoyable.  This doesn't happen.  You keep trying anyway.
That's For Honor.  It has this ability to suck away hours from your life because you think, like any fighting game, you've just got to make it click so you keep going to try and believe it'll be good soon.  It's impossible.  The game is fundamentally broken due to an incredible array of technical problems to balance issues, from input detection errors to connection problems the game just doesn't have the capability of being an enjoyable experience for most people.
Probably the most frustrating system in the entire game is an obviously tacked-on gear system to emulate some form of progression.  It takes an INCREDIBLE amount of time investment to start getting competitive equipment that makes combat anything less than an uphill battle unless you stick solely to modes that are largely inactive but disable their effects.  You can soften this system with real money because it's Ubisoft, but there's no avoiding it and it feels like few fights in the larger modes are ever actually in your favor.
Another frustrating concept is the team matchup indicator.  You are always on par or better than your allies, you are always ONLY on par with your enemies.  This is patently false.  This entire matchup display is completely falsified and has no logic behind it.  It's a slap in the face.  Beyond that, the matchmaking doesn't even try to hide it because it never finds a match before setting it to search for all skill levels.  Never mind the fact that the person using an AutoHotKey script to perfectly block every attack coming at him is on the opposing team in your first match, just don't try to report them because the report function is a placebo, too.
Funnily enough, around the same time I got this game, I purchased Call of Duty: Infinite Warfare, another depressingly bad videogame, but because it's literally unplayable on PC anymore.  I would still say its current state is a better game than For Honor, if only because it prohibits you from actually interacting with it in a meaningful way.
Now, I have a habit of making hilariously bad purchases I later regret to remind myself of why I keep most of my savings in a secure account out of my ready hands to spend it.  I spent $100 on this game and there's not a moment I don't regret it when I see this game in my steam inventory, but what I regret more is continuously spending time trying to justify that purchase, regardless of this horrendously negative review.  Don't be me.  Avoid this game.
I'd say Ubisoft should be ashamed, but they're basically thieves and con artists by this point.  I made a mistake.
As a horror game lover,  this game doesn't really give me the fear factor, hence, I'm sorry, but not recommending it despite everyone's positive review

There is not a whole lot I can say about Tormentum - Dark Sorrow that hasn't already been said, and more than likely stated more eliquently than I can say it. It is easy to manuever through out much like in Shadowgate (2014) the difference being that in a lot of screens you can see the main character in a third person perspective. The music, and ambient noise sets the theme perfectly. I believe I purchases this on sale for around $10, and it is easily worth the full asking price. It is not often (almost never) I will take time to review a game, but this one deserves that recognition. If you are a fan of games like Shadowgate (2014), Whispered Worlds, or Chains of Satinav you should do yourself a favor, and pick this game up the next time you have some extra money burning a hole in your pocket. I don't think you will be disappointed.

LiF:YO could be an amazing experience, 3/10.
This game can be fun with the right people, however after playing it on many different servers, I cannot honestly say they are that common to find!
Let's clarify somethings about how I would review a game, and why I would ever give it a negative one; for starters I am a fan of the whole Early Access, I love supporting developers whenever I got a few extra dollars without hurting my wallet too much - This game, I bought last Christmas for my cousin, my friend, and myself to all join up on a server, do whatever it is we do in games, and enjoy it. Now, the fruit of my review begins.
When things are simple, you enjoy it, you enjoy it without ever knowing why until something more advanced finds you and steals you away. At the time we began, healing was horribly broken, never working - things seemed useless but the menu was beautiful. We sat around and dug holes or flattened the ground. Nothing mattered, the need for hunting or fighting did not cross our minds. Then that was the day we all just.. Stopped.
Somewhere between stupid fun and idle stalling did we fall off of the bandwagon of "LiF:YO", not because we were given something under false pretenses, but because the world, as big and beautiful as it was had been deprived. Animals turned all the way up? Might as well make it "Fight Eachother 2014 - 15", there were no animals to kill half of the time, you kill ten and then you wait hours for them to pop back up. You go to YouTube, to watch the videos detailing LiF as an MMO, and come to realize that was ANOTHER game -- not this one. At full price, even now, post-release you will without doubt enjoy the game in its fullest; because no matter what they do, I fear the game is at its peak. You build, and build, and build. Hunting? Only do it to build the stuff you need - you will never find animals much anyway.. I wanted to love this game, I thought I did. Then like I said, I fell off of it, I fell back on my feet and
reminded me, reminded me of something great..
, too feudal anyway to be playing a game post release that is just as, if not more broken than it was back in Early Access - Oh, the most exquisite thing was the altering of the menues. WONDERFUL! Full-game complete!

It's not what it promised, not what I wanted.

This is one of those 'neutral' reviews which we can not make on Steam, though because my feelings tend to be more negative than the other way around, I'm going with the red thumbs down.
80 days looks pretty groovy, the UI and grahpics which might not be AAA still struck a chord with me. As did the fact that this is one of those 'story telling games' where your decisions determine the path you're going to take, and thus how the story continues.
However the problem arises when the decisions you make, aren't actually all that interesting. As opposed to making the player wonder how their decision pans out, it gives you an uninteresting outcome. Which then makes you not really care about any forthcoming decision making. As mentioned in another review, this game is very wordy. I don't really see that as a problem, however it is when it isn't captivating me with those words. And that's what's happening in 80 days, throughout the game.
The only time I felt my decisions gave me a satisfying outcome, was when at the end of my game I was faced with starting a mutiny on a boat. The mutiny failed, however that was the only time where I felt the story I was 'creating' was grabbing me. And that was well at the end of the 80 days time period. So everything before that: meh.
Which brings me to a complaint that was brough up by another reviewer. This isn't a game you're supposed to finish in 1 playthrough. You're supposed to do things differently and learn from prior games, to be able to make that 80th day deadline. However the only time where I learned to do something differently in a next game, was again with the mutiny scenario. And I wasn't going to make it even if it had succeeded. There's no real learning point, as you don't really know what you did wrong, other than try a different path. And there are loads of those.
But then we're back at the game's scenarios and decisions not really being engaging, and after 1 play through I didn't feel like doing it all over again. I can see 80 days being a good game to other people, as it's not really 'bad'. However I personally wouldn't recommend it to everybody. Hence the neutral/negative conclusion.

I felt like an updated review was needed. I've been looking at all of this negative feedback that BeamNG.Drive has recieved recently, and from what i can see, people aren't really understanding a few things.
First off on my reasons for liking this game so much, i played a previous game to this, called Rigs Of Rods. Rigs Of Rods (Or ROR for short) was a very dumbed down, barebones version of this game, and i very much enjoyed ROR as it ran perfectly on my previous very terrible PC so i was almost stuck to playing ROR, which gave me a long time to play the game, download thousands of mods and clock some huge hours in game. And for anyone who's played ROR, this is ROR, but everything that ROR needed, including a HUGE graphics overhaul, i mean seriously, the required specs of this game are no joke, it's simply beautiful for what it is.
Now, onto what others appear to be saying:
The first elephant in the room is:
IT'S NOT DONE YET. EARLY ACCESS MEANS
Theres still more coming to this game, so you can't unfairly leave a review saying "wasn't worth what i payed" as this game isn't done yet.
The second:
I've seen quite a few negative reviews surrounding this game just being about driving around and crashing into walls/objects. Reviews like this make me feel like the user hasn't actually explored all of the games options/settings, as there's scenarios to complete, maps to explore and even a story mode on Utah which i personally think is an awesome little thing in itself. To further back up my previous point, the mod base for Beam is HUGE. There's absolutely loads of different mod sites for Beam, which can add new aspects to the game.
Having over 400 hours in game which yes, before you say those are legit hours and i have played this game for a while now and through the updates the team are constantly adding new maps, cars, configurations and other things into the game which make things that little bit easier.
Heres the part which i guess many will be wanting to know:
Should i buy this?
BeamNG.Drive is NOT currently a finished game. So why would i be pushing you guys to buy this? Well, as of right now you won't get all the features in game, but what you will get is a beautifully textured and detailed engine with the best crash physics to date in any game that i have seen. I remember as a child playing Burnout Paradise on the Xbox 360 and remembering how awe-inspiring those crash physics were, and how you could actively see your car getting bent up/damaged and BeamNG.Drive puts that game to shame in the physics department. There's more to come yet, and i'm proud to say i've been backing this game since release and will continue playing this game for many years to come. The fact this also has full support for 900 Degree racing wheels such as the Logitech G920/G29 and the G27 and many other wheels is just fantastic.
Should you buy BeamNG.Drive?
(As long as you meet the required specs to play the game of course to prevent lag/ a ruined experience..) yes,   yes,  and YES.
I don't even know what I'm supposed to be doing in this game. Nothing is explained and it's not clear what the goal is or why you should care about any of it.

If you like slamming and pushing other drivers off the road, the new Flatout is probably not for you.
It's overall a really OK racing game but unlike in previous titles (or, true Flatout titles which are all released prior to 3) the physics engine is really bad. You can still destroy street signs and what not but slamming other drivers feels really bad - there is just no force to it. When I hit someone's rear with 200kmh in Flatout 2 I could be certain they won't bother me again any time soon. In Flatout 4, however, when you hit someone's rear at 200kmh, their car slightly jumps and you see a few sparks - that's it. In the best case, they lose control over their car but nothing more. Maneuvers like that are REALLY dangerous as most of the time other drivers will just "shrug you off" and you will suddenly find yourself losing control of your own car while they just continue racing as if nothing happened. Same goes for trying to push other drivers off the road - it's like they are driving on rails.
tl;dr: Flatout 4 is not that bad of a game but if you are that kind of person that likes to fully slam into an opponent that has just overtaken you, you won't have a good time with it.

I'll get to the point.  Recommended?  Yes.  But that comes with some caveats.  See below:
Good:
- Its a return to Flatout 2 & Ultimate Carnage.  Its quick, and its fun to play.
- Some of the new stunts are fun, once you unlock them :| (flatout mode below)
- Graphics are well done, as is the sound.
- The addition of track modes: assault (gain powerups and nitro from ramming others) & carnage (as much scenery as possible) add a different spice to races.
- Steam workshop support will soon be active, theoretically meaning an increase in community generated tracks/vehicles(?) after release.
Not So Good:
- The career mode is a grind.
- Flatout mode is also a grind
- A greater range of tracks would have been nice.
- There appears to be an absence of a "tournament" mode to play multiple stunts/tracks together in one go.
- No stunts initially in online MP.
- Derby matches (apart from CTF) are a mixed bag.
- The music is a bit cheesy in parts, but thats probably to be expected.
Conclusion:
I've dropped some time into it, and its proving entertaining.  Is it worth the US$40?  Its a judgement call.  For people who have been missing a Flatout fix its worth it.  Alternatively, wait for a sale :)

As of release, Dead Sky is quite possibly the worst game I have ever played. While the concept sounds interesting on paper, the execution is far from resembling anything that could ever be mistaken as a fun diversion. Even the title screen comes off as clunky and amateur. And I wish I had heeded the warning bells that screen set off in my head, because the gameplay is far worse. It's actually kind of an impressive achievement, come to think of it-- Dead Sky is so void of entertainment value that it is impossible to even revel in how bad it is.
Zombies are supposed to be the pizza of videogames; even bad pizza is still pretty good. And yet Dead Sky somehow manages to make even killing zombies feel boring and tedious. I can honestly say I have never regretted a purchase as much as Dead Sky. Even if the game was free-to-play I would not recommend that anyone play it. There are better trainwrecks out there. Don't even bother rubbernecking this one out of curiosity.

Poor oversight by Magic 2015 developers in the game.
Positives include a catchy theme song, ability to construct a deck to however you like, storyline is not a bad inclusion, opening more boosters to provide anticipation and excitement.
Sadly however the negatives definately out weigh the positives.
You are restricted in deck building to a limited selection of cards after you have completed the campaign unless you which ti invest in "boosters" to increase your card pool. Matching up against others who have superior cards or/even duplicates or sets of 4 card(s) whom have purchased additional boosters, not only makes deck building difficult, ineffective but also increases the likelihood that you will be demorilised over and over again in matches against other opponents in 1 v 1 or free for all matching.
I generally enjoy purchasing this product for the puzzle games, Last turn puzzles a few years ago were amazing and difficult/challanging. 2014 however showcases some very sub par puzzles games and this year, well, there are none.
I played one game of free for all on 4 v 4 and I felt so far away from the game table I requested my flatmate to provide me a magnifine glass. myself and another player also realised 4 turns in that we had already lost when one of the players threw down some superior cards for which we had not even access to.
This put me off continuing playing this game into the future as really there is no point unless I am wishing to invest into this.
Suggestions would be to at least bring "two headed giant" match making back, a level par card selection by perhaps charging a set $15 fee from the start and not this "micro transaction booster option" which is poor oversight in my opinion and perhaps even a tournament mode where equal par magic the gatherers could paticipate tournaments of 10 players etc, round robin to then provide a level based system and a decent points rating for those wishing to climb to the top in rankings over time (by winning more tourney's etc)
Rating,
interface, music score, Story concept 6/10 (as what else can you do with a story really)
gameplay campaign 5/10 (as well the AI seems to get the perfect run of cards sometimes :S)
Deck building feature, 8/10 as this is very flexible
Card selection 2/10 (extremely limited unless additional investments made)
gameplay vs human 3/10 (for the reason you will become frustate that you are unable to build a deck that is consistent without investment into more booster packs)
Overall I would probably rate Magic 2015 4/10

username: The Rt Hon. Persona non Grata
text:
An ambitious game with a well defined market. Recommended to any military enthusiast.
Scope and scale are both impressive. Maps measure in the hundreds of square kilometers, the paltry 4 maps (Apex DLC included) is slightly disappointing, but their sheer size compensates for this deficiency. Weapon customization and weapon choice is vast, the same applies to uniforms, vests and backpacks. Vehicle variety is not as great, but nonetheless extensive, with CAS, air superiority jets, utility and attack helicopters and VTOLs. MBTs (4) is however, disappointing.
Unrealistic and inauthentic elements do exist however. Vehicle behavior is odd, multi ton tanks are brought to a standstill by rocks and ditches. Aircraft performance characteristics are regrettable, departure from controlled flight arising from low air speed high AOA induced stalls feel too brief and recovery is obtained too early for the heavy CAS jets. There is a lack of sophistication in jet aircraft behavior. It is clear in-game physics are not refined, with the modelling of inertia and momentum being an afterthought. Tanks lack the full gamut of features they ought to possess. There is no integrated FCS with lead indicators for MBTs, MRAPs, APCs, and SPAAGs. Tank shell ballistics are also done very poorly. Firing of the main gun on an inclined surface affects shell flight path exaggeratedly, causing unrealistic levels of arc and deviation. The effects of APFSDS shells on lightly armored vehicles is poor. Some lightly armored APCs can resist what in reality is a multi megajoule shot. Tank damage models are also fairly armature, for example the carousel mounted ammunition of the T-100 when struck does not detonate, catastrophic kills are hit and miss. Tank components were clearly not laid out, and disabling of the engine which should inflict a mobility kill is not implemented. Engine destruction should cut power to the tank's electronics and turret, this is however, not the case. Explosive Reactive Armor (ERA) is also not modeled, which would be an excellent defense against shaped charged shells. Penetration mechanics are overly simplified, this is disappointing as the effects of composites and ERA on chemical energy warheads are disregarded completely. Radars aboard the air superiority jets of the ARMA 3 Jets DLC have their radars implemented unsatisfactorily. Radar aperture is fixed, the mechanical scanning of a PESA was not even a consideration, and the lack of Helmet Mounted Displays (HMDs) aboard advanced 5th Generation jets is incredibly eyebrow raising.
Infantry combat is well implemented, with weight considerations to weapons, equipment, and ammunition. Weapon sway varying across weapon weights is obvious, recoil feels significantly detrimental to firing, and fatigue is incorporated, requiring brief breathers between sprints for weapon stabilization. One small gripe being that there is a noticeable lack of scopes with sub milliradian divisions, but this is an insignificant criticism. Destruction of certain structures with large high explosive shells is possible, and penetration of surfaces with varying caliber performances at the small arms level is modeled. This is impressive, giving utility to rounds like the .50 BMG, 9.3cm x 64mm, and carving out niches for the .50 BW.
The game is not user friendly, appealing to consumers with strong interest in military simulation, available tutorials in game are lackluster at best, controls and key bindings require experiential learning and external tutorials, making beginnings difficult and frustrating.
Ultimately, though the flaws of the game are rampant, it is the harmonization of the combined approach of air, sea, and land made easily accessible to all, coupled with the fact that there is no direct competitor or substitute to ARMA 3, that make it a huge winner. The game is established in such a way that facilitates communication through an in-game voice chat, bolstering the social element and adding value to the game, enhancing consumer satisfaction. The creation of a militaristic atmosphere, with gargantuan maps and large scale conflicts, is unparalleled across the market.
I have great memories of this game, sadly there are no more to come.

Having to pay for premium cards, thereby making this somewhat ofa  pay to win game really really bugs me, but it doesnt ruin the game, except for much of the random pvp, which if your like me doesnt affect you at all.
Now for the bads:
The User Interface is bad. All of it. This is not an overstatement, there is no aspect of this game's user interface that either is not buggy or is poorly designed (most of the time its both)
There isnt much of a point in listing the bugs here because they are common and infiltrate nearly every aspect of this game's UI. Unfortunetly this occassionally screws you over in matches. So far ive had a mulligan that did not bring my new hand up so I can view the cards, and an inability to look at anyones' graveyard even when it should have come up automatically to choose a card from it. I encountered both of these within my first couple hours of play.
Design wise, the best way to describe the UI is that every choice was made to make it look fancy and new happily at the cost of usability and ease of use. Pressing the start button when opening it has about a 3-5 second pause before the game reacts, with only about 1 second being the transition effect.
Another thing to mention is that the AI is absolutely terrible and in no noticeable way improves from the previous games even slightly. Ive had duels where the AI did not pick up on the fact that one of my creatures could become flying easily due to its own ability, and instead it attacked with its only flying creature, leaving it defenseless from the air at about 2 health left.
The only multiplayer options anymore are free for all 2-4 player, having removed 2v2 since 2014 and another gametype since 2013. 2v2 (which was called two headed giant) was the third most played gametype.
This game is still fun so its not a terrible buy, but beware that you are going to have to endure many annoyances and that this game feels like it needed 7 more months to finish, with missed features and bugs, both serious and minor, that are exceedingly common.

I really tried, but this game was unbelievably generic and stupid.  It was almost written and programmed with the target demographic of teenage boys and people who haven't played a decent shooter since the early 90's.
And perhaps that's just it - they attempted (and failed) to make a piece of video game nostalgia that gives a middle finger to the games that preceded it, as if it's doing something better by being simpler (and dumber).
Here's a Halo joke, here's some big-breasted women in private school uniforms, and here's a bunch of random set-pieces with moving targets to shoot.
The whole Duke Nukem Forever design timeline is a real shame.  I heard the developers kept scrapping each current project when a new game engine was released, rebuild for the new one only to do the same once a NEWER engine was announced.  This is really telling and goes back to my early point that these developers started working on this project during a simpler time in "shooter game design".  There was still an audience for ultra-violent, silly shooters that were devoid of puzzles, platforming or paid DLC.
Basically an "early 90's shooter ethos" mixed with an "updated" engine minus time/patience to polish off the jaggedly, crap-covered edges equals Duke Nukem Forever.
Rest in piece, Duke.  The king shall be hailed no more.

80 Days is a VN "choose your own adventure" style game, in which you are Jules Verne's valet in his attempt to get around the world in 80 Days, based on the novel of the same name. Its dripping in story, with references to various other novels such as journey to the centre of the earth. You are placed in a steampunk universe with gyrocopters and winged mechanical birds flying you around the globe. One playthrough the mysterious Black Rose may offer you a chance to run away, another you may solve a murder a la Agatha Christies Poirot. This is the highlight of the game, the writing is great, the choices are great, there is no real criticism of the writing, I had a lot of fun finding the different stories.
The graphics have a charm to them, on the main you will be looking at a map of the world, with the occasional picture of you flying in a blimp or talking to a train conductor. Its good without excelling. Lets be honest though, if you are buying this game for the graphics, you are buying the wrong game.
The gameplay slightly lets the game down, I found the appeal of buying and selling items wore thin, as did being locked out of certain routes after 5/6 playthroughs. In a game that is meant to be replayed, I thought the gameplay ran thin rather quickly. A "free mode" of sorts with unlimited money/health would have helped a great deal, also, I now hate Manilla.
Would I recommend this game? Yes, played in bursts its great, but its not something I could replay for days. I would advise playing it every few weeks to keep it fresh.

I felt like an updated review was needed. I've been looking at all of this negative feedback that BeamNG.Drive has recieved recently, and from what i can see, people aren't really understanding a few things.
First off on my reasons for liking this game so much, i played a previous game to this, called Rigs Of Rods. Rigs Of Rods (Or ROR for short) was a very dumbed down, barebones version of this game, and i very much enjoyed ROR as it ran perfectly on my previous very terrible PC so i was almost stuck to playing ROR, which gave me a long time to play the game, download thousands of mods and clock some huge hours in game. And for anyone who's played ROR, this is ROR, but everything that ROR needed, including a HUGE graphics overhaul, i mean seriously, the required specs of this game are no joke, it's simply beautiful for what it is.
Now, onto what others appear to be saying:
The first elephant in the room is:
IT'S NOT DONE YET. EARLY ACCESS MEANS
Theres still more coming to this game, so you can't unfairly leave a review saying "wasn't worth what i payed" as this game isn't done yet.
The second:
I've seen quite a few negative reviews surrounding this game just being about driving around and crashing into walls/objects. Reviews like this make me feel like the user hasn't actually explored all of the games options/settings, as there's scenarios to complete, maps to explore and even a story mode on Utah which i personally think is an awesome little thing in itself. To further back up my previous point, the mod base for Beam is HUGE. There's absolutely loads of different mod sites for Beam, which can add new aspects to the game.
Having over 400 hours in game which yes, before you say those are legit hours and i have played this game for a while now and through the updates the team are constantly adding new maps, cars, configurations and other things into the game which make things that little bit easier.
Heres the part which i guess many will be wanting to know:
Should i buy this?
BeamNG.Drive is NOT currently a finished game. So why would i be pushing you guys to buy this? Well, as of right now you won't get all the features in game, but what you will get is a beautifully textured and detailed engine with the best crash physics to date in any game that i have seen. I remember as a child playing Burnout Paradise on the Xbox 360 and remembering how awe-inspiring those crash physics were, and how you could actively see your car getting bent up/damaged and BeamNG.Drive puts that game to shame in the physics department. There's more to come yet, and i'm proud to say i've been backing this game since release and will continue playing this game for many years to come. The fact this also has full support for 900 Degree racing wheels such as the Logitech G920/G29 and the G27 and many other wheels is just fantastic.
Should you buy BeamNG.Drive?
(As long as you meet the required specs to play the game of course to prevent lag/ a ruined experience..) yes,   yes,  and YES.

So, this was recommended to me after enjoying the four parts of Peter Jackson's Sorcery!. However, unlike Sorcery! I did not enjoy this one as much. I am sure there is a plethora and depth to this game that I barely scratched with my 5 hours of playthrough, but I was not satisfied with the story telling or gameplay.
I went through one playthrough, made it 61 days through the north pole which I felt confident afterwards that may have been one of the easier runs perhaps since much of it was standing still waiting for something to happen with little decision or choices to make. There was some cool story telling at times, but the dialogue as an American player felt like I was trying to understand European culture or at least UK English to understand certain "ways of life." There were quite a few words that I never use or have rarely seen in my lifetime and I don't account that for a lack of education, but just not understanding the certain style of the European language used to make the game.
To top it off, right as I got to day 30ish and into the artic the game started to eat away at my CPU taking 98%-100% power at a time. Noteworthy, I never ran into the issue in any Sorcery! game and this is a 5k desktop computer; I run much more demanding games than this title. I tried to google a fix, but found nothing besides restarting; which I begrudging was worried that the game wouldn't save so I just slogged through it which probably added another 20-30 mins.
The difference I feel with Sorcery! and 80 Days is two things. The story telling and the mechanics. For the story telling it is lightly flavored text and only mixed with some small story based on where you travel; like the artic had a short arc as well as each city if you stayed there, but after all was said and done, that was it. You are here or traveling there for a bit and you move on to the next location; nothing felt meaningful. There were light dialogue options to choose from, but not all of them felt like they had weight; sure, some helped "us" live in the artic, but I think I could have easily done it without any item or any dialogue assistance. (Maybe the medicine was the only choice that was key for survival. Not sure though).
And the mechanics, like the story telling, is also very light. There are small interactions with inventory and money management, but I never used the bank once. I sold one item for about 8k and came back with 4k (and the 20k prize). I never felt short on cash. I also could never tell what the Figg/Fogg guy thought of me really. I tried to look for a stat screen but was unable to find one that incorporated it.
Overall, it’s a quick adventure and that’s it. I am sure there are optimal routes and other cool short stories to read, but Sorcery! was built on the foundation of Peter Jackson's novels. They only thing that Inkle had to do was to build a foundation of a game with playable mechanics that would match the novels. This game showed a difference in focus where half was for story and the other for mechanics. And it turns out to be a light adventure game set in a steam punk 1800s worlds. But this isn't the game for me and can't recommend the title like I can for Sorcery!

Basically a choose your own adventure type story. The 80 days target is mostly just a motivation - it probably takes more effort to "lose" than "win", although there's obviously a challenge in doing things as fast as possible and you can also challenge yourself on things like spending the least money. The interest entirely comes from the really fascinating setting and the stories that get told through it. There are so many different paths, cities, items, people, so many different ways to play through it. Because of the map there are a few "bottlenecks" that you're going to see most games but most of the game you have a ton of different choices. Random events and your own choices mean there's often new stories even in places you've been through multiple times before. There's the occassional annoyance (eg getting given items in events that don't fit in your luggage, iirc it means other stuff gets chucked) but it's best not to worry and just focus on the story, which is really well written and really gives a lot of room for your own interpretations and thinking through the implications of it without leaving things out or being mysterious. Really great game.

I picked this game up on a whim and have been pleasantly surprised at just how much fun I have been having with it.  I highly recommend this game, as it is fun.
Originally, my intent was to get some driving games to use my shiny new racing wheel and pedal accessory.  The steering wheel works well-enough in this game, but a controller is, honestly, a better fit, withthe exception that I still prefer to use my racing wheel and pedals on Time Trials.
I have never played any other Flatout titles, so I cannot compare, but I am not biased either.
I have come to view this game as a more realistic and more grown-up version of a certain Kart game that involves plumbers, anthropomorphic turtles, and gluttonous dinosaurs.
You race in your car through various tracks, complete cups, unlock further cups and higher difficulty levels, and there is even a mode that gives you various offensive tools you can use against your opponents, which I thoroughly enjoy.
The other racers are all distinct, and, after playing and racing against them a while, I have noticed that they have certain tendencies, which is pretty cool.  Some of them are focused on speed and being in front, and will usually compete with you heavily on the Fastest Lap Time, others are aggressive bulldozers and will do their best to knock you silly.  Some are insanely reckless, you will see them stomping their Nitro hard and then will, invariably, see them spinning through the air in a spectacular crash, while some are much more careful and you can actually learn from them by following them and seeing how they handle the trickier parts of the track.
The tracks are also fantastic!  There is not a hige number of them, but you will race them forward and backward.  While that may seem insignificant, it does make a great difference and will absolutely make it a completely new track for you.  Each track has varied paths throught it, some are the shortest, some are the least cluttered, and you must be quick to decide whether you want to take a shortcut and gamble on your driving abilities, or go to a path apart from other racers to build up some momentum.
The physics really impress me.  The crashes feel meaty and if you mess up and slam into the wall you will definitely feel it.  Hitting other cars is also satisfying, especially if it is the jerk that has constantly slammed into you on a previous run and caused you to go from first to tenth due to a spin out or slamming into the wall.  The different conditions require adjustment too, driving through mud on a rainy day is vastly different than driving it without the rain, which is where the different vehicles come into play.
There are quite a few vehicles to buy and upgrade in career mode.  You can have volkswagen beetle like buggies, pickup trucks, caddilacs, jeeps and others.  Each one has its own strengths and weaknesses.  The pickup truck is very good at taking punishment, has a decent top speed and is generally rather stable, however it is slow on acceleration and its inertia may work against you from time to time as you slam headfirst into a pile of rocks.  The Jeep is my nemesis, I appreciate that is it a very fast, stable, and overall great car, but it is tiny and overturns at a stiff breeze, it is definitely a car for a much more skilled driver than I.
There are many different game modes, from career, which will have you race, do destruction derby, and time trials, to Flatout Mode which assigns you a car and gives you a specific ruleset.  Either do a stunt, such as flinging your driver out the windshield into a baseball bat, or drive fast to try to prolong the inevitability of exploding, or Carnage mode which is a "race" technically, but you are gauged on how much chaos you cause to scenery and other drivers, with your position in the race serving only as a multiplier to your points.  Destroying a fence when first will get you many more points than when twelfth.
Overall, this game is amazing, I wish more was done by marketing to get the word out, because this game is incredibly fun.
p.S.  I cannot comment on multiplayer as I do not have much interest in it myself, but the prospect is an intriguing one and I will definitely give it a whirl one day.
UPDATE:  i have recently switched over to playing the game exclusively with steering wheel and pedals, and the experience is even better now.  I can confirm that this game works very well with a racing wheel and pedals.

The game features a career mode with car purchases and upgrades; third-place finishes in each cup (a series of races on specific tracks) is required to unlock the next set. The FlatOut mode includes a mix of non-traditional game modes, and quick play and multiplayer modes are also available. In addition to traditional races, FlatOut 4 features assault races (with powerups), carnage races (where you score is based on damage caused), a variety of physics-based stunts (including long jump, high jump, golf, and curling), and destruction derby arena modes (including capture the flag). Causing destruction will award nitro, which can be used for quick bursts of acceleration. It is sometimes difficult to tell what is considered a “solid” object and what is not (Telephone poles? Destructible. Trees? Not). The handling is a bit loose, and there is occasionally questionable physics when hitting objects, causing spins that result in poor finishes. The AI is good enough for an arcade racer, piloting through each track appropriately and being aggressive with human drivers and other AIs. While not approaching the high mark set by FlatOut 2, FlatOut 4 is certainly a competent arcade racer and successfully eliminates the odorous smell left by FlatOut 3.

Like most free-to-play games, Anno Online starts out at a brisk pace but after you have invested enough time to be interested in the game, it gets slower and slower - unless you spend money.  All "free" games have to make money somehow and walking that fine line between being frustrating enough to make you buy things and so frustrating you quit playing is the difference between success and failure.  This game can be played with no money at all, but only very slowly.
Fans of the game like to point out it doesn't require money because there is no "winning" the game and that's true.   It's a city builder and that genre doesn't usually involve competition.  But it's a very repetitive city builder that goes at a snail's pace.  The advice one hears most often in the game's chat is "patience".
Pros: the graphics are beautiful; the software doesn't crash; the chat and moderators are helpful and the first city on the first island is a lot of fun.
Cons: the game has lots of lag; only happy talk is allowed in chat; all the cities are just like the first city; the sea battles are repetitive and mechanical and endless; the trading ships are surprisingly underdeveloped - they goe A to B and that's it, plus, they have to be stopped and reprogrammed to make any change in cargo (takes half an hour); leaving the game unattended for a day invites disaster; the challenges are more inventory management than strategy.
I played for a long time and that should cause a "Yes" recommendation, but to be honest, after the first couple of days I kept on playing more out of stubborness than enjoyment.  In retrospect, I wish I had picked a different game.  BTW the game takes so long to open I usually leave it connected all day so the hours I've logged are not actual playing time.

If you pay the $35 for this game, you will be paying to skip content. Winning games to unlock boosters is the whole point of DotP, so buying the complete version basically means you've wasted not only the extra money over the basic version, but also the money for the basic version. All. Your. Money. Wasted.
The "pick a deck, but you're stuck with it" gimmick is bad design and the devs are bad for doing it. No preview of the decks, just a vague description that in my case was totally misleading. I chose Red->Black which was described as "focusing on stealing your opponent's creatures and sacrificing them for fun and profit". Yeah it was just a plain RB aggro deck with 2 Act of Treason and 2 vampires that could sacrifice creatures for a +1/+1 counter...in a 60-card deck. 4 cards does not a focus make.
But that bad design was merely irritating, not game-breaking. I could live with it.
The deck-building feature is good, it's about time that they added it. However, they didn't actually add it. They replaced all other features with it, for a net loss of game. Let's see what the trade off was for something that should have been a standard feature years ago:
No more Two-Headed Giant, either co-op vs AI or multiplayer.
No more Planechase multiplayer.
No Challenge puzzles.
No Sealed campaigns.
Is all that worth it? Hell no.
This is a blatant money-grab by Wizards, who clearly fear losing players from MTGO if they add too much actual gameplay here, which is completely stupid as the two games serve two different fanbases.
I have nothing but disgust for the design decisions of this game. Definitely do not recommend.

Magic 2015: Another entry in the "We know you want Cockatrice but we're not giving it to you" school of M:tG games.
Compared to 2014 (in my opinion, the best of them since 2012, still not saying much), the game is, overall, a complete step backwards with few exceptions. Near as I can figure, 2015 has a grand total of three positives going for it:
* The initial deck selection isn't bad. You pick your base color, and then a modifying color (yes, you basically do have to start with a 2-color deck, but you can get around that fairly quickly -- see below). The base/modifier colors do create different decks, even if you swap the order; for instance, I started out trying Black/Blue, and ended up finding the Blue/Black deck being closer to what I wanted. So you've actually got a pretty good range of selections from the current Standard lineup to build from.
* You CAN, actually, create a completely custom deck from your available card pool in 2015, which is a MASSIVE improvement. So, play through the campaign a bit, unlock some cards, and then build something resembling the deck you actually want to play.
* If you're really tacky, you can simply buy foil "stickers" to apply to your deck, 30 for $1. So for $2 you can have a whole-foil deck, land included. Normally I'd say this is ♥♥♥♥ing stupid, but considering they're digital cards, screw it, if you want your deck to be obnoxiously holographic, go nuts. It's cheap.
That being said, the negatives:
* Overlay/gameplay-wise, not much has changed since 2014. The actual gameplay is the exact same (taking a page from Madden here I think), but the menus have a fairly annoying "wipe" kind of effect when you click on something that doesn't initially show that your click actually registered. A pretty minor grievance, but a grievance nonetheless. Oh, and by the way, if you want to cycle which mana you tap, the button you're looking for is LCtrl -- which makes no sense, since otherwise everything is accomplished via mouse. Everything. Except for that one ♥♥♥♥ing button.
* Simple, small things that were in previous incarnations' campaign mode just aren't there. The small, gimmicky side-matches you could play either for the ♥♥♥♥ of it or to unlock more cards just aren't there anymore. I have no idea why -- it would take hardly any manpower for the devs to have included an "all-Plains-and-Suntail-Hawk" deck -- but they didn't. The little challenges like that, parallel to the campaign, helped spice it up a bit, especially if you're struggling against a certain deck. But, again, you can build a completely custom deck to handle it if you'd like, so I suppose that's a minor trade-off.
* Multiplayer is lacking in so many damn things, and this is really where the game ♥♥♥♥s up. All you can choose is how many players, 2-4, are in the match; no alternative rulesets like Two/Three-headed Giant are even options. This goes without saying, but if you were hoping Commander/EDH, or anything other than (basically) Standard would be available, you're screwed. Hope you like the 2015 set because that's pretty much all you get.
* Oh, did I mention the Sealed Play feature of 2014 seems to be completely gone? Granted, if you can make a complete custom deck, I'd rather do that, but in order to get the cards you want you have to truck through the campaign -- which is, needless to say, not the same thing at all.
Magic 2015 is, generally, a step back from 2014, in my opinion. Too little, too late, Wizards added in custom decks and stripped the hell out of other features many players enjoyed. If custom deckbuilding was all it would take, there's no reason for the DotP games to even exist -- M:tgO and Cockatrice both provide that. If you spent the time and/or money in 2014 to have a handful of solid decks, stick with it; 2015 simply isn't worth the money to migrate. If you haven't, meh, give it a shot if it's cheap. It'll probably be the last game of its sort since Wizards recently announced that they won't be publishing Core sets anymore and the Standard rotation will cycle about twice as fast in the actual card game now, so... it's probably time to just play other formats, honestly.
