So the game has changed dramatically and in theory the changes are good. They obliterted the model of premade decks with twenty unlockable cards. Instead they give you a gradually building pool of cards with which to make any number of decks you want to make. When I head about this plan, I was initially excited. I like flexability, and more practice for newer players building decks is always a good idea (the game is aimed at newer players.) The execution, however, was poor.
You initially pick one deck archetype to start the game with, and that deck is the deck you are stuck with. Which wouldn't necessarily be bad, if you could make an informed decision. But there isn't a deck list for any of the archetypes, which is just poor game design, and leads to regret if you don't like your deck two games in, like me, and wanted to change but found out that the only way to change decks was to build a brand new one. I espcially don't like this idea for new players as it can lead to a great deal of frustration if your deck matches poorly with another deck or challange, or if the new player is unsure how to perfectly utilize the cards.
Now one might think that this mistake was actually intentional. There are in game purchases for either booster packs which give you ten "premium" cards that you can use to bolster your underpowered deck, or you can purchse entire planes worth of cards and nab that "collection" of cards. DO NOT DO THAT. Premium boosters offer cards you can not otherwise attain, and I suppose that they would be helpful, but overall its not worth the admittedly small price of two dollars a pop. However buying a collection of cards means you are unable to unlock cards from that plane now. And that brings me to the fun part of the game.
As you progress, after the inital furstration of the deck being awful, you really feel like your deck grows because of your victories. This sense of improvement and accomplishment is nice, and brings back faded memories of grinding in Diablo for better loot, or for you younguns, Borderlands 2. As you can imagine, buying those cards kind of eliminates the fun of the game. It is interesting and nice to also build decks from your collection once it reaches a critical mass. But getting there is going to be a rough time. With the elimination of any of the more casual variants like Archnemesis and Planechase, once you collect the cards, the only real draw is competitive multiplayer, and that can be a bit... tiresome. Coming from a seasoned (more than fifteen years) player, the multiplayer in this just annoys me. Newer players will be scared away by people like me, and experienced players will find decks that they created feel underpowered and unfullfilling, as the concepts are generally halfbaked and under realized. Cards are artificially capped, with mythic rares taking up no more than one spot in the collection, rares only two, uncommons three, and commons are a full four. I can not understand why they would do that. There is no reason other than keeping those cards feeling special to new players to cap the quantities in that way. While it may make Mythics and rares feel cool and different, players will ultimately be annoyed that their decks can't rely on those cards to come through, as there is only one floating around. Experienced deck builders will carve our a spot or two for truly great cards, but newer players will either not use them, or be continually frustrated as they almost never draw those sweet cards to help them win, and they haven't learned how to build a fundementally sound deck yet.
And yet for all the problems, I like the game more then I think I should. It's a nice break from other games with a solitare like quality, where you can log on quick, play a few games and bolster your collection, get a nice boost of achievement, and go about your day. But it does not have the same kind pop to me that 2012 or 2013 had for me. Bringing back a casual multiplayer variant, or adding actual planeswalker cards would help immensenly. And for the love of God expand the collection. Its just stale at this point. I know the review is negative, but at a decent price point of twenty, its worth your time and will quietly entertain you. Magic, at the end of the day, is always going to be Magic, and that's awesome.

text:
An ambitious game with a well defined market. Recommended to any military enthusiast.
Scope and scale are both impressive. Maps measure in the hundreds of square kilometers, the paltry 4 maps (Apex DLC included) is slightly disappointing, but their sheer size compensates for this deficiency. Weapon customization and weapon choice is vast, the same applies to uniforms, vests and backpacks. Vehicle variety is not as great, but nonetheless extensive, with CAS, air superiority jets, utility and attack helicopters and VTOLs. MBTs (4) is however, disappointing.
Unrealistic and inauthentic elements do exist however. Vehicle behavior is odd, multi ton tanks are brought to a standstill by rocks and ditches. Aircraft performance characteristics are regrettable, departure from controlled flight arising from low air speed high AOA induced stalls feel too brief and recovery is obtained too early for the heavy CAS jets. There is a lack of sophistication in jet aircraft behavior. It is clear in-game physics are not refined, with the modelling of inertia and momentum being an afterthought. Tanks lack the full gamut of features they ought to possess. There is no integrated FCS with lead indicators for MBTs, MRAPs, APCs, and SPAAGs. Tank shell ballistics are also done very poorly. Firing of the main gun on an inclined surface affects shell flight path exaggeratedly, causing unrealistic levels of arc and deviation. The effects of APFSDS shells on lightly armored vehicles is poor. Some lightly armored APCs can resist what in reality is a multi megajoule shot. Tank damage models are also fairly armature, for example the carousel mounted ammunition of the T-100 when struck does not detonate, catastrophic kills are hit and miss. Tank components were clearly not laid out, and disabling of the engine which should inflict a mobility kill is not implemented. Engine destruction should cut power to the tank's electronics and turret, this is however, not the case. Explosive Reactive Armor (ERA) is also not modeled, which would be an excellent defense against shaped charged shells. Penetration mechanics are overly simplified, this is disappointing as the effects of composites and ERA on chemical energy warheads are disregarded completely. Radars aboard the air superiority jets of the ARMA 3 Jets DLC have their radars implemented unsatisfactorily. Radar aperture is fixed, the mechanical scanning of a PESA was not even a consideration, and the lack of Helmet Mounted Displays (HMDs) aboard advanced 5th Generation jets is incredibly eyebrow raising.
Infantry combat is well implemented, with weight considerations to weapons, equipment, and ammunition. Weapon sway varying across weapon weights is obvious, recoil feels significantly detrimental to firing, and fatigue is incorporated, requiring brief breathers between sprints for weapon stabilization. One small gripe being that there is a noticeable lack of scopes with sub milliradian divisions, but this is an insignificant criticism. Destruction of certain structures with large high explosive shells is possible, and penetration of surfaces with varying caliber performances at the small arms level is modeled. This is impressive, giving utility to rounds like the .50 BMG, 9.3cm x 64mm, and carving out niches for the .50 BW.
The game is not user friendly, appealing to consumers with strong interest in military simulation, available tutorials in game are lackluster at best, controls and key bindings require experiential learning and external tutorials, making beginnings difficult and frustrating.
Ultimately, though the flaws of the game are rampant, it is the harmonization of the combined approach of air, sea, and land made easily accessible to all, coupled with the fact that there is no direct competitor or substitute to ARMA 3, that make it a huge winner. The game is established in such a way that facilitates communication through an in-game voice chat, bolstering the social element and adding value to the game, enhancing consumer satisfaction. The creation of a militaristic atmosphere, with gargantuan maps and large scale conflicts, is unparalleled across the market.

This game is such a simple concept, but still entertains me when I return to it. Being an arcade style game, the story is nothing special, the character is bland, but it still has it's charms. The weapons feel like they have impact, and you can choose to run and gun, take out the enemies in front of you, or save time and ammo by running through the mobs awaiting you. Looting houses is fun, sorting out the things you need and the things you dont need, but why not be able to explore the house? It could be a bit boring if it wasn't done right, but it would be more entertaining than a blank menu, and all the zombies stopping dead in their tracks until you get out. It's a good game, but a flawed one. I like it, especially the fact that there is 2 player local co-op. I give it a 6/10. It's worth a try, especially if you feel like a good arcade game.

I thought -- I hoped -- that for $4 this might be worth it; it's not.
PREFACE: I had Duke Nukem, Duke Nukem 2, and Duke 3D with some of the expansions (and also Shadow Warrior, which used the same engine). I have more hours than I can count into playing Duke 3D and building tons of levels to share with friends. Had I money at that time, I would have been one who pre-ordered Duke Nukem Forever.
PROS:
Well, the voice actor sounds the part.
There are some neat mechanics that could have possibly been something (ego increases, etc.)
CONS:
Hitboxes are wonky, as is physics in general.
Enemies can shoot through solid (unbreakable) cover. For example, I got shot through a building or wall multiple times.
The controls are unweildy at times. When on the dukeburger level, I touched the conrner of a box and bounced at a diagnoal midway across the room to my death.
Speaking of death, some of the checkpoints (particulary where the controls are aweful,) aren't any good. Why not just let us save?
Several areas are just boring and repetitive. Stand here and shoot for several minutes.
Definitely moves away from the original in some of the worst ways.
The difficulty settings feel weird and untrue sometimes (caveat: limited experience with that).
EDIT: Forgot about getting stuck on terrain and invisible walls! Several times, I've jumped places only to find invisible walls causing me to miss or fall to my death. In the monster truck portions, they'll cause the truck to flip kicking you out and leaving you vulnerable.

Tormentum takes torture, darkness, nightmarish fiends, and makes them into beautiful art. The themes of Tormentum are something like Hellraiser mixed with Lord of the Rings. Massive dark castles and monsters are everywhere. The game itself is a grand example of how to do a point and click, adventure style game. Story is interwoven beautifully as you make your way through the dark corners and blood splattered hallways. All the scenes are visually striking but never aim to needlessly shock. Nonetheless you feel a bit off guard when roaming from room to room. Not knowing what lies in store for you. The music matches perfectly with the game as well. Along the way there is the usual amount of puzzles and item interaction one could expect. With obvious cues and signs of where items go usually. However the game does flow at a good pace. Never letting you rest or linger in an area for too long. Getting stuck or lost is rare but can occur. The game also throws many decisions your way. Some of the dark denizens either need your help or want to harm others. How you approach these tasks can alter the ending of your game. Adding a decent amount of replay. In all I had a really great fun time with Tormentum. The genre of Point & Click games is a little over-saturated. Making it difficult to capture my attention. Tormentum not only captured my attention but tortured my eyeballs! I couldn't look away and wanted to see more!

Very simple options with this one: Sliders for music and sound effects, and full-screen or not. In addition, there are nine languages to choose from.
If you play the demo, you'll find that the game seems to be more of a puzzle game than an adventure, with just a few screens and puzzles before moving on to the next area. This does NOT hold true for the rest of the game. You'll be locked out of some areas once you leave them, but there are plenty of locations to move about, puzzles to solve, and story to discover as you progress.
There are no hints, no skips, and no map. I did not have any trouble completing the game, nonetheless. Nothing I came across was frustratingly hard, and the only real problem I had was missing obvious things on the screen, like something I needed to interact with or an exit I simply didn't see. :p
Every screen scrolls left and right a bit, depending on where your cursor is. Although it would have been nice to just see the full scenes, some of the puzzles involve this scrolling mechanism, so I can't complain.
Speaking of the puzzles, be VERY CAREFUL when you are solving them, and really pay attention to what you're doing! Sometimes there is more than one way to solve a puzzle, and your actions really matter in this game. Your decisions count, so choose wisely.
The art style is dark and disturbing, but also beautifully done and very evocative. Combine this with the well-chosen music tracks, and you have a deeply environmental experience that will question your morals and life choices.
For the achievement hunters like myself, there are 34 achievements to obtain, which will require you to play through the game at least twice. I'm pretty sure most people won't mind going through a second time, as there are two endings!
There is a lot of bonus content to look at, which is not necessary to complete the game, but will enhance the experience. Some of these things will earn your achievements (such as reading all of the books,) so be aware of that.
While
is on the short side (around four hours for my first play-through,) the multiple endings and fascinating world which the devs have created make it absolutely worth owning. Definitely recommended, and I'm looking forward to OhNoo Studio's next game~! :D

This is what Tormentum starts with, a well known quotation from one of the most popular philosophers Germany has to offer. What defines human ethics? Is reason the source of morality? You should know by now that Tormentum neither answers this questions solely nor tries to do so, but stimulating the player’s mind with radical issues presented in gruesome but hand-painted actions and pictures instead of reading Kant’s essay might work better, at least for gamers. Your actions and decisions will affect your story, always leaving you behind with one question left. Did I make the
choice?
Introduction done. Don’t worry, this is not about philosophy, it is about
, a game that looks like our worst nightmares got caught and painted by H.R.Giger. Some of those bad dreams might even haunt you after the game is over but even then you just can’t stop looking at every small detail, whether it looks amusing, terrifying or violent. Speaking of terror and violence, we should take a look at Tormentum’s story. You are...well. Who are you? You are somebody,  yet no one. A poor creature wearing a capuchin, that gets imprisoned in an old, horrendous looking castle, threatened with torture and punishment for sins you cannot remember. Survival is your only thought and thus keeps your motivation alive even after having seen the suffering your new home has to offer. Prepare for morale choices that will not only affect yourself and keep that one thing in mind: Nobody is what they claims to be.
While Tormentum does look like a classic point-and-click at first sight, it uses some hidden object influences, mixes it up and combines them with classical puzzles and riddles. These are not unbeatable since you will find many clues but expect to be fairly challenged. May it be the right time on a watch, a certain melody that needs to be played or a man-eating worm that blocks your path, you will love the variety. There is no button for highlighting things, some objects have a unique glow instead whilst others can be hard to find sometimes. Additionally, objects can neither be combined in your inventory nor used for multiple actions. This may sounds simple but it fits the idea Tormentum wants to convey. The only time this really bothered me was early on after the start where you get confronted with many different scenes and tasks. If one link is missing in the chain you get stuck forever, running through the same backgrounds multiple times. These are eyecatchers even after passing them again and again, so do not lose  your confidence, there is a clue or hint for everything.
Before listing major points, I want to take a second look at the atmosphere Tormentum creates. I can’t talk enough about the graphics, or better, art OhNoo Studio created here. There won’t be many scenes you may find peaceful or cheering though, but would you really expect that to happen when a game is called Tormentum? You will witness pain, torture and suffering, everywhere. One can only imagine how a world would look like where evil lurks everywhere and redemption seems to be the only escape, but if this world really exists I fear it would look like Tormentum. Creepy People and Creatures, a dying land, epic but disgusting monuments, fire that rains from the sky, everything brought to life or death with hand-drawn masterpieces. Whoever created the soundtrack and effects should be awarded, too. My first impression was a bit monotonous but it quickly became the perfect skin for its cadaverous body. Emotions can be heard without even knowing what happens in the current scene.
Seeing this game getting Greenlit made me proud and happy since I backed it on Kickstarter myself, but when it got released the two of us couldn’t match. I am not a fan of Hidden Object games and playing the first couple of minutes I felt that this was not the game I expected. My opinion changed as you might have already guessed.
Once the story gets its hands on you, luring you with choices, challenging with puzzles, playing with morality and disturbing with violence, Tormentum starts to become more than just a piece of unforgettable sound, visuals and artwork. Staring at the screen for more than 5 minutes, pondering your next decision, you will ask yourself again: What is the right choice? Whether you know Kant or not, this will affect you.
Verdict: 8,5 / 10

80 Days feels like a mixture of a boardgame, a choose-your-own-adventure book and interactive fiction. It has atmosphere in spades, and a huge replayability value. It's not for the impatient, as there's a lot of reading to be done. It's not just an interactive story, however, as there is plenty of strategy involved: picking your route, managing your funds and inventory,  deciding what to do in each location and so on, and so on.
As in the Verne stories, Fogg makes a wager and attemps an around the world trip with Passepartout, his valet. There are a lot of added elements that make Verne's world into a steampunkish alternate reality dreamscape, that's occasionally hilarious and sometimes very dark. The writing is of very high quality, and even re-doing the same segments in multiple playthroughs doesn't feel like a chore, partially because there are multiple ways to deal with nearly everything.
The game also makes good use of Steam's achievement system. There are lots of achievements for finding various events found in the game, and dealing with them properly. It really helps keep the game alive, and getting 100% will keep one occupied for a long time.
80 Days is a masterpiece and a steal at this price (10€ at the time of writing).

80 days - To travel around the world, west to east from London to London. In what is a story based game about adventuring, route optimization, wondrous stories and relaxing rides through an alternate 1872 as the valet to a well known gentleman who has made a wager.
Along the way you will need to manage funding, items, packing, and selecting the routes to follow. It sounds simple, but it is complex enough to keep you busy.
To get it out of the way, yes, this is phone game. Do not let that scare you off, all it truly means for you as a PC gamer is that even your most outdated toaster can run it, the controls are simple and they do not need to be any more complex to do what you need to do. Game mechanics themselves do not suffer either, with a great majority of your options being simple choices in dialogue. Choices that actually do matter many times, with stories to tell you that I found surprisingly pleasant and interesting to read.
You can embark on an adventure and enjoy a richly filled world while balancing your own interest at exploration and your task as valet to keep monsieur Fogg in good condition and comfortable, on track to win his wager. It is not difficult to make it in 80 days if you try and plan things out in advance, but often there will be opportunities and potential rewards just a little off your chosen path. A lot of tempting things can drag you out to somewhere you didn't intend and it can both be a great boon to your funds and travel time or a disaster. With every city and most travel lines in the game having their own or connected stories, you will need multiple playthroughs to see them all. And even then it may not be likely unless you actively try.
Losing is alright as well. The wager won't bankrupt you, and you will be able to just try again. After all, why bet only once? A playthrough will take about an hour, perhaps a bit more or less depending on how much of a rush you are in.
But then there are some things that you should probably not get very hyped about either. Racing other people? Live multiplayer feed? Unless you actively go looking on the map for them, you likely won't find others except near the start. Even then, there is no interactions with them and I have yet to notice any sort of multiplayer feed. At best there are some icons on the map of where others went before you, and some things you aren't told and have to find out the hard way(Leaving a train at a midway stop when you have a ticket to the final destination of the train voids your ticket. You aren't allowed to get back on with the next train passing by. Some routes don't let you resume at all if you buy only a partway ticket, and so on)
The game is surprisingly easy to break as well, crashing or freezing if you try to do too much at once. A good autosave system helps with this, so you likely won't have issues- Just start it back up and you're back to where you were.
But in the end, these are small issues that don't actually hold it back.
80 days is a great game that tells you a story, while giving you full control over the story it tells, with excellently fitting graphics and amazingly done mood setting. Its flaws are few and easily forgivable, with a very competitive price to make it definitely a worthwhile buy.

BeamNG interview between me and myself.
Me: So how do you like BeamNG?
Myself: I love crashing cars!
Me: There are many games where you can smash cars. What makes this game so great?
Myself: Three words. Soft. Body. Physics.
Me: Soft body physics? Can you elaborate?
Myself: Realistic and unlimited vehicle body deformation. More than any game before it. Before BeamNG there was Rigs of Rods. Burnout 3: Takedown has the best vehicular damage in the Burnout series. But that game did not simulate every component of the vehicle. Carmagedon, Dirt, Grid, Flatout and Crashtime all have pretty amazing vehicle physics. BNG is just leaps and bounds ahead of everyone.
Me: Would you recommend the game, even in the early access state?
Myself: Absolutely yes! If your PC can handle it. This is probably the only thing holding the game back. The game is still a work in progress so at times the game runs great, other times not so much. There is a mod community already making vehicles for the game. These can be hit and miss as different versions of the game come out compatiblity changes. So if you find a car that just falls apart you might have to uninstall that mod. The developer content in the game is great so far. Constantly adding new vehicles, maps and scenarios to play. I just love to load up a map and play around with the many vehicle types. It's essentially a physics playground of vehiclular vehicle slaughter.
Me: Wow! that is a lot to take in. Hopefully this answered some questions for the community looking to buy.
Myself: Well if you want you can swing over to my profile page and check out some of the screenshots that I took in game.
Me: Great. I will. Thank you for our time.

Overall, the graphics are good. The textures, reflections, particles, bloom and subtle motion blur definitely work quite well together.
The UI is obviously built for a console, and even with that said could still use work. The mouse doesn't work on any of the menus, which kinda sucks, but isn't a huge deal to me. My main problem with the UI is the reward claiming. It goes through each individual reward separately, which makes you want to spam the button to continue. This can cause you to accidently start up another championship/race. It's quite frustrating.
I feel the AI in this game
need some work. It can be pretty inconsistant and unpredictable with you either leading by 30 seconds or losing by 30 seconds. The characters also seem to be pretty bland. One of the things I really liked about the Bugbear FlatOuts was that each AI had their own "personality." Each character had their own background and driving style, making them more memorable and allowing you to actually have rivalries with them (Yes, I'm talking about you Lei Bing and Jack Benton)
For the asking price of $33.99 (at the time of purchase (and yes, a friend did buy it for me)), the game really isn't worth it. The car list is pretty weak for current standards, there aren't many tracks and the campaign feels like too much of a grind. Hopefully the devs will release some free content updates in the future.
The vehicles really seem out of place is most cases. Their proportions seem off, as well as their overall style. The cars really don't look like they belong in the same class. The different classes are basically just the same cars with different modifications and slightly faster, and the extra speed doesn't mix well with the tracks or AI.
Oh boy, where to start. The people who worked on the tracks must have been completely cut off from the people who did the physics. The tracks are laid out pretty okay (some tracks could be better), but the physics
don't like them. Small bumps seem to be the hardest thing for the cars to handle, often ending in your car spinning out, flipping and bouncing off multiple walls. The wheels also seem to act like spheres rather than cylinders, causing your car to flip while randomly try to climb walls. Moving onto the stunt mode, the character ragdolls aren't, well, good. For example, I was playing the new Cup Pong mode and my ragdoll kept spazzing out and either bouncing out of the cup or just getting stuck in the side of it. The vehicle impacts also seem a bit buggy with small taps sending you from full HP to a sliver, making the derby modes really frustrating.
Performance is okay, but there are some pretty significant problems. The FPS holds up okay(ish) for most part, but there's a few hitches and a ton of stuttering no matter what visual settings are being used. With VSync off, the screen tearing is unbearable. But with it on, the FPS fluctuates all over the place, but is still surprisingly playable. There's also no other AA options except for FXAA which kinda sucks.
I had to make a separate "Neutral" section just for this. The way this game feels hits pretty close to home. It's trying to be a FlatOut game, but can't quite pull it off. To be clear, the game is free; payment only gives you access to two one-use-only-ever chests of resources which you don't need one bit. There are also a couple DLCs, but if you look at development/patch notes you realise the vanilla game is rich and you won't want to pay for the stupid DLCs even into late game (e.g. there's a SP-only dlc - for the incompetent only). Please read on.
3 races to choose from. Build your city, your army, your garrison, whatever labour forces you may want. Two very important factors that I find separate this game from those you may think this is similar to (involving MMO strategy games with building a settlement):
1) You can't be attacked when offline. If you're not logged in and playing, you can't be attacked - meaning you don't need to worry or dedicate ANY time to this game. (You also have a cancellable 24hr-game-time-only battle protection for noobs, after which you'll have a great base. Additionally, battles are always between similar-strength forces).
2) Your buildings can't be destroyed beyond 1% health. No conflict you will ever have will reset your city. Your buildings will be repaired over time and you'll just lose a token amount of resources, from what I understand you'll even get a few crowns (useful for upgrades or renaming units etc).
I recommend, if you have any interest in a forgiving MMO RTS game with visual battles and really quite rich content, you should download and try a couple of the races. Read the descriptions to see what you'd be interested in and have a go. Just be wise on how you spend your crowns in the beginning as they're earned through quests (story line), battles, daily-gift of 1 crown if you login and trading in gold. P.S. you will want to make gold one of your primary mining operations, because if you shop around at some NPC towns/cities, you can usually buy more than 100 of any resource with 100 gold.

Here's the deal: people are comparing this game to Doom or Boarderlands, but there's something huge missing from that analysis. Both Doom and BL2 are known for their excellent level design and composition, making for an experience that has pacing and balance. *Shadow Warrior lacks this in every way*
Though the game plays like a fast-paced gibb-fest, and moderately interesting loot is found aplenty, the somewhat proceedurally generated levels quickly come to feel just like something you need to get through in order to confront your objectives. The impulse to explore and discover dies away, the mind starts to notice reused templates throughout the levels, and battles seem to have no pacing or balance.
I was a big fan of SW1 and the old-school series. Unfortunately, this iteration falls far short of the bar its franchise has set. I feel a little bad giving such a harsh review of such a beloved series, and other aspects of the game do shine (weapons, upgrade system, enemy types), but level design is such a defining aspect of the overall experience that I just can't give the thumbs up.

First off: I really, really like the game. It's all cycling-lovers have and riding stages is a great experience. Unfortunately, that's where the fun ends.
Why I do not recommend the game:
1. Crashes, many other reviews already mention it, the game has been up for nearly a year and it still has the amount of crashes you would expect from a game in early beta. It is at an unacceptable level, such that I wonder if it's even responsible for steam to offer the game, as you're buying a flawed product.
2. The management part of the game lacks, the interface is clumsy to use, for example if you want to assign cyclists to a training camp you're unable to see the breakdown of the cyclists (which is very annoying if your starting a low level squad with many unknown cyclists). Generally there are just not many things you can influence from a manager's perspective on the long run.
Concluding: I love the concept of a cycling manager game, however the game is a faulty product which feels like it's in beta. This is unacceptable for such a long running series. Cyanide needs to step it up and make their game actually playable.

1. There really aren't a lot of cards to choose from. (Not really a bad thing in my opinion but it does limit your deck building options.)

I totally loved this game! It made me buy the Penumbra saga right after I finished this one. I'm really into horror games, having played since gems like the first Alone in the Dark, but few things have scared me as much as this game did. The story is also deep and original, finding a good balance between detail and mistery. You know there's a lot behind what you see, but you can only grasp a small part of it while you're playing. Which, in my opinion, helps you get into the plot and the mind of the main character.
Best thing about this game for me, something that shares with the second installment of Penumbra, is the fact that you simply can't fight back. You are defenseless against the monsters. And that, compared with usual games where you simply fill their putrid bodies with lead, makes this one actually scary. I lost count of the times I stood hiding behind something, holding my breath and hoping for the enemy to just leave the damned room...
There's maybe something that could make a player feel less scared, though I didn't notice it in my first run. You can just run forward crashing into all the monsters and, well, yes, they are ugly and they kill you and... then you re-spawn nearby and keep going. And the monster is usually gone for good. So I guess some players may find that silly and feel less opressed during the game.
Anyway, here are my general thoughts:
Pros
+ Great and scary atmosphere
+ Amazing storyline
+ Nice level of difficulty, not challenging for pro-gamers I guess, but will make casual players enjoy
+ Decent graphics and cool physics
+ Nice music, with helps creating the atmosphere
+ Did I say it's scary as hell?
Cons
- Monsters just knock you down and leave you unconscious, then go party elsewhere
- Not really long, but with more than enough content in my opinion
- Mostly straight-forward, don't expect an open world
- You may suffer a heart attack

This is an interesting specimen. Sure, zombie games are dime-a-dozen at this point and at first glance this'd seem like a side-scrolling ripoff of any other modern zombie survival game like DayZ or Left 4 Dead. It's rather different. It blends certain RPG elements with a myriad of weapons and a beat-em-up map layout.
The object of the game is to cross several streets littered with the walking dead in order to reach the survivors after a zombie epidemic plagues the city. Along the way you can loot buildings, trade supplies and save at shops, and, of course, kill the undead. The enemy variety is neat too. You get several different classes of zombies with different amounts of health, damage outputs, and attack styles. For the most part you get ones that walk towards you and attack. Eventually you reach spitter-like enemies that fire green globs. Considering each direct hit takes away 20 hitpoints (You start out with 200), I'd suggest dodging those. You also have a couple zombie bosses.
Overall it's a fun game to burn time on. You have different gamemodes and if you have friends around you can join up on LAN and fight zombies together. Although online capability would really be the best over anything. So, if you have a few dollars to spend, I'd recommend picking this little gem up.

By raising $11,000 on Indiegogo, Tormentum: Dark Sorrow proves that point and click adventure games still have an audience. And at first glance, it's easy to see why: not only did OhNoo Studio create a hellishly beautiful game, they lowered the puzzle difficulty so as to appeal to a larger audience.
Speaking of puzzles, let's talk about game design. In Tormentum, players do not control their avatar directly; instead, they click left, right, up or down in order to progress through a series of moderately interactive screens. As to the puzzles themselves, they appear in two forms. The first requires players search for a particular object, such as a bone to appease a hungry animal or a key to unlock a prison cell. Secondly, Tormentum is filled with mini-games. These mini games often possess puzzle elements—for example, adjusting a set of gears to open a door—but not always.
Experienced point and click adventure fans may have noticed that I didn't mention item combinations. That's because there aren't any. OhNoo Studio ditches item combinations in order to lower their game's difficulty while providing a minimalistic inventory system. Does this decision pay off? In the end, I have to say no. The puzzle design in Tormentum never strays too far from easy, and genre veterans will breeze through this game.
That said, easy puzzles shouldn't distract from the game's biggest triumph: tone. All of the art in Tormentum is hand-drawn and disturbingly ghoulish, with many monsters seemingly torn from the pages of a H.P. Lovecraft novel. The world alternates between horrible, bleak, and ravaged. No one finds goodness in Tormentum, a sentiment echoed by the game's ominous and occasionally plaintive soundtrack.
With decent gameplay and strong art, I'd consider recommending Tormentum were it not for the game's terrible story. OhNoo Studio bundles two video game clichés with a vague plot and obvious morality system. Amnesiac protagonist? Check. Absolving murderers good and killing innocents bad? Check. The nail in the coffin is the game's English translation: though Tormentum is more or less devoid of blatant errors, several awkward phrases took me out of the story.
When I think of Tormentum, I think of missed opportunity. What if this game had put a price on being good, encouraging the player to make the evil choice instead? What if the developers had fleshed out the plot? While Tormentum: Dark Sorrow could have left me contemplating life, OhNoo Studio settled for style over substance. This point and click adventure will have its fans, but don't count me among them.
FINAL SCORE: 5.8/10

This is a great game with stacks of depth that I would wholeheartedly recommend... If I could get it to work on Windows 10.  Unfortunately I just get a black screen every time and none of the fixes that worked with Win 8.1 seem to help.
As a bargain bin hunter I didn't expect much from a $5 game, but I was very very surprised.  Unfortunately this was all in the days before I acquired Steam (Before Steam?  BS?  Probably not a good acronym) but I'd probably estimate that I easily played over 1000 hours of this game, because it generally followed the trend of how much I played AOE2.
Pros:
Trading is very fun.  Trading is also a completely valid way to play the game - don't wanna fight?  You don't have to!
Some challenging scenarios and ways to play.  Playing as a pirate is a real challenge in this game, as literally everyone will try to sink you, but you're also trying to steal as many ships as possible.
Variety of missions.  I never did find all the artifacts to get me that steam ship (mainly cause I kept deciding to become a pirate)
Operating businesses and towns.  Building your own town is a real labour of love, as you have to make it viable - trade ships won't visit you unless you have goods to offer at a competitive price.
Smashing the French, sinking this ships and stealing their towns.  But seriously, the French have the worst ships.  Capturing towns is also a fun challenge, as you have to defeat the nation's military presence/fleet to a certain point before you can capture a town, and once you capture a town the logical consequence happens - that nation increases their military presence again, so you can't just go around easily capturing towns.  In my opinion, it is a challenging but rewarding experience, and there's nothing better than reducing an enemies' territory to one measley town.
Cons:
Grinding.  Ooh baby, there's plenty of grinding.  Take two horny teenagers, put them in a flour mill in hell where there is much gnashing of teeth, and you still don't get close to how much grinding this game can involve.
Learning curve is steep at first.  Trading is pretty easy but you don't start with much, so you have to take on missions to towns you haven't discovered yet, which might just get you sunk by pirates or military convoys if you're not in every nation's good books.
Combat is alright.  This probably isn't a con, but it's pretty easy pretty quickly.  You'll be able to take on a military convoy with 5 Ship-of-the-Line's with one military corvette because you're a bit more nimble.  AI will always use chain shot and try to board you no matter what.  The duels with enemy captains are fun the first time but a joke after that.
All in all, great game, and I'll never stop trying to get it to work on Win 10.

Visually it's H.R. Giger meets 80's Metal Covers - Rad! It's not really a "normal" Adventure but rather a puzzler. Your character doesn't walk around and there's not too much to interact with and there isn't really any dialogue choice. Instead you move the mouse around seeing whats there in the scenes and hunt for the items to solve puzzles at every corner to advance while looking at the insanely pretty scenery. Usually I'm not into that type of game, but the quality and way how the world was drawn and the resulting atmosphere hit a nerve that made it very interesting to me and I welcomed the change in gameplay. The puzzles start easy and get progressively harder, but you probably don't need a walkthrough unless you get impatient at one or two confusing spots. It does have two endings, but despite that replayability for me is not very high since it's pretty linear with not much to do. I enjoyed my time in this dark and twisted world nevertheless and all my desktop wallpapers are from this game right now :D
If I do want to play it again though, notes to myself: Don't become a serial killer again, as much as you hate it let people live. And save the girl.

I was excited for a prospect of an actually decent new Flatout, but "decent" the most you can describe it as.
It's worse than Flatout 2 and Ultimate Carnage in just about every aspect. In most it's only
worse, it's no Flatout 3, but "better than Flatout 3" is a hell of a low bar to clear. It feels like Flatout Lite – there is a sense that they tried to recreate the old ones, but it lacks their best and most fun aspects and moments.
The driving is, put quite simply, not fun. The crashes lack any punch. I notice an opponent in front of me spin out and get sideways, nitro into him at full speed, and for that effort I'm rewarded with a
which the game is happy to tell me was a "great slam". It actually felt like my car slowed down before the impact, as if to avoid the collision like I was playing full-assist mode in a circuit racer.
The cars basically have three control types. All Derbies are understeering bricks, all Classics are spin-happy nitro machines, all Ultimates (or whatever the third one is) are 6x6 offroaders. None of the classes have any variety in character.
Speaking of character, the cast of 7 (FO2) / 11 (FOUC) fun and varied opponents with actually different AI parameters have been replaced with two facial models caked in various forms of makeup, who drive exactly the same. Did they honestly think we wouldn't notice? Not that FO2/UC's opponents were some kind of RPG-esque well-written characters (they had a car set, a paragraph of bio, a "photo", a color scheme and some AI parameters tweaked), but this game manages to avoid even that.
The Assault mode, which is essentially the only addition to this compared to FOUC, feels like a better fit in a kart game and has been better done in several of them.
The music, after FO2 which basically defined my tastes for next 5 years and FOUC which, while not as impactful, still added a few bands to my notice list, is uninspired and lame. Most of the songs are in the genre of what I'd only call "whine rock".
Even the graphics, which you'd think would be the one area where it's stupidly easy to improve after
are worse. Not from the technical standpoint, they've got the fancy reflections and godrays and whatever from the latest set, but it looks straight up worse because the environments are grey, the cars look dull, and the details are low-effort.
Worst of all, this game gets
. The races quickly become a grind. The stunts are a snorefest. (Seriously, how do you make flinging yourself into a Beer Pong cup uninteresting?) The derby is a succession of lame-feeling hits and watching the health bar go down.
Maybe, if it was the only game in its genre, I'd be okay with it, as it has occasional cool moments and is, at the very least, competently made (as opposed to Flatout 3). But seeing as Flatout Ultimate Carnage is right nearby on Steam and
, there's just no point in buying this game.

So I bought this game on a whim because a friend of mine ask me to buy it too, and I did, and I did not regret.
Beforehand, I read all the review that is people deemed most helpful, saw that it got a lot of bugs here and there, unplayable graphics, etc. And you know what? The first time I ran it on my laptop, it got shutdown my laptop right away when I'm loading the world from some server. Disappointed? Very. I could run Fallout 4 on my laptop albeit getting 20-28 fps so I wonder why can't I run this game? Simple, the optimization at release is quite poor. So I did what a someone with a brain will do, play it on my PC. And thankfully, it run greatly.
No gamebreaking graphic bug encountered, which seems to be the main complain of most reviews here, no crash at all from all of my time playing this game, and I can play this game flawlessly albeit it does hit 22 fps in dense forest.
So we have that out of the way, now what will you expect by buying this game? Firstly, one thing that you can expect is poor optimization, yes I admit the graphic is quite heavy even for my spec which could run witcher 60 fps with high 1080p setting, and fallout 4 flawlessly too. But it's understandable since almost everything can be interacted with, so the game is heavy because of that. And no, if you compare it to fallout 4, that game is still light in building things since you didn't interact with most of the game, just place things on the ground, while in LiFYO, YOU CAN TERRAFORM THE TERRAIN, my suspicion is that the game is heavy because of this, but let's leave it at that. So, heed that recommended spec before you buy it, does your computer spec meet or above the requirement? If yes, you don't have to worry a thing (possibly), if no, buy it at your own risk. Luckily though, the dev is quite fast on implementing fast hotfixes.
Secondly, this is not a simple survival building crafting game, where all you need to do is know the recipe, have the material and then voila, it appears. Nope, you need to LEARN HOW TO DO IT FIRST. It got a complex skill tree where there're a few skill you need to learn first before you get to the skill you needed. Tedious? Very. Boring? Not so. Which is why having a group or making friends in-game is very valuable. You don't need to be a jack of all trades, you just need to focus on what you want to be, and ask for help for something that is outside your capability. You could learn how to do it, but it will take a lot of time, and don't forget about that skill you want too, it takes time too.
Wiki and youtube is your friend, seriously. They might be outdated but they are still relevant as much since it's still the same. The only problem I had with the wiki is, it's not very complete as I checked it a few days ago, some detailed bits are missing but the general explanation should suffice, if not, check the youtube, there's a lot of let's play and tutorial for life is feudal.
Third, The UI in this game is simple enough. There's status bar, hotkey bar, general info, chat panel, etc. You can customize their position too with F10. Also the cursor and the movement mode can be switched with tab. Like the name imply, cursor mode is used to navigate to panels, while movement mode is used for camera while moving and interacting with the world. The interaction follows Ultima/Wurm online. Whereas right click to something brings up the context menu, and it doesn't take too long to familiarize with this system. Right click on the ground and it shows a square tile which show how big the area will be affected by terraforming or what we can do with that area. It's not everything has their keybinds, but each things have their context menu, and you can set the default action to do something to the left click, so all you need to do is point something and then left click.
Lastly, this game emphasis on player to player interaction, so roleplaying is what it is in this game. You want to roleplay a blacksmith? Go ahead, level up your blacksmith skill, then advertise your service to some guilds or tribes you found. If you're lucky, they'll accept you as their own or you get tricked or worse you could be killed right away, the choices is theirs to make.  I warn you there's no human NPC in this game, only animals and such, so there will be a lot of human interaction.
tl;dr
great game, very VERY time consuming, you have been warned,
not for someone who wants a quick/easy/simple/straight jump to the action-ish game,
needs time to learn the mechanic and enjoys the game,
if you're familiar with ultima online/wurm online or the like of it, you'll feel very nostalgic,
lots and lots of player to player interaction,
heed the recommended spec,
no gamebreaking bug which I encountered so far,
buy it if you like it and it's at your own risks

It's hard to describe really what's so great about this game. But no other shooter really communicates the idea of fear for their life to the player like this one. One peak can mean the difference between life and death. You could be coming across an enemy force that will have you dead before you even know they exist. Swift and sudden death can come at any moment, which really makes you have to commit to your decisions on the ground.
PROS
Singleplayer gameplay is fun, but short. However, joining a multiplayer group or clan is really where this game begins. I play this game for the military-simulation aspects, so I can't comment on the Altis Life and Epoch versions of this game.
Operating on such an in-depth tactical level with your team, is one of the most rewarding things I have experienced in video gaming. It's not that you can't do it in other games, but even in Battlefield, things are moving so fast that the game doesn't really allow the time for tactical decision making like Arma 3.
CONS
Optimization is not terrific, but can be quite tolerable with upgraded hardware and tweaking in the settings. Although, I have seen this range drastically from person to person.
There is a steep learning curve, and finding the right people to play with can be tough. In my group alone, it takes about 3-4 people per person to get a new, solid member of the team.
SCORE
9/10. Optimization is not great, but the gameplay is so intoxicating that I actually forget about my frame rate.

Flatout 4.... it's not bad, but it's not great either.
As someone who still plays Flatout 2 somewhat regularly, my biggest gripe with the fourth installment in the series is that it's just too arcadey. "But it's an arcade racer! It's supposed to be!" I know. Let me elaborate.
Flatout 1 and 2 were by no means simulation racers or even simcade racers (think GRID). But at their core, they were still grounded in reality (save for the driver ejection mechanic). The races were simply races. The cars weren't crazy or silly and they all made sense within their class. Derby cars were mostly used/junked race class cars, and the street cars were mostly just normal sports cars. In FO4, you find yourself racing:
- An icecream truck
- A modern sports car
- A 50's sedan
among others, all within the Derby class. Sure they're junkers, but the wildly varying styles racing together leaves a bad taste in my mouth.
Adding to FO4's silliness is the customizable nitro trail including confetti, bubbles, and money. This is completely optional but it feels more at home in Rocket League than Flatout. Additionally, FO4 features a car combat game mode that involves magically shooting oversized projectiles at other racers. Fun, but not really what I've come to expect from Flatout.
However, the game is gorgeous. The driving mechanics are really solid (the crashes feel a little lame this time around though). And I really like the environment/track design.
I wanted Flatout, but got the love child of Dirt: Showdown and Mario Kart.

80 Days presents a simple but unique premise for a game: to make an interactive variant of Jules Vernes' "Around the World in Eighty Days".
Players take on the role of Passerpartout, assuming his roles of planning out each leg of the journey, managing finances, and making sure that Master Fogg is in good spirits. Choices are a crucial part of the gameplay, as the player's actions not only effect the immediate consequences, but also add up across their journey as a whole, making no two playthroughs exactly the same. This alone adds a great deal of replay value, but the large amounts of text and minimal graphics might not appeal to everyone, and some may only be satisfied just finishing the game once.
I quite enjoyed making many trips around the world in this game, but truthfully, I can only seriously recommend it to those with interests in geography or classical literature.
FINAL GRADE: B+

The Read-A-Game genre is already too full. This is a fact in evidence. That being said, this game is good enough to push a whole shelf of Hatoful Boyfriends and Cinderses into a circular file for. Subtle to the point of obtuseness, its core purpose hides like a cat, leaping out to swat at you and leaping back in before you can really get a handle on it. To fully understand the setting's meaning and your place within it, or even the full breadth of your own character, you'll be many playthroughs in, but to simply have wonders to gape at a few hours will give plenty to see.
One thing worth noting, though, is that actually winning the wager is meaninglessly easy. The only way to lose is to intentionally wander off; any course that points vaguely eastward will get you there in 70 days or less. There is no challenge to be had whatsoever unless you go for the 50- and 60-day achievements, and those who come in looking for a game about finding a way to get Around the World In, say, 80 Days will find themselves disappointed.

Hello! Let me start by saying this. I wanted a game that I could command large masses of troops to attack strongholds. After searching EVERYWHERE I found this. This game exactly fit my needs! Now I am going to let aside my desire for games like this for the rest of the review to keep it biased.
Ive been playing this game for about 80 hours now and I fell in love! I only have one friend that plays this so we usually attack together. The game is way more fun with friends! Now on to the things I need to explain.
First if you don't care for the tutorials provided at the main menu you WILL be lost completely! I rushed straight to the game and couldnt figure out anything. Please Please do them. Next the Global chat and Disscusion page are needed! The in-game help is very minimal and you will have a lot of questions. Next this game has a lot of bugs!
Now a lot of people say this game sucks because it crashes all the time and has slow battles. Do not believe them all. I can run this game at lowest graphics 50fps on my 3gb ram 1.2ghz laptop! When fighting large masses of people it is true that the frame rate drops. For me prop to about 3 or 4fps, I dont really care though because it picks back up after a few seconds.  Now on to the pros and cons.
Pros:
1. Awesome Gameplay and Idea
2. Great Potential
3. Friendly Community
4. Great graphics as a whole
5. Good money system
6. Very complex and soooo much to do

Cons:

2. Bugs
3. Lack of tutorials and guides
4. Not very easy for new players to begin (goes with con 3)
5. On my bad laptop takes around 10 to get the game loaded to my city (Again my laptop is bad)

Finally my over view
This game has grown a top from "Dawn of Fantasy" with new updates and bug fixes. I really enjoy this game and wish it does good in the future. I can spend hours a day on this game seiging new cities and taking territory. You can also do online coop quests with random people is you feel like it. It is Massively multiplayer and PvP! For those who NOT RECOMMEND Nether, either you are some frustrated WarZ players or you haven't played enough of the game.
People complain that you die easily for players that have full gear, but since I can remember this happens with EVERY scavenging-survival games. There WILL be good players who will help you with supplies or even guns, and there will be players who will kill you on sight. It's part of the game, and that's what makes you feel afraid of dying and losing hours of looting and leveling, but as I said, It's PART OF THE GAME.
Here are some features that make Nether a great choice between WarZ and DayZ:
1- Immersive Gameplay: No, I'm not talking about some creepy and badly-placed ambience sounds. Nether will make you feel literaly inside the game. It's atmosphere will make you♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants when it's nighttime and you hear a Nether (monster) nearby, or when you hear shots from the distance without knowing if it's a guy killing Nethers to survive or hunting down other players.
2- Easy loot, easy life: I'm not sure if the spawn-points for the items are all pre-determined and will never rotate or something, but It's easy to find items like Pistols, food and bandages. Within 30 minutes I was able to find a Shotgun, Mini-Uzi and tons of supplies. Of course, it depends on your luck, purely, but it's not like you'll walk a thousand miles without finding a single can of food.
3- They're NOT Zombies: I like zombies. Everyone likes zombies. But in a world that survival games are all pre-determined by zombies, Nether innovated with these new creatures that not only make the game different, but enables the devs to explore a new level of map design. The Nethers (monsters) can teleport to where you are (IF they spot you), so you'll not be able to run if a Nether spot you, but there are nearly no monsters on the streets if you compare it to DayZ or WarZ. So it's like this, if you can stealth, you'll be fine, if you've been spotted, you have to kill them silently, otherwise you'll alert other Nethers and cause a chain-reaction.
4- Urban Environment: It's purely a city. There is no jungle or giant forests. The map it's huge enough tho. Since it's Alpha, the map is limited, but the amount of details that you can find in this game is remarkable, and you can notice the details on the very first time you jump into the game. There are underground subway stations that you can explore if you have enough courage. And EVERY street is different. It's not a bunch of copyed buildings and houses and blocks, you will rarely feel like you're lost because every street is different.
5- Buildings with levels: Since Nethers can teleport, they will be on rooftops and they WILL chase you even if you enter or climb a building. There are many buildings that you can enter and get on higher levels, but nothing unfair like multiples multi-level building with multiples windows that will make you get hit by a sniper without even knowing where he is (it happens sometimes tho).
6- GORGEOUS graphics: Unreal 3 does NOT disappoint with the graphics, and even tho you can notice some flickering when walking above some objects or climbing a staircase, the beauty and details make it worth the play.
7- Player leveling: You earn levels when you kill Nethers and players, and the skill-tree is actually VERY useful. You upgrade your melee and you can block an attack, upgrade it again and will increase your damage and decrease your stamina use when swinging your weapon. You NEED to upgrade your character. If you're level 1 and find a Sniper Rifle, you'll not be able to shoot a thing since your aim will be extremely shaky and unstable. You can level up to lvl 20 (I think), but if you die you'll spawn level 1 again.
8- In-game Market: If you kill monsters they're likely to drop certain itens (I guess) and money (I guess too) that you can use to sell and buy things on the Safe-Zone. You also can store things on your safe-zone so if you die you can retrieve it later if you wish. You can buy guns and ammo and food too. I'm not really sure about in-game transactions, but they say it on the website that there are not. But actually there are, but I'm not sure if it's only because it's Alpha or if they will make it permanently. I totally disagree with these micro-transactions tho.
9- Missions: You can grab a package and deliver it to another safe-zone in exchange for money and exp, and if you're lucky enough, you'll find tons of items during your trip to the destined area. Nether-Surges happens too, wich is like a massive Nether-spawn in a random area of the map, so look out when this happens. The Safe-zone can also be attacked by Nethers, and you need to cooperate with players to restore the "nether-shield" and make the Safe-Zone secured again. So it's not like you'll jump into the game, grab some guns and kill people, you have some objectives that you can do, if and whenever you want.
10- It's Alpha! : The game is not even finished, and you can notice the amount of details that the Devs are pouring into this game. They also HEAR the feedback from the community and improve/add features as people play and give them their opinion.
So, if you still think Nether is NOT worth playing, I suggest you to gather some friends and play it together as a Team. Of course, if you play it alone it will be boring sometimes, and if you get killed you'll be really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥because you lose EVERYTHING you have, but hey, It's part of the game, and that's what makes it really fun and immersive.

After my problems at the release of the game (The game didn't launch the whole launch day and i only got it fixed the day after) I have been enjoying the game a lot.
If you are a cycling enthousiast looking for a game to play of the sport you love, then this might just be your game. For other spports fans, i'm not so sure. The game is very complicated in some aspects, and can often seem quite confusing for people not watching real life cycling.
The game is enjoyable and has a large learning curve. There is a high ceiling for skill level, as the possibilities of strategies are ENDLESS. This can also been as one of the biggest weaknesses of this game though. Because this game can be very confusing and complicated for some people, it can draw people away from playing this game. Most of all people that have no clue what they are doing. (Attacking with their riders from the start and such).
Overall this new edition of the pro cycling manager series has seen minor but great improvements.
Would i recommend it to people who have never bought a PCM game? Yes.
Would i recommend it to people who bought PCM15? Not as much.
There are only minor improvements to the gameplay (New hud design, which is amazing btw, small improvements to career and pro cyclist), as the biggest change was the overhaul in the online mode.
Would i recommend the game to people who skipped PCM15? Yes.
The new pro cyclist mode has been improved, and as for that the game can be a total bombshell of new experiences.
So to conclude, i would recommend this game, but only if you know what you are doing and what you need to do in the game.

The Duels of the Plainswalkers (DotP) series has always been my secret pleasure since I stopped playing Magic the Gathering in high school. It had simplified one on one duels, challenges that were a nice and fun extra if you wanted something to work your brain and learn new strategies for Magic, a Bonus mode like archmage or plainschase that added even more depth to single and multilayer matches, and plenty of decks to use with over hundreds of cards. The series has also had the mode made DotP series extremely popular Two-Headed giant which is two vs two action that could become extremely strategic and to be great at the mode required communication between teammates which was a great addition to the Plainswalker series.
The campaign mode in 2015 is dull and can be very frustrating if you didn’t purchase cards packs which to mention compared to previous editions of the DotP series, to unlock all the cards without grinding is expensive and purchasing the complete package doesn't give you all the cards, there are still premium boosters to purchase for two bucks a pop. You are stuck using one deck until you have unlocked enough cards to make a second deck. The story has never been a main point to the series which is why there has never been a good one. They don't matter, it has always been about the gameplay.
DotP 2015 takes away everything we loved in the series, challenges, two-headed giant mode, a bonus mode to mix things up and gives us the ability to customize decks and a large variety of the cards. The issue is the menu's are the worst they have ever been, you get kicked out of a room after you have played a game online and you can't change your decks in a room forcing constant inviting the same person over and over if you're playing with a friend or want a rematch. Over time the process becomes unbearable that you will prefer one of the previous entries in the series compared to this one.
The ability to create a deck is stunted by one thing, you will always see the same builds over and over with slight differences. This is due to the fact that most of the good cards in a color are very few so more players are more likely to use them and cards that combo with them in order to win more games.
Magic 2015 is just a spit in the face to fans of the series, it asks for more money f you don't want to spend hours upon hours grinding and be able to compete in the online competitive multiplayer than any digital Magic game in the series. The menu system might as well be the challenge mode considering that it is the most clunky and unresponsive menu ever. The multiplayer aspect has been ruined by not being able to play two-headed giant or have constant friendly re-matches without getting kicked out of the room. The only pro about this game is that it's Magic and Magic is an excellent card game and has always been.

Amazing game, I'm surprised at all the downvotes but I realize I shouldn't be. Most of these people have only 2 or 3 hours played and have no idea wha they are talking about.

This game's multiplayer is brutal and unforgiving. If you lose its because you were outplayed. Most people believe they are way better at video games then they actually are. They will load this game, pick a character, not practice againts bots at all or memorize even the most minimal part of there move set, and then jump straight into multiplayer. Then they will charge into a losing fight and get rolled when there button mashing spray and pray is easily countered by the most basic block/dodge/parry playstyile known by most who have put in an ounce of effort.
This is the turning point for most gamers. See its alot easier to say ''this game sucks'' ''I lost because of lag'' ''Characters are unbalanced'' than it is to say ''I got rekt because this player was better at that aspect of the fight then I was, I will need to work on and improve that''. These people have this insane delusional mindset that they are the master of all games now and for ever and can make no mistakes, so if they lose its because of broken mechanics. Yes it can be very frustrating, I've had to restrain my inner child from chucking the mouse across the room several times. However once I cool down I get a feeling of genuine happiness because it has been a really long time since a game caused me to become emotional, and that tells me there is someting special here.
Are there problems? absolutely, every game has problems. Is there a meta built around counters? maybe, I'm not good enough at this point to know, and the vast majority of people I have played against are not either. I'm not saying this game is perfect, there is no perfect AAA title. What I am saying is that this game is a breath of fresh air in a gaming generation that has a building model of ''sell the player of a big flashy cinimatic experience, hand hold the player though non challenging gameplay so that he feels he is good at games, player is good, game is good. Player gets on average 8 - 12 hours of gameplay to finish the story and do some of the side points until eventually moving onto the next flashy title, rinse and repeat''. Ubisoft is one of the star catalyst for this buisness model.
I'm not one to write reviews, and never ones that are so ranty. However I really like this game and feel it could really be something great once Ubi fine tunes some things and the hype crowd moves on to the next distraction. If your looking for some really visceral melee combat with a refreshing (Not revolutionary, but refreshing) combat system, and like a game that challenges you and gives you something to sink your teeth into, you won't want to miss out on this.

The 'Duels of the Planeswalkers' series of games have been declining in quality in recent years, and
is no exception.
While the out-of-game interface looks pretty at first glance, it is considerably clunky to handle. The transitions
to finish before you can click on anything else, making navigating just the introductory cutscenes tiresome, let alone the rest of the menus.
Players of the 'Duels' series have asked for complete freedom in their deck-building many times over the years. With
, they get it. But nothing else. A lot has been cut out of the core Duels experience in favour of the deck-building system: the long-time favourite Two-Headed Giant gametype; a second gametype (Duels 2012 had Archenemy, D13 Planechase, and D14 Sealed Deck [does that count?]); and challenge scenarios where you have a single turn to win the game using the cards given to you.
Although most of the time, the single-player campaign feels like a set of challenge decks. As I've played Magic for almost a decade now, I naturally set
's difficulty to the highest possible... boy, was that a mistake. The AI makes perfect draws and plays, to the point where I get the feeling their decks are just plain stacked. Even on the lower difficulties, some campaign matches played out the exact same way each time I faced them.
It's enough of a challenge just getting started in the campaign: you choose a two-colour deck with which to begin, but you don't know what's
the deck until you're playing it. I ended up with the green-white build, and only because it actually won me the last tutorial game. My preferred choices of white-blue and blue-green didn't stand up to the red-green stompfest that you have to beat to get started on the story proper.
I cannot recommend
under any circumstance.
Postscript: If you are looking for an MtG game on Steam, Duels 2012 remains the best of the series, as I see it. Closely followed by D13 (marred only by its focus on single-colour decks instead of a balance of one, two and three-colour).

Port Royale 2 is a 17th century Caribbean themed trading/piracy/military sim. It's the basic mix of buy low, sell high, build up some cities to further expand your trading horizons, build up your fleet, engage in some piracy or privateering. It's a great and easily accessible intro the genre.
However while accessibility is a perk of the game, it's also its downfall. The game is shallow and the economic simulation is basic. For instance cities not receiving sufficient supplies will rarely shrink so you'll have a huge array of countries willing to buy whatever product you might have at max price. And the economy is also mostly static. There are some irrelevant short term events (famine for instance increases food consumption x2) but with effectively infinite money to be had everywhere you look you'll probably never even notice these events. The ship combat is enjoyable at first, but weak AI becomes a problem once you learn the system, though that's pretty par for course in this genre.
However, in spite of the limited depth it's still an enjoyable game and also has an excellent interface. Things like auto-traders can be heavily configured in a very intuitive fashion.
If you're new to the genre or just looking for a relaxing and stress free romp through the caribbean then this is a great buy. If you're more experienced in the genre or willing to tolerate a more steep learning curve (but experience a far richer and more dynamic game in return) then Patrician 3 might be more up your alley.

I'll start by saying that I don't recommend this game, in it's current form at least, and I'll explain why.
Honestly, this game is infuriating. Sometimes you feel like a badass, but every other time you have to question what is wrong with the janky and frustrating controls and mechanics. The combat is sophisticated, and between guard breaking/interrupting, parrys, blocking, dodges, and more, one has a lot of options for how they approach a fight and what they have to consider. It's incredibly idiotic on Ubi's part then to only tell you the bare minimum you need to play, even with the advanced tutorial, as there are mechanics the game never explicitly tells you. Every attack, for example, has some degree of homing capability. This isn't just the character taking a step as they attack, but them straight sliding forward a nearly absurd distance to hit you. Not only is there this weird homing, but some attacks are deceptively slower than others, with no real reason why. Conqueror's top heavy for example is slower than his side heavy's, and there isn't anything special about his top heavy that would justify it being slower. Parry and guardbreak interrupt timing are okay at best, and bs at worst. There's a clear indication on attacks for when you should parry, but it's like you have to ignore it and parry a quarter or half second sooner. Guardbreak interrupts are really broken, as there are certain times you can and can't. Certain heroes, like Conqueror, can't interrupt a guardbreak if a light attack is blocked, or a heavy attack. I'm unclear as to what classes this kind of thing affects, which is really bad. There are some other situations as well, but just the fact the game only tells you when you should interrupt a guard break, but never when you can or cannot.
This, and other strange things that happen in this game, really ruin the whole experience for me. I'm really not trying to dump all over this game, as there's a lot of potential in it and I want to see it succeed. As the mechanics are now, and with the addition of an ambiguous p2p connection, whether fighting is smooth or clunky is simply too variable. There's a story in the game as well, and it's kinda trashy in my opinion, but the multiplayer is really where it's at of course. Too bad its' just to haphazard to be enjoyable for any longer than an hour at a time, maybe.

I can't be the only person who's gotten a pirate ship or spaceship and spent all their time hauling junk around to sell. There's something quietly gratifying about buying low and selling high, and so there should be no surprise there are games that exist to scratch that itch. Port Royale 2 does just that on the surface, and then surprises you with several more layers of fortune-seeking options.
You play an aspiring merchant in the Caribbean of the 1600s, starting with little more than a sloop and some sacks of money. Your ship will get you around to the many ports, each modeled in simple, charming Stronghold-esque 2D. The buildings that comprise each town determine what goods they produce from a list of about two dozen, and the rate at which they consume them. Your job, then, is to learn which towns need which goods, and where the best place to buy them up is.
It's not as simple as finding a town that makes shirts and a town that grows cotton, though. Each location is constantly producing and consuming goods, and their prices are determined by dynamic supply and demand. So, if you bring a huge load of cotton to shirt town you might make a pile of money, but turn around and do it again and that cotton might be worthless because they haven't used up the first load yet. Success in the mercantile business means making circuits around the sea, picking up whatever you can at bargain-basement prices and unloading it at whatever port happens to need it. The world map helpfully displays what good a town needs the most at the time, but there are plenty of other traders who can beat you to the punch.
The dynamic, living world of Port Royale is what keeps it fresh and entertaining, because not only will demand flip on you, you can be the agent of that change. Strike enough deals in a town and they'll grant you building permits to set up your own farms and workshops, allowing you to add new production sources across the map. With enough capital you can move away from buying and selling random goods and instead working your own supply chains for pure profit. You can have enormous merchant fleets at your disposal, moving around huge loads of goods or broken up across the Caribbean to beat the other traders to the punch.
Somehow the developers didn't think that was enough, so if you want to eschew the merchant life for full privateering, even that's an option. Any ship can be designated a warship and outfitted with cannon and sailors to take on pirates or merchants of other nations, or even besiege and ransack ports. Governors in major towns will even give you missions to eliminate particularly troublesome captains if you need guidance. There's real-time combat between ships that's functional but basic compared to other high-seas simulators, and comes with the odd handicap of letting you command one ship at a time while your opponents have their full fleet.
Still, the combat is an engaging and welcome addition atop the robust economic simulator, and it isn't even the only one. You can also choose to ferry around settlers and construction materials to help grow towns, gamble in the many taverns of the world, piece together treasure maps, and more. A series of four extensive tutorial scenarios will help you get a grip on the game, and then you have four challenge scenarios or the wide-open freeplay mode to enjoy. The chunky 2D graphics might not have aged very well but they certainly don't detract from the relaxed atmosphere, and the soundtrack is exactly what you'd want in a low-key trading sim. Anyone with even a passing interest in being a high-seas merchant is sure to find something to enjoy here.
