Amnesia:  The Dark Descent is, overall, a relatively descent game.  It reminded me very much of a first person version of the old-school PC games where you had to find random items and figure out what to do with them.   It's not a difficult game (2/10), but it makes up for it with story (7/10) and mood (8/10).  Overall, the gameplay is creative (7/10), putting the player in the position of a terrified psychotic lost in the dark hiding from monsters rather than an ardent hero defeating evil.  The sound effects and music (8/10) are good, but the graphics (5/10) are mediocre, even for the year it was released.  It's a short game, very short (2/10), and can easily be solved in a single sitting if that's what you're looking to do.  There is very little if any replayability (2/10), except if you just want to experience the ambience one more time.  I did not experience a single bug or glitch (9/10) playing or setting up this game except that it required a windows automated compatibility repair in order to play in 1080p, which is really not a big deal.  Finally, there is basically no player input for character customization (2/10) and the player experiences the story with no inputs into it or decisions regarding it except for once; though, to be fair on the character side, this game has no numerical statistics other than the character's super simple and not important health and sanity levels.  Overall, I'd give it a 52%, making it in the realm of what I would consider to be games that are recommended but just barely.  Might as well give it a go, though.  Seriously, it won't take that long:)  Thanks for reading!

Tormentum.
A game that takes the aesthetic freedom of point n' click games to a whole new level. First and foremost, the art and absolutely gorgeous. It carries the game beautifully in all its grotesque detail, lurid colors, stark portrayals. The art is emotional, evocative, and truly does touch your soul in both good and bad ways.
However,
is it a good game?
Yes...and no? But yes.
Tormentum is something of a newer variety of point and click games. Ones that focus a lot more on the logic puzzles rather than the classic Monkey Island style of "try this with this, and maybe this, and maybe if you're lucky it'll work because why not". They're very straightforward as point and click games go and with a few exception, very finely crafted.
But with that, they're also very easy. In fact, your typical point and click gamer, especially of the older variety, might find themselves a bit miffed at just how straightforward these puzzles are. Almost to the point I couldn't help but think to myself, "how on earth am I doing all this so easily and yet so many others in this setting have utterly FAILED?" And that can be a bit of a damper simply because for the most part, just about anyone can cruise through the game with nary a problem. There's just about no challenge.
I'm not quite sure I can bring myself to call that a flaw though. The amospheric aura of the game combined with its crisp--though admittedly not nearly as talented as its visual art--writing and very lean, clean cut gameplay really just allows you as the player to truly focus on the game for what it is. And that is an evocative art gallery of introspection. Just like any other wonderful piece of art. This is one of the few games I've ever played that leveraged a morality system...and still made me question my choices. Where the results of your choices oftentimes came back to haunt you later, leaving you thinking to yourself "...oh♥♥♥♥♥♥..did I...did I ♥♥♥♥ up? Was that REALLY the right decision?". And it's absolutely beautiful.
Another thing to note about the game that could be construed as a flaw is its length. It's pretty short. Anywhere between 2 to 5 hours. It does have some replay value but the game is still short despite that. But in all honesty, I find that length for better rather than worse. Any longer and the game might be overstaying its welcome. You really don't want to become desensitized to an artstyle like Tormentum's.
And one more thing. I'll admit that I was a tad bit disappointed to see that the game didn't have as much...uh, grotesque, visual torture as I had thought based on the demo. That's...probably a good thing. And in all honesty, led to a far more cohesive game probaby. But I'll just throw out there for those who were looking.
All in all, I highly recommend Tormentum for anyone who is willing to go through a dark, surreal, and visceral visual journey of the mind and eye. With that being said, I do not recommend this game to anyone who's a bit on the squeamish side and probably not for minors. The art can be very grotesque at times in a pretty disturbing way. I also caution veterans of the point and click genre to approach knowing that the game is pretty darn easy. And finally, I don't suggest this game to anyone who's searching for something with a more adrenaline tick. The game is eerie, but it is by no means "horror". And anyone who would not enjoy point and click mechanics simply has little to find here outside of the aesthetics.
But really. Play this game. It's well worth the money. And then some.

Short and sweet: If you like realistic sims (specifically Medieval era here, hence the name) than this is your game. Mind you, the developers did a weird turn and released a somewhat different version of the game than what we had been testing throughout Alpha, so some repetitive glitches have been reintroduced. I'd say overall the Devs made a really poor decision by calling this a "released" product, and I fear that the hopes of their MMO and sales will suffer as a result. Nevertheless they're chipping away at the bugs currently, and I cannot recommend this game enough for the older generations out there that want a gritty, realistic experience.
Kids should probably stay away. Not enough graphical prowess, steep skill/combat curve, and no magical doodads to fiddle with.

While rather basic in gameplay, I find myself very much wanting to recommend this game for various reasons including its storyline and its immersive steampunk napoleonic setting. If you are in any way a fan of "around the world in 80 days" or if you are intrigued by the thought of travelling the world in an 1800's steampunk world, then I strongly recommend this game to you as you will find a lot to enjoy.
When it comes to gameplay, there is an aspect of money management which involves buying low and selling high in different places, and then choosing an appropriate mode of travel between each location (fast, comfortable and expensive, or slow, uncomfortable and cheap), You have to keep your master happy but also remain responsible with his/your funds throughout the journey. Despite this, the games primary focus is the text-based character interactions and the thoughts and descriptions of the player character when visiting new cities and travelling in different interesting vehicles. The game also features several dialogue choice segments which can influence what other people think of you and your masters opinion of you.
While I have not yet made it all the way around the world in either of my playthroughs (It takes probably a good 3 hours to do so), I find myself frequently wanting to come back to it but rarely end up gettting around to it, hense my fairly low play time. This game is a delight to play if you are in a lazy mood and want a chilled out but entertaining experience that will last an hour or two until you put it aside for next time. Furthermore, this game has a fair amount of replay value as you are able to choose your own journey (you will not get to visit every city / country in one playthrough due to your 80 day / turn time constraint). All in all, as far as casual games go. i give this an 8/10.

A quite intriguing WWII Shooter from the start, but it falls off heavily in every single aspect after 4-5 levels.
The game reduces the Sniper Elite series to a core, removing many action and openly kissing its own shoes with its oppressing and, after the first time of seeing it, very boring and annoying kill-cam mechanic. The Stealth, which was the main emphasis in earlier titles. was also limited down by removing the option to vary in speed and giving the enemies the ominous, omniscient "I SEE THAT FILTHY AMERICAN AROUND THE CORNER"-ability, which kind of destroys the point of having any stealth at all.
The combat heavily suffers from unpredictable movement patterns and instakills from most weapons, making the player unkillable within cover. Regenerative health doesn't help that. Even on higher difficulties the experienced (meaning: has played a videogame before) player wont die ever if its not from some cheesy event-trigger that spawns a squad in his face. And yeah, those happen alot.
And last but not least, while dealing with a realistic topic, the story feels as cliché-ridden as a late 2000's sitcom, making Russians the main antagonist in a rather insulting plot sourrunding some german-socialist conspiracy while still sticking to the gameplay as the main aspect. IMO a shooter like this has to pick: story-driven or gameplay-focussed. Trying to combine both, at least in this case, worked out to be a sloppy and tiring mess, hardly describable as fun.
Also, multiplayer doesn't feel any different as single player, no real cooperation whatsoever.
Play something else, maybe an earlier title, and expect improvement in Sniper Elite III. That trailer looks promising to me.

I LOVE THIS GAME!!!!!!!!!!!
In short,
PVP is a BLAST
Campaign story is intriguing (I have yet to beat it) its also has Co-op mode as well.(Enemies do have double the health in this mode)
It has Level progression with unique characters to play and their abilities that can become unlocked while playing both single player and multiplayer (Single player abilities DO NOT transfer over to multiplayer mode). You can unlock abilities with steel in Multiplayer. I do not recommend this method as you can unlock them by simply playing the characters of your choice and leveling them. Also it has a hint of RPG elements with the gear/loot you can uptain in multiplayer.
Drops (Armor/Weapons) after a round is ended or bought.
**Gear and perks are only applied in 4vs4- Skirmish / 4vs4 - Dominion/ 4vs4 - Elimination or custom modes(if you wish).
They DO NOT apply in 1vs1 and 2vs2 duals!
Yes, There are microtransactions in this game (as are with most games these days)
you buy steel for cosmetic looks, emotions/executions. You can also earn this steel by playing muitlplayer games (any mode) after a round is finished or by completing Bounties that the game provides, Also In single player there are hidden breakable objects that provides you some steel as well.
Of course you can just buy the Steel if you wanted to.
You can get Gear by using the Scavenge Gear or as i like to call it "Try your luck" at getting random gear (weapons/armor perks) using the Steel you earned.
the picks are
- Basic pack
- Weapons
- Armor
- Premium  (best chance to get rare items)
If you are going to use this system be warned its only applies to the character you choose.
(Side note, do not do this until you reach reputation level one. Thats getting the character pass level 21)
As for the "connection issues" I was at NAT "Yellow" or moderate" connection. After reading the Ubisoft support page --
I found UDP port 3074-3075 was the cause of my problem.
After opening these ports on my router my connection went from "Yellow" to "Green" (NAT OPEN)
I have since had ZERO connection problems (able to play game after game without losing connection) however, From time to time i would receive a server full message or when someone disconnecting for unknown reasons. (none of this fault is Ubisofts)
If you wish a more in depth review please keep reading.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Now that's out of the way,
As far as the gameplay goes, It's fun!
Some may call it "Rock,Paper,Scissor,"
but I think its more"Rock,Paper,Scissor,Laser,Spock."
There is more then one way to stop or counter moves, not just blocking in the directions they are swinging at you. hence the "Rock,Paper,Sissors" gameplay I keep hearing about
to simply put these individuals are one tracked mind and can not see the other options available to them.
Practicing your Character(s) of choice and learning the ALL moves is key. (As it is in any game we play).
Take your time, there are many ways to learn and still get XP/loot  without getting your keyboard/mouse or controller all salty from PvP gameplay. Oh, and I do recommend a controller(I use a dualshock playstation 4 controller)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Multiplayer modes (where you will spend most of your time)
1vs1- skill is needed in order to win. If you are new to the game i recommend playing Vs BOTS. This is the best way to learn a new character and still get XP/Loot (In my opinion)
***** Gear stats have no effect
2vs2 - skill is needed in order to win along with a skilled teammate. (unwriten code of conduct in this mode- Do not gang up on the last survivor wait until dual is over. Of coruse this is not always followed and some salt might be split if not done so)
***** Gear stats have no effect
4vs4 - Dominion reminded me a bit of (Dynasty warriors™)
3 control points to capture with the middle point (Point B) having a wave of minions that must be pushed across or cleared to a line in order to gain control of that point.
Also, there are buffs and ability(s) that your character can be used (Yes, Gear stats does play a part into this)
4vs4- Skirmish is (Dynasty warriors™) lite. No real mass of minions on the battlefield however there are "Captians" that are harder then the normal minion and a few straglers of minions you might encounter here and there. No points to control but there is a point system in place when a team reaches 1000 points they win (provided they kill the remining hero's)
there are buffs and ability(s) that your character can be used. (Yes, Gear stats does play a part into this too)
4vs4 - Elimination is kind of like 2vs2 but with 4 player, there are buffs and ability(s) that your character can use. (Yes, Gear stats does play a part into this too)
and in this mode is where the MOST complaints come into play about the (unwritten code of conduct)
Characters are Diverse in play and style, (some are easier to learn then others)
Vanguard Heroes- Adaptable/Straightforward (Good Attack range/High Health)
Assassin Heroes- Mobility/Counters (Fast attacks/Strong attacks but cant take hits)
Heavies Heroes- High Defense/ (Hard hitting/slow but excel in group combat)
Hybrids Heroes- Combination/Range (Range fighters, Each taking a bit from the other groups to make something truly unique.)
Some Heroes have bleed affects which can be a pain at times, learning how they apply it and knowing when to step back or counter guard is critical to stop this techniuqe
Some Heroes have stuns or on hit kills, again learning how these are uses and when to Side step/guard or counter guard is important.
Some Heroes have counterattacks and knowning when not to heavy attack or make you self open to a combination attack is key to success.
As you can see each hero is unique in their own way, Practicing against each of these heroes will help you understand the games mechanics. You will learn what to do and when to do it.
As far as the story mode is concerned, I haven't finshed it yet.
I am only at part 1.6 "Wolves among sheep". I have been playing the campaign in "realistic mode" only (yes, it can be challenging at times) its only because I don't know any of the Kinghts moves by heart (still learning them)
So far the story isn't bad, I wish I could talk more it but I can't.
having some Steel hidden in the single/co-op campaign is a nice little perk to make you want to complete the storyline.
Thanks for reading this and hope to see you on the battlefield!

Port Royale 2 is an excellent game that features: trading, battles, wits, economics, wits, battles, buying new ships to hold more goods, economics, battles, wits, quests, gambling, production and a few other things.
When economics come in you have to know what town needs what and what towns has what that town needs, when you find two towns close to each other that needs what the other has, you make a large profit.
When battling comes in you have to make sure that you have traded enough stuff to buy armaments to fight pirates and enemy nations, so that you can capture or destroy enemy convoys to allow you to trade more, and make money.
When production comes in, you can build production facilities that produce: tobacco, wood and various other commodities, so that you can sell them to towns that want said commodities.
Gambling can be accomplished by going to an inn and betting how many points you can get in a card game, if you get as many points as you bet you earn as much as you bet, if you don't you lose as much as you bet.
Buying ships allows you to carry more goods, and carry more firepower.
Quests are given by governers of towns, quests can range from destroying ships, to delivering cargo.
Rating: 9/10, a nearly perfect game, if you ask me. Especially when it is on sale.

OK, this♥♥♥♥♥♥is good. The reason I don't play horror games is because there aren't many good horror games. I don't like something jumping in my face and screaming and then disappearing. That's not horror. That's stupid. That's what most of the horror games do.

Amnesia tries to teach gamers and developers alike that "proper horror" is not just about jumpscares. It's about atmosphere, lighting, sound effects, voice acting, music, level design, story, the feeling of dread, the constant fear of being hunted, and generally just about anything that creeps you THE ♥♥♥♥ out and makes you NOT want to move forward from any safe areas.
Let me elaborate on that stuff if you want to read:
+ Atmosphere: You feel like you are actually in 1800s in a castle haunted by something (not gonna get into that too much). + Lighting: The really clever use of lighting (or the lack thereof) contributes to your fear and makes you turn your lantern on (which runs on limited oil which you find rarely :3 ) and thus you are left with a stressful situation in which you either choose to navigate in dark (reduces sanity which has other consequences) or spend your oil (and risk being left in the dark later in the game).

2008: Bugbear released FlatOut: Ultimate Carnage for PC. It was a remastered verison of FlatOut 2, with some new modes, different soundtrack, and new cars. Bugbear just unknowning released their last FlatOut game.
2009: The publisher, Empire Interactive, filed for backrupty, and shutdown. Bugbear lost the Flatout IP, where it then went to another publisher, Strategy First. This publisher hired Team 6 to work on a new FlatOut game.
2011: Team 6 released Flatout 3: Chaos & Destruction for PC. The game was recieved horribly, with bad AI, bad physics, horrible optimization, lacklust map design, boring gamemodes, and awful car damage. The game was nothing like the original FlatOut games, and became one of the worst games on Steam.
2014: Bugbear released an early access game called Next Car Game (Now known as Wreckfest) to Steam. They said they wanted to go "back to their roots" with a "core FlatOut racing experience" and a "tactical damage system" inspired from the Destruction Derby games. Instead of being the fun game they hoped, it turned into a simulator years later. This means that any "roots" they wanted from FlatOut were gone. Fans lost hope that there would ever be a new FlatOut game.
2015: A new game called FlatOut 4: Total Insanity was announced, being made by two new developers, Kylotonn Entertainment and Tiny Rebel Games.
2016: Bugbear released another early access game called Stuntfest. This game is based off the stunt ragdoll stunt mode in FlatOut. Instead of making the comsumers happy, it made them mad since they thought the stunt mode was going to be included in Wreckfest.
Now it's 2017. FlatOut 4: Total Instanity released for PC. Does it live up to it's predecessors?
FlatOut 4 isn't the Bugbear style FlatOut we wanted, but I will say that the game is okay, but not amazing. It has issues that hold back it's potential at restarting the FlatOut series.
I was disappointed at the lack of settings. This game does run over 60FPS. I have everything on the highest setting, and the game looks good, but lack luster. Pop in of props, and shadows are very noticeable. Textures, and particle effects look amazing, although the sparks are too overexagerated. Some of the images, like with loading screens, are a bit blurry. The optimization could be better, as like I said before, the pop in is bad, so I wonder if they did that intentionally to make game run better, without actually optimizating it properly.
We were promised it, given the tools to do so, but it never happened.
The menus look great, much like Bugbear's menus, but they are too cluttered with items that can confuse the player.
(I only used a controller) The handling is arcady. It's an improvement over the horrible unsteer seen in FlatOut Ultimate Carnage. Using the e-brake is also much more improved, but you can still spin out.
What an awful camera. It sticks too close to the car, violatly jerks around when spinning the camera, jumping of a ramp, or getting hit by a player. Boosting is even worst, as the camera shakes so erratically my eyes started to hurt.
The gamemodes are very interesting and fun. The races are filled with destruction. Career can be  grindy at times. The demolition derbies are totally different, as they aren't realistic as previous titles, but still as fun. The new assault mode uses powerups to slow down, and wreck the enemies. It's like Mario cart on steriods, it is crazily fun. The stunt arena is back, with new challenges, and previous challenges making a comeback, like the Rings of Fire. These gamemodes are fun, and will have great replayabilty.
Where is everyone?
I was hoping for the return of cars from previous titles, but was disappointed to see nothing. However, the cars in the game are good, and have their own unique personality.
Just like FlatOut Ultimate Carnage, the customization is not very extensive, with limited color changes, and no really visual changes, other than the exhaust color. They do still have the useful upgrades with engines, chasis, wheels, etc.
The vehicle damage is very interesting. They deform way more than the other games, but in a very unrealistic way. Many times the bumpers don't fall off, and the doors clip through objects when opening. It just doesn't look right.
The tracks are full of props, scenery, and plants to destroy. The tracks aren't nothing special, but they set the mood for FlatOut 4 very nicely.
Like I mentioned before, the props physics are improved, but I noticed that when a prop was stuck on my vehicle after a while, rather than flying off, it would simple disappear. Other times I drove right through them, without any hit detection.
The physics have been improved for props, but worse for cars. In FlatOut Ultimate Carnage, props would be your worst nightmare. Not only would they slow you down, they usually would flip your car, and spin you right around, messing up your race. Here, the props still have an impact on speed, but they usual don't flip, or spin the car. Now when it comes to vehicle physics, it's a different story. Coupled with the bad camera, may times the vehicles physics will screw up when hitting jumps, getting knocked over, and hitting other player vehicles. They don't feel natural, as the cars seem extremely heavy. In FlatOut Ultimate Carnage, the cars felt more appropriate when it came to weight, and the physics didn't freak out like they do in this game.
One of the big things with FlatOut Ultimate Carnages was the characters you raced against. They had a personality, some were more aggressive, others were more tactical. FlatOut 4's characters feel unspired, and empty. They don't feel different, and sometimes it can be hard to tell who drives what car. In FlatOut Ultimate Carnage, you knew who that b*tch was coming behind you to take you out.
The vehicle AI isn't the smartest. They tend to crash themselves. However, they can be aggressive. I have gotten spun out many times by drivers, and they love grinding with other cars. The AI is easier than FlatOut Ultimate Carnage, but they can still put up a fight.
Compared to FlatOut Ultimate Carnage, the ragdoll physics are horrible. They don't look natural at all, as they look very stiff, and can clip through objects easily.
The sound design in this game is meh. Some cars sounds good, while others sound like vacuum cleaners full power. Also, you don't really hear the roar of the other cars in the game.
The soundtrack consists mostly of rock, heavy metal, punk rock, and rock 'n' roll. I personally don't find the soundtrack that interesting, as FlatOut 2 really nailed the soundtrack, while this game misses the mark in interesting, and enjoyable music. It doesn't set the mood very well, causing the music to feel out of place with the gameplay.
FlatOut 4: Total Insanity sticks to some of it's Bugbear roots, while creating new ones. I still recommend the previous titles, compared to FlatOut 4 (except for FlatOut 3) This game is okay, but I still recommend this game, as the game is still enoyable, even with it's flaws.

Let me get a few things straight:
This game is short. As an avid gamer but inexperienced in this genre, it took me about three hours to complete. Unlike other games of this type, I never found the puzzles to be too hard or too easy. Only once did I have to look up a hint which turned out to just be me not paying close enough attention. If you're looking for a serious mental struggle, you may not find it here. But, for someone who approaches this game more casually, I loved it.
Normally I try to look at how many hours I get out of a game compared to what I pay for it to find some balance. This game gets a bit of an exception just since I enjoyed myself so much. Normally I'd say a game this short would not be worth the price (and that may factor into your decision) but for me I am happy to support this developer and hope they make more in this vein.
There are moral choices in the game, which is hardly a new idea, but it's interesting to see how the game has subtle changes based on the decisions you make. The end result is more or less the same, but still, it's fun and gives it a level of replayability just to see the other options.
To me the story was interesting to follow and gives you just enough answers to understand what is going on but just enough mystery to make you wonder more about the world and what it may hold. I'd personally love to get to see more like it. Is it completely original? No, but it does what it does well.
The art alone is no reason to buy a game, but this game has some of the coolest I've seen in a while. It is detailed and interesting but not too cluttered, which is important for a point-and-click if you ask me. Gives me serious H. R. Giger vibes and as a huge Alien(s) fan, keep it coming.

The "choose your own adventure" genre is really interesting: in its original form (printed on a book, that is), it was fun for the first few tries, but you could get tired of the lack of interactivity, even though it offered more than one path to follow, which was already more than traditional books.
As a game genre, you can introduce more elements to the story and add a layer of gameplay to make your choices matter even more and really immerse you in the adventure.
In 80 days, you play as Passepartout, Phileas Fogg's valet, in an adaptation of Jules Verne's classic novel.
How much does the story differ from the original one? Well, I won't go into details because this is a spoler-free review, but the world is completely different from the one in the book (and from real life history at the time). The main theme is steampunk, as you will encounter various wondrous machines, contraptions and robots throughout your adventures.
The writing is witty and immediate, with a focus on the character's thoughts (he is, supposedly, writing on his diary), so it never gets too heavy or boring but doesn't skim over important parts of the plot and adds nice details to make the world come alive.
The art style can be described as "inky", with a focus on blacks and shadows. My only issue with the visuals is the fact that the 3D globe is a little too shiny, and sometimes you can even confuse the land with the sea because of the lack of clear, defined lines. It would be nice to have a way to change the color of the land and the sea to better suit the player's needs. The game runs absolutely fine, and it will do so on pretty much all machines.
The sound is limited to ambient sounds and some background music, but it does help you focus on what's going on in the story.
Gameplay wise, apart from the multiple choices, you also have to manage your budget, plan your trip to the next city, buy and sell items (some of which help you during challenging weather conditions), keep Fogg alive and, of course, make it back to London within 80 days (although the game does not end if you fail to do so, you always make it there eventually).
80 Days is not too difficult (as far as I've seen there's no true failure state), but it does offer a challenge in the form of indirect multiplayer with other Passepartous around the world.
The game is both turn-based and real-time: the hours of the day pass by as you wait, but you have to take some set routes from one city to the other.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game and I'm probably going to buy anything Inkle makes if the quality remains this high.
Sorcery, their other narrative-driven game series, is also really good, so if you enjoyed 80 days you'll most likely love that one as well.

80 Days is bar none the most sublime video game reinterpretation of classic literature I'm aware of. It's a travel game/choose your own adventure version of Jules Verne's
with writing that's not only engaging for the player, but
, and in the process does a very good job of presenting a larger living world beyond the player's reach. It's only fitting: you are after all just the valet of a man whose mere whim has you both traveling around the world, where you are in turn subjected to much larger twists of fate.
It's heavy on the reading of course, but rather light as a game, and there's generally no reloading saves if you click a choice you didn't mean to. For a globe-trotting game, its graphics toe the line between stylishly minimal and plain austere. I still highly recommend it for literary and adventurous types.

Lack of content (pro or con depending on your view) - This is a sandbox game, you're given tools to play and there isn't anything else. This is a very fun "choose your own adventure" style game that put's you in the role of the valet (and decision-maker) in the Jules Verne challenge to get around the world in 80 days. For an added twist, the setting is changed to a steam-punk variation of the original mid/late 1800s setting. In practice, you are doing two things: (1) reading through the (text) story, and making decisions that affect each little vignette (and affect what routes you know about), and (2) making strategic decisions about where to go, what to buy and sell where, what to spend your time doing, and what to spend your money on.
Pros:
+ You've got a lot of choices of what route you take around the world. Your decisions really do matter.
+ Good replayability. Although the game can get repetitive if you take the same route, each route has its own story. I always found myself wondering what would happen if I had gone another way, and this makes me want to play again.
+ Interesting stories unfold at each location. Depending on your choices, they can resolve in different ways. A number of the stories I played through were really quite engaging and well-done.
+ Challenging game mechanics, but not frustrating
Cons:
- As I said, the same events happen at the same locations, so if you play multiple times, you'll have to mix up your routes or else play through the same stories over again (much like if you were actually reading a "choose your adventure" book).

This is an interesting take on Star Wars, the Old Republic timeline. KOTOR 1 was astronomically critically successful, so I'll assume familiarity with that. This sequel to that legendary RPG takes things further and is 100% worth your time.
Bioware's KOTOR 1 was about Good vs Evil, and was groundbreaking with its moral decisions and player agency. Obsidian's KOTOR 2 is a deconstruction of the more normal Good vs Evil themes - it goes deeper into questions of what makes right and what makes wrong. It's not just about choosing to be good or choosing to be bad - Obsidian put more effort into making the themes more nuanced than that, and often the player will second-guess their choices and think very carefully about such things as greater goods, or ends justifying means - moreso than in the more straight forward KOTOR 1, anyway.

KOTOR 1 is a great game and one of my all-time favorite RPGs. KOTOR 2 one-ups it in narrative and maintains the same gameplay and structure that made KOTOR 1 great.

Be sure to get the Sith Lords Restored mod that is on the Steam Workshop. KOTOR 2 was originally released in quite a rushed state (as Obsidian games unfortunately often are) but that mod "restores" much of the missing content and really improves the base game.

This game is in early access. This is the firstmost important piece of knowledge that anyone going into this game should know. It's not perfect, and it's nowhere near done, but so far it's pretty fun.
Graphically, the game looks alright. It's the Unreal Engine, so you have to take into account that it'll sorta look like many other Unreal Engine games, with texture loading and light shafts. The art-style is dark, and apocalyptic, with the Nether looking scary, as they should. The city and it's many buildings look very good so far, with a real downtrodden and over-run look.
The game sounds decent, with the Nether themselves being the most impressive. Their ambient screeches feel right at home and help with immersion. While many sounds are there, they aren't very impressive, with firearms being the main offender. They just sound weak, and should have more of an "oomph." While I think that there should be some reverb added in so to give an "empty city" effect, I could live without it.
The gameplay so far is something that you would find similar to DayZ or Infestation. You explore the city for supplies, fend off against Nether and opposing players, and mainly survive. Although the game does have rudimentary missions that you can do in it's current state. With every Nether kill, you gain experience, which you can use to upgrade your character with skills that allow you to block, sneak around better, have more health, and hit harder.
Overall, the game is pretty fun as it is. It's dark and atmospheric, and it differs from many other "zombie" survival games due to it's variety in enemy types and the general enemy itself. Although I wish that the Nether "threat" was more, as it would definitely reduce PvP, it's pretty good as is.

I am a long time Magic player and I have played all of the Duels games released so far.  This is the third of the games that I have purchased on Steam, and let me tell you it is a disappointment.  The card collecting is nothing like the the previous installments.  There's virtually no replayability in single player unless you really want to dedicate the time to opening enough random cards that you may actually collect each one.  And even if you collect each card, what will you do with them?  The pool is so weird and scattershot in terms of mechanics and card quality that it's just silly.  Multiplayer is a joke, as in everyone else is also limited to this strange selection of cards so games end up usually uninteresting and just waiting for someone to draw that bomb.  It has no point.
I must also mention the aesthetics of the menus.  It's 2014 as I write this , and maybe it's a bit cliche to state, but holy moly talk about dated looking menus.  It's like navigating a flash-based website circa the year 2001 complete with unwelcome dissolve animations and unacceptable load times.  Yes that's right, I hope you enjoy menu screens because you're gonna spend a lot of time trying to get around in an ugly and clunky system.  Not to mention the layout and navigation of the game screens, which for some reason change every year.  I don't get it, isn't this designed with controller support in mind?  Why is everything such a pain to navigate with a controller then?  And why is it that using a mouse instead is somehow no better?  Everything about this seems like it was designed by 15 year olds, no joke.  It's a whole lot of "Wouldn't this be cool?" instead of what it should be, which is "Shouldn't this be seamless and functional considering this is the fifth version of this game we've put out?"
I honestly regret buying this game, especially at full price.  Yeah I've put some time into it but just in the hopes that it will become fun.  It has not.  For what it's worth 2014's "sealed" mode was a huge letdown coming from the point of view of someone who plays MTGO exclusively for the limited tournaments.  But you know I've sunk a lot of downtime into 2014 because the theme decks were fun, and there's a concrete goal of unlocking the next card for that deck and figuring out how to tune what you have into not only playable but just downright fun decks.  2015 has no such charm.  It's a complete step backwards in the series, there is absolutely no improvement in this version over the previous versions.  They had a single good idea -- custom deck building -- but top to bottom this game is executed poorly and not worth your time or money until it gets some very deep discounts.  If I can just convince one person to trust me and spend their money elsewhere that'll be good enough for me.

Is it worth the wait? Of course not, don't be ridiculous. How could any game possibly be worth waiting 14 years for, especially one that only ever aspired to be a low-brow comedy first-person shooter? There's no reinvention of the genre here, no real attempt at grandeur. More than anything, Duke just wants to party like it's 1997.
Check unrealistic expectations at the door and forget the ancient, hyperbolic promises of self-deluded developers before you even consider buying this suddenly corporeal ghost of PC gaming history. The development-time-to-awesomeness ratio isn't impressive. If you can do that, Duke Nukem Forever can at least mostly succeed in its aspiration. After all of its tumultuous history, it's ended up as an entertaining FPS wrapped in juvenile, smut-laced humor. Its gameplay is a hybrid of old-school and new, and it won't wow players with stunning visuals—its window of opportunity for that passed years ago—but it does put on a good show of alien♥♥♥♥♥kicking by working what it's got.
The Cycloid is one of the cooler-looking bosses, but his bark is worse than his bite.
Like a hyper-violent, over-sexed Peter Pan, Duke Nukem refuses to grow up. Though 12 years have passed since the events of Duke Nukem 3D, he's the exact same trash-talking, cigar-chomping, muscle-bound man of action, still rocking that '90s-style buzz cut and red tanktop. The source of his superhuman action-hero powers is his own ego, which doubles as a literal recharging shield over his (also recharging) health. It's reinforced by an entire world of people who worship him as an infallible man-god and sex idol—women want him, men want to be him. He's the stereotypical teenage boy's power fantasy personified and turned up to 11. Sure, he's a ham-fisted action hero parody, but Duke remains one of the most memorable characters in gaming history for a reason: he's simply more fun to play as than SERIOUS FACE ARMY MAN.
As two-dimensional as Duke himself, the story gets right to the point: intergalactic sex-criminal aliens are re-offending, and Duke must defy orders and step in to defend Earth's chicks. Even that flimsy B-movie tribute plot is resolved (sort of) half way through—DNF becomes simply about shooting aliens 'cause they're ugly, and bits of the script are little more than profane Mad Libs. Lazy writing or pointed critique of the state of story in first-person shooters? I prefer to think of it as the latter.
Incoming canned goods!
Reloaded
Action-wise, the single-player game fulfills its obligations as a successor to Duke Nukem 3D. It's fast-paced run-and-gun battle against diverse, love-to-hate 'em monsters, using weaponry ranging from conventional boomsticks toover-the-top sci-fi, and fought through a long series of corridor levels where there's almost always something unique to see and interact with. Almost every original weapon (except Duke's boot) returns—and after taking the Shrink Ray and Freeze Beam for a spin, it makes me wonder why few shooters have appropriated the joy of killing enemies in two-step attacks. Sure, shrinking enemies and then squashing them or freezing and shattering isn't as efficient as double-tapping to the head, but it's more fun. There's also the Devastator, a ridiculously powerful, double-barreled, rapid-fire rocket launcher that never pauses to reload until it's spent.
I just want to be looooooved!
Duke's trusty pistol, shotgun, Ripper chaingun, and rocket launcher may not be anything particularly unique or special (and certainly not realistic, lacking even a hint of recoil) but they're loud and potent alien killers. The new weapons, a rail gun sniper rifle, an alien laser, and a triple-missile-launcher called the Enforcer Gun are pretty ho-hum—no new classics here. The biggest sadness is that DNF has adopted the Halo-style two-weapon system, which frequently forced me to abandon my beloved Shrink Ray for lack of ammo. Even with all of that heavy weaponry, I still died quite a bit—despite the regenerating health system, Duke Nukem Forever is one of the more challen­ging shooters I've played in years.
At least the signature remote-detonating pipe bombs, laser tripwire mines, and Holo-Duke decoys (plus melee-enhancing steroids and pain-mitigating beer powerups) exist outside this limitation, allowing you to set all manner of devious traps in the diverse range of linear, corridor-style levels and lure enemies into them. Duke battles the aliens through his high-tech Duke Cave, his self-styled opulent casino, the aliens' disgustingly organic hive (complete with Prey-style sphincter doors that open when tickled), a Vegas skyscraper, a Dukeburger restaurant, Hoover Dam, construction sites, Nevada canyons, underwater, and more.
This little piggy is coming for blood.
Oh yeah, and there's a shameless strip club level with no combat—it's mostly a showcase for boobs and a playground for the many interactive games (pinball, air hockey, billiards, video poker) and gross-out moments in the bathroom. No two settings are alike, and with plenty of Easter eggs scattered around that boost your health when interacted with, exploring the world is a frequently rewarding high point.
Blast from the past
At the end of these levels lie some old-school-tough boss battles. Almost all of the hulking beasts took me out at least once before I figured out and exploited their attack patterns (notable exception: the final boss). Fights against a mothership, a massive alien queen, an underwater leech, and others are more about the spectacle of fighting huge unique monsters (plus an excuse for Duke to nut-punch something for an ego boost) than creating interesting gameplay.
It's Duke vs. Goliath.
The old-style design is probably due to the fact that DNF should've come out years ago. (Hell, 2K's recommended PC is built from five-year-old hardware.) Here and there, it shows; while alien monsters look pretty cool—particularly the iconic Pig Cops and flying, tentacled Octabrains—humans and many of the environments look well behind the curve. But thanks to the aliens' comical massacre of EDF (Earth Defense Force) troops, you don't spend a lot of time looking at people, so it only really offends when the incompetent President waves his unarticulated fingers in your face.
Pop culture references are similarly out-of-date—even growing moldy. Considering that the freshest ones I caught date back all the way to 2004's Team America: World Police (excluding reenactment of Christian Bale's 2009 meltdown in the opening and a crack at Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare tacked on at the end), most of Duke's one-liners were probably recorded in the early half of last decade. Though Duke still delivers several chuckles per level by quoting '90s films like Pulp Fiction and Starship Troopers and jabbing at Halo, it's noticeable that he's been living under a rock for quite some time.
Eh, it's Vegas. They were probably going to tear that hotel down and build a bigger one anyway.
Meatheaded
I encountered a lot more puzzles (of the jumping, physics, and switch-throwing varieties) than I'd expected, and few are befitting of Duke. Dropping barrels into one end of a shipping container to tilt it and create a ramp is too mundane a task for a super badass—Duke's not making fun of the puzzles other shooters started using a decade ago here, he's imitating them. Poorly.
The more innovative puzzle gimmick is shrinking Duke down to a few inches tall and sending you scurrying through levels made for man-sized play. Being action-figure sized gives you a new and interesting perspective on the world—jumping around a vast kitchen battling rats and mini Pig Cops among the shelves while using mustard jars as cover is a very different experience, and one encounter in particular makes an epic battle of what would normally be a one-shot kill. However, running any significant distance on tiny legs can get tedious.
80/100

After all the problems DotP 2014 had, I was really hoping that the devs had taken a step back and rectified the issues with it (deck construction locked into Sealed mode, bad challenges, restrictive campaign, etc.). Instead we get a barebones version of MTG that does everything wrong that it possibly can. Problems are apparent right when you start up the game; the UI is slow and heavily animated, obviously being designed for a touch screen interface. Instead of being given 1-2 prebuilt decks like in the previous two annual releases, you are given a choice between deck archetypes. However, you have no idea what cards are actually inside your deck before you lock in to using that "Intro Deck"-strength deck which can really screw you over at the start of the game. For example, I picked a supposedly B/G Reanimator deck but the only reanimator card in it was Rescue from the Underworld (a high costed, slow reanimator that requires saccing a creature as an additional cost). Because you are picking an archetype and not an actual deck, you also don't get unlocks specifically for your deck; while this gives you more freedom in deck construction, new players will be baffled about what they should add to their deck or how to edit it properly. A "Suggested Cards" tool is available but it isn't very trustworthy; using it with my best deck (G/W tokens), two of the three recommended cards are Phytotitan and Pelakka Wurm.
While you can finally build your own decks with DotP 2015, you will really struggle to put something playable together without buying cards for real money. Buying all the cards in the game will cost you $20 and individual "planes" of cards will cost you $5 each. If you could just drop $20 on unlocking everything in the game you would be looking at spending only $30 total on DotP 2015. Of course, it isn't that easy... many of the best cards available (including Stoneforge Mystic, Doubling Season, Kozilek, and more) are locked behind "Premium Boosters" which give you 10 random cards for $2 (physical boosters in Standard cost between $2-4 and have 15 cards each). Last year's gambling mechanic was bad but it was only restricted to the Sealed Deck mode. DotP 2015 has essentially become Pay2Win with these boosters because the cards inside can be used in any game mode, including online.
Speaking of online play, there barely is any! 2-Headed Giant has been removed for no reason and no other game modes have been added. You can only play 2-4 player FFA with your custom built decks; no Archenemy, no Planechase, no new modes. With the addition of deck construction and the rise of popularity in Commander/EDH, it is really disappointing that even that wasn't added.
The only good thing that I can say about this is that they finally added non-basic lands. Deck construction is a nice touch finally but the rest of the game has suffered for it. It seems that in order to release the same game on every platform they had to cut content to make it work on mobile devices. DotP 2015 has a tedious, boring, and grindy single player campaign, no Challenges, no multiplayer modes outside of FFA, and no tools to introduce new players to MTG except for the tutorial. This is the worst DotP game made yet (even worse than the original DotP which was removed from Steam) and not even fans of the series should bother with this blatant cash grab.

Beautiful, dark visuals (occasionally outright grotesque), nice animation and visual effects, topped with a quality brooding sound track that merges with and enhances the game’s atmosphere. Puzzles tend to be on the easy side, and making the "right" choice during moral decision time can require a little pondering - but usually fairly clear. Plot and particularly, character development are on the "light" side. I've read many short stories where I feel more invested in the struggles of the main protagonist. Dialogue is passable.
So, what it boils down to is that Tormentum is a visually stunning and atmospheric work of gaming art, let down somewhat by weak character development, an undercooked plot, and puzzles that may not be challenging enough for the average point and click gamer. This said, it would not be fair to say Tormentum is a case of style over substance, because so much of the game's substance lives in its visual and atmospheric qualities.
With pros and cons weighed I would recommend this to anyone looking for a dark fantasy fix.

As someone who has not read the book, this game has given me a profound appreciation for it. This game, though not terribly long, instills that age-old feeling of seeing the world and experiencing new things. I was expecting a slog, I was expecting it to be terribly boring as it seemed like a text game, but I found myself enamoured with it completely.
I had several moments I legitimately regretted not being able to do, from the jewel trades of the orient to trying to rekindle the romance of the woman from Mongolia, to the mutiny of San Francisco. The world was fashionable and entertaining and retained that incredibly important feeling of adventure.
I found glee in both being a good valet, and a bad valet, I found myself both sympathetic to forign governments with their armies of machine men and to the revolution in the heart of a woman found in the snow, nearly dying.
You get to have really divisive moments where you can choose to show your humanity or retain the steely veneer of a professional Valet.
This is a game I would let my kid play to not only allow them an understanding of geography & risk-taking but to give them an understanding of the scope of our world. This is a great, game, maybe not Game of the Year, but a damn good game to sit down and feel the wind in your hair and rekindle the sense of passion one would feel from travel.

As of writing this one week after its "commercial release" I would say that this game is not currently worth the full price they are asking for it simply because it should never have been "released" as it is. I waited until they announced it was being released as I want to be able to play the game rather than constantly reporting bugs, however this game is nowhere near in a releasable state. Frankly it is still an Alpha game and every single play session I have entered into leads to yet more bugs and issues that quite frankly leave me frsutrated and enfuriated. Saxxon, the companies modrator on the steam forums, replies to complaints in snarkiness and with sarcasm and constantly compares this "release" to that of Fallout 4 because "that game has bugs too!" when the fact is that Fallout 4 does have bugs but is still more than playable with minimal stress or concerns whereas I am unable to get through 20 mins of Life is feudal without finding something else which is either broken or was simply half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in development. This game's "release" in no way compare's to Fallout 4, and for that matter I wouldn't compare it to Arkham Knight either which in istelf had a nightmare launch. Frankly, the release of this game is by far the worse PC release I have ever been a part of and what really pains me about that is that the concept of the game in itself is a very good one.
Frankly I am disgusted that the company went straight from Alpha state into "release" completely bypassing the bug detecting beta phase and that they then have the ignorance to have someone like Saxxon treat new players concerns with derision because "well it's not that bad". They made a business decision to say that this game was finished and releasable and so with that there comes higher expectations as to the actual standard of the game and quality of the gameplay. At the moment this game fails on both fronts simply due to constantly encountering game-breaking bugs when trying to do the most basic of tasks. Do not be fooled into thinking that this game is as polished as other games as it really is not, and even now you are paying to participate in an Alpha even if they have removed that from the description. Be prepared to encounter lots of graphical and gameplay issues and also be prepared to submit a lot of bug reports.
The real sad thing is that most of the bugs I (and my girlfriend) have encountered are things that should have been fixed in early alpha stages and so it disheartens me a lot to think that the developer now believes the game is adequate for release. It points to the fact that either the Developer is not actually taking note of issues and fixing them, or that the majority of players who particpated in the original Alpha didnt actually start over from scratch and build things for themselves and instead joined ready built servers. I have read a lot of forum posts from players who quite clearly just joined a pre-existing server where things were already built and so they skipped the majority of the grass routes "find this and build this" content early on. There really isn't any other explanation for why some of these bugs are still in the game at release.
There is also a hell of a lot of mis-information on the internet about the actual workings of the game. The Life is Feudal Wiki being one of the main sources as it seems to be rediculously out of date when you try and look things up. This leads you to look for things that it says you need only to later find that you actually don't and that the process has now changed or become more complicated in some fashion. This is very concenring too considering that the company believes that the game was releaseable and yet they can't even be bothered to update their online information source when they make major changes to the game.
I am extremely frustrated and dissapointed by this game simply because the concept in itself is great. I WANT to like this game and I have been forcing myself to play it and to fight through bug after bug to submit the reports to hopefully get them eventually fixed. The problem is that I simply can not morally support a company who force out a turd and then try and tell you that it is chocolate and that it tastes good because someone else's tastes worse. I have read a lot of forum posts in the last week and Saxxon's demeanor has led me to write this honest review. When a company charges people to play an Alpha version of a game, they damn sure need to listen to the feedback they are given and they need to listen to it with a smile as far as I am concerned. We are playing it more to help at this point than for any real enjoyment of our own and so when you read someone dismissing legitimate concerns simply because they can't be bothered to face the reality, it really frustrates me.
Right now in it's current state I do not recommend this game at it's full listing price. If you see it at 50-60% off again (as it was on its launch week) then by all means buy it but do not expect to play it every day unless you are mentally prepared to encounter a lot of bugs. This game is not worth the full price which is a real shame.
I do have hope that eventually they will get the game in a good and playable condition but I am not expecting that to be anytime sooner than 6 months or so from now, maybe even longer. This leaves me very dissapointed that they have considered "releasing" the game as they have. I will edit this review as and when issues become fixed and the game becomes playable and enjoyable but for now I would say save your money and wait for a sale. I still have hope that this game has a good future, but right now that future seems far off and my hope is not as high as it once was.
EDIT 1:- Well my initial review was written at approx the 40 hours of game time mark, and now since I have doubled that and am at approx 85 hours, I figured i'd update my review to show if anything has changed. Sadly, It hasn't. The more I play the more I see issues which should have been fixed months ago. The in game systems such as Herbalism or Animal Taming are rediculously bloated and make the game a tedious grind more so than any other game I have played, and to make matters worse because the developers have relied heavily on Random Number Generators for everything in game it actually leads players to argue at how easy/hard things are to complete. What people forget is that because the game randomly assigns all recipes to you in something like Herbology, what works for you will not work for anyone else and so if you find it easy it is because the game has made it so the most common herbs are the important ones where as for everyone else the important herbs are the most rare. There is no definitive "the game is easy or hard because" simply because the RNG decides that every time you click create character. The RNG's seem to be everywhere too, such as in taming an animal. I have had one boar that would tame after 5 apples, but then another takes over 50. When you are playing the game as a single or co-op player that is a ton of resources to lose just for a single animal, but the problem is that you have no idea how many you will use until you have used them. Animal taming has many other flaws too such as the idea that you have to chase the animal until it tires itself out which again seems to rely on an RNG as to how long you will have to chase it for. Just today myself and my girlfriend had to chase a horse from dusk one day until the following morning in game and at no point did the horse tire out. It just ran and ran and never stopped. Another major issue is the fact that the animals can run straight through anything that would stop you, so they will literally pass through a tree trunk, stone wall or garden fence whilst you have to run around them. For a game that is supposed to be realistic, more and more I see issues that are simply unrealistic.

I first played this game over 2 years ago when it was offered through EA games website.  Until they shut it down because no one was playing it anymore.  I noticed it was offered through steam and I wanted to come back for 2 main reasons.
First, to see if anything had been changed, improved in all that time and the most important one was so when I wrote this review it would be as accurate as possible.  Yes, I did forget about this game and most of the content in 2 years so I wanted to be accurate.
First of all let me give you my recommendation, NO, please do not download or play this game.
For those of you with no patience it is sid meyers sim city meets micro transactions.
The game is a browser game port that requires flash to play.  It is hardwired so that it prefers google chrome flash over adobe flash.  Up to a few days ago if you had a semi modern pc or laptop you could not even get into the game because it did not recognisze a 64 bit flash version as a valid one.  Yes, it was a straight port over from browser to steam.
Okay I will step up on my soap box, I personally do not think browser games or phone games belong on steam period.
Now I will step off of my soap box and tell you why this game, this Anno Online is bad.
Before I do that I want to give 2 points away to those few people who give this a positive review.  It is not pay to win, there  is no PVP at all, barely any combat I will go into that in detail in a bit.  Let us call it what it is, pay to play.  There is someone in the forum who claimed to be able to unlock everything for free but he did spend over 400 days doing it.  I can not confirm or deny it but it does sound about right.  Let me give you a warning here.  If you ever miss one day logging in your loyalty program will drop back to day 1, even if you did spend 2 years playing it.
My second point I will give those few people with a positive review is if you are going to write a review, good or bad please use more then 1 word so it is helpful.  Okay got those out of the way.
The game is pretty staright forward.
Your little ship shows up on a new island, you build your first house and your first woodcutter.  Total population 1, yeah.
Then you will spend the next 8 to 10 hours depending on how familiar you are with sid meyers sim city games to grow your population from 1 pioneer to 1500 vassals. You will make houses, farms, markets and wells, maybe a church here or there.  Then you scratch your head and go, hmmm, now what.
Now you hit the first pay wall.  Your little settlers are asking you to give them linen shirts which takes hemp which your main island does not have.  So now you have 2 choices.  One you can go to the market place and buy a little island with hemp or build an explorer ship and hope to find one.  This process can take anywhere from 1 day if you are really really really lucky to a week to a month depending on what you find.  This is assuming you managed to avoid all those pop ups for micro transactions getting here.  So for arguments sake, you really "don't" have to buy your first island it just helps.
Then you have your little island.  You think, lets rename it hemp island or something.  Nope, you can not rename any of your islands or ships.  You repeat the sid meyer city building, a few houses, a few woodcutters and some hemp farms.  Now you make your settlers on your main island happy right??  Ah, not really.  What you find is that the little trade ship you can build, or buy can haul back about 5 shirts.  It will take you at least another little hemp island and another trade ship to make any kind of progession in game at all.
Okay so you are still playing, you have your little hemp island and your main island with its 1500 vassals.  By now your pop up help menu has annyoed enough to no end that you will start trying combat.
Combat involves 3 ship types, the brig, the caravel and the galley.  Each one is good against one type, poor against one type and even against ships of the same hull.  You will line up your little ships, hit attack and they move forward like in a chess match and shoot cannons. Period, plain and simple.  Of course you have gem items like chain shot or smoke screens or repair kits to make it a bit more interesting.  For arguments sake, yes you can make these if you get cannon balls as a reward but you will use up way more then you ever get.
Still playing, wow, if you managed to finally unlock the next section you will see that your little settlers now are asking for more goods that you can not make on your home island or your little tiny hemp island.  So now you hit your second paywall.  Do you buy a medium sized island, or a large island or a huge island.  Keep in mind they cost up to 19,000 rubies or $60 each and you can own 12 islands currently.
In my opinion you can buy the stand alone pc copy Anno 1404 and play it for about $10 and have a better, more complete and fun experience.
For a better all round experience I would recommend you pick up any of the Patrician series games, where you can actually move your ships in combat, fire the cannons etc.

Ah, DROD, the Dark Souls of puzzle games, where knowledge is key, and Second Sky, the best way to end a long time series.
Second sky is a product of love and a big collaboration from the original developers with long time community members and level creators. This is shown in every facette. The world is filled with details and lore, every room has new puzzle concepts or advances the really long and epic story to it's ultimate conclusion. Expect twists and turns and great written dialogue on its way. Funny, philosophical, thought-provoking or just some good old character drama. It's all there and even if this game as a whole doesn't look like that, the Lore behind it is absolutely fascinating with its different types of societies and factions that work on very different ideologies. The "Empire of knowledge" is one of the more interesting "evil" factions I know of in a game.
The game itself is classic DROD gameplay with new mechanics and as a first time in the series, some dungeons will force you to go with another weapon than your sword. Every weapon has new rules, but they are easy to understand. For example, the baseball bat like weapon doesn't kill an enemy but you forcefully push the monster for 1 tile and it only goes splat if pushed against a wall. It's fun to play with this and other weapons. They feel very different and the dungeons are all built around the new possibilites of the weapons for even more creative puzzles.
Can I recommend  Second Sky to new players? Ahh, no, you'll be overwhelmed, not in the good way, more in the math class room and you can't comprehend what's going on type of way. For DROD you have to train your brain and let it do some rewiring. The phenomena was discussed in The Witness a lot but also applies extensively to DROD.
With Second Sky it's like playing the Witness3, not a pleasant idea unless you want to feel like a big dumb pile of meat.
DROD has a very linear difficulty curve though and you'll be smoothed into the puzzle concepts with each entry.
Most veterans now say skip KDD though and play:
- Gunthro and the Epic Blunder
- Journey to Rooted Hold
- The City Beneath
- The Second Sky
Also as a good starting point you can check the unofficial wiki for elements and monsters here:
The lore section isn't really filled out though.

Alright here is my review of the Early Access of Nether.
This is a First Person Survival Horror RPG (possibly MMO) title with alot of great potential. Being it's a beta, the game does have some bugs, and collision issues, but those collision issues also occur to enemies. (Watching a Golem "bounce" on a car for 2 minutes is pretty funny).  Here's some of the basics on the gameplay:
You start with creating a custom character before plunging into the open world. You'll find yourself with a Skill Tree, a Money display, and Gold Count (For Believer's and Chosen they get in-game gold, which isnt that great unless you wanna buy colorful gasmasks and such).  When you start in, your equipped with a Kitchen Knife, and a 8 Slot Backpack.
You must play the game slowly and strategically to avoid death, as this game runs a permadeath system, and it will clear your levels too!
On your travels you will come across mutant creatures. Here's a list of names of what to expect:
Crawler
Shrieker
Golem
Watcher
Nether
Stalker
(I may be forgetting one other name.) These creatures at first will be hard to battle, as they do teleport around you. For newest players I recommend upon leveling up, to put a skill point into the Melee tree, So you can learn to block, which will negate the physical attacks of most of the creatures. Once you make a good strategy to fight, then you will be fine, just dont take on a group of 3-4 Nether creatures without a some sort of gun.
These aren't your only enemies at the moment, PvP is a biggy in this game. Which I personally dislike, but have overlooked it as I have managed to stay out of the way of other players, or, kill them first.  Most players are out to kill and loot your body. Many will loom around outside Safezone's waiting to strike someone who thought they were safe. Others will traverse Rooftops, surveying the ground for supplies, and their next kill. You are never really safe in this game, and maybe that was an aspect the developers meant. You will find yourself in a panic, trying to hide from creatures, trying to outrun and gun players, and of course all while finding supplies.
Within Safezones you have the opportunity to make purchases AND BANK YOUR ITEMS. This is an absolute part of keeping your supplies, as YOU WILL DIE, many times.  I think some players over look this ability, but its so essential. However, sometimes, Safezones will fall prey to Nether Attacks and Surges., when this is about to occur, the game will prompt you roughly 10 minutes in advance. Its best to grab what you need and run for the next Outpost. Attacks usually last an hour of real time. So it will be a while before you can come back.
Amongst those, there are Supply Drops in game that last 15mins. If you have no supplies as it is, and are no where near the drop, forget about it. The loaded players will be there first with rifles and guns waiting for someone to try to grab loot. Its an easy bait for a not so smart player. If your decked out, and think you can grab the loot, then go for it. But bring ammo and a decent ranged weapon, you'll want to pick off enemy players  before moving in.
As for objective? Survive. Its that simple. Its a sandbox of sorts, and you choose what you do, as long as you manage to keep yourself alive. Don't overthink think this one. Think of this as a Fallout MMO, minus the futuristic feel, the mini-nukes, etc etc.
The Best Way to Play: Bring a friend into this game! Seriously, your not gonna be able to trust anyone else in the game, so have a friend tag along. The added teamwork will improve survival. If your a lone wolf, be smart, know your surroundings, and keep a low profile. Nether creatures are easy to sneak past, as they rely on hearing and a close proximity of sight to find you. Other players are easy to avoid to, keep low and track them till they move on, if its someone with a gun, then keep a close eye on them, chances are, they will shoot you if they see you. If its some new player with just a Kitchen Knife, don't be an a-hole, leave them be, you were new to this world at one point too.
Where to Loot: Best places are normally lit up, so scavenge Ambulances, Military Trucks, Convience Stores , and Gas Stations. I find Gas Stations best as they have money, food, ammo, and maybe even a weapon at times.
Overall: 8.75/10

OVERVIEW REVIEW
Ok, lets get this straight, this is not a perfect game, but that depends on what you get angared upon more: lack of content, bugs or optimization and gameplay. This game has a lot of things to give and has no lack of content whatsoever.
The play style is like a fuse of fast paced rts, total war, campaign and city management and has it's own play style. As for bugs... they are out there and they will outnumber your men.
Content and Playstyle
----------------------
The content they give you is to choose from 3 races, very interesting, wide, unique and original races: Humans, Elves and Orcs
(I chose humans because I always do) You start off by having a village and a town elder instructs you how to manage it with a very funny and old langauge. As humans you will start off with simple quests like slaying ogres, trading with towns and training simple soldiers like swordsmen, macemen, halberds, archers, cavaliers and so on who you will upgrade later in game to royal troops like knights, and beasts like minotaurs, dragons, dwarves and wizards. You also start with a hero who you will upgrade along the game. Troops are also upgradeable and leveled, troops will gain experience in battle and you will be able to upgrade their attack, health, speed, defense etc. Is there something else... Oh yes! You can siege AI and player castles and take their loot, you will have to find out on your own how it works, there is also a vassal and diplomacy machanic with AI, you can take over castles to become your vassals and interact with lords through quests and such.

I have 3 major gripes with the game in it's current state (as of 2/16/17).
1:P2P
For those that don't know matches are not completely Ubisoft hosted, they are only a small part of it that makes sure that players are connected to the ubisoft network. Matches are hosted using a p2p system that connects players to one another to form a match lobby. P2P does not exactly work well with a game like For Honor. Such problems like; lag, connection stability, disconnections, rage quiting(yes it does happen quit a bit). All of which can ultimately crash a lobby and leave a lot of frustration.
2:Guard Breaking (2/23/17 Update! They reverted this back to state that it was in Beta)
In combat you have 3 stances; Up, Left, Right. You can Block and attack from all of these stances, but you can also be guard broken. Now this can be ountered BUT from beta to release there was a change, and not for the better in my opinion. Currently you can't counter the second you see that your opponent is guarding breaking you, before you could counter it the second you saw it. The reason I have a problem with this is by the time the system allows you respond you've already been stunned and more then likely giving your opponent the upper hand in the fight. I found this change frustrating upon release to that point that I feel it's pointless to try and counter it.
3:Ladders
How can ladders be such a big problem? Let me tell you, as far back as alpha and to release ladders have been unreasonably dumb. If you attempt to climb a ladder while your opponent slides down it into you, it will knock you off and deal an enormous amount if not killing you first. This also works the same way going up, if you manage to hit an apponent above on a ladder it with knock them off without question dealing just as much damage. From my time in the beta and after release a fair amount of players use this tactic to their advantage often.
4:Matchmaking (I know I said 3 but this is minor compared to the rest)
A fair a few times now I've spent atleast 3-5 times queing for a gamemode for it to fail either because the lobby was full or the connection just failed  to connect to the lobby.
But all and all here are my cons and pros.
Pros:
Beatiful Graphics
Decent Hero Customization (not enormous amount but more then enough to make everyone look different from one another)
Fluid Combat (when P2P plays nicely)
Cons:
P2P
Current Guard Breaking System
Ladders

Tormentum is a point & click game set in a dark world with soundtracks and art style that make it unique in its genre. The story is fairly simple and revealed slowly bit by bit, with a great twist at the end. There are no combat mechanics or even player-controlled movement, and yet at no point have I felt these things missing. You navigate the world room by room, relying on your perception to interact with your surroundings, picking up items and using objects. Collectables have a slight shine to them, which makes it a bit easier to spot them and you won't spent much time hunting down items. The game involves a lot of puzzle solving but most of them are easy enough, with only a few that can make you stuck on them (especially if you missed the hints). The graphics in this game are pure works of art, and the eerie soundtracks complete the depressing, grim feel of the world you are traversing. Every now and then you will have to make a moral choice, and these choices will essentially decide your ultimate ending. Wish the game was a bit longer, but it's not too short as it is. It would also be great if there was voice acting instead of just plain text. Overall, Tormentum has enough replayability value for at least 2 playthroughs and a total of 5-6 hours of entertainment and is in my opinion definitely worth the price.
+ A well told, easy to follow story with a great twist
+ Awesome graphic style
+ Excellent soundtracks
+ Simple but powerful moral choices
+ Striking, interesting characters
+ The atmosphere is very well set and realistic
- A bit short
- Most puzzles very easy
- No voice acting (except intro)

What seemingly starts out as a strangely random and certainly frightening sequence of surreal experiences quickly turns into a deep search for what your soul truly harbours. A multitude of choices, sometimes harder than you might think, will be brought before you in this game, and it is up to you to decide if your fate can still be changed.
Tormentum: Dark Sorrow can easily be finished within less than 5h, but considering that only half the achievements and one of the two possible endings can be gained with one play-through, you will definitely be incited to attempt a second one and, in doing so, question the choices you have made before.
You won't regret plunging into this nightmarish world that reeks of inspirations such as Giger, Bosch, Poe or Frances, and that enchants with atmospheric music and sometimes profound dialogues. The difficulty could have been raised a little, seeing as most of the riddles can be solved in hardly any time, but in the end that simply makes the game more appealing to a broader audience.
