When I heard about this through Kickstarter, it was the one and only time I have ever backed something. Why? Because I adore NEKOPARA. It's the VN that got me into VNs, and the one I compare all others to. It's also the only VN I still really watch, and have sunk hundreds of hours into it's three volumes (four, if you count 0. Most don't).
Do I regret backing it? Not remotely.
However, that said, the 'yes' recommendation for this isn't as pure a yes as I give the VN originals. Don't get me wrong, I loved this OVA. The characters really came alive in it, and the way it stayed very pure to the original was impressive, to say the least. Very few video/film adaptions of books/VNs manage.
And yet, this OVA doesn't quite feel like true NEKOPARA. I think the reason for this is because it just wasn't quite long enough, and was missing far too much content. And no, I don't mean the H scenes. What, as a writer myself and almost compulsive reader, I loved about NEKOPARA was the deep character and plot development throughout. The OVA, whilst true to the plot for the most part, tried to pack a very extensive plot into too short an OVA. The result was a lot of cut content, and not necessarily in a pleasing manner - especially since a lot of the cut content is the stuff concerning the growing relationship between Kashou, Chocola and Vanilla, which is pretty much absent during the OVA, and was pretty much the focus of the VN.
I'm not saying this should have been longer. I imagine the effort that went into what came out was extensive for all involved. Asking for more would have been cruel, in a way. And yet, that said, there was a lot of stuff missing, a lot of development that just didn't make it into the OVA. And without it, it doesn't have the same impressive feel of the VN. To be honest, without it, sections of it just rush through without any real explanation or plot, and if I didn't know the VN so well (perhaps TOO well), some of the OVA doesn't really make sense.
Was this OVA worth backing? Yes. Do I regret doing so? God no. Would I recommend watching it? Definately. But I think that, to be frank, if it's a choice, you're better off with the VN, unless you dislike the reading part. And unless you speak Japanese, you'll still have to read the subtitles anyway, which are kind of annoying with the steam video player - which isn't the OVA designer's fault, far as I know. This is the only video I've ever watched on Steam, after all.
I've run on a bit more than intended here. I usually do :) Overall, whilst I would recommend this OVA to anyone who enjoys NEKOPARA, if you haven't read the VN, go with that. It's a lot deeper, and makes a lot more sense. This is great fanservice, so to speak. But for those unfamiliar with the world of NEKOPARA, it's a little hard to follow at times, and lacks the strong story of it's source material.

Pretty solid visual novel/text adventure-type game with time & money management mixed in. Better suited/designed for mobile/handheld but works fine on PC.
You start in London and then slowly make your way east through a variety of cities. It seems like each of the many cities are uniquely described and you often meet interesting personalities who can hinder or help your progress.
There is a steampunk aspect to it (a lot of mechanical contraptions, robots/androids, artificers' guilds) and alternate history type of things that clearly distinguish this world from the real history. So the most education you'll get is geography (learning where cities are located), the rest is flavored/inspired by the real world but not something you should take seriously.
My favorite part of the game was finding and dealing with the events that occurred. Sometimes events can have different outcomes when you bring items from previous locations (like the Artificer's Medallion).
You have four options in most (but not all) cities: Market, Bank, Explore, and Sleep/Depart. The Market is where you buy and sell items. The Bank is where you can withdraw money after waiting a period of time. Explore is used to find routes out of the city. Sleep/Depart is to move to the next day or view routes out of the city.
Items come in four varieties: Travel items to keep Fogg in good shape while travelling under certain conditions, Conversation items that allow you to ask more questions about routes, Commodity items that sell well in certain cities, and Route Maps that show available routes in a region.
You have three options that can appear during travel: News/Wait, Converse, and Attend. News brings up a one-line headline on world events that usually doesn't affect travel. Converse is where you talk to learn about routes and destinations and use Conversation items. Attend raises Fogg's satisfaction with your service and his health by a few points.
Some other notes:
Worth a look if you enjoy VNs/text-based adventure games.

To catch up to the times and when this review was written, it's about the rerelease of Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic II - The Sith Lords, which was meant to, as previously said, catch up with the times. However it does feel awfully detached from the original Xbox version of the game, of which this rerelease seemed to have been aimed to recreate.
First off and foremost, the native widescreen resolution is, simply said, very nice. Being able to launch the game straight from Big Picture Mode with a controller while kicking your feet upon the coffee table and relaxing on the couch staring at your TV is somewhat reminiscent of what it was like to play it on console many years ago. However, with it being "native", there was a very large
on
side of things, as it was simply just the widescreen modification that users could have done themselves on the older release of this game. What that entails is that the text on screen, on a TV, is relatively difficult to read without squinting your eyes until they turn red. Needless to say, they just added something that many have been able to do through WSGF for some time now.
Secondly, the controller support. Pardon my barbaric comment on this specific topic, but WHO DESIGNED IT. Absolute RUBBISH. I still haven't figured out what the triggers are supposed to do, they added a mini pop up window. A POP UP WINDOW. With functions that were previously mapped to dedicated buttons in the original version of the game on the original Xbox. Furthermore, they excited everyone with the additional controller support, however, it seemed to have been a last minute after thought by those who were porting it. They had the tools to make it original, yet they still screwed it up.
Thirdly, the action bar will always, I say again, ALWAYS, appear on your character's head. Unlike the original that we have come to know and love, they butchered this unique, simple and useful feature by, I don't know... Attempting to "generalize" it for all scenarios? Whatever the reason is, they butchered it. It gets in your view during combat or when you simply want to see what you are hitting.
Quadruply, they did not add a virtual keyboard into the game. I know many games don't have this capability, but guess what... It's 2015. People don't want to deal with the hassle of using a physical keyboard to type their name or save game title in if they are using a controller. They proved that controller support, once again, was an after thought.
I'm giving this port a 0/5
However, the game is receiving a 5/5, simply because it's KOTOR.
For any of those who don't want to deal with subpar garbage and wouldn't mind doing some simple set ups to get your BPM setup up and running with a controller and KOTOR widescreen that feels like the original, feel free to search for my controller support on YouTube by searching the following: SW:KOTOR [GAMEPAD UPDATE] [Dualshock 4 Support!]
I proved that I could make a controller profile, for free, that had nearly 90% replication using digital red neck methods of creating my own controller support. In fact, I took the two seconds out of my life to grab the KOTOR 2 manual and replicate the controls of each button and add them into a functional control scheme. The amount of downloads that my controller schemes have acquired and the views my videos have earned merely prove the requirement of PROPER controller support in such games, especially games that were released approximately 10 years ago.

This is a fun and simple game, within interesting visuals and cool music. It's nice to see a new type of rhythm game.
However, being a rhythm game enthusiast, there is one thing I can barely bear:
Your score for each level is your highest streak, meaning that if you miss a single note halfway through the stage (which is almost always the case), you're fated to get a C rank or lower. You could simply chalk this up to difficulty, but missing one note out of five hundred at the wrong time can feel random and unfair.
For instance, I'm currently looking at an end screen: 393/399 hit, 92% accuracy. Not bad, right? Nope, it's an E rank.
Compounding this, It's difficult to get started in the game because the training system is rather misleading. The Streak training (the default) is
what you would normally see in the game; the Rhythm training is much closer to the actual experience. Once it clicks, though, you'll suddenly be able to beat the first level.
One last point of contention is the level editor, or rather, the lack of one. Creating a level basically means creating a Lua script that draws the game board every frame. This allows for very flexible level design, but makes it nearly impossible for someone who doesn't already know how to program to make levels for it. It's no wonder that there's only one level in the workshop, and it's very simple compared to the built-in levels.
Despite these flaws, the game itself is quite fun. The mechanics are simple: Look at the small square, and press the corresponding key on the beat that it becomes the big square. As the levels progress, interesting effects are added on which tempt your eyes away from the squares. The music and effects are well chosen, and are definitely worth the difficulty of getting a C rank on the previous level to experience.
All in all, a small fun game that's certainly worth $4.
I'm designing a level myself and I'm also planning on making a video guide for non-programmers, so maybe we can get that workshop level count up.
(Edit: After writing this, I noticed this game is apparently about "human adaptation to strange environments." That's still no excuse for using a terrible scoring metric, Undef.)

So as someone who has been looking forward to this game, it most certainly lived up to the hype for me personally.
I keep seeing negative reviews on P2P and Paid Progression, so let me first get this out of the way.
I've had 2 bad instances of Connection Issues since release and the same could be said for most of my friends, there's an issue here and there, but people are boarding this bandwagon and using against the good faith of the game.
The Paid Progression? The gamemodes where gear actually gives you stats are not there for a competitive feel, they are there for fun, Hack and Slash type feels! If someone wants to spend hundreds of dollars to get good gear to play Dominion or Skirmish, that's completely up to them! Gear is completely cosmetic in 2v2, 1v1. Where the beauty of the combat system lays. It's not made for big player battles, even then. I have beaten multiple players with higher gearscore than them. Gearscore adds a small amount of damage or other stats. Have no doubt, it's still a skillbased game. A Good player with bad gear and a bad player with good gear will get absolutely destroyed and anyone that's played the game consistantly will agree with me.
Now if you're interested in the competitive nature of the game, then it's for you. If you want it for the Story, it's short, it's there to teach players the combat system while offering dialogue and story, while it's amazing fun on Realistic and offers you cosmetic rewards and whatnot for battling through it, DO NOT buy this game for it's story.
But if you're interested in a adrenaline filled, intense combat experience within a competitive scene, then this game is most certainly worth a try for you. There has been moments where i've felt my heartbeat in my throat from an intense duel with a very good player.
Now, Ubisoft's attention to detail within it's appearance editor, is great fun! Playing matches to hope for some better looking gear is absolutely exciting! Hundreds and hundreds of different combinations to make yourself look and sound unique!
While the game has a few issues here and there, it's not something that's out of the ordanarry for a newly released AAA title, if anything it has much less issues than some AAA Games, i will say no names though.
I have played all of the Closed Alpha/Techanical Tests, Closed Beta/Open Beta. I believe i have the experience to forward this review.

As someone who despises jump scares... this wasn't awful. It relied more on atmosphere and a sense of dread (like any good horror game/movie should) to make it as creepy as possible. While there tends to be a good bit of back tracking, it doesn't get too boring because of the changing surroundings. The audio generally stayed consistent in volume, no sudden increase in sound or screaming (there is occasional screaming, but it’s often distant and you get use to that). Well, I found the overall game to be loud and volume not very easy to adjust (only had a scale from 1-10), but everything is loud to me. The graphics, while not horrible, are not the best. I found I had a consistent blurry line 1/3 up from the bottom of my screen when looking at walls through the whole game, and though it could be ignored, it was a bit distracting. A few finally things; the inventory felt a little clunky but never took away from the game, constant maintenance for your health and sanity are not overly difficult, storyline/plot was engaging and allowed for multiple endings based on final choices, and while there are ‘cut-scenes’ they seem to add more than they take away. I was able to complete the game and all its endings in 12.5 hours, split over two days. I highly recommend playing it at 4am.
This game offered an interesting (if not almost-accurate) depiction of the human psyche and its response to trauma, denial, and torture. When the description boasts that the game “pulls no punches when trying to immerse you”, I think they may have rather meant they ‘pull no punches’ when describing torture. While the act is never shown visually, the aftermath is very in-your-face and the audio is… chilling. I don’t recommend this for anyone who cannot handle sounds of bones breaking, flesh/bones grinding, what may have been chewing, or other fleshy, squishy noises. Written descriptions are also given occasionally, though only 4 are very notable for extreme physical harm.

This game was honestly terrifying for me. Because it's so well-renowned, many people think it's overrated, but I honestly loved it. Maybe I thought it was scary because it was my first real horror game playthrough, but I enjoyed everything about the game. The atmosphere, monster AI, setting - everything was fantastic. It gives you a false sense of security at the best moments, forces you to encounter the enemies, and eases you into the difficulty at a good pace. The game mechanics are great - stay in the dark to avoid danger, but don't stay for too long or else your sanity will drain, and when your sanity is low you're more likely to be seen - it's stuff like that that keeps you on your toes the whole time. I enjoyed that it wasn't just an "avoid the monsters to progress" experience, instead, it's very puzzle-centric and has a deep and thorough story as you recover your memories and the truth about your past. Overall I was thoroughly scared the whole way through, but it was satisfying enough for me to build up the courage to play just a bit more each time.

So... Arma 3... one of the most fun and stupid games you'll ever play.
I'll jump right into the pros and cons for those who just want to see if its worth buying or not.
Pros
+ Extremely customizable, if you can think of a scenario then (as long as you have the mods) you will be able to create it
+ It's great fun to grab 2 of your friends, throw down a zeus module, set up a town for them to take then laugh at them as everytime they kill an ai you spawn in another one on the other side of town.
+ The ai allow you to fill in the roles of people that you may not have for those larger scale scenarios
+ There are so many mods its ridiculous, one second your squad is tactically clearing out a town and the next you're in massive mech suits shooting at zombies as someone shoots at you from a destroyer class battleship.
+ Massive player base with a huge list of servers in different regions so if you don't feel like doing something yourself or with friends (or you don't have any) you can always connect to a server.
However as fun as that all sounds this games is not without it's negatives.
Cons
- Stupid DLC, I would seriously recommend buying arma 3 on sale and as a bundle. There really isn't much point in just having base game arma without the DLC bundle 1 or Apex as it severaly limits what you can do and in many case stops you from joining your friends and servers.
- the ai are uhh IDK, the ai themselves are a joke. Heres an example. I'm flying an apache at 200Km/h at 500 metres in the sky, however one ai sniper one shots me in the head and I've lost the helicopter.... Other times ai won't enter a building for some unknown reason, the ai drivers are rather dim and don't know how to not crash into every object ever, and if they do crash they become stuck there for all eternity. so aside from god like accuracy, idiotic driving and awful tacticul decisions they're pretty okay.
- Really you need the mods for this game to be interesting. Without the mods the gun sounds become flat and dull after awhile, you lay on an RGN frag grenade and survive it, also you can't climb over walls... only low level picket fences. the guys creating arma work very closely with the mod creators but really a lot of these things should already be in the base game.
- Ask any arma player for one word to describe the game. you'll start to hear a common theme. Buggy. Arma feels like the king of bugs. From breaking your legs by climbing down a ladder to being thrown over the map for no apparent reason, this game needs a lot of heavy bug fixes. Don't get me wrong a lot of these bugs have been sorted but seriously there are way to many still around.
- Have you ever wanted 40 different crouching positions?. Aside from the controls being more confusing than a spaceship or your friend's shower, they feel awful. Winning CQB firefights feels more like pot luck than anything. I'm almost scared to fight someone in a building.
A little wrap up of everything. Arma feels like a clunky buggy mess that survives on mod support. But by george it is heeps of fun. The literaly thousands of possibilities make it so the game never gets boring. I would recommend buying this game but only if you're going to through hours and hours into understanding it and how to work around the issues.

Age of Empires - in the first person! --Reviewed at 18 hours--
If you are in doubt about this game, I urge you to just jump in and YouTube & Wiki willing you will enjoy this game!
There is little to no tutorial and things may frustrate you, I would urge you to push past this and open up a world of possibilities
Not many games get 15 hours of straight play; Life is Feudal did it for me.
The game based in a medieval era urges the players not to play as a simulator but to think logically and forward think for your new character and live in the world grinding out skills to reach the next skill type that you need to progress your settlement. (So yes it is a simulator but not to the level that we have previously known it, you get invested in your players as you roleplay out their lives and complete many, many tasks)
As a SP game it will be hard to manage your land and its needs along with other players in the MP realm...
You may choose to be a travelling tradesmen specialised in your skill trading for what you need or you might choose to join a group and move forward in leaps and bounds for the greater good of the group... However be forewarned, as you grow into a large group the needs change and your supply of food and mining rewards may begin to find a low and risk everything that you have so far worked so valiantly for!
The depth of this game is astounding, the devs listen to the gitch reports and actively seek to fix them with frequent patches. Yes glitches do occur and there are other things that just don't match up; this game has come a long way from its alpha release in many ways and its current gameplay today proves just that.
The question is are you willing to fork out your own investment into a character and help etich them them into history.
10/10 for such vast gaming ideas
8(9) for current game state due to some stability issues
8.5 for graphics - this game is beautiful, however Nvidia uses may struggle; the Devs use ATI.
8 for sound - mesmerizing
10 for the right server and community input
Buy the game if you are on the fence;
buy the game if you doubt the glitches;
buy the game if you like medieval games;
buy the game if you like want minecraft with REAL graphics;
buy the game if you like Age of Empires, it's it in first person!

We have gone far in attempting to immerse ourselves with catgirls, just short of genetic experimentation (we have this stupid "medical ethics code" to blame). Our most successful attempt of catgirl immersion has been of the absolutely groundbreaking Nekopara series of visual novels that has been met with among the highest of praise from the world over, so good that almost every award ceremony has refused to acknowledge the series as it would completely sweep the awards. This revolutionary series has just branched out into the world of anime, where it continues to stay as fantastic as ever. How so, you may ask? Well, I can explain it easily. NEKOPARA OVA, much like the visual novels...
Most people would be lying if weren't interested in catgirls. But I can see why, as they may be a tad too advanced for our simple minds to comprehend. However, NEKOPARA OVA is able to condense the first visual novel, one of the biggest milestones in the history of catgirls into a single, hour long movie. The OVA easily introduces a newcomer to the concept of catgirls. It gradually drip-feeds the viewer ideas like "How are catgirls domesticated? How do they behave? How can I ♥♥♥♥ a catgirl?" These ideas and their explanations may be simple for those who already have experience with catgirls, however they are presented in such a way that it's impossible for anyone, inexperienced or experienced to be bored or uninterested.
These ideas are revolutionary, yes, however as with the visual novel, the other aspects hold on their own as is. The story, while simple in concept, is enhanced with the addition of catgirls, which adds many philosophical levels. The catgirls are all beautifully drawn and animated in a way that appeals to anyone. I do believe they are drawn too well, as it only reminds us of the fact that we will potentially never see catgirls in our lifetime. The catgirls however, are also written and portrayed fantastically; the voice acting would make you swear that catgirls truly exist, and the character interactions demonstrate the way that they are all top-tier waifus. We have the script to thank, which has in it some of the most genuine and realistic interactions possible for a slice of life, in addition to the story and the ideas that it presents to the viewer.
If you want catgirls, go and get the games. I haven't played them myself yet, but I've heard that they're...games. (Yes, you ♥♥♥♥ the catgirls, now go get it) If you
want catgirls, then feel free to spend 33.99 Canadian fun bucks on this OVA. Yeah, it's one hell of a steep price and I definetely wouldn't recommend it at that. You can get the entire series on sale and STILL have around 7 dollars to spare for the same price. It's your money and I'm not one to judge you and your fetishes.
My friend got this as a joke for my birthday. Fun little thing to do with some dosh that really wouldn't have been spent any better, honestly. After we both felt ashamed of ourselves, I sat down and prepared for the worst and...well, it wasn't bad. Take what I said before and tone it down, tone it WAY the hell down. Nekopara's OVA is a comfy slice of life, and I love slice of life. The characters are pretty cliche, but come on, they're fun to watch
they're catgirls! It's simple, adorable, is pretty damn well animated, and it's just fun to watch. It's definetely not worth 34 Canadian, but if you really have that much to throw at catgirls, then...♥♥♥♥ it.
Go do what your heart desires, and if that's catgirls, then so be it.

When I picked this game up in a Humble Bundle, I really didn't expect it to be so addictive! I was anticipating mildly interesting interactive fiction, and what I got was a smart, funny reimagining of Verne's novel, packed with interesting characters and seemingly infinite possibilities. I love the steampunk elements - they feel true to the spirit of the original, if not to the letter of it - and the development of Passepartout as a character is excellent. The writing is very rich, and there are some truly affecting moments.
Thanks to the ever-ticking clock you can't explore everything in one game, but every playthrough offers glimpses of possible adventures that you can seek out next time. Every time I finish a journey I want to start again and see what happens if I do something a bit differently - explore a new route, build different relationships, pursue a new achievement.  I've got so involved with this game that I still haven't got round to installing the game I actually bought the Humble Bundle to acquire...
With the new season updates this game is incredible now. Maybe a little bit expensive but it's definitely worth it.

I thought I would post my own review of this software, it miight have a postive rating, but I don't feel this software is very good.
The first thing that needs to be addressed is that, this doesn't use it's own firewall code, instead, it uses windows own firewall. So if you already have a security suit or third party firewall, then glasswire becomes pretty useless. And while I have used windows firewall for a bit, I used a third party app that controls the firewall better then what glasswire does. the problem is, this doesn't give you any real prompts if something is making an outband connection, or inbound connection, like some third party firewalls do. Sure you can block apps that are already running, but then again, I would rather have a prompt if something is making a connection.
If you want better firewall control, or a better firewall period, (third party) then I suggest you look else where.
Which leads me to my second major gripe with the program.
The bandwidth monitor.
as it stands, the bandwidth monitor is also next to useless. why? because of a silly design choice or bug, and the devs refuse to fix it, even though I brought this to their attetnion a long time ago, (last year infact)
basically, it tracks over last month as well as the current month. so if you are on the 5th of June, then instead of showing bandwith only from that month, it also includes bandwidth from last month. this makes finding out how much you used pretty annoying, not without having to manually set the dates and sliders to only show the usage from the month you are on. What is worse is, the devs refuse to fix this problem in V1, currently released version) and said that this will be fixed in V2 (and seems that is taking a very long time, as they been saying that will be here X then Y then goodness knows when.)
But what is staggering is why this was like this from the get go? why does the bandwidth monitoring spread over two months? and why are they refusing to fix this when it should be an easy fix? So while the software might seem useful on the face of it, I can't recommend it. And as for when V2 is coming? I have know idea, info on that seems very thin on the ground, and V2 should properly track the full month and not half a month. But still, why not fix this in V1 and why was this even released like this I don't know.
Anyway, I have ditched the software, found a better firewall and bandwidth monitor, and gave up waiting for this so called V2.

At 0.3 hours I really, REALLY wanted to vote "No" out of frustration.
At 0.4 hours, things clicked; I beat the first level and I decided that "Yes", I would recommend this game.
The most frustrating hurdle is finding the "correct" rhythm with which to play the game, and learning to "read" the squares.
Despite what the first level says, it is *NOT* "easy" to pick up and play immediately.
Bind the keys to whatever is most comfortable for you (I did ABXY), and spend some time in Training getting the timing down. Wherever the "little box" is, that's the next button to press. The "Big Box" moves to the location of the button you're supposed to be pressing. Make sure you hit the button at exactly the same time as you hear the "beat". Too early, and it counts as a mistake of the last "beat". Hesitate, and your rating will be poor.
Just when you start to do well, the game starts changing colors, altering animations, and jittering like crazy. The first animation shift hit me like a brick wall every time; Here I am without even a half hour of game time or a single level under my belt, and already the game is trying to throw off the controls and rhythm that I'm still struggling to learn.
The music is good, which is crucial for a title like this. Workshop support seems interesting, though I haven't played any custom levels yet.
If you're thinking of buying this game: It's like the sadistic lovechild of Super Hexagon and Bop It, conceived on a bed of nails. I think "relaxing" is a bit of a stretch, but it's definitely a game that puts you in "The Zone". On the Port Royale 2 fansite they state there is two option available, either play it on XP or buy the 'Reloaded' version.
I guess Steam doesn't have that version.
I have since managed to get the game working, here's how:
1) (Possibly optional) Try setting your launch options as "-32bit" (without quotations)
2) Select browse local files for Port Royale 2 from the Steam menu, scroll down and right click PR2.exe and select Properties and then select compatibility mode for Windows 98/Windows ME, then click apply.
3) Finally change your desktop resolution to 1280x720 (this is the key part). You may also find that simply by changing your desktop resolution to 1280x720 that you won't have to bother with the other options.

// BeamNG.drive is a 3D Racing Simulator: //
// Schuitje82 - Extended Review //
When I made this review the game had been released in Early Access.
There is no influence from the maker due to a free key or any other reasons.
Title: BeamNG.drive
Genre: Race, Simulator,
Developer: BeamNG
Release date: 29 mei 2015 (Early Access)
Why I wanted it, and maybe you will too?
===============================
Personally I love race / car simulator video games.
If it's a racing game like Forza or a Sandbox simulator I want to play them all.
I've watched some movies and reviews about this game and wanted to know for myself what this game is all about.
Yes it's a simulator and oh yeah.... you can crash your car and it’sreally AWESOME!
Still, I wanted to try it myself and make a review about it.
Core Gameplay:
============
This is a pure simulator, so if you are looking for a racing game, maybe this is also something for you.
You have some different modes to choose from, like Scenarios such as Freeroaming.
Scenarios are  for the people who like to have a goal while they play around with the simulator.
I must say there are really very many modes made for you to try.
For example: Road Race, Jumps, Full Circuit Racing, Rally Croos Long Courses, Destruction Derby (multiplayer) and much more!
The Free roaming is really cool for the player who likes to drive around the levels the Dev's made for us.
You can choose already from 10 massive levels that you can drive and play through with all the cars that are ready to pickup from the car list.
If you think, “What kind of levels?’ for example:
You can choose from giant cliff, Derby Arena, Small Island, USA; and East Cost, USA as a Raceway to go high speed.
So these modes give you many hours of fun and in the future they will add campaigns for more ways to play.
Last option and I think the coolest is the "Add Content" option.
What makes this game really cool is that you can add your own levels and mods to it that other people have built for us.
Check the MOD section on the online website to see all the crazy and cool things other people have made for this awesome game.
I geot excited after every page seeing what all people have made for this great sanbox simulator !!
Graphics:
========
The first thing that makes this a nice simulator is the graphical part. (In my opinion.)
Everything looks really amazing and that was the first thing i noticed about the game that made me want to try it.
Not only the roads, but even the tree's a looking amazing. What appeals to me most is the car detail!
For example the car interior, engine, and everything else looks really amazing,.
aAnd let’s not forget about the damage that can be done to your car!
If you crash into a tree, your car’s hood folds like a piece of paper.
I think they did a really great job with this aspect of the game!
The onOnly thing I think is annoying sometimes: with a small crash even when there isn’t any huge physical damage, your car can get stuck and not be moved / driven.
Controls:
=======
I played the game with my keayboard as well as my Xbox 360 Wireless controller.
I can recommend the controller because you have more feeling with it.
For example, make sure to remember that  when you take a turn, sometimes your car brakes out and with a controller it is much easier to control and recover the car.
I'm happy with the dev's choice for controller support because many games I play in early access does not support this.
The cars feltels really weird in the beginning when I played the game, only after some time did I get used to it.
Every car feels slightly different, which and still makes it fun to play and try every car that I can choosice from.
They did a really good job with the different roads, likeand I mean is whean you go offroad racing.
Multiplayer:
=========
Still this is a early access game, but there are some crazy co-op local co-op things to do.
Like destructiiton derby, that is a lot of fune to play with up to 4 players local.
I hope the Dev's can add online multiplayer modesmode to this, so we can all drive all together!.
Overall:
======
This a really fun and well madegood and fun Car simulator where  you can have hours of fun!.
TheGame game wais only released infrom 2015 and there are allready so many community mods we can try out!.
It's a nice project with very much potential to it.... so Dev's keep up the good work.
I give this Simulator a 9/10 score.
A job well done !!

80 Days
Or, more aptly, "Around the World in 80 Days".
This game is fun. Set in a steampunk 1700s (?) world, in which the artificers guild has amazing contraptions that can help you get around the world, you play Passeporteau (spelling?), the French serving man to a wealthy English gentleman. He made a twenty-thousand pound bet that he could get around the world in 80 days, and it's you're job to accomplish that.
You can go just about any way you like, through just about any cities you desire, in your attempt to race around the globe. You have to manage your money, and your Monseur's health, in order to complete the trip. Buy and sell goods to keep the income flowing, or visit a bank, and never look back. The artwork is fantastic and the music is simple and charming.
The one thing I really didn't like about this game was the... what's the word. Dialogue? Monologue? Thought processes?
I don't know what to label it. The game is told past tense, through the Diary of Passeporteau. By selecting his conversation options/choices in the diary, you tell the story that is told in the Diary. A very interesting and fun mechanic. Kingdom Wars is truly a unique take on the RTS (Real Time Strategy) genre and is truly worth a try for both fans of the genre as well as those new to it.  People who are fans of city-building simulators will also find much to enjoy in this unique title.
While Kingdom Wars has gone through many changes, some good, some less-than-desirable, overall the experience is really something that has to be experienced to understand it.  The very early stages of the game can be somewhat confusing, however it is my understanding that the developers have addressed this issue in the time since I was a new player.
Although there is the option to spend real money (in fact, I obtained my copy of the game back when it was still a regular purchasable title) the game truly is "free to play" in the sense that, while you can beef up your army using real money purchases, you will not be penalized for not doing so.  When PvP occurs (which is largely optional) players are matched up roughly based on the strength of their armies.  This is not an absolutely perfect system, however it vastly eliminates the possiblity that your opponent will have an absurly stronger army than yours via real money purchases.
Also, both the PvP and the PvE aspects of the game are truly exciting and offer an experience not found in other RTS games or titles from other genres.  While similar to PvP, the PvE side of the game can be better tailored for those who like a more relaxed approach to playing.
The thing I like most in the game is the building of one's kingdom, which is a gradual process that can take weeks or months to expand, depending on your playstyle.  It is really fun to carefully plan your defenses out and try to set up ambushes for would-be attackers, while at the same time it can be very engaging in that you take semi-permanent losses from battles, so you are encouraged to really think things through.  This is the most true for the human race (who specializes in defense) however all of the races, humans, elves and orcs, have an aspect of this.
The different races play quite differently and I actually have yet to branch out into the orcs and elves, but their playstyles are all unique and offer a vast amount of play time should you choose to explore all three.  Even with only having focused on one race, I have spent many hours on this game and feel like I have only scratched the surface.
This game has its rough edges, but the developers are serious about making it as polished as can be and have been working hard to make many changes that both improve the gameplay and well as the look and feel of the game.  Bugs have been being addressed over time and overall the game can be played and enjoyed with few interruptions caused by bugs.  The UI (User Interface) could use some attention, however it is still quite functional and usable after some experience with it.
Overall, this game is really fun (which is the most imporant part to many people) and worthy of sinking at least a couple dozen hours into it before deciding if you like it or not.  Do not be fooled by the graphics or the first few minutes of the game - this game is huge and in a very good way.

There seems to be consensus among point&click adventure developers that puzzles need to be as convoluted and nonsensical as possible. Tormentum does not follow this rule. In fact, Tormentum altogether drops combining items. Most of the puzzles are logic and sequence puzzles, and most have accompanying notes laid around the area giving hints. As you may imagine, this makes a lot of the puzzles easy. There are a few puzzles that you are given and instructions for (or that I did not find hints for) that relied solely on guess and check; and I was stuck on these for no small amount of time.
Other than the above mentioned puzzles, I only have one complaint for this game: It’s short. I finished it in a little over 3 hours and in one sitting. Otherwise, this game is fantastic. The art is incredible. The music is good. The story is sparse in all the right ways, and more than simply interesting enough to keep me engaged. There is a good and bad ending (decided using a simple moral system; kill or don’t kill etc…), and of course I got the bad ending but this has little impact on the story outside of the ending.

I was happily surprised by this game. I got it on a whim when it was free for a day, thinking it would be some basic, yet fun arcade type shooter. Instead, I got a gorgeous looking, yet easy to run game, with solid gameplay, and decent story.
I'm running a HD 5850, yet I can run this game with all settings on full (except supersampling, which I didn't feel I need) and with V-Sync on, I'm getting a solid 60 FPS.

Where to start....
First, I gave this game a thumbs down because there isn't a "Meh" option.  It's not terrible, but there are definitely better games out there, and I never recommend that anyone waste their time.
I tried really hard to like this game.  I gave it every possible chance to impress me..... but, no dice.  Frankly, it is under-featured, the gameplay is dated (at a date somewhere around 1991), and the development team seems so obsessed with controlling possibly offensive content that they have gutted any form or fashion of customization.  If you do play, take care choosing your nick-name, since it's the last thing you get to customize.  All island and ship-names are generated by the game.  So much for immersion.  I got saddled early on with two islands with the same name, and no options to fix it, which was prohibitively confusing, considering you have to coordinate shipping routes between these islands to grow the economy.
As far as city builders go, again, it's a "meh".  With no competitive play and the weakest PVE system I've seen in years, building and upgrading are monotonous and repetitive almost to pointlessness.  It was only a sense of "this game can't break me"  that got me to care at all.
So, now that the reason for the thumbs down is out of the way, here are the good points, kind of.  I have only played on the UK "Mermaid" server, so I don't know if all of these factors are consistent from server to server.
The moderators:  The mods were polite, and as helpful as they could be.  Apparently, however, their powers don't extend much beyond kicking people from the chat and answering an occasional question.  Twice I have been told by moderators that they had no experience with the Steam Client, and thus couldn't help with Steam-related issues.
The players:  This is the friendliest, most helpful game community I have ever seen.  The global chat looks like a constant beginner's tutorial, as players take time out from their own game to answer questions and fill in the gaps for the un-necessarily cryptic quest instructions  and inadequate game documentation.  Why did I play for seven weeks?  Because the players were fun, even if the game wasn't.
The price:  It's free.  I have, however, played many, many much better developed free2play games.
In the end, it's a shame, because there are building blocks here that could have been a really good game TWENTY YEARS AGO.  But, it's 2015, and experienced gamers (of which you will not find many on Anno-Online) have expectations of gameplay, challenge, immersion, and graphics that this game does not meet in any way.  I would seriously recommend to the developers that they play some of the games made by the competition, and get some idea of how a contemporary city-building game should look, play and work.
Lastly, I am a longtime fan of Ubisoft games.  If you likerd their blockbuster titles, or even the Anno franchise, do not assume that this game comes anywhere close to the quality of those games.

It goes without saying that Duke Nukem Forever isn't an amazing game, but I think it gets more hate than it deserves. The writing is pretty awful most of the time and the jokes are a collection of time capsules full of internet memes ranging from Team America quotes to things that even people at the time the memes were popular might not recognize like GI Joe PSA Edit references, and some of the gameplad setpieces just aren't fun at all, like one where you have to drive a monster truck through a level and constantly stop to get gas. But when it does do things right, DNF is a passable shooter, and if nothing else it's at least fairly interesting in its design. The 10 years of development show very obviously, and the game is pretty much a random collection of ideas thrown into a game, so you never know whether you'll be shrunk down to size jumping through a Rats version of the Duke Burger kitchen or sent to a strip club to collect items for a dancer. The thing that this game is most notable to me for is the almost excessive level of interaction in the environment; you can use microwaves, poke power outlets, and more. You can probably name any number of FPSs that are more fun than DNF, but I doubt you can name one that not only lets you use the water cooler, but also individually switch on either the cool or uncool water. The result is that the best parts of the game are the parts where you aren't actually in combat, and can just enjoy the environment and find all the things you can do in it. It doesn't make up for the rest of the game's frequent mediocrity, but it's something that I wish more games did.
It's worth noting that the DLC, The Doctor Who Cloned Me, was not made by 3D Realms, and as such it's a lot better. It still has a few pitfalls, like the return of Dylan, one of the worst characters in gaming history, and the final boss is a bit of a letdown (the boss in the middle of the DLC is a better fight, really), but it's actually funny for the most part and parodies things that are more relevant to the time it released compared to the original, and the campaign as a whole is more fun than DNF. It's decent enough that it's worth the $5 or so the collection goes down to when it's on sale. DNF as a whole isn't a game that you should buy at full price, but it's not the Big Rigs of its generation like people will try to convince you it is.

What is Magic 2015 - Duels of the Planeswalkers?
Magic 2015 - Duels of the Planeswalkers is based on the best-selling collectible card game "Magic: The Gathering". Like in each PC instance, with the exception of Magic The Gathering Online, the rules are dumbed down and a pre-set of cards is given to make the game appeal to more casual gamers that don't want to invest hundreds of dollars and still play with nice decks against each others.
The basics of the game are explained in my review for Magic 2014, so please look there, including the comments section:
What are the differences between Magic 2014 and Magic 2015 then?
Well, first of all you can now freely build your deck from a given card pool for which you can unlock booster packs by winning games or paying real money. While it doesn't sound bad at first, two factors greatly diminish the value of this novelty to the DOTP series: First of all the card selection is horrible, several combo cards are added without their counterparts, making it difficult to build a good deck. Second, some cards are real-money exclusive, which requires around 16 Euro to unlock all so-called "premium" booster packs.
The multiplayer experience suffered greatly by the exclusion of the Two-Headed Giant mode where two players could play against two other players cooperative. Another removed mode is the puzzle mode where you could solve 10 puzzles, i.e. pre-given positions where you had to defeat the opponent. Instead a forced tutorial was added that goes over one full act, only afterwards are you allowed to get an own deck, and only after the next act to freely build your deck. This horrible design choice leads you to having to play through the first part of the game with the starter deck which you can't exchange for another starter deck. Those decks, of course, have misleading descriptions.
As for achievements, most are nicely done again, only the 100 multiplayer wins are a very bad achievement, since without the Two-Headed Giant mode there is no real incentive to play multiplayer with not fun decks against other people with not fun decks. The 1v1 battles for that achievement should be done with a friend, ensuring you also can get other achievements easily.
Another thing that really bugs me is that although the title is "Magic 2015" the signature cards of that addon are not included in this game - Waste Not would have been a real addition to the game, allowing for really cool effects. Instead you have cards you either know from the older games or that don't have much synergy. You want to create a deck of your style? No good mill, no good burn, no good anything - a green-white token deck or red-blue control deck without any real opportunity to draw cards is the highest of feelings you can get.
On the positive side, several new effects were implemented, such as multicolor lands (finally!) and Monstrosity. And as the title says, planeswalkers are... wait... still not implemented!
Recommended: Play inofficial mods for Magic 2014 instead, and do your own deckbuilding with inofficial tools there. Many effects of Magic 2015 are already possible there, although quality varies. And yes, you CAN have planeswalkers with unofficial mods in Magic 2014!
Even as a die-hard DOTP fan, I can't recommend Magic 2015!

A very engrossing and very deep 17th century economic simulator.  You start as a small time trader with a small ship, a warehouse, and a purse of gold. From there you buy goods cheaply at one port and sail off to other ports and hope to find one that will buy those goods at a high price. Once you obtain enough capital you increase in rank. Rank increases allow you to hire more captains to have separate fleets, and obtain more building permits in different ports.
The economic depth is amazing. Each port is capable of producing 5 different goods. Some goods production is dependant on having a supply of another good, and that's where you the trader comes in. Do you want to buy rope from Port A? Then they need a good supply of hemp from Port B. Furthermore, once you obtain a building permit in a particular port you can become a greater part of the local economy by building your own warehouse and then manufacturing facilities. If you are smart enough and have the gold you can buy basic crop plantations in one port, produce that good cheaply, haul the goods to your advanced manufacturing facility at another port to cheaply produce the finished good and sell it for a massive profit. For extra profit you can also build housing for the new workers for your faciliteis and have them pay you rent. You also make money buy shipping in surplus workers from other ports to the port that now needs those workers.
Not that there aren't plenty of obstacles to stand in your way. When the game starts out in free play there are no pirates active and no nations are at at war.  As the game progresses the four nations, Spain, France, England, and the Netherlands can and will end up at war with each other. You can attempt to stay friendly with each nation and continue selling to all sides or offer to help one side over the other by raiding ship, blockading ports, and attacking ports.  Doing so rewards you, but at the cost of not being able to do business with the other nation until you repair your status with them.
Piracy is your other main concern. Pirates start off weak, with a single ship, but quickly grow to a major problem. They will sack ships, and invade ports. The sacking of ports is of great concern if you have a warehouse in that town as they will steal all of your stored goods, otherwise it is a great opportunity to sell the newly ravaged port fresh supplies. You can mitigate the risk of having your favorite port raided by pirates and enemy nations by donating cannons and paying for soldiers at your personal expense, and it is VERY expensive, so don't bother until you are wealthy and have something worth protecting. You could try to kill the pirates, but the game will not let you attack the pirates base until it randomly shows up on the map. Once you do know the secret location you must have a both a massive (expensive) battlefleet and a letter of Marquee allowing you to attack them. Why you need permission to kill non-Marquee Letter holding pirates is a bit of a mystery. That is about as historically accurate as all the white guys who work on your sugar plantations that you pay wages to.
While the game is incredibly deep, it suffers from having ZERO in-game help or tutorials. It took me three full days of playing to realize I could have my warehouses auto-buy goods when they were cheap so that I didn't have to micro manage them. The same is possibly with your trade convoys but I haven't been able to fully figure it out yet. Finding an online guide is a must for full enjoyment.
There are even deeper aspects of the game and economy, but it would take a book to get in to them all. If you are a lover of deep economic sims this game is 100% for you.

I have not had this much fun in years, or for as long as I can remember even. I am usually very hard to please (and certainly not a Ubisoft fanboy), but this game keeps amazing me. It's difficult, but not too difficult. It has modes that require teamwork, and modes that only depend on your own skill. Overall, I feel well-satisfied in my need for CO-OP and 1v1 action.
The classes are incredibly fun to play, and while they are fairly quick to learn (in contrast to games like Mortal Kombat), they take a long time to master. There are great customization options for each character, in both cosmetics and animations, allowing you to really implement your own preference on your favorite character. The in-game currency can be bought for real money, but is also fairly easy to earn with daily quests and contracts. Using micro-transactions is NOT necessary to be a good player.
I have only had ONE disconnect in 17 hours of play. The game usually finds a new host if the current one leaves, and the matchmaking is quick and always tries to find a player close to you of similar skill (which I can confirm, having often faced players from my country). If you have bad or unstable internet, then yeah, you might have a bad connection.
Now to the best part: The mechanics are unmatched, and hands down the best fighting system I have ever played. There is so much depth to it, yet it is intuitive and easy to pick up on, allowing you to enjoy every minute right from the start. Of course, you will benefit from spending some time in practice to learn a character (or playing Story mode) before going online.
The attention to detail in a lot of areas is also fantastic, and shows that Ubisoft have really made an effort here. The game looks great, and animations are very fluid and realistic. Is it perfect? Probably not. There might be balancing issues, bugs and so on, but so far I have had an absolute blast without exception. With the seasons and rounds in faction wars, I have every belief that Ubisoft will take good care of this game long after it's release. This game is here to stay, because it is really really good, and not like any other fighting game I have seen.
TL;DR: I have had one disconnect in 17 hours, and ping is good in 90% of matches. The fighting mechanics are the best I have seen, and ridiculously addictive. So much depth, yet so easy to pick up. If you have decent internet, and you enjoy improving your abilities and understanding continuosly while having a blast... Well, I'll leave it at that.

Frustrating. The idea is you are playing through Jules Verne's book Around the World in 80 Days, but as Phineas Fogg's valet, which is an odd choice but not bad. You choose routes from city to city, hopping or crawling your way across the various continents. If you make it back in 80 days, well, I don't know because I didn't make it either time. If you don't, the game rather lamely laments and starts you over again.
The first playthrough was fine. I made obvious mistakes, but did well on money. I narrowly missed the 80 day mark (arriving in around 86 days), but I saw it coming and understood based on some of the circuitous routes I ended up taking in pursuit of good market deals. The narrative was fine, and I was kidnapped and narrowly escaped cholera and packed all sorts of guns across America.
The second playthrough was aggravating to the extreme. I remedied the errors of routing I had made before, and so made excellent time across Asia. Then I was stopped at the Pacific coast, as each city I came to gave me routes only to other Asian cities, effectively halting any progress westward. I went from Vladistok to Yukohama to Pyongyang to Manila, finally losing a week for a bank withdrawal (having lost my money idly wandering), another week to cholera, and then finally managed to get to Honolulu, broke and nearly dead.
I recovered in America, made good sales, recouped my money, made good time to Chicago, then suddenly had the same problem. No routes across the Atlantic. Chicago to Atlanta to MIami to Port Royal to Port-Au-Prince, and tere stopped, broke and in cities without banks, so my only option was to return to Washington. I had lost nearly 40 of my 80 days with unavoidable game circumstances, making what should otherwise have been a sure thing impossible. Frustrated and finished, I closed the game and uninstalled it.
If it were a game of better money balancing vs. route planning, I would support it more. But bad luck or dead-end routes have little appeal. Also, I would prefer if the rather tiresome interruptions would serve to give more real histories, rather than the fantasy stories it presents.

Let's get started with saying this game can be described as a disturbing, sick, abnormal, and a worrisome looking game. I guess that could be your opinion, but I think Tormentum - Dark Sorrow looks amazing. Every area looks like a classic heavy metal album cover coming to life! I'm a metal fan so this is right up my alley, but what's interesting is that the game's main soundtrack I wouldn't say is metal. It still fit perfectly as an eerie melody that made the life of the game intense.
Alright so you know how much I like the look, but what is the actual game. At its core it's a point and click game with smaller puzzles blended in to keep things interesting. The puzzles were exactly how I like them in a point and click game. Challenging, but not to the point where you feel the guilt to check a guide.
The smaller puzzles I mentioned are pretty straightforward. Like moving some cogs around to connect two ends, or figuring out a jig saw type puzzle. They were a nice change up from going from place to place. There's also times you'll come across patterns mentioned on signs, and other places. This is where the notebook you carry comes in handy. Your character will automatically sketch out the details. Now you can look at this pattern at anytime while looking at a puzzle that requires notes.
I want to mention this, but not going to spend too much time on it for worry of possibly taking some mystery out of the game from you. Tormentum features some choices throughout the game, and let's just say there is more than one ending. I loved the ending I got to this game, and that's all I'm going to say.
You can probably tell that I enjoyed Tormentum - Dark Sorrow a lot, but I have some issues I want to bring up. The main one is that I feel like there isn't enough options in the game. There's a couple like volume control, language selection, and a full screen mode. One option for a monitor resolution would be nice. I would have liked the game to take up more of my monitor. As you can see it there's black around the square of gameplay. I would have liked to have the option to do some sort of zoom in to take up more monitor space.
The other option I would have liked is the ability to control the camera, and make it stay still for the most part. Whenever you move your mouse the screen moves a little. It's not a big complaint, but took me a little time to get used to it. Then the last thing is more of a small annoyance. Everytime you pick up an item it zooms into it. While most of the time this feels right because it goes into more detail, it's not always necessary. When someone would give me an item it'd just be easier to just pick it up off the ground, than have to zoom in to do it. Also once you zoom out you can't zoom back into that area the item was in so I think it's a little unnecessary. These complaints in no way ruined the game. I just want to make this clear. There just things I'd would have liked to see in the game.
Final Say: I'm positive about Tormentum - Dark Sorrow. I gotta recommend it to you if you're a fan of point and click games. I do wish it was longer as it took me three hours to beat it, but there is more than one ending. So the replay value is there if you want it. Still with the artwork, music, puzzles, and story, Tormentum - Dark Sorrow gets my approval.

I'm not surprised at how much I enjoyed this game. It's a "Choose-your-own-adevnture" style game that is largely told through the story. You do have a limited inventory that you have to manage, but other than that it plays almost more like reading a book. There is some strategy, of course, and I can see myself playing through this again. After an initial failure of getting stuck in Russia, not being able to afford my way out, I figured out what I was doing, and made the trip in 74 days in about two hours playtime.
Aside from the adventure and story telling that make this game enjoyable, I really appreciated the decision-making process. In many instances you have to move quickly because you have a choice of taking the fastest route out of the city or exploring to find more options but possibly costing yourself more than a day. In some ways this game reminded me of the board game "Tales of Arabian Nights" as you often make decisions that seem like they will have one outcome, but something entirely different (for better or for worse) happens!
I also loved how you could see the progress of other adventurers traveling at the same time as you; this really helped it feel more like a race.

High above in the sky, locked in a cage in your gown of shadows, held from the most steampunk aircraft ever seen in a game before, across from a beauty and the beast esk monster, is where you begin this dark point and click adventure. You play as an unnamed character in dark robes, who has been captured by the dark guardians of the tower for some treason that your soul has committed. The lore and story are slowly explained to the player, that never really gives the player too much detail, creating a minimalist effect that really made the gameplay experience enjoyable. I feel like some point and click games today flood the player with story, so playing this was a sigh of relief.
The gameplay in Tormentum follows the basic structure of point and click adventure type games. Items are found that you can pick up and put in your backpack, that might solve some of the puzzles later on in the game. This process is repeated throughout the entire game, but is kept interesting with the great number of interesting and enjoyable puzzles. Most of the time, there are cheat sheets in other locations that provide the player with graphical representations of how to complete a puzzle in a different area. This keeps the games difficulty balanced and gameplay enjoyable.
The artstyle is unique and breathtaking when first seen, because it doesn't follow the conventional scheme of pretty games today, because Tormentum is incredibly grotesque in its detail. Every point of detail in the game has something amazing on it. The tables with blood dripping of them, to the human remains being electrocuted in the death chambers, each scene is as amazing as the last.
The player enters a throne room with a rather wicked looking court jester sitting by the castle throne. You approach him and he tells you to kill a certain prisoner with this special knife he provides you, whilst offering the player a hefty reward. At this point in the game, the story hadn’t been described to me that much, and so I had to make the choice that my guy told me too. These choices are dark, and usually represent a good/evil decision the player needs to make.
The games length is around 5 hours for a single playthrough. These 5 hours weren’t just a 5 hour grind of ‘gotta go here’ and ‘gotta do this’ but instead was an intense and rewarding diegetic experience. This game has plenty of  replayability with the choice system inbedded in the game, giving each playthrough a different experience. Tormentum is less a video game you play for enjoyment and more an experience that people of dark adventure would love. I would recommend Tormentum to anybody who sounds like this would be their style of game, and when it’s selling for a price point of less than $15 AUD, it’s a steal.

God this game is SO MUCH FUN! I was very sceptical to be honest, I love well written and well told stories, I'm a huge fan of visual novels, but as games I often find them boring or not catchy enough.
80 days is different. There are no(!) huge walls of text, the steampunk element is simply charming and very well integrated into this classic story, characters are awesome and fun, and well, I just love it.
Somehow it actually made me feel like I was travelling the world. You really have to try to find the best route, keeping in mind the time it takes to travel, where it wil, take you, how you will be able to continue from the next point, costs, luggage, etc. There are several little side-stories (which I mostly missed so far becaue I was a very well-behaved british gentleman and in a great hurry!) but from the hints I got I can already tell they side-stories are awesome as well.
Despite a looot of time spent on trains and airships I did not get bored. There were no long waiting times and I always found something to do and interesting tidbits of information that were more or less helpful for the journey. The Cholera outbreak in Manila scared me, as I was stuck there for a few days, but alas, Mr Fogg escaped unharmed. And me too.
Uhm. Yes. Where was I. Anyway.
Let's make this a bit more organized:
PROS:
- Fantastic adaptation of the story
- Beautiful graphics
- unexpectedly interactive
- very well balanced game elements
- lovely steampunk elements
CONS:
- none that I could name right now.
If I had one wish, i would ask for more detailed and more varied graphics for the different cities one visits on this journey. But they are already nice.
I finished the game once, and I already can't wait to play it again. I will never forget the romance I had in Dallas, but there is so much more to see!
I want to take the route through northern Africa, and I simply have to see South America, and there is something going on in Vladivostok that I have to discover, and so much more. The sheer amount of content in this game is amazing.
Again, it is not a hard game, it is not very difficult and demanding, but it is so beautiful and so much fun.
80/80 wonderful days of travelling.

Get nether they said..... It'll be fun, They said. This game is a graphically enhanced version of infestation: Survivor Stories. You wander around a massive city aimlessly looking for loot to survive which is great if you find something. In my several hours playing this game I managed to find a grand total of 2 ranged weapons and only scraps of food and no health kits. I point out health kits because there is no other way to heal at all so you're stuck looking for loot with only a thousand total health pool and no health kits to help which puts you at a servere disadvantage should you encounter any enemies because not only are the enemies quite hard to kill but health loss is almost garanteed when fighting in melee.
This brings me to combat which is one of the better parts of the game when it comes to NPCs melee combat requires you to be on your game, nethers can teleport anywhere around you so you find yourself listening to portals and moving fast to try avoid being hit, This also puts a really nice twist on ranged combat too because you can't just spray and pray. Where the combat gets bad is PvP which is mainstream shooter mechanics with skills, sounds great right? Wrong. Because you lose your skills every time you die getting your skills off the ground is near impossible without a ranged weapon (Which barely exist at loot sites) which means you often die before you have a chance to become good and that means those who have been playing since day 1 and not died end up getting all the loot rewards while those new to the game have no chance to win at all.
In conclusion what this game needs is less reward for being a bandit and more rewards for killing the nether just like Infestation: Survivor stories. It's a shame because the game has amazing potential but it's ruined by people who have more experience with PvP shooters.

There are walker mechs :D
And even while you're in a space battle you can break things out a lot: teams can go inside their own ships and repair hardpoints. You can even launch drop pod incursions into enemy battleships and commandeer them - WHILE there's a full fledged space fight outside. The scale is like Planetside 2 but with Capital Ships. But, it's also not like Space Engineers or Shattered Horizons either - ships won't be split in half and you wont be sucked out into space or anything; the interiors are the own 'counterstrike map' and so is the space that the ships occupy. So, if you easily get disorented in 3D space don't worry, there's not a lot of that happening.
The AI 'grunts' that make up the rest of the servers normally when there aren't enough players, are generalllly kind of herp a derp when it comes to reacting to close quarters weapons fire, and oddly seem to love crouching toward most of their objectives, and look around and the oddest places, but they are surprisingly hard to hit at range and offer up legitimate target practice. The AI's ability to detect and evade incoming projectiles is also really solid, so they even put you through your paces trying to dumbfire rockets at their vehicles.
I wish the mech walker was shown a lot more love, as it is way more difficult to maneuver than it ought to be, given that it doesn't pivot at its waist or anything and it just feels like a bad nerf for it, like nobody would seriously choose to bring something like that into a real combat scenario like that if it wasn't designed to pivot - it has no other distinct advantages aside being small and cool and it can jump (but not crouch) and runs at a very uninspiring stride speed, esp compared to vehicles like the jeep that are tuned up for Rocket League. And, the mech is just super awkward all the same to play with on the default KB+M settings - idk why its feet aren't steered just like you would the tanks in the game. They aren't even controllled like a big infantry either. They're just - haphazardly controlled. I hope they do something about it, but they're still fun to use don't get me wrong!

I had a lot of fun playing through this with a friend of mine. The game feels good, and the double-jump and dash allow you to zoom around the map and over the heads of approaching enemies. The weapons feel great to shoot, especially with an ice upgrade, shattering your foes to pieces. There is a wide variety of enemies, and many have weaknesses that you can capitalize upon by choosing a weapon with the correct elemental upgrade (toxic, fire, ice, and electricity). There is an extensive equipment and skill system, allowing you to choose and min/max a certain playstyle. However, the upgrades (which seem to be mostly randomly generated) can clutter things up after a while. Enemies drop a lot of upgrades, and soon enough you'll be swimming in them. Other rough spots of the title include the way in which you learn of enemy resistances/weaknesses. Elemental resistances and weaknesses are written in the same color and font, and when you are getting bombarded it's difficult to discern which is which. Additionally, 90% of the dialogue is pretty groan-worthy and adolescent. There are a few chuckles to be had, but they are few are far between. However, the menu music and especially the final boss music are incredible. The confusion in pinpointing enemy stats doesn't constantly occur, and it's easy enough to ignore the dialogue, so it's easy to recommend this title. A neat melee/gun hybrid FPS.

This game is like pizza which have all your favorite ingredients in in and a few strange ones. If you can look past the surprise toppings, you will like it, if you find them ruining the whole pizza you'll hate it, and if you find them actually adding to flavor as a whole you'll love this game.
Combat is great, star of the show, even better than first part, it may very well be the best first person shooter (more like slasher, heh) experience I had throughout my gaming life. Very tight controls, fast, aggressive, easy to finish off enemies and make it look cool at the same time, never bored me at any moment. Outstanding weapons feel, dismemberment system, destructible environment (not everything), tons of explosions, even some minor details like flashy way of reloading the shotgun — it's all adds up to the great result.
Soundtrack and humour are both awesome and on-par with first part. Visual eye-candy is somewhat worse, I think, probably due to semi-randomized level generation system. Shadow Warrior from 2013 was entirely hand-made, and wins out in terms of visual style when compared to it successor. Still looks pretty sweet to me (except a few places, that make you blind with bloom turned on). Storyline is a bit worse than in the first part, but still okay (at least it logical from start to finish, which is rare nowadays).
Main thing that makes people love it, like it or hate it is randomized loot system. Many aspects of your weapons, skills and character as a whole could be randomized through dropped loot. Sorting out the dropped shinies can very well turn people away from game, because interface is not very well thought-up, and the amount of loot that needs sorting up through is pretty big, and it eats time, this precious time you could be having fun, slicing and shooting stuff up in amazing combat, you know? Of course
sorting is done, combat usually becomes even better, as the enemies freeze solid from your sword now, or you wielding two pistols instead of one, or shoot three bullets at a time instead of one, or charge your shots for bigger damage, or made them explode,  or... some another nice upgrade you gave yourself, there's actually quite plenty.
The trick, for me was to get some experience through learning with sorting out process. Once I decided what variants of loot do I want, and what goes to junk/sell list immediately I got from awful 10-minutes loot-sorting pauses after every mission to pretty quick 1-min "automated" process and the game graduated from "amazing but flawed" to "pure awesome" category.
So, at the end I ate my pizza, and loved it to the last Wang of it ;)

A flawed classic. There are so many ways to complete quests and different dialogue choices that change the story. The combat can be unbalanced when you get your first lightsaber and you just spam master flurry attack. Once you get a lightsaber, there is no better weapon and you might as well duel-wield them rather than go two-handed as you do more damage overall. You actually don't get your first lightsaber until 7-10 hours into the game. Instead you have to build it by completing optional quests (make sure to look up the Nar Shadaa one, it is very easy to screw up the quest that gives you a part). The lightsaber is teased multiple times throughout the first two planets, but it isn't a let down when you get it. Instead, it opens up new unlockable moves such as using force jump to jump thirty feet and stab a guy and a dialogue tree to become a true Jedi or Sith, which unlocks more moves!
TLDR: If you can get around the crashes and performance issues, you can find an experience akin to Bioware's Mass Effect series (they also made KoTR1) and Fallout New Vegas (which was also made by Obsidian).
Update: Whelp, they updated the game. Now there aren't any bugs, crashes, or performance issues. Now you can also use a controller, which is awesome as I first played this on the original Xbox. The story is still pretty sweet and so is the combat, but it can be quite unforgiving if you don't pay attention and blaze through everything without reading (Hint: you may think force speed is trash, but it allows you to attack two extra times each turn you attack. Master flurry also gives you an extra attack with no downsides, so spend those rare upgrade points wisely!)

In my opinion what lies at the heart of the zombie apocalypse genre is the nerve-wrecking paranoid survivalism. How well does this game pull it off? Not exactly great but definitely better than most zombie games I'm aware of.
The major flaw of this game is its backward difficulty curve. In the beginning I had only a crappy shotgun, a handful of bullets and a death wish. And that was great because when I inevitably run out of ammo, I had to run from building to building, praying that inside I'll find at least a couple of bullets before the horde of working class gentlemen chasing after me proceed to chew off my face. It was tense, stressful and absolutely awesome, just the way a true zombie game should feel like. Unfortunately, by the time I reached the last streets (a.k.a levels) I had so much money, ammo and medkits, I was practically immortal and all the challenge was lost. In short, the game is rather unbalanced.
Besides the few times when the game crashed and cheered me up immensely, there isn't really anything to complain about from the technical side.
The music is pretty decent but definitely not memorable.
Criticizing the graphics feels a bit awkward considering the fact it's written in the goddamn title what you are supposed to expect. Desperate lack of resources hiding underneath pretentious retro banner.
However, despite my rambling, I enjoyed this game a lot. It's in no way deep, is a bit clunky, but it has a sense of style and what it does, it does well. It's definitely worth checking out.
