It's definitely EARLY access as I write this (Jan 2016), but if you're willing to put up with some kinda crappy level design or overbearing bugs, it's definitely worth spending some time with. For an example of the kind of frustration you might have to put up with: a lot of times your car will slightly go over the edge of the road and you'll have to restart -- this is especially true for scenarios involving large vehicles like the cement mixer. (Might be tolerable for driving game experts, my mom gave up immediately.) More unfortunately, isn't really a "racing" game yet, since there's not much in the way of AI that (I could find), or two-player split-screen, which is a little disappointing. I also can't seem to get the (much-tauted on their website) one-click mod installs to work.
In other words, it's much more of a physics playground with cars right now, but some of the scenarios offer fun challenges.
So far, the best scenarios that I've found are the single player checkpoint race-against-the-clock ones. There are a few with crazy jumps and things, which are cool, but my favorite by far was one with a big classic truck hilariously falling apart within three minutes or so. You gotta reach the end before falling apart, but you gotta master the turns because the thing is crazy top-heavy and will flip with ease. My dad and I had a real blast playing this one. He was totally into it. Good time spent together. That right there makes it worth my purchase money.
But again, it's early days. I'm sure most of this stuff will change and a lot will be added. It seems like the core physics in it are pretty great, but how the cars interact with the road often debilitates them TOO quickly. The menu system has a really snazzy material design aesthetic, which I believe is a newer addition. (The rest of the interface needs to catch up!)
I took a chance on this because it seemed a lot different from the cookie cutter racing games out there, and it is. But they have a long way to go to remove a lot of frustration factors and add modes I really want, like local splitscreen races and actual AI.
Got my fingers crossed for much more!

The best description I have for it is Call of Duty mashed with Chivalry but polished and optimized. Each faction has a drastically different feel (though this isn't terribly important as any class can be played in any faction in multiplayer) and each class has a different feel and plays differently from the other classes -- even superficially similar classes like tanks, vanguards, and assassins play differently from the other classes in their subclass (superclass?).
The gameplay itself involves running around in third-person. Combat involves chain attacks stringing together heavy and light (hard to be more descriptive as this varies a lot depending on the specific class you're playing as). Blocking/parrying is of the high/left/right persuasion where you match your guard with the direction of your opponents' attack (this is more intuitive than it sounds), though some classes have to time their blocks more precisely and some have abilities to block attacks from all directions. Dodging is forward/back/left/right. It's not going to have the same pace as something like Dynasty Warriors or even Skyrim but if you can figure out those combat systems you can figure out For Honor's.
Game types vary from team duels to team deathmatches to team zone controls to personal duels.
Overall: if you like competitive team-based games, this is a good one. If you don't, you won't like this game.
Edit 03/10:
Now that the game has been out for awhile, it's glaring flaws become more and more glaring.  Class balance is poor.  Group balance is poor.  Matchmaking is terrible.  The worst aspect of the game, however, is the community.
It would be one thing for the usual community whining about how other people are playing; that's to be expected.  Instead, the hate and sheer intensity of the trolling is actually bad enough it detracts from the game.  But being that this is the internet, that's to be expected and can't really be blamed on the game itself.  However, given the way the P2P matchmaking works, if anyone in a match quites, it's likely to crash the match for everyone involved.  This happens with the exact frequency you'd expect it to happen: any time someone is about to lose.  This needs to be addressed immediately or the game is simply not worth your money let alone your time investment (to say nothing of the money the game wants you to spend on it internally).  We either need dedicated servers or when one person leaves a match they should be the only person to leave.
Edit 06/18:
Class balance is still iffy.  They did open up the game to be able to fulfill all Contracts and Orders (sort of a daily quest) against AI (excepting Duels) which is nice in that people are less likely to deliberately crash the match.  However, rather than making matches more stable, they have decided to institute a matchmaking penalty for leaving matches early; so if someone on your team is playing like a jerk and you leave, you're now penalized for not wanting to play with a jerk.  Another boneheaded design choice from Ubisoft which further tarnishes a game that desperately wants to be amazing but is so throttled by poor choices it never quite achieves that goal.

The game is heavily puzzle-based, and reminds me of Coktel Vision's titles, such as The Prophecy, as well as those of Dynamix, like Rise of the Dragon, or Heart of China, and even more recent efforts by companies like Daedalic Entertainment, such as the Deponia and The Dark Eye series. Tormentum boasts striking visuals, is very reminescent of the art of Zdzisław Beksiński, and H.R. Giger, and has an atmosphere similar to that found in FROM Software's "Souls" games.
The puzzles are never too complicated as to keep you stuck for hours. Highlighting effects ensure that you will never spend too much time pixel-hunting down the items needed to progress. The story is cryptic enough to keep you guessing, until the end (no spoilers here). Multiple choices with consequences not immediately obvious also ensure you will want to do more than one playthrough.
I heartily recommend this game to adventure game fans. The presentation (both the visuals and the music) alone is certainly worth the price.

Having played in Beta, and having sunk a decent amount of time into the game, I have to say the game itself is very, very, very solid. The campaign is really little more than bot matches, as several people have noted, I was dissapointed in the story, but playing against other players in multiplayer really is alot of fun.
The community, insofar, is great. Most (a truely significant) players refrain from being ridiculously irritating, preferring to actually fight and win over simply tossing an opponent over a balcony. A single mistake can leave a player open to deadly assaults from the opposing combatant, just the same as a screw-up on the enemys part can turn a game around. Every kill is satisfying on a personal level, compared to other games (like battlefield) where one can gun down four or five enemy players with mechanical precision.
There are levels, which mean little, other than what sort of cosmetics one can unlock, and use of battlefield feats, and what gear is available. That being said, higher-level gear tends to come with significant drawbacks, and as someone who has earned their equipment and levels as opposed to buying them, I still do lose to players that are 30 'levels' lower than me, and 50 levels lower on equipment. And when I myself was a lower level, I'd also wiped the metaphorical floor with players who really thought that they could 'pay to win' on day one, carrying equipment/levels that took me three days to earn, a very, very satisfying catharsis. Skill matters much, much, much more than equipment. Several of the game modes use basic-stats only, ensuring a level playing field, though you get to of course, wear and display the pretty trinkets that one has earned or purchased.
The game itself runs extremely well, even on lower-end systems, and every game I have played ran as smooth as butter until problems came up. When this game works, it's very enjoyable, and almost worth the price.
I say almost because Ubisoft is Ubisoft. My favorite example of this is AC: Unity. Where they forgot to release modes, and included pretty much unobtainable equipment for a damn good long time after launch. All recent Ubisoft titles have an Achilles' Heel; For Honor is no different. The games major weakness comes in the Peer-to-Peer connection. People will be unable to join your party. You wont be able to join theirs. Matches will randomly kick you. Matches will randomly kick all other players. It doesn't always happen, I often can enjoy three or four games in a row before the bugs rear their ugly head (namely failed to connect...to everything.), and I have to restart the game. And between the loading screens, I had actually managed to cook myself dinner over the course of three games. If a game goes down while you're in it or a player disconnects or the server switches hosts, the game might give you errors every time you attempt to join a game. A client restart (in my case) seems to fix it, but by and large, these frustrations could have, and should have, been taken care of by the developers. As a paying customer, one should not have to apply duct tape to a merchant's product to get it to work as intended.
-If- you can deal with the frustration of the consistently unstable multiplayer...the game is a great. A little polish to the diamond in the rough, and it'd be phenomenal. The game gets a very, very, very grudging reccomendation from me. But Ubisoft should get a boot to the head.
Overall, a great multiplayer game that's been hobbled by it's own developers. Heres hoping Ubisoft doesn't decide to blind and castrate it in the future, too.

You have been captured and placed in a cage below a zeppelin, little do you know that this is the start of something that can decide your fate. Well I guess now you know, or do you? Come journey through this dark world of twists, turns and decisions, and see what might be lurking, waiting for you.
Tormentum: Dark Sorrow was really a breath of fresh air, well actually to be honest given the feel of the game it was probably slightly poisoned air, but that doesn't mean that this game was here to kill you, then again maybe it was. Wow, this is one of those games where I want to tell you about all the interesting little twists, but to do so would ruin it for you.
What I can tell you is that this is a bloody point and click adventure. You are a nameless, hooded, being that has been captured by a group that is hell-bent of purifying the world, and the way to do that, of course, is through torture.
There's going to be many obstacles and different types of puzzles put in your way, but I'm confident that if you pay attention to your surroundings you might be able to find hints to help you conquer some of the more difficult ones.
Graphically I was really surprised by this game, there's not a whole lot of animation to this game, and it is very side-scroller-ish in appearance. The thing is that each scene looked so polished, and yes many times slightly creepy, but that just fit the feel of the game perfectly.
This game is around 2 and half hours in length, and when I got to the end I was both relieved and saddened. I wish that there was more because I was so invested in the game, but at the same time I was relieved that I had reached the end. Speaking of ends, there are multiple endings to this game, so if you are looking to maybe correct some of the actions you did in the game, you might be able to change your ending.
With all this being said, I have to say get this game. It might not be for everyone, but those looking for something polished that has just the right about of twists and turns, and difficult decisions, this is a game that you can't afford NOT to have in your collection. This game gets a 9.4 out of 10.

Tormentum is a puzzler at heart adorned in an adventure cape. Thrown into a prison for reasons unbeknownst to you, you are supposed to escape your cell and find your way out of whatever location you are in.
For all the imagination that was put on the world design, there is never really any motivation for you to do anything other than to just finish the game. You will encounter multiple characters, each with their own plea and moral standing, and depending on who you assist, the game will generate one of two different endings.
Each new location presents a puzzle or an element that you will need to solve one, and their designs are absolutely striking. So much work has been put on each set-piece and all for good reason. Simple in its approach as it is, Tormentum is a beautiful game that justifies its asking price just for its aesthetic, and at $11, coupled with some interesting puzzles, it’s a bargain.
Pros:
– Beautiful landscapes and art direction specially if you are an H.R Giger fan.
– Balanced difficulty curve that has the game starting♥♥♥♥♥♥easy and ending mind-numbingly challenging.
– Great use of sound and ambient
– Multiple paths that will lead to one of two different endings.
Cons
– The story is too simplistic and almost laid out for you from the outset
– Some puzzles are obtuse and others are too simplistic.
– What ending you get, evil or good, is dependent on your decisions, themselves dependent on visual cues that are not clear at times.

The artwork in this game is pretty fantastic. It's like I was walking through the nightmare of some metalhead, and it was pretty gruesome. You're surrounded by the twisted souls of people being punished for some vauge sins they supposedly committed, and the wardens of this place are even more warped. Suffering seems to be the fetish of the day as you wander through this decrepit world, and no one is who they say they are.
You're given moral choices to make throughout the game, and while some seem rather obvious, others are not so clear.
There are two endings depending on the moral choices you make. Good, and Evil. On my first playthrough, I committed two evil choices, and the rest were good. Didn't matter, as I got the evil ending. YOU CAN'T MAKE -ANY- EVIL CHOICES IF YOU'RE GOING FOR THE GOOD ENDING. One evil choice is all it takes to get the evil ending, it seems. There isn't a balanced system for measuring the moral choices at the end, so keep in mind what ending you want to pursue before beginning a playthrough.
A lot of the puzzles in this game remind me of those brain-tester minigames you'd find on the Nintendo DS or some online flash game, and those are the only ones that present any kind of challenge. The rest of the game is finding objects hidden in the environment, and giving them to NPCs or completing mechanism & puzzles. Nothing in this game is really difficult at all, as some of the NPCs will outright tell you how to solve the puzzle, or make it entirely obvious. So, the puzzles and minigames felt really tedious. Only some felt necessary to the story, but even then, not at all challenging.
The story was ok. Can't really give anything away to those who are adament in playing the game themselves, but it was ok. No real character development, as your interactions with various people are brief. The first words out of 90% of the characters you encounter will either be "Fetch me this" or "Here's info on the next objective". The only character that made me feel -anything- was the rat-man you encounter in the beginning of the game...but even then. Nothing deep or impactful, just a bit of...surprise.
There are a few bugs in the game that make it feel a bit like a buggy flash game. Sometimes I'd get stuck on a close-up of an environment when picking up an object, and I'd have to restart. The credits for the Good Ending also have a bug; where one image will get stuck and the credits won't even start to roll. When that happens, you don't even get the achievement for the ending (for all those looking for total completion).
The Ending itself is also abrupt and lacking, as it was just -over- after you count up your moral choices.
My verdict:
The gameplay & story are very lacking, but the art is pretty cool. Get it when it's on sale, and it'd be worth it. However, as it is right now, I don't really recommend it.

This is going to be a highly controversial opinion, but in all fairness, I like this game. I played it a few years back on the 360 and hated it... the load times were abysmal, I died a lot (especially toward the end) and it didn't mirror the cool graphics of the game I saw a person on Youtube showoff (later I would find out it was the PC version, which has marginally better graphics)
Fast foreward a few weeks and I manage to obtain a version of the game (don't ask me how :P) and play through the game on all four difficulties. I always had a forgiving nature of notriously bad games, and this is no exception. Gameplay can be fun (if highly unfair later on Insane difficulty) and addicting.
I am not blind to its faults. The game can get really brutally hard. You will learn to hate most of the game's turret levels (the one at the beginning of The Mighty Foot is not that bad) and the Octoking, Pool minigame, (This mini game needs to die in a fire...) Energy Leech, and the Mothership are some of the most annoying aspects of the game.
Ignoring challenge (as it is very much possible if highly frustrating) this game is quite fun. I never grew up with Duke Nukem and wouldn't even play M rated games cause my parents were restrictive till much later. There are some questionable moments (The infamous Hive level... though I am personally not bothered by this level... shows how horrible a person I am) and the gameplay is unfairly hard at moments (Crash Course I am looking at you) but if you give it a try and don't let people's overwhelmingly negative opinions about things affect your enjoyablity of games, then this game can be quite the fun experience.
A fun thing to do once you beat the game on all four difficulties is to cheat. Unlimited ammo + Unlimited Health + Insta Gib = absolute god mode and revenge against all the brutal segments that this game has to offer. OctoKing give you a hard time during Insane? Why not turn on unlimited health and Insta Gib and laugh as he falls into bloody chunks.
This game isn't as bad as people say and I get that it is about disapointment over the hype, but I haven't experienced that hype and didn't even know it existed till I saw that video.
Give this game a try if you can overlook a few flaws, it can be quite the underrated treasure.

Actually, Shadow warrior 2 (2016) had much potential to be good product and even might be such one now.
It feels very nasty to write negative review for it. Flying wild hog are one of the best developers of nowadays. They put much effort into optimisation, visual, animations and etc. I liked, how much did the firearms become useful in compare to the previous Shadow warrior (2013), I liked multiple quotes, bossfights, variety of enemies... Soundtrack, especially the composition written by Stan Bush!
So what did actually spoil the game enought to write a negative review? The only and obvious answer are rpg elements in casual form, that presently became cancer of other genres. Instead of handcrafted levels with complex architecture and interactivity, like it was in Shadow Warrior(1997), we get small sets of prefabs with limited thematics for procedure generating, that make a lot of places look monotonous despite of being vivid and pictorial. Moreover level desing doesn't suppose any interactivity, like it was in SW (1997), but is suited for (although good) fights only.
Another flaw is looting random garbage, that drops from enemies in large numbers and starts to irk very soon. Subsecuently, this proceeds to the arms, that are, in spite of abundance, in many aspects act similar. Furthermore, three upgrading slots for each of them demand annoying frequent reconfiguring each time to get any notable characteristics.
Out of this, another demerit feature are different types of enemies and corresponding weapon configurations (poisonous, shocking, combustive), that set some of them about invulnerable or immune to anything except for special conficurations of weapons and feel as (or really are) bullet sponges.
And, I suppose, as the last of flaws - grinding requiring leveling.
If you, yes, you, find this nasty features - everyone's worst nightmare, entertaining, feel sure to enjoy the game. It has no any other flaws and it's developers deserve to get payment for their work. Hey, what are you waiting for, I'm talking to you!

As a fan of the first Knights of the Old Republic, I don't know why I skipped out on the sequel until 2015. It's a good thing I finally played it: KOTOR II: The Sith Lords is a deep, thought-provoking experience and a worthy follow-up to its famous predecessor.
Known for feeling less like Star Wars because of its many shades of gray, KOTOR II has you search for answers about your past while playing as a fugitive of sorts, the supposed “last jedi knight” that Sith all over the galaxy are eager to capture. You pick up a number of colorful companions along the way, and it is these characters and their nuanced perspectives that form the backbone of the story. The gameplay is much the same as the first Knights of the Old Republic: pausable real-time RPG combat, with tons of force powers and weapons to experiment with. Playing with the restored content mod (a piece of cake to install), I encountered very few bugs, but some of the new content stuck out like a sore thumb; I thought, “Yep, that was added in later.”
Even with the fixes, KOTOR II still has some lingering flaws. The graphics have not aged well, and the game drags in places due to excessively large environments, minimal guidance (not clear where you need to go next) and too much dialogue. It's all well-written, yes, but trimming it down would have helped the pacing by making events proceed faster. As it is, the game feels too long at 40 hours, and I probably won't be playing it again any time soon.
It's still totally worth it, though. KOTOR II is a very good RPG that I'm glad I finally got around to, and it feels good to know that quality content like this is available on Steam at such a low price.

Duke Nukem 3D is one of the most hilarious and badass games I've played, I'd figure Forever would be as badass as it's predecessor. I mean, this game took 12 years to make while suffering engine and team changes during it's development. Well, no. This game isn't as badass nor as funny as 3D.
What 3D has that Forever doesn't is an open world to explore. You could find many secrets and easter eggs in many places in 3D while Forever is linear and would've been better suited as an on rails shooter (Virtua Cop for example). 3D could let Duke hold a variety of weapons to hold onto. Forever has a measly 2 weapon slot (4 if you even bother to look in the game options). While both games have pop culture jokes, 3D's jokes are still memorable to this day while Forever is just too in your face about everything like the power armor is for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥joke. Speaking of power armor, Forever has regenerating health.  Let that sink in.
Overall, Forever will never be as good as 3D, but that doesn't mean it's that bad.
Duke is still funny with even more awesome one liners, a variety of things to interact with, decent graphics with a steady FPS, smooth controls and some fun levels to play in. Forever isn't a masterpiece like 3D but it's not a terrible game. It has a ton of flaws when compared to 3D, but it's better than any other modern FPS out there. It's just a decent game. Some might enjoy it, some won't. It's just a matter of preference. Just get 3D instead if you don't have it or if you do have it, just get Forever during a sale. Also, F*CK Gearbox for almost ruining Duke Nukem and Aliens.
TL;DR: FOREVER IS A DECENT GAME.

So to get started, I tried this game seeing it as one of the few free to play games that actually get a positive review average from the relatively critic community of Steam.
The game plays out as a normal RTS, where the player gets to build his city in a relatively small (2v2 in rts standards) map in which he can do "quests" in order to gain resources faster. You slowly get to fill your map of your stuff, and when you want you can go to the world map, drag your city units and resources into armies, and send them to global cities for whatever needs to be done, be it trading or combat.
The economy system is alright, focusing on standard RTS resource gathering or buildings that provide small amounts of a resource over time. It is definitely not a hard game to get in to and my only mechanical complain would be that the combat animations are rather, well, ancient but I should say that the variety of units and their abilities is on par with other top quality RTS games.
The problem with that game however in my opinion is that it is more of an MMO than an RTS. Going around with battle protections and the like, and a community of approximately somewhat less than 1000 players per server spread over 3 factions things are veeery slow. I had to spend all the playtime I spent just to finish the quests of my map area and then all I could do was wait. Not wait for something to happen or wait for something to wear off or wait for any quests to open, just wait. Instead of being able to move in some sort of pvp or pve zone as you would expect from an MMO you can only grind resources in your solo map, so you can build units and send them to enemy cities. Thing is with all players being in that grind mode, sending units alone even if you get the maximum amount possible won't do jack.
All in all for the game to be enjoyable you have to cooperate with an alliance otherwise any sort of expansion stays imaginary. This does not only mean finding an alliance of other people, being accepted in it etc etc but then having to co-ordinate your actions. And while that is normal for an MMO and something some may see as an asset, there are so few people online that this is not feasible. Currently each faction is dominantly 1-3 full member alliances(aka guilds) of some players who were obviously the first and new players cannot contribute anything to that.
For that model to work(which is really nice and creative in thought by the way) the game needs a much much bigger amount of players, which is obviously not getting, because there are just better options out there that do not require so much time.
So while it might feel somewhat harsh, despite obviously a big amount of work put into this game, the system around it makes it the playground of those who hopped in first and for everyone else after it is a little more than a waste of time.

I've followed this game for about a year now and finally got around to purchasing it.
The game is still fairly barebones, and lacks many ease-of-use features- there is no workshop integration, meaning that you have to install mods manually, and sometimes the menus can be finicky.
However, the amazing soft-body physics are hard to beat- nothing is more satisfying than watching the car you're driving crash and crumple realistically when you crash, or letting AI vehicles destroy each other with spectacular results.
In addition, the modding community is quite active in the game, and the dedicated mod page on the beamNG website, although still relatively small, is growing.
The game's development team also deserve some praise for creating an all-new physics engine to simulate vehicle activity as well as releasing updates in a fairly timely manner.
Overall, if you prefer a driving simulator that emphasizes realism, then the game may be for you. Try out their demo on the BeamNG website - it gives a sense of the game and allows you to try the physics out before you buy it.

Anyhoo, saw this originally on Kickstarter a while ago. Developer wanted one pound and it'd be successful. After verifying that a pound meant a British unit of currency and not a trick to rip the flesh right out of me, I decided I was going to jump on it for the hell of it. Then I saw for a few more pounds I could be listed in the credits. Bonus!
I like indie games, and I like the classics. This is both. In case you don't know your history, the title is a reference to the first video game a lot of us ever saw in the arcade: Space Invaders. This game was so old school it was in black and white, except if the owner of that particular unit wrapped colored cellophane over the display. Not a joke, they did that. But it was the '70s, so they wrapped it around people and whole islands for all I was paying attention at the time. Whippersnappers think maybe that was kidding too. Kids these days have no idea. Yes, get off my lawn.
I had a point at one time... Oh, right, this game.
If you like Space Invader clones, this is one of the better ones I've seen. It adds color and a more frantic pace. It's a little more streamlined than the version released to Kickstarter supporters, so it's even better than what I paid for.

Hey, now that I think of it... Since I was a Kickstarter supporter, does that mean I got this key for free and have to mention it in the review? Well, sort of yes, sort of no. I paid the Kickstarter fee for it, he just couldn't guarantee keys at the time. I'll mention it anyway just to be safe. Heck, just having my name in the credits (I mention that yet? It totally is!) means I ought to mention it.
Game, uh... Colors, indie developer, cool music at times, twist on classic gameplay, graphics that aren't AAA game polished but at least better than the typical indie stuff, and powerups, and so many flying saucers he must think this is the '70s or something (wait, that title again). All we need are pet rocks and disco lights. Maybe we put a checkmark next to disco lights looking at the screenshots and thinking back. Probably a pet rock too somewhere, but I've played the Kickstarter version more than this one so far. Is that a cliche? "Ignore Steam's hours on record, I've played another version to death, I swear." Well, doubters... just check the credits.
Anyway, if you like this type of game, you should like this one. It's got an authentic vibe to it, not like someone who thinks Space Invaders is about condo squatters or something. Space ships, explosions... what more do you need? But if you demand schmancy VR stuff or emergent personalities or anime♥♥♥♥♥♥(not that there's anything wrong with that), you probably won't find it here. Unless that's a powerup I didn't get yet.
And did I mention you should like totally check out my name in the credits, dude? It even matches my Steam name, more or less (just a space difference, which is fitting I guess). So you can verify. Just only do it if you want a game that's like an LCD trip down Random Access Memory lane. (I probably stole that line unconsciously from somewhere cool. Game appears fun at first but there is a fundamental design flaw.
When a player makes a mistake there is no way of telling what they did wrong.
For example when I play Overwatch, I can get better at the game by just playing the game over and over. This isn't the case with "For Honor". You literally have to study classes and watch video guides on how to each class operates in order to get better at the game. Idk about you guys but I already do enough homework at college. I don't need my video games adding more.
Any game designer knows that a fundamental part of a fun gaming experience is letting the user know what they did wrong when they made a mistake. It's disappointing to see such a large company overlook such an important aspect of game development.
I believe their skill matchmaking algorithm isn't quite up to par yet either. So many of my multiplayer matches have been beyond one sided that the losing side gets so discouraged and then just gives up. Once again, not a fun experience for the winning or losing side. Another feature, (which is larger than you may think) is good/evil decisions. Some of these choices are a little hard to decide which is the good or evil choice, and this has a HUGE consequence at the end of the game. The story is great, artwork is great, spooky atmosphere yet not scary, good puzzles that stay on the same-ish level of difficulty throughout the entire game, and I only got stuck once and required a guide, but you can definitely do it without one.
I will spoil the end so avoid the next line if you do not wish for it to be partially spoiled. I REPEAT: SKIP THE NEXT LINE IF YOU DON'T WANT A SPOILER!

Most (almost all) of my time played was from my first run through, with what was probably half an hour or something like that just going balls to the wall to run through again (not sure exactly, just an estimate) but it is an enjoyable game, and is definitely worth it in my opinion.

You create whatever "class" you want, which is determined by the gear you choose (limited by how much you can carry and your XP progression - but very balanced and fair).
Game play speed is moderate - nothing crazy like CoD speed (run 'n gun junk), but not as slow (i.e. tactical) like ARMA/Squad/etc.
Graphics are good.  A few textures here and there need to be updated from the 1990's, but overall, very good.
No problems with performance - seems to be optimized well.
Negatives:
Player-base is small.  Many reviewers complain about this, BUT WHERE ARE YOU??  The player-base will only increase if you start playing....come on guys & gals.
Regardless, it's worth the price.  When more people discover this gem, the player base will no longer be an issue!  Buy buy buy!

Duke Nukem 3D is one of the most hilarious and badass games I've played, I'd figure Forever would be as badass as it's predecessor. I mean, this game took 12 years to make while suffering engine and team changes during it's development. Well, no. This game isn't as badass nor as funny as 3D.
What 3D has that Forever doesn't is an open world to explore. You could find many secrets and easter eggs in many places in 3D while Forever is linear and would've been better suited as an on rails shooter (Virtua Cop for example). 3D could let Duke hold a variety of weapons to hold onto. Forever has a measly 2 weapon slot (4 if you even bother to look in the game options). While both games have pop culture jokes, 3D's jokes are still memorable to this day while Forever is just too in your face about everything like the power armor is for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥joke. Speaking of power armor, Forever has regenerating health.  Let that sink in.
Overall, Forever will never be as good as 3D, but that doesn't mean it's that bad.
Duke is still funny with even more awesome one liners, a variety of things to interact with, decent graphics with a steady FPS, smooth controls and some fun levels to play in. Forever isn't a masterpiece like 3D but it's not a terrible game. It has a ton of flaws when compared to 3D, but it's better than any other modern FPS out there. It's just a decent game. Some might enjoy it, some won't. It's just a matter of preference. Just get 3D instead if you don't have it or if you do have it, just get Forever during a sale. Also, F*CK Gearbox for almost ruining Duke Nukem and Aliens.
TL;DR: FOREVER IS A DECENT GAME.

This is an amazing game, but it was rushed to be released and so it has many game-breaking issues. To fix these issues, and add the content that was intented to be in the game, I reccomend downloading the TSLCRM mod and the M4-78 mod. Those are the only "mandatory mods", so after that you can get any other ones, provided they're compatible. This game picks up a bit after where the last one left off, so I'd reccomend playing that one first.
STORY (Minor spoilers)
[Canonically, the protagonist is a human female named Meetra Surik]
You play as the Exile/Meetra Surik, a former Jedi who fought in the Mandalorian wars under Revan(The first game's protagonist). However, the Exile, like her name suggests, was exiled from the Jedi Order for going against them by leaving with Revan. This is just the Exile's backstory, as the game picks up on Telos, a space station that is barely functioning and soon going to explode. The Exile must escape the station and return to her ship with the help of 3 companions you find along the way. After that, depending on whether you want to play as a good little Jedi, or an evil Sith, you will try to find all of the leftover Jedi to get their help and find out why you were exiled, or to murder them all, with the help of 9 companions you find scattered around the galaxy.
Pros
+ Interesting, suprising ending based on your choices in the game
+Solid, tactical gameplay.
+ Not just an open world, an OPEN GALAXY
+ Each companion has a rich backstory and companions are actually very useful
+ Detailed crafting and upgrading systems
+ Great replayability
+ Filled with great Star Wars lore
+ Your actions affect the entire galaxy and many of the people in it, including your companions
+ Prestige classes change things up early/mid-game
+ YOU CAN TURN YOUR COMPANIONS INTO JEDI OR DARK JEDI!
+ When you reach end-game, you will be god-like with your force powers; On my way to the final area, I was clearing rooms with just one shot of Force Storm.
Cons
- Dated graphics
- Game breaking glitches are present without proper fixes
- Dialogue can be strange and confusing at times
- In many cases your quests will fail to update or you'll be clueless on where to go
- Some game-breaking glitches can be exploited and make the game too easy
- Game rarely presents the player with a challenge
Mixed
-/+ Forced to use certain companions at times
Final Rating
This game is a solid 9/10 for me. The game is NOT perfect because of the heavy amount of glitches present, yet the gameplay and story make up for it. I reccomend this game for ANY Star Wars fan or RPG fan. Buy this game!

Duke Nukem Forever if a FPS game that is a direct sequel to Duke Nukem 3D, came out in 2011, was developed by 3D Realms, Triptych, Gearbox, Piranha and it's famous for taking 15 years to complete. As you can see, it kind of had way more expectations that it should be, making people wait forever. While non-awesome spin-offs and even FPS Duke game on GBA were coming out.
It also came out for PS3 and Xbox 360. They are known for having technical troubles like framerate, some textures are always low-quality and long loading times. Also, didn't get patch which gives player an option to increase amount of weapons he can hold up to 4. Yea, PC is the way to go.
Shame that DLCs aren't available in Russia, maybe I am missing out on some good single-player stuff. Can judge only base game.
Multiplayer community isn't dead, there are a few people playing it regulary. But you will only get Deathmatch and Team DM modes. Sadly, all of them seem to use infinite ammo mutators.
And this game had a huge development history. In nutshell, one of the main people in 3D Realms wanted to make it the best game ever and so they would go and chase the goose of what was cool at current time, often going to change engine and having to remake stuff. All while they were throwing oil into fire of hype, screwing around publishers who really wanted them to just release something already, while giving no final product.
There are interesting trailers laying around. Like, the game started as a Half-Life clone set in some desert with female AI running around and even turret section that you all love. Then went into something with tentacle-infestation, though they say that a lot of stuff in 2001 trailer was made up for it. Then it went into more sci-fi-like stuff of clunkyness, then into more of Halo and such.
Just don't tell me about "looked ten times better", I have enough experience to know that stuff always looks better in trailers than what it truly was. Not to mentioning that some stuff didn't look particulary interesting.
And you know, that's the way development hell works: you don't spend time polishing and adding, instead you often remake core because you got better ideas all the time. And it just can go on forever when trying to reach perfection, especially during those times when technology was moving fast!
In the end, 3D Realms finally started to fall apart at "so I heard Halo is cool" iteration. In the end Gearbox, Piranha and Triptych (apparently fired DNF developers) ended up glueing and polising single-player part, adding multiplayer and spend 1-2 years doing legal mumbo and some stuff. And so they finally released at least something out of that embaressment. While also making people hate it because they had to fulfill all their "once Duke Nukem Forever comes out" joke promises. Now we have to do "once Half-Life 3 comes out", but it's not as fun because Valve promised nothing and don't even plan or tease anything.
Dammit 3D Realms, if not your stubborness we would have had an interesting Duke FPS franchise that would follow FPS genre evolution.
Anyway, the plot of this game is that aliens came back, all while Duke was enjoying his infamousness, having saved Earth more than once. And it doesn't take long to find out that Aliens are here to wreck and and grow huge tentacles everywhere and to ruin Duke's little ego paradise.
The setting and Duke in this game is awesome. They didn't just take some generic game and slammed Duke's one-liners on top, aka Manhattan Project. They took what makes Duke game a Duke game and increased it by two times. Remember how people would give you example that in second level of Duke 3D you can shoot at ball on the billiard pool to make them roll around and that it somehow makes the game better than Doom (it doesn't)? Well, now it's an actualy playable mini-game winning which will increase your Ego (still doesn't make it better than Doom, STFU)! Actually, there are a lot of interactive fun stuff to do that increase your max Ego, what a wonderful idea for Duke 3D sequel.
All while going from the silly stuff like Duke's Vegas location, into the depressive The Hive, all while giving lots of variety and pacing. Platforming is nice, yes, don't tell me things. Shame that it's linear, more than say HL2.
Heck, remember those maps for your favourite old FPS where you are a tiny being placed in a huge room of a house? Jumping on bed, hiding behind boxes, exploring mouseholes and such. Well, you now finally get to experience such thing in single-player campaign of Duke Nukem Forever! I think it's the first in single-player FPS games. Maybe.
It's a shame that toward the second half, when you go into Wild West thing and Dam, it deflates down. To be honest, Duke 3D deflated down fast as well, but not as hard. Not to mentioning that developers later released Atomic Edition which had awesome episode, being sorry for all non-awesomeness in base game. Then again, Forever got some "Doctor Who Cloned Me" DLC and people say that it's better too.
Not as much fun interactive stuff. Not as much sillyness. And when you will be exploring dark generic corridors of the Dam you will be wondering if you are playing a proper Duke Nukem game or some kind of Duke It Out DC.
As for gameplay, Duke doesn't need any stinking syringes to eat out of medkits and is powered up by his allmighty and menly EGO alone. In other words, it follows some of the modern popular stuff, like here you have both regenerating Health and regenerating armor that is his Ego. Don't worry, monsters are now more vicious and you can't just camp behind a single barricade or anything because some can correctly teleport behind your back.
You also have only 2 slots for a weapon. Game is kinda designed around it, by trying to make you swap weapons by throwing lots of them and always giving RPG and ammo for bosses when you need, while each of them has low ammo. So stop it with always carrying RPG around. So it's not as tactical, but lets you relax and change around. You can also execute some enemies with melee punch or kick if they drop onto knees when almost ran out of health. Doing this will restore your Ego immeditly. Freezer weapon is actually balanced this way: it's not all that strong, but it gives 100% chance for execution to gain ego back during battle.
And even then you can increase amount of slots to 4, but game was designed for 2, so I would recommend to stick to two.
Items are more useful now too. Holoduke is now actually useful, as it also makes you invinsible to monsters. Steroids are now useful too since boosted melee can now 1-2 hit enemies. What was the point of these two in Duke 3D anyway? There is also beer that makes you take less damage and infinite dark vision where you can actually see environment too. Heck, pipe-bombs and laser-mines are now throwable by a hotkey, making them so much more comfortable and useful too. Awesome.
I still miss more of mazey/sandbox feel of Duke3D levels, with all situations and angles you could get yourself into, but eh.
There are also more good bosses. And music is sadly your everyday orchestra, outside of multiplayer penthouse thing.
There is competetive multiplayer too. It's old-school in a sense that it's chaotic and not too enganging outside of that. Explosives seem to be more powerful than everything else, RPG is the top weapon. Laser-mines are everywhere and are hard to see unless you slow down. Pipe-bombs are too good too.
It also isn't so fancy technically, a lot of people experience lag. Also, no ragdolls, all Dukes always gib for some reason.
There is also leveling, but it only unlocks cosmetics for Duke and stuff in your penthouse. Which is fancy idea, though doesn't feel as good when ugly wooden boxes of "yet to unlock" stuff litter the house.
Eh, it's a pretty good game. Or at least fine for what it is. Or at least people can now move on from the Duke Nukem Forever development hell.

Probably the best old school FPS I've played in a long time. The mixed RPG elements work well for the most part, adding a lot of variety while still staying true to the original (e.g not becoming a grind fest). Very large selection of satisfying weapons that's entirely customizable to your liking with different element/ammo/fire mode/whatever mods. Toxic shotguns, fire chainsaws, freezing dual blades etc all possible, pick whatever you like. There's also lots more unique chi powers compared to the first game, and new movement abilities, letting you kite enemies a lot easier (kinda reminds me of Painkiller for some reason as I was always bunnyhopping there, now I just fly around :P).
The levels are absolutely huge and fun to explore, and sometimes look pretty gorgeous as well. Open-ended approach to missions is cool too so you can do everything in your own order. The game ran okay on high-medium settings with my specs (960M GTX, i5 6300HQ).
Downsides? It starts off really cheap, the first mission didn't really sell me the game at all, but thankfully it opens up from there pretty quick. Compared to the first game, the plot is probably a lot weaker as well, or at least I felt that way at the start, and secrets aren't as present as in the first one. The upgrade system is a bit too overwhelming as well and should be toned down, you get too many powerups all the time and it's a lot to manage (not a biggie for me though).
Once the game opens up properly a few missions later though, it gets really fun. I'd really like to see SS4 made in a similar style as it feels very innovative.

First thing's first, I put this game off for way too long and having just beat it I felt the need to post a review for it.  I had heard the game was terrible and, as I didn't want to ruin the nostalgia that I felt for Duke Nukem, I decided that I was going to avoid this title.  I was so, so wrong to judge this game before experiencing it first hand.
The game may not be perfect, but it is definitely fun.  I found it to be as enjoyable as any first person shooter that has been released in the last few years.  Duke is back in all of his glory and the gunplay is a blast.  His crude one-liners are more than welcome after the decade plus that I've waited for a worthy return and I found myself laughing frequently.
The mechanics of the game run flawlessly.  I didn't experience a single issue the entire time I played and the aiming and character controls are top notch.  Every single death and missed shot in the game felt like it was 100% my fault and not some aspect that was overlooked by the developer.  Another aspect of the game that I enjoyed was that, although the number of weapons to be found is about on par with the other games, all of the remained viable throughout the game.  They all have their pros and cons that you can use to your advantage for each situation that you find yourself in.  It also should be mentioned that, unlike the vast majority of FPS games out there, the game never felt monotonous to me.  One moment you'll be running and gunning, the next you'll be platforming after being shrunk down to the size of a can of soup, and the next you'll be manning a turret as hordes of alien ships and reinforments are en route to kill you.
There are two parts of Duke Nukem Forever that keep it from being an absolute gem, however.  First, is the restriction on the number of guns that you can carry.  Duke Nukem used to be a walking arsenal.  Every weapon that you found in the game you kept for the rest of your campaign and could use it at any time as long as you had the ammunition for it.  The second improvement to the game that could have made it a classic would be the vehicle controls.  Driving Duke's monster truck, while fun to run over aliens with, was a bit more of a hassle than I would have liked.  It wasn't absolutely terrible but it was enough that I was less than excited when I saw it ahead of me and knew that I would be driving instead of running and gunning which I would have preferred.  Fortunately, you don't spend very much time in it.
I recommend this game to any first person shooter fans and especially to old Duke Nukem fans.  I had a blast and played it from start to finish in about ten hours over the course of four days.  This -is- the worthy successor to Duke Nukem that I had hoped it to be and I had to get the word out about my experience!

The free-building of decks had long been expected, and when they finally added it, it mostly sucks. There are other things that make this a bad game. Here are my complains:
1- When you start, you pick a combination of two colors. You're given a deck in that combination and you must start with it. When you win you earn cards. Simple, right? Well, not that much. This starting deck is awful (no matter what combination you picked, they all s.u.c.k. I just can talk about two combinations, but for what I've read in other reviews, it's the same for everything else), so you may need to play a lot before winning. And when you start winning you're given like 2 cards. Seriously. Just until you beat the first "boss" you are awarded with more than 10 cards per match, which is cool, or well, would be cool if the cards were useful.
2- The card pool is poor. there are few cards and the ones available are mostly bad cards. You must play a good while until you have enough cards to customize your starting deck, let alone build one from scratch. You start with 26 lands, which seems an awful lot for me, and that get you constantly mana flowed. Go figure: at the beggining you are so limited that almost half your deck is lands. You can disable auto land-filling in the options if you want to change that, which will be useful until you have something decent to replace the lands you take out. Also, (this may be just my skill level), I have not been able to create a deck that stands good against all opponents. I know this is, almost by definition, impossible, but in previous year's Duels, the decks were more or less balanced and had some rather solid base that allowed you to build your strategy against different opponents, which meant that any single deck was able to overcome the complete campaign. In Duels 2015, I have been in the need of making an entire specific deck for a specific opponent. Try to  use that deck against the next one, and you're screwed. There's few (if any) flexibility.
3- The description of the starter decks is crap. Take this: the red-black one is supposed to be FOCUSED in stealing your opponent's creatures and sacrificing them for your own benefit. Cool sounding? Well, in your 60 cards deck (26 of  which are lands, remember) there are 2 cards that steal creatures from your enemy and 2 that can get some benefit of it. Good luck making that "strategy" work.
4- The menus are awful, you have to stupidly scroll through it, instead of a convenient and simple list as was Duels 2014 main menu. It takes a lot of scroll to get anywhere. Selecting your deck is a long tedious process, instead of being able to simply pick a deck at the beggining of a match. Are those menus good for tablets? so some people say, but I don't give a flying ♥♥♥♥, I'm using a PC. And even if I were using a tablet, I'd prefer a simple list that lets me see all that is available in a menu. Also, sometimes when you click, the game does not respond, forcing you to click for a second or third time before something actually happens.
5- Microtransactions. This is not particulary bad for me, since I never make in-game purchases in any game. But be aware that if you want all the possible cards, the price of the game goes, in total, to $40.
6- No extra game-modes. Just campaign and free for all. I loved the coop two headed giant, now it's gone.
7- Decks in campaign mode have access to a totally different card pool than the one you have, usually with cards much stronger than the ones you have. Take this example: a match against slivers. On turn 5 i was crushed by 5 trampling slivers, the weakest being 5/5. It took me like 6 tries to beat the slivers. And do you get some slivers for your pool after winning? Nope, you don't.
This game had a huge potential, and it was totally wasted. Not buying next year's. They have lost a fan.

This game is ridiculously short. My first game took me around two hours (probably a bit less, but I kept AFKing so I can't say for certain); my second game only took me an hour (I made the opposite choices as the first game and skipped all previously read dialogue). If you're an achievement hunter, three runs is the most you'll need to get them all.
As for the puzzles, they're extremely basic. The only puzzles that can't be immediately solved happen to have a hint on a scrap of paper nearby. None of them require much thinking.
I found the story to be underwhelming. I expected much more because of the high quality of the art. At the end of my first game, I honestly cared very little for the main character. The dialog is fine, and there are some notes and journal/book pages that give you some background, but it never felt like there was enough.
As a game, I feel like it didn't deliver. It was short, easy, and had a basic story that seemed to only be there as an excuse to show off the artwork. As interactive artwork, it's quite creepy and grotesque and beautiful. Honestly, I think they could've just sold this as a digital artbook and charged quite a bit more.
As stated at the beginning of this review, if you're interested in the artwork, then it's definitely worth the price. If you're interested in a dark fantasy game with a rich world, good story, and solid puzzles, then I think you'll be disappointed.

Challenging puzzle game.
These are 36 puzzle devices that are each different and each give you no hints on how to solve them. Like an IQ test, you'll know when you get it right. Sometimes you get more feedback along the way, sometimes less, and there are some common elements between the puzzles that may help you figure them out. Which I haven't. Not all of them, anyway, and that's why I think this is challenging.
You can skip a puzzle if you get stuck, but the number of puzzles you can skip seems to be limited. The puzzles are original enough that I think them fun. Yes, there is a light flip, but then there are some light flips with different takes on them that I haven't seen before. There's a match-2, but it's only part of a bigger device. There's been thought put not only into the packaging, but also into the puzzles themselves. I'd say it seems to be short, but then it is also cheap (especially now that it is on sale) (and I'm still at 30/36, so who knows how long I'll take to figure these out).
If you like your brain cells challenged, get this. Recommended.

A surprising solid third-person shooter. I was expecting nothing more than a wack-a-mole shooting gallery with clunky controls. However, Sniper Elite V2 is a no-nonsense sniping game which is fun to play and of decent quality. The bullet cam and sound are especially commendable. What's great is how you can adjust the difficulty; including the bullet physics. The game is intuitive, fast-paced and has smooth controls. It works well with both a gamepad and mouse & keyboard. Mechanically, the game is robust and this becomes apparent in multiplayer. It's no Gears of War, and the cover system is a bit fiddly but other than that, one would be pushed to find more flaws in a sniping-focused shooter which delivers all the action without the camping and bird-watching. Sure, the campaign and levels aren't exactly epic and lack the excitement of sniper missions found in other shooters, but overall Sniper Elite V2 is worth playing if you're after a fun sniping experience.

Angels Fall First (AFF for short) by Strangely Interactive is a First-Person-Shooter that includes battles on land and in space with different objectives. Fighting over territory, hacking terminals, clearing landing zones, destroying weaponized satellites or boarding battleships.
The well customizable infantry can use all sorts of vehicles ranging from buggies to mechs and tanks, from small interceptor spaceships and bombers to huge battleships that are also extremely customizable.
You can play online on servers with other players or offline with and against AI on land or in space. And even if there are servers with lets say only 3-4 people on it the other empty spots will be filled with the amazing AI this game has to offer.
AFF is running on the 2010 Unreal Engine 3. And while the engine is a tad old Strangely Interactive is managing to create breathtaking maps, weapons and vehicles. Everything got a lot of detail in it, especially the maps, wherever you go you will find someting to explore. Be it alleys and buildings on the urban streets of Irega, space-gas-pumps in the cloudy, creepy spacesector that is NB3345 or spacedocks, terminals and halls on Lukather.
The effects in AFF look very nice and add a lot to the scenes. When firefights break lose there are bullettrails, plasmashots, explosions and lasers everywhere without obscuring the scene too much. It makes big fights, be in it space or on land, feel very powerful and fun.
Scenes are presented in the right ways. There are day and night maps or maps that include both in different game modes.
You can clearly see that the devs put a lot of love and effort into designing this game.
Everybody can create loadouts for their footsoldiers and vehicles with a system that gives you three budged caps, "Commanding", "Support" and "Combat" that weapons, armors, enhancements or accesories use. Leveling up those budgets by, for example, commanding soldiers on the field, healing allies or killing enemies increases the caps on them to allow for more customizability. Even though that gives higher level players more to put on their guns and equip more kits like grenades that blind and create smoke at the same time or automated turrets at the same time it does not makes them stronger in 1 on 1 combat against lower level players because even starter players can allready use every gun in the game, may it be with less other weapons, kits or attachments. The balancing is very fair.
The gunplay in AFF feels very good, weapons kick and feel heavy, it just feels very good to use them. Recoil control is highly awarded but usually easy to manage.
They range from machinepistols, SMGs and revolvers to assault rifles, machineguns, snipers, grende or rocket launchers and plasma rifles.
And even better feels the dogfighting in space. Boosting around to chase your foe, evading missles or flying through astroids like your name is Han Solo, it all just feels very satisfying.
There spaceships for every playstyle and situation, interceptors, assaultships, bombers, boardingships, agile battlecruisers or heavy frigatesand a few more.
You can customize the capabilities and weaponry of all of the smaller fighters in the same manner you would make loadouts for a infantry soldier.
Every map got its own objectives and one of the most fun is boarding the battleships or spacestations on space maps. First you fight for defensive postitions in space, than you get a few battleships, launch boardingships and protect them, you need those to get into the enemies hangars. When that is done you deploy inside the foes ship or station and fight your way through to objectives to take out. You either do that to destroy single battleships or take out their systems or to win over something to win the match. Fighting inside a space object in tight corridors and huge hangars is just too much fun. It is not unlike Battlefront 2006 but a bit harsher, heavier and requires a lot more strategy.
Something that can't be missed is to talk about AFFs community and devs.
AFF sports a very active Discord that is used to chat about the game, off-topics, read up on what the devs are working on or future updates or submit bug reports and ideas on what to improve on. Whatever you have to think about AFF you can discuss it there. With one of the nicest communities I have ever seen. No matter your question, there will be someone to answer it.
And now for the best part. The devs are a few of the msot active members on the server. They care about the community a lot and take to heart, what we got to say. They let the players be part of their project.
We organize groups to play with every weekend and of course when people are interested also in the week.
Even if you don't have anything to say it is very much worth joining the Discord server!
AFF is a very good game, even in Early Access, don't let that scare you off. If you like games among the lines of the old fashion Battlefront, Elite, Battlefield 2142 or sci-fi, shooters and strategy this game is definitely worth checking out for you. And while everything may seem a bit overwehlming at first it is not that hard to get into and have fun.
The game got its hickups, bugs and problems, but none are gamebreaking. The balancing is already amazing, the gameplay fluid and the maps gorgeous. Report your problems and the devs listen.
When I played the UT3 mod "Angels Fall First: Planetstorm" a few years ago I already thought "This game may be the future". Now that I play the standalone I know that this game is the future.
I love AFF, that is for sure.
I thank you Strangely Interactive, with my heart I do. The industry needs more devs like you, more passionate people like you.

Strangely addicting...
Maybe I am just a fanboy. Back in the 1990's my Mom would take me to the "Crossroads Flea Market", a dirty building full of merchants selling shoes, clothes, trinkets and videogames, shareware video games like Wolfenstien 3D, Commander Keen and Duke Nukem.
So my history with the Duke goes back a long way, I have great nostalgic memories of the awesome 2D platformer. Duke 2,  I played a bit of but not much. Duke 3D came out and I was enthralled. This was one of the first games that we played over LAN and set crazy pipe-bomb traps. I played Duke 3D again recently on my 360 and noticed how high the difficulty was and how obtuse some of the level design was. As a teenager Duke was the man, as a middle aged man Duke is terrible person.
Duke Nukem Forever was something I followed since those first trailer appeared. After a decade, I admitted to myself that the game would never be released. Then it was announced, then released on PS3, 360 and PC. I was in disbelief. What kind of game did it look like? Well it looked like a single-player, linear, cheesy and throwback kind of game with crazy setpieces.
Now I pre-ordered this game. Played it through on my 360, bought and finished the single-player expansion and came to a few conclusions:
If this game was released 10 years ago, it would be hailed as an awesome "modern" sequel to Duke Nukem 3D.
If this game was released as a "budget" throwback game, no one would complain.
The load times suck on consoles.
Look, I am a middle aged man now. I have no problem sitting back and rolling through a single-player shooter in 8-10 hours  that is a bunch of stupid fun with some nostalgia thrown in (Dr. Proton!). The PC version is the best with 4 weapons and way better load times. I played through it again on my steam link (while the wife was work and the kid was asleep) and it was a fun, mindless distraction. The environment is interactive, the game play is uh "varied", vehicles, shootouts, mini-games, vlts, poop-throwing etc... The game sure isn't for everyone, the breaks in action and the bizarre sexual attitude towards women come off as way to creepy these days, but bottom line:
It was fun and that's what videogames are supposed to be.

MTG 2015 is a net gain of zero for Wizards of the Coast.  In a nutshell, the expanded deck builder and revamped multiplayer came at the expense of playability and variety.  The DOTPW series remains a better option than traditional MTG or MTG online for players who don't want a large investment of time and money, but it is far from perfect.
MTG 2015 did and excellent job on the deck builder/booster packs.  Booster packs are now earned following most campaign and multiplayer matches, and the set complements the base decks very well.  The multiplayer mode is much improved in terms of speed and reliability.  Unfortunately, the planechase and two-headed giant modes have not been replaced, but the faster gameplay is a welcome improvement.  Pay-to-play is still present, but has been scaled back to allow success without additional spending.
The user interface and menus are fashioned after a tablet OS.  Regardless of your gear, it responds as a touchscreen tablet would: slow, stuttered, and at times unresponsive.  Visually, it is appealing (provided you maximize the graphics), but after a few minutes of navigating the menus you won't care.
The mandatory tutorial would be bearable were it not for the voiceover.  Think nagging mother meets special education.
One of the most frustrating themes of the series is an apparent lack of play-testing.  MTG 2015 is no exception; browse the forums and you will see thread after thread lambasting Wizards of the Coast for their shoddy execution.  Beyond the more obvious glitches, a number of poor choices in button  placement and user interface render the gameplay clumsy, yet unforgiving.  One of the more glaring oversights is the continue button: as your main phase comes to an end, the continue button becomes the skip attack button.  This sort of haphazard design should never have made it into the final product.
The script is hilarious.  I'm sure this wasn't their intention, but it is laughably bad.  The best part about beating the game was the three minutes of mouth-breathing, sophomore attempts at fantasy writing.  The game is worth beating, if for no other reason than hearing this gem of a script.
When all is said and done, the game is still worth its price.  For $10, you get access to a wide variety of cards and decks, all of which can be used in an improved multiplayer.  The user interface and gameplay seem to have regressed in functionality, but the game looks good.  Gameplay issues aside, DOTPW remains a quicker and cheaper alternative to other MTG venues.  Consider this title recommended with reservations.

A very fun and well done game, but that could be a lot better with a more balanced difficulty and more upgrade options.
The premise of the game is simple: you were captured to participate in an alien battle royale and to earn your freedom, you must fight your way through waves of enemies and three bosses. As you defeat enemies and the crowd cheers on you, you'll get power-ups and weapons to use. Weapons run out quickly but the faster you kill enemies, the more items the crowd will give you. And at the end of each section, you'll fight a boss. Defeating a boss makes the next dungeons harder in some way, so once you've learned about each boss and what they change after they're defeated, knowing the proper boss order becomes important. And as you defeat enemies, you collect some special coins that will then unlock new weapons and items to use.
As a fast-paced roguelike game, Satellite Rush is a really fun game to play, with a challenge level that will keep you on your toes at all times. The game isn't very long, but because of how difficult it is, it requires some time to beat as the player gets a little better on each attempt.
That's where the game's two main issues arise.
The first is how extremely unbalanced the difficulty level is. Of course, as a roguelike game that isn't very long, some challenge is to be expected, otherwise the game would be completed way too quickly. However, even with that considered, the game can be extremely unfair to the player, as the player is often thrown in rooms that are absolutely crammed with enemies, sometimes with literally nowhere to run and nowhere to hide. And because the game becomes harder as the player progresses through it, there are times when the difficulty becomes almost unbearable.
It would have been a lot better if the game had difficulty levels to choose from or unlockable difficulties (you defeat the game once and the next game has a higher difficulty).
The second issue is the lack of upgrades. You unlock three weapons, then three items and that's it. It's pretty easy to unlock those and once those are unlocked, there is no other use for the coins you collect. Also, items obtained after you defeat a boss are fixed - which isn't bad per se, but some more variety would have been good.
One solution to this would be to have the coins collected after all items are unlocked become usable to buy upgrades for the character - as an example, using red coins for health upgrades, purple coins for fire rate and green coins for speed. That way, the coins would still have some use and the player could use those to beat the game if the game is too hard for him/her.
Despite these issues, it's still an extremely fun game to play and highly recommended.

I recommend this game, but for reasons different than most others. I went into it with every intention of immersing myself and really getting creeped out by the game, but it didn't work, even though most times I was playing it I was in a dark room by myself with headphones on at night.
Still, maybe I'm just desensitized to Gothic horror like this. Regardless, the game has a pretty solid atmosphere and excellent sound design. Stand still and you'll hear a creak that oculd either be close or far away, or maybe a distant whail of pain. There are lots of details in the sound department to really help you get into it.
The story is also solid enough. You play as a guy named Daniel, a man who wakes up with no memory in a castle somewhere. Nearby is a note from himself telling him to go to the darkest depths of the castle and kill the baron there. You learn things through notes lying around (like in most horror games) and as you go on, you learn the dark truth behind the castle, Daniel, the baron and why the monsters in the castle pursue you relentlessly.
Additionally, there's a sanity meter. Remaining in darkness or looking directly at the monsters will drain your sanity and as it deteriorates further and further, your vision distorts and the camera might shake, or fall or something along those lines. It leads to some fairly intense encounters with the monsters you are helpless to defend yourself against. Do you hide in the dark and risk losing further sanity until the thing goes away? Or do you turn your lantern on to preserve some sanity, but risk being spotted?
So while the game failed to really scare me, I still enjoyed my time with it. It has a solid atmosphere, story and set of gameplay ideas that help it stand out and unlike its copycats like Outlast, it relies more on subtlety than jump scares to scare the player. Plus, I got it for free during a recent sale. It's worth looking into for horror fans despite the fact that, if you've played other games like Silent Hill 3 or regularly expose yourself to all manner of horror media, you aren't very likely to get too scared.

is a top-down shooter that features some rogue-lite mechanics such as permadeath and randomized levels. These features are complemented with a great looking set of pixel art, a pretty fitting soundtrack and what could be described as a retro inspired sci-fi setting.
You play as an office worker who is captured by aliens and taken aboard the Satellite Moebius, an arena where you’ll have to fight for your life against waves of alien enemies. The concept is pretty simple, your objective is to, hopefully, get out of the arena alive but while attempting to achieve that goal you’ll also have to entertain the alien crowd. As you start killing enemies in quick succession the crowd will eventually start throwing power ups and weapons into the arena, so it is in your best interest to kill as many enemies as quickly as possible.
Upon entering the game you’ll have to choose one of 3 doors to enter, with each one leading you through a different path and eventually to a different boss. If you manage to defeat the boss you’ll be able to choose one of 3 different upgrades and after that you’ll be teleported to the first room and you’ll be prompted to enter one of the two remaining doors. This time the path you’ll choose will have more and thougher enemies and if you manage to the defeat the second boss the process repeats itself, eventually leading to a final boss. Each one of these paths has a different colour assigned to them, and it is that colour which will determine what kind of coins enemies drop when they die. Once you get a certain amount of them you’ll unlock new items.
In terms of gameplay, Satellite Rush is pretty straightforward and anyone that has played Isaac or any other game in this genre will feel right at home. The only thing I believe I’ve never saw in other games like this is the fact that when you shoot your character actually slows down, so you can’t just run around shooting enemies while they follow you because they might catch up. You use WASD to move around, arrow keys to shoot and you also have a designated key to pick up and use items. In terms of weapons, while you’ll most likely spend a lot of your time with the basic pistol, you’ll also spend a lot of time with weapons the crowd throws at you such as, machine guns, shotungs, rocket launchers, flame throwers, and other sorts of crazy weapons such as laser based weapons that fire in a V shape. Besides that, the crowd will also give you power ups which are a one time consumable item such as, bombs and shields. Considering you’ll be able to keep the alien crowd entertained, the gameplay will vary a lot, one second you’ll be firing rockets from afar against enemies that explode when die they and the next second you’ll pick up a shotgun and you’ll have to go close to the enemies in order for the bullets to actually hit them.
Satellite Rush is a pretty fun game to play given the fact that is still in early access, and that kind of leads to one of my complaints about the game. As of right now, you’ll probably see everything the game has to offer in less than 10 hours, but I’m hoping that before the game releases it will have more enemy types (which there are quite a few already), more power ups, more boss types, more weapons and perhaps a little bit more of variety in each level.
Overall, I think that for its current price there is no going wrong with this one, especially if you’re a fan of the genre. It manages to keep the gameplay diversified enough so that you don’t feel like you’re doing the same thing over and over (even though you kind of are) and the game seems to go towards a humorous retro setting. If you’re not sure you’ll enjoy it just pick it up and if under 2 hours the game doesn’t manage to grab you just ask for a refund, for me all it took was a few minutes.

Satellite Rush:
~~~~~~~~~~~
The alarm clock went off at 6 am, showered until 6:15 am, finished breakfast at 6:30 am, walked to work . . . abducted by Aliens around 7:15 am, been given a colourful necklace and a gun thingy at 7:30 am, find myself in the middle of an arena being watched by strange Aliens at 7:35 am. Well, what do you expect when you are an office worker?  Hold on, I have really been abducted! AHHHHHH!
Satellite Rush is a top down shooter action game where you take control of an office worker who finds himself in an interesting situation, to say the least. You will have to fight to survive and clear the Arena (corridor) of the Satellite Moebius one by one, by killing Aliens and destroying several robots along the way. You will also have to entertain an unconventional and tough audience (full of Aliens, of course), by eliminating all enemies as fast as possible or by creating a chain reaction with explosive barrels within each arena. Then they will cheer you up and even throw you some fabulous goodies for your effort; these items will help you to reach the last arena and hopefully beat the boss of the level.   Each time you eliminate an opponent, a coin will appear at the spot where your enemy has fallen. Make sure to pick up all coins before exiting an arena. Each time you reach a specific number of coins you will be able to use a new weapon from the audience.
I really like the introduction cut-scenes when you load the game – they’re funny! You will be able to test your skills in three different arenas with each one slightly more challenging than the last. The level randomisation aspect will give you good re-playability but keep in mind this game is still on early access and shows great potential.
Good pixel artwork, nice soundtrack (especially the samba track), you will smile all the way to the slaughtering arena!
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good pixel artwork
-	Level randomisation
-	Good soundtrack
-	Fun and addictive
-	Achievement and Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Needs to be more challenging
Who told you being an office worker is a boring job? Today is your lucky day, you’re playing for your life on Satellite Rush!
