Good things about the game:
++ Awesome art. Really, every single scene and character in the game is painted beautifully and with so much detail. Every screen is a feast for the eyes in some way, with its own dark, twisted world. Imagine someone like Geiger doing a video game. This game is proof that we do not need to be stuck in pixellated art for adventure games.
+ Atmosphere: the feeling of oppression, mortal frailty and fatality of the world comes across well. Everything attaches itself well thematically to what is going on and almost every little thing has some dark twist about it.
+ If you are afraid of the incredibly obtuse puzzles, you have nothing to fear in this game. Despite the twisted nature of the world, the puzzles are logical and the game isn't afraid to give you open hints as to what you need to do.
+ Different environments: again, every screen looks and feels different. Are are unlikely to see the same wall twice and the game does everything to vary the nature of the environment. The environments are actively part of the story rather than lazily copy-pasted all over.
+ The story had a surprising twist-ending (well, it surprised me).
Bad things about the game:
- The puzzles will not be challanging to a veteran adventure gamer. There are one or two puzzles where you can figure things out without the game giving you a solution but that's about it. However, the game still holds interest to them for its art and atmosphere.
- Not enough oppressing/depressing music! I recall only one instance in the game where the music actively contributed to the scene. Otherwise it is fairly muted or I don't recall it at all.
- The story does have you start with amnesia but for one driving memory. However, the character's identity is not imporant to the plot (until the end) and the story actively works with this rather than just use it out of laziness.
- The game has a moral choice system but it is rather transparent and predictable where it goes. It falls into the trap of "doing evil for evil's sake" and rarely really tempted to do evil. Evil needs to be something that the player would chose from something other than sadism (or amoral selfishness) and good needs to be the hard, unrewarding thing to do or even something you wouldn't think to do.
- I don't really call it a negative but the game has no hint system or even a point-of-interest highlighter. The game is design well enough that you don't need them.

Kumeric Labs is an independent development studio from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Their studio is one that was founded out of a number of friendships who had a shared passion of gaming. The studio was established back in 2012 with five fresh university graduates. Less than twelve months later the quintet decided to turn their passion into a reality by deciding to create a permanent dedicated gaming studio. In the time since they have added seven more people to their team bringing it to a well rounded twelve passionate staff members. Satellite Rush is their debut title.
It is a top-down shooter that features pixel art graphics, randomized levels and roguelike elements. The team have endeavored to mesh a number of well known games and media into one singular title with influences taken from Super Smash TV, Binding of Isaac and Douglas Adams with a garnish of sci-fi imaginarium. The player gets to take control of an abducted office worker and play through Satellite Moebius which is an intergalactic space arena where he must destroy enemy aliens and robots that have been programmed to kill you in order to cheer up the television show’s audience.
I’ve found the game to this end to be a highly enjoyable experience. If you’re good at games such as the aforementioned The Binding of Isaac you’ll find yourself at home almost immediately. The game play can be fast and frantic which keeps you on your toes constantly. Players determine which of three doors – red, green and blue – they wish to go through and complete each room in the corridor chain before returning to tackle the next chosen door. You need to clear each arena before you can take on the next challenge but in order to do that you are aided by the dropping of various power ups and tools when you kill certain enemies. One of the smaller problems that I had with this system was that rather than having a certain time to use these power ups you’ll lose their ability when you move into the next room. I’d like to see the abilities featured on a clear timer rather than losing them because many of the power up weapons will unlock when you’ve just cleared a room making many drops almost entirely pointless.
The graphics, sound and atmosphere are almost perfect for the game in its present state. There have been some very wise game design decisions implemented into the game already. The game is colorful and vibrant without being overly so. The level design has been carefully thought out and meshes quite well with the atmosphere. One of my favorite aspects of the game is the sheer amount of enemy types. They help present new challenges in each randomized room making no two rooms let alone full games ever truly alike. Thus far I haven’t particularly noticed any of the typical downsides that this can often lead to such as games or rooms feeling unfair.
At $4.99 Satellite Rush is exceptionally well priced for the quality of its content having successfully passed from Steam Greenlight into Early Access. The game has a lot of potential and room for growth, even being as solid as it is already, and a game that I am eager to keep up to date on.

The art alone is enough to make playing this game a worthwhile experience. Amazing atmosphere, world, story, characters, themes, music, and engaging but not frustrating gameplay. I would love to see more of this universe. This game combines the decision making elements of games like the walking dead with classic point & click elements. But the puzzles are easier than classic point & click games and there are no dialogue trees.
This was the perfect game for me because I love mini puzzles and I HATE dialogue trees. There is dialogue, but it's concise, relevant, and interesting. The mini puzzles were cool, but not so difficult that you have to spends hours trying to solve each one. This was the first game I have played without using a walkthrough at some point. Most of the time I knew what I needed to do, and could rely on the in-game hints.
The main reason to play this game, though, is for the story. The only downside is, like most games of this type, I wish it were longer. I have 9 hours on record but most of that was from the game running in the background while I was doing other things, or asleep. Ideally I would like an adventure game to last 20 hours, but given the level of detail of the artwork, that would be unrealistic.
Edited to add: this game has no voice acting which I think is perfect. I hate voice acting unless it's really really good quality. The silence is eery and fits the atmosphere. Basically, everything about this game is perfect. I am now really sad that I've finished the game. Anyone who likes point & click games should really just buy this right away.

The game is fun to play. The kit out system lets you customize pretty widely, even with low loadout setups; notably, there are some break-points that will make certain setups much more powerful, but the game does a good job of making every effective, without being too powerful.
You're going to have a learning curve, when you first start. I highly recommend loading up the single player mode and learning some of the weapon options. Alot of the information about different loadouts isn't very clearly communicated; you're going to have to experiment to figure out what works where, and why. To add to this, there are alot of weapon options that're very good at one or two situations; It requires some experimentation to figure out what to use where, and what a good 'all purpose' load consists of.
Playerbase is small, but the game's AI is still fun to play with; most matches tend to be four or five humans and the rest of the forty slots filled with bots. Hopefully it'll grow.
Gunplay feels a little clunky, still, but has actively improved over the time I've had the game. It fills my 'I want to play a shooter' niche, pretty solidly.
Overall, would recommend; you get more than your money's worth, as long as you understand that you're buying into a pretty complicated, team based shooter.

Duke Nukem: Forever has recieved many mixed opinions throughout its time with new players and those already acquainted with the Duke Nukem franchise. I myself was an avid fan of Duke Nukem 3D on the N64, and played it regularly with my brother anf friends for a long period of time. So, being familiar with Duke Nukem myself, I can say that my review will be based a little on my appreciation for Duke Nukem franchise, however I will try to be as unbiased as possible.
Duke Nukem, having previously saved the world from the alien invasion, is now regarded as a celebrity and world superstar amongst the global population. The aliens once again attack the earth and steal the babes (only the hot ones) in search of revenge against their nemesis and planet earth. As a result, Duke Nukem goes back into action to save the world from the aliens once again.
With a really nice graphical update from its predecessor (this game has been in development for a
), as well as Duke's classic inappropriate wit, I definitely enjoyed reliving the Duke Nukem experience. Some may say it goes a little over the top, however Duke's personality as well as those of other character such as Captain Dylan, make this a very comical FPS experience, with plenty of cheesy lines and film references to boot. Although a simple storyline (very typically Duke Nukem style), the FPS experience is still enjoyable, with classic weapons such as the shrink ray, expansion ray, trip mines, holo Duke etc. Ego boosts such as lifting weights, or shooting hoops can increase your ego (which acts as a health bar) as you progress through the campaign. As well as ego boosts, there are also other hidden Easter Eggs to find, making the levels fun to explore. A game worth getting for any Duke Nukem fan in my opinion, especially during the sales, and also worth playing for those new to the franchise.
Pros
+ The full Duke Nukem experience with bucket loads of comical quotes and references
+ Classic enemies and weapons
+ Hidded Easter Eggs (Ego boosts + more)
+ DLC for an extended storyline, which is also great fun for those who love the base game (cheap on sale)
+ Achievements
Cons
- Fairly standard FPS mechanics
- Some frustrating and tedious section (such as using a turret against incoming ships)
- The occasional bug can make AI enemies and companions become stuck
- When pig cops jump at you they kind of float in mid-air towards you rather that having a fluid jump
My Score: 7/10

For better or worse, Duke Nukem Forever has all the qualities we now associate with modern FPS games.  Linear, corridor-like levels.  Recharging health.  Epic set pieces.  Vehicle sections.  The ability to carry only a few weapons.  Turrets.
As a huge fan of Duke Nukem 3D (I played through the original when it was released and still play through much of it yearly), I would be lying if I said DNF is a worthy successor to that DOS classic.  However, Duke 3D still works and we can always go back and play that whenever we want to.  The sad fact is, if you want to sell a FPS today you need to compete with COD, and that means playing by modern FPS rules.  A game like DUKE3D, with its large and sometimes mazelike levels and enemies that can tear through you in seconds, could not be released today by a major company.
Which is not to say that DNF gets a free pass for its faults.  The strict limit on the number of weapons you can carry means it very seldomly makes sense to take the risk of carrying some of the more unique weapons.  I played through the majority of the game with a pistol, shotgun, minigun, and rocket launcher, and while I wanted to play around with the freeze ray and shrink gun, they just seemed like suboptimal choices.
The vast majority of the game takes place in linear corridors, though this is sometimes broken up by larger areas you need to travel through in vehicles.  There is one section toward the end where you finally get our of a corridor and under water, but your oxygen is so limited that you basically have to follow a "corridor" of pipes letting out crucial air bubbles.
The corridor design works sometimes.  Toward the end there is a stage where you have to escape from a collapsing structure and even though it is totally linear and you cannot fail, it's pretty exciting the first time through.  The intro level is also pretty fun just because there is so much going on you forget you are travelling in a corridor.
Sadly, the middle sections (a good 1/3rd of the game) are extremely dull, and have you (literally now) running through corridors fighting the same 3-4 enemies, never in any real danger because of regenerating health and generous checkpoints.  Never mind the awful parts where Duke is shrunk down- this works nicely the first time it happens and you get to explore a "giant" kitchen, but the game repeats this trick another couple times and it gets dull quickly.
The weapons all feel pretty decent, though some of them (minigun especially) should have packed more punch.  There are also plenty of items to use.  They add some flavor to the game, but I was able to get through the game with no problem without using them at all.
The game looks surprisingly good with all settings turned up to max, especially considering how much review at the time complained about how dated it looks.  I ran it on a top of the line gaming laptop hooked up to a nice monitor, and it looked really decent.  Granted, much of the game takes place in a hallway.
I didn't touch multiplayer.
As for the Duke stuff... as a fan of DUKE3D it was nice to see how a lot of stuff was updated for this, from the enemies, to the items and weapons, and the one-liners.  There is some really childish/lowbrown "humor" here that was totally absent from the classic game.  DUKE3D had some raunchy locations, but avoiding stooping to such low levels.  This stuff is few and far between though, and the Duke character is still charming.  Just like in DUKE3D he is a mixture of cool and lame, an action hero who doesn't realize that he is a little out of touch with the times, but at heart a decent guy who wants to save the world.  I especially like his final one-liner to the end boss, which is so ridiculous and over the top that you imagine he was trying to come up with the ultimate macho burn but instead came out with this crazy nonsense (though true to his word he does exactly what he promises).
Duke Nukem Forever is not nearly as bad as its reputation would have it, and I certainly enjoyed the ~10 hours I put into it to completion.

This game was my most anticipated title of the year. The first one blew me away, and I couldn't believe it didn't get more attention for being so visually spectacular and fun (first person melee combat is rarely good or visceral in the way that SW2013 is). The sequel is good, but they throw out the linear story-based game with a simple ability/weapon upgrade system in favor of a mission-based shooter that feels more like Borderlands than anything else. Wang is still funny, the environments and shadows still look best in class, and the gun and swordplay are still super satisfying, but the pacing is wrong. Stopping to loot, and spending a lot of time in menus modifying weapons and equipping new ones feels more monotonous than it should, and turns it into something more reminiscent of Borderlands than SW2013. They might've gone too far in a few places, here.
Seems like a lot of people had the same issues. I kind of wish they had just stuck to their guns and given us more of the same type of game the 2013 version was. You can see what FWH was going for pretty clearly; they wanted to include a ton of weapon variation that the 2013 system just wouldn't have allowed for (that game played more like an old school shooter where there's x # of total guns and once you have them all that's it). Including claws or dual swords wouldn't have been easy to do unless they were purely a cosmetic change. But the benefits of having a bunch of extra weapons were outweighed in my opinion by the tedium of equipping and socketing them.
The last problem I had with the game was the sidekick character. Kamiko just doesn't have the same impact or rapport with Wang/the player that Hoji did. Hoji's story in the 2013 game was surprisingly poignant, and by the end of a game that was supposed to be about murdering the ♥♥♥♥ out of demons as a man whose name is a euphemism for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥shouting puns about it every few minutes, I was actually emotionally invested. Hoji was a friend. Kamiko clearly detests Wang until like, 2 or 3 missions from the end, when she kind of has a make-or-break moment of "oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ this guy holds my fate in his hands I need to stop being such a♥♥♥♥♥♥to him." It's abrupt, it doesn't work for me, and I didn't care about her at all.
Shadow Warrior 2 is still worth a look to anyone interested. Even with all the flaws, the gunplay and visuals are so good I still rate it an 8/10 at least. But I would highly recommend newcomers trying the 2013 game first. It's a better, more compact experience, and regularly goes on sale for like $5. The writing is better in that game and doesn't try so hard to recapture bottled lightning.

Satellite Rush is a tricky arena shooter with a cheerful, colourful setting that disguises the fact you're a random bloke who's been abducted and has to fight for his life!
It's a fairly typical action-roguelike set-up. You choose from a red, green or blue door, then have to clear out a series of randomly allocated arenas, and finally a boss. Repeat until you've won all three doors.
The crowd thrill meter at the top is a clever way of adding urgency to the game. If you string together kills, the meter goes up into the rewards zone, and cool temporary weapons will spawn in the arena. But it will continually tick back down again, forcing you onwards. I'd like to see them do more with this concept.
Gameplay review video, including two bosses:
I liked how the aliens have a variety of attacks to learn, encouraging you to come up with strategies such as who you'll need to kill first. But there needs to be more enemy types - some of the existing ones are a little dull.
The persistent unlockable system is a familiar way to encourage you to play again, and the door choice at the start allows you to focus on the upgrades that suit your play style, which is cool.
But the runs behind each type of door don't feel hugely different, which is a shame. A much wider selection of arenas and level styles seems crucial for long-term replayability.
Also, the control of the player isn't very slick, with eight directions of movement (and only four to shoot). He can feel lumbering and unable to dodge stuff. It helps that you run faster when not shooting, but getting out of a tight spot is often just not possible.
As is often the case with action-roguelikes, the game starts off slow and gets more exciting as it goes, so once you've played the game a few times the early parts can feel like a chore to get through. The game takes off once you've got the crowd meter high enough for weapons, but if you get the wrong arenas, this might take a while.
The bosses are tough, so they're satisfying to beat. Some of the bullet hells are a little silly, given your character isn't that manouverable, but bosses do become much more beatable with practice.
So overall, it's got a few problems - one of the major ones should be addressed by new content being added over the course of early access, but it's the basic control of your character that might put people off. I enjoyed the game enough for it not to bother me too much, especially given its value price point.

I just finished playing Tormentum - Dark Sorrow, and there are very few games these days that I can sit down and play for several hours at a time but this was one of these games. In fact, I sat down and didn't get up before the credits were rolling, which does say a lot about the phasing of this game. It took me about 4 hours to get through, which for me is well worth the asking price. (Might have to check out some of the other endings as well)
What really kept me engaged in this game was the fantastic setting, wonderfully rendered, incredibly creative environments and characters are scattered around. And even with very little dialogue per character you still get a great sense of who they might be by just looking around and taking in their surroundings. Presentation really sells this experience.
The only thing I could possibly comment on is the difficulty of the puzzles. This is rather difficult to predict as a game designer when using somewhat pre-used puzzle designs, how much their audience has already experienced those types of puzzles. For me having played quite a few of these games, none of the puzzles felt very challenging, so they ended up feeling a bit routine like. There is a good variety however, so at least you're not doing the same ones multiple times.
Overall, fantastic experience, one I'll be keeping with me for a while to come.
Thanks to the developers for providing something very interesting and pleasing to the mind.

Much like many of the recent views, I purchased this game via the Humble Narrative Bundle. As the Bundle's title suggests, I purchased six story based games (my favorite type of games). I had always seen advertisements for this game both on Steam and on the App Store. I decided to forego reading any reviews until at first experiencing the game. 3.1 hours in and I completed my first 80 days, I must say this is probably one of the most replayable games I have played. I am eager to try out many different scenarios, including attempting traveling the globe beginning east, as opposed to the west. I want to give out as little as possible, as this game must be experienced, however the objective of the game is to go around the world in 80 Days (beginning in London) with your master Monsieur Fogg. After this, everything is up to you!
After my first playthrough, I already miss the characters Monsieur Fogg and Passepartout. The writing is intelligent and there are always twists and turns happening in the game to keep one engaged. There are so many cities to visit! You have the option to visit over 200 cities, and the time crunch to get back to London was thrilling. Another option is try to go around the world visiting the least amount of cities. There are so many hidden gems in this game I have yet to explore but cannot wait to! I am absolutely loving this game so far and would've gladly paid full price. It is a fun adventure with superb writing and multiple enthralling twists and turns.

At the time of writing this review, I have done a single trip around the world which took me about 2.7 hours.
I'm VERY glad I didn't read a single review of this game but saw it rated very positively here which prompted me to get it in the latest Humble Bundle because most of the reviews are blatantly spoiling one of the best twists in the early stages of this game which blew my mind and which make this game VERY different from the Jules Verne affair which was fantastic in it's own right. This game does take heavy inspiration from the Jules Verne novel but adds it's own unique twist and spins a narrative around your actions that is VERY compelling.
You start as Passepartout, the valet of Phineas Fogg who has just made a wager where he must travel around the world in 80 days. As the valet, you must plan your travels across the major cities on the globe and ensure you meet the goal and win the bet for your master. You must decide upon your mode of transport from one city to the next, manage your finances, go to markets and buy and sell goods which will fetch you some profit with which to pay for passage to the next city. You will face many situations and forced to make choices along the way which shape the narrative of the game.
What sets this game apart is it's one of the first games I have played which is narratively focused where your actions will ACTUALLY AFFECT THE OUTCOME. As enjoyable as the Walking Dead series by Telltale games is I never feel as if any of my choices leading up to the end ever mattered leaving me only with a binary choice of some meager description. This game is so refreshing in it's beautifully written world which changes as you make choices along the journey and in the cities you visit. The way you interact with people you talk to, the decisions you make, the items you buy, the paths you take, every single one of them shapes how your journey goes and whether you actually return to London, the city from where you begin this epic tale, on time to win the wager for Phineas. There are also so many references to the original which are done brilliantly yet subtly which I absolutely loved.
For all the praises I have been singing about this game, truly there is but one, though enormous, demerit to this game. One that would almost make me not recommend the game. For all this amazing story-telling along the way, what they give you at the end of the journey as a "journal" of your travels is so pathetically sparse and idiotic in it's presentation that I almost don't feel like playing it again. What happened to the grand tales of my fight on a train, my almost missing a boat, my meeting the owner of a freight company and other such amazing little stories? All they show you are logs of what happened and the date AND THAT'S IT!
If it weren't for the pure joy of seeing your journey unfold before your very eyes and the amazing number of branched paths that are possible and events that you may face which I very much look forward to finding, I would have completely stopped playing yet I find myself wanting more. I want to experience that thrill of exploring and finding people, nooks and crannies that show me new things along the way. And grudgingly, I will go through the game many more times and will surely forget the issues along the way because this game truly is a joy to play.

Quite a nice little puzzle game in the style of "The Room", but it's lacking any story, and graphics seem to prefer style over design: It looks nice and shiny, but the game is buggy, and controls are clunky. There's quite a number of times where you have to turn a dial, and it feels like a mobile port designed for touchscreens, not for mouse users. The dials go everywhere exept for the one place you want to set it, and though it forces the player to think a little bit harder because brute forcing becomes neigh impossible due to frustration (turn three dials with twelve settings each …), it's no fun even if you know the solution.
There's no feeling of reward - though the sales pitch tells a story of a not-so-distand furture where personal data being stored in elaborate boxes, you never get to see the contents of the box you've just cracked. There's some blue light, and that's it, next box. I imagined myself in the role of a professional cracker who constantly keeps asking himself "Why the hell am I still doing this?". Even my Windows 3.0 Mahjongg game rewarded me with a fortune-cooky-style saying if I solved one. Here, I get nothing. Okay, there was some
in the end, but it didn't even look
.
As for being buggy: The boxes sit on a kind of desk, where you can turn them around (and a little bit up and down), zoom in and out to find details (not that looking for minute detail is required for more than one puzzle). It happened four or five times that I found myself trapped inside the cube (thus knowing they are empty and not worth the efford), and hitting Escape in order to get to the menus leads to the images rotating maniacally, forcing me to end the game via task manager. Made me twitch and felt cheap.
Still, it's a recommendation. I payed less than one Euro in the summer sale and spent a couple of hours with twisting, turning (and cursing dials). You can replay the puzzles, but why bother? It's play and uninstall, there's hundred of nice (or not so nice) puzzle games on Steam, but I had some fun, making it fifty cent (or so) well spent.

I have been a player of this game since Aug of 2013, when the game was only browser based and in beta. when I first started playing there were several bugs, but in the past year (2014) most of the bugs have been cleared, and a lot of new content and changes have happened.  This game is constantly changing and always for the better.
Unlike most Free to play games, Anno Online has NO PVP, which makes for a different environment.  My fellow players and myself have a very helpful community VS one out to kill each other.  Another thing that sets Anno Online apart from the others is that you don't need to buy the ingame currency to get anywhere, all you need is a little amount of time... I didn't hit the top population on the starting island till a year after I started playing, but no other player insulted me, or kicked me out of their guild because i hadn't hit the "End Game".
Game play of Anno Online is very much like Anno 1404 AKA Dawn of Discovery (in North America), Except for a few major changes;
1) There is no Spice/indigo/silk Islands - all the oriental goods that you made in 1404 are instead Sold by a NPC vendor
2) Monuments -  In Anno Online Monuments are 100% different and there are more monuments than in any other Anno game.
3) Island colonization - there is no NPC stealing the island you wanted in Anno online, you find islands for yourself and only yourself, they are 100% random and very different... but i will admit it's hard to find just the "right" island
4) Interactions with other players - you help your neighbors in Anno online by sending buffs or your constructor over to their islands, and in turn you get rewarded for some of it... there is no hostile interactions between players.
5) Construction - in Anno online, you can move buildings with no resource penalty but deleting you only get back 1/4th of what you put in. VS other Anno games where if you put a building down you have to delete to put it somewhere else, which in most missions you lose 1/2 resources.
6)Combat-  In anno games you control the ships and they fight the other ships in real time with little to no rewards... in Anno Online, Possibly cause it's too much strain on the servers the combat is Turn Based, but every combat you enter gives you rewards, these rewards can be spent on fun things to boost your economy with one issue, it's a strain on your economy early on to be building up and doing PVE, and many veteran players suggest doing the PVE to mid/late stages of the game.
Now it isn't a proper review without posting a few negative points;
1) Zone locks- these freaks of nature can hurt, and sadly seem more frequent now with more players coming in from the steam community, but there is 2 ways that I know BB handles these... first is the auto script, it runs every day at midnight server time (8pm eastern time)- 90% of zone locks are fixed this way... I have had a zone lock and the auto script handled it.   The other way is BB has to go in and find the error, sadly this takes time and can take from days to weeks to even a month in some cases. however sad you do get reimbursed for time lost.
2) Minor combat bugs - since this latest patch these might not show up... but on some maps after attacking and winning a boat may get 'stuck' and becomes unusable... i haven't seen if the map is still in the game after this last patch but they can happen if near an island for combat.
3) Construction- losing 3/4 of resources spent is a major blow if you built the wrong building.
4) early game - it's slow... very slow but that's why we have our friendly chat system to make you forget how long something takes.
5) As with all multiplayer games, Trolls  just can't avoid them on the internet.
6) This one is more personal- can't use steam client with the web started accounts.  This is something I would love to be added in the future.
7) lack of a 2nd ruby cutter... would be nice to cut rubies faster... but it's again a personal complaint.
All in all I like the game and would recommend it to others!

It's a puzzle game where it took me literally an hour to beat all the 36 puzzles it has to offer. I was hoping for a bit more, since I really love these types of abstract puzzles where you aren't given any explanations, just a problem for you to solve. I guess I've been spoiled by games such as the Room-series, where each puzzle builds upon the previous one. Here, you're presented with a self-contained puzzle every single time, just with a new mechanic thrown in and later on you'll get puzzles made of combinations of all those mechanics.
Most of the puzzles are straightforward enough, where it only takes you seconds to realize what you're being asked for and it also takes no time at all to achieve the win state. Other times the principle is really easy, but the way getting there takes some time. And by far the fewest are puzzles where the solution itself is quite roundabout but the way to that solution is fairly easy again. I guess that this keeps the frustration level fairly low, since there was never an instance where I felt like giving up, but I'll also readily admit that at least 2 or 3 puzzles got solved entirely by accident. I didn't even brute-force them, I just started entering "solutions" and the game just played the congratulation-melody without me ever knowing what I accidentally did right. The first couple of levels are entirely tutorials so hardly a lot is being asked from the player. Some levels actively try to fu
ck with the player by giving false clues, but that's kind of a di
ck move in a game where you're never given clear explanations. But thankfully those are extremely few and far between.
The presentation is pretty good, it looks better than a puzzle game has the right to be, but I would've liked some actual music instead of the same repeated audio loop of rainfall. I guess for $3 you can't ask for much, but I really wasn't anticipating such a short session when I booted up this game. Oh well.

For those of you who've played M&B Warband, what you'll find is a somewhat more limited but much more story-driven game, set during a very dynamic era in Eastern Europe's history. It's somewhat more limited as there are fewer 'roleplay' options and the economy seems less well developed, It's much more story-driven because instead of the over-arching "take over the world" objective, you have three different stories (Cossack, Muscovite, and Polish) you can engage in and leave 'on the back burner' at any time to return to the free-roaming sandbox world, which still exists largely unchanged from Warband. AI improvements: By default, a pike and shot formation will shelter the shot under the pikes. Ideal for defeating cavalry. Musketeers can kneel and fire. Reloading can be achieved on the move, though at a walk. In terms of the engine, WFAS and Warband are essentially identical, so expect smooth performance on any remotely reasonable gaming computer even at maximum settings.

Duels of the Planeswalkers finally gets deckbuilding, but at what cost? Slow, unresponsive UI, a starting experience that is frustrating because you are forced into playing with mediocre cards for hours, and a shockingly overt pay-to-win structure where lots of good cards are locked behind Premium Boosters that you can only buy with real money. Lack of puzzles is also a large disappointment for me.
All in all, I would recommend staying away from this, even as someone who enjoys Magic regularly and has been buying the Duels of the Planeswalkers series annually.

When playing through the game, be sure to install the Restored Content Mod and the M4-78EP mod. These will allow you to play the game as closely to how the Obsidian development team originally wanted the game to be played. This is easily my favorite Star Wars game to date, and it is also in my Top 5 favorite games of all-time. At the time of this review, I have only played 1 playthrough on Steam. I completely engulfed myself in the game and did not skip through any cutscenes or dialogue. I did skip through Peragus though (because I find it to be more of a tutorial level than anything) by using the Skip Peragus mod.
Pros:
- The main questline is very elaborate and well thought out. There are also many sidequests to do along the way that will enhance your view of the galaxy.
- The seemingly unimportant dialogue choices you make during the game can have significant effects down the road.
- I felt that this game was much more visually appealing than the original KotOR. It also seemed to me that the game ran smoother as well, although that might just be me.
- The characters that join you along the way have their own pasts and interesting stories.
- Subpoint: Depending if you are Light Side or Dark Side or Male or Female, you get different allies along the way. You can also influence them more depending on which way you side.
- Many unique and interesting force powers learned along the way.
- There is a "prestige" system setup for later in the game. In the beginning you can choose what type of Jedi you will be (Guardian, Sentinel, or Consular), but around level 20 you are given the option to become a better version of one of those.
Cons:
- The game does have its bugs (the TSLRCM should fix most of those problems though).
- Gaining the influence of your allies is often difficult, or even impossible, if you are of a different force side as them (i.e if you are a Jedi, it'll be harder to gain influence from one of your allies who leans more towards the dark side).
- I wish there was just a little bit more to the end of the game. *SPOILERS* I felt that after you defeat Darth Traya, you should be able to go back, see how your decisions affected the Republic, and then go off into the Unknown Regions in search of Revan.
- There are places where I thought were just a bit too thin. Like could they have given us a little bit more?
- Even though the game supposedly levels up as you do, you basically are able to just plow through everyone without even trying.
Conclusion: 9/10
May the Force be with You.

Shadow Warrior 2 was my first forray into the Shadow Warrior franchise. Until the release of this all I had to go on was my friend doing some streams and screenshots from older games. I really didn't know what to expect except for shooting, living beings being dismembered, and wisecracks.
Shadow Warrior 2 was a funnier game than most other games I've played. Lo Wang always had some wise crack at the ready in cutscenes and most of his references, while some of them dated, didn't really make me groan like the writing in a game such as Duke Nukem Forever. With his constantly foul mouth and how characters reacted to each other, my time in Shadow Warrior 2 was a fairly enjoyable experience. The only problem I'd say is his one liners got old real fast. Hearing the same line three times in a row really makes the writing wear out it's welcome.
The gameplay itself is solid at it's core. Movement and combat both feel polished enough, provided you don't get stuck on the geometry of the map or accidentally dash off a ledge like a moron (like I did a few times.) There's a wide variety of weapons for you to use against enemies to satisfy your style of play. Like swords and knives? You got it. More of a shotgun kind of person? There's plenty to choose from. Want to just run through guys with a chainsaw? Go for it!
The game also give you a few powers to tackle your foes. Summoning spikes to impale enemies, vanishing and launching a surprise attack with your swords, something akin to a force push from Star Wars, and more.
Try to hide the smile from your face as you lunge dual wield swords into the chest of a Yakuza thug. I bet you can't.
For all the praise I give this game I have a few complaints, and yes the main one is the ARPG elements present in the game. For lack of a better term I describe them as tacked on. I can't really feel immersed when choosing what upgrades I want to put into my weapons takes a large chunk of my time that could be better spent killing anything in my way. It also leads to the most attrocious inventory management I've ever had to deal with. You can organize equipment in only two ways, and it's item level and quality. You can't really separate by stats, abilities, or anything else, which makes slotting upgrades a chore.
I also had a slew of graphical issues and my rig is not that bad. My graphics card may be three years old but I had some of the worst loading times I've ever seen in any game (on a solid state it was unacceptable), moments where my game would freeze briefly if too much was going on, and low framerates were common problems. And this was on Medium settings. This became such a problem I think it messed up my ability to play with my friend online.
I give this game a cautious thumbs up. If you have a decent enough rig, like the series, and/or feel the need to feel like a superhero give this a try. Just be wary that the whole ARPG element is something other games have done much better. But at least the enemies don't feel like bullet sponges like other games in the ARPG style I've played.

Let me first state this for the record. This game, has great potential. It really does. The developers of this game really do care about this game.
However with that being said, this game is a bug-glitch ridden mess that is holding hands along side a microtransaction system, That offers cosmetcs, and also "preminum" accounts, booster, etc. You name this game has it on the microtransaction side. This is not how you do microtransaction, btw. It's either one or the other, not both. Doing both may or may not work. In this case it doesn't work, in terms of concept and execution.
They shove it right in your face the whole nine yards, "Hey tell your friends about us!". Yup, i mean all of our friends play videogames, i mean yeah ALL of our friends...... >.> not only that but this game randomly encourages you to do so, and also suggest to sign up, and god knows what else. Anything to get their game more attention and care, and also $$$$
Since gathering resources might take awhile, and you might need the few extra crowns (which by the way can be obtained through quests, or *ding, ding* you guess it. BOOSTER PACKS! :D) expect to not be stocked up for a long while. But even then the proccess is really, really, slow. Unless you have upgrades and you communicate with the community.
It just isn't the microtransaction system that is also plauging this game, but like what i previously stated before, this game is a bug-glitch ridden mess. The army's AI is chidlish, making illogical decisions that baffles you, plus the "co-op" system in this game is a complete joke, no lobby, but through a random selection of players or friends that, and oh by the way they must meet certain requirements in order for you to play with them. So if you are X, 1, 2 & 3 and your friends are, Y, 4,5,6 guess what? can't do it! Must be on the same page. But even then the game's cp-op system is still broken. the PVP has the same system, and runs just like the co-op system. You can tag team against players and what not.
Now. How is the rest of the game?
Well it's like Stronghold. You rule your own little "territory" in various landscapes, races, etc. All of which have their own set of skills, abilites, quest, etc. You can't customize your character, and if you want your character to have a name, must buy, buy, buy a renamer thingy in order to do it. In your terriotry, you see your land grow, however bewarn, upgrades require certain techs, large amount of resources may vary, and guess what? CROWNS! GLORIOUS CROWNS! :D
Also these "VIP" status buildings, and upgrades? They require an insane amount of supplies and CROWNS! so don't think getting to the top is going to fast and swift.
You can create alliances, but it costs......CROWNS! :D as Buzz Lightyear would say: "Crowns. Crowns, everywhere!". You must be invited by the clan leader in order to become part of the alliance, yup kiddes you have to make a ton of friends in this game if you want to be apart of it on a larger scale. The tutorial does it's best, but honestly, if you played Stronghold, and a Total war game, then it shouldn't be a bother.
Now, unlike a Bethesda Game Studio game (Oblivion, Skyrim, etc.) there are no radient quests, the quests are given to you, so don't expect it to be quite fun. And unlike a Total War game, there is no real panic with the peasntry and such. Which would've been nice to have in this game, as it gives players an incentive to think about their territory first.
The lore is alright, i guess. For a medival game it does the job right.
One more thing, if you don't have a good rig. expect big performance issues, and even if you lower down the settings, the game still has weird performance issues, etc.
So in the end. Despite the patches, the issues are growing, and with this absurd and constant in your face "give us promotion" and also, buy, buy, buy! I recommend, NOT playing this game.

One of the best Star Wars RPG's i've ever played. On par with the first KOTOR, this sequel takes place 5 years after the events of KOTOR 1 and are an extension of the great sith war taking place 4000 years before the Battle of Yavin and the destruction of the empire's ultimate weapon. The story follows a jedi exile, canonically a female, however a choice of male doesn't affect the storyline in any way besides dialogue options, and is a story of loss, betrayal, ardousness and above all redemption. From amazing scenery, to great weapons and an addictive turn based combat system with pause features, this game is one of the most enjoyable from bioware and an integral part of the star wars canon of the Old Republic days. It isn't the graphically advanced games of new, but this in my opinion is the last requisite on a list to enjoy this game. Amazingly done voice acting, dialogue is on point, fantastic environmental work and just a great RPG game that really makes you feel like the hero, or villian if you want to be. choose your path, paragon in action, or a devil in disguise, you play as jedi or sith, be aware that each choice has repurcussions! and the fate of the galaxy will once again rest on your shoulders. An exceptionally made game, easily a 9/10 and even a 10.
Would buy it for any price, and would suggest playing the first to grasp the entirety of the plot and story linearity, however is not required. Great game and an absolute Star Wars iconocism.

80 Days is a charming game where you must plan your journey to cross the world in 80 days (or less!), which is a lot harder than it might sound. You must juggle departure times, funds, and your luggagge if you hope to make it back to London in time to win the wager, and even when you think you've got the perfect route, accidents can happen occur along the way.
I bought 80 Days as part of the Narrative Humble Bundle, so I didn't pay full price for it, but I think it's probably worth its retail price--there's a lot of replayability in this game, as you're never going to be able to visit every city AND make it back to London in time, so you have to prioritise different tasks in different playthroughs. But I think there's more than enough content, particularly as you get to choose different responses and thus provoke different outcomes to the situations you and Fogg find yourselves in.
My only complaint, really, is that the game will show you other players' progress as you're playing, which isn't particularly obtrusive but I found it kind of distracting, and I can't find a way to turn this off in the game settings.
Nonetheless, I fully recommend 80 Days! It's a lot of fun if you like choose-your-own adventure-style text games, and it's a lovely new take on Jules Verne's original novel, with a whole host of secondary characters. The game also feels very progressive in the right places--a lot of female characters, particularly women of colour, play prominent roles within the side stories in positions of power or academia, and there is at least one storyline where you, as a male character, can kiss another man.

This game is one of my top recommendations to people. If you want a game that will tell you amazing stories, this is it. It also does a fantastic job of making you feel like you're on a journey as you only see snipets of characters' lives before you are whisked away. The writing is superb and the simple presentation encourages your imagination to run wild.
Gameplay-wise it's very simple. It's most like a visual novel with some very simple time, inventory, and money management to push you along.
Representation-wise this game is also fantastic. The world is a crazy steampunk Victorian era. Half the drivers, captains, and pilots as well as incidental characters are women. The racial diversity is also plentiful, as one would hope of a game about traveling around the world. Additionally, half the romance options are female and half are male.
If you're turned off by all this SJW crap, you should play the game anyway. It all works in service of building a unique and varied world that's not just entirely populated by white men with brown hair and giving you a sense of the rich tapestry of people that inhabit the entire world.
Overall, you should absolutely pick this game up. It can get a bit repetitive as you repeat travel routes and stories multiple times, but it's not so much that it's a deal breaker. The game is also available on mobile devices, which perfectly suits the traveling nature of the game. I highly recommend you try it.

People wanted this game to be bad, and that's the only reason people say it's bad.
The game is far from perfect and the wait for it was far, far too long, but that does not mean it deserves a score of 52. The three main points people bring up for why this game is worse than the holocaust are very easily countered and I honestly don't think can really be used as "cons" at all.
1.  Duke Nukem is too sexist.
The fact that this complaint actually gains any traction whatsoever is really, REALLY stupid and it kind of pisses me off to some extent. Really? Duke Nukem being sexist? WHAT A HUGE SHOCK! That's the entire point, don't you guys remember? I could understand if you didn't find the jokes funny anymore, but that's not the devs' fault because they aren't any less mature than the ones in Duke Nukem 3D. If you didn't find the jokes funny then you simply grew up and don't find it funny anymore. Duke Nukem games aren't supposed to be some deep observation of the human spirit or the definition of heroics. Duke Nukem games are about guns, boobs and swearing. You get all three of those in this game, if you didn't like them here then you didn't like Duke Nukem 3D either.
2. The graphics are terrible.
Uh, no, they really aren't, especially for 2011. It looks almost as good as Far Cry 2's max settings or even RAGE's high settings, just without DOF. This game looks REALLY good.
3. It wasn't as groundbreaking as Duke Nukem 3D.
Seriously, guys? Duke Nukem 3D wasn't very "groundbreaking" either. The engine it used had already been used to make Witchhaven and Powerslave (on the PSX and PC, not on the Saturn) and DN3D didn't do anything with the engine that those two games didn't. Another thing I'd like to point out is that Quake came out before this one did, and Quake is an actual fully 3D game, DN3D is still 2.5D. Hell, Marathon came out a full two years earlier and that game's engine stomps BUILD's testicles.
Was it a disappointment? Yeah, of course it was. I was pretty disappointed with Half Life 2 because the violence was somewhat toned down and there weren't nearly as many weapons or enemies to fight. I felt like I waited too long for something that would have more in certain areas but way less in others. Disappointment does not mean horrible, though. Is Half Life 2 terrible? Not in the slightest. Is Duke Nukem Forever as good as Half Life 2? No, it isn't nearly as good. At the same time, though, Duke Nukem 3D isn't way more amazing than Doom 2 or Marathon or Quake or System Shock. All Duke Nukem 3D ever was was an interactive mid 90's action movie. Duke Nukem Forever is the exact same thing, except this one wasn't released in regular theaters and only got distributed through Grindhouse because there's quite a few♥♥♥♥♥♥here.
I give Duke Nukem 3D 7.5 out of 10 and DNF 7 out of ten. Fight me, nerds.

Tormentum has just made it into my all time point and click adventure favorites list, and I'll try to briefly explain why...
1) The gameplay does not suffer from crazy logic like so many other point and clicks. There is no ridiculous logic like "combine the frog with the book and use it on the bucket to open the chest" that so many other titles are guilty of to create the illusion of complexity. Puzzles here are straightforward yet challenging enough to make you think. In terms of the environment, as long as you are paying attention you won't often find yourself resorting to having to click on everything everywhere to progress.
2) Unlike many other titles in this genre, there are multiple endings depending on your choices (of which there are many) in game. Replayability!
3) This game is beautiful. The art direction is both moving and disturbing at the same time.  H.R. Geiger comes strongly to mind.
The only drawback to this title is that it will take about 3-4 hours to run through the story once. Subsequent runs will be shorter.
All in all, despite being a little short this title is well worth your money.....especially if you feel drawn to point and click adventures but regularly get put off by some of the tropes of the genre

I sat up all night playing this game. I didn't mean too, Having just installed it, I'd planned a quick look before I went to bed, then I started my journey...
For a game that is mostly just text, with a smattering of route planning and luggage management, it conjures up a wealth of vivid images in my head. Just like a good book in fact, only it's you (in the guise of Passepartout) in the book. It is a completely unique experience, I'd never come across a game that engaged me in that way before. At no point in the journey did I want to stop, even though a part of my brain began nagging at me that dawn was breaking.
I nearly died twice, once in an airship crash and then again when I had a bit of a run in with some slavers.
Then there was the incident at the market in Lisbon. In some ways I don't like to mention it. It was a heart-stopping moment of my adventure. Less than 24 hours from London and my literally world collapsed. I found myself back on the desktop, the game had crashed! Were my 78 days of travelling going to end so ignominously? With a shaking hand I at last found the courage to click on the button that would bring things back to life. Perhaps, just perhaps, there'd be an autosave that meant I'd only have lost a day or two of my trip. In all my excitement it had certainly never occured to me to make any form of manual bookmark.
I needn't have worried, the creators in their wisdom had tracked my progress right down to the moment I'd made the ill-advised visit to the market. I was back at the hotel, all my bags were where they should be and my master was waiting for me. In my relief, I abandoned any thought of making a last-minute deal in the markets of Lisbon and hurried aboard that last airship to London.
Somehow I (or maybe that should be we) made it, with almost two days to spare and money in our pockets at that!

First of all, I DO recommend Rainbow Six SIege. It's an amazing game, and the devs are still working on it and trying to improve in every way possible, BUT
In the newest update, among other changes, 8 maps were removed from the ranked gameplay and 2 from the whole game, and it has been announced announced that might happen in future updates too. I understand that some of these maps were not suitable for ranked gameplay, but that doesn't mean that the players that still wish to play those maps should not be allowed to. I feel like the game is heading to a cs-go-like direction, where the goal is not to have fun playing the game, but winning it by playing it as the rules tell you to: You have these 9 maps, you have these peeking spots that you can use, now play. And, sadly, people are going with it. It's losing the need for people to use their brain and inventivity, adapting to the environment to outweigh the enemy's advantage, and limiting them to a few simple instructions.
Again, this game is still good, but this review is made in hopes that the R6S team will reconsider removing features fron the game, and hopefully coming up with a better solution, that doesn't involve limiting gameplay, and in hopes that this game won't lose it's identity, turning into another competitive shooter where winning by following some strict rules is more important than actually having fun overall.

I seriously can't get enough of this game. If you want to be a hero and help other players out, you can do that! If you want to be a villian and kill them in their weakened state after they get attacked by the nether, you can do that too! The world has come to an end, and all you care about is the melted ice cream!
I love the atmosphere of this game. It feels a lot like the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games, except not as desolate and lonely because there are actual people (virtually) in the map, and they don't ask how you're doing, 'bro' in a russian accent. The scavenging aspect really appeals to me, because it instills in you a sense of urgency with everything you do: you can level up and find weapons all you want, but at the end of it all, if you don't have food, you die.
This is what gives the more villianous players the right to kill without discretion. And you know what? I don't really mind. That isn't how I play, but I don't care if it's how some others choose to go about finding food. If I wanted to play a boring game where all I had to worry about were the zombies (demons?), I'd go play something else. When I jumped onto a server for the very first time, the first thing I see on the chat window is:
First guy: (name) You friendly?
Second guy: Yeah
First guy: (Name)... I'm trusting you bro
My eyes widened and my heart started racing and I was like "So that's how it's going to be..."
Whenever you die, you lose anything you had on you (you can put items in the global inventory to save them for a later character), and your skills get reset. I don't really mind this as well, because it would get boring if there was no penalty for dieing. I can see how I may get tired of it later on, but right now it just keeps things intense and keeps people from becoming complacent. Besides, you can find equipment fairly easily, so starting over isn't as bad as people would have you think.
The playable map is enormous, leaving a lot to explore by yourself or with friends; And this is only a small portion of the map of the surrounding area, leaving it open for expansion when the final game is released as well as future updates. The chances that you would come across a ne'er do well are so slim, that when you finally get sniped, it's such a treat that you can only shake your head and go "This kid" because the fellow has probably been watching that particular alley or intersection for hours, praying that he didn't choose a bad location to hunt, and then he sees you, the person who's made his day.
On a final note, I bought this game during the christmas sale from steam, and I guess I was part of the 1%< of people who couldn't sync their steam accounts to their nether accounts and therefore couldn't play. Upon writing this review (12/27/2013) the issue hasn't been resolved, so I can't play it without them giving me a guest key to use, which I've been playing with. However, this shows that they haven't left the minority of us who can't get in at this time blwoing in the wind; I posted my problem on the troubleshooting forum (after trying everything on my end to get it working, of course) and they gave me the guest key.

Flushing my money down the toilet would've been a better choice than buying this game.
- The game crashes constantly, even on high end machines, often in the middle of a match. Sometimes, it crashes the entire pc, forcing you to restart and lose the progress.
- When you start, you're prompted with a choice of ONE deck. The hints are very misleading: i chose the white/black deck that was described as removal based. Total removals in the deck: 3. You can't change your choice and you're stuck with your deck for the start of the campaign, unless you manually edit the save file.
- That goes without saying, the deck is EXTREMELY UNDERPOWERED, regardless of your choice. You'll have a hard time beating the early battles, even if you turn down the difficulty to Arch-mage. Be prepared to grind your way through HOURS of frustrating losses, as the AI "cheats" constantly. The only way to go around this is turning down the difficulty to Mage, then suddenly every match is a piece of cake but no fun at all.
- Even if you somehow manage to beat the AI, you're rewarded with a single booster pack. There's no guarantee the cards in the pack will boost your deck, they can be any color and, yes, you'll get doubles. The strongest cards, though, can't be obtained this way: they're reserved for people that BUY booster packs.
- NO 2HG, no Sealed Play.
- Clunky menus, that force you to go forth and back to check your progress.
- The "free deck building mode" is a joke. Despite what the description on Steam says, you'll be very limited with your choices when building your deck, unless (of course) you don't open your wallet and start hunting for premium cards. Building a decent monocolor deck is nearly impossible.
Magic 2015 is built around a single purpose: frustrating the player to the point of buying more booster packs through microtransactions. That is all. You won't enjoy this game unless you throw in it a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of money. Even buying the complete edition (30$) won't get you 100% of the cards available, but will leave you at around 90%. In the end, to get the full experience you'll have to pay the same as a AAA+ retail game and that is if you're lucky.
This franchise has suddenly turned in a Pay to Win product, and that means that, at least for me, this is the end. I won't buy any more games from Wizards, ever.
My piece of advice is to turn to Hearthstone: it's still based on booster packs, but at least it doesn't FORCE the player to spend money just to enjoy the game. DON'T BUY THIS GAME.

One aspect I really like is the courier system where you ferry packages from safezone to safezone for large amounts of money and XP.
TL;DNR: Game needs a bit of polish and expansion, but the framework is there for an excellent scavenge/survival game.

I want to love Glasswire.  I really do.  I am a network design engineer by trade and finding something consumer oriented that has a decent amount of information is tough.  I thought glasswire was the ticket.
Used it for hours and loved it - found that it detected some obscure network traffic and showed some good source/destination information.
While it found some good traffic - it COMPLETELY missed over 6 Mbps of traffic from a few different video sites when I was going through a app detection testing round.  I had taskmgr/resourcemon/Glasswire next to each other and Glasswire underreported network traffic by a huge margin.    While going through Resourcemon,  I found it also completely missed several other applications that were consistently using bandwidth when Glasswire reported zero throughput.
If they fix their app reporting then i'll give it another shot,  but until then, stick with using Resource Monitor to look at your process tx/rx.
You cant recommend or rely on an application that misses on its core functionality.
EDIT:  Developer responded and provided some information which unfortunately, didnt apply to me.  They suggested reboot, but unfortunately that wasnt my issue as I had it installed over the course of several reboots.
Developer response:
GlassWire's normal desktop installer warns that to pick up all new connections you may need a reboot, but we don't force the reboot because some people find that annoying. We will try to add a notice about this on Steam also.
We use a well known and trusted Windows API to detect traffic and it's very accurate.

I got this game two weeks ago when it was free and had just finished it today. It took me so long because I wanted to play the game the way it was intended: In the dark alone with great headphones.
The game isn't too long, and for 20 bucks it shouldn't be. The game is, however, filled with great story, intense moments, and fun puzzles. Personally, I liked the idea of the sanity mechanic which can only be maintained by making progress in the game. This helps make progress all the more rewarding especially after stressful parts. The developers also did a great job easing the player into the world and putting the player up against nothing they can't handle early on, while still making it very intense for the player. I have heard from friends that this game sometimes locks up at certain points like when enemies spawn. Others play just fine. My only technical issue came when a scripted event would happen. When something intense, yet expected, was about to happen, my screen would freeze for a split second. Honestly though, it didn't ruin it at all because events that were unexpected played right away, almost as if they were optimized or something.
Lastly, I would like to point out that there is developer commentary in the game that can be enabled from the options menu. As I would like to try my hand at real game making eventually since I am currently in school for it, the developers provide some really excellent insight on making their game and creating games in general.
The atmosphere was awesome, enemies were terrifying, themes were solid, game world was sound but I cannot recommend this game for 20 dollars because to me, there is just not enough there. If you can find it on sale, for any less, buy it. If you really like horror games and have some how never played this one, get it now.

TLDR:
I have minor connection issues, Microtransactions don't really matter, and ITS VERY SKILL BASED,Yes even guard beaking. Highly recommended. Refer to conclusion
Microtransactions:
They honestly don't even matter. Yes you can buy steel and then use that to buy scavenger packs(Supply drops) but good gear doesn't drop until usually Reputation 1(prestige) and even then the gear drops based on hero level and current gear level for said hero, so you have to play the game to actually "pay to win" but even then, you still have to have a certain amount of skill. 1v1 and 2v2's don't use gear level so its purely skill.
Connectivity:
While I'm still very disappointed that its peer to peer in 2017, I only had issues on launch.
The BAD Connectivity:
Because of peer to peer, people have the need to rage quit and it causes reconnection which can revive someone you already killed or just be killed. This is an issue but I grew up with it, so I'll live.
Skill:
Thats right I said skill. People complain about guard breaking and spammers and I did too for a while. In order to be an effective decapitating machine that every one wants to be, you have to actually know advanced mechanics of the game. When someone spams a guard break you can counter it(if you need help message me, you don't need reaction time, just good hearing) if someone attacks the same way you can parry it and make it very punishing for them. YOU WILL NOT WIN EVERY GAME, I dont care how good you are there are always better people.
Price/Season pass:
For Honor follows the same model Rainbow Six Siege does. Everything is free but season pass holders get 7 day early access and don't have to pay for new heroes.
Steel Grind:
Yes steel is a b***h and a half to get, your daily quests should give you 600 a day and beating the campaing on hard gives something between 5-7k steel. Weekly quests can give steel but not commonly. Honestly just play have a good time and your steel count will shoot up. P.S. You don't need to buy heroes to play them, you just can't customize them.
Conclusion:
I haven't felt the addiction to a game like this for years. For honor is highly frustrating but very rewarding. With my minor connection issues I have no axe to grind here. The grind is meh, just pay attention to the way the game works. You can counter all "cheese lords" with skill. Season pass works like rainbow six's does. Microtransactions are mostly for cosmetics. Steel is hard to get for a reason, Ubi doesn't want a bunch of newbs running around with the mythic skins, however they can if they choose to pay $20. I love this game personally but not everyone will.

I love this game. It's way more substantial than I expected going in, meaty in terms of story but also fanciful and whimsical at times. Plus, on my first playthrough I released an Indian rebel from British forces.  I also met a mechanical dragon, flew on the back of a giant eagle-mech, spent some ghastly time in a Russian jail, and got delayed on a ship where I led a failed mutiny.
I definitely lost some time in the beginning due to not understanding the mechanics at first (time passes while you are trading in market, etc.), but just barely made it around the world in 80 days, with the kind of nail-biting, edge of your seat decision-making that feels like a great accomplishment in the end.

This interactive narrative of the steampunk variety encompases the adventure of Passepartout, a french valet who provides service for his master, Phileas Fogg - of whom has wagered £20,000 that he can travel around the world in 80 Days. This immensely dialogue rich game immerses the player in a world (with a little imagination) not too dissimilar from our own. Set in the 1872 it explores not only the geological but plunges into the philosophical and ethical as you converse with people around the world in every country.
While the visual aspect of this game belies it's touch-screen origins it did not detract from the overall aesthetics as the vector heavy, high contrast, less-is-more approach to the graphic content more than made up for this very slight shortfall. 9/10
The audio is palatable for a few hours as it assists in immersing the player into the world it offers, however, depending on your sensibilities, it may take a single playthrough to notice the looped tracks. Personally I played through twice before switching to my own playlist. I can appreciate the attention to detail of the composition of these tracks and how they seem to draw the player ever along on their global trek changing slightly to befit the corresponding country. 6/10
This game has a ridiculously high replay value and I relished the opportunity to play through again and again as not only did I want to explore and discover the seemingly limitless paths spurring me on to London but also to follow in my footprints yet again to uncover a conversation I had missed or a city I had passed on a rail journey of which we did not disembark to explore. 9/10
Regarding gameplay I cannot speak highly enough. It was refreshing to play a character that you could flirt with two young ladies leaving France for a holiday, or have a romantic interlude with the muscular captain of an ice-walker. The dialogue and response options were also a breath of fresh air, this character could have shortcomings or may have a grandiose personality, or a penchant for mischief. Being able to choose your character's personality as you go really made it a giddy experience and a reminder that even if you try your hardest you can still fail; which is just another one of the positive aspects of this game. While I did found the audio a little repetitive, the immersiveness, replay value and relaxing aesthetics make this a game I shall continue to enjoy for many more hours to come. 10/10
Overall I love this game for many reasons. From the simple and elegant visuals, the rich story, the depth of the dialogue through to the gameplay and replay value. 9/10
TL;DR:
Audio 6/10
Graphics 9/10
Replay Value 9/10
Gameplay 10/10
Overall 9/10 - would happily repack luggage again and again and again...

In the headquarters of the DotP team, the UI guys are meeting for the first time. Years of technical experience and traning are behind them. They're going to make the best damn UI you've ever seen. "Right," says Stefan. He has dark hair. He is from Stockholm. His wife is pregnant, but neither of them know it yet. He pauses to pull a pencil from his pocket, and licks the nib. "Does anybody have any ideas?"
"Well," says Linda, "I think we should star-"
"MENUS," screams the Menu Goblin, who is perched naked in the corner, covered in baby oil. He is making too-intense eye contact, and stroking his own frail biceps.
Linda tries to smile. They tolerate the Menu Goblin, because he ate the DotP '14 team when they let their guard down. Killing him will only spawn two more of him. So sayeth the old texts. Linda has just finished design school. She has a bright career ahead of her. Against her better judgement, she tries to be diplomatic.
"We already have a menu menu, and a menu menu menu," she says, "don't you think that's enough menus?"
"MENU," screams the Menu Goblin. There is anger in his voice. His nostrils open and close furiously. "MEEEEENNNNUUUUU."
He peels a boil off his arm, inspects it with a single beady eye, then eats it. "Menu," he says. He raises a single finger, and wags it. "Menu menu," he says. The UI team nod, trying not to make eye contact with each other. There are too many menus already, but the madness of this creature drives them deeper into hell. Dante could not have imagined these layers of pixels going down down down.
"Menu," says Stefan. He swallows. He is trying not to cry. He nods, "yes, we need another menu. A menu inside the menu inside the menu inside the menu inside the menu. What a wonderful idea. Thank you for your input, Menu Goblin."
"Menu," says the Menu Goblin. It nods, then picks at a boil on its thigh. "Menu."

After many months of this game being dead since the developers sold the game to another company they finally bought back the rights to edit the game. Game is still the same since before they abandoned it and they said they will continue to add more items into the game.
