Nether History:
Nether game about around 2012 and was Early Acces and the basic version was priced at 30$ for basic version, 40$ for some other and 50$ for the best. Back then there was microtransactions, so all those masks, skins, and Nether potions used be only bought with gold, or you had to open them with golden keys which was a real pain because 5 keys costed around 7k. There was alot of running packages back and forth. But the thing about it is that there was no PVE or Singleplayer. So you had to do all these runs in PVP and along the way having to fight bandits off. Around 2013 the developers expanded the map which is the wasteland as you know today.(Best place to run package runs) A few months later they added a vehicle, or a buggy. This was actually extreamly buggy, the driver was never able to go out and it could only hold 3 people. If it touched any water all passengers would die instantly. Then around early 2015 the devolpers had sold the rights of the game to another company. So that company did nothing with the game and shut it all down. So most of the year it was down and nobody was able to play the game. Eventually in late 2015 the devs bought back the rights to edit the game and thats how we got to Nether Resurrected, they removed all aspects of microtransactions in the game and everything can now be bought with money. THey also removed vehicles like the buggy and motercycle.
And thats where we are today. Great game and cheap! But I had bought it for 30$ back in Beta.

I've clocked to 70 hours and I think it is time to give this game a review.
This game is what Star Wars battlefront 3 SHOULD have been. The scale of the battles, the initial infantry charge into the fight and the space battles are truly a sight to behold.
The gunplay is excellent and rewards recoil control. The weapons themselves feel very powerful in each of their own right and each weapon caters to what kind of infantry you want to be. The vehicles are good although they do bug out sometimes on terrain but that's just a small problem to deal with and nothing game breaking (though I do occasionally get stuck in terrain and unable to get out. Hopefully this will be fixed in the future.) There's also mechs in the game which is an excellent addition.
The space battles are truly eye candy. Never has game like this allows me to pilot a my own corvette or battleship. The boarding action from transport ships to the opposing team's battleship/space station has never been so immersive and I truly enjoyed every second of it. Never has a game like AFF made me feel like I'm truly in a CQB fighting within a space station or battleship.
Weapon and vehicle costumization, at first, feels overwhelming and utterly confusing but stick with it. This game allows one to tailor a weapon to fit your infantry fighting style. Want to go in quite? You can. You want to go in guns blazing with electric-coated bullets? You can. You want to snipe enemies with armor-piercing bullets? You can. With the addition of your own avatar's suit costumization, you can be nimble and move fast or a walking juggernaut with a massive handheld minigun.
BUT...
The AI bots in the game can range from being outright moronic to incredibly overpowered. In otherwords, it's inbalance. For example, during the assault on the final phase of the mission, your AI teammates can be incredibly stupid for the most part. Sure, during the initial phases of the assault, they can capture points and secure drop points for your team. However, during the final phase, they tend to gather at one place and just stay there, sometimes for the rest of the mission like incompetent fools. Only a few soldiers would go and take the objective but they would go in single file, one by one, to the mission objective, all the while being gunned down by the opposing team. Now, this is where my rant for the AI begins. The enemy AI is not good. They just cheat. Say that you have an assault rifle, customized with electric-coated bullets. Electric coated bullets, when fired enough, will cause the UI to short-circuit, spazzing out the screen. Unfortunately, the enemy AI is NOT affected by it, and kills you (sometimes instantly) with a well placed headshot with a freaking pistol. Sometimes, the AI can strafe and ALL of their shots hit you with FLAWLESS accuracy. They are a lot smarter than your own AI, because they tend to gather at the final objective. This, plus with your own incompetent bots, leads to downright frustrating games because no matter how tactical you play, or how hard you fight, the enemy AI somehow still has the advantage. It's frustrating and sometimes unfair.
With all that said, I still enjoy the game. This is truly a hidden gem, filled with lots of potential. Even in early access, this game has a lot to offer you. The devs are very active in the community and they even play their own game. I do hope that this game succeeds because I want it to. This game, for me, is a spiritual successor to Star Wars Battlefront 2 (2005).

So, I spent some time with Sniper Elite V2, here. Overall, it's a 6/10, and I will explain why.
Initially, I got this game on the day it was free, so it scores some bonus points for not costing me any dosh. I installed it right away, excited about a WW2 Sniper shooter! I went in expecting levels with a wide variety of paths, ways to complete your goals, and all sorts of neato things like that. However, I was somewhat disappointed. I write this on finishing the campaign on the Sniper Elite, or Hard, Difficulty of the game.
Over a mind numbing 8 or so hours of dying, dying some more, crawling before dying, and dying again, I finally finished. On these 8 hours, I have to say that the campaign is fairly linear in the paths you can take, with only a few special spots you can get up in that give you any real advantage over the super aim of enemy soldiers. There's not many ways to skin the cat either, when it comes to completing goals or shooting targets. There's one set vantage point, or one set way to stop a convoy of vehicles, etc. I will applaud the story, though, for obtaining my interest and keeping it through the duration of the campaign.
On the story, it's somewhat generic, and I won't spoil it in this review. It was enough of a fresh breath, though, compared to the games around it that it stands out.
Mechanics wise, the bullet drop is interesting. Not as punishing or realistic as Red Orchestra 2, but not as rediculously cheesy as a game like COD. The cover system is mediocre, with your body sometimes sticking out enough for enemies to be able to shoot you, and on sniper elite, this will kill you every time. Enemy detection works alright, and the AI is fairly cohesive. I found myself flanked from time to time, and they aren't grenade spammy.
I don't care about graphics, so that doesn't weigh into this score.
The multiplayer is fun with friends, and so is the co-op. Otherwise, don't bother.
Overall, this game is a short, interesting little game about killing Nazis and Reds. Would I buy it? Only on sale. Would I reccommend it to friends? No. 6/10, and I'll probably wind up getting more time in it playing co-op matches and free for alls with friends, and having a grand time of it.

When I was originally told to review Magic 2015, I was very disheartened. Not because I hate Magic the Gathering (I actually play it in real life and enjoy it quite a lot), but rather because I had already picked up the iOS version. If I was to review that, then no joke I would have given the game a 2 at very best. I won’t go into detail about the iOS version, except a simple warning: for the love of god don’t spend time downloading it. I went into the PC version in hopes that it was better than my experiences with the iOS version.
I’d just like to start this review off by saying I loved Magic 2014 and played it to death. Now, before I go into the game itself, I’ll just quickly run over what Magic The Gathering is. It can be played by a minimum of two players and there is no real limit to the maximum amount of people, so it’s really how many you can fit around a table, although most people limit their games to four players. After placing Lands, you can ‘tap’ these Lands for mana in order to cast spells and bring out creatures. All players start with 20 health and you win by reducing all opponents health to zero by attacking with these spells and creatures (although, with certain cards, there are special ways you can win). That’s the basic run-down of Magic The Gathering.
I could sit here all day listing all the mechanics and so on behind Magic The Gathering, but instead, I’ll just go on what’s new in this game. The story behind Magic 2015 is fairly simple, as it is with most Duels of the Planeswalkers games. Garruk has been cursed by the ‘Chain-Veil’, which is making him hunt down and kill every other planeswalker. Why? Erm… Because there wouldn’t be a game without some mysterious object making Garruk want to mysteriously kill everyone.
The music within Magic 2015 is quite plain, causing me to put my own music on not too far into the game. However, after playing Magic 2014, I was kind of expecting this to happen, so it didn’t bother me too much. But I was still hoping that it would be good music though.
One point which I really want to hit on is the new deck Building. In Magic 2014, you had Sealed Play, in which you opened boosters and made a (normally pretty bad) deck out of that. Well in Magic 2015, that’s how you play the main game. At the start of the game, you select a deck that consist of a combination of any two colours. You can’t see the cards within these decks, and the descriptions are very misleading. After selecting a deck and beating the tutorial, you open Boosters, allowing you to add to the deck and also make a new one of different colours. This is where my first niggle with the game comes in.
If you want a specific card, you’re going to have to do one of two things: Grind on the game until you get it from a booster, or… Buy it. With real money. Yes, Magic 2015 has micro-transactions which allow you to buy sets of cards for more than it costs to buy a booster in real life. Instead of progressing through the game normally, they’ve let people buy their way to the best deck that they could possibly have before they even start the game properly. A better name for this game would have been Money The Gathering.
However, the AI is fairly well balanced with its difficulty. On Planeswalker (Hard), it used all its creatures to the best of their abilities and often gets a good combo of damage on you by combining different cards abilities. Whereas on Mage (Easy), they don’t use abilities often, if at all, and they attack with creatures, even if you can defend against it and kill it without any casualties on your side.
I say that, until I got to the fight against Jace, just over half way through the game. I was playing on Archmage (Medium) with a red and black deck that was kinda slow. Because of this, he swarmed me and countered any creatures I brought out, and because of my slow deck speed, I could only really get one creature out a turn, meaning I was open all the time. This meant I had to re-make my ENTIRE deck. For one fight. I’m all for difficulty, but when I have to spend half an hour re-making a deck for one duel, it really ruins the fun.
Also, there are no other game modes. Before, there has always been a special mode (2012 and Archenemy, 2013 had Planechase and 2014 had Two Headed Giant). Well, none of those make a return here. All you have is a 2-4 player FFA. Which gets very boring very quickly, especially when the AI takes ages with their turn.
There are five chapters to travel through, each with 4-6 duels to fight within them. These duels are fun at first, but after a while, it becomes the same thing. The only duel which had some form of originality and fun was a duel in which you fought against your own deck. The campaign itself took me around 8-9 hours to complete, but around three of those were spent fighting and changing my deck against Jace.
It seems Wizards of the Coast have taken a step back with DotP, and it’s a big disappointment. Bad Deck Building, micro-transactions and lack of other modes makes for a boring and unimaginative installment of Duels of The Planeswalkers. If you must get one, get Magic 2014, but keep the hell away from this.
Pro’s:
It’s Magic The Gathering
Finally custom-build your deck
Balanced AI
Cons:
The deck building is bad
Only one gamemode
Boring music
Bad starting decks
Bad storyline
Microtransactions *-*

Dead Pixels is a great game to just pick up and play. It has really good controller and local co-op support that was a ton of fun for my friend and I to play (Him on a PS3 controller and me on a 360 controller). Dead Pixels has a good amount of content with a story and survival mode, that is fairly challenging and is surprisingly addictive. For a $1.01 it is surprisingly polished and has a pretty hilarious storyline. There is a large variety of zombies that all have different amounts of health and abilities. Also throughout the game you'll find many buildings to loot and traders to buy weapons and ammo, and sell valuables.
There are simple RPG elements throughout the game that allow you to upgrade your player with enhancments such as; Run Speed, Weapon Damage, Health, Melee and Strength. These upgrades all cost a pretty penny though, and I guarentee you'll be running low on money the first couple hours you play, just because of the mass amount of junk there is to buy. I find myself overencumbered all the time just because I feel like I'll use some items eventually, even though I usually don't.
The wide variety of weapons is also a really interesting mechanic especially since there limit to how much you can carry, also there isn't one dominate weapon for there is a down side to every weapons strengths. For example, the Chainsaw can shred zombies up but you need to get close and there is a limited amount of gasoline you can carry. The Burton assault rifle has really good range and damage, but blows through ammo ridiculously fast.
In the end Dead Pixels deserves a 9/10, It's a solid Indie game with no real downside except for the lack of online Co-Op. There is also no way to change options unless you quit to the launcher which got pretty annoying while setting up a keyboard and mouse, which most people won't have to do.

tl;dr: Shadow Warrior 2 is a good arcade shooter with elements from Borderlands mixed in, which are not not perfectly developed, but still make it a good game.
After the 2013 reboot of Shadow Warrior the developers could just made another game without major changes. But they didn't, they kept the core formula and added some new elements: the levels are randomized and built from a number of setpieces. But that makes the levels also seem random, they miss memorable places as they are all build interchangeable.
The biggest new features are the weapon upgrades. You get a big arsenal of weapons, including many meele weapons. From the classic katana, to dual energyblades, from the classic pistol and shotgun to lightning-generators and a searing stream of heat shooting out of a gauntlet, there should be something for everyone. Additionally, every weapon has three upgrade slots, which can change the stats of the weapon or add elemental damage. The problem is that you find dozends of upgrades in every missionen and sorting the out is very time consuming as the game is lacking proper comparison function. I think is also pretty revealing that there is a option to mark upgrades as junk to easily sell them at a store. They can also be bought from stores and later an option to craft upgrades is unlocked. Use three of one quality level to make on the next superiorer one. But since the stats are randomized its pretty useless. Just sell everything and wait from something good to drop (chances are high because of the high numer of drops) or show up in the store.
Their are four forms of elemental damage (fire, ice, electricity, toxic) and the enemies can be weak, resistent or immune to those effects as well as to the "normal", physical damage. But that is also randomized, so get used to groups of enemies were of two next to each other one is weak to a certain elemental effect while the other is resistant to that. I found it more effective to chose something both are not resistent towards. But it also makes it quite frustrating as the fights can drag on for minutes, not helped by the fact that every enemy has a large healthpool. The bossfights where a weakness in the first game, they are much better here. They are more diverse and require lots of movement. They bosses are also quite agile, a rocket launcher is pretty useless as they will always dodge the first shot. So using a instant hit weapon is most the time more effective. Compared to the rest of the game, healthpacks and ammo drop a lot, to the point where the mini map is filled with icons. That makes the fights quite easy, but they can drag on.
Meele combat is again an essential part of the game, there are lots of weapons and since the protagonist Lo Wang is very agile it should be very effective. But with enemies spawning out of nowhere, surrounding the player immediatly it can also lead to a death trap. Often times I was forced to use a meele weapon because I ran out of ammo, which is only placed scarsly in the levels and dead enemies don't drop it very often.
There are also passive skills which can increase dropchances, make abilies and weapons more effective. Those are unlocked by getting karma levels, which you get by killing enemies. There is no indication in the game as far as I'm aware, it just happens from time to time. Bu the skills are very powerful and worth the wait.
New is also a coop mode: the whole game can be played with up to four players and is very leanient with players dropping in, it doesn't matter where in the story everybody is and which level they've reached, everybody plays the mission the host players currently is on. But there is also no synergy between the players, as they game has to be beatable alone too. So the enemies have even more health and the quality of the drops doesn't seem to be much higher.
The story was point where the previous game rally surprised my as only rarely you find an FPS with good story if the name isn't Half-Life or *Shock. But the reboot had a really good story takling some quite deep stuff and of course had the great dialogues between Lo Wang and his companion Hoji. They added that as well, with the new sidekick Kamiko. Unfortunatly it doesn't work as well, the chemistry isn't the same. It feels that they've tried, but tried too hard to replicated it and then overshot the goal. While the story as a whole is good and has some good twists, but doesn't reach the quality of the predecessor.
A got to admit, at times I'm quite frustrated with the game, especially when the fights drag on because enemies spawn out of nowhere and have a ton of health. It doesn't make it harder, just longer. Still, the basis makes a good arcade FPS, but the new additions don't work that well. The ideas are good, but not as well executed as in say Borderlands.

Let me start by saying I love Magic: the Gathering.  I love the card game and I liked the earlier video game installments.  However, the most recent version of Duels of the Planeswalkers has been (to me) monumentally disappointing.  The entire game works like the Sealed Deck campaign on Magic 2014, which I though was an interesting concept at the time.  It was extremely challenging as a quirky off-shoot of how the main game worked.  Instead of starting out with a good, working deck, you had to hobble together a ramshackle deck to beat your opponent, which often required immense amounts of patients, do-overs and careful manipulation of your deck between matches.  I though it was fun after I beat the main campaign.

But now with 2015, that's all you have!  A ramshackle deck that barely works and a horribly frustrating method of unlocking new cards.  Worst of all, the card selection on the game is TERRIBLE!!  I can't stress that enough!  I typically play with a mono-Black deck, with plenty of kill cards and lifelink, but low and behold, none of those cards exist in this game!  No Doom Blades, no Murders, or Corrupts or Tendrils of Corruption, none!  The only kill card is a worthless 5-drop!  If you enjoyed the last installment of the series and/or enjoy playing Black, I would highly advise that you avoid this game...

This interactive narrative of the steampunk variety encompases the adventure of Passepartout, a french valet who provides service for his master, Phileas Fogg - of whom has wagered £20,000 that he can travel around the world in 80 Days. This immensely dialogue rich game immerses the player in a world (with a little imagination) not too dissimilar from our own. Set in the 1872 it explores not only the geological but plunges into the philosophical and ethical as you converse with people around the world in every country.
While the visual aspect of this game belies it's touch-screen origins it did not detract from the overall aesthetics as the vector heavy, high contrast, less-is-more approach to the graphic content more than made up for this very slight shortfall. 9/10
The audio is palatable for a few hours as it assists in immersing the player into the world it offers, however, depending on your sensibilities, it may take a single playthrough to notice the looped tracks. Personally I played through twice before switching to my own playlist. I can appreciate the attention to detail of the composition of these tracks and how they seem to draw the player ever along on their global trek changing slightly to befit the corresponding country. 6/10

It was refreshing to play a character that you could flirt with two young ladies leaving France for a holiday, or have a romantic interlude with the muscular captain of an ice-walker. The dialogue and response options were also a breath of fresh air, this character could have shortcomings or may have a grandiose personality, or a penchant for mischief. Being able to choose your character's personality as you go really made it a giddy experience and a reminder that even if you try your hardest you can still fail; which is just another one of the positive aspects of this game. While I did found the audio a little repetitive, the immersiveness, replay value and relaxing aesthetics make this a game I shall continue to enjoy for many more hours to come. 10/10
Overall I love this game for many reasons. From the simple and elegant visuals, the rich story, the depth of the dialogue through to the gameplay and replay value. 9/10
TL;DR:
Audio 6/10
Graphics 9/10
Replay Value 9/10
Gameplay 10/10
Overall 9/10 - would happily repack luggage again and again and again...

The art is obviously inspired by the paintings of Zbigniew Beksiński (sorry, it does not remind much of H.R. Giger - it is much less phallic for that.) The illustrations are top-notch, contributing greatly to the bleak setting of the game. However, there are barely any animations and the game cuts the scenes to a 3:4 format (leaving you with a black borders on the left and right of your display if it is widescreen.)
As dark as the illustrations is the setting. The corrupted landscape is full of twisted creatures and inhuman machines. It is foul, rotten, broken and crazy. It tries to explain itself in the finale, but even after that I was under the impression that it was grimdark for the sake of trying to be darker and edgier alone. The writing didn't help - you might be able to swallow it straight, but for me the dialogues sounded as written by a goth wannabe.
The game promises moral choices, and the bleak setting gives plenty of opportunities for that. You will be dealing with subjects like imprisonment, torture, murder, deceit and redemption. Unfortunately often the choices fall flat - since everything around you seems like an irrational nightmare there doesn't seem to be much incentive to care either way. However, your choices do influence the development of the story and do carry consequence for that twisted world.
Since you are constantly lost in the mad landscapes I was afraid that I would be similarly lost if the game's puzzles would follow a similar dream logic. However the game makes some effort to explain whys and hows of the crazy inhabitants and the machines littering the environs. It might not exactly make sense, but you should always know what to do. Why is the red ruby, that you snatched from the painting, used in a mechanism opening a door, and why is that mechanism located three floors below said door... that is a completely different question.
The game is rather easy. No puzzles are challenging to begin with, and for most of them there are solutions to be found nearby. There is however a good variety of those tiny logical puzzles, so you are constantly treated to something new. In the end, the game is rather short. The first playthrough took me 3 hours. However, I intend to give it another go to see the results of the other decisions. Replaying it will bring me closer to the advertised 4-6 hours of gameplay.

I wasn't sure how much replayability there would be in a mostly text-based story game like this, but I have only played through it twice so far and can already tell there is so much more waiting to be discovered with each playthrough. It's a fairly short game if you're just trying to make the 80 day limit, but there's a lot to see and do at every stop and on every transport. I already see myself sinking a ton of time into this one just to see what new things I can do and discover with each playthrough. The steampunk setting is really interesting and the text-based descriptions are incredibly vivid and almost make you forget it's text-based. My only real complaint is the unskippable opening credits. I'd really prefer to not have to sit through them every time I start up the game.
UPDATE, having explored a bit more in this game: I need to reiterate that the setting is absolutely fantastic. Every place you visit and every vehicle you take is fully realized with a rich backstory to discover. In one of my recent playthroughs I just kept going north until I hit the North Pole, and even fell in love along the way (so far the second same-sex romance option I've discovered - another point in this game's favor). I still haven't explored most of South America, Australia, or Africa yet, and I can't wait for my next playthrough to see what else this game has in store for our friend Passepartout.

Being an Ubisoft customer is like being a subject in laboratory experiment on behavior.  You're placed in this room, and in one wall there's a lever attached to a chute. Whenever you pull the lever, the drawer pops open and you get a cookie.
And it is the best cookie you've ever tasted. It's warm, and sweet, and just the right blend of chewie and crunchy.  It's hand down the greatest thing possible for a human to consume, and you can have one any time you want just by pulling the lever.
But after about ten pulls or so, instead of a cookie, an 8 ounce boxing glove mounted on a mechanical arm pops out and punches you hard right square in the nuts.  You pull yourself up off the ground struggling with this crazy feeling that is a gutwrenching combination of the pain of taking a shot to the pills, and the bitter shock of disappointment and loss, cause you really had your heart set on that cookie.
After some time, the hunger for that cookie grows and grows, and the memory of that gential-punch begins to fade.
So you muster up your courage, and pull the lever again.
And what do you know?  A cookie!
And it's glorious.
It's just as good as the first time.  It's the best cookie ever, and it'll never get old.  You'll never get tired of it, or crave a sandwich or pizza instead because this cookie is just that damn good.
You pull the lever a few more times, and get a few more cookies until one time you're not paying attention and WHAM! -another blow to the nuts.
As the days pass by, the frequency of getting punched in the nuts grows and grows, and the cookies come less and less often, until one day you realize that you get only one cookie for every ten pulls of the lever, and the rest of the time this 8oz boxing glove mounted on a mechanical arm pops out and strikes you right square in the nuts.
But OH MY WORD, that cookie...
It's buttery, and flaky.  It's filling, but not heavy.  It's got this curious blend of flavors, aromas, and textures that you just can't get anywhere else.
Every time you get your lips around that cookie, it makes you realize that it's all worthwhile.
You know without a shadow of a doubt that you'd gladly get punched in the testicles 99 times just as long as you know that somewhere in a hundred pulls of that lever you're going to get that perfect cookie.
I know that you have doubts.  I know you read the negative reviews, and you think "Yeah, makes sense.  That's Ubisoft.  The past few times I've spent money on Ubisoft I've regretted it."
Hey, I know how you feel.  You pulled the leverr, and you got punched in the nuts.

-the inability to play the story mode offline,
Each of these is a punch to the nuts.
But Brother, For Honor-the game itself- is a cookie.

Update: After playing this more, I've determined the game is fantastic once you understand the mechanics -- which can take awhile. However, the game is so extensive that every detail matters and I love it. Everyone says the controls are complicated, I disagree, the binding is very flexible. I find myself trying to do some Arma3 movements in BF4, which results in a "doh" moment, as well as trying to shoot a flare at an enemy position. If you play BF4, you might catch yourself doing this.
First and foremost, play single player and do some of the show case challenges, they come in handy in multiplayer when you're in a good squad. Multiplayer can get confusing real fast as every server has a different way of doing things (more on this later). Second, do some coop servers online. Lastly, do Apex protocol, which tests your skills and teamwork.Then go play one of the dozens of mods, from the original PUBG (you know it was originally an Arma mod, right?), to RPG.
Multiplayer: If there's one thing I'd say never do, is jump into multiplayer with less than 5 hours of gameplay time. You'll be confused enough as to how the server is ran than you will figuring out how Arma3 works. Some servers are casual and you just parachute in whereever you want, while others have a person that will assign you to a squad, direct you to a line for a helo extract, load out with whatever your squad leader says to have, and you will meet up with your squad talking like a commando. They may also only use Direct Communication, which requires you to be near the player speaking to hear them.

Nothing can compare to what Star Wars: KOTOR 2 is to me. From the ripe age of 7 years old, to coming on 19 now, this game has been a constant in my life. As a child, I played it because I loved Star Wars, and because I picked the first game up at Gamestop with my mother after graduating second grade. I didn't understand a lot of what was going on, but the gameplay kept me going on, and so did the fact that it was Star Wars. Over the years I slowly understood the story, the subtle way the game presented itself, and it hit me. This game is a masterpiece.
The Sith Lords is one of, if not the, best Star Wars game, hell, even Star Wars STORY, that's ever been made. It starts out much like the first game, Mr/Mrs Hero off to save the galaxy, but as the first game stayed on those tracks, the second derailed so hard it knocked our planet out of orbit with the sun. You play as a jaded, broken ex-Jedi, who until recently wandered around in a vagabond fashion along the edges of the galaxy, and you stay that way til the very end of the game. It's not a story about one man or woman, but about the entire galaxy and the people in it. It manages to humanize Sith, make you feel contempt for the Jedi Order. choose the fate of entire peoples and planets, all the while without having polarizing, lazy, and obvious choices during these things. There's no black or white in this game. Its, for lack of a better(and less cliche term), all gray.
Is helping an up and coming planetary government going to actually be good for the people of this planet, or is it going to give them hope for it to just be crushed down again?
Is this man, who is a Jedi master, really what he says he is? If so, then how can he sit and watch a planet full of suffering and do nothing? If he isn't a Jedi, then what the hell is he? Should he be punished for forsaking his responsibilities?
Will your actions on trying to heal a broken planet save it, or damn it and a galactic government into bankruptcy and its eventual collapse?
Is a culture based on war and battle so bad? Are Mandalorians the evil boogey men the Republic has it out to believe? Are the actions the Republic took during the Mandalorian wars justified?
Who is to blame for the Jedi Civil War? The Jedi, or the Sith?
Should a galactic republic enforce its laws with a religious organization?
Is the Force a force of good, evil, or is it amoral?
All of these things and more are the types of problems you're presented in Knights of the Old Republic II. The writing is great, the gameplay is great, and the story itself is god damn beautiful. If you love Star Wars, get this. If you don't love Star Wars, still ♥♥♥♥ing get this because it would be a disservice to not at least try and experience one of the best RPGs made so far.
*ALSO* Although the game is amazing, it is unfinished. But! There's a mod called The Sith Lords Restored Content Mod that tries to piece together the things they could and they do it beautifully. If you want the full experience of Star Wars KOTOR 2, this mod is a *must-have*.
UPDATE: Nominated this for the "Test of Time" award since its story and gameplay are STILL the best in a Star Wars game, and one of the best forr regular RPG's.

If you're new to Magic and you want to learn how to play, this game is fantastic on teaching you the ways of the basics and explaining what all the enchantments, auras, abilities, and everything else mean. This is coming from someone who had no idea what Magic really was until I played this game. Now I feel like an expert. The game runs you through every element (White, Blue, Green, Red, and Black) to make sure you get a feel for what each color specializes in. Then once you're about to complete the tutorial, it lets you choose what kind of deck you want to run with. And it's already pre-built, just for you, to ensure that you at least stand somewhat of a chance against the computer that knows what it's doing. Most of the time...
BUT
If you're an experienced player and you want to play it with your friends and see what kind of awesome deck you can make with the newly-implemented pre-built decks, look the other way. The pre-built deck system is not quite what everyone else was hoping it would be as every deck combination you could possibly use starts you with a vast number of inferior cards. Of course, there's supposed to be weak cards in every deck, but these decks are built with cards that don't have a fine and polished pattern that work efficiently. I guess that makes sense knowing that every card combination, whether it be Red and Blue, Green and White, or Black and Blue, has many ways for you to customize them to your own liking and build your own kind of strategy.
But here's the kicker; the way you get cards is by beating people with a very unefficient deck. If you don't go with white, you're likely going to lose a lot. And the designers planned that. Because once you beat Avacyn, if you can because she's the final boss of the first plane in the campaign, there's an option for you to BUY CARDS. Seriously. I'm not kidding. You can waste $35 of your hard-earned money to get every card IN THE GAME. NOT in as every card in existence. Every card that was PUT INTO THE GAME. And it doesn't bother telling you that either.
Now there's two things that aggravates me about this: First, people who have a lot of money now have the ability to create a terrifying-powerful deck just because they have money. That ruins the experience of learning how to use what you're limited to and formulating your own unique strategy. Now they can use all the best cards and get bored with the challenges and regret their purchase because they wasted their money on a game they'll never play again. Secondly, for the people who don't have money all over their floors, they have to constantly beat annoying people with annoyingly polished decks that crush you if you don't draw all your good cards early in the game. Constantly. And even then, the best card they could get is something that doesn't fit well in any of their decks. The booster packs you earn for beating the snot out of the computer will ALWAYS give you defective cards that don't help your weak deck. And the worst thing about it, is that if you can't do anything but lose and you think you made the wrong choice for what deck you thought would be suitable for your playing style, guess what? You can't change it until you unlock all the cards that would be in the other pre-built decks, or if you reset your profile and risk losing all the cards you so painfully earned.
This game is almost able to classify itself as a pay to win game. You know, like those games on the iPod Touch where you have to pay to unlock certain things that you need in order to progress in the game. Now I haven't spent thirty-five dollars, but just because others fell for it, that upsets me. You're stuck, so you have to pay. Unless you have a lot of free-time at home, which I doubt, or you have the patience of a god.
So in conclusion, only buy this if you have no idea how to play Magic and are interested in learning the fundamental concepts of Magic. Otherwise don't buy this friggin' game.

Gridd is a neon-cyberpunk game, where you control your craft and try to “hack the system,” while avoiding and destroying enemies. Behind simple concept there’s a good execution with well-detailed and thought out neon 80’s-like style. Think of Tron, a 1982 movie. The style of the game world vaguely reminds of a famous lightbike scene that the movie portrayed to us.
•	Simple, but action packed gameplay. You can move in 4 directions (up/down/left/right) and shoot. There are different obstacles and enemies that makes it interesting and engaging.
•	Difficult, skill-based gameplay with two modes: the arcade mode offers one same gameplay sequence again and again so you have a chance to study / adapt to it. Endless mode offers randomly-generated levels, so you’ll have to rapidly react to what’s happening on the screen since you can’t actually prepare for it.
•	Neon-Cyberpunk Style: glowing neon futuristic levels, with amazing particle effects, stylized enemy models and well-thought out obstacles. This gives a great vibe of “system hacking” like you would imagine it in 1980’s movies.
•	Music is repetitive, but not annoying: the music loop fits the game fine.
•	There’s not much in the game content-wise. Sure, different enemies and obstacles are there, but your ship remains the same and there are only 3 bonuses: health / shield / weapon upgrades. It gets repetitive after a while: Arcade mode throws the same level at you again and again. Endless mode adds variety, but somewhat diminishes the skills: since obstacles and enemies are random, you can’t learn the positioning and predict them in a timely manner.
•	Dying sequence deserves an extra mention: after you die, you are shown the final screen with score (acceptable). Then, after you have to press the button to close the screen, you get thrown to the main screen of the game (press start to continue), where you have to navigate to the game mode you want and pick it (more button presses). For a skill-based game that requires lots of retry attempts – that quickly gets annoying. Simple restart/retry button would make it so much better.
The game offers an engaging gameplay with exceptional style, but does get repetitive after a while since there’s not that much content present. I say grab it during 50% discount.

Mechanically: Imagine the most obstacle-course-like parts of Star Fox, with a dash of Space Harrier, topped with an infinite runner/infinite dodger/dodge-em-up/whatever the eternally mutating nomenclature is currently, and you'll be on the right track.
Stylistically: Pure 1980s neon tinged Tron meets Nightmares (the Bishop of Battle.) Grid lines, modern re-imaginings of vector graphics rendered in 3D and lit with bold colors. Essentially what you see in any of the screenshots is exactly how the game "feels" visually.
This is one of the finest examples of simplicity in design leading to greater things than one might expect that I've played in a while. The game literally consists of only two inputs and nothing else: move, and shoot. It has the simplest imaginable visual guideposts, as well: If it's red, avoid contact with it; if it's yellow, shoot it; it's metallic don't shoot it because it will richochet, and like red, don't crash into it.
From that barebones premise however, emerges a shockingly enjoyable and addictive experience. This game is effectively a true arcade game, and one I wouldn't have been surprised to find in actual coin op cabinets back in the day.
You dodge obstacles (and boy do they become demanding later,) shoot targets to increase your multiplier, grab shield, health, and weapon powerups, and try to progress to the end of the game. There's a brief hacking challenge wherein you shoot a target to unlock a numerical key sequence, then try to collect numbers to find the correct input. If you get one right, let it switch to the next number and try again. Once all three have been input, you open a "backdoor" which is essentially an extra life in GRIDD.
Every time you get hit you lose shield, health, and/or weapon upgrades. Run out entirely, and it's game over. There is no save functionality, and running out of lives in the main Arcade mode does mean starting over again from scratch. But the game is challenging and enthralling enough that if you're a fan of on-rails shooters and dodge-em-ups and/or infinite runners like myself, you probably won't mind replaying. Especially if you dig the visual and sound design.
There's an endless mode that saves your progress (measured in kilobytes of data obtained, increased by defeating enemies) through a series of sectors. I'm not certain whether this mode is a random selection of premade areas, or truly procedurally generated. In either case, it always feels different, and the challenge continually increases as you progress through higher and higher sectors. In this mode, here's no downside to dying, other than making only marginal progress in your kb bar for the sector you're currently in. So you can play Endless at your liesure, making it the less stressful mode despite it also being the more challenging of the two.
Pros:
FANTASTIC audiovisual design makes for a profoundly nostalgic look and feel that anyone who grew up in the 80s will recognize. Very atmospheric. Not sure how the A E S T H E T I C meme started, but this game embodies that vibe entirely.
Pure arcade action is brilliantly minimalistic in its mechanical design, but endlessly fun and addicting. (At least for me it is.)
Leaderboards and achievements, if you're into that.
Reminds me of the B-movie "Nightmares" from the 80s (the Bishop of Battle,) which to me - despite its poor reputation - was a staple of the gaming spirit of the decade I grew up in.
Endless mode is fun, gives a sense of progression, and is challenging. After completing Arcade, it's the only thing left to do, and gives you a sense of accomplishment as you make your way through progressively higher sectors.
Arcade mode is finely crafted and rewards practice.
Full controller support. (Using a wired 360 controller, personally.)
Runs great on low to mid tier hardware. (I'm running a Phenom II X4 965 BE, 8GB DDR3 1333, and a GTX 660 in Windows 7. Smooth as butter in 1080p.)
Cons:
Somewhat short (though there is still the endless mode which is... well... endless.)
Not much musical variety, and while feeling authentically retro and nostalgic, none of the tunes stuck in my head like (just the most recent example off the top of my head) STRAFE's did, or even something simpler like Bit-Blaster XL. Sometimes retro-centric synthwave style game soundtracks forego melody in the pursuit of pure atmosphere. It totally works, don't get me wrong... I just won't be bobbing my head to it. Perhaps for the best given the concentration required to play this at times, though.
No additional unlockables, modes, or features that I can see. So you have to really love the core experience on offer here. (Fortunately, I do!)
The camera doesn't follow your ship so much as the track, and since it's on rails, this means you can frequently be fooled by your perception and spatial awareness. A good tip is to keep your eye on your actual ship, not the camera angle, particularly when avoiding tough obstacles. There are moments when the camera focuses on an enemy instead of the track as well, which can make it difficult to tell how close you are to colliding with something. Pay special attention to your ship at all times. With practice, this will become second nature.
If you're fiending for an on-rails shooter that feels and sounds like all things 80s, especially if you liked movies like Tron or Nightmares and grew up with them, and don't require a lot of unlockable content or replay value beyond the old fashioned arcade joy of "can I make it further this time than my last run?" then I can highly recommend this game.
If you're on the fence, want more for your money, or don't feel like endless mode would be something you'd keep coming back to... maybe wait for a sale. Put it on your watchlist for future reference.
If you don't like the audiovisual design shown in the store page trailer, aren't a fan of on-rails shooters or hefty precision dodging, or you expect a lot of content... you might be better served elsewhere.

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: this game is beautiful, though in a very disturbing way.  The artist wears H.R. Giger's influence on his tattered sleeve.  Each screen is amazingly painted and animated, making this game a sheer joy to look at.
As for gameplay, if you're a fan of point-and-click adventures, this doesn't really add anything new to the genre, but it's a solid entry.  The interface is streamlined, with just a single skeletal hand to interact with the environment.  No "look," "use," "speak," etc icons to deal with like in Shadowgate or older Sierra titles.  This is more like the FMV Sierra adventures, like Phantasmagoria.
The puzzles are not particularly difficult.  The few times I found myself stuck, I just left the game for a bit, came back, and found that I had just missed another room or an object on the ground.  A lot of the answers are pretty well spelled out for you.
The story is pretty simplistic, but allows you to make a few choices along the way.  The decisions you make have negligible effects on the gameplay, but will affect the story.
Finally, the game is not very long.  I managed to wrap it up in under 3 hours on my first playthrough, and my second took me about 1 hour.
Tormentum - Dark Sorrow is a beautiful game, and one that is truly worth experiencing, but be warned that it's not particularly difficult, and it's over pretty quickly.

On my third run, I believe was my trip north, I made it in 50 days. That was quite adventurous.

Being an Ubisoft customer is like being a subject in laboratory experiment on behavior.  You're placed in this room, and in one wall there's a lever attached to a chute. Whenever you pull the lever, the drawer pops open and you get a cookie.
And it is the best cookie you've ever tasted. It's warm, and sweet, and just the right blend of chewie and crunchy.  It's hand down the greatest thing possible for a human to consume, and you can have one any time you want just by pulling the lever.
But after about ten pulls or so, instead of a cookie, an 8 ounce boxing glove mounted on a mechanical arm pops out and punches you hard right square in the nuts.  You pull yourself up off the ground struggling with this crazy feeling that is a gutwrenching combination of the pain of taking a shot to the pills, and the bitter shock of disappointment and loss, cause you really had your heart set on that cookie.
After some time, the hunger for that cookie grows and grows, and the memory of that gential-punch begins to fade.
So you muster up your courage, and pull the lever again.
And what do you know?  A cookie!
And it's glorious.
It's just as good as the first time.  It's the best cookie ever, and it'll never get old.  You'll never get tired of it, or crave a sandwich or pizza instead because this cookie is just that damn good.
You pull the lever a few more times, and get a few more cookies until one time you're not paying attention and WHAM! -another blow to the nuts.
As the days pass by, the frequency of getting punched in the nuts grows and grows, and the cookies come less and less often, until one day you realize that you get only one cookie for every ten pulls of the lever, and the rest of the time this 8oz boxing glove mounted on a mechanical arm pops out and strikes you right square in the nuts.
But OH MY WORD, that cookie...
It's buttery, and flaky.  It's filling, but not heavy.  It's got this curious blend of flavors, aromas, and textures that you just can't get anywhere else.
Every time you get your lips around that cookie, it makes you realize that it's all worthwhile.
You know without a shadow of a doubt that you'd gladly get punched in the testicles 99 times just as long as you know that somewhere in a hundred pulls of that lever you're going to get that perfect cookie.
I know that you have doubts.  I know you read the negative reviews, and you think "Yeah, makes sense.  That's Ubisoft.  The past few times I've spent money on Ubisoft I've regretted it."
Hey, I know how you feel.  You pulled the leverr, and you got punched in the nuts.

Awakened behind the twisted metal bars of your cell suspended far above the earth, a magnificently gnarled airship humming ominously above as it carries our mysterious hooded protagonist from their unknown past to a hellish new reality behind the confines of a massive and ghastly prison complex. Will you give in to your new existence of demonic incarceration, or will you find the will to journey into the pits of hell itself and find your freedom?
Tormentum is not a tale for the queasy, with brutal depictions of death, despair, and torture the imagery within is enough to make the average modern horror fan♥♥♥♥♥♥their pants in terror. The game comes from a seriously engaging and tasteful angle despite this, and everything is done in a fictionally compelling way that serves the narrative and not just for the sake of shock. The core element in Tormentum is atmosphere, and its surreal influences show to the very root.
The bleak path ahead is riddled with puzzles, mini-games and secrets keeping you just out of reach of your next step to freedom, the next diabolical room of traps and tricks and all forms of unholy devices. Each solution requires a keen eye and generally has the player glossing carefully over each hand-painted environment, which is already a real treat to behold on its own. Paying close attention to small details left across the harrowing stages leads you to discovering artifacts and symbols usually arranged in specific ways to clue you in on how to solve that specific area's solution, and take form as anything from candles being lit in specific order to create a pentagram of light across carefully arranged mirror surfaces to crudely decorated skulls that must be brought back to their rightful tortured remains.
The puzzles here are genuinely fun, as someone who generally hates them I didn't find anything in Tormentum to be tedious or long-winded. They reward those with an appreciation for the remarkable art and encourages enthusiastic exploration of the visuals surrounding the player. With many obstacles come moral choices, and many of the solutions face the player with painful decisions that weigh on your mind throughout, the betrayal of friends and murders of the seemingly innocent bringing you closer to your goal but further from humanity. The spirit of classic point and click adventure gaming is present, and you'll be completing plenty of satisfyingly simple and rewarding tasks and pushing for that next gruesome screen of beautifully detailed scenery though never without consequence.
The artwork itself is absolutely breathtaking not because it is pretty, gorgeous, or inspiring but because it is fantastically grotesque in detail. Every organic curve, every sickeningly moist surface of glistening quality and every rusted jag of blackened metal stand out with each transition of a scene, each one more jaw-dropping than the last. A brutal assault of rapid images portraying ruthlessly grim imagery, making escape the one bright glimmer of hope in our protagonist's peril. There's an unmistakable similarity to some of the most macabre and surreal artists from the organically twisted curves of Giger to the grand hellscapes of Bosch, combined with the likes of what could be straight out of a Dimmu Borgir album cover just for extra measure. And it isn't just the art; I've already caught several references to works of the surreal including the phrase "Fire Walk with Me", showing that these brilliantly demented creators have their influences set in the right place.
It's not just from these decadent and long renown artists that Tormentum draws its artistic influences from however, there are plenty of modern day touches that gamers and horror enthusiasts of every ilk will reminisce on from darkened knights dressed in twisted sets of armor akin to the foes in the Dark Souls series, to the natural feeling animations of Odin Sphere that move fluidly with every rising breath of a character or rusted movement of the cold metal environment around you. Tormentum has the makings of a classic, and if you aren't turned away by it's cruel imagery this is one ♥♥♥♥ed up trip worth taking.

An interesting if somewhat poorly handled official mod, With Fire & Sword is actually Mount & Blade's official release in Poland, pretty much setting up history from the 16th century or so as a framing device. One thing that becomes immediately clearis that this version of Mount & Blade is MUCH harder than its previous incarnations. This can be summed up in three simple reasons: poorer economy, less effective armor, and GUNS. The regional economy is falling on hard times and defeating even bandit infantry is much more difficult than is thanks to the fact that much of your armor is cloth and even low level enemies will carry rifles. Soloing is nearly impossible, so you will have to amass an army one way or another soon. If you're the kind of person who likes to just roam the map being a lone wolf, this is not the game for you, but if you enjoy building up a (surprisingly historically accurate) army and inflicting it on your fellow man, give With Fire & Sword a shot. The Nekopara OVA is a decent but expensive adaptation of the first Nekopara VN.
When it comes to the story, it's about as slice of life as it gets and while there's not a lot of depth to the setting or characters there's enough to basically allow for cute catgirls doing cute things which, based on the sales numbers for all the VNs and the number of backers for this project on Kickstarter, is certainly enough for a lot of people. I actually think the story improves upon what was featured in Volume 1 since it helps fill out some nebulous details in the plot and generally transitions better between scenes to tell a more cohesive story of the life of the twin catgirl leads and their owner along with the struggles they face.
The presentation isn't exactly top-notch and if anything, I think how characters are portrayed in the VNs is better but the animation itself helps to make up for the altered style. There's certainly a lot of things all the characters do that weren't or couldn't be shown well in the VNs and it was appreciated to see characters come to life in a more fluid, active way.
Sound work is generally good across the board. The cast that voiced the characters in the VNs also voice the characters in the OVA and overall they do a solid job even if the delivery isn't consistently strong. The major addition is the protagonist's voice actor and his voice work fits the character reasonably well. Music is about as good as those featured in the VNs and may sound familiar if only because of the stylistic similarity.
You might wonder then why I give the Nekopara OVA a red thumbs down of non-recommendation despite all the praise in the paragraphs above and it all comes down to the $30 price tag. I personally backed this for $30 myself mostly to help push the stretch goals near the end of the Kickstarter campaign and in addition to a key to unlock this to view (which is awarded at the $15 tier) I also got some additional cosmetic stuff including the soundtrack. While this is a little expensive for my tastes there's no questioning how much better value it is than to pay the same amount just to watch what is basically a 50-something minute anime adaptation of a popular visual novel.
Furthermore, for much less one can watch other anime adaptations of fairly popular media even on Steam itself. There's also plenty of less-than-savory ways to get this for cheap or nothing to the point I wonder if even a decent amount of money will end up being made from sales and whether it's a good idea to price this so high considering the campaign itself raised over a million dollars. It is no wonder then that there's plenty of forum posts criticizing how expensive the Nekopara OVA is. Heck, one could even buy all of the Nekopara VNs in their bundled form for about as much as this costs when it's at full price.
With all that said, if you have $30 to burn, want to throw money at NEKO WORKs. and you really want to watch this, I doubt what I've said is going to stop you. I hope then that you at least find it to be worth your money.

This game really is a two parter, as ground battles and space battles are separate.
Ground battles are good, but nothing too exceptional. A futuristic Battlefield is the best I can think of to compare it to, and while it's well done overall, it's nothing too original, at least as far as I can tell now (this comes from a Planetside 2 player, not a battlefield player mind you)
Space battles, however, are a completely different beast, and where the game truely shines. Capital ships are literally moving spawn points for fighters, on top of having a ludicrous amount of health. But what makes them truely unique is that, unlike ANY other game, the inside of the ship is fully navigable, an important feature since it can be boarded, and destroyed from the inside far more quickly than if the opposing team was just to shoot at it. And these ships are large enough to fully qualify as maps of their own, to make things even better, and the fact that battle damage affects it in real time can affect the gunplay inside thiose ships, since all large ships insides have various ways to react when getting hit: internal explosions, smoke, the screen having a shake so violent you could swear your character just got thrown against the wall, and more.
And it all makes for a very epic feeling, the only regret being that ground battles aren't as interesting.. maybe by mixing up the two, space battles controlling entry points for the ground fight? Would be a pain to achieve, but would be soooo awesome.
Also, while this game has a rather low population at the moment, it doesn't suffer from it as much as other games of its kind. AI bots are perfectly willing to pick up vehicles if all players decline the chance of spawning one, including battleships, and they will attemp even boarding actions if given the chance. It also mixes well with the fact bots will actively seek cover most of the time when shot at. In fact, the only thing it dosn't know how to do at all is provide healing support: I have yet to see an AI attemt to repair battleships subsystems, even when it's sitting right next to it. But the most important is that it means solo play is possible, and isn't a bad experience.
Overall, a great experience that deserves far more spotlight than it does right now, especially since, for an "alpha" it looks already like a finished product.
To the developpers... If you have the financial means to do it with the money from the early access, please, I beg of you, ADVERTISE THIS GAME. It definitely has the potential to be the next big thing next to titles such as star wars battlefront EASILY, as it delivers the same combined arms battle, and more. It deserves more players than it has now, and I would be extremely sad to see it die by a lack of players while it has so much to offer.

Options- Very few. 5/10

Stability- When I first played this game, I thought it was in beta. It wasn't. 3/10
Speed- Quick for an mmo-rts-rpg, but hamperred by Crowns. 7/10
Story- Aparently you can learn more of it by traveling around, but blocks of text aren't my forte. 5/10
Microtransactions- Most are cosmetic, but you can buy premium. At least it's not APB Reloaded. 8/10
If the game actually had some more depth to it, I'd suggest it, but there really isn't a "top teir" to this game, just more of the same. I enjoyed it for awhile, but in the end, it really was just meh.

Keep reading for more info and Pro's n Con's but it's really a fun game. I felt like I was a kid all over again ...
This genre mash-up has left me pleased with my purchase. But let's get to the real reason you're here, the breakdown;
[EDIT: 3rd Novemeber. Devs replied to inform that there is a tutorial being brought in with the next patch. Mainly to assist the mass influx of impatient gamers. Secondly, the UI is currently being revised and the hit 'detection' is currently getting worked on. So basically what you have is an active Dev who reads your comments and actively partakes in the community. Seriously, what are you waiting for? Buy the game].
- Combat; Alot of work went into the mechanics of the ground fighting.
- Smooth as a babies bottom.
- YOU CAN LEAN!! Why do FPS games always leave this feature out? It's starting to♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.
- Falling animations. E.g. I was in the hanger, heading to jump in a fighter (Think Battlefront 2 here) when an enemy shot the side of the ship and my character went stumbling across the walkway. Little things like this are a nice touch.
- Spawn locations make sense. No random spawning like battlefront/field.
- Small squads emphasis small squad tactics. Also make friends easier.
- Good selection of weapons. Each one feels different with a wide range of play styles.
- No set class system. You loadout your own avatar how you like.
- Armoured vehicles can be spawned at random, alot like SW:Battlefront heros.
- Drove a jeep into an airport walkway HALO style. Felt Very proud that day ...
- RPG Elements;
- So you have three categories to lvl up; Command, Combat and Support. Do stuff in this area and you lvl them up which gives you more points in that category and allows you to add upgrades to your loadout and carry more stuff.
- Persistant lvls.
- Not a quick thing to lvl them up. Might be a con to some people but it feels like you earnt your ranks so it's a nice balance.

- Space;
- I already mentioned that space combat feels like your commanding a pilot through 500 VPNs with an internet connection from the 80's but it still feels kinda fun and unique. Targets work alot like SW:Battlefront 2 (1995) so it should feel pretty familiar in that regards.
- Ship interiors feel polished with alot of eye candy.
- I stood on the bridge for the first time and realised that the ship was actually persistant in the battle. And here I thought it was a seperate world space ...
- Just like infantry, you can change your loadouts and weapons. So pretty cool.
- I also like the waiting periods for respawning ships. If multiple use the same station, it will load and launch each persons ship in que. Nice little touch there.
- User Interface;
- It's pretty detailed, with a good selection of crap to click on. (See cons for more details).
- Sound:
- Sound is a mixed bag. Music is pretty cool, like a military version of Skyrim thing going on.
- What sounds are good are REALLY good. Explosions feel heavy. Though I'm not a fan of hit marker sounds, they are satisfying either way.
- Community;
- Everyone is actually pretty nice, 'cept that guy who teabagged me, screw that guy.
Overall; 9.2
- Combat;
- Mech units feel like they are gliding. In all honesty, you could remove them and no-one would bat an eye.
- Driving in this game feels like dricing in GTA 1. Delayed reactions will have you driving into every wall/post there is.
- Hit detection is at times rubbish. You'll be saying "WTF!!!!" a bit more then you'd like.
- Zero tutorials. You're going in dry sunny, so bring you're own lube.
- Graphics feel dated (Though that is NOT a con in my books).
- Space:
- So, you get into your cockpit of pre-red mist and set out into thy yonder ... only to have your steering wheel replaced with a 1700's nautical wheel. Steering the sail boat Assasins creed 3 anyone?
- Oh you will die. Alot. Aaaaaand you still won't be good at flying. Just hope the skilled guys finish the objective fast so you can board the enemy stations/ships.
- I wish there was a better description for each weapon. It's hard to understand what each little things does/good for.
- User Interface;
- So everything looks like it's from Half-life. Yes, the menus and clickable shinies are all detailed and you can do alot of stuff, but it's so old. I mean, why are you so old? I'm afraid to sneeze the dust will blow off and there will be nothing left.
- Sound;
- You can tell the difference from things they put attention to and the things that are more placeholders. It's not really a con and just a reminder hat it's still EARLY ACCESS. So not a con really.
- Community;
- It's so small. Like, the kinda small you're always worried your ex is telling everyone you are. Dammit Devs, advertise your game already!!!!!!!
Final verdict - This game is probably better then all those AAA titles in your games list. An Early Access title that delivered the kinda game that just takes me back to a childhood dream and didn't give me PTSD along the way.

Tormentum - Dark Sorrow is a point and click adventure thrown into a damnable orgy of suffering, misery and despair in the visual trappings of Giger and Beksinski.  The art is easily the linchpin of this release, those richly hellish and tortuous scenes are so morbidly captivating and visceral that one has to question the mental health of the artist. It’s not just those wide panoramic vistas that give off a sense of infernal grandeur, it’s also the attention to detail in small objects, items obscured and a wealth of visually suggestive scenery and object placement that make the art direction and presentation so incredible. Feed into that the bleak and austere soundtrack and you have an audio visual phenomenon.
Gameplay is your standard point and click adventure types, you are to find items that they may resolve other problems that hinder your progress in the game, rinse and repeat. To this end the game employs a great number of puzzles which are fairly enjoyable and not too taxing, oftentimes clues given to you on how to solve them are found in other locations. Overall the gameplay is simple and for the most part is secondary to the experience, not so much in the sense it has been neglected, but more so that it is a means to an end rather than the core of the experience.
The lore and story are slowly bled out to you, never providing you with too much detail, but just enough dark particulars to provide a minimalist context allowing your imagination to run wild and give a few grains of morality in weighing up your actions. NPC’s are often times minimalist in interaction, but are quite capable of reinforcing the central themes to the game and giving it greater depth. This overall vagueness reinforces the crushing sense of despair and disorientation that accompanies you in the game throughout.
At certain points in the game you are presented with choices and whilst at face value they are your standard black and white good or bad dichotomy, the lack of guidance or understanding of your role in this world brings your own philosophical dilemmas into the fray. Can one kill for freedom? Is it a crime to punish the wicked? Is it my place to judge them so? Am I being lied to? Etc.
Gameplay is short, I would guess perhaps around 5 hours in total, but what an intense and rewarding 5 hours they are! Not forgetting that there is some replayability in making alternate choices in the game. However playtime is irrelevant, playing Tormentum is an experience more than a game, a quasi-philosophical interactive grotesquery of redemption and punishment set in the most horrific and stunning abysses.

CAVEATS:  1, I'm not a fanboy - I played Duke Nukem 3D as a kid, but other than that I really didn't care if or when this "next game" would be made.  2, I bought this during a STEAM sale for ~$5 which, quite frankly, was the only price point I was "ok" with.
PROS:
- Plenty of vulgarity / nudity / "suggestive content"
- A resurrection of the corny, over-the-top, mostly bulls hit FPS gaming of the mid to late 90s
- More interactivity and engagement than one might expect from a title like this (jokes, minigames, reactive environment, etc.)
- Relatively low key, low frustration, high gratuitous violence kind of gaming.
CONS:
- The entire thing is map driven... just like the old games.  And, just like the old games, each map could fit on an old 3.5" diskette.  I mean, on the one hand you can rest easy knowing you're *never* very far from a checkpoint / level warp... but on the other, the maps are goddamn small.  It's like traveling the world... 10 goddamn feet at a time.
- The game is old (4 years as of this writing), and plays even older.  Same stuff you heard at release - graphics are dated, engine is clunky, mechanics are simplistic.  For a Duke Nukem game, it's just fine.  For a "game we waited 12 years for", its an astounding disappointment.
- It's short.  It took me 10 hours on "standard difficulty" to just plough through the whole thing, and that was with me wasting time to do stuipd sh!t like "Win an air hockey game 7 - 0 at the strip club".
- The production values are rough.  The few cutscenes look like PS2 era graphics, or are literally "flash animation" type moving pictures.  After its done you can see that the "Triptych Offices" were an abandoned condo with a kitchenette and two chairs.  The game is an accurate reflection of what those kinds of resources get you.
So, why is this a positive review?  I enjoyed it.  As I said, I have no vested interest in the Duke Nukem franchise (trust me - I understand why they're upset), and I got the game for practically nothing.  As such, it's easy for me to simply not care about a lot of things.  If you're of a similar mindset, or can snag this during one of STEAM's sales (or both), I think it'd be worth your time / money. 80 Days is a video game based on Jules Verne's Around The World In Eighty Days. It tells the story of Phileas Fogg, who takes a bet to circle the world in 80 days, starting from London in October of 1872. You play as Passepartout, Fogg's new valet, who assists him on his journey. That is where the similarities end, though. The story takes place in an alternate history 1872, in a world full of fantastical technology such as automatons, underwater trains, flying machines, and even mechanical camels, but it's also very aware of contemporary political and cultural struggles.
The game part of this game comes in planning out your journey, trying to find the quickest path, managing your funds, and negotiating for lower ticket prices, seats on trains or zeppelins or submarines. BUT ALSO, you talk to people in the cities you travel to, witnessing or becoming part of the stories. For example, one path gets you involved in an Agatha Christie style murder mystery that you can try to solve. In my first game, I got arrested, organized a mutiny, accidentally blew up a boat, and lost a boxing match and still managed to get back to London JUST UNDER the time limit at 78 days.
The writing in this game is fantastic. It's a wonderful adventure, full of surprises and thrills and even heartbreak. Everywhere I went, I encountered people who touched the character's heart in unexpected ways. But I had to leave them behind, because the game is focused on the challenge. You're always moving forward, leaving things behind.
And the game also explores themes of anti-colonialism, unique cultures and how varied the cultures of the world are, as well as celebrating a diverse cast of adventurers, inventors, and even criminals (in my game, I had a romantic tryst with a woman who was an internationally wanted thief and cardsharp). All manner of people are represented and from my admittedly white perspective, it represents the world cultures in a way that is not exoticized.
The world is realized so well. The beautiful art is simple and evocative. The historical events represented are all affected by the game's fantastic steampunk-ish world, and your characters are not the focus of the world, just participants in it.
At it's core, it's an incredibly complex choose-your-own-adventure story, with hundreds of branching paths and possible narratives. There are 170 cities in the world you can visit, and in a single playthrough, you might visit 20, and depending on your choices, you might only see one possible part of the stories present in that city. Discussing this game with my girlfriend, my mind began spiraling from the possibilities of this story. And all of these possibilities are elegantly tied together with the focus on your goal and your relationship with Fogg as you go on this journey together.
This is a wonderful, beautiful game, and I'm certainly not the first person to see this; it won Time Magazine's Game Of The Year in 2014, and it was even nominated for 4 BAFTA awards. I highly recommend it to anyone.

Dynasty Feud is a 2-4 multiplayer focused platform brawler which boasts a huge roster of over 40 characters. It takes inspiration from games like Smash Bros. while also reminds me a little of recent similar releases like Brawlhalla both of which I have sunk a good number of hours into. I usually get tired of playing fighting games after a short while because regardless of the number of characters the game presents to you, the battles start to feel same after a while.
Dynasty Feud is a game that solely focuses on the multiplayer aspect and there are no bots or an offline story mode whatsoever for solo play. There is a very certain lack of content visible right from when you boot up the game and the game makes no real effort to try and hide it. You can either play Quick Play, Ranked Match, Private Match or train with dummies.
For a game which boasts of a massive roaster, it is important to get the tutorial right for the players to get comfortable with the different skills of the various characters. The training mode does no favours to the player in this regard as the dummies (not bots) stand at one place and fire lasers at you killing you in one hit.
Now the major problem with this is that since these dummies are not bots, they offer no actual challenge whatsoever while their constant respawing and shooting lasers do not exactly let you practice calmly. This training mode is one of the worst I have seen in a fighting game in a long time.
Let’s now see how the actual gameplay of Dynasty Feud fairs. The game starts off by asking you to pick one of the eight different dynasties, inspired by various pop cultures and references. Each of these dynasties contains five characters within themselves. The first one to kill the opposing dynasty wins the game.
Each character has a varied moveset with two special attacks of their own. To provide some lore to these dynasties you can read their backstories in the codex.
The problem with the gameplay is that the majority of the characters die in one hit, some taking two because of additional armour. This gives you little to no time to get familiar with the characters before they are killed.
Once you kill or get killed, the killed dynasty leader gets an annoy power which can summon flashes of electricity to giant balls. These annoyances make the game feel far less rewarding than it should be. There is no real sense of achievement and every kill you get just gives your opponent the opportunity to annoy you more and vice versa.
The abilities of each character being limited to only two makes it difficult to balance the game as some characters have overpowered abilities while others are just randomly given some trash powers. You cannot choose your own character line up for a dynasty aside from a local mode called “All-Star” making you play the characters you don’t like quite often.
Even though the visual designs of these characters are somewhat interesting, I never felt connected with them in any way. It makes one wonder if a smaller but more fleshed out roster would have been better for Dynasty Feud.
At the time of writing, the game also felt empty online. It took me over one and a half minute to find a match in Quick Play and that also was only 1v1. Going in to find 4 player online matches are very rare and the ranked matches are limited to 1v1 only which is an ongoing trend in many games of this genre. Playing locally is certainly more fun  but that can be said about most of the other games.
The visual design of Dynasty Feud is pretty average by today’s standards. While the characters are uniquely designed and there is a certain flair and charm in them, the backgrounds stand out like a sore thumb. From an artistic viewpoint, games like Brawlhalla has far more beautiful and charming aesthetic while a game like Brawlout has much more detail in its maps. Considering Dynasty Feud’s price and genre this comparison is bound to happen and I was never once enamoured by its visuals.
Credit where credit’s due, the sound design of Dynasty Feud is pretty good. Its main soundtrack is ambient and there is a certain level of ambiguity present in it which makes it sound really good to the ears. Certain sound effects like jumping, special moves and grunts are done really well and goes perfectly with the game. This is a sound design that is very good as an overall package.
I’d be wrong if I said if I didn’t enjoy myself for a few but fun moments while playing Dynasty Feud, but it is weighed down by the numerous problems plaguing the game. The fighting and mechanics never gelled together and the game never completely clicked for me.
It never fully capitalizes on its massive roster and instead makes a mess out of them with its dynasty feature. It also lacks in content at the moment and while the game has potential and does not do much wrong to deserve a negative recommendation, it is nothing more than an average platform brawler with a steep price tag.
