Dynasty Feud is a local AND ONLINE multiplayer one hit KO, fast paced, team based platform fighter game.
-Gameplay-
1-4 players with ONLINE support. I emphazise this because most games I've played and reviewed are local only. There are over 40 characters to choose from each with unique abilities, a great way to familiarizing yourself with the gameplay is through bot matches with different factions.
-Graphics, Sound & Artstyle-
While it doesnt exactly have memorable graphics or sound, the character design along with the level design for this game are clear stand outs in this, and the Dynasty Feud universe becomes immersive because you'll enjoy the characters
-Price-
The retail price is 14.99 USD
-How many hours estimated?-
ONLINE PLAY gives this game so much more life and the fact that people actually play this game online is a welcome surprise to me. It's hard but fun online but it shines obviously with it's local multiplayer giving you in my estimation well over 15 hours of fun gameplay!
-Buy it Now? Wait for Sale? Don't Buy?-
While the game doesn't have a story, the lore of the game is just as good. 40 characters and 8 DYNASTIES, and also the ability to create your own dynasty in ALL STAR MODE, picking your favorite characters (in a balanced matter) to take on other Dynasties. Matches can vary anywhere between 1 min and 10 mins, giving each gameplay a unique feel. Everyone I showed this game to wanted to play more of it, even myself and i was not very good at the game! Dynasty Feud is what indie games should strive to be, fun, fast paced and the ability to go online with friends! The only real downside to this game apart from a few quidbits here and there like some characters feel clunky, levels often get repeated way too much on random, the lack of bots to fill in a online multiplayer match, is that the game costs 15$USD. While it does offer a ton of content and replayability the most I would shell out for Dynasty Feud is 10$USD. Other than that, like I said, the game is great and Kaia Studios should be very proud of their game.

A charming little game set in an alternate late 1800's timeline. I'm hesitant to use the word steampunk, but the tech definitely seems to follow some of those tropes. Not to say that the tech is the focus; the game does a wonderful job of painting exotic locales around the world that are made all the more fantastic by this amazingly advanced technology akin to magic.
Based off of Around the World in 80 days, you play as the valet to a rich man who has taken a wager to travel the globe in 80 days. To do this you must not only plan your route using major cities as little event nodes in which small, choose your own adventure vignettes take place, but also must keep your prim and proper master in immaculate condition.
Or not. It is a choose your own adventure game after all! Your valet can be anywhere from a Batman-esque Alfred super butler to a brusque racist who cares little for these exotic cultures and even less for your pompous master (although if your master's condition drops too low I'm assuming you lose the game; I wouldn't know, I had to much fun being an Alfred type).
The game has loads of replayability as not only can you see your past routes but also the routes of other players. However, I did feel it was a bit short, and the events in each city node don't seem to have much variation, so once you explore them all, which will take a while, you wont have much left to do except try to speedrun the game and maximize your effeciency.
The atmosphere carries this game. If it didnt have such amazing and unique setting it'd probably be a completely meh game. As it is, I'd have to say the game is easily an 8/10 if you care about world-building or settings.

There's a lot to be said about this game. Both good and bad.
It has an amazing combat system, intuitive and clear cut. Although it has its gimmicks, those gimmicks are easily counterable by those actually skilled at the game. Great graphics, great aesthetics, and a downright avalanche of customization options and rewardable min-maxing. With a very interactive faction war to top it all off.
Everything it has to do for the player at face value, it does right.
The microtransactions and seasonal passes are not necessary but merely for those who wish to truly drop that much money. I have no complaints with those, but I would prefer to not see them on a game that's already so expensive. The UI is clunky and unintuitive at times, with not a very clear cut idea of what exactly you're doing sometimes. There's a few bugs and other errors that I feel like could've and should've been cleared out during beta.
And now for the nail in the coffin that everyone always goes to, the P2P connections. Why on God's green Earth does Ubisoft insist on this, I will never know. I'd love to see them finally step up their game and match up to all the other big triple A game companies for once, they make great games. They're just held back by their continued mistakes.
Overall, it is a game worth getting, and although I have my qualms, I feel it's well worth buying for all the options and gameplay it brings. It is in no way in an 'unplayable' state due to the connection issues, merely annoying for the price paid for the game.

This game has got to be one of the greatest I've played.
You begin with the character Naomi Xian, a chip off the old block kid, whose life becomes threatened when Australian invaders exploit the land. With nobody standing up to the Aussies, Naomi is quick to act fast and places the entire land in peril. Naomi then finds himself trapped in a world of drugs, money, fame, and power, forcing him to make decisive decisions that will impact him throughout the whole game.
With this in mind, the player has full control over Naomi through the perk system, skill tree, etc, and, through the RPG based aspect of the game, the player can develop Naomi into a complete versatile weapon of good, or evil - I personally made my first Naomi a level 13 Orc Mage hybrid with an Archer build.
Besides the story, and character, the game also offers immense graphics with minimal invisible walls - I repeat: minimal invisible walls, literally none. This, added with superb AI, offers an action packed game bursting with possibilities! This AI also includes real time situations with real time reactions; enemy soldiers will be able to manoeuvre around obstacles, definitely ensuring 100% that they will not go prone and stare at the obstacle blankly, whilst trying to fathom the meaning of "lyfe".
I highly recommend this game to anyone interested in any form of RPG, as the open-world design, with unlimited freedom, truly allows you, and you only, to choose Naomi's destiny...

The graphics are outdated and need some serious makeup, more so than Dolly Parton in the morning and as for customer service in trouble shooting it's scarcer than finding water on the sun. The reason for this is because the original company which developed this 'Humongous Entertainment' no longer exists and were bought out and bedded by more partners than Zsa Zsa Gabor.
This Humongous Washington based company was strictly focused on producing educational entertainment (edutainment) from which many franchises sprang such as Pajama Sam, Spy Fox and Freddi Fish. Even way back at the time of release (1997) this particular franchise known as 'Big Thinkers' of which there were 2 episodes with a 3rd in the pipework’s but thwarted due to the enemy of Bankruptcy. This series was never well received in comparison to the others and publically received reviews in the newspapers and magazines as something that is 'yawnful', 'dull', 'non-captivating' and that it 'failed to ignite'.
The problem all stemmed from the two main characters, your first introduced to Ben and Beck Brightly (actor Mike Shapiro and Actress Karen Kay Kody) through a jingle similar to an oompa loompa song on speed. Then they simply follow you around a house with zany animation transitions that would only make sense if this game was a MK Ultra experiment. They constantly spit out puns that will make you hiss like you’re a vampire being shown garlic and as said before you will want to have the cursor arrested for drunken and disorderly conduct.
The objective is to find 12 minigames in the house which will test you on various subjects from maths, geography, which colours make what colours, painting, joining pictures to words etc. Unfortunately there's no shooting gallery where I can enjoy a 'brightly' blood bath. Once you've been rewarded enough smart stars in each category you can travel to the garage where there is a big minigame which will test you on all random categories and reward you with big smart stars and a certificate which shows up in your lounge.
All minigames are unfortunately tedious thanks to a cursor which wanders around spasmodically like a fretted jumbuck. Everything being happy in game while you’re trying to harness a wild stallion cursor only compounds the frustration. Yes happy, happy, song, song, smile, smile, stab, stab, cursor, delete.

Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic I was nice; but in a way the story was somewhat predictable, certainly not in a bad way, but there were two main options - good or bad. So despite being a little dated by todays standards it still should be on any self respecting Star Wars fans list; even without the content mod it should still provide good fun and hours of gameplay. And for those who pay very close attention you can see where the Mass Effect series was born but in a different franchise.

Well as a more distant sequel to the first game, they give you KOTOR II.
KOTOR II has a lot more depth when it comes to gameplay overall and different battle interactions.
But at the same time is riddled with something im going to talk about.
The story aspect has been driven away from the traditional KOTOR/RPG style, instead of a two sided light/vs/dark there is a far more greyzoned area, which will make you think again of who is really right and wrong in your aspect.
There are several nods to the previous game (no spoilers) such as Carth, Bastila, your characters future fate, depending on what path you chose and descision made throughout the game.
This makes the story part a WHOLE lot intresting as it creates a dilemma where right is hard to tell from wrong.
Now enough about this, the biggest downsides to this sequel was the production period. The game was rushed, and a lot of content cut, no debate, and as a result there is a huge amount of content missing, and a lot of, and when I say a lot of I MEAN A LOT OF BUGS, some which may even be game breaking, to a point where you are forced to restart or go a load way back to a earlier save. (trust me I had to play through this twice to even get half through the game)
Now this can be fixed by installing the TLSCRM mod which, through amazing modders enabled players to play cut content with a lot less bugs, as well as fixed and missing dialogue and bug fixes in the game itself, honestly I can´t even think of how I would´ve gotten through the game without this mod.
Anyway conlusively this game is definitly worth it for the story, the combat is meh, and is sadly bug ravaged, execpt with the TLSCRM mod, which is practially essential.

Is the glass half empty or half full? This is the question that describes Shadow Warrior 2.
As someone who absolutely loved the first Shadow Warrior (2013) and played it multiple times (first on Normal and then on Insane and Heroic in parallel), I had a bittersweet feeling about the sequel. It incorporates many of the characters, art, and motives from the first game which make you relieve the memories, but the game itself is lacking in so many aspects.
The story is just a shadow of the touching tale from the first game. Those who played it, know that behind the facade of wang jokes, the game was actually telling a surprisingly deep story. The wang jokes are still there, but the rest is not.
Sometimes it feels like the developers were chasing the money, or replaced the story writers from the first game with a group of drunk teenagers. The ending is really terrible. The story leading to it is pretty bad as well and does not come toghether.
Carefully thought through, well-designed, memorable levels have been replaced by procedurally generated generic-looking maps. By incorporating diablo-like elements, the game departed what what made the first part so great, but did not succed in living up to the standard set by its predecessor.
That said, Shadow Warrior 2  is not a bad game and those who loved the first game may enjoy playing the sequel and seeing the references to the first game, but they should adjust their expectations. On a scale of 1-5 this game would be 3, and with a binary recommendation system it (barely) passes the "Recommended" threshold.
As someone who was really enthusiastic to preorder this game, partially as a way to say Thank You to the developers for all those great moment I had playing the first Shadow Warrior, I will think twice about purchasing the future sequel if it ever comes out. But hopefully, Flying Wild Hog will listen to their fans and will make a masterpice that is just as great as the first game.

This is a great game that is wholly different than when it was first published on Steam - disregard negative feedback that predates 12/12.
I bought it two days ago, and it's fantastic.  I had previously played Day-Z, which I was able to enjoy despite its unbelievable lack of polish, but eventually did drop due to its rough edges and the prevalence of cheaters.
When Nether appeared on Steam, I did my research and wrote it off as another War-Z - frankly, Nether looked like a buggy piece of unpolished, derivative garbage.  Fast forward to two days ago, I end up checking the game out at the insistence of a trusted friend - Nether KNOCKED MY SOCKS OFF.  Here's why:
I have encountered only a minor UI bug in my play thus far.
Nether feels like my Fantasy Fallout survival game.
Since Nether appeared on Steam, many bugs and complaints have been addressed (I have encountered NONE of the complaints that discouraged me from purchasing when the game was first released), and significant features have been added at a break-neck pace (e.g. subway systems added to the game world courier/collection missions, new enemies, etc...).
The decision to include a degree of persistence in the form of the Global Inventory (a 20-item bank that persists through death, only accessible in the few safe zones in the world) and cash (can be exchanged for supplies in safe zones; ~20% of carried cash is dropped on death; cannot be 'banked') actually RAISES the stakes compared to Day-Z (where death means a total reset).  In Nether, when I have valuable items, I WANT to bank them, whereas in games with no persistence, it's easy to achieve a zen-garden mindset where nothing matters at all – paradoxically, this adds to the suspense  by making death more significant, while at the same time softening the blow such that you have something to come back to after being (inevitably) killed.
This game is an utter delight.  If you played Day-Z, but were irritated at it's lack of polish, you will adore this title.  If you've never played Day-Z, but have a masochistic streak in your gaming tastes (i.e. you enjoy rogue-likes), you owe it to yourself to give this a spin.  As testament to this fact, I virtually never participate in community discussion (no forum posts, virtually no reviews), but felt compelled to write the above about Nether.
If you detest PVP – steer clear.  This is not a game for people who cannot handle 'losing'.

I had a chance to round up my TowerFall buddies last night and play Dynasty Feud in my living room using Steam Big Picture and a bunch of PS4 controllers. This game rocks. Dynasty Feud combines the sustained, tactical tension we love about TowerFall's one-hit-kill mechanic with the stage and character diversity of a Smash Bros. The "dynasty" mechanic--coming back to life as a new character with a different move set each time you die--is brilliant. It constantly shifts the feel of each match, and adds an almost Overwatch-like strategic layer to "hero selection" as you attempt to counter the other player's current fighter in real time. One of my friends is an illustrator, and he was blown away by Dynasty Feud's character design, to the point where he was wishing there was a single-player campaign. I myself could care less about story modes in brawlers, but it speaks to the strength of the characters that they make you naturally curious about their back stories. The art style and overall tone reminds me of Guacamelee!, another favorite.
We're looking forward to our next play session. We unlocked all of the clans except for the aliens! Right now I'd say we're in that fun discovery stage of a fighting game, learning each fighter's moves. Because the pace of the game is so fast (that's a good thing), you may initially experience some frustrating spawns, where you basically die right away before you figure out what's cool about your character. But when you do have that Eureka moment, like, "I can move around as this devastating tornado!,", "I  can reflect projectiles with my stubby punches", or "I have a shield instead of a dodge!", it's very rewarding. At first we thought the supers were OP, but after some experimenting we realized you can dodge, and in some cases shield-block, the ultimate abilities. If the game is this fun now, I can only imagine what it will be like when we know what we're doing.
You can't direct the wind, but you can adjust your sword.

This game really nails the "easy to play, hard to master" mantra. It succeeds at being accessible to all kind of players, but at the same time it excels at rewarding dedication and mastery.
It's one hit one kill mechanic is easy to grasp, and the aparent (only aparent) simplicity of mechanics makes for an easy adaptation into the game.
However, when you deepen into the game and realize the great amount of attacks and animations that really are available, you understand that there is much to be learned and mastered in this game.
Apart from the main fighting mechanics, the fact that you play as a whole Dynasty at once expands the possibilities even more. In order to become a competitive player, you will need to master not only every champion inside your dynasty, but also the champions of the opposing dynasties. This way, you will be able to wisely select your next champion to respawn once you die and counter your adversaries.
It can be enjoyed as a single screen local multiplayer, or online multiplayer. From my experience, the online aspect seems to be lacking some optimization, as I have experienced a couple issues while playing online. Though it works without problems most of the time and the local experience is just superb.
If you are into game lores, this game also includes a "Codex", which gives an accurate description of all the ~40 champions and also some tips. I really enjoyed reading through it.
Conclusion:
Easy to play, but with a lot of depth to satisfy serious players.
Playing as a dynasty really makes for an strong tactical aspect.
Original champions and mechanics.
Some online conectivity issues.
Can definitely work as a party game.
Recommended.

Several years ago I lived in a big house with a great number of people. I worked nights and the bustle and noise of so many people under one roof made sleeping during the day difficult. I remember coming home in predawn hours however, and brewing a cup of tea. I would take a fine leather bound volume of Jules Verne stories from the bookshelf on the mantle, and sit down to lose myself in strange places and wondrous adventures. I would quite often disappear from the phenomenal world and regain my footing in sublime places.
Playing inkle.Ltd’s spectacular
has taken me back to those days. The game mechanically is a grandiose, “choose your own adventure” tale of a man becoming a man of the world. Though minimal in execution, the game’s presentation is perfect for what it is. My first playthrough was a 3 hour time flash which, I swear, only lasted 30 minutes.
In these days of jagged and blocky 8 bit dark silhouette characters jumping around in pixelated indie games with nary a storyline at all, it’s refreshing to find a game replete with such an incredible amount of imagination put into it.
Playing Phileas Fogg’s ever loyal servant plucked right from the pages of Jules Verne’s novel,
, I got us both kidnapped by cultists in Calcutta. I delivered a baby in the South Pacific while sailing to Manila, and in Manila I contracted cholera. I flattened myself against an alley wall in Dallas, Texas as hooded members of the Ku Klux Klan walked past me, torches in hand. And in New Orleans, Death sat at my table in a bar, bought me a drink and kissed my hand.
No. I didn’t win the race, nor did I complete my world tour in 80 days. But I had (mis)adventures of a lifetime that made winning an around the world race (and the wager involved) pale dim. When the roads freeze and the wintry snow buries your front door, fix a mug of hot chocolate, indulge yourself in this wonderful game filled with beautifully crafted prose. You’re welcome.

This is a game that shines in gameplay, but by business practices, was shoved deep into the mud. It had so much potential to be something amazing, but either ignorance, or greed, has destroyed it. I shall explain in detail all of the positives/negatives of this game.
Positives:
- The gameplay is magnificent, smooth, and well designed.
- It is extremely well optimized for Nvidia, and I can run it on a relatively low-end GPU.
- The customization is there, with a lot of options to choose from.
- The classes all feel extremely unique as well in their playstyle.
- The story mode is of moderate length, and can feel fun on the harder difficulties.
- The game itself also looks utterly beautiful.
- AI is actually very competent, and quite fun to play against.
- If I were to rate this game on gameplay alone, it would be a solid 9/10... but unfortunately...
Negatives:
- Peer to Peer connection is atrocious, and should absolutely be changed. Some people (such as myself) can't even play 4v4s, and I have a solid connection. Other times, you will randomly get disconnected from a game despite having 0 lag.
- Mouse/Keyboard controls are unacceptable for a game of this decade. It feels like a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥port from console to PC. Anyone with a controller has an immediate defensive advantage in almost every way. You can immediately determine who has a controller, and who is using Mouse/Keyboard. It feels unresponsive, and honestly worse than Dark Souls' control issues. (This was a problem during the Alpha, Closed Beta, and Open beta, yet unresolved) It actually feels cheap when someone who spent money on a controller has a ridiculous advantage over you.
- No offline mode? Really Ubisoft? Not even an offline practice mode? That is atrocious. Some people around this world do not have godly internet connections, and allowing them to hone their skills in a practice mode during the down time would have been a natural step. The lack of ANY offline features is another example of Ubisoft's bad business practices, they ruin an otherwise good product because of piracy, and hurting the actual customers who want to enjoy it.
- The Microtransaction whoring is to be expected, and I honestly would expect it for the cosmetics, however Ubisoft offers a complete level-skip, which you can go straight to unlocking everything... which is a disgusting practice.
- Environmental kill worship? Let me tell you, this game has more environmental cheese than Smash and Soul Calibur combined. I died more times in the Story campaign on the hardest difficulty to straight up random environmental kills (One particularly bad one, I walked back 1 inch at the start of the duel and got insta-gibbed by a geyser and had to restart the mission) than I ever did to a bot. It also encourages players to use these cheesy tactics rather than using the well established fighting mechanics that already exist. Especially when you take into account the difficulty of escaping a guard break (which suffers in the P2P lag occasionally), one can find themselves winning a fight, only to eat a random guard break that passes through your swing, and insta-kills you by way of ring-out. Which is very different from a game like Soul Calibur, where only a very small amount of moves on each character ring out, and they are easily defended against.
- Lack of Tech information is really irritating. Almost all fighting games that you play, will list out everything from frame data, to COMPLETE moves lists of each and every character. This game just has icons, and minor information that you're apparently supposed to figure out yourself. Not to mention, minor details that are missing, like how long some characters get stunned for after a parry based upon your class. This game *really* needs an explanation of frame data, so you can know what attacks you can land and when, because in many cases, it feels like guessing.
- Another bit of cheese is the annoying 'Revenge' mechanic, which is just a crappy way of balancing 2v1s. Especially when people use it in 1v1s. There appears to be an unspoken 'honor code' among the better players, where you don't revenge in a 1v1, and you don't try for environ-kills. Yet, it seems, that in many cases you have no idea if a player abides by that honor code, until they're slamming you in the face in revenge mode. Honestly, revenge should not exist in a 1v1, it should only be built from blocking another player in a 2v1.
- Class imbalance that was known about since the beta, but not addressed. Now I don't claim to be a godly player, but I'm sure there was a way around making Peacekeeper/Valkyrie/Nobushi without giving them such hilariously cheesy effects like bleed and insane speed. Peacekeeper is ridiculously fast with its swings, and at low level play you almost only see spam with it, which is much harder to deal with (especially with lag/mouse >_>) than you might think. At the higher levels, I only really notice Warden/Kensei/Orochi/Berserkers being used. So these annoying classes might only be just that... annoying. Either way, some redesign should be done to make them better, and less cancerous.
Honestly, these negatives are so bad, that they drag the fantastic positives down to almost being meaningless. I do *not* recommend you buy this, until it is fixed, and *if* it is fixed.
Final rating: 5/10

Life is Feudal is a complex sandbox box, with a very open world. For those of you that remember it, it's VERY akin to the old Star Wars Galaxies (pre NGE)
Pro's:
-Complex Crafting system.
-Fantastic system to socialize, as it is impossible to pick up every skill
-Complex skil system that allows you to try new things, grow into new skills, and forget them if you don't like them.
-Fantastic challenge rating for skills: Easy to pick up, time consuming to master. You can grow, loot, and craft high quality materials.
-Great graphics. Really nice visuals on higher settings.
-Terraforming: Push over minecraft, you can literally level landscapes, dig siege tunnels, and build ramps. Or just flatten terrain so you can build a city!
-City building: Akin to SWG, you can drop down pre-generated structures, tools, build roads, claim ownership.
-Nothing is worth doing that doesn't take time to do: This whole game takes time. It's not a fast paced, get your guns in a day and rule the world. BUT... it is fantastic, and well conceptually well designed.
Pro&Con:
-This is an MMO Sandbox. It is what you, and others make out of it. If you want to be a trader or bar keep, you can actually craft resources, make food, sell high quality foods, trade for better resources, and even pray for absolution from your sins. However, for every peaceful choice you make, someone out there will want to be a rampaging psychopath that will run into your shop and wreak everything...
Cons:
-Right-click-simulator: The game is fantastically in-deptch, but in order to make it EASY to manage, it uses a right-click system. Where you end up openning that menu... A LOT.
-It doesn't like it when you alt+tab. Seems to work better on windows 10.
TLDR:
This game is a fantastic open world complex to the likes of SWG Original Release. It's got a deep crafting system and really encourages social play. So build your character, find new people, and start carving up your plot of land! Because this IS the sandbox game you've been looking for!
Epic game 10/10 would recommend. Wish the DLCs were cheaper though (but definitely get them when they are on sale!)

Another Game that was overhyped. For Honor is great conceptually, but lacks all the promised elements. If your looking for a asymetric fighter game, look elsewhere, For Honor has no real honor.
For honor is a hack and slash style 3rd person game where in a fictional land where 3 factions battle for dominance, the Legion(Knights), the Warborn(Vikings), and the Chosen(Samurai). For Honor features a Meta game by allowing players to engage in cross-platform fights for the land, and after every match, can allocate War Assets to particular engagement zones, which every 6 hours recieves an update, and those with the most assets in that area wins the area.
The biggest attraction of For Honor is the ability to play are particular faction, and engage the ither factions with your factions fighting style. Knights bearing heavy armor and heavy strikes are power houses, Vikings with little to no armor rely on aggresive advance and a combination of light and heavy attacks to overwhelm their opponents, and the Samurai, with medium armor and speed, rely on precision and speed to defeat their opponents.
Unfortunately, none of this is true. Ubisoft opted instead to allocate fighting styles to a class system, which covers up the fact that the fastest classes dominate all others. The Orochi for example, a Katana wielding samurai, has a attack chain of 3 light attacks, which interrupt all other moves. So the key to winning is spamming the Orochis fast attack, and dodging when neccesary, and spamming again. The knights in general are heavily armored, used as justification for hard hitting attacks they have, but are painfully slow. And vikings are a mixed bag, bringing hard hitting attacks with speed, the best of both worlds.
Another drawback is the throw system. For Honor features a guard break, essentially a unblockable stun which then opens the player up to being "thrown", or rather, dragged, in the direction of the attackers choosing, typically off of a cliff or into a spike wall, both of which are instant kills. In other words, For Honor lacks any real honor. Players opt to go for throws for easy kills  rather than play their class or fight. Why fight when you can win without effort?
The two primary modes to play are Dominion, essentially Domination for those familiar with First Person Shooters, where players battle for territory against other players and AI minions, and Elimination, a combination of duels  in open territory where players can interfere with other duels, tag teamming others for easy kills.
Another drawback is the Peer to Peer multiplayer. For those who do not know, Peer to Peer is a system, one of the oldest in fact, where one players internet plays host to other players. If the "host" leaves, then the game stops and finds another player to host, and if the game cannot find a player to host, it will end the match and kick everyone out. This is the source of the dropped games and poor connections, which will NEVER be fixed because the problems are inherent to the design, not some external source.
As one can see, For Honor lacks honor, polish, and balance. 3 of the 9 classes clearly out class the others and are the most used, ruining the game.
TL;DR
Pros
-great graphics
-interesting story
-Conceputally good
Cons
-Poor design, 3 of the 9 characters beat the rest, no reason to player others(Orochi, Warlord, and Valkyrie)
-Peer to Peer connection, the source of the drops and leaves players at the mercy of people with budget connections
-Lack of actual honor, players will spam and throw rather than make efforts to "git gud", expect to be thrown off cliffs or get gang banged by players
Final note: I may change my review in time if Ubisoft balances the classes and fixes some bugs, but I highly doubt it.

After reading a bunch of stuff on Sniper Elite V2, and realizing it was for free for a day, I decided to give it a try. At first I was very interested, and willing to let small problems slide because I wanted to be invested in the story and the gameplay. However, small things slowly began to build up, and the problems only seem to get more and more frequent.
Before I start listing the pros and cons, disclaimer. I did not finish the game as of now, have not played co-op or multiplayer, and I have only been playing on Sniper Elite difficulty. So take that for what it is.
Pros
-The feeling of the game is great.
-The bullet cam gives you real satisfaction. Nothing feels better than watching the shot you spent a good few seconds lining up play out before you. Nothing is safe from your rifle. Bones, organs, testicles and eyeballs are all shattered, pierced, and mauled in a wonderful display of gore.
-the overall item selection is pretty decent. I found I always had something for any given situation. Grenades, trip mines, and dynamite all played their part in my strategies.
Cons:
-the story, I personally found, wasn’t amazing. Usually all you get is a small mission statement spoken by your own character, and then are simply thrown into the action.
-the enemy A.I. is poor at best. Enemy snipers will fire at you, but not a single other soldier will react to this. Enemies will recklessly charge at you, which turn the fire fight into a shoot the duck game as you sit behind a wall and wait.
-Enemy placement between engagements can be extremely irritating. Sometimes you will have a firefight on the first floor of a building, and somehow the 15 enemies right above you didn’t hear a thing. Also, this game is VERY guilty of zone sensitive enemy spawns. Several times I will reach an in-between checkpoint, and suddenly a Nazi just appears in front of me out of thin air, rifle up and already firing. This makes scouting completely pointless, because it’s impossible to predict where they will appear.
-The sound mechanics are broken at best. As mentioned above, 15 men don’t hear a firefight right below them, yet for some reason they can distinguish the main characters footsteps from their allies. Also, the enemies voices (which they use WAY too much), have a nasty habit of being louder than they should be. Several times I would hear a Nazi with a voice level that would indicate he was in the next room, only to find the whole building I was in was completely empty, and he was actually outside, across a road, around 70 meters from me (the game told me so when I shot him in the head).
-the weapons are not persistent between levels. You will always start with the sniper rifle you were given, a Thompson, and the Welrod. It doesn’t matter if you spend the last mission painstakingly gathering MP 40 rounds, the main character assumedly just ditches them somewhere, and pulls another Thompson out of it his♥♥♥♥♥
In summary, although it had its moments, this game is not worth the price it charges, and unless you got it during the 24 hour period that is was free, you probably shouldn’t bother. It’s a great idea, cut short by poor A.I. and design errors.

Big Thinkers 1st Grade is a game for kids of 6-7 years old. In it, you have a brother and a sister that can tranform themselves in many things and that are explaining the games and encouraging kids. Ben and Becky are searching for Smart Stars around their house. And these can be obtained by playing minigames.
Each minigame is covering a field: for example, in the living room, kids can express themselves through an art activity while in the library, they can practice their geography without forgetting the time telling in the kitchen. Each activity met with success will be rewarded with Smart Stars that can be used for a challenge. Some minigames, like the time telling, have different difficulties: it can be more objects or thougher questions.
The games are really varied and use mechanics that you still find today in educational applications. So, yeah, I do think that Big Thinkers 1st Grade can be still in use nowadays. However, what may be a little hard to get past at is the graphics. What will follow is pasted from my review of Big Thinkers Kindergarten.
Not that I mind old graphics, as you know. After all, I began playing with Super Mario Bros and Doom II triggered a real passion. But some of them aren't aging well. Big Thinkers is among them. It's like seeing an old cartoon. True, back then, these were frequent in the adventure genre. However, today, it seems not at all clear. There are many information on the screen that it's nearly making you scream that it's not user-friendly. I understand that the education behind is probably the main reason but I don't care about words like Pantry or Rightly, though I suppose that for the kids, it's showing them something that is obvious for the adult.
Anyway, you can interact with nearly everything, as far as your cursor is a white arrow. As an adult, it can seem to be too much but for a kid, it's amusing. Myself, I got intrigued by what can happen.
If I have to say something for the soundtrack, it's correct. It's more the voice acting that is a pain in my ears, mainly Ben's voice. I'm always under the impression that he tries to be louder than Becky.
Big Thinkers is in English. Total English. I don't know if there were any translated version because it would have been interesting for the other languages. If as a teacher or a parent, you have no problem in English as second language, you can guide your kid in the game. If some activities can be easy to understand, like the art or music activity, self-explanatory or like the money one where you can guess that you need to pay items, others require knowledge of English vocabulary - it's nicer to understand the stories that the kid is imagining or the questions in geography. Anyway, 10 activities can be played by non-English speaking children.
Big Thinkers 1st Grade is a good educational game, whether for the classroom or for home. The graphics may have aged not so well but the rest is still "modern".
Ah and if you don't manage to find how to exit the game, put your mouse at the bottom of the screen, the menu should appear. It's sad that there is nothing to indicate it though.

KOTOR II is one of those classic RPGs I can replay over and over. This sequel was released in 2004 and is still a great game and remains extremely playable today. Even though Bioware developed the first KOTOR, they ended up handing the job over to Obsidian who, as always, did a fantastic job with their work.
The use of KOTOR II's Light Side/Dark Side system is a lot like the modern day systems of good/evil characters. When you as the  character does or says evil things then you grow more in tune with the dark side of the force. The contrast to this is of course, doing good deeds and saying not-so-evil stuff. This leads to the Light side of the force. In either case you will grow more powerful and influence those you travel with. This will also effect your force powers amongst many other things...
The single defining feature of KOTOR or KOTOR II is the story. Anyone who loves Star Wars must love a good mythos from the Star Wars world, especially one this early in the timeline of the Star Wars Universe.
This sequel begins when a stranger, oblivious to his past, wakes up in a Mining Station medical bay, only to notice no one is around. No one...except a mysterious elderly woman. Journey to several planets and cause havok or create order. Kill the weak or defend them. All the while, you search for the power to make you a Master of the Force.
- Great main storyline with various other mini-quests, all which act in canon with the Star Wars universe.
- Open world that you would expect from an RPG
- Choose what you say to someone carefully; You could end up in a fight or effect the story.
- Choose light or dark side; Your actions will decide what you become.
- Tons of lore from the Star Wars universe you can't find anywhere else!!
- Graphics are from the first Xbox generation, but it still holds today.
- Some of the voice overs for alien species are simply repeated recordings on loop.
- Occasionally, a glitch or two might happen
-
, but sometimes there are game breaking bugs. There are only two that I know of, and one of them ruined my first game. This requires the double save slow technique.
-
This is my favorite Star Wars game hands down. Many people also recognize this particular game to be LucasArts' crowing achievement. Obsidian does a great job with the sequel to Bioware's KOTOR and does Star Wars in general great justice.

This is an absolute gem of a game.
It is perhaps best described as an interactive novel set in an alternate steampunk 1872, warped around the writings of Jules Verne, in particular his novel 'Around the World in 80 Days'. You play the trusty valet/sidekick Passpartout, charged with getting your gentleman master Phileas Fogg safely around the planet on time and on budget, no matter what the world throws at you in terms of surprises. That said, some of the greatest adventures are not along the more direct or traditional Foggish route, and there are loads of little encounters with historical figures of the era as well, be they inventors, poets or adventurers. It can take a while to sort of the real people from the fictious ones.
The writing in this game is superb, and the many potential paths - some of which take a while to unlock or riddle out - offer great replay value. Going the
route won't likely be as appealing, as the story of each city or travel path is largely identical with each gameplay (there are factors that alter dialogue options, such as items in your inventory, past choices, and Passpartout's valeting skill) - but with the possible exception of Paris, you'll still have so much choice of where to go that this potential repeat has little consequence in your first few dozen playthroughs.
The only negative thing I can say about the game is that you cannot pause the clock (if it's running - it stops whenever there is something to read). This can make you miss vital connections because you suddenly realize you have too many bags of luggage when you attempt to depart, and by the time you've thrown surplus items away, the ship has sailed without you. Quite vexing, if you paid the captain thousands of pounds the night before to sail a few days early. :-p
You do not want to be a packrat in this game; travel light - the world is large and is begging to be explored. If you enjoy a good read and adventure, 80 Days will not disappoint - be it this game or the novel it is based on.

Written Review:
Dynasty Feud is a 2D multi player platform brawler title much in a similar vein to the likes of Super Smash Bros or Brawlhalla in which you are able to select one of 40 unique fighters to play as in combat.
What differentiates this from the likes of Smash or Brawlhalla however is the method of defeating your foes, in those games the goal is to effectively knock the other players out of the stage. Here things are a little more straightforward, simply hit the other player to win.
In fact the vast majority of the characters in this game will die in 1-hit with some exceptions here and there that takes 2, making this game a lot more tense than you would initially expect and creates a lot of room for strategy. Simply put learning the characters abilities and where you should position each character for an attack is key to succeeding in this title.
The game itself is easy enough to simply pick up and play however, but I personally feel this is one of those titles that’s easy to play but can be pretty hard to master as you will need to get a handle of controls before you will likely find yourself having a blast.
In fact my initial impressions of the game were a resounding….”meh”....And as I played more and more I started to get a handle on how the characters move and where I should position attacks resulting in my enjoyment increasing significantly.
Each of the 40 playable characters all belong to a specific faction, depending on which faction you are in, you will be able to access various abilities that can either help you or simply annoy the other players. These come in the forms of the Supers which charges as you fight allowing you to unleash a devastating attack that while can be dodged, will highly likely hit someone. As well as Annoy abilities.
Annoy abilities are designed specifically to….wel annoy the other players and can only be accessed while you are dead or waiting for a character to spawn, these will usually create visual effects to distort the battlefield making it harder for other players to hit each other or avoid stage hazards, or do simply but annoying things such as reversing controls for other players temporarily.
I myself am not too fond of these annoy abilities myself as they are….well annoying….but I like their addition nonetheless as it allows the defeated players to have something to do while waiting for a match to end.
If you are a Solo player however this game is not one for you as it is strictly an online only experience, with the exception of Training mode of course to get a handle on things.
Not only that but the game as it stands at the time of writing is pretty prone to a few bugs that happen pretty consistently which range from literally game breaking or a minor annoyance.
By far the most egregious bug so far is one i’ve found myself replicating surprisingly often, whenever I use the pirate faction of characters and activate the Super, I found that this around 70% of the time desyncs the game with the other players freezing the match in its entirety. Which truth be told is extremely frustrating, forcing me to load up a new game lobby before I am able to play again.
In fact desync issues can occur pretty randomly and I noticed this occur the most with 3 or more players in a single game, I am not sure if the player connections are to blame or if the netcode is a little buggy but it is an issue i’ve come across from time to time, usually things work out when I make a new lobby but it’s still an annoying issue that I hope gets patched soon.
Each of this games stages are well designed and offer a neat amount of variety, with even some stages offering minor destructible environments such as the bank in the wild west train stage and other hazards like the lava eyes in the skull island level.
I have to say as well that I love the overall Art Style of this title, especially in regards to some of the character designs. And the game soundtrack is pretty top as well, and while I don’t usually find myself humming a lot of the music excluding the pretty dope title screen theme, it’s all great to listen to.
Ultimately Dynasty Feud is a pretty fun game especially when playing with a group of friends, however I found the first hour or so when I was adjusting to the controls and gameplay style to be pretty mixed in regards to how I feel. But as I played it more I grew to really enjoy the title despite its bugs and quirks.

Another Game that was overhyped. For Honor is great conceptually, but lacks all the promised elements. If your looking for a asymetric fighter game, look elsewhere, For Honor has no real honor.
For honor is a hack and slash style 3rd person game where in a fictional land where 3 factions battle for dominance, the Legion(Knights), the Warborn(Vikings), and the Chosen(Samurai). For Honor features a Meta game by allowing players to engage in cross-platform fights for the land, and after every match, can allocate War Assets to particular engagement zones, which every 6 hours recieves an update, and those with the most assets in that area wins the area.
The biggest attraction of For Honor is the ability to play are particular faction, and engage the ither factions with your factions fighting style. Knights bearing heavy armor and heavy strikes are power houses, Vikings with little to no armor rely on aggresive advance and a combination of light and heavy attacks to overwhelm their opponents, and the Samurai, with medium armor and speed, rely on precision and speed to defeat their opponents.
Unfortunately, none of this is true. Ubisoft opted instead to allocate fighting styles to a class system, which covers up the fact that the fastest classes dominate all others. The Orochi for example, a Katana wielding samurai, has a attack chain of 3 light attacks, which interrupt all other moves. So the key to winning is spamming the Orochis fast attack, and dodging when neccesary, and spamming again. The knights in general are heavily armored, used as justification for hard hitting attacks they have, but are painfully slow. And vikings are a mixed bag, bringing hard hitting attacks with speed, the best of both worlds.
Another drawback is the throw system. For Honor features a guard break, essentially a unblockable stun which then opens the player up to being "thrown", or rather, dragged, in the direction of the attackers choosing, typically off of a cliff or into a spike wall, both of which are instant kills. In other words, For Honor lacks any real honor. Players opt to go for throws for easy kills  rather than play their class or fight. Why fight when you can win without effort?
The two primary modes to play are Dominion, essentially Domination for those familiar with First Person Shooters, where players battle for territory against other players and AI minions, and Elimination, a combination of duels  in open territory where players can interfere with other duels, tag teamming others for easy kills.
Another drawback is the Peer to Peer multiplayer. For those who do not know, Peer to Peer is a system, one of the oldest in fact, where one players internet plays host to other players. If the "host" leaves, then the game stops and finds another player to host, and if the game cannot find a player to host, it will end the match and kick everyone out. This is the source of the dropped games and poor connections, which will NEVER be fixed because the problems are inherent to the design, not some external source.
As one can see, For Honor lacks honor, polish, and balance. 3 of the 9 classes clearly out class the others and are the most used, ruining the game.
TL;DR
Pros
-great graphics
-interesting story
-Conceputally good
Cons
-Poor design, 3 of the 9 characters beat the rest, no reason to player others(Orochi, Warlord, and Valkyrie)
-Peer to Peer connection, the source of the drops and leaves players at the mercy of people with budget connections
-Lack of actual honor, players will spam and throw rather than make efforts to "git gud", expect to be thrown off cliffs or get gang banged by players
Final note: I may change my review in time if Ubisoft balances the classes and fixes some bugs, but I highly doubt it.

To start off my review of this game, let me start by saying that I am a huge fan of Star Wars and have been since a very young age; for as long as I can even remember.
I played this game about 4 years ago for the first time, shortly after I had completed the first title in the KOTOR saga (which I highly recommend playing prior to this game) and I have to say that, as good as the first game was, this outmatched it in so many ways:
As for the game itself, I cannot recommend it highly enough. There is real value in playing the game more than once, as the plot and characters/companions met through each gender are different and both light and dark side users will have compelling choices to make in terms of core storyline as well as companion storylines.
I myself have used a mod to skip the opening prologue (do not be fooled, the option to skip this in game at the very start is misleading, and I find the actual prologue VERY tedious and it takes at least 2-3 hours to get through on your first go).
I would definitely say that this game is not for those who want to rush through a game for the action and adventure. This is geared for people who enjoy a rich, compelling story which has depth, malleability and maneuverability in terms of what you get out of it at the end.
I got this in the Star Wars Humble Bundle, but if it goes on sale on steam for around £5/$7 I would definitely pick it up if you are a Star Wars fan and have played the prequel.

This game...
it is GREAT! If you've seen someone like Markiplier play this game, then you might not be that scared. But to get the full experience, I'd say you'd have to play it yourself.
Music: 10/10
The atmosphere was created by this music. If you've ever noticed in any video game, music is what subconciously creates your emotions. A sad death scene? Chances are there's soft piano or violin music playing. Final battle? Tense music that will keep you on your toes will fit the theme. This is a horror game, and the music, especially in headphones, will create the perfect environment for a game like this. The spooky sounds, the steady speeding up of the music when the monster is nearby, and the feeling that you are alone and it really creeps you out.
Gameplay: 8/10
I haven't tried out custom stories yet at the time of this writing, but I plan on doing so. The game is very well played, going through a scary area whilst looking for clues and notes that will help explain the plot. However, because the game is so large at times, you can skip over one room, either by not seeing it or by thinking it will have maybe one tinderbox, you could screw yourself over. There are so many rooms and areas you can enter at one time, making it difficult to sometimes find a key you need to progress through the story. However, when you complete a puzzle, it is very rewarding.
Mechanics: 9/10
The sanity mechanic is one of the most unique ways of making the game more realistic. If you encounter a monster, looking at it once will cause your screen to start swaying back and forth. The way to recharge it is by staying in the light, but this can be hard once you see the monster. When the monster comes, you have to hide from it in order to live, and it will notice if there is light near you. That defeats the purpose and you're dead, so you just have to hope that it goes far enough away so you can turn your lantern on again.
Verdict: 9/10
This game, from watching people play it, looked fun but it didn't look that scary. Now having played it myself, it is so much better, with the music creating the atmosphere, the sanity mechanic creating a realistic feel, and the gameplay making me afraid as I played. This game, especially when played in the dark with headphones, created a perfect environment for me to enjoy the experience to the fullest.

Have you ever wanted to be part of a team driving/gunning a capital ship, maneuvering, firing, repairing damage, then switch gears to join a boarding party on a shuttle that leaves your ship and flies over to breach an enemy capital ship where you sweep it deck by deck for infantry fps combat?
Yes, you can do that here.
Between the infantry fps ground maps, vehicular warfare maps, space battles, and wide variety of offensive and defensive loadouts from weapons and tools, AFF has an impressive array of combat experiences.  There's the makings of a great game within this early access.
So far though, the game lacks a bit of the polish you could expect from a AAA title.  Textures are fine but not super high res.  The physics of manuvering vehicles (especially in the air and space) can be a bit wonky.  FPS combat doesn't yet have that super satisfying smooth feedback loop that comes from seeing your projectiles fly from your gun to your target and register a clean hit.  Sometimes the hit boxes seem off, sometimes it's not clear where your bullet projectile veered off to or why, and sometimes the animations are just a bit too "jolty" which makes it hard to deal with recoil when you shoot.
Still, excited to see where this one goes.

Rating 7.5/10
Note: I played with the restoration mod. It is HIGHLY recommended that you play with this mod as it fixes a lot of bugs/glitches as well as restore lost content. It brings the game closer to the original intentions of the developers
The Good:
+ The game has a lot of robust options in how you build your character. You start by choosing between 3 classes: Guardian, Consular or Sentinel. Each class obviously focuses on different aspects of combat. Further in the game you can then further specialize your classes. You can fully customize your character how you wish between attributes, skills, feats and Jedi powers. All of this leads to many different options and replayability in how you design your character
+ The core aspect of the game is that as you can either play as a Jedi that is good or evil. Saving people, being kind and choosing the peaceful solution leads you to the light side while doing the opposite leads you to the dark side. Doing so leads to certain bonuses to your Jedi Powers. Being good means Light side powers will use less mana and dark side powers cost more and vice versa. I find the system to be very effective because it ties morality choices into game play, a feature that seems to be very lacking in today's modern games.
+ The second core aspect is how you respond and handle situations with your party members. You can gain or lose influence with them. If you gain enough influence with any particular party member, new dialogue options open up resulting in more background to the story, and/or stat increases for you or your party member. It is not mandatory as you can easily complete the game without gaining any influence with anybody but it adds a nice touch to the game and offers more options.
+ The story, although confusing in the beginning because it throws so much at you does get increasingly better. The story is presented very well because of the great dialogue options and fantastic writing. Obsidian is easily one of the best in the industry regarding writing.
+ If there is any company that can match or exceed Bioware in writing for npc characters its Obsidian. Every party member that joins you in your quest is well written and interesting. Every party member has alternative motives for joining you which makes things more exciting and not every party member gets along with each other. These ideas are explored the further you progress in the game.
+ Every planet you visit feels different. The game throws a few twists in for good measure to keep things fresh.
+ Well written Side Quests
+ mods
The Average:
Sadly there was no improvement with combat. The combat in the game is really showing its age. I never particularly liked the combat because it's not very engaging.
Certain force powers, skills, feats are game breaking while others are completely useless.
The Bad:
- The UI especially navigating to find items in your inventory is a chore and frustrating. The inventory screen is a long list of your items. There are options to filter the list based on specific items but this doesn't fix the overall problem of a bad overall inventory management system.
- The game forces you to do solo missions either as yourself or one of your party members. These sections are frustrating and awful only because the combat was never designed around solo play. This problem is further compounded if you auto-leveled up any of your party members. Playing a solo section with a party member that has all the wrong attributes/skills/feats is painful.
- Last few areas have cut and paste environments. Obvious that development was rushed at the end.
Conclusion
A worthy follow up to one of the best RPG's for its time. Obsidian once again shows that it is one of the best when it comes to writing a great story with great characters. It's sad that it takes a mod to fix a lot of the problems with the game. If you loved the first game then there is no reason not to love this one as well.

Now that they've Finally listened to the players and fans and allowed us to actually build a deck and use it properly the MtG games in my opinion are finally worth it.

There's no such thing as random in this game.

(even being 1 or 2 mana for every 3 draws).
I was starved 8 Games and Flooded 17.
She was starved for 13 and flooded for 15.
So we adjusted or Mana respectively , adding and removing no more than 4.
Each time depending on the method used we got starved more often or flooded more often.
This isn't a game breaking issue. Online against other people however it can become irksome.

actually random
Another issue is the game can't handle over powered cards, (See my Screenshots) you can break the game.

Now that the annoyings out of the way.
I'd still reccomend this game, it doesn't have much of a footprint , the art work is fantastic , the Campagin story is good and it's MtG. The game is fun , and even with the annoying little bits , it's still worth the 10 bucks and the Nerd rage on planeswalker difficulty to unlock all the cards.

((EDIT))
I'm adding this part here seeing as I just read a lot of reviews talking about "pay to win" and "slow interface".
1 - To fix a slow interface , play it in windowed mode. The slow interface is because the refresh rate of the game doesn't match your screens actual refresh rate (EVEN if you change it in settings) Playing it in windowed mode , will resolve this 9/10 times. Also to add on you can set your windowed mode resolution to 1920x1080 to mimic full screen and it will still resolve the sluggish issue.
2 - This is definitely not a pay to win model. You can unlock every card in the game by playing through the story. It's long and tiresome but it's a Trading card game. Deal with it or buy to unlock them all except the hidden premiums which you unlock through completion and achievements.
3 - The removal of Co-Op play. Yea this was a HUGE mistake on WotC part. Just stupid to remove the ability to play WITH your friends instead of against them. Really no idea why they'd do that.
4 - Someone added that now you can finally adjust Mana? You always could.
So to summarize;
- Don't be lazy and assume it's the programs fault when you get sluggish activity or lag.
It could very well be , it could also be your hardware. Find a work around , it takes maybe 2 min to figure out a system that works.
- Just because you can unlock through purchase doesn't make it pay to win.
Pay to win means you can ONLY get very HIGH end and RARE cards THROUGH purchase.
All cards you can purchase you can unlock in game with some diligance. That is by definition NOT pay to win. You're just lazy if you think it is.
- Removing Co-Op was idiotic
- It's not an Actual RANDOM shuffle
- Yay Custom Decks
- Buy the $10 over $30 and do the work to unlock the cards
- WotC For the love of God , don't tease us with cards we'll never be able to touch
- WotC Enough with the Character deck changes (Liliana's deck doesn't even reflect her anymore)
I will agree with the non-recommenders and say this.
The previous Magic (2014) was better. The only change they made that makes me want to play this over it's predecessor , is the custom deck.

Shadow Warrior 2 doesn't reinvent the wheel, but it sure knows how to maximize performance from it.
Moves, both for traversal and attacking. Are simplified and now can combo into eachother. So for example you can now jump off a roof while charging a stab attack, dash in mid-air gaining a huge amount of momentum, and simply bore through an enemy clear to the other side. It's moments like those that make the gun and sword play so much fun. That there's a variety and ability to customize gun attributes to your own playstyle makes things even better.
All the classic weapons are here. Rockets, chainguns, bows, nailguns, revolvers, grenade launchers and even chainswords. And that doesn't even cover all of the different guns, of which there are 3 versions. Military, cyberpunk, and demon. Some are better than others, but with the right mod pickups any weapon is viable.
On that note. Yes there is loot in this game, including some of those weapons. Which means shops and quests to sell and earn better gear are the bread and butter here. Shadow Warrior 2 now has more in common with Diablo than its Doom-clone roots as a result. It also means you will run into a problem when enemies might just be too powerful to deal with until you power up or use the right gear.  Especially if you happen to set off multiple groups of powerful enemies by accident.
On the graphics and sound side. The game is beautiful, but all the effects from yourself and the enemy can turn into a blur at times. Not that blindly wailing on guys doesn't work just as well and is just as fun anyway. It's just way too much at times, of which your graphics card will remind you. Speaking of, this thing is a beast. I ran this with a GTX 1070 TI, and it still gave it a run for the money I stuck in it. Keep in mind I also had everything on ultra though, so obviously you're gonna want to turn down the bling if you're on older hardware. The options to do so are plentiful enough to let you, so that shouldn't be a problem.
Music is a mix of heavy metal riffs, east asian traditional music. It can easily put chills down your spine during the low action moments and get you in the mood to slice heads off when the action heats up. My favorite is the Shadow Warrior theme reprised from the first game Flying Wild Hog produced. What I love about this mashup in styles, is that it creates an emotional center for the game that's reflected in the story. Shadow Warrior 1 for example, surprised many in how serious the story got about an assassin who's own name is a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥joke. 2 continues this by never letting up on the jokes, but still deals with noble sacrifices and sometimes commentary on the nature of man. Again, this is a game where the player character's name is a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥joke.
Even if you didn't come for the story. And you shouldn't anyway, even if it is pretty good. There's plenty to like here. I haven't even gotten into the 4 player coop aspect. Or the randomly generated levels and enemies that force frantic tactical and adaptive thinking.
Bottom line. This and Doom 2016 are possibly the bests shooter games to come out in the last 10 years. As always I'd still suggest taking advantage of a sale if you can. But getting it at full price is well worth it anyway.

It's been roughly a couple of months since the game hit Steam Early Access so I'll take my review here.
Objective: It's simple. Survive by any means. That includes looking for food, gear, teaming up with someone or if you wanted to , going the bandit route. Whatever the choice the keeps to the premise.
Gameplay: The gameplay has a solid foundation. Nethers (monsters in the game) will come looking for you if you shoot at anything, players can hear gunshots and all the normal things you would expect in a survival game like this. But there are a few kinks they could work out. For one thing, they recently put in Hang Gliders to let you glide if you were to fall from a skyscraper by accident. That is a great idea, but they could at least give you the option of deploying the hang glider before a person jumps off of the roof. The subway system they also recently put into the game is a great help to avoide Safe Zone campers.
Loot is somewhat rare, but it is common enough for a player to find at least a shotgun, handgun, better melee weapon, low end medical items, ammo, and some cash. The better weapons, backpack, and medical items requires the players to look for them within the world or to steal them from another player by killing them.
They have a sort of a 'Mission' like quest where you have to take a package to a certain outpost. (i.e MTO to WTO or Museum Outpost to Westside Outpost.) These missions gives out money and exp rewards based on distance the package has to travel. A loot drop mission where you can get some better gear (but this goes for the same for everyone since it will be announced globally within the server), nether surges (defeat a boss styled nether), and save the main safezone (main safezone will occasional lose it's Safe status. it's up to the players to restore the safe status by repairing the 6 anti-nether devices)
That leads to the skill tree. Obviously the longer you live/kill nethers, the more skill points you have to invest into your character's abilities (guns, stamina, strength, melee, survival, stealth). But be forewarned. If you die, you WILL LOSE ALL OF YOUR PROGRESS IN TERMS OF ITEMS, SKILL TREE PROGRESS, AND WEAPONS CARRY ON YOU. They have a Golbal Inventory that you can store items in. Up to 20 slots so you will have to piroritize what items you want and what items you don't want. They also have cosmestic items that does not drop on death and only drops when the player drops it.
The map is fairly small for the amount of players that can be on a server (64 players max) but when the game hits full release, the max expands by 3 times it's size. Keep in mind that it is only small for the duration of Steam Early Access/Beta.
I would have to say the best thing about the game is not in the game itself. The developers themselves are actually reading the forums and taking in the player's suggestions. The Subway system that was just put in. That was a player suggestion that the developers put into the game. So you have a voice to state what you want in the game.
Sound: It sounds exactly like you would expect in a post doomsday world. The only sound you hear is what you do to yourself (eat, drink, bandage yourself, etc), what you do to others (shooting them), and what you do to the enviroment (water splashing, crawling noise, nethers shrieking and teleporting to you).
Who should get this game:
People who enjoys the Survival games.
People who wants the Urban varation of DayZ.
People who wants to try the Survival games but don't know where to start.
Overall Personal Rating: 8.0

This is a significant departure from the early versions of this game, notably in that you construct your decks from one pool of cards, rather than having a number of decks with 40 odd extra cards to play around with. Is it an improvement? Not really. It could have been, but most of the cards in the game are completely toothless. So, there's nothing really exciting going on in this game.
The campaign was frustrating, as all of the starting decks were varying degrees of weak compared to your AI opponents. The other reviews are accurate in that you pretty much need to restart the game until you get a reasonable hand. What's worse, if you choose a deck that is awful, you have to limp through the game until others are made available, as you are forced to play with your initial choice (it was pretty funny to watch my housemate struggle through with a green-black deck).
The menus of the game are really, really slow for some reason. Added to which, it's quite easy to go into a game with the wrong deck by mistake, as it does not automatically select the last one you were editing. So if you want to mix it up as you grind, it's easy to mis-select, and then it's back through the slow menus.
Other reviews have complained that the game is a bit of a grind, but it's probably less in total than unlocking all of the decks in 2014. What bothers me is that some quite good cards are behind a paywall, and cannot be accessed through play. That said, the base game is quite cheap, so another $12 bucks or whatever is not too much, but the pay-to-win aspect is still bs.
The multiplayer suffers a bit from imbalance, as there are only a few viable combinations. In the limited time playing in multiplayer, I only really lost to convoke and other izzets, all of the rest being fairly beatable. Probably the extreme low point is the lack of two-headed giant. I don't know why they got rid of it, but giant was the big draw for me in 2014 and 2013, as it was for many other players, I expect.
Tl;dr:
Pros
-They finally implemented deck building.
-New pool of cards to play around with.
-Game loads quite fast in comparison to Magic 2014.
Cons
-Mostly uninteresting cards.
-Limited range of viable decks (also, I hope you didn't want to play creature removal).
-The game might load fast, but the menus are frustratingly slow for some reason.
-Unfair and frustrating power ratio early campaign (to mid-to-late campaign depending how poorly you chose and how committed you are to sticking with your awful deck).
-¡No Two-Headed Giant!
-Pay to win.
-Deck selection isn't as fluid or intuitive as it should be.
-No challenges.
In conclusion, it might be worth the $10, but if you were a fan of deck variety or two-headed, you'll probably find yourself going back to magic 2014, or to another franchise.

Despite the negative reviews, Duke Nukem Forever is actually quite a good game in its own right, as long as it isn't viewed comparatively to its predecessor Duke Nukem 3D.
The game's single player component is a linear shooter campaign reminiscent of the Halo series which featured regenerating health & a 2 weapon carry system. The latter didn't work too well in DNF due to the power structure of the game's weapon set, though upping the carriable weapons to 4 in the game's option menu resolves any issues. The game featured lots of variety throwing in driving, platforming, turret & minigame sections, which were actually excelently placed, alternating nicely with the standard first person shooting gameplay sections so you never had too much of one thing at a time. Wolfenstein: The New Order notably had a problem with doing just that as the game threw non-combat after non-combat section at you in the middle portion of the game in a maybe 4:1 ratio with the first person shooting & bundled up all of the game's fps at the beginning & ends, so kudos to 3D Realms/Gearbox for getting that right.
Forever's FPS component is actually a lot of fun despite the regen health, limited weapon capacity & the slow movement speed. Shooting aliens is still shooting aliens, & DNF does it well.
Story wise, it's whacky & expected. Basically the aliens from 3D come back to earth, attack & abduct all the women, & you, being Duke Nukem have to defeat them & save everyone. The writing frequently makes nostalgic references to not only DN3D but also other games from the time period like Doom & System Shock 2. The one liners are also enjoyable in the game, as always. One particular segment I liked was where Duke, shrunk to the size of an action figure navigates across a pantry shooting shrunk aliens.
The multiplayer is reminiscent of arena shooters. Despite having a 2 weapon limit in a set clearly not designed for such a thing, it also works quite well, the teamplay mode in particular
feature some cooperation between players using different weapons to their advantages.
Overall, DNF isn't a work of art, no one really expected it to be, & it doesn't live up to 12 years of hype, or the awesome 2001 trailer, or its predecessor Duke Nukem 3D, but if you were to use one word to describe it, it would be fun. DNF is just that, a whole lot of whacky fun to be enjoyed for the right price. I payed $7.50 & don't regret it.

Greetings fellow gamers! This is Gamer Guy (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of the Indie Adventure/CYOA 80 Days. 80 Days was released on Steam on September 28, 2015 by Developer Cape Guy ltd. and Developer/Publisher Inkle Ltd.
(NOTE: This game was NOT reviewed using a key provided by the Developer and/or Publisher, it was a game I purchased for my own account)
Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
Around the world in 80 Days, the novel. Fully playable, very Steampunk.
5/5 DO NOT MISS THIS ONE!
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
80 Days is, simply put, an absolute treat! This has easily become one of my favorite games as of late. WHat it is is a re-imagining of sorts of Jules Vene's classic "Around the World in 80 Days". Your master, upon accpetance of a wager, intends on circling the globe in under 80 days. You are his Valet and are in charge of not only caring for you masters well being, but planning his route. Along your journey you will engage in buying and selling goods from various markets to balance your funds (and to make your journey easier at times!). Another key component to the gameplay is the conversations. You must explore and converse as much as possible in order to find and open up new routes to facilitate your journey. Then, you must pick and choose carefully which of these routes you will take. The entire game is built around the CYOA mechanic, as you read through the incredibly well written dialogue you must make choices as to which direction the story takes as well. All in all, the writing is superb and the art and sounds are very, very beautiful. It is no wonder that Time Magazine gave it Game of the Year status for 2014. THis is also available on mobile devices, but the Steam version is well worth it. 5/5 and easily worth $10.
Happy Gaming!
