I don't know where to start! Life Is Feudal is by far one of the BEST sandboxes ive ever played. Its got unique systems and mechanics for crafting, forging, cooking, alchemy and other things like terraforming and logging. ALL of which have their own skill sets and levelling so you won't progess skills the same way twice, or find the same items & ingredients in the same place which is a nice touch. Depending on which server you are on, there are also variable stat & skill caps this means that if you specialise in a certain skill it can determine how useful you will be in building settlments, and once reach the leveling limit of one skill, thats it Reach the stat and skill caps and leveling up will be a distant memory as they will become rare occurences. This means prople of different skills will have to work together and pool resources and skills, especially if a battle takes place in nearby settlements/towns and repairs have to be made quickly. For example, one person of your group/guild might be a master blacksmith, while another will be a master Logger, so choosing which skill to level completely is CRUCIAL.
You basically start the game with nothing but food scraps and rags for clothes, so your first instinct is to create primitive gear which can be done quite quicker than you would expect. As you start to meet random people in your travels, you will also start to learn of the surrondings more and where developments have been started. I remember one time where I spawned into the world and I basically turned right and saw an ENTIRE FORTRESS built far off into the distance on the other side of an island, and as I explored around there was the odd camp/shack then a small town where groups have formed a guild. It cleary shows the sheer scope of how important working with people is in this game.
Another strong point is the combat mechanics, if you have played the Mount & Blade games you will feel right at home here with the directional movements and there are even group formations to be used in a battle! Formations like shield walls, phalanx/wedge, and defensive circle formations can be applied and changed on the fly in mid battle, VERY useful for when 2 armies or more are battling it out.
The final thing you will notice (and the most notable when you start the game and spawn into a world) is the graphics. At the moment there are Direct x 7 and 9 graphics, DO NOT let the discussions and reviews fool you! This game is a visual master piece considering the DX7 and 9 graphics closely resemble TES4: Oblivion's graphics, but with the fast approaching release date the Direct x 11 graphics will make this one of the most beautiful medieval themed sandboxes ever made!
Overall i give this game a 8.5/10 and thats just at an EARLY ACEESS point of veiw as Bitbox are at the moment of smoothing everything out for the release and beginning to implement future features upon post release. This has been one of the most comprehensive, immersive and challenging games ive played to date. Looking forwand to more!
11/10 would recommend this game to those who have never played sandboxes or similar themed games like MMORPG's as it is worth the experience.

Seeing as I have 500+ hours and this game is about to release I should put my opinions and experiences out there
We'll begin with the learning curve of the game. Personally, it took me and a few friends a week or two to actually get into the "mid-game" of Life Is Feudal. Through lots of struggling and crashes we eventually became the strongest and best on the server, we were addicted. For new players, this game is extremely difficult but very immersive. I can not stress enough to new players to push through the beginning grind so they can experience the rest of the game. I feel as if more stuff should be added to the beginning of the game to make it more fun for newer players, however.
The skills tree is very well thought out, however it features some bottlenecks that must be overcome. I very rarely say this, but I enjoy how this game forces you to play with friends to make the game a little easier. In saying this, roles come into play. Whenever we play, we usually designate a farmer, blacksmith and builder, as these are the roles needed to quickly surpass the early game. I almost always play the farming role at the start as I enjoy seeing how a few seeds that you scraped up from the ground begin to become a vast farm that surrounds your town. Most of the other skill trees in the game also flourish in a similiar way, such as going from constructing chicken coops and shacks to beautiful multi-story houses and towering walls.
During our time in Life Is Feudal, we rather quickly noticed the older aged community. We made many friends with people 20 or even 30 years older than us. The only major problem we had with the community was that some of the older folks (a lot, actually) disliked PvP and stuck to strictly PvE. This anti-PvP community here in Australia at least is quite worrying for the future of the game, as removing one of the main elements to a game like this makes it ever more boring. My group and I all enjoyed the threat of having some armed dudes try and take us down because they were worried that we would become powerful, and it would be great if one day we came across a server that didn't shun it. On the topic of PvP, the weapons and fighting in the game have come a far way, however I hope they do fix some little things in time for the MMO to avoid♥♥♥♥♥♥♥running about with no armor and bows just to get some easier kills.
Overall I look forward to the MMO and would recommend that you buy this game when it goes on sale for the release, and remember, life is feudal..

I wish there was a "mixed" review button on Steam. I don't want to recommend this game, neither do I want to not recommend it.
There are a lot of aspects about this game that I really like, such as the graphics, the optimization, the gameplay mechanics and even the campaign. There's just so much that could be done to make it better. The biggest thing that NEEDS to be done is dedicated servers; Ubisoft, you're charging a hefty £40 of our hard earned cash for this game, another £30 for the season pass AND you have in-game purchases? But you can't pay for dedicated servers? Hmm...
Now I've played some peer to peer multiplayer games before and the majority of them work quite well, it's just this one doesn't. I've played a few matches now and once it starts to migrate to a new host because somebody has left, the game has a tendancy to stop the game indefinitely, forcing you to alt+tab from the game and close the window.
The only multiplayer game mode which stands out to me from around the five that Ubisoft have generously put into this game (yes, five game modes for £40) is the duel/brawl mode. This is because this seems to be the only game mode in which players can fight fairly; it reminds me of a Souls type duel. In other game modes players are free to leave the brawl at any time, run off and pick up buffs and more health, and even liasing with other team mates so that they can all well and truly massacre you - although you should have won the fight fair and square. And then once you've been slaughtered by around 4 other players, somebody decides to leave and you all have to wait for the peer to peer connection to fix itself, infuriating you even more so that you alt+tab from the game and write an angry review (like me!).
Now, there are alternatives to this. Ubisoft has added the option to play with AI's, nothing but AI's, which I have tried because it is near impossible to play a full multiplayer match... This would be good if the AI weren't so stupid. ESPECIALLY your own team. We're talking one of your fellow AI team-mates standing around 5 feet away from you, doing nothing and watching your life, and dignity, being taken by three enemy AI players.
The campaign has started very well and I am looking forward to playing it. The graphics are outstanding and the game is very well optimized. The fighting mechanics are some of the best I've come across, if not THE best, and I believe future sword/slashing games should follow a similar style.
The game has a lot of potential to be really fun, and I believe it will be in due time. Remember, Rainbow Six Siege wasn't that great when it first came out - now it's praised. I believe Ubi will listen and make this a great game. So my honest advice is to pick it up then, not now.

WOW!!! Probably one of the best strategic First Person Shooting game. This game is so addictive that I put 190 hours within a month and still playing this game. Trust me its worth every single penny that I spent and I can't demonstrate how awesome the gameplay is.

Rating 7.5/10
Note: I played with the restoration mod. It is HIGHLY recommended that you play with this mod as it fixes a lot of bugs/glitches as well as restore lost content. It brings the game closer to the original intentions of the developers
The Good:
+ The game has a lot of robust options in how you build your character. You start by choosing between 3 classes: Guardian, Consular or Sentinel. Each class obviously focuses on different aspects of combat. Further in the game you can then further specialize your classes. You can fully customize your character how you wish between attributes, skills, feats and Jedi powers. All of this leads to many different options and replayability in how you design your character
+ The core aspect of the game is that as you can either play as a Jedi that is good or evil. Saving people, being kind and choosing the peaceful solution leads you to the light side while doing the opposite leads you to the dark side. Doing so leads to certain bonuses to your Jedi Powers. Being good means Light side powers will use less mana and dark side powers cost more and vice versa. I find the system to be very effective because it ties morality choices into game play, a feature that seems to be very lacking in today's modern games.
+ The second core aspect is how you respond and handle situations with your party members. You can gain or lose influence with them. If you gain enough influence with any particular party member, new dialogue options open up resulting in more background to the story, and/or stat increases for you or your party member. It is not mandatory as you can easily complete the game without gaining any influence with anybody but it adds a nice touch to the game and offers more options.
+ The story, although confusing in the beginning because it throws so much at you does get increasingly better. The story is presented very well because of the great dialogue options and fantastic writing. Obsidian is easily one of the best in the industry regarding writing.
+ If there is any company that can match or exceed Bioware in writing for npc characters its Obsidian. Every party member that joins you in your quest is well written and interesting. Every party member has alternative motives for joining you which makes things more exciting and not every party member gets along with each other. These ideas are explored the further you progress in the game.
+ Every planet you visit feels different. The game throws a few twists in for good measure to keep things fresh.
+ Well written Side Quests
+ mods
The Average:
Sadly there was no improvement with combat. The combat in the game is really showing its age. I never particularly liked the combat because it's not very engaging.
Certain force powers, skills, feats are game breaking while others are completely useless.
The Bad:
- The UI especially navigating to find items in your inventory is a chore and frustrating. The inventory screen is a long list of your items. There are options to filter the list based on specific items but this doesn't fix the overall problem of a bad overall inventory management system.
- The game forces you to do solo missions either as yourself or one of your party members. These sections are frustrating and awful only because the combat was never designed around solo play. This problem is further compounded if you auto-leveled up any of your party members. Playing a solo section with a party member that has all the wrong attributes/skills/feats is painful.
- Last few areas have cut and paste environments. Obvious that development was rushed at the end.
Conclusion
A worthy follow up to one of the best RPG's for its time. Obsidian once again shows that it is one of the best when it comes to writing a great story with great characters. It's sad that it takes a mod to fix a lot of the problems with the game. If you loved the first game then there is no reason not to love this one as well.

Maybe it is partially our fault as consumers, for not pouring money into this admittedly ambitious project early on, but Early Access is meant to be a place where serviceable products are made better, not a place where the majority of a game's story is held hostage until a critical mass of cashflow is reached. First if you buy Magic 2015, just buy the 9.99 version and consider buying some boosters later on (there are a maximum of 14 boosters which will give you all premium cards).  With 9.99 spent and some grinding you can unlock 90% of the cards in the game.
Overall thoughts:  I had a very nice experience playing Magic 2015 with only a few bumps.  First and formost the game is fun to play and there are a large number of interesting PvE computer enemies and decks to play against with interesting challeneges that will often require you to shuffle your deck around some to adjust against there tactics.  Likewise once you have unlocked a fair number of cards it is extremely fun to play online multiplayer against other players and see the different decks people have built.   There are quite a number of interesting tactics which work in the multiplayer games with the free cards available.  The premimum cards allow a few other tactics but really are not required to be competatively viable in multiplayer games.  I quickly worked up 50 hours of play over a week before my vacation and had an extremely fun time playing.  If you only buy the base game at $9.99 you should have a very fun time with your money really well spent.  I strongly recommend you do NOT buy the special or complete editions of Magic as you are really just unlocking content early leading to your playtime having very few unlocks as you play through (and spending extra money on something you would unlock for free).
Pros to Magic 2015:
Many PvE enemies are availble with interesting decks to play against.
The marjority of the cards can be unlocked for free.
The $9.99 purchase gives you many hours of enjoyment without requiring any addtional money spent.
The PvE game is quite challeneging and ramps up in difficulty nicely.
The updated UI plays well during games and is easy to learn.
Deck building works great and is quite balanced with the current available cards.
Multiplayer games are a blast and there are many interesting tactics that you can use.
You cannot get more copies of any card than you could put in a single deck, so you rappidly will fill out your entire card collection.
When buying premium boosters you know you will get the full set after 14 boosters exactly (you can't buy any more as your set will be complete).
Cons to Magic 2015:
Difficulty can be very high early for some players (lower the difficulty to the lowest when you start out).
Once you complete the tutorial you are locked to your current starter deck.
It takes a while to buildup enough boosters to build a new deck/color approach.
There are less immidiate features and game modes than past Planeswalker games.
Premium cards cost quite a bit for what ultimately is a small sub-set of the cards (~$30 for the 14 premium boosters).

To start off 80 Days is an interactive fiction game, so if you don’t like lots of reading, steer clear.  The game is an adaption of the classic Jules Verne novel about consummate British gentleman Phileas Fogg and his wager to circumnavigate the world in 80 Days, and does its own spin on it by adding steampunk. Now steampunk is usually squandered into just being greasy nerds covering themselves in gears and talking in bad British accents instead of actually exploring the punk part of the term, but 80 Days uses the trappings very effectively, adding on to the feelings of wonder and adventure as well as actually exploring the social and economic impact of such inventions like dealing with how they interact with the ills of the Victorian Era, but also the hope for a brighter future such innovations could bring as well. The world of 80 Days is also an interesting a mix of real history such as France still recovering from their humiliating defeat in the Franco-Prussian War that led to the unification of Germany and alt history such as the Zulu being a rising world power that successfully repelled British invasion. You play as Fogg’s valet, Jean Passepartout, and gameplay is strategizing your money and supplies as well as making choices to learn more about possible routes, win people to your side, and improve relations with Fogg, among other things. This game is dense as hell and there are so many places to go and people to meet on your journey that you will definitely miss out on a lot in just one playthrough.
Overall it’s a really engaging experience and to just give a more detailed example, in my first playthrough I took a northern route cutting through the Baltic and going overland through Russia. Hijinks along the way included getting caught in a battle between Communist rebels and the Czar’s mech-pilot soldiers in St. Petersburg, getting chucked off the Siberian Express in the♥♥♥♥♥end of Siberia after inadvertently deep sixing a young romance, getting waylaid to Beijing and seeing a Chinese opera performed by robots, delivering the captain’s baby on a boat from Honolulu to San Fran and running into a gang of Chicago hooligans that lifted houses off their foundations with their machines if they didn’t get paid protection money. With less than a week left and finding myself in New York, I sold all our stuff to take a rocket sub to Iceland, and after that finally made the worldwide journey back to London…82 days later.

But in the end it didn’t feel like a failure, it kind of felt like a fitting ending. Fogg and Passepartout didn’t make it, but close enough to still make it impressive, and their whole journey was a grand adventure and the two became close friends by the end of it. My two subsequent playthroughs were much more successful and were unique adventures of their own, such as solving a murder and going down the Amazon. And that’s what 80 Days really succeeds at and deserves the praise it’s gotten, really making you feel you went on an adventure. In conclusion, 80 Days is a fantastic adventure game and a must play.

This is really a great game, and far more unforgiving than I'd have guessed initially.  You are the servant of a wealthy man who bet that he can make it around the world in 80 days, as the title suggests.
And this world is really something.  The whole place is this incredibly realized steampunk alternate future where horses have been replaced by metal horses, and where pirates use airships to plunder over land.  I don't want to give anymore away, those are two early examples of the game's incredibly cool atmosphere.  Some if it is incredibly inventive, at least as someone who doesn't know much steampunk stuff.
And the game is, as I said, quite punishing in a fair way.  You can miss an entire day just by missing the departure of your chosen method of travel.  If 3 different methods of transport leave at 1:00 PM and you're still clicking the option to get an extra bag on-board at 12:59, you'll miss the train/ship/car/railroad etc.  It's both frustrating and realistic, seeing as they won't wait around for you all day.
The game is about managing the options for your travel amid various circumstances which present themselves in the game's choose your own adventure texts.  You go through multiple stages of dialog which can improve your relationship with your master, or with strangers, and perhaps net you items or new information on how to travel to another destination.
You have to be wary of your master's health, which decreases over arduous journeys, or he'll die.  You can buy gear which aids traveling over the stressful paths, like desert clothes or storm gear for oceanliners.  Be sure to get items from various cities to sell elsewhere, too, so you can afford transport costs.  There's lots of really funny, interesting things that happen and I've only gotten to day 70 on my first try (I had to restart because I screwed up).  There's an entire northern half of Europe, both North and South America which I've yet to even step foot in.
You really should get this game, and hopefully many more games like this come about in the future.  It's got great music, the writing is easy to read and not overly wordy (unlike lots of games which bombard you with text and then claim to have "great writing," such as something like Pillars of Eternity).  Even the globe of the game has a color scheme which reinforces the theme.  All the art is very pretty to look at also.
Just an absolute joy to play the game.  The myriad of choice supports multiple playthroughs, though you will doubtless run into some scenarios twice.  You can handle these differently to see what the outcome is though.  The game also reacts to your path and the number of days you have left in a way which seems really impressive; my master was not pleased when I decided to go west after heading northeast because it went against our progress, even though it meant we'd be able to do this quest and get tons of money while boarding the trains more to the south.
Definitely get this game if you like choose your own adventure style games, and this is a really cool introduction to the genre for people who don't normally play this kind of thing.
I played it for a bit thinking it would go somewhere or perhaps that there was some skill involved, but there isn't.  Gets boring fast and doesn't seem to go anywhere.
While still in development, what's here is very promising. Art style is undeniably charming.

Dead Pixels is the kind of game you would have played over and over again at the arcades 'back in the day'... at least if you're of a certain age. It doesn't pretend to be anything other than a side scrolling SHUMP, but it does it so well.
The feeling of panic as the horde swarm down on you, as you run out of bullets, as the heartbeat thumps over the audio as your health goes down works so well. The desperate search for a Trader to sell your unwanted junk so you can buy more ammo or the the life saving fireworks.
Yes, fireworks.
The premise is simple - survivor 20 streets to make it to the potential helicopter to safety. Loot/raid what you can along the way and find whatever you can to survive. Shoot zombies and steal their wallets, and find the trader to buy upgrades.
Easy.
Only, it can become challenging as various zombies start to appear, some with different abilities... and some that are incredibly hard to kill. By themself they're nothing, but when you get by that Zombie Wave containing various Zombie types... well you know you're in trouble.
All I can say is watch out for the rats, they're not bad.
You will finish this game in ~1 hour, however there has been an update that has included several different modes since it's release - such as survival mode (waves).
All-in-all it's a well presented, cheeky tribute to the games of old with a somewhat modern twist.

I often find that I miss a sense of mystery and discovery in contemporary gaming. This game is quite the exception! 80 Days is a charming "choose your own story" type of game in which you take the role of a faithful valet in service to Phineas Fogg, an English gentleman. Fogg has taken a bet, in now so have you! Your goal is to circumnavigate the globe of an alternate history late 19th century world filled with steampunk creations in 80 days or less. I found discovering unique modes of transportation to be an ingenius plot advancement device and I never knew what might come at the next stop. I'd like nothing more than to describe just a few of these fictional vehicles, yet to do so would ruin that sense of discovery that I've enjoyed so far.
So, aside from managing your master and deciding on your route, you must also balance your books and ensure you have funds to spare. Much of this is done by buying and selling for profit. This is all quite transparent and easy to understand. That is a boon to this title! Simplicity and ease is one of the greatest selling points of 80 Days and I would even recommend it to those who don't regularly play PC games.
I highly recommend this title to just about anyone. Whether it is the exploration, excellent writing and plot or the challenge of the unknown and a strict timetable, this title will not disappoint. That being said, do not expect to win on the first play through. This is a game that is highly replayable, and I would even say that it is a necessity. Safe travels!

This game is very interesting. While yes it is one of those "survival sandbox" games which has (until 4 days after this review) been in early access, it is also one of the most original and expansive of those on offer.
The game itself has managed a wonderful feeling of immersion in its own world/lore. When you play it you can be quite content with the feeling of actually being in the world your character is surrounded by. I will now break this review down into a few sections:
Gameplay:
This game takes a long time. That is a key point, do not expect to have a massive medieval castle and town within 5 hours of playing the game. Large parts involve effectively grinding (!FLUX! - players will know) to find the resources you need to construct/create the buildings/items you want. However teamwork is amazingly useful because it reduces the time needed to perform many actions. Such that imagine 1 person takes 1 hour to perform an action, 2 people would then take less than half an hour to do the same action.
Also as this is a survival game you need to gather food to survive. This is relatively simple if you have found a few reliably good quality apple trees. You will also need to 'rest' your character occasionally if performing tough work such as terraforming or construction etc.
This leads me onto another important point regarding skill progression. The game is designed, as I've said previously and as you will hear through this review, for teamplay. A limitation imposed by this is such that you cannot be an expert at everything! You have a limited number of skill points to distribute around the various skills (which unlock in a skill-tree type fashion). As you perform actions these skill points will be added to your skill in that action up to your limit (you can 're-spec' by downgrading your skills if needed). Because of this you will need a group to play with unless you set your game/server to have custom (default is 800 I think) levels of skill points.
Graphics:
This game has looked absolutely fine throughout its development but its looming DX11 release looks incredible from what we've seen thus far. Other than this I cannot comment much on this point other than it runs very well without many framerate dips etc. so seems quite optimised.
Music/Audio:
The sound quality is great with well recorded clips for all actions and a nice atmospheric background soundtrack, although if playing for many hours at a time it can get a little repetitive.
I'm not used to writing reviews (this is my first so I know I will have missed a lot) so please don't hate :P

Admittedly this is a reluctant Recommendation, if only because it costs next to nothing usually, especially when on sale.
Dead Pixels embraces the campiness I love, but mostly in its presentation and music choice, the game itself balances a line between zombie sim and arcade shooter. The sim aspect is simplified but can feel heavy starting out while the arcade shooter aspect kick in late game if you play your cards right. But that's really what this game has going against it. It's a slow crawl to the point where you have enough ammuntion that you can go wild and actually actively fight your zombie foes, otherwise you're conserving ammuntion and running away from loads of fights. Oh, and going hog wild at the beginning is the quickest way to screw you over for later. Choose your fights.
It's just not interesting, unique, or terribly fun until you sit down and spend some time with it. After that, as if you're filling some sort of play time quota, the game becomes quite hectic and entertaining. So if you're interested, I'd wait until it goes on sale. If the sequel plays up the arcade shooter elements more (because it's looking a lot better so far) and plays with the difficulty to match it, you might have a fun retro-esque game on your hands. Right now it's just... not.

Great sand-box multiplayer game. With a overall great community and interesting and engaging building/ crafting mechanics. Easy to learn and very hard to master. If you like medieval times, and working for what you get I recommend this game.
If you are the type of player that wants to run around killing people without putting any time in, I would recommend you look else were. Not to say your play style is not welcomed, but game mechanics make players wait days, and weeks before they can craft their first sword. After that you have to wait a few weeks before you can actually use any good gear. Simply put if you want things to be done instantaneous you will not enjoy this game. It is very slow paced, but personally I like that aspect.
If you enjoy making friends, and working together with other people, or to role-play heavily then I would recommend this game. The game mechanics forces players to work together to create any mid to end game buildings or gear. All skill trades intersect with each other, and all of them need each other's help. Because of this set up you will have to group up or trade if you want to create end game gear.
devs are very good about updates (even if they fall behind) and are constantly listening to feed back and improving the core mechanics. The game is a bit expensive but I believe that it is worth every dollar.

I'll be honest I originally bought this through Humble Bundle to get the AQWorlds bonus items, but was also interested in playing the game. After hearing that the developers for Dungeon Punks had been the ones behind Shadow Tale I got even more excited. I'm currently running through New Game+ mode and although it is a bit tougher without the shop its still quite good. I do recommend this game as I do enjoy playing it.
~I do like and enjoy this game because, its not stupid hard or stupid easy.
~There are upgradable skills, but they max out at level 2.
~I believe characters max out at level 40 or so. Update: Leveling goes beyond 40.
~Theres different weapons and shields for the six unlockable and playable characters. Some items are locked to two or so characters such as axes or maces.
~All six characters look different and have different skills. Only one female though (out of six).
~You are not limited or forced to play as any specific character unless you haven't unlocked them all yet as you can easily switch characters on the windship. In the combat areas you can switch between the teams of two and then switch to pick the exact character to play as.
~Shop is locked after beating the game and begining again in New Game mode + (Just a minor nuisance, but items drop more frequently)
~Some replaying of areas and grinding is required to progress
~Death penalty only seems to really hurt you in New Game + mode, as the cost to resurect goes up.
~Without the shop in New Game+ gold really stacks up and loses value. You can spend gold to enchant items, but I'm doing just fine without enchantments and I've got just under 800,000 gold saved up so far.
~One bugged achievement so far.

Dungeon Punks is a really fun Beat-em-up.  I highly recommend this game to those that like this genre or just want something fun to play.
There are 6 different classes you can play as, each with their own unique set of spells.  You can also buy equipement, which are class specific, to use in combat.  You can also gain levels which increases their overall power and use tome points to level up skills.
Each level you have to beat a boss to proceed to the next level.  The levels have multiple rooms, you go from room to room and fight enemies.  Along the way you may encounter NPC's that give side quests which will earn you gold and exp.
The best thing about this game is you have AI party members that tag along and fight with you.  Very refreshing to see, you can swap between party members as well if you want to play someone different.
One issue I have is the lack of healing in the game, there's not enough potion drops.  This kind of forces you to exit the dungeon early because your party members will die and you're left alone.  You can finish the level alone, but it's not worth the trouble.
From an hours to price ratio, you will definitely get your money's worth.  The RPG elements combined with the combat are very good and will keep you entertained for a long time.

I've played plenty of survival games in my time, and this is hands down my favorite.
The overall feel of a server's community entirely revolves around human nature. Some people want to be barbarians, some want to be bandits, a lot more just want to coexist. In the end, your experiences depend on which you choose.
Barbarians (people who run around naked screaming obscenities ad decapitating deer) tend to add a bit of comedic relief to the trying environment that is LiF, but may also come and burn your house down and steal your chickens.
Bandits come in two flavors. They either roleplay and hold you up much like a common highwayman, or run around in packs of 4+ and just kill some poor naked ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ under the illusion that they have gear worth taking.
Coexisting countrymen constantly care for each other like cousins. The core concept is to cooperate in a calculated campaign of carpentry, construction, calipers, and cooking. This competing collection of corroborative characters can, and commonly do, cause caustious- ok enough with the alliteration.
tl;dr If you aren't a bard or bandit you typicaly form a group and make friends through helping each other build a small settlement. If you are like me, you tend to do this with around 15 other people, the majority of which are on Teamspeak. The few times you get attacked either end in everyone dying or some lone wannabe bandit getting chased off by a dozen angry, heavily-armed and armoured peasants weilding the fruits of their labor as weapons of death.
To be fair, i have had my troubles wanting to play this game but this is for personal reasons. I can not handle stress due to a medical condition I have. This being said, you will stress a lot in this game. (Is that naked man on a horse really a bandit with his armour deequipped to lull us into a false sense of security, or is he some scrub fresh spawn that got lucky and found a horse already?) These are the questions that can get people killed, or get people killed. It is very rare for most people to trust one another on a server with known bandits and barbarians as they recruit more as the server grows. In the end though, this game is a delight to have in my steam library and I'm happy to have spent $40 on it.
Please read the comments to get a more updated look at my experience with the game as it develops.

As a side note, download the Restored Content mod for this game immediately. The developers did leave a minor subplot hanging, but left much of the content on the game disc, and a group of modders has helpfully restored it to functionality. Trust me, it's a delight.

Really nice and creative game. Having completed a trip a few times on Android I wanted to give it a go on Windows for the achievements and the comfort of a bigger screen and a mouse.
80 Days follows the story of the wealthy Phileas Fogg and his valet Passepartout. In the game you have to try to travel the world in eighty days (what a surprise!). How you do it is up to the player: will you try and brave the deserts of Arabi or take the long railway through the cold Russian lands? You can make a lot of decisions which make for a unique travel each time you play the game.
When you find yourself in cities, you have multiple options to pass the time: find banks to transfer money from London, visit markets to buy and sell items to help funding the trip or to ease the harsh travelconditions. You can also explore each city to find new travel methods and interesting stories about the city you're in. Each city has a nice story, some longer than the others, which can really add something to the experience or the trip.
When travelling stories will present themselves in which you can make choices what to do and what to say. These choices can really matter, so be careful what you choose. You can fall in love, get your airship boarded by pirates, strand at sea with no escape left; there's a lot to explore, discover and experience.
The world itself is very interesting. It's a futuristic steampunkish world with its own morals and codes. It's a world Jules Verne (the game is based upon his novel) has created and it's really amazing. The developers did a great way to shape the content to be a hommage to Verne.
Is this game something for you? If you like cool storylines with a great interactive touch this is something for you. It has a little bit of strategic management into it with the markets and the items you can find there, but also how you will travel and if you can persuade people to help you in your endeavor to travel the world in eighty days.

Transport Defender is an incremental game of the Clicker Heroes sub genre. However, the comparison is not necessarily fair as it stands far on it's own and is more innovative than your average idle game.
Transport Defender actually makes idling more compelling way of playing than many other incremental games, as it's possible to purchase automatic buying, automatic resets and many other automation via upgrades in the game (called Features in game, which there are hundreds of different kinds). The mechanics also include ascension types of resets that reset your current prestige resets while giving even larger bonuses.
The game also goes much higher numbers than your average incremental games as the number certainly don't stop with simple 32 bit floating point limits.
As for negative aspects of the game, the game tends to update quite often. While this can also be seen as a positive, the updates sometimes completely throw off the previous game balance. The fast iteration may be interesting but it may also devalue all your previous progress at moments notice. It also makes me wonder if all the updates are always that well thought.
The game is also interesting enough to play without paying for the in game purchases. For incremental game enthusiasts, I at least recommend taking a look at this game as it offers a somewhat unique take on the genre.

Let me start by saying that for more than 10 years, I've been waiting for a sandbox that would rival Ultima Online. Nothing could ever quite match up.
I seriously think this might be the one. And that's a big statement for me. *fans self* I'm getting a little emotional here.
What struck me about this game is that it is a challenge. I appreciate that in order to get somewhere in this game - to accomplish anything - you must really pay attention. You won't find random epic loot in chests. You won't get neat armor from killing a bear. Bears don't wear armor. It just makes sense.
I also really love that you can spend your time doing whatever it is that floats your boat. You don't HAVE to do anything to have a fulfilling game. It's a true sandbox.
Right now, I'm playing on a fairly small server. There are usually 3 - 5 people playing at a time. But already, there is community. I can imagine that it will only improve once there are more players coming in. Because there are SO many skills, and so many jobs to do, trading and building alliances actually has meaning.
Obviously because it is in alpha, there are some bugs and improvements to be made. I'm confident that they'll be coming in time.
There are some things that seem overly difficult, although it may vary from server to server. For example, on my particular server, apples never grow back. We must plant and replant. Food is quite difficult to come by. Foraging for edible plants almost never finds anything.  A disproportionate amount of time is spent trying to find it, and hunger levels grow quite rapidly. I spend alot of time catching my breath, and waiting to be able to play again. After all that mining and lumberjacking, I would have thought my character would be fit enough to run for 20 seconds! :P
Overall though, I really highly recommend this game. After just a few hours, I was hooked. There is a steep learning curve, but there are many resources online that will answer your questions.I'm very optimistic about this game's future, and I will definitely be spending a very large chunk of my time playing it. Goodbye, social life! :D
I recommend this game.   ...but maybe don't pay full price.  It helps.

I've been playing this game for about 2 days now and have installed 1 mod as well. Hopefully this review will help decide whether you want to buy the game or not.
First order of buisness is you need to make sure your computer is stable enough for this game, this is Beamng Drive, not minecraft. If you look at the photos and videos of the game on the steam page, it's a nice game, at high graphics resolution and settings. You can't just download this game on you average computer and hope for the best. I have a 750 GTX card and still experience some problems running the game, I HIGHLY suggest that you take a look at your PC'S specs and the games requirements first.
The second thing I have to say is that YOU have to keep the game interesting. This game has NO goals or objectives at all, so if your one of those people who has to have some sort of objective, then I HIGHLY DO NOT recommend this game for you. Sure, the game has "scenarios" but they're short, choppy and to the point. However, the developers do claim they're working on a career mode, you'd just have keep checking the offical website for updates, or steam too. Don't completely rely on that news, though.
The third and final thing is that you either like the game or don't. Theres far and few in between, but sadly, this is one of those games that you just have to try for yourself. You can read reviews and watch video reviews all day long, but truth be told, that honestly won't help. This game is what you make of it, I took a chance and bought it while it was on sale, and I thing it's a great game.
My overall opinion of the game, I give it a 8 out of 10. This game isn't perfect, no game is, but this game is slowly but surely working it's way up. I feel like once they add a career mode, this game will skyrocket to the top simulators of the year. Right now though, it's a crash and driving simulator, the physics in this game are outstanding, like no other, but the  catch is there's no objective. Do I like the game, yes, but do you like the game, thats for you to decide. People also gripe about this game still being in beta form. This game is nowhere CLOSE to being in beta form, just because it's on steam doesn't mean it's in beta form. It's also a very well polished game, to polished to be in beta form, sure there are glitches here and there, but thats mainly with mods in the game. Hopefully you've come to a conclusion about getting the game.

A rapid cacophony of impacts broke the monotony of driving, accompanied by the chatter and crack of automatic fire hitting the vehicle. The person next to me that I had been talking to was already slumped over and covered in blood by the time I realised we were in the middle of an ambush.
I jumped out of the vehicle, as it's wheels had been taken out by a 40MM grenade, and, because I had been shot in the leg, crawled my way into a ditch at the side of the road, where I passed out and died.
I think, after all this time, I can finally review this game.
One of the biggest things I noticed coming into this game is the learning curve, which is rather extreme. You will intially be very confused by things and some, the AI and the ballistics in particular, are very complex and not well explained in-game.
Once you overcome that, the game opens up and it's absurd freedom starts tp show- you can do ANYTHING in this game, despite it being presented as a military tactical game.
Multiplayer-
Modes and missions range from the Life and RPG simulation of everyday normality, people working jobs, driving around and having a police force, to the Survival and post-apocalyse gamemodes revolving around the pursuit of food and water, weapons and transport to stay alive.
You have the ever-popular PvP gamemodes such as King Of The Hill and EUTW, which bring a Battlefield style gameplay mode into Arma, and you have the original Battlegrounds, which was so popular it is now available as a standalone game.
Another side of the game is that of the clans and groups who take the base Arma's focus on the military and expand it, making the already impressive realism to ever greater levels, with things like new weapons, uniforms and vehicles covering every nation in the world, to advanced medical modes that take into account blood loss, surgeons and battlefield trauma / medical care to fantastic and impressive details.
Groups like these are one of the biggest attractions of the game, and range from small groups to friends to massive clans with over 300 active members- Arma can support over 160+ players in a single multiplayer game, in addition to hundreds of AI soldiers, so the scale of some of these groups in without comparison to anything else except EVE.
Arma has such a wide variety and depth to all it's systems, from how the ballistics and each individual round is modeled in the game, and affected by velocity, drop, zeroing, penetration against various materials from wood, brick, steel and body armor, to rounds being able to bounce and deflect due to high-angle ricochets on hard surfaces like concrete or vehicles.

That's just a single example, and the game covers everything from underwater combat and submarines, land battles with infantry and tanks with modular damage to systems and parts, making it possible to, for example, knock out a tanks tracks and turret without destroying it, leaving it totally helpless, all the way to next-generation jet fighters and advanced radar detection, thermal and IR technology.
You can go from using a submarine and respirators for a stealthy night insertion on a Greek coastline in 2035, to commanding a tank crew in a pitched battle in the Iraqi desert during the Gulf War, to evacuating wounded soldiers from thick Vietnamese jungles in 1970, before using an American aircraft carrier to stage for a dogfight above Russia in the modern day, all in the course of a few hours.
This is due to the huge modding and creation community for the game, who add a massive range of things to the game, from new vehicles, sounds, maps, campaigns and new missions, systems and anything you can possibly think of- Someone has either made it or is working on it- from ALIEN and Star Wars, RPG and Police cars, to every weapon and piece of equipment used by the British, American, French, German and Russian armies over the past decade.
On to the Singleplayer aspects of the game-
I put over 350 hours into the singleplayer content alone, and never even touched the multiplayer aspects until after that.
Despite it's reputation for it's MP based community singleplayer can still give people plenty of intresting missions, and Steam Workshop support for mods and missions is fantastic.
The base Arma 3 campaign is set in 2035, and revolves around NATO forces on the islands of Altis and Stratis (based on real islands off the coast of Greece) and their fighting with the native AAF armed forces and the more advanced CSAT, based on an Iran/ ME alliance.
The campaign does not hold your hand, and you are thrown into a situation where you are NOT the winners, being constantly on the back-foot and fighting with lesser equipment and as guerillas and insurgents fighting against a military with superior armaments to you, which is a nice change from the normal state of affairs in games, where you play the exact opposite.
The campaign is rather long and has both free-roaming missions and storyline missions to progress throughout it. I would estimate the base campaign to be about 20-35 hours long depending on difficulty, your style of play and if you do the optional free-roaming mission.
The AI are able to supress you, pin, flank and use a decent level of tactics, so it's often best to take some time to plan your mission in advance- What cover is in the area? What is the sightlines and visibility and is a stealth approach possible? Where are the enemy patrol routes and is there any chance of enemy reinforcements? What type of enemy soldiers and equipment do you suspect they have- nightvision, machineguns, marksmen, support assets like vehicles or static weapons can affect your approach to your objective.
The sandbox nature of the game means you can often go around or even totally avoid some obstacles or forces you might come across.
The Apex Expansion also adds a small COOP campaign, which has some great presentation and polish, based on Tanoa, which is a fictional island off the coast of Fiji, and is a utterly STUNNING looking map, well worth the price of the Expansion.
Apex takes place on the Tanoan islands, off the coast of Fiji and Australia, and follows a small, well equipped British special forces group, CTRG, and their fighting against the Syndikate drug Cartel in the jungles. As special forces you are often deployed at night, and have access to advanced equipment like thermals and night vision, putting you at a technological advantage over the Cartel, but the Cartel have greater numbers so a stand-up battle is often a fatal problem- it's often possible to avoid patrols and soldiers. Apex also adds a wide range of weapons including the AK-47M, AK-12, AKS-74U, HK-416 and HK-417, M249 SAW, MP5K PDW.
Performance and lifetime-
One of the biggest problems people have with the game is performance. Because of the huge complexity of ARMA, particularly in Multiplayer, the performance of the server and the mission is paramount- MOST of the highly popular and heavily scripted gamemodes will not get 60 FPS, regardless of settings, but with a good server and mission you can achieve 60+ FPS. The game is biased towards CPU clock speed, rather than the GPU like most other games, so a higher clock CPU sees much better performance than a GPU upgrade.
The game is constantly getting large updates even years after release, and the DLC's always come with free platform updates, adding new features like bipods, sound overhauls, new weapon and clothing features like thermal concealment, advanced helicopter flight models for more simulator-like flying, and many others it would take too long to list.
To end-
Arma is, put simply, the most widely varied and impressive game I have ever played, and the absurd number of hours I have in the game ( Over 4,200 at the time of writing) is a testiment to it's great community, authentic gameplay and varied experiences. I'm going to be playing the game for years to come, and Arma was an eye-opening intoduction to PC gaming for me.

Overall, Sniper Elite V2 is a pretty decent game, but it isn't a game 100% worth your time and money.
Pro:
- Awesome kill graphics
- Realistic bullet physics (e.g. wind, bullet drop, etc.)
- Recreated WWII environments (e.g. Berlin)
- Several ways to kill
Con:
- Doesn't reward stealth (no real challenge except not dying)
- Fairly linear map layout
I take issue with the last two, as it doesn't make the game a powerful challenge. Essentially, where Uncharted, Splinter Cell and Metal Gear increase difficultly accordingly, Sniper Elite V2 allows you to shoot your way out, and nothing worse happens. No heightened alert modes, no extra enemies barrelling in... there's not much about Sniper Elite V2's challenge.
The linear map layout? There are chances to flank the enemy and kill them from several angles, but there's a lot of places that could potentially be visited or explored, only to be blocked off by the lack of an action prompt. The several angles make less use in game, with the "shooting your way out" business making stealthy kills fairly redundant. Brothers in Arms makes a better, more realistic use of the several angles approach.
Notes:
- Have not tried multiplayer/co-op. No friends to do so.

17+ Hours in, my feelings on this game are pretty well summed up as mixed. I'll try and make it brief by breaking it up here.
Story Mode: Gameplay feels great, good way to introduce classes so they can be utilized in multiplayer (the real meat of the game), and does enough world building to give me some sense of purpose. Otherwise the story is convoluted, collectibles give length to the missions that they otherwise don't have, and the overall story telling is just.... so heavy handed and hammy in my personal opinion. The gameplay carries it through here.
Multiplayer: When it works properly? Probably the best melee combat I've ever played. Combat systems are well flushed out, mostly balanced, and diverse. 1v1, 2v2, have little to no problem. 4v4 battles however, we start to get into the REAL issues of this game that have been harped on a lot here. Peer to peer connection for a twitch multiplayer game in 2017 is flat outright unacceptable. I have some hopes that once the game shows long term profitablility (see example with R6:Siege) they'll shift to a dedicated server connection model. Moving off of that - I have some issues with the pay-to-play features. I don't think I've seen more pay walls in a non-mobile game. Ever. Ubisoft wants your money. Want to skip all the combat associated character progression? Don't play for 10 hours to get level 19 with a character, just pay us $5. Want the best equipment? Don't get loot from matches after those 10-50 hours, just pay us $5 and MAYBE you'll get your equipment over the 10 pack rolls.
Overall: Listen. The short and the thick of it is, if you've been starving for a close combat multiplayer game that took what was fun about the Dark Souls Multiplayer and improved it enough for it to be an Esport - this is the game for you. You'll overlook it's faults for the enjoyment of the gameplay. If not? Maybe this title is a miss/rent.

I HIGHLY enjoyed the game, don't get me wrong, but maybe my PC is just having some issues running the game (LOW FPS on low quality, or as low as I can get it).
I don't understand many of the mechanics and I felt like I was thrust' into it without any combat experience. Regardless, it was easy to adapt to. I enjoy the fact that the game adapts to 2 kinds of games at the same time; Space Battle Sim, and FPS Ground combat. It's diverse in the way people can get into the game and I think it's a nice touch for those that want to try a different style of game or just brawl the best way they know how.
For an game in Early access, I'm highly impressed. I rarely do flight sims, but this one change my perspective a bit. I do quarrel with it being a little hard to adjust to, but I'm managing. The ground combat is a bit rough with ai models doing the hokey-pokey every now and then (not literally) and somehow managing to miss the enemy entirely. Overall, they're very objective based and will stick to their orders (unlike me). As well as fighting, there is a bit of customization if you find yourself in the heat of battle and can't seem to progress, with the addition of a credit/combat point system based on objectives and control points (as far as I understand) under your control. Heavy guns for taking down the mass of hungry opponents, or precision weapons for taking down that pesky team leader.
Are there things I would change? Yes, of course.
For starters, I'd like to maybe see an implementation of basics, such as ground and space combat and basics of objective related items (how to capture, how to progress, etc.) Very minor and I hope easy to develope. Another would be fixing some of the animation and maybe tweaking the ai a tad bit; seeing as they shuffle around and don't provide a whole lot of support when attacking the main objective, or the enemy ai being TOO overwhelming in some areas.
Overall, fantastic game. I recommend to anyone looking for something Star Wars mixed with Mass Effect... The good Mass Effect... And the games George Lucas had nothing to do with... Those ones...

Recommendations can be a mixed affair. Would I recommend this game to me? Yes. It isn't expensive and I like the grind of playing through matches to collect all the card even more than multiplayer. I've enjoyed to some extent every release of the game. Would I recommend this game to any Magic: the Gathering player or gamer in general? No.
The deck building option is the best feature of this game. Any card you have can now be put into any deck you want. And you can create any deck you want. You get more cards by playing games. A win gives you a booster pack of cards. Simple and it works well enough.
Interface is one area where this game suffers. It's the best you could hope for a tablet game perhaps, but they didn't change it around for the PC. 'Lazy' is the word that comes to mind to describe this. It is frustrating to go through the UI knowing it could be much better for a PC.
There are no other options of gameplay. The other games had Archenemy (very fun), Planechase (not so fun with computer at least), two headed giant (always nice). There is a huge format they haven't touched upon yet. Commander! My lord it is about time they made an EDH release for the game. There are several other options as well. They could have a booster draft options that use only cards in your collection. There is so much they could have done. I don't know why they sat on their hands in this.
Another problem is that blizzard seems to want it both ways: charge to buy the game and charge for premium items. I know they need to monetize their product, but this is typically done through one or another. Not both. It feels lame that they keep trying. I hope none of you are buying that stuff. I'm guilting you if you are. You're encouraging bad behavior.
In summary, the build your own deck model was a huge step forward for the franchise. They just made several small steps back as well. If you've bought every iteration of the game so far and enjoyed it, you will enjoy this one as well. Otherwise, this isn't exactly the polished product you want to pick up.

17+ Hours in, my feelings on this game are pretty well summed up as mixed. I'll try and make it brief by breaking it up here.
Story Mode: Gameplay feels great, good way to introduce classes so they can be utilized in multiplayer (the real meat of the game), and does enough world building to give me some sense of purpose. Otherwise the story is convoluted, collectibles give length to the missions that they otherwise don't have, and the overall story telling is just.... so heavy handed and hammy in my personal opinion. The gameplay carries it through here.
Multiplayer: When it works properly? Probably the best melee combat I've ever played. Combat systems are well flushed out, mostly balanced, and diverse. 1v1, 2v2, have little to no problem. 4v4 battles however, we start to get into the REAL issues of this game that have been harped on a lot here. Peer to peer connection for a twitch multiplayer game in 2017 is flat outright unacceptable. I have some hopes that once the game shows long term profitablility (see example with R6:Siege) they'll shift to a dedicated server connection model. Moving off of that - I have some issues with the pay-to-play features. I don't think I've seen more pay walls in a non-mobile game. Ever. Ubisoft wants your money. Want to skip all the combat associated character progression? Don't play for 10 hours to get level 19 with a character, just pay us $5. Want the best equipment? Don't get loot from matches after those 10-50 hours, just pay us $5 and MAYBE you'll get your equipment over the 10 pack rolls.
Overall: Listen. The short and the thick of it is, if you've been starving for a close combat multiplayer game that took what was fun about the Dark Souls Multiplayer and improved it enough for it to be an Esport - this is the game for you. You'll overlook it's faults for the enjoyment of the gameplay. If not? Maybe this title is a miss/rent.

Being an avid fan of the first game, I was impressed by the news of a second one being released. The first Sniper Elite was overall a fun game to play, but suffered from significant bugs and a bland storyline. Inspite of having a lackluster story and rigid dialogue, what really gave the first game it's replay value was the immersion into what being a sniper may be like.  The game captured the importance of stealth, precision, and accuracy of executions in lieu of the run-and-gun Call of Duty fad. And can we talk about the bullet cam? Nothing brought joy to my eyes than getting to view the scenic and slow motion video of a well done shot.
This is what Sniper Elite V2 continued to do and even better.
PROS:
*Many of the glitches from the first one have been greatly improved. Yes, there still are the occaisional twitch body, but noe game is pefect.
* The bullet-cam is perfected, now including an x-ray vision kill shot. If something does not call for replay value like seeing a shot to the heart or gonads, then I don't know what does.
*Graphics are your average, but well-done nex-gen console quality.
*V2 allows for more of an open style of gaming. Sniper Elite eventually got boring because it demanded too much stealth to be considered incredibly fun.
* You can shoot Hitler... in the manhood.
CONS:
*Although better than the first, the storyline to V2 still seems bland and kind of monotone: Kill a target, save a target, save world from bomb, kill bigger target.
* The music, although on key to the original Sniper Elite, feels recyled and plays the same rythmn on and on.
* The enemy AI at times could be on par with the most lethal of assassins and at other times equivalent to a 5 year old.
REVIEW: 8.5/10
*Sniper Elite V2 is a solid attempt at reviving the sniper genre to something more than a bunch of twelve year olds no-scoping. If you could get through the rigid storyline and dialogue, this game will keep you busy for hours.

Early Acces Review:
Short version:
This game in one short sentence would be: A survival game a lá DayZ with RPG elements in a post-apocolyptic setting.
Rating so far: 8/10
The game is already pretty fun and i can see a lot of potential coming from the setting, developers and the game so far.
Pros:
- Awesome style
- Clear progression in-game (skill trees, levels, etc.)
- Weapons feel nice and balanced (guns&melee)
Cons:
- Texture pop-in
- Badly optimized
- Collision boxes wonky at some points, making it hard to traverse certain areas or let's you 'sink' into the terrain.
Long review:
The game has a great style throughout the whole game.
The monsters, enviroment, weapons and players all blend well together to give this game a good post-apocolyptic like feeling.
Guns are not super easy to find and it is best to expect to run around with melee for a while or at least use melee as your most viable attacking style.
But that is fine since the game features multiple skills to add things like defending, sneaking (and backstabbing) and flanking bonuses as your level up your character in the different skill trees.
Enemies are not all the same too, there are a couple different types of enemies whihc all have their different way of being a pain in your survival adventures.
For example, there are big, mean, high hp, high hitting monsters called golems which can punch you with their big hands/claws, but there are also human sized ugly guys with lots of humps that explodes when he gets hit.
These all require your to keep in mind their differences and look at how you will attack them or even if you have to run away for now.
The PVP part is pretty straightforward, you have safe zones which are pretty big and you can easily sneak out of base without people waiting you up at the gates.
When you die, you lose all of your gear you had on you at that moment.
In safe zones you can deposit stuff in your global inventory (basically, bank) which you can acces with every one of your characters you have/will have.
So if you die and you put your most valuable gun in your global inventory, you can pick it up with your new character at a safe zone if you so desire.
So far i haven't noticed too much PK-ing and they continue to work on finetuning how PK-ing works.
They just added somethign so that when you kill a player, you get blood on yourself which makes it easier for the Nether (the enemies) to find you, thus making it a lot harder once you decide to go on a full out rampage.
As for the amount of bugs and quirks, there are quite some out there.
I have had multiple times that i was under the ground after crouching in a certain spot for example, or that you couldn't crouch walk somewhere it looked like you could.
My computer is pretty high end, but the framerate isn't too good when putting every graphical setting on highest.
I hope to see some optimizations and bug fixes in the future and from what i can see from the patch notes, they have alrady been working on that, so i am pretty sure they will be able to optimize this game in the future even more for an optimal experience.

2015's installment of the annual Duels of the Planeswalkers video game is, in a word, mediocre.
In contrast to previous Duels games, Duels 2015 allows you to freely construct decks from one large card pool, rather than providing you with a selection of pre-constructed decks that cannot be mixed and matched. One might expect this to lead to a wider variety of decks seeing play, and to allow for greater individual self-expression. To an extent, this is the case. In practice, however, the fact that any card available to one deck is available to
decks means that, for balance reasons, Duels 2015's card pool ends up feeling somewhat bland and mechanically tame by comparison to some of the more exciting and idiosyncratic decks available in past games (such as my personal favorites, the "Up to Mischief" Faeries deck and the "Lords of Darkness" Demons deck from Duels 2014). That said, the open card pool was executed about as well as it could be; while there are a few deck archetypes that are clearly much stronger than others, that's the case no matter how you're playing Magic, and the higher-rarity (and therefore, theoretically, higher-power) cards being restricted to fewer copies in a deck than cards of lower rarities helps keep things unpredictable and forces you to play a little more thoughtfully.
With only a few exceptions, I found the AI battles in the single-player campaign also less interesting than the single-player encounters in previous Duels games. I did, however, appreciate the "Explore [Plane]" function, which added a quite large chunk of content to the game without tediously bulking out the single-player campaign.
Duels 2015's multiplayer function is actually a step backwards from the fairly basic multiplayer options of Duels 2014. The popular Two-Headed Giant team play mode is no longer available; the only options are two-player duels and three- or four-player free-for-alls. A minor loss, weighed objectively, but it stings disproportionately. I also, for the life of me, cannot figure out how to make the "invite player" function work for multiplayer matchmaking.
Duels 2015's user interface is, frankly, obnoxious. While the animations for the various menus may be slick and polished, they also add quite a bit to the time necessary to navigate them. It quickly becomes tedious. Additionally, it is frequently unresponsive to mouse-clicks, requiring several clicks of a button or rolls of the mouse wheel to have any effect. Something as simple and routine as clicking "Start" on the game's initial loading screen to access the main menu should not be an effort-intensive chore, but it is. If mere clunkiness was not enough to condemn this game, I have on more than one occasion
, which is absurd.
Many people have complained that Duels 2015 is "pay-to-win," in that the cards available only in the Premium Boosters that must be purchased with cash rather than unlocked through play offer deck-builders a substantial advantage. It's true that there are several cards only available through Premium Boosters that are quite useful, but at best the Premium collection takes bad decks up to mediocre; it is trivial to build a competitive deck with only the base collection. Especially with that in mind, Premium Boosters are unquestionably overpriced.
In summary, while there are definitely worse ways to spend $9.99, just buy Duels 2014 instead.

6/10  - One of the best shooters I've seen, that took some weird directions in its design that are complicated...
Good:
- Great Solid First Person Shooter
- Cool Weapons and effects
- Great AI
- Good Graphics
- Smooth Gameplay
- Ridable Ships and Tanks and much more
- Great Stage Design
- Good Music
- Decent FOV
- Shooting range to train in
- Good Voice Acting for the dialog spoken
- Love the Scifi world and Tech
- Cool mechanic that marks Leader orders on the map for the team to follow
- Lots of maps
BAD:
- No STORY... absolutely no dam idea what your fighting for or why its important, factions are just introduced fighting and you go in and shoot... this isnt like other shooters like COD or Battlefield, which at least can pretend to be based off of real life... this is another world, another galaxy, with no lore at all... you just shoot things.... albeit really cool things , a comic would help this out...or some depth to each faction or at least a likable character or two to introduce you.
- Intro and main menu were AMAZINGLY beautiful with 3d ships and bases rendred with the actual ingame engine, now its weird colorful still images of soldiers kinda sliding by, just seems like a big step down..all the awe and wonder kind of vanished, but maybe I just liked the space and scifi aspect more idk.
- UI / Interface is ....difficult to understand, I'm trying to warm up to it... as developers they must be used to it... but a new player will run like their life depends on it. Or stay and be confused as to how things work beyond main goals (take out the thing with the shield on it? how exactly?),The UI is nice and pretty, dont get me wrong, but the key parts like weapons and a few ingame objectives and functions are hard to get, and those matter the most.
- High learning curve.... this comes from the UI and trying to explain the game to others, for them just figuring out whats going on and how to use things or where to spawn was a challenge... the developers should focus on training , hints, and introduction to the equips, even if its an audio clip... the game is made...but its presentation is not complete...(How do you use the weapons?, how do you do certain objectives?, get tanks and vehicles on the ground maps?, selecting team leader vs AI?, Dropships and storming enemy ships? etc)
- Battle across the cosmos no women allowed... just a gripe of mine with shooters... In the future females still can't be part of what I can only understand as a large important battle for humanity... well... considering the armor style I guess it makes sense for women to be excluded... also a club in there that may explain things...
- Just little things that make a player pickup the game, understand whats going on, jump in and want to be part of the conflict. Rather than see alot of options and layouts, scratch their head put the game down for another time.
CONCLUSION / TL:DR
The odd changes to the main menu and difficult UI in terms of picking weapons and knowing objectives. Also learning the game takes time, combined with the lack of story may ward some players away, but underneath is an incredible shooter that does everything right as far as mechanics, AI, gameplay modes, usable vehicles, scenery , music, voice overs , and more... This game is a Beautiful fully functioning Sports Car or Jet plane, that is scratched all over with no paint job... functions perfectly, but not enough people look at it, so no one knows...and the manual is in another language... and its a shame...because it seems they are adding unnecessary parts rather than glossing it up.

Kingwom Wars I still remember my thrill when I heard about this game being released. If I had to explain this game in one sentence it would be: The game is like Travian, Tribal Wars, ... but in real time 3D RTS mode.
I have little play time on steam, that is because steam release was buggy at start, it payed off more to play using official launcher, meaning not using steam. The gameplay is simple, you start with a town which you upgrade. It has no deep depth of techology, it is rather simple and straight forward. You do not even need super strong economy to get decent army. I mostly play Elfs since I find their economy and troops most suitable to me (Archers :) ). Game has single player and multiplayer side which do no differ too much. You can play singleplayer offline with no problems, multiplayer gets you closer to other players. Multiplyer is same as singleplayer but you can go into CO-OP battles with other players, either with or against them. Maximum players inbattle are 2v2, which is kinda limiting. Guild/Clan/Alliance has meaning in terms helping each other during attacks. Game itself looks like Total wars series where troops and cities are managed on global map, while battle itself is in spirit of total war series where 2 armies clash. Combat system is same as with total war series archers(mounted, foot, crossbows), infantry(heavy knights, pikemen, swordsmen), cavalry (one type mounted knight, elfs have mounted archers), monsters with orcs etc. Each unit formation could lvl till 20 and had stat points for you to manually upgrade which provides decent ammount of depth. Each unit type has its special skills, where some have to be researched using crows, which are acquired with battles and quests.
At start it was that simple, during time game developers kept close contact with comunity and invested great time to fixing bugs and providing new content. At release time game was once time purchase, now it is free to play model with premium. New content added mages, dragons, dwarfs, new heroes/special units, sieges but for all of it you need massive ammount of crowns which arent easy to get. There are also some bugs where you spend 250 crowns, but s*it happens, server reverses your upgrade and town state and u lose 250 crowns which finally made me quit game.
Game itself is fun and worth playing, developers are moving forward and wont forsake the game, but KW2 is comming and you can feel that they are more focused on that release. Have fun it is nice game.

Big fan of Smash Up!, owning a physical copy and becoming very excited upon finding it online. But like some other people have found through play, the online copy is extremely rough and not an enjoyable experience. Just by playing three games against bots I ran into various errors in gameplay mechanics, such as minion powers not being calculated properly upon base breakage, issues in card effect sequences, and base powers not triggering correctly. It is quite frustrating to have a base break and not get the correct amount of points. Fundamentals like this have a huge impact on enjoyability. I also found the card interactions to be rather clunky, lacking a fluidity that doesn't seem like it would be too hard to implement.
Another complaint is the online due to the lack of players. Since the game itself is rather unrefined I am not surprised there is a very small player base. The chat is virtually non-existent most likely to stymie any potentially negative dialogue, swearing, etc, but this really impacts game start ups as you can't communicate with others if you should wait for more players or just get started.
The small faction base is another source of disappointment, as part of the fun of the original game is the expansions with their diversity of factions. This feels like a really rushed product that is not worth a $15 investment whatsoever. These issues will most likely be a deterrent to newbie players and veterans alike. This is extremely sad is it is an addictively fun card game and an improved game would be quite enjoyable even with only bots to play against. Really hope the game is fixed up in the future, but until things change stay away!

Both Necrologue and Twilight of the Archaic (a sort of expansion to the mod) do a good job of reproducing the Penumbra atmosphere, so if you didn't get enough and simply must have more, you should definitely give these a try. The main problem, however, is that it is just more of the same. Too much for its own good, and most of it is just filler while you backtrack through empty recycled locations, mostly borrowed from Requiem. Necrologue takes about twice as long to complete as both of the original games combined, with Twilight taking about as long as Requiem. It's certainly cool to see how old locations tie together to form a believable station, but it also evokes a strong feeling of deja vu.
Storywise, there is nothing really new here either and Necrologue mostly just ruins the good plot points from Black Plague by resurrecting fallen characters and pretending their deaths didn't happen. As much as I disliked the official ending, it did a good job of tying the story off, making the likes of Necrologue unnecessary. The writing is quite bad, with notes and diary entries being outright cringeworthy. There is even some nonsense about genetic experiments and superhumans in Twilight of the Archaic. Computer terminals couldn't be reproduced correctly on the Amnesia engine and should have been omitted altogether, instead of leaving cryptic manuals explaining how to close programs with the Jump key. New enemy types look like something out of Silent Hill and do not make much sense. Many of the puzzles feel like busy work, especially in Twilight.
None of it is nearly as good as Penumbra was, and while the atmosphere and the terror are still there, both Necrologue and Twilight of the Archaic are mostly boring and just tarnish good memories with cheesy, unnecessary endings.
