Okay, I know my game time is not enough for some of you. But hear me out... And of course take your time reading this.
Now in all honesty, Kingdom Wars has it's ups and downs. Let's not forget this is a review...
Now let's get down to business shall we?
First off the game is amazing to some (If not most) gamers who prefer Real Time Strategy games. Now this game, has that kind of gameplay. But in this game you have two kinds of maps... The local map, and the World map. Now I know this sounds pretty straight forward. But if you're confused on what I mean by local map, and world map. Let me explain. The local map is the map you're currently playing on. Be it your City or just a battleground. Now the world map. Is used to access these other local maps. But you can access your city all the time, anytime. (Except during a battle)
Now on to the game itself. The game has a lot of bugs, like some quests don't get completed or you can't do some quests because the game bugged on you now you have a quest you cannot finish. But with that aside.. The game features the basic "Group troops" meaning that let's say you train a Swordsman. You don't get A swordsman. You get a group of swordsmen, And they can replenish their health over time and increase in number again. (If you have played Dawn of War or any other game that has this feature then you'll understand this quite quickly)
Now the controls itself is a bit "off" for most. Since it is a bit sluggish and downright broken at some point. But that doesn't mean that the game is unplayable. It is in fact more challenging to actually move your units to where you want. Rather than the fighting itself. But luckily the developers actually do fix these things (Provided it gets reported to their forums or something) and they release a patch to fix it.
Now most of you want to ask the same question I asked before? "Is it pay to win?"
I'll tell you.. It's not pay to win, yes you may get some Booster packs. But that isn't going to help you win if you just mindlessly charge your units to their deaths. (Trust me.. I got experience of this. But I didn't buy anything.) But the game actually rewards you for your time on it. Yes, it may be a bit long. But think of this game as a hobby or something. Because you can't really stay on for a long time. Especially when you have battle protection (Battle Protection timer moves when you're online!)
And also I did mention about the time based rewards. Now it's not really that the devs are gonna give you rewards based on how long you play.. No, that's not it. The Time Based reward is that you've built up your city and now you can do anything you need to do. Be it getting resources, building armies, heck even gathering the In-game special currency of Crowns! (By the way you can convert your resource Gold into Crowns in-game. And no.. This does not cost you real money.)
So to end this review. Since I'm quite losing myself in my own words. This game is a bit like a Beta that needs more fixing, but is already good enough to play. Not saying it's a GREAT game, but a good enough game to play and pass the time.. And remember... Once you start playing, don't let your Storage reach it's cap!
7/10 Play this game to pass the time, and help the devs improve upon their game!

A lot of critics, and it took a good week or two for this game to actually run, but I like it.  I played DotP 2013 and 2014, and DotP 2015 does add quite a bit more with the deck building.  I've played Magic since 1994, and I do not pretend that this game is an exact simulator of the actual card game.  If you have that in mind, this game is fun and offers a challenge.  It is an enjoyable Magic-like game, where you encounter the same themes from MtG cards.  If you buy all the best cards, to craft the same deck some other person conceptualized and won a tournament at, to stomp everyone you meet, you won't enjoy this.  You actually have to think and work at it.  Consider it a draft, where you get what you get and have to craft something usable to beat the competition's better deck.  Yes, it might take a while and be frustrating at times, but why buy/play a game that you can just walk through with no effort?  I'm having fun and have beaten several of the opponents.  i'm looking forward to many hours of fighting/struggling to get through.  Put yourself in the right frame of mind, and have some fun!

If you've ever played the Epic War flash games, it's like you have your base send units against their units until you kill their base. You can give orders to your units of course, but the unit control is pretty straight forward. Advance, hold or retreat. Now I dont know how many different kinds of missions there are going to be. But for the most part to my understanding, you have to defend your base and build up an army to be able to go out and destroy theirs. There's usually hidden goodies laying around off the path between bases. This was the first mission in the alpha, and I was already going to enjoy the game as it was just like that.
Now there's an open exploration mission (the new first mission) and honestly it was alot of fun just going to all the objectives and seeing what I could find between them and getting ambushed a few times. There's ruined buildings and there used to be a dungeon but I think that's down for maintenence at the moment as there's rocks blocking the door to the dungeon. There's been alot of small little surprises added every update that honestly make it pretty fun to play through all the missions each update. Now by this I dont mean "wow an entire epic dungeon that wasnt there before" in every level each update. Once there was a small dungeon added with a little orc guy patroling around which made it come to my attention, this time there's trees and hidden goodies laying around inside them.
This game makes my inner nerd come out because of what it's growing into. There's currently only one type of hero you can recruit, the warrior, and as basic as that sounds, he has a skill tree and randomized stats when you recruit him. I cant wait to see all the different hero types and what all their skill trees will be like.
I've talked to the dev about potential ideas alot before, so I'm probably more excited than I should be. There's alot of thigns he wants to do that I wont throw out there because people will complain if it doesnt make it in. It's mostly just ideas that would be cool if they made it in the game and whatnot. But I'm so excited to see how this game grows. But dont be a stranger, talk on the discussion board and see what all this game can grow into.

I think you will need to enjoy the reading aspect, at least to a light degree; if you don't and just want to skim-read the story or click through randomly, then you may miss the point (and your way), as the real charm of this game is in it's "dynamic writing", and how these literary adventures tie in with your race against the clock.
One thing I was particularly dubious about before playing was mention of the steampunk aspects, such as walking cities, as I thought these may destroy the immersion ... however the steampunk is not an odd distraction but rather a fundamental and fully integrated component of this Jules Verne version of Earth, and as such plays a full and refreshing role in each story, that could otherwise I think have felt rather stale.

What an amazing game. A literary classic told through fitting music, charming art that while simple never becomes boring and surprisingly deep and involving game mechanics. I was physically unable to stop my journey once it had first begun, and though much of it was played relatively safe there was still plenty of close shaves and action which made the entire experience one of the best adventures I've had in a game in recent memory. Sadly, I did not make the first trip in 80 days, in part due to poor planning but also from being marooned on a small island in the middle of the pacific ocean where Mr. Fogg almost left his senses. I am already excited to start my next playthrough, with so much of the world left to discover I believe it won't be the last one, either.
If I had to have one complaint, only one, it is that I felt like I experienced an abnormally high amount of female characters compared to male ones. From my start in London, over Paris, Copenhagen, into Russia and across the middle east, East-Asia to New Zealand and into the dark heart of Africa and back into Europe, the amount of male characters I encountered could be counted on one hand (and left me wondering where they all were. Replaced by automatons?). On one hand it was humours, given the game takes places in an (albeit fictional) period of time where women were not often seen in these very male-centric professions, on the other the almost total lack of male characters (and the game at one point describing a grizzled boiler-room engineer as a petite Indian women in a beautiful sari) took a little away from the overall immersion, and I had to wonder if it was intentional or if my route just happened to let me encounter every possible pilot, captain and engineer of the feminine persuasion. Either way, I guess I'll see if this changes on my further adventures.

Charming, intelligent, and moving; a steampunk-flavoured choose-your-own adventure brought to life by spare but lovely visuals.  The writers and programmers have created a rich and beautiful world burgeoning with fantastical mechanical conveyances and automata, burgeoning with old traditions and fomenting revolutions.  You play as one Monsieur Passepartout, loyal French valet to the phlegmatic and inscrutable Phileas Fogg, gentleman explorer and Englishman's Englishman, encountering men and women of all nationalities, political persuasions and walks of life.
As the player, you are never told what to think or believe, and you may shape your own character to be as sceptical or open-minded, as cynical or trusting, as you wish, although, as in real-life travel, the greatest rewards come from openness, curiosity, and acts of kindness.  The interface and inventory is simple but effective, presenting the player with choices in dialogue, traveling routes, and buying and selling of items, with the constraints of time and money encouraging resourcefulness and essential tradeoffs.  Will you attend to your master's wishes, or pursue your own romance?  Go whale-hunting, or play it safe?  Help out the revolutionaries, or the local colonial government?  Cannot recommend this one highly enough.

The video is a template of "How not to Make a Good Fan Service Anime".
In general, this anime is more or less a replica of the well-received Nekopara game, which in fact restricts its manners to express the characters. The staff struggled to make every second, every frame to act exactly same as the game, which turned out to be overkill.
The graphics is of decent quality, defeating most of the OVAs and quite a few popular animes available on the market. A few defects are visible, but they do not affect the main experience. (However, I am still disappointed of this "decent" quality considering this being a million-dollar kickstarter project.)
The hero, Kashou, is a voiceless character in the game. The anime provided a quality act and design of the character,
The framework of two main characters, Chocola and Vanilla, was not even built within first ten minutes. All the audience saw was something they would have viewed in the game, which had been only 2 minutes long even if they do not skip the dialogue. On the other hand, a newcomer may be lost what the anime is about.
The plot goes on in a stream of consciousness (not the good side of it). Things jump out without a foreshading. Fir example, characters suddenly decided to run outside, like just because they came up with it, but not because of a progress of the plot. After Chocola ran outside the screen, the hero suddenly walked in the park with her in the next scene, like he had superpower and could teleport.
Understanding cat girls act and think differently from human, it must be noticed that their emotions must be expressed in a way the audience can follow and empathise. The cat girl laughs in one cut, and suddenly bursts into tears in the next - this happens and loops a few times in the anime, and the viewer simply won't get why. I would agree this expression style would work well in a drama show, but doubt its effectiveness in an anime.
Though it is subjective to judge a voice actor, I would state that the actors are not doing as good as in the games.
Most part of the anime looks simply like a celluloid coloured version of the game (this become annoying when I realise the game already has Live2D). A speaking charater occasionally stands in the far corner of the scene. In the scene where Coconut eats a whole piece of cake, the cake seems to disappear from the spoon rather than being swallowed.
In conclusion, a $15 Kickstarter backer tag is fair for this piece of work, but you won't want to spend a full $30 on it.
My personal opinion? If they proceed to release a sequel, I will be a backer the first time without hesitation. After all, Nekopara's been one of my favourite character combination since Chocola was still called Chocolate.

Although the game is still in early release and I think the game could have potential if some of the gaming mechanics are tweaked, the biggest let downs on game are it's core components, PVP, Loot and Leveling.
Player interaction - every person I have encountered are hostile so you can't team up, and they only seem to camp safe zones popping off new players searching for items to enter PVP with; so its knief vs automatic rifle or sniper!
Loot - If you can get away from spawn sites before campers get you, finding loot isn't too hard, but carrying limits are way too high to make it a valuable practice as you have to get past campers again to sell it.
Killing Nether is pretty easy but after killing 36 of them in a row, they didn't drop a single item and I only levelled twice, so I can see why camping is so practical in this game which makes it worthless.
Levelling - Whats the pont?  As soon as you die, you're back to level 1, all that grinding for nothing, I can understand losing loot on your person when you die as long as you could store provisions in a safe zone, but losing levels only feeds PVP camping and defeats the purpose of having a levelling system.
In short good idea and potentials there but until the camping and levelling is sorted I'm staying clear; the bugs I could live with but pointless mechanics make this a waste of time.

UPDATE JULY 2015:
The game has now received a major patch, 10 years after the release, which is crazy! This makes it easier to recommend, since the patch allows you to play in higher screen resolutions, has a neat selection of achievements and most imprortantly allows the Steam version to install the famous Restored Content Mod. This replaces a significant amount of the cut scenes and dialogue, thus improving the story a great deal.
n.b. - neither the patch nor the mod fixes the litany of bugs that plague KotOR 2 (some of which can be game breaking). 'The Sith Lords' remains an unfinished game and something of a chore to run - but what works is still very high quality, and now there is more of it.
====
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
====
Knights of the Old Republic 2 had an extremely hard act to follow (Bioware's original is damn near perfect) and very little time to do it in. That a game this good was written and put together in only a year speaks volumes about Obsidian's skill with role-playing and story.
Gameplay, graphics, sound and pesentation are near identical to KotOR. Though little improvements have been added everywhere from the voice acting to the design of the Jedi robes, it almost feels like a very compehensive mod more than a game of its own. But KotOR's strength is the immersive, rich adventure it adds to the Star Wars mythology, and this sequel wisely puts all of its effort into the same area, with impressive results.
The plot follows immediately from the original (playing the sequel first is not recommended) and follows a similar structure and creates a similar lead character, but the much darker, more thoughtful tone becomes apparent immediately and just keeps growing. The great strength of KotOR 2 is its cast of characters - especially your mysterious mentor Kreia and sidekick-with-a-past Atton. These two (and a few others) are written and played with a subtlety and depth that the first game lacks even in its best moments, and manage to create a rivalry between the two games. KotOR is consistently fantastic, but KotOR 2 has moments of something better. It's a more cerebral, more thematic, sober affair than almost any other Star Wars story out there, and all the better for it. Where the first game apes the films to a fault, the sequel is compellingly unique.
It can't be denied that the game is buggy, inconsistent in its difficulty, tone and plot, very linear in places and has a very flawed ending (developers have admitted having to cut large sections to meet unreasonable deadlines) to the point of its last hour being barely compehensible. The first 90% of the game is solid, but newcomers should expect some headscratching during the endgame. It's not a gamebreaker, but it does marr (ha) the overall product.
Its confusing cliffhanger ending was eventually resolved in a disappointing novel from Del Rey, but the game itself may leave you frustrated. That said, the not-quite-finished product is packed with exceptional characters, moments of brilliant dialogue and world-building, and the overall gameplay remains great fun. The game experiments a little too, helping to develop the Bioware-style RPG model: you are able to train followers to become Jedi knights, for example, strongly effecting their character arc and role in gameplay. Some missions require you to play without your party, or without your player character. Puzzles often require creativity and thought and can have multiple outcomes.
For fans of quality RPG writing and those looking for a darker, more pensive Star Wars - and especially for those who enjoyed KotOR - it's an easy recommend.
Expect broken rooms, missing voice files and a deeply confusing plot. But for a year's work, it's amazing.

I usually do idle games on my phone, but this one looked neat so I decided to give it a try. Good choice. Though it's still an idle game and thus primarily something that's happening on its own, the sheer amount of options makes it a lot more involved and allows different players to actually progress in different ways. Some of the features actually have negative effects, so it makes you keep on your toes rather than just throwing your resources at everything in front of you.
I've now got over 1000 hours in on this and there's no cap in sight. And if there WAS it might not be there long, because the developer is very active and frequently adding new features and tweaking old ones--so it's basically part of the gameplay to keep adjusting to which features have become more or less powerful.
It's a nice fun thing to have going on in the background. It doesn't make noise, and doesn't interfere if you want to run a second Steam game at the same time.

Going to be completely honest here, this is one of those games where you have to put time into it to see that it's a hidden gem buried under a bad reputation.
I can tell you right off the bat, the voice acting in this game is semi-lame, the dialogue is semi-cheesy, the running animations look like your character has a damn d*ldo in his buttcheeks, and I'm not trying to hate on it nor am I trying to be funny, it really does lol. The camera also seems to be a little motion-sickness inducing for some but personally it doesn't bother me, this is coming from someone that gets motion sickness very easily in car rides, and a tiny bit in VR. HOWEVER, as a fan of The Elder Scrolls series and open world games in general who has put hundreds of hours into Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim, I can tell you that this game is like a poor mans version of those games but in 3rd person....... and it does a surprisingly good job. It's nowhere near as bad as the first one was, though the first one is really fun if you give it a little time, it'll catch you off guard. I think the biggest thing that hurt the first game was that the voice acting was absolute dog sh*t to the point it almost felt deliberately comical, and the animations were like staring at a flip book, literally.
As for Two Worlds II, The magic system in this game is amazing, giving you the ability to create your own magic spells, similar to TES Morrowind (the old game, not the ESO dlc), for those of you familiar with that. If you're into magic then I'd honestly say the magic system in this game alone is a reason to buy the game, no joke. Personally I hate playing mages but this game makes being a mage so much fun. Probably one of the best spell systems I've ever seen. The melee combat is somewhere in between fluid and clunky, but feels alright. You can also buy your own house in the game. You can upgrade any weapon or armor as well as dismantle them. You can enchant them with different kinds of gems and can even fuse gems to make them more powerful. There is an arena mode in the main story campaign, but you can't access it just yet (reminds me of the arenas from Fable 1 and 2). You can increase your reputation with different factions, and from what I understand this makes prices cheaper when buying from merchants (at least that's how it worked in the first game so I'm not sure about this one). The world map itself is pretty big, with plenty of quests that don't really feel like fetch quests, there's some good variety in the game. There are tons of different enemies to face.
The story itself is okay and seems to pick up after the first game, but seems done a lot better in this one. The multiplayer in this game is surprisingly really fun and addicting, you just join a server and jump in with your friend in a starting town which acts as a social hub and you're able to play missions with your friends or alone. There are different types of modes such as Duel, Deathmatch, Adventure Mode (quests to do), some sort of Defend your base mode?, hell you can even buy a village once you have enough money and can upgrade it and defend it, etc. Multiplayer runs solid, I played with my loved one and neither of us had any problems.
The game runs really well, ran it on both computers, i7 6700K 4.00ghz overclocked, GTX 1080ftw, 32gb ram as well as an i5 3.2ghz, 16gb ram, GTX 970 and had zero issues, no frame drops, no crashes, nothing. Even on an older rig I had years ago with 4gb ram and a dual core with a GT 240 card this game still ran fine. I've seen some people saying the game runs like garbage, and maybe for some the game does, but it's hard to tell whether or not it's the game or simply just their machine and they're too dumb to realize it, but Idk for sure.
Anyways, I recommend getting the game when it goes on sale again, and maybe even pick it up for a friend because personally I think it's worth it. There may have been a few things I missed in this review, but I will say this...... don't listen to what I or anybody else says about the game, the only way you'll really know if it's worth your time is if you give it a chance and invest a substantial amount of time into it (10 hours no less) before deciding. It's sad to see a game that is surprisingly really good and with much potential get sh*t on over an unstable foundation it was built upon. Don't be close minded. I'm not saying it's the best game among it's type, but it's certainly far from complete garbage that's for sure. (My opinion of course).

Smash Up is a fantastic card game for up to four players.  The basic rules are very simple.  And as long as you have at least one person who knows what's going on, the game is very easy to follow.
Smash Up, the digital game, however, is a mess.  It's still Smash Up.  It's still kind of fun if you REALLY, REALLY like Smash Up, but the UI and the way you interact with the cards is horrendous.  It's a mess.  It's clunky.  It's hard to follow.  And, with what little experience I had with this game, not many people were playing online.  That means you're stuck playing against bots.  That means you're stuck playing against bots with the vanilla game's factions (plus Geeks).
I do have high hopes for the game, though.  If they dramatically improve the user interface and add drag-and-drop functionality, this game could be a winner.  It's frusturating that they failed to copy an already great existing UI - Hearthstone.  Just copy that.  I can picture it in my head right now.  Copy that and you're golden.
I think hardcore fans of the card game will struggle to find a reason to stick wtih the digital version for very long.  It's just not ready for primetime.   And it's certainly not worthy of your $14.99.  Pass... for now.

I love Smash Up, I own the physical game and a couple of the expansions. It is one off my favorite games to play. So, you understand why I was excited when this came out.
But so far, I'm kind of disappointed. I've only tested it out a few times (versus the bot)  and already have come across issues where some cards don't play right, or do something they shouldn't have done.
For instance, in the Trickster faction, there is a card that prevents an opponent from playing actions on their next turn. I played this against the bot anf then, on it's next turn, they played an action! This shouldn't have happened, since my card should've blocked it.
Some of the other issues I encountered might just be down to the game's understanding of the language used on the cards. In one game I played an Armored Stego coupled with an action that protected it from an ability. On my next turn I played an action that allowed me to select one of my played minion's power score and destroy the opponents minions there (with power less than my minion). I chose my Stego (power 3) and the bot's minions (all power 2) should've been destroyed. Instead what happened is it only destroyed the action attached to my Stego. The action attached to the Stego dictated it's destruction if an ability would AFFECT the Stego. The action I played to destroy my opponent's minions didn't affect the Stego. It wouldn't have been destroyed, moved, or returned to my hand. The action merely allowed me to select that Stego's power score, not affecting it in any way.
Because of this misunderstanding in the card's language, my Stego was destroyed and the opponent won the game.
These are extremely frustrating problems that I hope will be fixed. Once they are, i'm sure this will be a much better game.

As it is the first Duels of the Planeswalkers to really focus on building your own decks, releasing you from merely playing pre-constructed decks or that poorly implemented draft mode of 2014. I'd reccommend this game to anyone interested in MTG, and fans of the series.

While the card pool could always be more expansive, and therefore, better, the available cards selection is already pretty good in the base game, something I imagine they will add onto as they release DLC throughout the year.
I would not, recommend buying any of the 'unlock' DLC, for it merely allows you to use all the cards you can easily open up for free by actually playing the game. Another Con would be the lack of planeswalker cards (despite the name) , and the lack of any new modes, much like the previous three years introduced. But For only $10, and the ability to make your own decks, I think this is worth a purchase.

80 Days is essentially a choose your own adventure story inspired by the Jules Verne novel
, set in a steampunk Victorian world with mechanical automatons, airships, a walking city, and further fantastical marvels. The game places you in its narrative as the valet of Phileas Fogg, a gentleman adventurer propelled onward by a wager to circumnavigate the globe within the titular 80 day period. On this journey you will explore the world's cities as you chart your own course to make it back to London before the clock runs out, balancing Fogg's health and your monetary funds as you plot and trade your way across the world.
As 80 Days is essentially a text-based game (though it is dressed up quite a bit with an attractive interface and travel graphics reminiscent of the
movies), its success lives or dies on the quality of its writing - and it manages to live quite large. The story woven in your character's journal is superbly written, and you find yourself heavily engaged as you decide the course your character will take and the way they react to events while exploring the game's cities and interacting with some of its characters.
It is a short game - easily playable in just a couple of hours depending on how well you do -, but features fantastic replayability. Though I'm not usually one to revisit a game like this, I'll certainly be going on another journey soon, as there's just so many different cities to visit, and you could easily play the game many different times before repeating a single step of your journey. Adding to this is that the game's parameters change as you play through on different starting seeds (there are 8, which you advance through in order with each subsequent playthrough), each slightly altering items available for trade, available travel routes and departure times, as well as introducing new elements to the game's story.
It's a cute little game that I thoroughly enjoyed - well worth the low price of its $10 entry.

Let's clear a few things up from the beginning:
-This is not a difficult game - I was able to make it around the world in less than 60 days my first playthrough without so much as discomfiting Mr. Fogg.  Although it is possible to "lose", winning and losing are not really what this is about.
-This is not a particularly "fun" game.  The pacing and story-bound nature of this title don't really lend themselves to instant gratification.  It is far more contemplative than that.
-This isn't really a "game" at all.  As other have mentioned, it is much more a choose-your-own adventure book, heavily steeped in a strange alternate reality that we might call steampunkish, but which is really a close modern approximation of what Jules Verne's imagination produced.  If you don't enjoy reading, steer clear of this one.
With all that out of the way, I really enjoyed my first play through, and look forward to completing several more.  I think the format of the game lends itself well to multiple replays, as there are numerous routes and methods at your disposal to get from one place to the next, and the time requirement makes visiting more than a handful of locations during a single playthrough difficult. How replayable it is after more than a handful of playthroughs is debatable.  I'd guess that after about 4 or 5 circuits (about 8-10 hours) you'd have exhausted many of the locations and dialogue, and it might start to get a bit stale.
My only real gripes are that the interface is slightly wonky for keyboard and mouse, as it was designed for iOS.  I had a hard time figuring out how to get from "planning" back to where you could go to the bank, etc while in a city.  Turns out you have to click on the city you're currently in to go back.  Also, it should be noted that on PC this title is 10 bucks, whereas on iOS, it is 5.  I think the experience lends itself better to a tablet as well.  So there's that.
Overall, if you enjoy books and reading, and especially if you are a Verne fan, you'll likely love this.  If you dislike reading and are looking for action and excitement, you'll probably hate it.  If you have an iPad, consider getting it on there vice PC.

“I have entered into the service of a new gentleman. It would seem he is a gambling man.” Orchestral music with a sense of urgency starts up as the globe begins to turn around its axis. Right off the bat, 80 Days gives out an intriguing vibe. The journey begins in London and, as everyone knows, follows the adventures of Phileas Fogg as he attempts to circumnavigate the world in 80 days. In this take of the Jules Verne classic novel Around the World in Eighty Days, Fogg takes a backseat to his French servant Passepartout. Players assume the role of the valet who is in charge of picking the route, handling the funds, baggage, and taking care of Fogg himself.
The game distances itself from its inspiration even further thanks to its setting. It is still set in the second half of the 19th century, but 80 Days boldly embraces a steampunk theme and an alternate take on history, which simply makes perfect sense. As you travel the world, you will discover strange means of transportation, automatons, and a mysterious guild of creators called the Artificers. There is something interesting to learn about each city, sometimes without ever even going there.
80 Days is designed as a roguelike and it is intended to be played over and over again, discovering new routes, visiting new places, and experiencing a new story. 80 Days is quite an undertaking regarding the storytelling. There are massive amounts of text here with choices at every turn. Even though the choices primarily impact your experience, sometimes they also have more tangible repercussions. For example, your actions might get you imprisoned in Russia or your intended route might get drastically altered after a scuffle in the middle of the ocean. The most remarkable thing about this game is that each playthrough is totally unique thanks to this emergent method of storytelling. You never know what is going to happen next and where you will ultimately end up, which truly contributes so much to the game’s sense of discovery and wonder.
The writing is interesting and strong throughout. Each part of the trip consist of these lovely mini-stories with unusual and fascinating characters. However, there are also these separate conversations that you can engage in while travelling from point to point and they feel completely different. They are very poorly written and they simply feel completely unnatural. The main purpose of these conversations is to determine new routes and find out information regarding valuable items and trades.
Outside of storyline choices, the gameplay revolves around managing all aspects of the voyage. As Passepartout, you will need to choose the best possible route, taking in mind the price and conditions of each trip. A cheap trip in a run down car or a shanty boat will take its toll on Fogg, lowering his health. He won’t die if his health gets depleted, but he won’t be able to travel any further until he recovers. You can tend to him during travels, or buy items that you can use in order to increase his health points. You can also buy outfit sets. Some sets will nullify negative health points while travelling by train, others will provide bonuses when riding on horseback. Outfits can also help negotiate faster departure times, so that you don’t have to be stuck somewhere for two or more days. Sleeping in hotels instead of the streets with homeless people and dogs will also help keep Fogg’s health up.
Going around the world costs money. There are several ways of earning enough of it to arrive in London on time. You can take out a loan in a bank, but you will have to wait for the money up to a week – depending on how much you want to withdraw. A more efficient way is to buy items along the way and then sell them in cities where they are worth much more. However, this approach may take you off your desired route. But it is actually this kind of unpredictability that is most appealing about 80 Days. It should be noted that you don’t really have to make it back to London in 80 days. You can just explore and go wherever you want. My first playthrough took over 100 days. You can play the game in any way you like. You can race the clock and try to beat your best time, or you can simply unwind and just take in the sights.
Even though the game actually gets more interesting on repeated playthroughs as some additional routes and storylines open up, I have also experienced moments of boredom. Certain stretches just feel a bit laborious and dull. I also have to say that the interface is somewhat clunky, especially when you want to do several things in a hurry (visit the market, check your luggage) before your transport departs.
The game sports a clean art style that is pleasing to the eye. The music is also good, but there is not a lot of variety there. Overall, the production values provide a sufficient amount of atmosphere, but I was left with the impression that more could have been done to give each location a stronger sense of place. For a game that is all about travel and discovery, locations could have had more of an awe-inspiring impact from an audiovisual standpoint.
80 Days is a unique and imaginative game that serves as an apt and worthy homage to its inspiration. It manages to bring so much of its own regarding the storytelling and world-building, and it competently mixes multiple styles of gameplay. This is one grand voyage you should not miss out on.

3D Realms, Triptych Games, Gearbox Software and Piranha Games really knocked it out of the park with this game. After 15 years of development hell the first true masterpiece in video games is here.
The game takes a lot of cues from modernist fiction. Much of the game is about topics such as sadness, loss, addiction, alcoholism, failure, family, mental health, morality, PTSD, fame, chaos, masculinity, spirituality and isolation. The structure of Duke Nukem Forever reinforces this and the entire game is split up into vignettes all structured like a recursive fractalic ionizing radiation symbol.
The game is set years after the first alien invasion and chronicles the post-war life of duke much in the same way the Greek dark age poem The Odyssey talks about Odysseus' struggle with post-war life and the hard transition for him. The game picks up shortly after the alien war. Duke has fallen on hard times, after an unsuccessful spout in politics, his failing business ventures leave him facing bankruptcy. The game switches then to 7 years later, duke is no longer remembered as the savior of earth and is forced into private life as a used car salesman married to a woman who doesn't love him and who is cheating on him. Duke falls into a deep depression and visions of his past haunt him at night, slowly the visions creep into the day and this vignette ends with a violent outburst in which duke believes the aliens have come back to earth.
Now it's 3 years later, duke is an a mental facility dealing with the horrors of his past. His wife has left him and he struggles with a lot of health problems in this chapter. One of the patients in the facility recognizes duke but slowly over the course of the vignette the player realizes that the patient thinks that Duke is the great king Gilgamesh a champion of masculinity from the ancient near eastern epic poem.
Duke next transition is into the desert, set only a year later duke is living on the outskirts of Las Vegas. Duke is forced into an emasculating job as a male ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who is forced to do disgusting acts for peanuts. Duke is slowly drinking himself to death in an attempt to kill the pain in his life. At several times during the course of this phase in his life he wanders drunk through the desert, in the last of this section Duke is lost in the desert for 40 days before reaching civilization and being tested with addiction by a strip club and gives into his desire. This section mirrors the temptation of Christ but twists the ending.
The next section takes place only 3 days later, Duke is an emasculated, mess of a man make impotent by the drink. Duke jumps off the Hoover Dam but fails and lands onto a child.
Duke wakes up in a prison hospital missing his left leg. Duke has been sentenced to life without parole for drug possession and killing the child at the end of the of previous chapter. In the hospital the doctors discover Duke has prostate cancer from the steroids duke took during his youth. Duke loses all masculinity after his surgery and develops into a fat, sexless man confined to a wheelchair. Duke yet again falls into a deep pit of depression and wants to kill himself but just can't do it. It's implied that Duke is bottom to his cell partner. Duke dreams of the aliens from Duke Nukem 3D returning and him regaining his former glory and fame. Duke wakes up and starts crying, he reflects on his life and all the paths that brought him to his current state. Duke hangs himself in his prison cell.
This game is a truly bold move for the franchise and has entered gaming into a brave new world of creativity and story telling.

TLDR: Rage Quest offers a unique and complex battle system that has a bit of a learning curve but is challenging and rewarding to play.
Rage Quest is a game with a simple story and complex gameplay. The game itself is relatively short and took me 6-7 hours to get through when trying to finish all the content. Although the story is dry and parts of the game is clunky and slightly unintuitive the meat of the game, the battle system, is fun and satisfying.
The battle system takes traditional tile based combat and puts a spin on it making timing as well as strategy matter. Removing the traditional turns, each move used by the player as well as enemies has a charge time as well as a cooldown, all visible on the map. This means that timing your actions allows you to and prevents enemies from dodging attacks. The game gives the player three categories to freely sort their actions (abilities, items, movement, defense) into, and only one action from each category can be performed at once. This means that you are able to bring a maximum of 12 different actions into a stage but only 3 can be used at the same time. A player may choose to attack with three different attacks at once but they will not be able to guard or evade while doing so.
All of these aspects gives the combat of Rage Quest surprising depth (as well as somewhat of a steep learning curve). The amount of unique abilities and items allow for a plethora of ways to approach each stage and good balancing helps this. Rage Quest's levels are quite difficult and do not pull any punches even at the beginning. Each encounter is tense but very rewarding to complete, especially when done by a strategy of your own devising (after perhaps failing a few times).
With almost 70 encounters throughout 4 worlds to fight through, Rage Quest provides a decent amount of content for its price.

This is a neat idle game for people already used to how idle games work.
An interesting take on an idle Galaga-esque title, Transport Defender does a great job of balancing those who prefer to play idle, and those who are actively playing. You have the option to freely fire your main cannon, and click to increase your other weapons "overdrive", or damage multiplier.
The game struggles with the idea of ascending/prestiging. The cargo that you receive unlocks upgrades that are poorly explained in the tooltips, so in a lot of circumstances, you're buying something you'll have no clue of the actual usage, but are forced to buy it to progress to the next upgrade set. Eventually you'll get the hang of it, but it's frustrating that the tooltips are long and confusing, rather than short and neat.
Overall, it's a good game to play alongside your other idle game offerings, it's definitely one of the longer idle games I can leave running without having to babysit, and the options for auto-buying weapons and upgrades make it a must-have if "set it and forget it" is your forte.

FULL IN-DEPTH REVIEW. 100% ACCURATE
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
This game is just simply fun. It brings me back to the good old days of Life Sims. In that regard, this game is a European-Life Sim. It's just kooky fun all around.
The atmosphere is relaxing and quirky. You get to play in this big old castle with warm fireplaces at every turn, and plenty of exquisite wine on every shelf.  The music is soothing, and is only matched in that respect by the game's warm, colorful eviroment.
The Story is simple and sweet. You play as a man named Daniel. Daniel is having a vacation in his Uncle Alexander's luxury masion castle. Daniel and Alex have little quirky aventures together while in the caslte, and learn the valuable lesson that family always comes before property and wealth. The in-game story that you can complete through minigames is heartwarming, and really complements the hundreds of hours you will probably spend on various fun attractions in-game.
The Castle is filled with Uncle Alexander's loveable servants, who all have distinct hilarious and quirky personalities. Some are pretty clusmy, and knock over stuff in the castle. It's just funny. Some will even play games with you like Tag and Hide-and-go-seek. Playing these games fills up a "fun" meter that can improve your gameplay experience with various quirks. It's basically like the Fresh Prince's butler, but slightly less Black and more English.
Overall, it's a great, casual game with fun around every corner! I reccomend everyone pick it up.

MFW all the weebs and neckbeards take their autistic screeching from the battlefield to Steam reviews =.=
Taking a break from liberating the holy land to bring you this review:
For Honor has completely reinvigorated the fighting game scene. Best action, hack-n-slash, strategy game I have ever played. There's a hero to match everyone's play style. Do you like to tank in MMOs? Want to
tank hits? Try the Conqueror. Like Assassin's creed? Try Peacekeeper. Just want to play and bash people's brains in? Try the Warden.
Honestly, there's a big learning curve. The first thing you should do is complete the story to get a feel for all of the heroes, and THEN do the AI matches - those AI are pretty challenging! Don't go into PvP not having learned the game and think you 360noscope everyone else.
I see a lot of the complaints about microtransactions...Guess what? YOU DON'T HAVE TO BUY STEEL TO BE GOOD AT THIS GAME. The only big ticket items are the cosmetics. All of the heroes can be unlocked with the Steel you get for completing the basic and advanced tutorials. Additionally, you can spend ~$20 to unlock all of the feats (skills) for your heroes, OR you can take 1-2 hours for each hero and level them to 21. This is more of a convenience factor, because it is extremely easy to unlock all the feats.
I do agree with the other reviews on the connectivity issues. Sometimes my friend and I have to restart our games because there's an error with our connectivity or whatever. It's pretty annoying and Ubisoft definitely needs to address these issues.
Overall, if you appreciate smooth AAA-graphics, like a good challenge, and aren't afraid of dying a lot, then this game is a must for you.

-sigh- This is me rewriting a review for a game that I truly believed in. I have nearly 200 hours in the game, which probably makes it look weird that I'm recommending that you spend your money elsewhere. Just hear me out. Let's just make a pros and cons list:
Pros -
Monsters in the game are super awesome -- concept-wise that is.
The game's "story" and concept are great. The story isn't really known though or even spoken about in game.
Cons -
Anybody remember War Z/Infestation Survivor Stories? Well, this game has kinda fallen into that category.
The game is unfinished, no matter what anybody says -- some buildings are unfurnished or don't even have stairs to climb them, there are a lot of spots where you can clip through something that would otherwise be solid in any other universe and the overall game play mechanics seem a bit janky.
There are only a small variety of monsters to fight.
I previously would've said this is a great pack-rat game, but they've limited your space in bank, so... Nevermind...
The devs don't really listen to the players.
Feels like ever since Puppet left, hackers haven't been getting taken care of.
The support team is not super responsive or helpful when they do respond.
PvP is very rampant with hackers -- this is not technically a problem with the game, just the people; but it IS a problem nonetheless.
Let's just have on the record that I REALLY appreciate the pros of this game; but, there is no way in hell that some cool monsters and a practically ignored back story can save this game for me.
So, be wary if you wanna try out this game. It was once a game of huge potential, but I think the devs lost a lot of interest in it, which tanked the community and the overall fun of the game.
If you are considering picking up this game, I highly recommend you don't. There are plenty of better and more finished games out there.

However the counter continues to count down even when you're not logged in. In Kingdom Wars the counter only goes down when you're LOGGED IN! Meaning if you need to take a break and let things farm in the background you can sign off and come back later without loosing that starting protection.

Here is my final review for the release game.  I had to change my thumbs up to down, but I hope someday to turn that back around.
First off, I love the concept of the game.  This game shows a lot of potential and I believe someday it will come through.
Second: the final release is missing key components that I would advise people to wait for at least a year, possibly two before buying the product as it.
The first issue is Game Master management.  Game master management is an essential tool for running an MMO, MUD, or other server in a way that an end user playing the game cannot understand.  To keep GM workload under control you should have a a screen that runs seperate from the game, you need to have extensive user control tools that allow the game master to isolate and talk with a problem player, to record chat and actions on selected players, and increase or decrease stats, plus run server variables and camera shadow players.
The second issue is that the building art is limited.  In a game where you do not hand design buildings, you should be able to reset building facades. This is not implemented.
Third, while there is a coin system after a fashion, there should be a GM controlled money system in place.  Again this should be handled by a control panel.
Finally, under the hood there is an extensive guild relations tools available, but there is no way to use them.
This game WILL be a winner, but wait for the GM tools to mature before jumping in.

One word.  AWESOME.  This game is being designed to be effectively limitless in possibilities, realistic ones at that, and the current limits, considering it is still early access, are constantly being expanded.  Great appearance helps as well.  PvP is fun.
The one note that I will make is that this game is not for the weak of heart.  To be successful takes a LOT of time and effort as well as a group of friends.  It is incredibly difficult to setup a successful community with a cooperative group of 10 people, and even more difficult to do on your own, though it can be done.  This isn't the result of a game flaw, this is how the game is intended to be.  Forest disappears very quickly once you start constructing even small buildings, as the materials gained from harvesting things like trees is pretty realistic.  Unlike other games, new trees don't just sprout up in their place, you need to plant more.  Planting is easy, but even with ideal weather conditions it takes real life days (up to a week I think) for the trees to mature into a useful, harvestable material.  This is just one example.  This game is difficult, and it is meant to be.  One HUGE advantage from this is that there are far fewer♥♥♥♥♥hats that just run around abusing people for the sake of doing so, and most of the time if someone does that they are banned.  The rationale is that if you want your character to be a bandit and steal from others, that is fine.  But if you're just going to grief people, that drives players off, resulting in smaller/fewer groups building on a server which ends up in server death.  The requirement of cooperation really encourages players to respect one another.  Players are also less likely to risk losing things, such as weapons, attacking other people unless there is a good reason, as replacing them takes a significant amount of time, work, and help from other people.
If you truly enjoy survival this game is for you.  You can always setup a local game and adjust the difficulty to be easy to do on your own, but most servers do NOT do that.
Definitely a great game with a great future.

Tried this game in very early access and it was unplayable so I avoided purchasing it. After watching its progression, I decided to get it. However I’m a bit disappointed with the purchase. The game really does feel like it was a way of testing the game for the MMO version as most negative reviews state. The game itself is a great idea, which is basically a realistic medieval sandbox survival crafting game. Yet there are things hurt the Life is Feudal: Your Own version and also still make it seem like its early access. How the developers handle it, will determine the games overall success. I see potential, but with all the issues I simply cannot recommend it.
- Developers actually followed their roadmap.
- Both the graphics and the environment are beautiful.
- Game offers unique ideas and systems, making it stand out from the rest.
- Game has a heavy grind with noticeable progression.
- When playing on a public server, you’re forced to play daily with long hours. If you’re not playing a public server, you don’t experience the full game and miss out on the features which stop you from losing interest in the game. On a public server you need to keep your monument up, watch your crops before they die, and if you play on a server with judgement hour, you need to defend your base. If one person falls behind on their chorus, it impacts everyone. It feels like I sold my soul to the devil or am paying a monthly subscription.

Just the pressure makes you want to quit. The developers should find ways to remedy this issue. Time and days will fly by quickly and you will separate yourself from reality and family. It’s scary and I much rather invest my time and effort in things that actually matter in life. Unless things change, I might abandon this game all together.
- The terraforming feature is not as fun as it seems. It requires real life days to get the layout that you want. It doesn’t matter what settings you have, it’s just way too slow. Makes you appreciate games like Don’t Starve and Haven & Hearth which don’t include terraforming whatsoever.
- Optimization doesn’t seem like it exists. I can’t tell for sure what’s causing this absurd lag spike that lingers for minutes and keeps coming back continuously. Developers said it was the server but no one else on the server is experiencing the same issue and nor is my older computer which has worse specs and is using the exact same internet I have. It could be the game, the server, or my computer. What I do know is that I’m having difficulty playing a game that lags so badly even though I have recommended specs.
- Game is not polished and doesn't feel finished. I'd personally call this an early access game which is not even worth the price tag.
- The game has numerous of bugs and glitches. Some of these type of issues may make you question if you should even continue playing the game.
- The combat is not balanced at all and needs some serious improvements and additional features for it to be considered functional. Combat is based around exploits currently not skill, making it simply not fun. Imaging working hours and hours for your things only to have some player who logins during judgement hour, exploit the game to get the upper hand of combat, and then stealing your stuff. Thought combat was going to be much more strategic in this game, I was wrong.
- Survival in this game is just too easy, making it feel non-existent. I wouldn't call this a survival game.
- Servers are capped to 64 players by the developers not the hosts. This drastically hurts your experiences because even with a full server, you will hardly find anyone. Also server get full frequently, which prevents you from playing. Unlike other games, you can’t just join another server because all of your progression is on that server that’s full.
- Mods aren’t officially supported. We’re dealing with private servers, mods should be expected.

So I've gotten a decen amount of time with this game, and I'm going to say its far an away an improvement over the previous styles of the game. First I'll get my main gripes out of the way.
1. No Two Headed Giant multiplayer mode. This was a great game mode, no idea why they didn't include it, it was in the two last versions of the game. Just plain, WTH?
2. The menu system/UI. There is a lot of animation and blur effects while navigating meus that are unskippable and take time. Basically 5-8 seconds to go from one menu to the next section. It's annoying at it's worst. Also there is a blur/field of focus effect in game that makes cards illegible unless you zoom in on them. It can take 15-20 seconds to back out of all the menus far enough to quit out of the game. Also just annoying but not game breaking.
3. The sopratic advertisement for the MtG 2015 core set. They will flash this ad at you in game, maybe 1 out of 5 matches that you launch. It's mildly annoying.
4. No more creating a deck of 40-100 cards. All decks have to be 60 cards. Not sure why they did this.
5. No longer a "random deck" option during a match. I used to love having it pick a random deck to play with.
6. Premium Boosters. So they're geting into the pay to win category with this. (Given that the physical card game is quite inherently pay to win) But you pay 2 dollars to get a booster of powerful premium cards you can't unlock otherwise. This is bound to♥♥♥♥♥♥off other opponents online if you play with decks relying on these cards.
7. There are key vital cards missing from MtG 2014, that the NPC players will use against you, like Rampant Growth, and the artifacts that heal you for each color card you play. (Maybe they will get added to the Premium card collection later?)
Everything else is golden, it's basically the Magic game I always wanted them to make. You no longer "unlock decks" and then grind through 40 wins with that deck to access all its available cards, and then customize the deck with only the deck specific cards. All that is gone. Now you start with a premade decks, and with every win you get a booster that earns you cards to your collection. Then you can go an make a custom deck from your collection, with NO LIMITATIONS! Build any damn deck you want, you're no longer trapped in premade template decks. Also the Sealed Deck concept is gone, because this new way of custom decks makes it obsolete.
I've read reviews complaining that there is less in this game than previous iterations. When it comes to Two Headed Giant I agree. And yes the Challenge mode is gone, but to me I couldn't care less, it was a silly thing, a puzzle game made from magic cards that was all about precision timing. Everything else, is a consolidation into a more functional and efficient format. It's kinda like arguing that 1 lb of popcorn is more better than 1 lb of gold, because it has much more volume. Volume doesn't mean value, and this game has more value.
Previous versions had the "grind" as I described to unlock every card in a deck, and this game has a grind too, but it is much more pleasant. It is the grind to unlock as many cards as you can to complete your collection. You're now unlocking cards that go into your universal collection that you can use in any number of custom decks. That makes tham way more valuable, and you time way better spent unlocking them than in previous games.

Bottom line up front!
Pros:
+Takes less than two hours for a full playthrough.
+Tons of replayability
+Great visuals; it reminds me very much of a well-designed board game.  The conveyances in particular are well rendered, which you may see in the screenshots.  The map itself is very nice.
+Good ambient sound and music
+It's a piece of interactive fiction with a story to tell.  There aren't "wrong" choices, just different ones.
+The Phineas Fogg health mechanic is EXCELLENT!  Instead of managing your character's health, you are charged as Mr. Fogg's valet.  You may abuse him or care for him as your whim dictates.
+The system is relatively intuitive and operates very much as though you had a globe and touch-menu available in your room.  They ported it from iOS or whatever very well.
+The game autosaves often, which offers an easy way to treat this as a casual game.  I did not mind that I couldn't manually save given the relatively short amount of time it took to play a journey.
Cons:
-Every journey (so far for me) starts from London to Paris.
-Playing through a journey sort of wears out the fun.  Each journey builds toward the triumphant return to London (if you make it!), so for me starting a new trip right after completing one felt more like a burden than a truly new adventure
-Each city, conveyance, and character has its own art, but really the only striking art was the conveyance.  The characters are very much colored cameo/silhouettes, while cities are a bit forgettable.
-No tutorial or other instruction is readily apparent.  It took me half an hour to figure out that it was easier to use the arrow keys to switch between possible routes and an hour to figure out that my character needed particular equipment in order to negotiate quicker passage with the available conveyances.
In all, if you're even considering getting this game then I recommend it.  It's a nice way to while away the time on a lazy afternoon or quiet evening, offering a bit of adventure to contemplate.  The script author is an excellent writer, and I very much enjoyed seeing what she came up with.  I think it's a good bargain at $10.  That's how much I would spend on a two hour movie and I expect to get quite a bit more time out of this game than that.

Considering this game takes its inspiration directly from my favorite novel by Jules Verne, whether or not to play this game was a no-brainer for me. This game is a great example of an interactive novel. You are Passepartout, Phileas Fogg's valet, and it your job to plan the route that will take you Around the World in 80 Days ( I couldn't resist). As you plan your route, you have to manage the finances which involves purchasing gear that will help speed up travel or be more comfortable, or purchase artifacts or luxury items to sell in other parts of the world. The routes you can take depend on what maps you have, and who you talk to. There are so many ways to travel around the world, and so many side stories to be discovered. Expect multiple playthroughs to discover them all. The only potential drawback with this game is that you have to read everything. There are nice backgrounds to each place you go but the game relies on the players imagination to visualize a great bulk of the action. Overall, this is a very fun game with loads of replayability.

Note: I haven't played enough of this game to gleam it's true quality, being only 1000 waves in at the moment, so take this review with however much salt you wish.
This is more or less your typical idle game fare, only this time, clicking BOOSTS your total damage based on a mechanic known as overdrive, which you learn about from second 1. Overdrive decays at a fairly decent rate so you need a decent click speed to build it up at first, but it's not completely needed.
First spell has a 120 second cooldown, and it maxes out overdrive, which maxes out at x9. Overdrive builds at a rate of 0.5 per click, but decays by 0.1 every second roughly. Overdrive affects ALL your weapon damage, making it useful and also easy to "abuse"
Spells after that give you various boosts to offensive and utility aspect. 2x Fire Rate, 2x Money Reward, Damage x2, +50% Critical Chance, 5x Critical Damage, 3x AOE Size. All these spells last 20 seconds unupgraded.
After is a spell that gives 10 levels to a random weapon, then the spell that resets all cooldowns, and then a spell that gives you the Peestige resource, cargo, based on sector, duration and cargo bonuses.
Overdrive you start with, other spells unlock after every 10th wave.
Cargo is the Prestige Currency. You use it to unlock "MK Upgrades" Color Crystals, Features, and more weapons. ON the transport, there's little brown 'X's Each weapon occupies it's own X, making there 33 weapons in total.
Color Crystals just change projectile color, Features are hte most important at first, however.
Features will unlock a large majority of hte more useful effects such as lowering waves per sector, which is 15 normally, so you want that for sure later on. Other effects include: Enabling Autobuy options, which are VERY useful, More Damage and Money, damaging effects upon ability activation, and cargo.
The game progresses more slowly than most other games, you'll find yourself pushing to sector 400 for your (roughly) first or second "Transfer" which is the Prestige function, it'll get you more cargo than a "Free Portal" which is kinda garbage as it only got me 10% of the owed cargo since it's not affected by duration or sector % bonuses.
I pushed to 1000 for my 2nd transfer, which only took a while with autobuy, so I keep the game running even while out in town, at work, or at school, and let autobuy do its thing.
Was able to get around 20K cargo, and I spent most of it on new features and unlocking them, as bought features start at level 0, and must be bought to activate them. Rest of it ,I spent on upgrading my Tsar Cannon Monument and Second Hand Shop features.
The Coin currency can be found periodically, and at random, all it requries is playtime (I believe) to accumulate, and you can use it to further increase your carbo bonus with 30 coins. The formula for it is 1 + 0.2 Multiplied by the number of times you've bought this upgrade, or [Upgrade level] X 1.2 which means it'll become more effective with every purchase after about 2 or 3, but then fall off after (probly) 20. since the bonus with it would likely be less than 10% with every upgrade.
If it's not obvious, I really enjoy this game. It's a more chill, relaxed idle game, and though you CAN breeze with active play, it's not too designed for it as some features can allow you to auto-cast certain spells, such as the first one.
Favorite part though is how Transfer reward increases based on how long a run lasts. The longer the run, the larger the bonus. If you ask me, all games should utilize this since it allows longer-term non-rush builds to be alot stronger, which is something some games don't do, and those games will usually just make progression walls that require long-term builds.
Only progression walls in this game, is based purely on your damage, enemy health, and the cost of feature upgrades/purchasesor weapon purchases.

The OVA is finally here; and surprisingly it dropped a couple days ahead of planned release. Having watched it just now, guess I'll give you my thoughts on it.
But before I start, I'd just like to mention that I was among the Kickstarter backers, donating a whopping $200 USD (or 170 euros) to get to the t-shirt tier. So I'm in no position to complain about the price of the OVA.
The OVA is basically all of Nekopara Vol. 1 compressed to an hour-long anime episode. Due to the disparity between the length of the VN and the length of the anime, some scenes had to be cut; these weren't really anything important, as it's mostly the interactions with customers as well as the... 'bonding' parts, but I do miss them a bit. That being said, the scenes they DID include in the OVA are the ones moving the plot forward, and I'm not complaining!
In terms of graphics, it's pretty solid. The artstyle is definitely recognisable and animations are quite smooth. Bonus points for including chibi-scenes!
Music: mostly remastered tracks from the original VN, but some new tracks are also included. The OP and ED are entirely new to the series, and in terms of enjoyability definitely above average.
I'd give this OVA a solid 8/10.

Taking a break from liberating the holy land to bring you this review:
For Honor has completely reinvigorated the fighting game scene. Best action, hack-n-slash, strategy game I have ever played. There's a hero to match everyone's play style. Do you like to tank in MMOs? Want to
tank hits? Try the Conqueror. Like Assassin's creed? Try Peacekeeper. Just want to play and bash people's brains in? Try the Warden.
Honestly, there's a big learning curve. The first thing you should do is complete the story to get a feel for all of the heroes, and THEN do the AI matches - those AI are pretty challenging! Don't go into PvP not having learned the game and think you 360noscope everyone else.
I see a lot of the complaints about microtransactions...Guess what? YOU DON'T HAVE TO BUY STEEL TO BE GOOD AT THIS GAME. The only big ticket items are the cosmetics. All of the heroes can be unlocked with the Steel you get for completing the basic and advanced tutorials. Additionally, you can spend ~$20 to unlock all of the feats (skills) for your heroes, OR you can take 1-2 hours for each hero and level them to 21. This is more of a convenience factor, because it is extremely easy to unlock all the feats.
I do agree with the other reviews on the connectivity issues. Sometimes my friend and I have to restart our games because there's an error with our connectivity or whatever. It's pretty annoying and Ubisoft definitely needs to address these issues.
Overall, if you appreciate smooth AAA-graphics, like a good challenge, and aren't afraid of dying a lot, then this game is a must for you.

A Vampyre Story proves to be a quirky point and click game with great writing and a cute art style.
The story follows Mona De Lafitte and her bat friend Froderick as they try to escape Baron Shrowdy von Kiefer. The plot doesn't take itself very seriously at all and is filled with cheesy puns and references but still has a genuinely interesting cast of characters; Mona herself is charming with a ridiculous amount of denial about her vampiric nature, while Froderick has some very sarcastic lines that would often make me laugh. The animations can be a bit off at times but the designs have a lot of personality and the voice acting is really high quality. Like other point and click games some of the solutions to the puzzles are absolutely ridiculous, admittedly I did have to look up a walkthrough a couple of times, but they were still pretty fun and gave more opportunities for the fantastic dialogue to shine through. I've seen other people talking about issues with the game running, but apart from a weird instance where some of the cutscenes repeated themselves I didn't have any problems at all.
Once I finished I looked up some information on the sequel and it doesn't look like we'll be seeing it any time soon, which does put a downer on the experience as it means that (spoiler) the story remains incomplete due to the cliffhanger ending. I would love to get a continuation to Mona's journey at some point, but I had fun with what we've been given and could see myself playing it again in the future. Overall I had a great time playing this game and I would definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoys point and click adventure games with a sense of humour.

This game falls along the lines as other "survival" titles such as DayZ and Infestation (WarZ). Although I have not played the Stand-alone version of DayZ, this title, Nether, is leaps and bounds over Infestation. However, currently there are mechanics that mimic different aspects of Infestation (WarZ) which I hope that Phosphor Games will take notice to and change.
The biggest change that I believe needs to happen is towards the Nether creatures themselves. They are relativily easy on their own, even in groups of three or four against a single survivor. This then leads to the only viable opponent being the other players of Nether. This in turn removes the survival aspect and just turns the map into an online CoD match. If I wanted to play a round of Deathmatch, I would pick up a copy of one of those games. This game needs to be different in this respect, or it may find itself lacking like all the other "survival" fpv titles, which would be quite unfortunate. The spawns will need to be strong enough to force the players into working together, otherwise you will not be able to play the game prosperously.
All in all, for being a game in its' pre-release stages, it plays rather well. The skill tree is implimented, there are decent loot spots, etc. However, the biggest problem is the loading server list. While your client pings the servers, the program locks up for a good 1-2 minutes before you can do anything. This, as you can figure, is quite annoying. The next biggest issue is the fact that about 1% (according to the devs) of the Steam population trying to attach their Steam accounts to their Nether account are getting errors and are unable to even log in due to the inability to prove their purchase through their linking of the accounts. I, thankfully, did not run into this hiccup. Although the forums are ablaze with posts from individuals who are.
My overall rating for Nether would be a 6/10. They would be able to gain those four remaining points by fixing the freezing/Steam Account issues and alter the Nether spawns to support more of a "survival" aspect of the game. If you're looking for something like Infestation (WarZ), then this is it. If you're looking for something more, don't buy just yet. Wait for the actual release and see how the reviews are then.

Longer review:
The visuals are really good and well optimised. The atmosphere, from sound effects to lighting are really well done. Random events can make groups have an activity to do instead of wandering around. Starting off is rather difficult, you have no money to get equipment, you have nothing to start off with and you have nothing in your bank. To truly start, you have to do a few deliveries to save some money for health items. This would make you go through a few lives as you normally lose a lot of health during this. Some Nethers are too powerful and too difficult to avoid, ensuring in almost certain death. Too many players Kill on Sight (KoS) and this is quite aggrivating. There isn't really much else to it though right now, so it can get quite boring at times.
So all in all, its well designed in most areas, but starting off and players ruin some of the experience. The developers are active in the community which is fantastic.
So far I'd give it a 6.5/10 but I'm confident this will increase more and more as time goes on and with the developers constantly taking in feedback

Kingdom Wars (Race: Human)

Resources are gathered by peasants (stone, wood, gold, food - though food is a bit different as you can slaughter pigs that are "fattened" for a large food income). Each peasant unit takes 1 population space and costs some food.

For quite a while I had battle protection as a starter player. This battle protection gave me enough time to form an army, walls and a wizard. Wizard is an extremely strong unit. Maximum population number of town is 90 I think - you can increase the initial low population limit by building houses - also, you can have initially up to 5 armies outside of your town on map - each army has 60 population cap (Normal units take 1/90), wizard takes 10 and costs 120 crowns. Crowns are gained either by paying 5000 gold (daily limit of bought crowns is 30) or winning a pvp/pve battle (siege or army fight) [You can get 20-40 crowns for winning when attacked by enemy player in your town). A wizard needs further spell upgrades to be able to cast spells (10,20,40,80 and 150 crowns - example for lightning (of the Deep) wizard: shield,drain stamina, buff allies, large aoe attack, teleport) so it's very expensive unit. Once I got the wizard and trained him to get to higher level and bought 2 spells (shield gives him extreme resistance to everything and aoe attack kills everything sooner or later) I was able to siege enemy castle with one man - the wizard.
This happened when I finished building my inner stone wall and outer wooden wall (There are 2 types of wall - One made out of wood and the other one is made out of stone, stone is very expensive and there is inner (cheaper) and outer part - outer is much more expensive than the inner one, it's like a second layer of walls) and placed trebuchets on them (you can build trebuchets, rock throwers (close range) or hot oil thingy that pours hot oil on top of the enemy) on top of stone walls. I recalled all of my peasants into my middle part of the town. I chose to fight the enemy. I placed my archers on the wall - on the side from where the enemy was coming. He started attacking my town with trebuchets, he focused on my outer wooden wall and used fiery stones that set the area around my walls on fire. I had plenty of stone in my town and you can buy stone during battle for gold if you have market built so I started aiming all of my trebuchets (the ones on the walls) at those trebuchets. In 4 minutes the enemy trebuchets were destroyed. Then I opened the outer wooden door. As I expected, enemy archers started pouring in, hoping to shoot my people, cattle and soldiers. As soon as they passed my gate I closed it behind them. They were trapped in my outer wall part of town. I started ordering all of my elven rangers (best archers in game, I got them from befriending one elven town and buying them in it) to increase their rate of fire and fire at the enemy archers. Then I opened my inner gate and sent all of my unicorns (also elven unit, they use them for gaining gold and as a cavalry. My wizard kept placing defencive shield on my rangers and they kept firing while unicorns were slaughtering the archers and crossbowmen. They died in 2 minutes. Only thing that remained were enemy melee units behind my wall. I sent my archers to shoot them from safety of my walls and aimed my trebuchets with another 3000 stone remaining (Enough for a long time of constant firing from few trebuchets). The enemy surrendered before I managed to obliterate the rest of his army. I got 28 crowns. The whole siege was like 20 minutes long.
I find this game very nice - also, any units you loose during the pvp or pve fights is dead permanently (except wizards, main hero and other heroes like them)

This review will be about what you need and should expect from the game/simulator
1. This is a extremely demanding simulator. This isn't because it is horribly optimized but because of the calculations your Pc has to make. One example of this is spawning in a vehicle that has 4000 beams. You may be thinking "4000 beams that's nothing" you are simulating 4000 beams but it's 2000 times every second 4000X2000 = 8,000,000 calculations I have a quad core 3.2 ghz processor it runs this perfectly fine
2. If you aren't someone that can stand repetition this isn't for you. You repeat things alot.....well sort of. You do crash over and over but how you crash is what changes. You could do a vertical jump at 60 mph Hit a wall at 100mph or do a head on collision with each car going 150mph. It all depends on your mind. I've done nearly everything imaginable and I still come back to experiment.
TLDR :don't like repeating don't get this if you're not creative and want to be directed
