As a long time fan of Magic The Gathering, it pains me to say that I would not recommend you buy this game. While it does finally let you build your own deck and manually change how many lands are in said deck, this year's version is quite stripped of content. 2HG, Planechase, and Archenemy were taken out (or just never implemented) for whatever insane reason, sealed play  is nonexistant, and no challenge modes.

Ah, Duke. Duke, Duke, Duke. We've waited for so long, and what did you give us?
A decent game, to be honest. But that's also where it stays. It is so "in the middle" it almost hurts.
The gameplay is cool, but it doesn't reach the testosterone-pumping "♥♥♥♥ you, alien" vibe of the original. My main gripe is the two weapons limitation - WHAT the actual FECK? *EVERYTHING* about Duke is over the top, and y'all go castrating him with two guns at a time. Eugh. But you get used to it. The old guns kick♥♥♥♥♥ and the new guns are meh at best. Nonetheless, killing aliens is still satisfying and it's fun to shoot stuff, which is what this game should've had more of.
The EGO system I actually like, and it's cool that they tied environment exploration and doing random activities to the actual health system - if in Duke 3D the only reward for giving a stripper your dollar was a pair of pixelated♥♥♥♥♥♥ in DNF you actually get a small health boost. Well done.
The graphics, meh, yeah, whatever. You could say they should be better, but I kind of get they can't be a big wow given the amount of hiccups this game has had since its development.
My main gripe is the pacing. It wants to cater to the brainy side of the player by offering some sort of puzzle every now and then, but all it does is slow down the game. Some sequences, like the "mini Duke", are AWESOME, while others are a boring chore.
I still gave it a "recommend" because I think it's a solid game with a lot of minor things dragging it down from being really good. It's still worth a playthrough. Get during a sale, of course.

(Stay clear of the starter edition this game does go on sale , the starter edition is a mega grind to get anywhere)  So after 500+ hours of gameplay I can say I have never been addicted to a game as much as this. The previous addiction of mine was the free to play game planetside 2 which has a strong focus on team play and tactics. This game could been seen as an evolution of another game I picked up a year previous to this one. That game would be CS:Go a game which is a staple in the fps industry. The concepts of CS:Go are simple and I will not knock the game however the simple fps concepts have been expanded and adapted in this game.
The adaptation and evolution hasn't created a carbon copy like many other fps out in the market but adds a lot more elements and variables. The biggest element of all as advertised in the destructive and interactive maps offered this adds a whole new level of tactics and gameplay that CS:Go never offered me. The gadgets are unique to your chosen operators which can been seen as loadouts, they all add something different when attacking or defending that is refreshing to see. The devs continue to work on the game and bring out new content, however they made the choice to pause on such content to work on the overall health of the game. In this I say in part has been very useful but given the size of the dev could have been done in a greater and better way. This game is a solid fps game however isn't a perfect execution, it has a few grievances with me personally that need to be addressed, these issues have been addressed in a much preferable way in CS:GO. The content should also get a reworking at present all new operators are unlocked through an in game currency you can earn from playing the game. This currency is rather easy to obtain but the operators are all priced the same, apart from the original operators. They should at least think about decreasing the amount needed to unlock operators each year so the most recent ones cost the most and so on as that would be fair. There are a few other issues but I feel overall in time these will be addressed the devs are very active and hope to keep the game alive for years to come. I can only recommend this game to people looking for an evolution of this genre and want a game that require more thought.

A Vampyre story has good kind of cheesy jokes, creative puzzles, fun characters and very good voice acting.
There are very few games in this genre where I actually listen to every single line of the dialogue. When you start randomly clicking just to hear a pun you know you have a good adventure game. It seems like no matter what you do it will trigger another joke.

Main characters have something to say even about most useless combinations that make no sense. Like you can click "Talk" on any object that can't talk and you will hear a unique comment instead of -can't do.

Also, you can press space to speed up walking or text. Very nice feature that some games do not have.
The story is not complete. However, a good story leaves you wishing for more. I don't think it will happen but I would love to play another one.
I think the most important thing for a point&click game is fun writing. I wanted to listen to every single line of voice acting which is something that most games can't do to me. After seeing all the terrible reviews of this game having played hours of it I decided to make my own.
Pros:
Excellent graphics, I have no problems whatsoever.
The gameplay is fun yet can be quite hard to learn.
Customisation of your characters is extensive with colored patterns and ornaments.
Cons:
Some characters are really unbalanced, Lawbringer being too slow to hit anything that isn't a heavy character, Valkyrie using a wet noodle for a weapon.
The timing of counter guard breaking has been reduced to a very small time, making guard breaks spammy as hell.
Guard breaks + 2 hit attacks allow for easy wins with some characters if your enemy is new.
Neutral:
Microtransactions and the season pass, these can make some people disgusted and just not buy the game entirely, just know that you don't even need to pay a single penny for anything, be it gear or cosmetics. Sure you can pay like £4 to unlock all the 4v4 feats on a character, but you can earn those after a bunch of games.
Connection issues are a problem yes, but they do not happen literally every game, maybe once every 4th game you get a connection error or a player disconnects, or you may not be able to join one game. Some complain about insane lag issues but I have gotten none.
Skill curve, later on when you win games you'll come across players who are very good at the game, no matter what level you are on your character. You'll get matched up with prestiged players when you can only be level 4 on your Warden. It is good if you are skilled yourself but awful if your learning a new character.
The Campaign is basically one massive lootfest which gives you 5k steel (currency), emblem pieces and cosmetics, but its pretty much disguised itself from being one large tutorial. Everytime you start a mission you are constantly given tooltips on how to play, even after replaying on a higher difficulty.
Apparently there are also some people using cheats online, such as instant parry, blocks + counter guard breaks, I never faced one though.
Is the game good? yes, but there are issues. Will it get better? Probably.

1) Navigate to Program Filesx86
2) Select "Steam" folder
3) Select "SteamApps" folder
4) Select "Common" folder
5) Select "A Vampyre Story" folder
6) Select "Game" folder
7) Scroll down to "Main"
8) Right click "Main"
9) On the Compatibility tab - click "Run this program in compatibility mode for:" and select "Windows XP (ServicePack 3)" from the drop-down
10) Also under Settings: check "Disable display scaling oh high DPI settings"
11) Also under Privilege Level: check "Run this program as administrator"
12) Click the "Apply" button and close the pop-up
13) Back in the "Game" folder, locate the file named " libpandadx9.dll "- click the file name and add a 2 - libpandadx9.dll2
14) Click "Main" and start the game
15) Set Anti-Aliasing to zero
16) Exit game, go back to the Game folder, remove the "2" from libpandadx9.dll2 so that it reads libpandadx.dll (ignore the pop-up warning)
17) Click "Main" again and the game will run perfectly with all the cutscenes

Hi guys, This is a PSA more than a review as I feel a couple of tweaks and options make this game way better.
First make sure to enable these two Options under Interface (scroll down)
1. Inventory Action Confirmation = OFF (this makes dissasembling scrap SO much easier, and believe me.. that's a lot of your inventory management)
2. Show Looting Animation = OFF (holy caterpillars, when I found this option it was a game changer. No more groaning when looking at 30 slaughtered savannah wildlife corpses piled around you, just tap tap tap and it's all in your inventory.. no crazy long animation or inventory sorting.)
Ok now those out of the way, something a little trickier but will much enhance your visual experience without any bells and whistles added. You might notice this game has a fair bit of blur and most of it can be turned down or off in your visual options ( AA, Motion blur 0, Depth of field 0, Bloom 0 because ew) But some cannot be turned off, like the blur while running or DOF when talking to characters.
We can fix all that plus add a little more Field of View AND removing the annoying and performance hungry fog that clouds up your screen with going to the installed folder of Two Worlds II where the .exe is, create a folder in that called Parameters and within that create a new text document called autoexecgame2.txt
paste the following inside the document:
graph.SetFastRunSpecialEFX 0
Graph.enablefog 0
cam.bank.move 0
Cam.Talk.DOFAmount 0
engine.fov 60
You can adjust the FOV to your liking (it goes from 45 to 80, 45 is the default.. talk about claustrophobic. I like 60)
Now you can save that and then rename it to autoexecgame2.con
When you start the game it will automatically apply that to the configuration and Voila, much better experience!
Also you might notice with 10/10 view distance huge chunks of landscape will refuse to render in the distance (ocean, etc). Apparently it's a graphics bug from the latest DLC patch affecting the base game, just turn your View Distance down to 3/10 and they will be gone. Doesn't seem to make a huge difference other than a bit of pop-in LOD's other than that.

An excellent game overall, that will immerse most RTS players for at least a good few hours.
Its fairly simple, with a very traditional setup of the three factions with strenghts and weaknesses. such as the Humans being the most durable overall, the Elves essentially having the strongest units but with greater weaknesses, and the Orcs being oddly enough the most frail but boasting the ability to quickly amass an army of considerable size at reduced cost.
(Please note: This is more of a quick run-down of some of the features in the game, than an review. The idea is that you can more effectively decide if its features appeals to you, rather than read someone trash n praise it)
Leveling up your units!:
This game relies quite heavily on the concept of your troops not simply being something you purchase enough of, in the right combination but actually take into skirmishes to level up or train at friendly strongholds, to then tailor suit what stats you want to improve, such as more health, damage mitigation, health regeneration, stamina, and so on.
Eventually you will pretty much max out all the stats but at that point you have spend quite a lot of gold on that unit, and considering its still very likely to get inconveniently killed while you look the other way you learn to pay special heed to keeping your investments alive and well protected.
Special Units:
Every faction has an array of faction specific units available to them, but theres also a common pool of special units available to all the factions. These units have roots in all three main factions, but theres also units from unplayable races, such as Dragons and Dwarves. These units almost always costs you Crowns, which is a measure of wealth and influence that you can spend on recruiting considerably attractive units to attack your enemies or defend your homeland.
Quest line:
Theres an rather involved lore in the game, and its often very nicely attached to the characters you interact with while playing the main quest line. As you go through the main quest of your faction your tasked with defending your homeland, your kingdom, and waging war against the two other factions in the game, and often also your own.
Due to the somewhat sandbox-like nature of the game, the senarios you find yourself in is often rather interesting and gradually gives you useful rewards that greatly benefit the construction of your homeland, giving a smooth progression of your homeland, the story of the game, and your involvement in the game overall.
Traits and Regions
In the MMO portion of the game, after choosing a faction you will be asked to choose a region and two traits.
These are important and should be chosen to match how you prefer to play the game. If your a "turtle" and enjoys defensive gameplay then naturally you may want to choose the most defensive region and traits, but if your more into siege and conquest than naturally you would do well to take a region that reflects that better.
Either way, your choice of region and traits will play an immense factor in the performance of your strategies.
Choose wisely. :)
Non-Mandatory PvP
In the online MMO portion of the game you may be attacked by enemies at any time, but you need to actually accept the battle. Should you choose not to, or let the timer run out you will forfeit a small portion of your resources as a tribute to be left alone. Even if no resources are available fighting PvP is never mandatory. As you start out with a new homeland you will have 24 hours of real time protection against PvP attacks to get you started. Notice that this time is only ticking while your in-game. Additionally, every time you pay a tribute or conclude a PvP match you will be given a small PvP Protection time.
It is also possible to purchase PvP protection for Crowns.
The graphics, performance, and the gameplay itself have gradually improved over time, with updates coming out frequently enough for a game you only pay for once. (Not including the micro transaction-like boosts available in the market, and additional features)
The gameplay in singleplayer, whether in the online MMO world or not, is very stable but once you have an actual fight not against the AI, but another player it soon becomes a bit of a mess.(This includes co-op aswell) Reasonably playable, yes, but still very annoying at times. However, they have worked hard to improve this game and the future update expected to come out this month, which will apperantly overhaul the entire thing onto a more stable engine will hopefully bring back much of the player base and thus hopefully bring some more life back into this, in all honesty, very awesome game.
(If you wish to know more details about the game, i have found a wiki with more details for you)
Yes, it does have some problems now and then but this game does deserve a chance if it calls out to you in general.

Disappointed. This is how I feel after beating this game. I was really hoping for something clever or subtle, for example the Shadow being an hallucination, Alexander being a good guy, and Daniel being the actual murderer (of William Smith, Doctor Tate, Prof Taylor, etc). But no, it's a blunt and bland story, like a plate of beans without seasoning. Daniel is
being chased by an eldritch abomination. Okay.
It's a puzzle game combined with a point'n'click, really; no idea why "Action" is there in the tags. You pick objects, combine them or use them on other objects, pull levers in the right order to turn a machine on, etc. It feels like playing Riven or some other Myst game, but in the setting of Stephen King's
(spooky mansion lost in the cold woods, with a huge steam machine in it), or the classic Atari Game
. The "scary" part is incredibly overrated: monsters are scarce, you can outrun them easily, and being killed makes you respawn in a ridiculously helpful place with the monster most likely being gone. Plus the game is heavily scripted, so you know pretty much exactly when a monster is gonna appear (when you solve a puzzle, usually). With the difficulty being so low, it's hard to actually feel stressed. You kinda have to force yourself to be scared, which is pretty weird. I must admit that the first hour sent some serious chills down my spine, but you get used pretty fast to what A:TDD has to offer, sadly. Screams in the background become just... well, screams in the background.
The graphics are sub-par for a game released in 2010 (they look pretty damn close to 2001's
rather than 2010 games such as Mass Effect 2 or Bioshock 2) but I soon figured out that it's very probably for the same reason as in
: physics. You can throw, move, displace a lot of objects, and that can take a toll on your computing power. The engine is very good though, and I thoroughly enjoyed launching boxes at chandeliers and watch them swing and twirl. That was great.
The fact that there's zero HUD and you only know your health is low because you see everything in red works way better here than in Brütal Legend, honestly. It fits the æsthetics of the game, where pretty much everything is implied rather than directly shown.
Æsthetics and atmosphere are clearly the strong point of the game (despite the not very refined textures). Especially the AWESOME music, reminiscent of Shadow Man and Diablo II, and brilliantly composed. That and the sound design in general. The voice acting is campy, but quite reasonably so. The attention to detail is variable: on one hand, I absolutely loved when the painting of Alexander changed after you discovered the skeletons. On the other hand, seeing the same 3 paintings and 5 books everywhere was rather annoying. Why would the mansion have 100 copies of this book named Pflanzenreich? Unless it's an encyclopedia in 100 volumes, of course.
I liked the fact that there weren't any cutscenes, but rather narration
Half-Life allowing you to actually walk and look around during it. I also liked the fact that you had no weapons, no magic powers, no ways to defend yourself. I mean, maybe you could have punched or kicked the Gatherers, or use the countless hammers laying around as arms, but no. It isn't explained why you can't, but you can't. When you get attacked, two options: hide or run. I only wished the monsters weren't so easy to outrun though, or that getting killed wasn't so damn convenient.
The "Sanity" meter (which actually measures anxiety, obviously) is an interesting thing. But the effects of losing your sanity should be a bit more than blurry vision and hearing insect noises. After a while I just stopped lighting candles and torches or even using the lantern, and ended the game with 40+ tinderboxes in my inventory and enough oil to refill my lantern 10 times. These things should have been rarer to find! They are EVERYWHERE. Again, I really don't understand why the game's difficulty is so damn low.
I'm also kinda shocked by how awful all the fonts look on screen. Why? Couldn't they at least have been antialiased? There is a LOT of text in the game, why make it unpleasant to read? I'm sorry for ranting so much, but Amnesia could have been a great game without all its flaws. I would have liked to know more about the origin of the orbs, what is the "true home" Alexander talks about... I was kinda addicted to this game, I'm not even sure why, and played it all night long (and also a bit during the day, but that was less fun) for two days straight. Something kept me going to it. I had to go on, I had to finish it.
But like a plate of beans without seasoning, it was filling, but not satisfying.
5,5/10.

This is not an easy game to pick up.  The learning curve is steep and success requires the investment of significant amounts of time.  That said, it's game with immense scope and huge potential.  Once you master the basics of how to "level" your character, the gameplay is quite enjoyable.
The game is not finished.  I hope to see significant polish put on before official release.  That said, unlike many other games that need not only polish but also substantive content, the majority of the game already exists and it is solid.
The emphasis is on realism: Say you have a animal hide and you need to dry it (one step in the tanning process).  You've built a drying rack (not too hard) and are ready to start.  There is no simple button with a quick progress bar: it takes an hour of actual time for the hide to dry.  Nevertheless, there are occasionally activities and game mechanics that need polish and certainly don't feel realistic (Hares drop chicken meat when killed?  Did I miss something in biology?).  Overall, the core is solid.

I haven't owed the game for that long but damn... I'm impressed.
Gotta say that this is probably the most enjoyment I've had for some time in a multiplayer setting. The level of customization in your loadouts for both your character and vehicles is enough to keep me coming back, trying out new combinations that'll be of more use to the team. Plus with the levelling system, you'll be gaining experience in three different catagories: Command, Support, and Combat. This will increase your "budget", allowing you to have more supplies and weaponry to  take with you onto the battlefield.
Infantry combat is decent enough, there is that early access feel to it but it's kind of excepted from an early access title. The movement is a nice pace, not too slow and not too fast. I also personally find the gunplay feels satisfying, especially with the fairly good sized arsenal to pick though.
I'd have to say though, the one thing that made me get hooked were the maps that took place in space. Not only do they have pretty solid space combat with good number of ship types, but for the larger ships, you have the ability to walk around inside them. While inside a ship, you can head to different terminals and man different weapons, as well as repairing any of these terminals to keep your systems running FTL style.
Best of all, you have the capability to board enemy ships, allowing you to fight against the crew on their own turf and damage the systems from within. When a ship is destroyed, it won't just explode like you'd usually do, but you will have a count down until the ship self destructs. This will usually give you enough time to make it to the ship's hanger and evacuate in a fighter.
For negatives, there isn't really anything I can complain about that isn't in regards to the game being in early access. Some guidance I'd give the creators is to set up a way for people to escape the smaller sized ships, as currently, you'll have a 30 second countdown to detonation but as far as I know, there is no escape pods or anything. Other than that, work on some optimization as it has some slowdown here and there at times, clean the UI abit as it can be a tad overwhelming with all the indicators and information it throws in your face, and add a little more oomph to the explosions. Especially the ship explosions. >:D
Overall, this game has some massive potential and is definetly on the right path. As of writing this, the game is currently 30%off, sitting at 13.99 canadian which I feel is a more than fair of a price. Just be cautious as the player base is VERY small, thankfully the game supports some fairly decent AI, but I feel that this game is only getting started and that over time, we'll see the community grow.

Bugginess/state of the game:
I've spend a few hours on the game. And it's occasionally buggy and not well optimised. But hey, they're not hiding the fact it's not finished. It's playable, that's the most important thing.
If you can't handle a crash once in awhile, don't buy it.

Gameplay:
I personally love it. But if you're an impatient man, do not buy this game. Doing things takes time.
In most survival games you have a full fledged base in maybe a week or even less.
Here 1 weeks worth is having a small house and furnace (if you play alone) or a village with wooden palisades (if playing in group).
Now this game is not meant to be played solo. Many server have the recommended level cap.
This effectively limits you when you play alone, as you can't have all stats maxed. You can do everything decently, but not perfectly.
There are server where the cap's been increased, so you could technically be a one man powerhouse.
But more often than not, expect there to be roles. Towns tend to have a dedicated blacksmith, carpenter, tanner, etc...
This game takes time, especially being a bloody herbalist..... there's just so many freaking herbs.
If you don't have patience, don't buy it.
If you like a community and working in group building up a medieval society, go ahead. Expect to shovel a lot of dirt leveling out land though.
Watch out for bandits aswell. People still love free goodies.

This game *does* have some bugs remaining. I had some sort of memory leak (or other compouning problem) and sound issues after playing for awhile. It became unbearable after something like 5 or 6 hours (but my system is pretty high-quality, so your mileage may vary). However, a simple restart of the game solved the problem and only took a minute. This is not game-breaking.
I love this game... but it won't be for everyone.
Some things to note:
A) Most servers use conservative server settings that are pretty close to default.
B) At default settings, things in this game can take a long time and a lot of effort to achieve. You'll have to earn it.
C) With default settings, you almost cannot survive alone. (Farming/nature lore can both allow you to forage for food, but cooking requires multiple skill sets that will almost undoubtedly require multiple participants. If you plan on jumping into the game with no friends to help you and with no idea what you're doing... you will probably fail.
D) Some servers have much more newb-friendly settings... look for high level/stat caps and high resource gather multipliers/exp multipliers.
E) Part of the appeal of this game *IS* the fact that it takes so much effort to be successful... reaching a milestone can be very rewarding. I'm looking forward to getting my first shack built.
F) There's a lot to learn about this game, the wiki is your friend.
G) Something that I had to find out through experience and lots of looking online: Many abilities require advanced skills with a skill level of 0... but they must still be unlocked to be used, and many require lots of skill levels in a prerequisite skill to be unlocked. IE: cutting billets for cooking fuel requires lvl 0 carpentry, but carpentry doesn't unlock until lvl 60 logging.
H) Working with terrain is tedious and very time consuming... don't plan on getting in here and levelling mountains like in minecraft... you'll be digging the rest of your life... it's just implausible.
I) The skill system is very detailed and random events can occur. I cut my hand while trying to forage and it bled for like 10 minutes. Not life threatening... but interesting. This game feels kindof like Neverwinter or D&D meets ARK set in medieval times.
J) There's no magic (although prayer can have supernatural effects [including teleportation]).
So far this is just a description of the main points of the game as I see it at the moment.
Now for the good and bad.
GOOD:
-Devs are pretty active.
-Plenty of servers with a variety of settings.
-Very playable, few bugs.
-Very unique.
-Highly replayable. (partly because of how limited you usually are in character development)
-Very conducive to roleplay. (Though it's often not required/expected)
-The music. (I love it, totally my own opinion)
BAD:
-A little expensive for an alpha game.
-Graphics are very mix-n-match. (IE: character model looks amazing, but the hair models look atrocious... kinda weird)
-I love the focus on team-play... however, there *needs* to be a single skill set that will allow you to survive in the wilderness on your own. Sure, you won't be eating cake... and it's likely you'll spend most of your time hunting/fishing/gathering to support yourself... but it seems unrealistic that you can't have a single survival skill that enables you to build a simple campfire, hunt/fish, and grill up a bit of dinner. This could also make for a new skill tree leading into "scouting" skills.

Penumbra: Necrologue is a community-made mod that brings an ultimate conclusion to the story of Penumbra games, telling the final part of the tale involving Philip, the Tuurngait and the Archaic Caste, along with the story for other characters that were involved as well, even actually involving Penumbra: Requiem as well
Necrologue stays true to the other Penumbra games, both in gameplay and story. Everything is there - the puzzles, the monsters, the low light vision, etc. Like the other games, Penumbra: Necrologue isn't so much about jump scares or creating a disturbing atmosphere, as it's more about surviving in the darkness, avoiding creatures while unfolding the story in the game. And story is where the game really excels at, developing a complex, well-made story that maintains its quality from the first game to the very last one.
The Twilight of the Archaic add-on also adds a little more to the story of the game, telling the story of two other characters - one that wasn't involved with Philip and back when the Penumbra storyline originally started, before Philip's arrival, and one that was involved in Philip's story.
Necrologue has a few issues - mostly FPS drops and a few crashes during Twilight of the Archaic. Personally I also found a bug during the game that almost halted my progress, but I found a way around it. Fixing these issues would greatly improve the game, but it's an amazing quality mod nonetheless.
If you enjoyed the original Penumbra games, you'll probably enjoy Necrologue as well. And because it's free, it can also be played on its own, though in this case the story probably won't make much sense, as you'll be missing a lot of the story from previous games.

The reviews of Magic 2015, here on steam and throughout the interwebs, have been unanimously negative. I agree with the overall sentiment of said reviews, with special disdain for the increased amount of micro transactions sprinkled throughout the game. Every iteration of Magic since 2012 has had micro transactions as a way to decrease the amount of grinding necessary to unlock cards, but what's interesting about this iteration is that the campaign play-through, including completing every "exploration" for every plane will unlock most of the cards with very little grinding necessary thereafter. WotC has charged more for unlocking less. The plan, from my perspective, was to lock the player's deck choice, forcing battle after battle against AI opponents with powerful decks while utilizing the weakest form of whichever deck the user selected. The player then is confronted with two choices: sit through loss after loss (you'll lose a lot in the beginning btw) and slowly unlock cards through boosters (some of which may or may not have anything to do with your deck archetype) or pay 20 dollars to unlock every card available in a booster pack normally unlocked through winning matches. There are also cards that can only be unlocked by purchasing premium booster packs.
What one gets from the purchase of Magic 2015 are the campaign, cards, and the ability to fully customize one's deck. Multiplayer has been severely truncated and only now consists of 1v1, 1v1v1, and 1v1v1v1. The removal of Two-headed giant was extremely disappointing to say the least, but I have recently learned that one team can only have a total of 4 of the same card. I don't know much beyond that when it comes to multiplayer rules governing the universe of magic however. Challenge mode has been removed as a category and implemented within the achievements. The issues is that instead of clicking on a challenge without having to worry about decks, one may need to rework one's deck to complete these challenges because specific cards must be utilized. For example, one "challenge" requires one to kill an angel with Shadowborn Demon. If you don't use a deck that includes black mana, you'll have to modify. Unfortunately, there is only 1 Shadowborn Demon card in this game, making the completion of this achievement based largely on luck and staying power (if the card is pulled late game). I use life-gain by default so I got lucky because I was able to build up enough life to withstand the onslaught; but most of the creatures cast by Avacyn are flying and if decks have no way of dealing with that, it will be a grind.
The animation on every screen is terribly long. Choosing to go forward to another plane or back to the main menu is a chore because the animation cannot be overridden or skipped and it cycles through every choice before going to the first one. For example, if one wishes to go back to the main menu, by clicking "Esc", to play multiplayer, the animation will start at the end of the selection and work its way down to the first selection. Check the status of your card collection? That selection is close to the end, so one must wait until the animation completes, cycle to "Card Collection", click it, and wait as the animation cycles through the other choices (about half a second), load, and then display the card collection.
All in all, what one is
for is full deck customization. It's an extremely high price to say the least. It almost feels like a punishment; WotC gave us what we wanted but had to take back other things to justify the action.

First impressions video:
80 days is a text based adventure game where you, the butler of a fine English gentleman, must accompany said man on a journey around the world. It is based off of the famous novel
by Jules Verne. The game consists of travelling between cities and dealing with events that occurboth within the cities and between them.
Most of the game occurs in a text based setting. You read a description of were you are, maybe a bit of dialogue, and you choose from one or more choices. Admittedly a one option choice isn't really a thing, but that's just nitpicking. The writing is clever and works well for the style. I highly recommend using accents for the people (especially if you don't know who they are yet. Gruff, English women are always good fun).
The game is procedurally created each time you play. That means a good amount of replay value.
The art style is simple and vivid. It isn't so elaborate that it pulls the eye away from the reading, while still having a good amount of character to it.
Overall, this game is worthy of a recommendation for the price of $10. Go circumnavigate the world you crazy explorers.

You, the valet Passepartout, embark with your master to win a wager: Travel Around the World in Eighty Days!
The dynamic story is different every time you play: based on the cities you decide to visit or the people you happen to meet. The world is beautifully described and you will even catch a glimpse of the politic affairs playing in the steampunky world you live in. The game allows for multiple playthroughs, because of the huge amount of different cities to visit, the randomized seeds for the world and ofcourse the urge to beat your friends or your previous records!
My personal record is 75 days, and during this particular journey I walked the ocean floor, was kidnapped by dangerous pirates, traveled both with a walking AND a floating city, crashed a hot air baloon in the ocean, only to be saved by a handful of fishermen.
I came across a lot more of interesting stories, but I won't spoil them all, they're for you to discover!
The game is based on the 1872 novel "Le tour du monde en quatre-vingts jours" by Jules Verne and the story viewed from Passepartouts perspective, just like Jules Verne's book.
The only improvable annoyance I found in this game is the 'conversation'-option you'll get during travels. It is a good way to learn a bit more about the possible roads you can take but it feels like more like some random generated lines than an actual conversation. However, the backstory of the vehicles you use are superb.
Easily worth the 10 bucks in my opinion. A perfect game to play on a relaxing night, it feels like you're reading a different version of Jules Verne's novel.

As someone new to the game looking for a less expensive way to get familiar with the mechanics I was really excited to give this a shot. The tutorials were exceptionally comprehensive and helpful, the cards themselves look great, and I had the chance to learn offline. All of those things should have lead me to a great experience, unfortunately I hit a wall very early on. The list of cons starts with the lackluster background visuals, slow iOS style interface, and insane difficulty spike which left a sour taste in my mouth. When it came to the first story quest line I made short work of the initial three enemies leading up to the first boss, Avacyn, this is where I started to lose interest in the game. Initially I thought players were meant to struggle with the healing play style of her white deck, but after four or five failed attempts I lowered the difficulty only to experience the same issues another two or three times. I realize that the game is meant to trick you and teach you to adapt, but this first experience made for a long five hours of play. It is safe to say that I love Magic the Gathering (or what I have played so far), but maybe real cards would be better suited for me.

A Vampyre Story is a 2008 horror comedy graphic adventure set in Europe during the 1890s, and follows a young female opera singer, recently turned vampire named Mona with her trusty sidekick bat companion Froderick as they attempt to make the journey back home to Paris.
As with any graphic adventure games, puzzles feature heavily. Most puzzles are creative and challenging and have a logical solution. I didn't however like a particular "Mix Potions into Different Potions" type of puzzle as it seems too over-used in graphic adventure games. It shouldn't be too hard for seasoned adventurers, although for me, I have to refer to the walkthrough more then once. Overall it took me around 15 hours to complete the game. Your mileage may vary.
This game introduces the concept of an "idea icon" in the inventory. Lets say if you attempt to have Mona take a sword, a sword-specific icon, not the actual sword will be added to the inventory. If necessary, Mona will teleport back to the sword, grab it, and teleport back to use it where she's supposed to. While unique, I thought it to be unnecessary. Nevertheless this is one of the game's unique way of distinguishing itself from other titles.
The voice acting for all the characters were pretty well done, but I especially enjoyed the playful and witty interactions between Mona and Froderick. Fantastic chemistry between these 2 characters and I really enjoyed the work done by their voice actors. The game also has a very beautiful orchestral and very professionally done soundtrack.
That said, there are also some serious shortcomings to this game.
Firstly, I understand that due to the age of this game, there are some people who are complaining that it doesn't even run on their computers. I am lucky that I am one of the few who have no such issues running it on Windows 10.
Secondly, there is no way to play this game in widescreen mode. The whole game is permanently stuck in a 1024x768 resolution with a 4:3 aspect ratio which means you will never be able to get it to play in fullscreen and will always have 2 thick ugly black bars at the side. In-game video resolutions are even lower then 1024x768 making the whole game look extremely dated in 2015.
Then there is the cliff-hanger ending. This entire game is only Chapter One and I understand that it was originally intended to be the first of a 4 part series. Sadly it seems that while a sequel was announced back in 2009, nothing was ever heard of it ever again due to some budget or legal issues with the publisher. As of 2015, it has already been 6 years since the initial 2009 announcement of the sequel. I highly doubt that it will ever be released.
Overall Rating: 8.0 / 10
Despite its low resolution, aspect ratio and other technical issues, I actually enjoyed the game very much. The cartoony 3D art style, wonderful soundtrack and whimsical story really brought back many fond memories of the good ole days of point-and-click graphic adventures.
If you can look past the technical issues that I mentioned and don't mind that the game ends at a cliff-hanger and is unlikely to ever release any sequel, I'd actually recommend this title to anyone who enjoys a good funny story with moderately challenging puzzles.
If you're sick of stupid childish Bioware ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, try out this awesome self-aware Obsidian craftwork, where the setting serves the story and not the other way around.

I really wish I could recommend Sniper Elite V2... but I just can't. Which is weird because it's a game I enjoyed playing a lot.
Let's start with the good things. Like many said before me, the sniping mechanics are incredibly well done. Sure, some would argue that you shouldn't have to adjust your scopes for a 100m shot, but the maps are relatively small, so it's kind of necessary to have such a drastic bullet drop in this game. It makes the gameplay more challenging and definitely more fun... and that's just the ballistics. The bullet cam and the X-ray vision are what make this game very unique. I don't think I've ever enjoyed sniping so much before.
BUT
These surprisingly fun sniper-sections of the game aren't worth the 20€ you'd be spending on it. (Thank god I got it for free...) Why, you may ask? Because not only the campaign lasts only like 6 hours at most (played on the highest difficulty, which is the only way I would recommend playing this game), only half of it will be spent sniping like that. Which should be okay since you don't want to get bored, obviously. Variety is important you may say, but sniping is literally the only thing they got right in this game... and after an hour of gameplay, you're gonna wish you could just snipe from your safe vantage point again, instead of attempting to sneak through an army of enemies, then inevitably fail.
You may have guessed by now that this game is supposed to be a stealth-based one. A mixture of sneaking your way through to the objective, then assasinate X and hunt the rest of the enemies nearby. That's how it should work.
Guess what: it doesn't. Most of the time you're given a very linear map which is almost completely impossible to sneak through. There are other times where no matter how good you are, you literally can't be stealthy: as soon as you arrive to a checkpoint, you trigger waves of enemies coming at you, no matter how sneaky you are. Then you're left there alone, against hundreds(!) of commies or Jerries with your trusted sniper rifle... and nothing else, since your SMG is♥♥♥♥♥♥weak and carries up to 2 magazines at once, and your pistol is either used for stealth play (which is either useless or non-existent most of the time), or you could grab a Colt and attempt to benefit from the power of the .45ACP round and its rate of fire. Good luck with that.
So the game forces you to snipe even in a CQB situation, which is absolutely ridiculous. You better grab your Gewehr 43.
Even when stealth play is given, you'll just find it faster, more effective and more fun to shoot your way through the enemies anyway. The other features of the game (setting up traps for your enemy, using distraction, the controls, storyline, co-op and multiplayer) are either laughably bad or just plain useless.
TL;DR: Fun sniping, bad everything else. Worth it if it's free, not worth it if you have to pay for it.
5/10 for the amazing sniping parts

I usually refuse to purchase ANY early access game that has less than a average, 300 player base..but there are always exceptions to every rule. Angels Fall First is one of those few exceptions. What seperates this game from many of the other early access games is their development team. The development team is very active, so much, I can personally guarantee you that you can reach one within less than 10 hours. Either through the community forum or on their discord channel. Another reason is that developing this game isn't their full time job, which means any funds they get from purchases goes into their equipment and strategies for improving and populating this game.
As for the game itself.. it functions fairly. You can battle on the surface of a planetary map or soar in space in fighter and capital ships. The most interesting mechanic of all, is you can fly your boarding ship at an enemy captial ship and board it and take the enemy ship out from the inside out. Again, the player population is extremely low, but the matches do serve us up bots (who are not that good, except space fights). The game's playable, many things that can be done on the battlefield, just no one is playing..they are chilling on their discord channel, waiting for the next big update that'll drastically improve the game. So unless you and others buy in and share your input, the speed at which this game gets update will remain slow...but they've said time and time again, it will get done...nothing in the real world is stopping them thus far. FORWARD FOR THE UNITY LEAGUE!

Life Is Feudal - A lot of people buy this game with bad expectations.  They play games like ARK, DayZ, 7 days to die and Minecraft, and expect a 'medieval survival/builder sandbox' game to be comparable.  What they don't realize, is that they're idiots.
Recent review I read:  "I logged in for 2 minutes, saw the game sucks and got refunded".
This is the mindset for why this game has mixed reviews, NOT because the game deserves mixed reviews.
Life is Feudal is a 'realistic' survival builder, which is something these kids don't understand, because none of their games are realistic.  To them, realism is finding a brand new machine gun in a box, or building a base in 30 minutes, or punching a dinosaur unconscious so they can tame it with berries, and that my friends is the grotesque standard these dumb kids are comparing this game to.  Don't listen.
This game is it's own genre, and it can't be compared to anything else.  Everything takes time in this game.  It will take you days to build your first house, and weeks to build a settlement.  And THAT is why this game has the GREATEST community I have ever seen in an online game.  This game is all about teamwork... not the solo game experience.
And just so people know what this game is being developed for... this version of the game is the groundwork for an MMO version, where a much larger world will be occupied by thousands of players.  This is by far the greatest survival/builder game I have ever played, with the best community I've ever played with.  Thank you 'Life is Feudal' developement team for creating a game for adults that scares off those with attention deficits.

There's something to be said for the increasing number of remasters on the market these days. I'm not a particularly big fan of them, but if they are being made, they must be selling. It's quite peculiar, though, to see a video game straddle different forms of media, to re-tell Jules Verne's classic tale of Phileas Fogg and his 80 day trip around the globe, and in a choose-your-own visual novel, no less! True, it isn't a direct re-telling, in fact it's almost entirely original material, bar the initial bet that sees Fogg traipse across the planet. But if 80 Days can rekindle my love for the written word, then I'm all for it.
If you've previously read Around The World in Eighty Days, you can pretty much forget everything you thought you knew about Fogg and his valet, Passepartout's, journey around the globe. While Fogg is still a stuffy, well to do type, and Passepartout attends to his every whim, the world around them is drastically different. The age of steam, gears and machinery has taken hold, and it's up to Fogg and Co to take advantage of it to arrive back in London before their 80 day deadline is up. A fortune awaits them if they can make it back in time, with bitter defeat and ridicule being the only other option - a fate worse than death!
Setting off from London, they can travel to any of a large number of cities, all across the globe. There's very little in the way of restrictions to stop Fogg and Passepartout,well, aside from their bank balance.
Their journey is set against a beautifully-rendered interactive globe, with sprawling travel routes running like a circulatory system across the planet. Each city they visit has its own story, people, market and events. So whether you're in Paris sipping coffee in a cafe, or stealing heavy machinery with a mining crew in South America, each location feels unique, and most importantly, authentic - no mean feat considering the truly monumental scale of the game.
Being men of the world, Fogg and Passepartout bump into all kinds of characters. Sometimes, you'll get a great tip about places to visit or faster travel routes, other times, you might end up comatose in an opium den, only to end up on an airship going in the wrong direction. Mon Dieu!
Traveling across the world isn't cheap, and whilst Fogg is a wealthy man, you'll still need to watch your expenses. Fortunately, you won't be shy of an opportunity to earn some coin. Marketplaces are a great spot to pick up trinkets, travel-appropriate clothing, and items that might be worth a bob or two in other parts of the world. Failing that, Passepartout can always dress up as a bearded lady in the circus.
Money affords Fogg and Passepartout comfort and luxury, but some routes may not be so accommodating, meaning traveling can impact their health. If you've managed to collect appropriate clothing sets for your journey, like scarves and hats, you can lessen the damage done., but some times you will be left with no option than to rest. You can keep Fogg in tip top shape by attending to his needs whilst you travel. It's amazing what a cup of tea and a tidy moustache can do! Just don't drink the local water.
Make no mistake about it, 80 Days is a gorgeously detailed book, rich in detail, and with more than a few laughs thrown in for good measure. Developer, Inkle, has crafted a gamebook so lavish with descriptive language that its easy to become engrossed. It doesn't matter if you win the bet or not, so long as you enjoy the journey, and trust me, you will.
80 Days is a wonderful re-imagination of Jules Verne's classic book "Around The World in 80 Days"

This would normally be a neutral review, but I tend more towards the negative.
I loved Shadow Warrior 1. It had a clumsy, one-dinensional generic story to begin with with yakuzas, katanas and you get the idea. As the game progressed and the story blossomed, ending in a very fine story arc. Besides that, it was and is one of the best paced FPS games out there, with pacing similar to Doom (both the old and new one), Quake1, Unreal Tournament and Alien vs Predator. It was quick, fun and immersive.
I bought SW2 the day it came out, I loved the first one, the second game seems to be the same, what could go wrong?
Well, everything.
It runs great and it did run great even on day1. That's a plus. The graphics aren't so nice and detailed (check Deus Ex: Mankind Divided for a comparison), so this explains. The levels are big, but the populations are generated random. So normally this would be a huge plus, but in the first Shadow Warrior, there were a lot of carefully balanced fighting arenas just like in Doom and this was a huge benefit to the level design. Not anymore.
The story is worse and in some cases, it doesn't make sense. Yes, Shadow Warrior 1 had its burlesque moments too, but they made sense and as the game progressed, it got a more and more dark and serious tone. In case of Shadow Warrior 2, it is just fluctuating.
The thing however which kills the fun is the crafting system. Shadow Warrior 1 had some weapons which were completely useless on higher difficulties, and some people were complaining about the large number of skills and choices in the menus. So guess what? You get more weapons (with some balancing issues) and you get a loot system you can attach to some of your weapons. A loot system which with its attachment focus is similar to Sacred 2's system (it was a bad one but still acceptable for an RPG). So instead of fighting through hordes of enemies in a fast paced fighting game, you end up looking in the menus and farming the shops to try to get one item spawn you can get. With an inventory which is list based, so not really user friendly.
For a single playthrough, if you play this for a story, the looting system wont spoil the fun, but the story isn't that great either.
If you like endless grinding and organizing records in a badly sorted list get this. If you are too old to grind some game to get better gear to grind even more, then skip this.
Btw: Yes, 10 hours is enough to go through the whole game and check NG+ a bit. It is short if you don't like mindless grinding.

I don't see Beamng.drive as a game, but more of a very open sandbox. Essentially you have several maps and many cars to choose from. You have maps that take you through cities, forests, rivers, freeways, dirt paths, racing circuits, hills and much more. You also get a really diverse array of cars ranging from trucks, commercial vehicles, sudans, supercars, vans, coupes, SUVs, classic cars, compacts, musle cars and the legendary three wheeled pigeon. Of course you can drive these cars around just like any other racing game, but you can also customize your car in the config menu and save it so you can drive it later. Now the best part of Beamng.drive is it's crash physics. Guaranteed there is no other game that can match the physics beamng.drive has. When you crash the way the car crumples feels so natural and the damage is realistic as it effects the cars drivablity allowing you to see how the impact effected the car. With such great physics you can create your own senarios and see how the event plays out. Somthing I think is over looked about this game is its modding comunity. Suprisingly on Beamng.drive's website there are a large amount of high quality mods you can add to your game. The mods can add extra maps, extra car configurations, entirely new cars, apps, skins, senarios and sounds. Personally I would recommend the mods Satuma 210, ETK S Series and Fait One just to name a few. Overall Beamng.drive is a must buy for any car enthusiast who loves to crash but doesn't want to kill themselves in the process.

While not for everyone, I found 80 Days to be a fun and unique experience.
80 Days has three main mechanics. First you need to plan routes around the world in order to complete you journey within 80 days. This is an interesting mechanic since you need to carefully plan your route but not take too long or you can arrive too late for your preferred form of transportation and have to wait losing precious time. You also need to handle your inventory buying and selling goods that will help you on your journey and help fund your travels.
The biggest mechanic in the game is the story itself. Most of the game revolves around interacting with the people and events you encounter on your journey. This requires a lot of text reading with the occasional option to decide how the story plays out. This is main reason why I said that the game will not be for everyone. If this doesn't appeal to you, you won't like 80 Days. If you like a good story though I think you can really enjoy 80 Days.
If you like the idea behind the game and like a good story that requires quite a bit of reading you should really enjoy 80 Days since it is a truly original engaging experience.
Note: I received a free review copy from the developer.

When this finally came out, the general responce was that it was crap. So, I avoided it until this recent sale. I must say that the opposite is true. It would seem the nay-sayers were probably not born yet, or too young to play the originals, especially Duke3D, when it was the latest and greatest. Yes, there was a time when Duke3D was a techical marvel!
DNF is exactly what a sequel of Duke3D should be. But where Duke3D was risque, DNF is soft core porn.
The game has scores of references, if you look for them.
DNF is Duke3D and Half Life 2's love child...in a good way. DN's monster truck even sounds identical to the buggy in HL2.
DNF seems to avoid all of the single player FPS quagmires: There are no jumping puzzles, no cheap bosses, and only 1 very short conveyor-belt-with-pistons-of-death bit.
The major change is that health is now replaced by ego. Which replenishes after a time. This makes sense for the character and stops you running around avoid fights while looking for health like a wimp.
All in all, this game is brilliant.

I downloaded this after mentioning to a friend of mine that I want to jet off and board things and whatnot, and he recommended Angels Fall First.  I'm glad he did.  It's chaos to start off with, and it can be difficult to tell what's going on HUD-wise, but after a couple of matches I understood what the important symbols were and how to handle myself.
XP and upgrades
Everything is unlocked from the beginning, but your loadouts (and you can customise every single vehicle, every armour slot, every gun etc) are limited in total cost, with 3 different measures - Combat, Support and Command. You can't deploy with a loadout that's over your limit for any of of those, and as you gain xp for killing things, supporting your team and taking objectives respectively, you'll earn small increases to these caps. While the caps increases are small, your first 10 point upgrade feels like the world just opened up around you, and that one extra mod you wanted is available, or you can completely rejigger your loadout.
Maps
I've played for a couple of hours so far, and I've only once seen the same map twice. There are lots of avenues, multilevel positions, mounted guns, staircases etc everywhere, with open areas for your LMG, and closed in sections for the underbarrel flamethrower on your LMG.  The level design is pretty great, and I've had my share of murdering a dozen guys from a fortification, and getting blitzed by a runner with an SMG zipping from cover to cover.
UI
Here we could use a little work. I've had a handy little comment below correcting me on this, which is nice.  It's still a bit of a pain, but yes, the tacmap -does- tell me what everything is, so I just need to commit those to memory.  You can check the weapon stats by clicking on a weapon, clicking on stats and then hovering over other weapons. I haven't had a chance to check it out since they let me know... 9 minutes ago, we'll see if that makes my decisions easier.
Graphics
Here AFF has a bit of an issue. It's running on Unreal Engine 3, and it looks like a 2012 game, if we're being generous. Just like a black and white movie, you get used to it after a bit and it stops bothering you, but the graphics are pretty chronic.  Don't let that stop you from buying this though, the gameplay is solid, and the devs are working, even now, to improve the game.

This little gem of an adventure game grows on you. Despite the main character being from Paris and talking in a German accent, the game is a suitably silly vampire story about an opera singer (who doesn't really believe she's a vampire) trying to escape a castle in Draxsylvania and get back to Paris. Her comedy sidekick bat sits on her shoulder and supplies plenty of sarcasm. There are some memorable characters, the voice acting is pretty good, and there's lots of jokes on just about every clickable object.
The controls are decent, a few of the puzzles are illogical, but otherwise bearable, and the story gets better and better as the characters grow.
Be warned that it ends sort of abruptly and was supposed to have been a two-parter, but the second game was never made. Some sort of information about that would have been nice up front, but it doesn't actually matter much. It's not too much of a cliffhanger, and the game is enjoyable enough that you can't really feel mad about it. If anything, you're sad you can't spend more time with the characters, but a prequel is in the works, so here's hoping.

I tend to judge stories by the intensity of the dreams they give me. By this standard Amnesia is a hell of a game. Though unlike in Outlast I didn't make my flatmate dash in to find out why I was screaming, the level of suspense and menacing environments had me on an emotional knife edge most of the way through.
It's more subtle than a lot of its rivals. Enemies stalk you from the shadows and though the plot has some intense (distressingly delightful) violence it's often suggested rather than given in 'look at this!' moments. Your imagination does the work (hence the nightmares).
My main problem was the difficulty of some of the puzzles. Granted I'm never good at these but I wandered around confusedly more than usual in parts of Amnesia. I thought some of them were set up a bit too mysteriously, which actually replaced suspense with frustration as I was left clicking on everything in sight before eventually stumbling across the solution.
But considering how it dares to give such a complex story in a very fragmented fashion the game works well, and I love how the truth is revealed agonisingly gradually. If you're sick of dreaming about exam results or turning up naked for work then Amnesia is for you, but beware - it could be worse than either...

This review is split into two parts as there are well.... two games, Necrologue as you know but also Twilight of the Archaic which is playable by right clicking on the game from you're steam library.
While it holds the name of the older game series "Penumbra" It is a mod for Amnesia: The dark descent and as such requires you to own a copy of Amnesia itself on steam. If you have a non-steam version the mod can be downloaded and installed from sites like ModDB. This is a free game so this review will keep that in-mind when analyzing it for its gameplay factors and graphic fidelity.
First Impressions remind of exactly of my experiences in the previous Penumbra games. It looks the same, it plays the same. The story apparently follows the previous title Requiem but I've found from playing the other titles story is not overly important here. In the end it’s a Horror/ Puzzle game and does not have a very strong storytelling aspect unless you read deep into it yourself either online or through the text based notes you find in-game.
The game itself is 8 hours long which is the perfect length for even a paid title, no issues there.
The horror elements are mostly that of jump scares, such as sudden doors slamming shut, something moving out of slight the moment you see it, lights suddenly going out, walking around the corner into an enemy and so on. Other than that there are the enemies that are monsters, dogs and spier looking things that will walk around in certain open areas forcing you to avoid or run to get from one place to another.
Puzzles...... Most of the Puzzles are fine, take a little bit to work out either using basic problem solving or just doing random things till it works. However and that’s a big however, a few puzzles of note really bring down the game a few points. I remember getting stuck on 3 puzzles, 1 of which I worked out with a friend the other 2 I had to look up online.
The first was a formula to create acid, you were supposed to match the formula to the periodic table while using a note that briefly describes some of the components that might work. For people unfamiliar with the periodic table this is very difficult to work out or know that it’s even relevant.
The second was a code for a door you had to figure out. You find a piece of paper with 4 strange symbols on it that look like something from an unknown language. First thing that comes to mind is count the number of lines connecting to each symbol as there are 4 I assume the code is 4 digits long. Nope, that doesn't work. Ok, I'll go look around for something else, Nope nothing in the whole area. My notes might say something about it, Nope! Nothing there. Ok let’s look it up, nothing online so I watch a video.... oh you’re meant to count the points connecting each edge of the lines.... well how about adding some dots so players can figure it out logically. There is nothing within the game or on the paper that warrants me to count non-existent edge points.
The third was the best of all. A small Maze towards the end of the game with buttons on the walls that displays different letters. I assume it’s either a code or a word. I write down the letters and can’t find anything to resemble a relevant word. This time you don’t even have your notes and nothing is in the area to give any clues as to the mystery word. Fantastic game, a must buy for anyone looking for a game that combines Battlefront, Homeworld, Battlefield 2142, and a solid space flight sim like Tie Fighter.
On foot FPS, jump in a tank, take an objective, jump out, steal a fighter, escape back to base, board a transport ship, assault an enemy capital ship to board and destroy it on foot.  You can do all this, online or offline with bots with tons of maps.
This is the game I always wanted.
Only thing is, it's still in early access and it does show.  The game is perfectly playable and fun, but just still rough around the edges.
-AI needs work.  Not in the accuracy department, just in the intelligent behavior department.
-Needs better UI for controls, like radial menus for the command menus so you can issue them without having to search your keyboard for different keys.  Being able to pop up a radial menu and quickly issue commands with only the mouse would be preferable.
-UI needs some work in general to make the gameplay a bit easier to understand.   When customizing vehicles a lot of the text runs off of the description boxes so you can't tell what certain things are supposed to do.
-A LOT of keys, could be pared down a bit more and consolidated.
-Needs more tutorial missions that focus on specific types of vehicles, their uses, and allow you to use them in a combat situation.
-Really, a short 5 or 6 mission storyline would be the way to go after the current tutorial.  That way you can have the player re-apply all the required mechanics in a combat situation.  It would reinforce what they learned during the tutorial (which is a lot to ask for the average player to learn, you have to reinforce it), but it isn't as chaotic as a general skirmish map.
-Once finished and released this would be a GREAT game to port to consoles.  Devs would make a ton of money from it too, hopefully they do that after it is polished up nicely.

Finished three times so far, excellent game. Here is a quick summary:
Pros:
+ Price:Worth ratio is very, VERY high
+ Melee combat is very satisfying and very well executed for an FPS game
+ Upgrade system allows firearms to perform differently
+ Skills system allows you to tailor your character the way you want to play it
+ Online co-op (but there is a big negative to this as well)
+ "Semi-procedurally" generated maps
Neutral:
o Loot oriented game
o Great successor
o A lot of weapons
o Attention to detail is amazing
o Excellent graphics
o Level and art design is very well done
o Soundtrack is awesome
Cons:
- Inventory system requires attention. Filtering options are direly needed
- Firearms require more love
- Some upgrades have big drawbacks, especially at early levels to make then worthless
- Some game mechanics require (more) explanation, and some don't make any sense
- The negative of co-op: Currently, anyone that joins a game is an "apprentice" in essence, and the host is the "master". Apprentices don't progress in the story line as far as I can tell. While I appreciate online co-op, not allowing players to progress in their own game will probably keep them away from joining a co-op game till they finish their game at least once
Personal/Extended Points:
+ I don't know why they added "semi" in front of "procedural". This is what a lot of games out there already do, and they just call it "procedural". Technically, "semi-procedural" is right, but still. Compared to other games that semi-procedurally generate maps, this one has bigger chunks, but the detail went to them is great
o Loot! You grab a lot of loot. In addition to upgrade gems that go into your weapons/armor, some weapons and some skills are also loot. Some may dislike it, but personally I like loot-oriented games
o Not exactly like the previous game; new additions and changes may not be well received by those who love the previous game, but personally I like every new addition and change
- Left unchecked, your inventory will become a massive clusterduck and finding something useful will be really hard
- "Fire mode" upgrades take valuable upgrade slots, making them perform poorly to melee in comparison
Overall, I enjoy the game a lot. There isn't much left to do for me, so I decided to go on multiplayer a little, and it becomes much more fun in multiplayer of course. I really hope they'll release free & paid DLCs, because this game has insane potential. As I've said, money well spent. I'm looking forward for the future updates and DLCs as this game has become one of my favourites.

*This review is written from the perspective of an experienced player in both the paper game and the Duel of the Planeswalkers series.*
Magic 2015 is the newest game in the annual Duel of the Planeswalker series. Other than the beautiful yet short cinematics and the fact that the game is a licensed Magic: The Gathering product, there are very few positive things to say about this game.
The user-interface is done in a clunky, slide-show format, making only four options visible on the menu at a single time. Numerous game modes present in prior editions have been removed. The Two-Headed Giant (cooperative) format for multiplayer will be the most noticeable for many players, who probably purchased the game for multiplayer games. The Challenges (puzzles) and Revenge Campaign - a second campaign with more difficult opponents, which appears after the completion of the original Campain mode - are also no longer present.
The largest and most noticeable change to the game is the way decks are chosen and constructed. The prior editions of DotP contained numerous pre-constructed decks. The player unlocked additional cards for your deck by playing and winning with it. the player would then use the cards you received to improve their deck, win more, and repeat the cycle. In Magic 2015, this is no longer the case. Decks are now individual constructed by the player from a card pool. With every win, you unlock boosters, which contain new cards for your card pool. Besides who makes the deck, it would still seem that the player win cards to improve their deck to win more cards. This is not the case however.
One of my favorite parts about the prior DotP games was the pre-constructed decks. The decks were mostly balanced and - barring a few exceptions - almost all of them were playable with zero cards unlocked. This was great for new players. They could learn the mechanics of the game without being punished for lack of experience with deck construction. Many of the decks were well constructed and included cards that I simply cannot afford to play in real life. This was great for experienced players on a budget, such as myself. The deck construction was constricted, but that kind of constriction prevented too large of a metagame from forming. I'll stop lamenting, but I guess my favorite part of the old DotP games is that every deck was playable to everyone, regardless of a player's skill level.
With Magic 2015, the player starts the game by choosing a deck archetype composed of two colours. Once the player chooses their deck, they are stuck with it. These are the only cards that they're going to have to play with until deck construction opens up. This is not a good thing for new players, who will be stuck if their skill level is not enough to overcome the handicap of terrible cards. Once a player has won a few matches, they will have unlocked a few booster packs. The cards in the packs by this point will likely not be enough to make a new deck, and if so, not one of any value. In fact, one of my largest issues with the game as a whole was that the card pool was terrible. Green decks have Cultivate, but no Rampant Growth. Red decks have Shock and Bolt of Keranos, but no Lightning Bolt. Black decks have Assassinate, but no Doom Blade. Griselbrand is all but unplayable in a Black-Green deck designed to get him onto the field.
Regardless of how terrible the cards in the card pool comes my other large issue with the game - the metagame. The other DotP games had a metagame, but it is much more mild than the metagame of Magic 2015. This game's metagame is similar to that of Block constructed. In time, only certain decks will be viable in multiplayer, making multiple other decks and cards unplayable. By creating a card pool with flexibility, Wizards of the Coast only limited the amount of playable cards even further.
If you want other decks to be useful, then you may have to pay. Pay real life cash. Monocolour decks benefit greatly from their respective Paragon, and a Five colour deck is only justifiable with Maelstrom Angel. These cards are only available in a Premium Booster, which are two dollars a piece with no other way to unlock them. I would have rather payed $20 for a game with all of the card unlockable in game, than $10 for a less than complete game. If you want a card game where your cards are determined by chance, you have infinite flexibility of card construction, a strict metagame, and pay real money for cards then play Magic the Gathering Online. It has all of that and more.
In short, Magic 2015 falls short of Magic 2014 by trying to be Magic Online. Magic 2015 has less features, a terrible card pool, a strict metagame, and a pay to win mentality. It is neither a true DotP game or MTGO/MODO. If you want to play real Magic in a digital format, then invest in MTGO/MODO. If you want to play a smooth game with smooth decks, get Magic 2014.
Positive:
- Beautiful cinematics
- Magic: The Gathering licensing
Drawbacks:
- Poor user interface
- Poor deck construction
- Poor card pool
- Locked content
- Removed cooperative multiplayer
- Removed Revenge campaign
- Removed challenge feature

This is my first review, because I feel that I have to recommend this game, but also warn you:
Life is Feudal is still in Early Access, but currently offers a lot of different mechanics. Finding yourself washed ashore on an big island with nothing on your body except for something to eat and some rags, you have to create everything in the game from scratch. You build your own tools from branches and stones, find some roots to eat and create your first Tiny Shack. All this building, crafting and planning (terrain flattening alone is an art/skill) takes unbelievably long time, which may annoy some people. If you are extremely impatient just skip this game - it's nothing for you.
On the other hand it is extremely satisfying to create your own buildings. Until I had a forge (which is needed for nails, for example - so a rather basic building), I spent around 20 hours in the game. When the forge was finally done, I was just proud of myself.
One reason it takes so long to achieve process, is that many activities take a lot of time: snapping a branch from a tree? Around 2 seconds. You need 20 branches for a building? Click 20 times on the same tree and simply wait each time 2 seconds. This can be annoying with the time, so better get used to it and watch TV on a second screen.
Having friends that play with you is not only nice, but highly recommended. With on character you aren't able to succeed in the various skill trees (or if you try you end up as a bad jack-of-all-trades, who is able to some jobs a little, but nothing really good). The strange server structure (everyone can host a server) leads to a huge variety of servers, leaving the "public" servers rather deserted, so don't count on meeting many people around there.
As already mentioned, there are several skill trees, like Herbalism, Carpentry, Smithing, Hunting and so on. Each of them uses different mechanics, so it is fun to try them all out. Some of them are extremly fun (building, carpentry), some of them are okay/highly repetitive (mining takes literally hours...) and some of them are simply boring and stupid (especially herbalism). At a later point you need high level material (like steel and mortar) so called Flux which can only be gathered by Herbalism people, who have to search for hours one small area of herbs and then combine them in an annoying mini-game and hope for some luck.
The second rather bad mechanic is the whole fighting module. Right now you can hunt animals, some agressive like wolves or boars and some peaceful like sheep or deer. The AI of these animals is simply stupid, you have to shoot them with around 10-15 bullets of your sling to kill them. During this annoying process they do not move a bit (or run away like 5 squares then stay still again). Even the dangerous species try to attack you only once, after you land one successful shot, they stand still like all the others. Even achieving higher levels of weapons (you have to learn Throwing Weapons, then get hit with Leather Armor on, then learn Crossbows and THEN you are able to use Bows) does not significantly lower the time you need to hunt an animal. This is truely unsatisfying and outright bad right now. If the fighting against other players should feel the same like fighting against animals, this would be desastrous.
TL,DR:
++ Extremely satisfying to build structures
+ Great when playing in small communities
+ Different mechanics to learn with each job
-- Huge effort of time neccessary to achieve something
- Long waiting times during processes
- Difficult to learn (Wiki helps a great deal)
- Combat Module isn't any fun
All in all I can recommend this game if you are looking for a challenging medieval-crafting-simulation. If you are impatient or believe that this game is all about building forts and playing knight, go away. You will be disappointed. But if you like grinding for ressources and want to build a small village with your friends - this is your game (Early Access and all).
