I rate Duke Nukem Forever 3/5. OK but it certainly does not live up to the genius of its predecessor.
It is an extremely linear game and as a result severely lacking in replay value. There are almost no true decisions to be made in this game. It almost plays itself. For that reason (and due to the relatively simple controls) this would be a good game to play if you had never played an FPS before and wanted to learn (but UT2004, a very different kind of FPS, is even better for this). The game has good graphics (in a style sort of half-way between Doom 3, Prey and Half Life 2) with an engine that seems closest to Prey's graphical engine. There are moments of irritation in this game and moments of greatness (the monster truck travel section was great). This game however loses itself in its focus on Duke Nukem's personality rather than on the potential of its various environments (In Duke Nukem 3D it was the amazing environments and complex level design that were the actual focus. In that game Duke seemed to merely be there along for the ride in many ways). Overall, Duke Nukem Forever is less intelligent than its predecessor and feels like a game paying homage to its predecessor (and it largely fails to be satirical). Parts of the game often remind me (perhaps this was done intentionally) of a few other games; mostly Doom 3, Half Life, Prey, Revolt and even, occassionally, bioshock. The jokes made in the game often feel stale or fall flat and Duke's personality (and the game's focus on his personality instead of on the potential mysteries of the aliens he's fighting or the possibilities of his environment) is even irritating at times. The game is often exciting (at least the first time through) with some parts reminding me of parts of the Alien and Aliens movie/game franchise (good but possibly derivative). The Steam version of the game I played ran wonderfully and had very few bugs...but with such an extremely linear game (no branching side-paths, no alternate endings, etc.) there's not much here to be buggy. Somehow this game was at once exciting...and boring...in different ways. The sexism in this game was no worse I think than that found in Duke Nukem 3D..but it would have been nice (even predictable for the modern social climate) if the game had an equal/opposite female heroin that Duke could "interact" with from time to time (like an ex-girlfriend or something), but alas no. Duke Nukem's personality alone does not provide enough interest for a game to focus on in such an exclusive manner...the result was somewhat irritating.

The graphics were fine, and some of the character models were great even (Cossack, anyone?). The problem I have with this game is the controls or to be precise, the delay with buttons pressed. They tried to make the attacks look more natural like the fighting style, but thanks to the attack animations  being mostly unique for each character, some characters have really cheap and exploitive button combos.
I would recommend it if you want to watch the CPU fight each other for 5 minutes. If wanting to play the game yourself, it shall be too annoying to like it for long.

As with the first KotOR, this game does an excellent job of expanding on the Old Republic storyline. Many of the great elements of the first game are present in the sequel, for better or for worse, but I'll get to that in a bit. I prefer dessert first so I'll lay down the sweetness before the ricecakes.
Pos+
$- The skill/feat system is greatly improved. While it keeps the origional, point based system, it makes it much easier to create a character you can call your own.
$- The class/prestige system is one of the most notable improvments. Not only giving a vastly superior starting point, but also allowing you to really embrace the Light/Dark side powers and choice system.
$- In keeping with the player driven, "morality" system, I will note that the game does not "punish" you for choosing Dark side actions like it did in the origional.
$- The speeder racing minigames are vastly improved and are far more rewarding than the origional.
Neg-
Rather than dollar pointing the negitives, I will simply break this down to the single greatest reason why this game is not as great as the first, even though it is great. It is a CLONE. Players may or may not be aware of this, but the development changed hands between games and was greatly rushed in comparison to the first. The result was a storyline that simply "continues" where the origional left off, and falls short of finding its own identity. Normally this would not be a problem as it is a sequal, but it uses the events of the first to cover up the lack of origionality and noticably underpolished graphics. For those who don't understand what i mean, examine the growth that occured between two other Bioware titles, Mass Effect and Mass Effect 2.
All things considered, KotOR 2, is a solid game with a great core in a fantasic Galaxy far, far way. A galaxy that is inhabbited by beautiful landscapes, complex stories and passionate, often "insane" people (his name is StarKiller, Mr. Lucas, and he is your fault).

This game has an amazing concept, and when the game works, it plays really well. Don't think of it as a Dynasty Warriors or fast pace action game. Think of it as a fighting game, or Dark Souls PVP. The controls are solid and I can't find any glaring balance issues so far. The single player campaign isn't too bad, I thought the premise to the story could be better, seeing as they had such a great foundation.
Gameplay aside, there is a myriad of issues that plague the game. Some are unintentional like network issues, and some are self-imposed.
Some people argue that the network issues are client-side, but most people agree that it is on Ubisoft's end. I can only play 2/3 of the matches to completion due to getting dropped from the game. Which is disheartening when it takes a few minutes for matchmaking to find me game, even with an open NAT.
My biggest issue with
, is it's blatant "Free to Play" architecture. This game was designed to be F2P. Plain and simple. If I was a gambling man, I would wager my house that
will be free to play within 2 years, and that's being generous. The progression system is slow, only sped up with premium currency that
be acquired through gameplay, but realistically obtained with real money. When I first loaded the game up, I honestly thought I was playing a F2P title. If this game was free to play, it would be amazing, but I paid $60 for it, and all I get is the feeling that Ubisoft just wants more money.
Complaints aside, this game has/had potential. I don't see myself playing this game anymore and I deeply regret buying it. I might give it another shot when they get the network issues sorted (They should have had a BETA to sort out the network issues....oh wait.). I'd wait for it to go on sale in a couple months to try it if your interested, but a majority of the player base will be gone and it'll probably take 10-15 minutes to find a match.
EDIT: I recently got a "free" 10 day VIP status from Twitch Prime, and I've been able to play with increased XP and money gains. The progression feels much better, and is how it should be for everyone. There is more than enough stuff to spend "steel" on, don't make it pretty much mandatory for people to spend most of it just to level up at a reasonable pace. My opinions still haven't changed. It's a decent game at it's core, but the business model is (quoting a commentor) cancerous.

I think that it's important for people to remember that this game is in Early Access Beta so it will obviously be rough around the edges. Some problems that I have noticed are that enemies can sometimes glitch to where you cannot attack them, but they can attack you. Several times I would get stuck on the street curb and have to jump to get unstuck, etc. While these bugs are annoying and break the immersion and fluidity of the game, there are many aspects of which to commend the developers for. Gunplay and melee combat feels solid, and you never feel overpowered or so underpowered that the game loses its fun factor. The world's atmosphere is pretty awesome. Think of it as Fallout meets Walking Dead.
The most immediate comparisons will be to DayZ and, unfortuately, Infestation: Survivor Stories (The War Z). While you can definitely tell that Nether took inspiration from DayZ, I would not call it a clone. There are some things that DayZ does better, and there are also things that Nether does better. One thing I immediately like better about Nether over say DayZ is that when you start the game with just your kitchen knife, you still have somewhat of a shot at surviving. I mean sure getting in close quarters knife fights with the Nether who can teleport and knock down your health pretty quickly isn't the best idea, but running into a few of them along the way to find supplies doesn't mean that you're done for. Also there has been talk going around the internet about how the same attorney who did the licensing (or whatever you want to call it) for Infestation: SS / The War Z also did the licensing for this game. However, that seems to be about where the similarities stop because I can tell you that the Nether is in every way a much higher quality game. I can't assure you that you're going to like it, but just because you didn't like that game doesn't mean that you shouldn't give this one a chance.
All in all I definitely would reccomend Nether. Whether you are looking for an alternative to the other survival games out there or maybe just an alternative to the standard FPS games, Nether isn't one to pass up on in my opinion. Although imperfect in its Beta form, the developers are really showing some serious potential for this game. It has a great foundation and I am 100% confident that it can and WILL only get better. **updated June 30th 2017 with Discord link**
Although comparing Angels Fall First to Battlefront seems an injustice to this game, it's probably the best starting point in bringing people up to speed on what this is. This game mixes it up with infantry, and vehicular combat, including light vehicles, tanks, aerial vehicles that can all be customized with various loadouts. While the comparisons to Battlefront are all but inevitable, I do feel the maps very much remind me of a mix of Enemy Territory: Quake Wars and Planetside 2 in design, and do mean that in the best of ways.
Aside from the mixed combat with more boots on the ground, where Angels Falls First really impresses is in it's more space oriented battles. It's huge flagships, frigates, fighters, bombers and more. The larger vessels being able to be breached and boarded by infantry making for some risky plays and interesting encounters even in the depths of space.
Now while I do recommend this game if you are willing to ride it out and be patient, I will state a few rough areas and current issues:
- Don't expect a large group of people playing all hours, most larger games are organized on their Discord channel. (link below). That said it's still fun to go smack around some bots alone or with a few friends.
- While huge improvements have been made to the UI currently, there's still some room for improvements in readability and presenting information to the player.
- Some weapons I feel could use some adjustments to their handling and time to kill.
Anyways, in it's current state, it's quite feature rich already, with a wide variety of maps, tools, weapons and vehicles. There's still work to be done, and the developers seem eager for feedback from the community as well as dedicated to delivering on their promises.
If you are into sci fi pew pew combined arms battles akin to Enemy Territory: Quake Wars, Planetside or Battlefront, give this game a follow and consider purchasing it as well.

Before I begin, I should mention that I have not yet completed the game, and that this is merely a first impression account. I've only played Amnesia the Dark Descent for about 5 hours now. I can honestly say, however, that from the moment I started the game I was hooked and was reeled in violently. As soon as the game begins you're already struggling and battling with the darkest recesses of your sanity (both in game and out). In the game, you're tasked with exploring a dark and slowly decaying castle, finding notes scattered here and there, and trying to piece together a strange story. My very first thoughts were that it echoes the essence of Resident Evil and Outlast, minus the guns and bad dialogue from the former and the nightvision camcorder of the latter. Instead you carry around a lantern as a light source, and while you're not being chased around by zombies and psycho inmates, you're being chased by ♥♥♥♥ed up ghosts / hallucinations. What fun!
The physics in this game are damn good, and since the game relies on physics to solve most of it's puzzles, it'd better be. I mean seriously, if you're tired of being terrorized, you can play a little game of basketball with a skull that you happen to find stashed away in a desk somewhere to kill the tension. The controls are very responsive and lightning quick, and comes in real handy when you're surfing the in-game menus and mixing chemicals and such. I've found that in similar games to this, the controls will feel sluggish, and menus will just be complicated as all hell, just to add some degree of submersion I suppose. But not in this case. A game that's been expertly crafted by the creative minds at Frictional Games does not need to rely on complicated♥♥♥♥♥♥just to help with the illusion. They know to keep it simple, and I deeply acknowledge that. The lighting engine in the game is astounding, with scarcely lit candles and torches creating an unprecedented atmosphere, casting eerie shadows everywhere. It's really a cool effect, but be warned, stand in the dark for too long, and you slowly start to lose your sanity! With the help of tinderboxes scattered left and right, however, you can choose to light some of the extinguished candles and torches littered throughout the world of Amnesia and create a trail of illumination. Light too many though, and you may not have a spot to hide from the monsters lurking around. Ironically, hiding in the dark will save you more times than you think. With that said, the graphics in this game are superb, and in my opinion can easily face off against some of the next-gen titles of today.
In conclusion, I gotta say that when I am done playing this game, I look forward to playing Frictional Games' earlier titles. Then maybe eventually I'll be ready to play their newest entry, Soma, which looks pretty damn awseome. As I mentioned before, I'm only 5 hours into Amnesia the Dark Descent, but you know what they say: first impressions are always important. Because of this, I have a feeling that I'll continue supporting Frictional Games in all that they do, including any and all future projects they may yet release. I've got a long road ahead of me, but for now I can definitely say that they've gained a fan :-)

This is the best large scale fps I've played so far. AFF has space battles and BF2142 style combined arms warfare. It's only weakness is that more people need to play this. Vehicles are earned as you score points in a match. This solves 2 problems: 1. New players shouldn't be able to yoink vehicles from people who know their stuff. 2. It encourages you to play harder to earn a vehicle. The mechanic is similar to spawning as a hero in Star Wars: Battlefront, but you just respawn in a vehicle. Both factions have different weapons and vehicles for each category.
There are no classes in AFF. All items are unlocked by default, xp progression just allows you to add more stuff to your loadouts. That way you can't drop ammo, health, and carry a LMG with an underbarrel rocket launcher in the same loadout until you're much more experienced in teamplay.

Magic 2015 is a game based on Magic: The Gathering where you collect cards, build decks, and battle opponents. They've made several Duels of the Planeswalkers games, and I've played all of them.
Magic 2015 is a huge step forward for the series, yet also a huge step back. It's really pretty frustrating.
This game finally implements the one feature people have been asking for since the beginning: the ability to make a custom deck from scratch. You get a pool of cards that builds over time, and you can build your own deck out of the cards you have, and it's a major improvement. The game has several ways of helping you build a deck, or you can hand-select each card, like I did.
If it wasn't for that, though, this game would be among the worst in the series. There's a somewhat diverse selection of opponents, but the difficulty curve is all over the place. It puts you against a big green deck really early, and that's a tough deck to face with only a handful of starter cards. The puzzle mode from previous games is gone. No alternate play modes either, such as Archenemy or Sealed from previous games. What's worse is that the card pool, even when you've unlocked everything, just isn't quite diverse enough, so there aren't that many great decks you can build out of it. If my opponents can make a Sliver deck, why can't I? As a side note, the menus in this game are really slow and animation-heavy. Magic 2014 had way better UX design... what happened?
The microtransactions in this game aren't as bad as the infuriating Sealed Deck mode in Magic 2014 (I'm still mad about that), but they keep a few cards locked out of the main game unless you pay more to unlock them. They're good cards, too. The white Paragon, for example, would be an amazing inclusion in the Convoke deck. I think they're usable in multiplayer too, so this could be called a pay-to-win mechanic (you can still build acceptable decks without those cards, but they really help).
There are two other pluses that I haven't brought up yet. Fighting random opponents in single player is a good inclusion. I wish there were more, though... there are only a small number of opponents per location. Also, as someone that follows the card game's storyline, it's nice to see what actually happens to Garruk (and Ob Nixilis).
Ultimately, I would still recommend this game if you're interested in Magic, though I don't think I could recommend it over Magic 2014. They're not asking for much with the $10 price tag, and I don't regret having spent the money on this. Magic is still fun. Also, it's nice to build decks from scratch for a change. For now, steer clear of the extra paid content.

80 Days is a fantastic story telling adventure that sees you travelling around the world making quick decisions every where you go.
I started off heading eastward to Paris before visiting many, many other cities and each and every one of them has a story to tell and depending on what you decide within the stories you could end up one way or another.
The first time I tried going around the world I made it JUST in 78 days!! After a few unfortunate mishaps and decisions I could have made better!
But what I love even more about 80 Days is the fact that once you finish your around the world trip the next time you play it, everything is different you get different items to start with in London and instead of heading South why not even head North? 80 Days is a real gem and you can spend hours on end plotting your way across the world, YOU are in control and it's up to you to decide how best to arrive back in London!
I highly reccomend the game to anyone who's ever been a fan of 80 Days around the world or interested in travelling in general, there is so much fun to be had!

I've been playing the Magic PC games for several years now.  While I appreciate some of the things they did with this release, ultimately I don't think it is worth the money or the huge time investment.
Pros:
- Actual deck building where you can use any card from your collection, building new decks from the ground up.
- Unlocking booster packs after wins is fun and prolongs the amount of time you can have fun playing the game.
Cons:
- You can't complete a set of 4 uncommon or rare cards, at most you can get 3.
- The interface this year is very clunky and slow to navigate through, feels like it was made without any regard for the PC market.
- The starter decks are awful, and you can't select a different one if you hate the deck you selected.  If you're getting stomped early on, it is very difficult to earn enough cards via winning to change your deck.
- I did list unlocking booster packs as a pro, but it also gets VERY grindy.
- Microtransactions are required to unlock the most powerful cards.  I believe its something like $38 to unlock all of the "premium" cards in the game.
For $10 it's not that bad, but I won't be buying the game again next year if they don't rethink their strategy with this game.

Eh, it's okay. If you already really like Magic and are the kind of fellow who bought every single other DotP game, you're gonna be addicted by this until you've got every single card unlocked (too bad there's the unholy Premium set which costs a small fortune to unlock). However, you will also be very frustrated because this installment in the series is in a lot of ways inferior to the others. In either case, I wouldn't really recommend this game.
If you're new, I urge you to buy DotP 2012, instead. The decks in that one are the best - there are some really awesome decks in that game.
And that already leads me to the biggest problem with this one, in my view. There are enough people who have written about the abysmal way the game starts you off (which, by no doubt, is designed that way to make you pay money to unlock cards quicker). It is abysmal. And it also leads me to my main problem - the card pool is severely limited.
I have picked the Black/Red deck at the beginning of the game. It was based around stealing creatures and sacrificing them. One of the best things about Magic in general (and, notably, the other DotPs) is that you get to improve the strengths of your deck as you go along and collect cards. I eventually saw that I was unable to do that. Sure, I got stronger cards which made my deck stronger - but only very few cards improved on the theme of my deck. Eventually, I simply won because I got to draw and play those strong cards, not because I utilized the mechanics and themes of my deck to their fullest. I thought that I just had poor luck with my booster. I didn't. There simply were almost no cards at all which built on that theme. The best permanent card which allows you to sacrifice creatures was already in the deck.
As I found out about that fact, I abandoned the deck and made a series of other decks, which all disappointed me in the same way - there was little possible interaction between the cards, or the interaction was simply too weak to hold up against the extremely powerful decks you fight in the campaign. Even if you just want to make a powerful deck with strong cards, you will find that, for some unknown reason, certain mana ranges only have rather weak or situational cards to offer. Eventually, I managed to make a deck I had fun playing, and also was able to win with, by combining three different colors so as to have more choice in cards (something which I highly recommend if you find yourself in the same position I was in).
The card pool is cripplingly small. By now, I have unlocked every non-Premium card and have already taken a closer look at the cards available. A lot of really popular and neat card archetypes just simply aren't there at all, or are extremely underrepresented to the point that their corresponding cards aren't only very poor representatives of their archetypes, but will also take you a long time to find in the first place. Since I have always heavily prefered Red and Black over the other colors, I mainly noticed which of their archetypes fall into this category; these would be: black reanimation, black sweepers, big black demons which require sacrifice, red board-changing sorceries, red sweepers, red creatures which come back from the graveyard, etc. But I have also noticed that decent blue card draw is very hard to come by - let that sink in for a moment.
Let's go back to DotP 2013. The decks weren't quite as good as DotP 2012's, but I still clearly remember some of the decks in that game (while I remember none at all from Magic 2014, on a side note). That game made me learn to appreciate Phoenix creatures, and I had turned into a bit of a fan of them. They may not be very impressive as you initially play them, but as the game goes on, you'll be more than happy to find a Phoenix in your graveyard, and some of them lend themselves to some really tricky plays. There's nothing at all which resembles that archetype in Magic 2015, not in Red, not really in any other color, either.
To add insult to injury, if you play the game on the harder difficulty settings, your opponents will have access to strictly better cards than you have. Sometimes, you may find yourself facing off againt a deck using a similar theme as you are, but with much, much better cards, and more cards to fit the theme.
There is also a lack of just plain gimmicky cards. There are very few cards which would lend themselves to have a deck built around them. Give me Coat of Arms or Adaptive Automaton and I will build a deck around whatever creature type I like. Eh, probably not, since I could only put two of either one into the deck because of how the deck building is limited in that regard - you may have 4 of the same Common card, but only 3 of the same Uncommon, 2 of the same Rare, only 1 of each Mythic Rare.
In fact, there's very few cards which promote any creature type. From the top of my head, I only remember there being some cards promoting vampire creatures, for some bizarre reason, and also one card making beasts stronger. There's also a creature which makes goblins worse, so there's that.
Even the Premium set sucks. There's some interesting cards, but also some really bizarre picks. The Premium set seems to be aimed to promote mono-colored decks, but with the most boring of cards - cards which simply say they promote a certain color, but don't really fit their color. There's no fun in Mono-Black without Corrupt.
Take it from a maniac who has unlocked everything in the game - the card pool sucks and you won't have a lot of fun with it.

Though I generally approach mobile ports with a certain scepticism, I found it impossible not to like this game.
Being designed for touch-controlled devices rather than for PC the gameplay would probably suffer if it wasn't for the fact that there is practically no gameplay.
Assuming the role of trusty
, you simply click your way through the interactive texts as you plan ahead for your journey around the world, manage your budget and attend to your duties as
loyal valet. Be it inquiring fellow travellers about possible routes, preparing Fogg's shaving water or just making conversation to improve his mood and constitution.
However, the game is obviously based on Jules Verne's famous novel and if you've read it, you already know that travelling won't be a walk in the park. There await countless random events; technical malfunctions, robbery, mutiny - even death.
But fear not, for you will also encounter various characters with the most interesting backgrounds whose friendship (and sometimes even love) you can win and who will often aid you on your voyage.
The story feels surprisingly thorough and responsive, considering it used to be "one of those pesky mobile games".
In pretty much every situation you have 2 or 3 different (text) options to choose from and alter the progress of the overall journey.
They managed to create and maintain a perfect balance between wanting to make haste in order to win the bet (circumnavigate the world in less than 80 days) and wanting to explore foreign culture. A perfect balance between "I can't wait to continue on my way because I'm keen to visit new cities and countries" and "But I also want to explore this city some more and learn about its recent history and its people".
I think this is probably the greatest plus of the game and the reason it feels so incredibly vivid, almost as vivid as the actual novel.
Throughout the adventure Passepartout will also develop in a certain way, depending on the choices you make. So it's entirely up to you if you want to be the exquisite Monseigneur or a sly daredevil - or maybe it's for the best of your gutless character to stay out of trouble and keep quiet?
Concluding my impressions after almost 3 hours into the game I can promise you that if you are a fan of Verne's works, there is no risk at all in buying this. I can also wholeheartedly recommend it to historically interested people, since you get to learn quite a lot about the time the game is set in.
Just make sure to keep in mind that it's more of a strategical exploration game with lots of text.
Ultimately, if you're still not sure whether to buy or not, just do it. The limit of 2 hours for the Steam refunds is more than enough time to get a good impression of the game.

Who else remembers Star Wars: Battlefront? Not the remake. Oh god no not the remake, I mean the GOOD ones. The halcyon days where you had an entire battlefield to play with, could seamlessly transition between infantry/vehicle/air combat or just man a turret and mow down the AI hordes. Ever long for that feeling where you badass your way through dozens of enemies, take the point or clear the map singlehandedly after your AI team bumbles itself to death?
Seems that the dev team of Angel's Fall First does too because their game plays very much like it, and is possibly even more enjoyable.
There is a backstory, but frankly for it to matter at all you have to go looking for it; its not important. You're here to shoot things. You have an army at your back in either blue and yellow flavour and if you stay alive long enough the computer might throw a tank, walker or gunship at you to mix it up a little. Alternatively you can select a space map and be killed by destroyers a lot whilst trying to strafe them, hop in a dropship and board capital vessels to wreak merry havoc from within, or dogfight enemy interceptors trying to do the same you your own.
One of the first things that will strike a new player is the sheer number of options thrown at them. The game comes loaded with the standard array of weapon attachment customisations along with some more esoteric stat modifiers to nudge some extra performance; it also comes with customisable vehicle, suit and aircraft loadouts that might be more familiar to Planetside 2 players. These range from nigh useless to frighteningly powerful, and it can take time to rigure out which is which. A player will progress in three different areas- combat, command and support, having to meet culmulative requirements in these three areas to equip certain gear and upgrades.
First of all, the good. This game is packed with options, allowing you to customise your style or just plain switch things up when it gets boring. It successfully manages huge and I mean HUGE battles with AI, and players working on the assumption that the AI will be a crapshoot might find themselves having to re-evaluate that assessment. The AI work in squads, will actively try to outflank your position or retreat and call for heavier support if they feel overwhelmed. Your own AI likewise seem rather competent but will generally get told to hold the fort or go support an objective the AI randomly assigns whilst you are busy channling Thor.
The space combat likewise extremely enjoyable, since it manages to include a full range of specialised ship types, from small interceptors, beefier torpedo bombers and moving up to the multi-crewable corvettes and frigates. The larger ships all have interiors, and the biggest of them can be actively boarded and sabotaged from the inside out- allowing a plasma-slinging match to rapidly become an infantry fight with one well placed dropship, or your menacing battleship that enemy corvettes and bombers can barely tickle to wind up adrift and blazing if you tune out the boarding alert. These ships also serve as mobile bases for fighters and have turrets that can be crewed.
Much like the aforementioned Battlefront, the game allows you the ability to sequence different maps to create your own campaign: start out in deep space, then move to a planet's orbit, fight your way through a ruined city, an open industrial wasteland and finally assault a barren fortress. However, it does lack a structired single player mode- the best you can get at time of writing is a CYOA style solo map mashup.
This game is not without its criticisims. The weapon design is clunky and questionable, and the graphics are not exactly bleeding edge. It seems to take an enormous amount of bullets or bombs to actually kill something with most weapons, and when maps are this large an effective range of 30 feet for an assault rifle is somewhat dissappointing. The AI commander, should you choose to use it, is often fickle in what objectives it wants you to defend or capture, and whilst the AI on both sides likes to coordinate it never seems to have heard of 'cover', 'concealment' or 'a grenade is not the weapon of choice when someone is actively stabbing you in the face'.
The map interface is too vague for my personal liking, and the plethora of sub-menus can break the gaming experience somewhat. It can often be hard to tell which side is actually winning, since any ticket or control system the game has, or the location or relative importance of an objective is not immediately obvious. In addition to this, the selection of maps is still somewhat limited (but fortunately growing with each update) and not all were thought out as well as they could be- in particular one example where the AI will continually request you to destroy an air dropped spawn point (no small feat) that will be redeployed if so much as a single enemy remains in the vicinity for a punishingly short duration.
The game also does a very poor job of telling you what progress you have towards being able to summon a vehicle or capital ship to the fight- this function seems to be based on individual performance on one or more of the C/C/S categories, but the lack of instructions or tutorials makes this function baffling- especially as the AI seems not to be bound to similar restrictions in many cases, and it is common to be facing down several Javert Class destroyers whilst your own team can summon nothing more than corvettes in answer.
Perhaps the largest criticisim is the seemingly barren servers. This is a game that was made for grand scale fights, and is frequently completely deserted. AI can and do compensate for this somewhat, but the true joy would be to play with friends against capable enemies.
Overall I would have to give this game a yes. It has some way to go and still feels low budget and unpolished, but for what you get it is well worth the investment as a hop in/hop out battle system of the original Battlefront/Planetside ilk; more developed and current than the former, and less bafflingly grindy and frustrating than the latter. There is a great deal of potential here, and the technology now exists to make use of it.

While not some high profile release with an impressive story and hundreds of hours of gameplay, I enjoyed my time with this game.
Story
The game has three scenarios, each with a different story. Dead Pixels is the first one, this is rather basic. The dead are returning from the grave, you must reach the airport to escape the town. The second is The Solution in which you are a convict sent to the town to attempt to do something about the zombies. The final one is Last Stand where you are a survivor who was unable to reach the airport, and must survive for as long as possible.
Presentation
This is pretty good. Some basic blocky graphics, similar to the kind of images you would expect from a Sega Genesis / Mega Drive or Super Nintendo. They certainly work, you won't have any trouble noticing a zombie against the background. Each zombie type is different enough that you know what to expect from them when you get close.
As for music and sound effects, these are good enough. The music isn't memorable, but at least gets you in the mode for dealing with zombies. As for the groans, gun shots and other effects, they are fine.
Controls
I played this with a wired XBox 360 gamepad, as the game was originally released for the XBox Live Indie library and had the controller in mind when released. Because of this, I can't confirm how good other control methods may be. What I can confirm is that it works great with the gamepad, using the triggers and bumpers to fire you current weapon and throw grenades in either direction. The left analog stick will move your character and the face buttons will perform actions like a basic melee attack and using doors.
Gameplay
Now for the important part of the review. In this game, you will play a character who will keep going right past groups of zombies, traveling several blocks in order to reach his goal and escape, unless you are playing the Last Stand scenario, where you simply try to survive as long as you can. Obviously, the rotting corpses will do their best to prevent you from doing this, by attacking you using any method they can, some even spitting at you. Now, you do start with a weapon and some ammo, but firing madly into the groups will expend your limited bullets quickly. However, by entering buildings along the way, you will find various items left behind by the previous inhabitants. You can take weapons, ammo and other items from these buildings, but be sure to not overload yourself if you wish to continue escaping. In two of the scenarios, Dead Pixels and Last Stand, some buildings will also contain survivors willing to purchase items from you, as well as selling some of their own. They will also allow you to exchange cash in order to upgrade skills, like weapon damage, inventory size and movement speed. When playing The Solution, these survivors are no longer around, but you do have a choice of characters, each with their own skills already for you to survive.
Lifespan
Provided you enjoy the game enough to continue playing, there is a good amount to do. The game has 4 difficulty settings, each of which extends the number of blocks you must travel to escape. It also supports co-op if you have a friend willing to play with you. It also has 30 achievements to earn if you are interested in collecting those.
In the end, while I admit this game isn't perfect, at the price of $3, you easily get what you paid for in terms of fun.

I have a blast playing this! And it feels like it's truly is an understatement since I am pretty much speechless when I finished this brilliant mod! Penumbra Necrologue seems like it was made by Frictional, themselves. A mod that nailed every aspect from the Penumbra  trilogy, the setting, atmosphere, narrative, puzzles, soundtrack, everything. It's not just effort that is shining there, it's love and passion toward the series. A desire to 'properly' end the haunting adventure of the luckiest unluckiest protagonist, Philip. A must have if you have and love the Penumbra trilogy. And I'll elaborate why.
Penumbra Necrologue starts off right after Requiem. Again, you control Philip, as he dive back into The Shelter, from his 'Safe Haven', and he must to face the consequence for the action he has done in the previous game, as he tries to escape from The Shelter and his ever decaying sanity. Necrologue isn't about revelation, well..though of course it eventually does, it's about an escape, from the Shelter, past mistakes, and regrets. It gives a subtle yet gradual feeling of ascend rather than a descend on Overture and Black Plague.Most of the notes, journal, and story elements are trying to wrap things up, while adding depths to the whole story / history of Penumbra, making things more interesting (in a mysterious, and at times dreadful way) while staying in canonical.  Sure, some things are left open for interpretation, but they carefully choose what needs to be told, and what doesn't need to. And I'm pretty satisfied  with it.
Nailed! Graphical style, atmosphere, level design / layout. I feel like playing a Penumbra game in a true and finest form. From the crumbled and literally complex, office complex, eerie corridors, narrow, maze=like sewers and tombs, and a creeper feeling I get on the mines. It's so Penumbra from every inch, with a far better graphic and effects. Making it creepier than it already is. It's what it feels like if Frictional did make Penumbra on their HPL 2 (Amnesia) engine, and it actually looked better than Amnesia itself. It's a mod that use the full potential of the provided engine and tools. Necrologue obviously has the technological advantage, but what makes me had a lot goosebumps is, well apart from the eeriness of course, is the amazing set pieces, level designs, and transition. I can feel the Half Life influence on it. The original trilogy has a great level design, but lacks the mind blowing transition (I don't expect that kind of thing in the first place), Overture is mine area focused, Black Plague is an office complex focused, Requiem is a..randomness? But Necrolgue.. it combine all three of them, in fact, we revisit some of the most notable places from past games, like "that hallway" from Overture, the first place of Black Plague, and the tomb of Requiem. And it surprisingly realistic! They don't use a particular place just for the sake of nostalgia, but it does tied up to the story, and add a feeling of natural connection between the structure and environment of The Shelter, making it a seamless experience from one location to the other. Just like Half Life building-city-forest dynamic. It keep giving you a fresh environment to explore without sacrificing a sense of belonging and progression. It just naturally flows.
Walls cracking over there, floors about to fall on the other side, insects crawling in and out the hole, wind blowing, a leaked gas, sounds of rusty pipes, and sometimes even complete silence, with an eerie music on the background, and "the whispers".  It gives me chills and a sense of cosmic fear and dread, give me an uneasy feeling while there's actually nothing there. Also, the voice acting is pretty decent, especially Clarence. I love how they nail Clarence's voice and personality perfectly.
Again, it's Penumbra on it's true form. The gameplay is true-to-root Penumbra. A game of hide and seek between a helpless man and the vicious Tuurngait with many clever physic based puzzle. I really like the placement of every monster here. the inclusion of The Hunter is a surprising and terrifying addition. The greatest fear in a horror genre is when you don't see it, when you feel like there's someone stalking you in the dark, the feeling of constant uneasiness. Necrologue understand it very well, the never ending eeriness is the scariest part, what lurks there? What's that sound? Should I go there? Should I shine my flashlight there? Though I don't find the puzzles is a step up from Black Plague, since it seeks the return of semi-obscene item placement and hidden switches from Overture and some otherworldy one from Requiem, though not as "annoying" as both of it, Black Plague still has the most believable and naturalistic puzzles than those 3. But I get it, Necrologue tries to combine all of the elements from the original trilogy. Also, I find that how the puzzles from revisited areas are already solved, and most of them need to be resolved with a nice twist.
One of the best, most memorable, scariest, and true to ti's source material mod. It, in a way even pass the quality of Black Plague, which in my opinion the best Penumbra. A mod made with passion, talent, and a lot of effort. It nails every aspect of Penumbra, yet manages to stand original and fresh with a well thought of narrative and design. Necrologue most definitely worth to carry the title of Penumbra, as it wraps up everything, giving a satisfying conclusion, adding necessary depth, and open some things for interpretation. The seamless, Half-Life influenced set pieces and transition is perhaps the best improvements over the original trilogy. A mod that exeed my expectation of what I thought a mod is, so brilliant, it goes beyond the boundaries of the capabiliy of what 90% of other mod don't do. Yup 90%, there are a few mod that reach it's level of awesomeness, like Black Mesa and Underhell. Necrologue certainly joins their ranks.

: Life is Feudal: Your Own
: Action, Indie, RPG, Simulation, Early Access
: Bitbox Ltd.
: Bitbox Ltd.
“Realistic medieval multiplayer sandbox with terraforming, free preset and modular building construction, rich crafting (smelting, forging, farming, animals breeding etc.), survival, no target physics based combat, original combat formation system and numerous other features.”
**Do note that this is an Early Access game, things will still change.**
My first impression when I tried the game is that the way the game is presented is very good. It's set in a medieval environment, your character starts off in a woodland area, the land is a mix of untamed forests, grass and water. The buildings and tools represent this era very well, a lot of effort has gone into the background. I like the realism behind the crafting system too, like if you go to fish, you won't always catch a fish. It's relaxing as well when you're not getting attacked every five seconds by the wildlife, which gives you time to do things. The game starts off with you having to explore, forage and prospect the land to find and gather materials. From these materials you craft primitive items that allow you to fish, chop trees, dig for ore, and from then on you can choose what you want to specialise in as well. There is a limited number of points you can pour your points into, which means you will end up focusing on one or two skills more than the others. For example you may choose to build a farm, and learn to cook and tend to animals. Or maybe you want to learn how to build a house and design it with different architectural styles. Perhaps you want to create potions. Or learn to forge armour and weapons. So you choose to focus on the desired skill tree until you are able to make the higher end materials.
This is good because with each player specialising in an skill tree, it means there is more chance of cooperation happening, for players contributing to build a village or a working clan, rather than running around killing people straight away. You can adjust the max learning points from server to server, but limiting it persuades people to work together for the greater good.
This is one of the things that lacks, and I feel the need to say it. The learning curve in my opinion is really hard, and it's difficult to get into the game if you don't have any friends that play it, who can help you to learn it. I liked the fact that the game requires you to be patient. It's not the kind of game where you can mindlessly run around and get everything you need in less than an hour. It's the kind of game that will require a lot of time for you to be able to get even some of the things you need. It's a slow paced game, but things are sped up when you do it with people - which means once again the game is encouraging cooperation.
The controls are ok, but the main problem is that you need to tab for virtually everything, which gets pretty annoying. I would prefer the viewing and gathering to be different than needing to tab for it each time. The screen freezes with wherever you tabbed so there isn't much free roaming/observing. The movement of the character is good and quite smooth, but the rest is clunky.

I really liked the music in the game. The game is very slow paced, and the music fits in perfectly in the background, nice and relaxing for something that you will end up spending a lot of time on. It changes when you go into combat as well.
I think the learning curve is really hard, and this needs to be mentioned for players who may not have so much patience with this. There's a lot of things you need to do, with your inventory you need to point and click for everything, and each action takes time to process. With the character creation menu as well there is no explanation of the skills you'll be putting your points into, which is a shame because these will affect the outcome of what you do in the game. For example one of the skill trees just says "Forestry", but with no detail as to what this means. What will forestry allow you to do and craft and how you can do it within the game. This would benefit enormously from having a small description underneath for each skill and talent.

This game is as much about the journey as it is about the destination. A playthrough may only take as much as an hour and a half, but with the sheer number of locations you can visit and perils or intriguing events you might experience on your way, the game not only encourages but almost demands multiple playthroughs to fully experience all the intricate details that can be found if you are willing to look for them.
Although the game can feel sterile and cold on the surface, its polished exterior soon reveals a world inhabited by multitudes of interesting characters. Who is the mysterious stranger aboard the train? Perhaps they require you to deliver an important item to a distant location. Perhaps they can offer you information about faraway routes and trade opportunities.
People might seek your help or attention, but will you risk getting involved in the matters of their lives, or will you ignore them as you set your sights on completing your journey faster than anyone might have imagined?
If you like a good story and don't mind a bit of reading, this game is full of excellent adventures for your choosing.

Angels Fall First is a great game. You've probably heard the basics, but once again I will say them. This game is a objective based first person shooter. You may command either other players or ai across a large playing field on numerous maps. A higher score is rewarded with vehicles to spawn in.
The gamemodes are first an objective-based gamemode. This will have you capture, defend, or destroy certain objectives. If you are attacking, your goal is usually destroy & capture until you get to the end under a time limit. The defenders defend, recapture, and sometimes destroy the source of the attackers. The other game mode is your average conquest territories gamemode. Both of these apply to land & space combat.
As a stand alone FPS, the game suffers from a lack of anything unique. Point, shoot, kill, very basic. As a combined arms combat the game does well/alright. Vehicles may spice up the battle, but there are better games for these situations. Overall, the game is decent like this.
What draws most people into AFF is undoubtedly the spectacular space battles. Whether it is objective or territories, you can do multiple amazing things during the combat. You could hop into a fighter or bomber and attack enemies head on. (May I add note I love how these ships move and handle.) But there's more. You could pilot an entire Battleship in the battle as smaller fighters fly around you. And if you please, you could get up and walk around in these monsterous ships. Angels Fall first really highlights the scale of these massive ships and the combat around. You could also join a raiding dropship and board an enemy captial ship to take out the systems from inside. Vehicles you could call in are Corvettes, Destroyers, Frigates, and Battleships. Overall the space combat is why I bought this and I stayed around a little for everything else.
Now things aren't all perfect, as the game suffers from two major issues.
The first issue this game suffers from is a low playerbase. Because the developers are not putting much into advertising, there are barely any people on the official servers. The AI is decent and could give you a challenge, but it is a lonely feeling having no one to fight against in this type of multiplayer-oriented game. And the players that do hop online are always on password-protected servers for whatever reason. Without a proper playerbase, the game is quite boring.
The other major issue this game suffers from is the unbearable GUI. It's messy, overlapping, and all over the place. It is painful to use and needs serious updating. I can't say much about it because personally it's only a minor problem for me, but I know people do not like it.
TL:DR
+Satisfying fighter combat
+Interior of Capital Ships (Walking around, destroying from inside)
+Pilotable  Capital Ships
Neutral: Decent combined arms warfare
Neutral: Few weapons to choose from, but customzing weaponry is important
-Lack of proper playerbase
-Messy GUI
-Spaceship movement partially clunky. Moving the mouse is perfectly fine, but if you're increasing speed, decreasing speed, flying up/down/left/right then you press the button and the speed changes almost an entire second after. This is really frustrating, so I usually only end up moving the mouse and thrusting to maneuver.

Note: I don't really play multiplayer unless it's with people I know, so I can't offer any info in terms of playing multiplayer with randoms.
The best way to explain this game is to say that it takes the most exciting part of other sci-fi games and puts you right in the thick of the action. From space battles that involve entire fleets down to street-to-street urban combat, you're given more freedom and choice than any game I've played with a similar scope. If you've played the Battlefront games this all may sound familiar, and it does definitely feel like an evolution of that concept, but there's more here than Battlefront ever had. Every ship in a fleet engagement is pilotable, and with the relatively simple command interface, it's easy to give orders on the fly.
The AI bots are surprisingly intelligent, but they do seem to have some trouble with pathfinding in vehicles. In close quarters environments they sometimes can be fatally slow to recognize an enemy running around amongst them, but I've seen that happen enough playing against actual people in other games that I'm not too put off by it. The game allows for all 64 potential players to be bots, which means singleplayer is more viable than most similar games.
The game used to be a little clunky the last time I really checked it out, but as of the time of writing it runs smoothly and without issue. I haven't experienced any crashes or undue slowness and my aging graphics card has no problem playing with the settings turned all the way up.
My only real complaint is the relative lack of a sense of progression. The current system allows you to gradually increase the amount of gear you can put into any one loadout, but every weapon and upgrade is available from the start. To be fair, this is more of an issue with my personal preferences than anything that is objectively done wrong; this system would probably be welcomed by people who like the game but can't devote the hours necessary to unlock the best toys.
There's a good variety to the weapons and upgrades available, and nothing feels gimmicky or out of place. The player and vehicle customization is probably my favorite mechanic; between all of the options on offer pretty much any playstyle will find a nice home here.
As fun as the vehicles are, I wish more levels included them. At the moment most non-space missions are set in urban environments with infantry being the only option for either side. Those missions still manage to be quite fun on their own, but the vehicles provide a little more flexibility to the way the individual matches play out.
Space combat is fun and engaging, with essentially three layers of fighting going on at any one time: the capital ships duking it out amongst each other, the strike craft trying to protect their bombers and transports while shooting down those of the enemy, and the boarders who can disable individual weapon systems on the capital ships or even sabotage the core to bring the whole thing down. Infiltrating a battleship, destroying the core, and stealing an enemy fighter to escape seconds before the ship explodes is a moment that most games would spend the entire time building up to: in AFF it can be your day job.
In short, I'd like a story mode and some unlockables, but the game's in early access right now, plus my opinion might be in the minority, so I can't really complain either way. If you want intense large-scale conflict then this is definitely worth checking out.

Dead Pixels is a zombie shooter with an 8 bit graphical style, which means alot of gamers will automatically ignore it. We must see at least one of these every week. But wait! This one is actually worth your time. The story and core gameplay are simple. Survive the zombie outbreak by running through several side scrolling streets, shooting or avoiding zombies. However, look a little closer and you'll find a surprising amount of depth. Killed zombies drop money, and buildings can be searched to find better guns, ammo, medkits, buffs and loot. Traders will buy and sell items, as well as permanent stat increases for things like health, movement speed, carry weight and weapon damage. This opens up several playing styles. I haven't encountered any bugs, and there's nothing major to complain about. Dead Pixels will only last a few hours, and it won't make any GOTY lists, but for £2 this is excellent value for money and definitely worth checking out.

Bought it, beat it and I will NOT be investing any more money into DotP. I faithfully bought every DotP game since the first, because it introduced new gametypes and a wide variety of decks (All prior to 2014 on Xbox, and the last two on Steam). DotP 2015 is a sad installment geared to milk your wallet. Given all of the features that were removed, I would have expected this to be the first in the series.
Paying for variety in a TCG is a form of paying-to-win, and it should not be present in the digital game version that's intended to be an introduction to new/casual players. The physical TCG and MTG:Online already support the hardcore P2W market, and they do so while including a secondary market for the players to feel their cash dumps have provided worth: thus justifying their continued spending. This game introduces the former and excludes the latter, which I find to be greedy and insulting.
After all the value Wizards of the Coast gave players in their previous DotP interrations, I find it hard to believe that this game was a result of their design decisions alone. It seems to me their new parent company had a major say in the outcome of this poor product.

I heard about this game after meeting the creator at a local meetup and trying a brief demo. The developer kindly offered to provide a key for me to try the game out and the demo was intriguing, so I decided to give the current version a whirl. I enjoy Norse Mythology and FPS games with RPG/fantasy hybrid elements, so the premise definitely appeals to me. So far, I'm really enjoying the game!
As it turns out, the game is a bit more reminiscent of something like Serious Sam in that the focus is on progressing through fairly straightforward levels while battling waves of enemies. The action can get pretty intense, but there is also a surprising amount of strategy based around when to use your various spells. I'm not particularly adept at FPS games despite enjoying them, so I liked that I could often engage with the enemy mobs at my own pace once I became more adept at using my freeze spells and relying on my support NPCs for cover.
The game is definitely in an early stage of development, but it's already showing plenty of promise and I think it has a lot of potential to be a gripping, fast-paced FPS full of arcade style encounters with large, varied mobs of enemies. Don't go in expecting Skyrim or Deus Ex levels of complexity, but if you're looking for some simple and fun combat-oriented arcade action give this one a try!

For instance in the 'kitchen' there are about 16 points where you can easily fail. If you fail at the end you have to retry them all. This soon starts to be a grind instead of fun. Still the game is fun when you can continue. So on a scale of ten I would still give it a 6.5 in comparison with DN3D. In comparison with other recent games with a savepoint system and no-cheats (i.e. lowering my personal standard) it would be an 8.

This game deserves to be so much better known than it is! My dad bought it on release with our first computer back in the late 90s and it is still his absolute favorite game now in 2017. I used to spend hours watching him play it, and even now it's still a ton of fun.
I think what really makes it is the level of detail. The developers clearly spent a lot of time working on the lore. Each of its faiths has a great, distinctive feel. Every unit has their own separate portrait and voice prompt (these get repetitive but really add depth). The combat is really clunky and can be very challenging and seemingly random (I tend to just autocalc everything if I'm being honest), but there's just something so satisfying about building up your awesome army and conquering your neighbors.
Although it can be kinda easy to get stuck in a gameplay rut, there's a decent amount of variation to be found through the various faiths and lords, the map editor (completely change up the map or even build your own... it adds way more variety than you'd expect), and the story mode expansion. That being said, I really wish this game had gained the popularity needed to get a sequel (or two or three). It would be awesome to see a more modern take on this. One thing I'd really like to see added is more expansion to the economy. A more robust trading system and financial management would really help the endgame (at which point your only options are really to kill off all of your allies, wander around fighting random dungeons, or just quit your hard-earned game. Boo!).
If you like strategy, fantasy, or especially both, this is definitely worth a try.

"Always bet on Duke." So reads the catchphrase to the manliest of men's latest outing. A testosterone fueled rage across the state of Nevada in search of serious payback. An unrelenting rampage of gunfire, one-liners, dismemberments, eviscerations and urinating on your foe's cerebral cortex. Nothing quite like it. Except that I wouldn't bet on it.
The thing about Duke Nukem is that you're looking for that 90s feel of a game. Where you shoot before asking questions and where cover if for the weak. You go, face first into the fray, killing and disrespecting the invaders of earth as you brutally reduce them to porkchops. Which makes it so weird that
holds you back for what seems to be a large portion of the rather short game. The first hour is spent toying with lewd buttons, curling dumbells and drawing♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on whiteboards. The following shooting section is to brief to qualify for a jump in adrenaline and all the subsequent shootouts are few and far between.
I mean, think about it; You're Duke Nukem, the blueprint of masculinity. Any blogger from Tumblr would cry in irreversible horror at the binary gender appropriation this man radiates. Yet the game makes you look and play like what Arnold "The Governator" Schwarzengger would refer to as "a girly man." You are weak; you can't take a lot of punishment, and when you add up the score you don't really murder that many aliens. It gets worse. As the game progresses, you're sent into more and awkward set piece stages that have no place in a testosterone fueled shooter. It even sends you to fight a boss underwater. Something the game wasn't calculated to handle as the swimming controls are set in stone and you're even weaker than before.
does have its moments. Usually in the form of banal comedy or the sudden change up where you're shrunk to seven inches and you have to ride an RC car through a hotel while dodging kitchen appliances. At times you'll have fun with the physics engine while playing a game of pool or you spend a good few minutes listening to Duke's baritone giggles as he slaps a set of mammaries that are attached to wall (true story). However,
is lacking in so many areas, and in particular the design and refinement that you'll be glad when it's over.

Before actually trying this game out I decided to watch the trailer. I came to the conclusion that this is pretty much kiting the game. This is an early access title so clearly it is not final, with that being said this review is only for the current state of the game now.
If you like kiting around mobs that get stuck on terrain and are not much of a threat while shooting fireballs, then this is the game for you. The only other useful spell is your ice golem pet who can distract mobs and also get stuck as well. And while there is some enemy variety, the AI is pretty basic but some will actually block/parry your fireball or dodge roll out of the way. Some will use abilities like aoe heal and various melee abilities that can reach you out of melee range. The bigger mobs tend to get stuck on the environment or each other.

Good game, but has a few flaws.
My main annoyance is the game is very oriented towards save-reload gaming. Why:
- Death of your character = lose game.
- Enemy units pop out of fog of war and kill you the same turn. Much farther sight range would have been useful.
- Game loves spawning "marauders" (neutral units) that kill you randomly for above reason.
- Loss of any regular unit is very devastating early and mid game, so you end up replaying battles a lot until there are no losses (generous auto-calc also encourages this).
- Early game quest to free Great Temple doesn't permit any mistakes for harder factions.
- Stats are rarely explained by the user interface (e.g. spell effects) and so a trial and error approach is necessary.
There are all these cool things to research and build but you're not going to be able to afford them unless you expand wide and subjugate AI factions; i.e. there's limited opportunity to expand on neutrals without conquest. This is basically fine, but game would have retained more flavor if keeping other factions alive longer.
Tactical combat is generally hard to control, you need to be paused so much to issue orders that it's pretty similar to turn based combat regardless. If you want a modern game that is pretty similar and IMO has better tactical combat, have a look at Age of Wonders 3.
Factions are very asymmetrically balanced in the unmodded game, but this isn't necessarily a bad thing. Also, the AI probably cheats a lot but it doesn't really matter that much due to the focus being on less on pure strategy and more on the overall role playing experience. Only persistent annoyance with AI is its diplomacy which again is inadequately explained in the user interface leading to frustrating experiences.
Most of my play time with this game comes from a decade ago (before Steam release). If you can live with the low resolution graphics, I recommend it if you're a fan of Age of Wonders, Heroes of Might and Magic, and similar game series.

This is a game about two warring alliances. Basically the russian sounding folk versus the british sounding folk. There is no pay to win. There is no additional buying crapola. You get the game, grab a server, and PLAY.
The game itself has some excellent mechanics, even though it is a Ue3 styled game (need an engine update?) as in you earn points by doing the three following: Combat, Leadership, and Support. Support is by far the hardest to achieve without having to enter some kind of combat situation. Leadership is easy-ish: Become the Commander and gain 1k-2k points per round. Combat, even easier - POINT 'N SHOOT! Certain weapons require certain points to achieve, while your three bars fill up with your loadout. It actually takes honest, hard working, blue-collared, red fingered gamers to take this game head on, which si where you finally come in.
In the official servers, there are bots and players. Players are at no point mean or dirty players, and they actually offer a significant challenge as there is no ranking system to keep higher skilled players from the newbs. Which is alright, you still gain a hella lot of combat points for getting your tush kicked. You lose, you win. You win, you win. Bots are... Alright. They could use a little extra go-go sauce in their systems, and they will be good to go. Fun lasts forever.
There are two kinds of maps: Spaaaaaaaaaaace!!!! and BOOTS ON THE GROUND. Both are extremely fun. The space part, in my opinion, is very difficult because those space bots are very good at flying and I am not. Capture space objectives, spit fire at space... Thing object #2... And win the game! Boots on the ground is when all those lovely bots now are armed with randomized gear, and will tear into your rear end with a spiked firetruck dipped in acid like a kentucky derby race where all the horses are on fire. Capture the objective and holding points are all fun and find and dandy, and it actually offers a challenge.
Commanding your units is not difficult at all. Whip up the ol' TacMap, click on a squad, right click objective or area. Boom, you just made +35 points for Leadership! Or, you can use your C key and tell everyone to ♥♥♥♥ off over on another objective, your choice. Squads can move about, delegating orders and doing their buisness the hard way. Fun!!
Overall game rating? Easily a 9/10. Needs a little more love around the maps, the AI for the bots too, and maaaaaybe add  even more content...

This game is extrodinarily fun. Space battles, ground battles, and pretty much everything that they involve respectively (except for space-ground battles.)
Positive aspects:
- Quite a few different maps and different modes for some of the maps
- Graphics, while not EA's Battlefront fantastic, are good.
- Loads of customization options.
- The battles can literally go any way. None of them will go the same as the one before it. I've had missions where a lucky rocket has taken out an enemy landing-pod (acts as a spawn point) and forces them to use the pod they used when they origionally landed, way back at the start. Other missions my team has been devastated, with a capital ship laser accidently slicing through our own frigate, or enemy gunships destroying your team's only tank just as the enemy get one.
- Lots of AI support
- Battles are really tense. Just that feeling of trying to desperately hold back an enemy force from taking a bridge with only your squad, while your teammates are being gunned down in the process. Or trying to hold an overpass in the night, fires blazing and tracers whistling everywhere.
Negative:
- UI is pretty awful. You can ignore it mostly when playing (except for health and ammo and small things like that), but still.
- Lots of bugs still (it is Early Access, with a small team, it is to be expected
- Online community very small (by buying and playing online, you can change that)
- Gunships are a 'little' difficult to control, but I never get them anyway XD.
Overall, you should buy and play. I think it is worth supporting the devs on this amazing project.

This game is rewarding, challenging but grindy as the @%#$. To be honest though, it really works here.
There is a ton of buildings to build and it would be a shame if you could simply make them right off the bat. This game takes time, and patience and when you finally build your first home... it feels great. Although one might argue that it takes to long, that one should also understand that this game is a prequal to an MMO. So the grind is required.
If you don't like grinds, then simply make your own server with the click of a button and alter the skill cap and skill gain as well as plant growth rate, or animal feeding rate, ect. Now... about that skill cap. I personally love the idea of a person needing to specialize in something. The problem? If you pick the wrong class tree to go down... you waisted a lot of time, so go online and look up a tutorial, because none exists on game. However, as I like descovering things as I go, I ask around a lot and for the most part it's a good community.
Now, about that combat! I am garbage at PvP so it always kinda sucks when someone raids my town (without walls) every day at the same time. And sure, while it may annoy me a little, i must say it adds a sense of realism to the world. The times back then sucked without or even with walls. Raiders bring it all together though and make the world feel alive. While I trade with one town, another is pumping out♥♥♥♥♥hats to attack me on sight. However, the combat itself kinda feels... like trash and quite unpolished. But then again, keep in mind I am not one for PvP so it could be that I suck. I guess there is only one way to find out.
Gathering is tedious and terrible but honestly very very important. You need it to make everything. I am not just talking about gathering sticks and stones... I am talking about gathering ore (which could take forever - This is not minecraft - move along) Or gathering 5 out of the (what seems like) 50 types of plants out there so you can make one item that is needed in ALL bigger buildings... Get an herbalist people... you need them... and they are playing the worst this game has to offer so you can makes walls and houses, and maybe one day even castles.
All in all this is an interesting game that is okay. Not great but certainly not bad. I would simply recomend getting this with a group of friends. But not so much if you are a solo player.

18 hours on hand, 100% completion of everything but Zendikar set and all I can say about it is it's hit and miss..
Deck building is both hit and miss ... you can only have 2 rares, 3 uncommons and 4 commons of each cards.. this hinders deck building but was probably needed for balancing reasons so while it makes niche decks harder to build it keeps decks centered around one color from being completely ridiculous, I vote this part as a step in the right direction though various decks require you to buy 14 premium packs to unlock all of them (Less if you get lucky on the packs and are looking for a single specific deck) which is a step back, it's worse than unlocking 2 new decks for a fraction of the cost in a lot of ways. That and the seemingly random selection of cards with very little cohesion makes themed decks very restricted..so while they took a step in deck building freedom the tiny pool of cards is incredibly hindering the actual number of useful decks you can build. Premium packs in general are idiotic in general since when 2016 comes out you have to start all over and pay all over again, at that rate you might as well play MTG online.
Multiplayer is a blatant miss, it's almost like they threw it in at the last minute and had absolutely no focus on it. 2 headed giant removed which was a huge bonus for 2014. You can't swap decks inbetween duels which leads to most people just scooping up the fight and leaving before it's done as soon as they feel (or know) they've lost.. no reason to stick around if a deck completely crushes yours since you can't swap decks inbetween fights, you've to leave the current game then change decks before joining a new one.   This is crushing to me considering multiplayer extends the life of games like these dramatically, with most of the cards unlocked I'm finding little point besides unlocking the rest before tossing the game away and shrugging off 2016.
Give the game 1.5 out of 5 stars. Singleplayer is still there and they attempted to move into the right direction with deck customization, but the multiplayer was murdered, extra content removed, premium packs required for vastly improving deck building options.
Challenges no longer a part of duel of the planeswalker? Miss.. those were interesting and fun parts of the series,

Adding full deck-building to the latest version of Stainless Games' series of Magic the Gathering games is almost worthy of a thumbs up recommendation, but poor design decisions keep it from getting a recommendation.
The UI is uber-clunky and frustratingly slow in its transitions, mouse clicks take a while to register and sometimes don't seem to register at all, and some of the more frequently addressed buttons are tucked away behind a fair amount of erratic scroll swipes. So, despite a few shortcuts provided by the bottom-right corner avatar pop-up menu, there is a lot of unnecessary action required when navigating the menu.
A minor gripe for experienced MTG players is that you're being forced to at least partially go through a tutorial session that explains the most basic game mechanics. Not being adequately informed that the deck you choose to play the campaign with is going to be the deck you are stuck with until you manage to unlock a fair amount of cards that will allow you to adjust the deck to your liking, is an unnecessary nuisance that should annoy both experienced and inexperienced players alike. While these two gripes are not a deal-breaker per se, they do make you question the developers' design choices. If these choices were made for their for 1st MTG:DotP games, they might have been understandable; however, for them to make these decisions for a 5th incarnation of the game is incomprehensible. The design curve for an annual game series such as this should easily show an upward curve, and not a downward one.
Some cards can only be obtained by purchasing premium boosters, and you will have to spend at least as much as you spent on the base game to unlock all of those. While that is a pity, it is another pity to find out that many of the great cards played by the AI are not at all available for the player.
The biggest fun should be found in deck-building, and then trying that deck out against real opponents. However, despite its size, the card pool is a bit underwhelming in terms of what it has to offer and generally steers the player in the same direction; fast aggro-decks. While there doesn't seem to be an awful lot of opportunity for creative deck designs as of yet, seasoned players of this game series will be aware that more DLC is to be expected, which might spice up the deck design possibilities some more.
So in conclusion, full deck building is the long-awaited great step forward, and it certainly adds alot to the fun of the game, especially in multiplayer games, and with that step it's finally approaching the feeling of the real game, but it's very likely that we'll only see the proper implementation of it in the next incarnation of this game.
