I only have a half hour of game play at time of this review, but have plenty logged on this title before it was brought on Steam.  Lords of Magic is a turn based strategy game that has an interesting mix of real time strategy for the battle environment.  There are 8 Faiths (ie races) in the game, and you pick to play as lord of one of them.  At the start, your main objective is to stop the Lord of Death as he seeks to subjugate (or just destroy) all else that will not obey him.  You can choose to be that of the Elves of Life with essentially the best archer units, or perhaps those of Order who are essentially the heroes of Arthurian legends, or any other Faith.
I've liked this game a lot because of how you can work with the other Faiths.  Say you're leading Life and liberate the Great Temple of Water (each Faith has one), they'll agree to join you (provided you're still on good relations) and their Lord will be come your heir.  So you essentially have two "lives" to work with while building up both regions.  You can still trade for resources, units, or research in other games but I always found that kind of alliance interesting about this game.
The RTS battles are more fun for me than the mass army battles.  In this game your army has a max of 12 "units" in 3 squads.  Each squad is composed of a hero/champion/unique unit and 3 generic units (footman, archer, calvary, scout, or summoned creature) and you can mix and match these as you like.  In battle, instead of having a host of units to macromanage you only have that small squad to micromanage long set paths in the various maps (some are open areas while others have corridors to bottleneck).  I've found that to be far more engaging.
The research aspect is only about the spells you have at your disposal.  If you don't use mages at all, then you actually don't even need to worry about the research (which is composed entirely of having a few mages in a building and waiting the number of turns needed based on the levels of the mages).
The other interesting part of this title (that they fortunately included) is the Legends of Urak quest pack.  Ever wanted to play out the story of King Arthur?  They have one for that.  What about Beowulf?  They have one for that too.  There are a couple other legends you play out the story off and it's adapted to the units and systems they have ingame which puts an interesting twist to it.
I'll definitely be putting more time into this now othat I have it again.  Who knows...maybe I'll crush everything as Balkoth as I unlocked him with a bit of a speedrun I developed (check my guide if you're interested).  Or perhaps I'll slowplay it again as Life like I did when I first played the game.  Then again, playing out as King Arthur would be fun again too.  I remember that took me awhile, but perhaps I can do it quicker this time too.
I realize this is a long review/diatribe but if you're a fan of simplistic land management blended with squad based real time strategy combat then I think this would be a title for you!
EDIT: The only bad thing I guess is that they didn't add an ability to play windowed, or work in the Steam overlay.  It plays just like it did when I first enjoyed it though...so there is that. ;)

I wouldn't say this is a bad game per se, but it's definately a bad pc port. The biggest selling point of this version of Magic was the Deckbuilding experience. It works fairly well but when you build your deck you are forced to scroll the cards horizontally, instead of having them shown vertically or in a grid fashion that is easier to navigate with the mouse.
There are fairly good filters to filter out the cards you don't need while deck-building but there is no way you can filter by card name or card type. So say you have to look for a specific red card, you'll select "RED" in the filters and then go through all the red cards (at least they are ordered by mana cost) until you find your card.
The "Card Collection" menu that lets you see all the cards in the game and how many of them you own is done fairly well but lacks an important feature: you can't scroll down with the mouse wheel. Unnecessary and annoying.
The menus navigate fairly slowly and are obviously intended for a gamepad, but in the end this is not as annoying as one might think, luckily you usually don't spend a lot of time navigating the menu anyway.
As many others pointed out already the start can be quite problematic if you buy the standard 10$ version of the game as some of the deck combinations you can choose from are fairly weak. For example I went for the Black/Red deck while a friend of mine went for the Blue/White one. I had several problems in almost every match of the campain to the point where I had to put the lowest difficulty setting to even have a chance of getting through while my friend had almost no problems whatsoever at the highest difficulty setting. In fact it took me twice as much to get to the end of the campain because I kept losing.
I must point out though that when you start to get to the end of the campain you will probably have unlocked enough cards to have unlocked (the games does this automatically when available) another starter deck, so you can always change your starter deck if you think what you are plaing with is really horrible.
In conclusion I reccomend you to NOT pick Black as a colour of your deck as i did because it sucks (at least at the start), turn down the difficulty setting if necessary and in 10-18 hours you should be able to get to the end of the campain having unlocked about 30% of the total cards of the game.
Regarding the premium boosters, i'm not going to address the issue pay to win. What I will say is that it will cost you 25 euros to unlock all the premium cards. Not more, not less. These cards are about 20% of the total. They are in some cases better than their basic counterpats, but in most cases they are not too powerful, at least in my opinion. I suggest you go through the campain, then if you still enjoy the game and want to play more, the game might be worth those 25 euros more.

I recommend picking this game up for a casual game experience and fun times.

So, I've played the game for about 15 hours.  I like it, and it's very playable, but the Microtransactions are.... wacko.
In the beginning, the game was furiously hard.  I started with one and only one deck made of commons, and immediately had to fight a single color recycling zombie deck.  And next a deck using fancy multilands.  I had literally ZERO cards beside the deck (which I felt had been overhyped.)
Unlike Hearthstone, the game only gives you one deck, and I was starved for any new cards.
I purchased a microtransaction to unlock all the sets, (because I'm an idiot, and I thought since the card logos all said MAGIC 15 I was not actually getting any of those other sets... ) and suddenly I had EVERY CARD.  The set went from 5% to 87%.   I had maybe ten legendaries, multiple copies of rare cards, and so on.  I also stopped getting reward packs for defeating the campaign bosses.
I actually rather wish I'd only bought one expansion set, but there is no undo button.   I am not a 'cheat code' kind of guy.   Still, it wasn't *totally* game breaking.
I really wish they had studied Hearthstone a bit better, giving players several deck for free, giving smaller rewards more often, giving card rewards for playing, and allowing players to gradually develop.
The game does have an auto-deck feature.  I can insert one or more cards, and the AI will make a deck around those cards.
If someone bails from a duel, I believe the AI takes over.
There are several minor tweaks and gripes.  There was nowhere in the tutorial where it said "PRESS CTRL TO CHANGE HOW MANA IS TAPPED"  I have some trouble seeing the opponent's cards when they come out, and can't read them without zooming and checking INFO.  I can't even LOOK at fancy lands without clicking off a setting.

My oldest brother owned this game when I was a kid, and I would frequently watch him play on our Windows 98.
Lords of Magic is a classic game from the 90's, overshadowed by bigger titles such as Heroes of Might and Magic, King's Quest, Quest for Glory, and Baldur's Gate. It is a mix of strategy and RPG - you create armies that explore the world map, collecting resources, traversing dungeons and fighting neutral monsters/enemy factions to level up.
The game takes place in the high fantasy realm of Urak. Balkoth, the loyal discple of Golgoth, the god of Death, has gone on a rampage throughoutt the world, ravaging the kingdoms of the other seven faiths - Life, Order, Chaos, Fire, Water, Earth, and Air. You pick one of the seven mentioned faiths and choose what role your Lord will be - Warrior, Thief or Mage.
When you enter the world, you will discover that you only have your Lord and a small army accompanying him/her. Every faith starts off in a weakened state, except for death and the faith "opposite" to yours (for example, Order's opposite is Chaos). Your first objective is to explore the area around your faith's capital, fighting neutral enemies and gaining strength. Once you are strong enough, you will need to take your faith's "Great Temple", which has been overrun with monsters. After you do that, your capital will swear fealty to you, and you will begin your quest to kill Balkoth.
Each faith has its own unique units, and they all have different strengths and weaknesses. For example, Life has some of the best ranged units in the game, with strong magical flying units. However, they have weaker melee units. Fire has units with very high attack, but low defense, and many of their units have low movement points.
The game does have some flaws, however. Combat has a tendency to be a bit clunky at times. The learning curve for the game, in my opinion, is very high. Finally, computer players will act oddly. For starters, they will often split their armies into tiny, easily defeatable groups. Secondly, there's diplomacy - the AI doesn't understand what a fair bargain is. Playing as Air, I once had Order ask me to give them my Air Drake (the legendary creature for Air) in exchange for a hound (an Order scouting unit). When I declined, my relations with them DROPPED because they were♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off with me.
All in all, I find this to be a very enjoyable game, albeit with a few flaws. It is a solid 8/10.

Rating: 9/10
Pros:
-Works like a Facebook game, you can log out with peace of mind knowing that players cannot attack you unless you are online. And you get rewarded for daily log-ins!
-If you are a rich and prosperping player, you might be able to pay them off with gold or stone, etc.
-Feels like Stronghold - but without the pesky tasks of "cleaning up gong" or "peseants stealing from our granery sire"
-Mobile armies: You can build a force and level them through campsites and taking on enemies in the wilderness around you, making you stronger and your units stronger for battles to come.
-Well designed lore of castles and beautiful landscapes.
-No "PayToWin": As they say in the news on the game "this game is designed to avoid the pitfalls of FreeToPlay games....focusing more on skill and persistance than bigger wallets"
Cons:
-Very wonky (slow) combat. You have to make sure you units don`t get stuck and cluttered as they will get moved over by the smallest force if you`re not careful.
-Co-op is not as smooth as I had hoped, while you can send supplies to your friend, getting them to play with you to aid in a quest or seige is a bit frustraing if you dont pay close attention to what you are selecting.
-Npc workers [peasants, etc] tend to get stuck up in hills or behiind fences when chopping down trees.
-The initial title screen has very LOUD audio - first tiime players make sure your audio is turned down some or your ears will get blasted away. While this is epic sounding, if any player has their volume up they might get quite a surpize once the tittle screen loads.
-Slow loading screens between transitions. [ While this really isn`t a *con* it can be annoying waiting for that bar to load up when there is little to nothing in your home city to load ] Another transition issue is between begining to seige and actually entering the seige. These problems are on and off, and while I havea solid internet this *may* vary between players.
Overall this game as great potential to kick out Stronghold and its gong-infested cities and brings forth a potential for a shining sheild in castle-sim-like games.

How many games had you played, That is based on Real Time of stragegy?
How many games had you played, Like Starcraft 2, And you hates having to rebuild everything?
How many games had you played, Where you just want to control your own soldiers into battle
How many games had you played, Where there is no actual pay to win features? [Like path of exile!]

Well, This is one of those game, And It's free.
After years, Not alot of players get an opportunity of a decent gameplay where everything does not prevent them from trying to advance in the game.
The best thing is currently about this game is;
- The developers do interact with the players once the while, thus making the game much more enjoyable for the players
- Instead of going the dull ol' fashioned where in Starcraft 2, You have to rebuild from ground one, You can skip that.
- There are three races in the game; The human, The Elves and the orc. They have their own way of survivals, Learn it.
-  Got dwarves. All race can have 'em. Dwarves. Dragons too.
- There is no literal pay to win feature. Those who do think there is, is just thinking pessimistic. The reality is the Crown systems does not prevent pay to win, rather Crowns can be obtained via having vassal towns, Players Versues Players, completing quests, and clearing reigons of NPC. The crowns are essential to many mechanic of the game to unlock better equipments and building upgrades that will determine the player's activity in PvP and PvE. In addition that the only two things that are locked are Skrimishes and Single Player Campagin, but those two do not influence the direct gameplay of original. becuase Single player campagin will be the same as MMO-verisoned, The difference is no player versues players and does not requires internet connection. Skrimishes on other hand is a 'Testing Ground', Where you trains your tactic and you can use said tactics to your gameplay, but It won't influence the gameplay via units, resources or any means. rather just a training ground.
- CO-OP Player versues Environment, Your best friend can help you take on Dagbor!
The downsides, however. . .
The Downsides only not so permanent and may be gone in next updates, and some downsides are from the player's gamestyle.
- The game have bad server hosting, Meaning you can accidently lose connection or reception to the server. The worst to experience is a rollback, however you can solve it by validating the game via Steam, And If it does not solve, then you can go to game's file and go to the game's forum, then place down the Log 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 into the techinal support thread and state what happened to you.
- The players will alway use a wizard of the Deep. The Wizard of the deep is the wizard designed for player veruses players combat and will wreck most of your army. It's expensive immortal [Immortals unit cannot die, They will lose a few level, but they cannot be killed permanently.] unit that cost at most 120 crowns, excluding the cost to get the spells required. The Wizard of the deep can be a major turnoff for many players who are forced to face them in combat because It's designed to destroy majority of army before wizard get defeated.
- Lack of players also make community small. only 150 players strong per day, and sometime peaking 200, and lowest is 95. The community is not average toxic, and can be friendly at most time. Some players are willing to assist you in understanding the game mechanic, but most are usually quiet and/or the chatbox is not working for them. It's the common issue in the server host connection that Chatbox servers does not connect successfully to the other players sometime and breaks, Not allowing the players to communicate with the community.

Let's see... where should I start?
First and foremost, Angels Fall First has immense potential. The basic shooting and gameplay mechanics are sound. The combat is objective oriented and players are organized into small squads. There are also a variety of weapons, attachments, and tools to choose from for your loadouts for yourself, your fighter, or your vehicle.
However, Angels Fall First is not without its share of problems, mostly, if not all, early access related. The UI is quite frankly atrocious and confusing. The developers have a new UI in the works though, so this should soon be remedied.
The next biggest problem for me is the lack of faction flavor. While there is some loose lore, there is little to nothing in the battle to give the factions a distinct personality. Given the current stage of development, it makes sense that this would, and probably should, be given a low priority at this point in time.
Lastly, it has a small player population. It isn't that the game is dead, but rather it has yet to grow. Once the game has seen more polish and becomes more fleshed out, it could easily support a healthy community.
So here is what I reccommend:
Buy it, see how the game evolves first hand while also contributing to future development and marketing
Or follow it and take a "wait and see" approach.
If you are looking for immediate quality, ignore this game for the time being and check back in 6 months.

Something I want to get out of the way real quick, people should not persuade you away with the player count. First, this game has had no advertising yet. The developers are using EA funds to fund an ad campaign to get this game out there and already have a lot of hookups, so buying this game would help it grow by more than just adding another player. Angels Fall First is something I've been eyeing since shortly after it came to EA on Steam. It's not something I got very hyped for or watched closely but it always kept my interest. I finally picked it up for $14 on sale and honestly I would have paid more. This game took me by surprise. It fills a crack that has gone unfilled since Battlefront 2 and much more.
If AFF had the title Battlefront III, I would welcome it with open arms and be surprised at how much they evolved and expanded on what made Battlefront great. Things like making capital ships completely pilotable, function similar to the ones in battlefront. All large ships (Corvettes, battleships, capital ships) have very detailed and beautiful interiors, some of them big enough to be their own infantry map. The detail in them is just amazing, the command bridges feel like command bridges. You can watch through the window in real time as the battle rages around the capital ship as fighters, bombers, frigates, and capital ships engage then retreat into the barracks to stop boarding enemies. I compare this game to Battlefront a lot because it has some very key mechanics that are similar. It is it's own game, though. It's definitely unique enough to not be an attempt at a BF remake/sequel, and that's good.
Pros:
- Large, detailed maps
- ~15 Maps between land and space, some are similar
- Large scale battles
- Good gunplay/combat
- Squad commands and hierarchy
- Encourages team work and cooperation
- Many ways to play between three roles/ranks: Combat, Command, and Support
- Large variety of weapons, armor, equipment, deployables, general customization for your player and nearly all vehicles land and space
- Large variety of vehicles
- Progression is subtle but helpful
- Offline Battlefront instant action-esque skrimish mode with up to 64 bots
- It's a very enjoyable experience
- Dedicated developers
Cons:
- Feels dated (but not entirely a bad thing in my opinion, will explain in conclusion but it may make some wary)
- Small player base (read top paragraph before making a decision based on player base, please)
- 64 Bots can cause higher end PC's to lag
-
It's now public.
- AI isn't great. Can perform most functions but a tad unresponsive.
- Some small but noticable model errors (bridge trusses not connected, weird normals)
Overall I can't recommend this game enough. It feels like a really good, before it's time, old game. The textures, animations, and UI give it the look of an older game, but the gunplay, content,  mechanics, overall execution, and scale make it feel fresh and satisfying to play. Little things like the in game HUD customization, working/informative on-ship displays, offline/lan/bot playability, real time 3d/moveable map, and attention to detail makes it feel like the developers really want you to enjoy and experience the game to its maximum potential. All of this for under $20 and no extra bull♥♥♥♥♥♥

I do not do reviews on games.... But this one I owe a review to.
First off, most of all the negative reviews are from players that have not put in the time that is required to enjoy this game. It's really sad that a lot of the negative reviews have given this game a Mixed review status. I have seen one review 0.4 hours invested and they said the controls are broken....
So before you start playing this game, please go to youtube and search for LiF Basics 101. You will learn A LOT of invaluable information. There is a learning curve to this game and you really never stop learning simply because there are a TON of details about what's going on that you will discover. This will make you more valuable to the community of players which is I believe what this game is about. Playing with others!
With that out of the way, this game is amazing. They have come along way since the beginning. The graphics are fantastic. (When you start the game is automatically on low settings you need to adjust it!) Sure, just like every single game out there, room for improvement, is a valid complaint. But in the end, this is one of the best sandbox games out right now.
Hard work pays off in this game. It will take some time to gather, build, level your way to what you envision. The reward is great once your done. Do not come into this game thinking that you can just gather a ton of stuff and instantly build stuff. It will not happen. (Unless you take the time to find a server that has high leveling etc.) You most likely WILL need help to do things. It is the way this game is supposed to be played, get it in your head. Sure you could play solo.... But it's going to be a long road.
TLDR:

At first glance this game appears to be "Pay-to-Win" but after playing it for some time now,  I realized the following :
1.) There are 6 card pools in this game -
Innistrad
Theros
Ravnica
Shandalar
Zendikar
Premium
2.) 5 of the 6 card pools are completely free as long as you are willing to invest the time to play games and win. You get a booster pack of 10 cards for each victory within the "Explore Realm" mode. You get a smattering of cards here and there for playing the campaign as well.
3.) I unlocked 4 of the 5 Realms for free (I bought Innstrad for 5 bucks before I realized we were getting free booster packs for winning within the "Explore Realm" mode). So WoTC / Stainless has given away 5 of the 6 card pools.
4.) I also unlocked 14% of the premium pool for free along the way (random draws in the free booster packs I was unlocking)
5.) There is nothing game breaking in the Premium Card Pool. I have competed quite well w/o having the premium cards.
So overall I can not honestly say this is "Pay-to-Win."  I think WoTC was more than generous to make 5 of the 6 card pools unlockable and even allow a small chance of getting premium cards in your random draws (In the booster packs).
As far as the game itself .... it is merely a re-skin of the last 3 editions with the same mechanics and glitches. Some minor cosmetic alterations have been added. The game table is drab grey with confusing geometric designs on it. The table now opens up and makes a huge red line across the table for Combat. Clunky mechanic IMO. the game menus are absolutely horrible. They are slow and come with an annoying "Muwaaaaaoohhhhhhhh" type deep bass sound that will drive one insane after a few minutes lol. Overall though ... for 10 bucks and the ability to get most the cards for free .... this is a no brainer for any Magic fan.
** EDIT** 2-8-2015 -  This game has been out now about 7 months and it handed people what they were clamoring for from the release of the original DoTP ... Full Deck Customization. The ability to build your own deck from scratch. All the crying and complaining for years people did to get this ability and all one sees across the table are what I call "Cookie Cutter Clone Decks." Copies of the pre-built decks within the game with slight modifications to them. I can count on 1 hand how many original themed decks I have seen across the table from me in MP games. It is like people lack the imagination, skills or abilities to create something original. You know from the 1st land practically what type of deck someone is playing anymore ... it has become that predictable. I see this problem as a direct result of the publics' general "I want the easiest possible win with the least amount of work" type mentality anymore. There is a sore lack of creative genius out there as it pertains to deck making. This problem will not be solved anytime soon as long as the general public is wanting that easy win quick gratification for little to no work type mentality. Now to sit back and watch the guilty burn down the house with their flames lol.

I decided to write this review because of the huge number of strange decisions the developers took on this game, and because I find this game really controversial and find myself really torn in my opinion about it.
I play it and will play it, especially if the multiplayr manages not to completely die, but more on that soon..
First of all, the huge letdowns -
The card amount is actually really low which dissapoints me a lot, and the amount of multicolored cards is shocking, as there is only 1 for each 2 color combination, I dont really understand that decision.
And to get to the worst, and I now fear ultimate downside to this game,
It feels like such a sucker punch by the makers, and complete lack of interest in player feedback, to simply not include a favourite mode like that in this game.
And as a result of this, the game's multiplayer is pretty dead, at times, there are like 20 games in total, but at the time of the writing for example, it was only three 1 vs 1 games and thats it.
And lastly, the game menu is a disaster. When you start the game, you have to press "Start" to get to main menu.
Well, I manage to press "Start" 5 or 6 times before it decides to react, it is that unresponsive, and the entire game menu navigation is cluttered by useless animations that slow the progress of getting to where you want down, and it is annoying to say the least..
As a person who owns every Magic game so far, Im just sad based on how the makers approach player feedback, or rather, how they ignore it, and sad to see what they do with this franchise, as it would deserve a quick responsive menu, larger selection of cards, and great choice of game modes, not actually lesser number of them than before..
There are good points about this game too, mainly the single player part which is pretty varied and can test you against all kinds of gamestyles.
And of course the fact you can make any deck you want, any combination of colours and cards you have, and any number of decks except, as I mentioned before, the total amount of cards to choose from is in my opinion dissapointing.
Based on everything said above, I cannot really recommend this game right now for anyone who would expect a great multiplayer experience. It is fun to play but it can get really hard to impossible to play a mp game.
I for example prefer to play 4 player game instead of the missing 2HG mode and thats the least played, and as a result, sometimes I simply dont get to play it when I want to because there is no one playing it, not very good for a game just released..
If you were a single player only player however, you may still want to consider it.
Fun gameplay but you may wish there was more cards to choose from, bad sluggish menu may annoy you, but the gameplay may still be worth it.
Missing 2HG mode, very low amount of games hosted at the time of the review, a disastrously annoying menu navigation on a pc, and last, but not least for me on win 7, 6core phenom cpu, 8gb ram and Gigabyte 7950 HD 3gb gpu, a shocking amount of crashes, mostly during menu navigation, so anyone with a similar pc setup beware.

This game had the best graphics I had ever seen on the PC when it first came out. I was 12 then and I still think the gfx are pretty good. That was the main reason why I shelled out $40 at the time, not knowing that it would end up being one of my favorite games of all times for other reasons too. Namely the excellent soundtrack, 3D world map that makes for interesting exploration (even though originally there was only 1 map in the game), immersive diplomacy, good thief abilities for spying on or stealing from the enemy (also it's fun decimating weaker enemies with just 1 thief as they can "hide in the shadows") and a ton of spells that I never even got around to trying most of. Many artifacts to find for the champions, although it's often annoying to not be able to use them as they are often faith dependent. The combat system is clunky and somewhat tedious but basically strategic with missile units and mages usually doing most of the damage. It is often simple to trick the computer by having it chase one of your melee units around while you fire on them with missiles, and the enemy doesn't evade well if at all. I suppose you could have an army of mostly melee units, but you'd better find the best ones in the game because most of them are pretty weak. The redeeming aspect of battles is the rpg-like element of experience points that levels most units (not all) up to 5, and champions much higher.
I always preferred playing as the Life faith, and it may be the easiest one to start with as they have the best missile units (archers) in the game. A tip would be to free your great temple as soon as possible (before the first 7th day) in order to start gaining followers for gathering resources and creating new units. New followers arrive to your empire every 7 days, depending on how much "Fame" you have gained.
I really hope they fix the "Pegasus bug" as I have already run across 3 of these level 8 creatures and it takes an entire army with my best champions to take one down, usually losing a couple units in the process. Not neccesarily a bad thing as it adds challenge, but I really don't think a level 2 hamlet is supposed to spawn this creature.
I really really hope they make a Lords of Magic II, or at least an HD update for this game!

So another classic arrives on Steam - as with many of these presumably the primary audience is going to be people that played them (often for many, many hours/days/weeks/years) when they were originally released, but as long as you can overlook the aged graphics and the lack of modern conveniences it should still be a fairly fun game.
When you start a new game you can choose to be a warrior, mage or thief and then you can choose to be any of the eight elements, give you 24 fairly distinct hero variations you can try out. Once you have chosen you will appear on the main game map where you can see various buildings and places to interact with, where you will find monsters to defeat, giving you the ability to summon creatures to aid you, hire more troops that can gain experience with you, wizard towars research new spells, towns where you can direct the locals to work in certain industries to increase your income of the various resources in the game (fame, gems, ale, etc), so you can support larger and better armies, and also other heroes to aid you in your quest.
You can also find a number of artifacts which give many different bonuses to your heroes (or not as some you will find will only be useful for classes/elements you can't currently recruit). You can conquer the town/temple of other elements which will allow you to hire more heroes of that element to aid you in your quest.
The one area I always found weakest in the game is the combat - it is played in pausable real time (one of the main ways it differs from early Heroes of Might and Magic titles), and while okay it largely reduces to just everyone attacking each other in a big blob (apart from the missile/spell casters). It never felt very strategic or interesting, and I always tend to autocalc whenever I can get away with it, as you end up having a lot of fights during a campaign.
Overall this is a fun title, if very old and creaky, but it does guide you along a bit at the start of the game, although there isn't a huge amount of hand holding here unlike most modern titles. The user interface is okay if a bit cryptic, but it flows fairly well if you are willing to work with it, so overall I would recommend even to people new to it if the overall theme interests them, and the feel and flow of the game are different enough to HoMaM that fans of that series will probably like it, as it is different enough to not feel like an older and harder to use entry in that series, while still being in the same ballpark in terms of overall gameplay.

Daca analizezi, povestea nu a fost stralucita sau memorabila nici in primul joc. Stand aici, scriind aceste randuri si incercand din rasputeri sa imi aduc aminte bucati din povestea primului Shadow Warrior. Aici lucrurile stau mai bine. Exista o noima de naratiune coerenta, cu toate ca este segmentata de ceea ce jocul numeste o harta si eu motivul pentru care am petrecut prea mult timp in meniuri. Dar ajungem si acolo.
Low Wang, mare Don Juan si mandru spadasin, dupa ce a facut tandari un demon… sau mai multi, in primul joc se pare ca s-a reintors la vechile obiceiuri. Ai una bucata mercenar, care se baga pe unde nu ii fierbe oala, ajunge sa isi imparta corpul cu o fatuca dupa o succesiune de evenimente magice, iar acum trebuie sa opreasca un inamic mistic. In cunvinte simple, povestea nu se i-a prea in serios, nici nu trebuie luata, principiu fiind ca trebuie sa arunci in aer Yakuza sau tai… dupa preferinta.
Am spus mai devreme ca am pierdut prea mult timp in meniuri si am amintit de un sistem de harta. Ei bine, lucrurile in Shadow Warrior 2 s-au schimbat in spre rau. Harta leaga foarte mult gameplay-ul de un sistem de progresie artificial delimitat. Nu mai exista o harta mare pe care cauti chestii, ai multiple locatii cu checkpoint-uri si misiuni pe care trebuie sa le indeplinesti. Pentru ca acum ai misiuni principale si secundare. Toate gasindu-se pe harta si putand fii accesate oricand dupa terminare. Nu este o idee rea, ofera rejucabilitate, dar in momentul in care te lovesti de sistemul de loot din joc, totul se schimba.
Daca ai un comportamentg obsesiv-compulsiv, atunci o sa iubesti acest joc. O sa stai sa colectionezi la idoli si alte zdranganele, unele dintrele ele legendare, dar cu niste statistici de mai bine le lasi jos… Asta ca sa nu spun ca armele fixe din primul joc au fost inlocuite cu un sistem de pick and swap, unde poti sa echipezi cam 70 si un pic de arme. Ideea nu este rea, doar ca unele arme sunt legate de misiuni, ergo sistemul de progresie artificial de care aminteam mai devreme. Armele la randul lor se pot schimba intre ele si upgrada, folosind alte zdranganele pe care le gasesti dupa ce omori demoni. In total trebuie sa echipezi o groaza de zorzoane magice si talismane, pierzand din gameplay ore bune, doar mesterind la statistici. Plus ca sunt total debalansate, asta la data redactarii acestui review, cele de nivel mare fiind de multe ori inferioare celor albastre, care teoretic sunt doar magice. Nu legendare! Putand sa trag o paralela intre lansarea Diablo 3 si acest incident.
In fine, pe langa faptul ca sistemul de inventar si misiuni e tembel, jocul chiar este distractiv. Odata intrati in misiune, structura cu toate ca repetitiva, este distractiva, iar modificarile nu sunt doar de ordinul statisticilor, ci si estetice, putand sa inserezi diverse elemente precum foc sau gheata. Impactul armelor a ramas la fel de satisfacator, dar nu la toate armele melee, existand si exceptii. Dar in mare parte sentimentul de impact si forta in momentul in care dai cu sabia intr-un demon este acelasi, usor imbunatatit la capitolul fizica. Plus, daca mai ai doi sau trei amici destui de dementi si obsesivi compulsivi ca si tine, sa isi construiasca ei cel mai ever tare build, distractie placute. Asta e jocul pe care il joc atunci cand te-ai plictisit intr-un final de Left 4 Dead, ai descoperit ca exista Vermintide si vrei ceva mai light pentru vineri seara. Sistemul de Co-Op, cu cat de bagat cu forta este, are meritele sale. Shadow Warrior 2 este distractiv, are momentele sale, iar sistemul de generare automata a nivelelor tine lucrurile fresh. In doi insi, este distractiv. In patru este bestial. Te distrezi doar gasind noi metode de a sectiona inventiv un demon, avand un picut din umorul provicial de tip Borderlands, iar daca te lasi prada momentului, chiar te poti distra. Lectia este ca trebuie sa te mai si relaxezi sa te bucuri de un joc care nu prea se i-a in serios. Co-op OK, un pic repetitiv, mindless, light la capitolul strategie, bazandu-se mai mult pe reactii rapide si loot-ul cel mai „ciumeg”.
Vizual, nu pot spune ca am avut foarte multe reprosuri de facut primului joc din 2013. Shadow Warrior 2 este extrem de bine optimizat. Se vede ca s-a depus multa atentie in meniuri, dar aici este un lucru bun, existand optiuni pentru optiunile de mai sus, putand sa faci jocul sa ruleze de cele mai multe ori perfect. Ce si-au facut aparitia totusi din trecut sunt timpii de incarcare. Distractie placuta la privit tavanul sau realizat ca trebuie sa cureti tastatura sau mouse-ul. Pe un hard de laptop, ai sanse sa si adormi in timpul ecranului de incarcare, depinzand de cat de obosit esti. Sigur, cand intri in joc esti întâmpinat de o lume limitata de pereti invizibili si tinut constant de manuta, doar, doar Low Wang nu pierde drumul. Totusi, lumine, cu toate ca realizate procedural, arata bine. Motorul grafic al celor de la Flying Wilde Hog arata senzational cam pe orice masina veche de 5 ani. Vizual, este de bine… dar sunetul? Ei bine aici este si mai bine. S-a pastrat umorul detasat si s-a introdus o norma de normalitate in poveste, prin prisma copilitei din capul lui cheliuta, iar dialogurile sunt redate delicios. Replicile intre Wang si fatuca respecta radacinile jocului, atat ele cat si muzica, astfel pachetul fiind complet.
Este un joc cu acel ceva care il putea face sa fie fain, dar acum e cam … ok. Shadow Warrior 2 nu este nici pe departe un joc rau, isi merita banii, fara doar si poate, dar o sa isi gaseasca o nisa de jucatori fideli care agreaza acest gen de hoarding. Astia sunt aceasi indivizi care au cumparat Dead Island, ambele jocuri incadrandu-se … cam prin aceasi categorie. Este placut vizual, are parti bune, este super fain in Co-Op, dar numai cu prietenii, mai spargi si un zambet, zece, dar nu este pentru toata lumea. Daca iti place sa stai sa colectionezi iteme prin jocuri si sa buchisesti la sisteme de inventar gandite in iad, atunci, ai dezlegare de la noi sa cumperi Shadow Warrior 2. Altfel este doar un moft pe care probabil o sa il scarpini la primul Winter Sale.

I've been looking for a game that melds a lot of features from some of my favourite strategy games into an online environment, a game that is set aside from others within the same genre, and this really is it. The game is not pay to win and is paced really well, it's not slow nor is it fast, you really feel rewarded from what you receive through the steady rate of progression. The quests help to push you in the right direction while you're starting out, and after just a few hours you'll be making some really steady progress toward the more end-game options.
Positives: As mentioned previously, the game is not pay to win, finding a game like this that is both enjoyable, f2p, and not pay to win seems to be the gaming equivalent of finding gold in your back garden, for this I am very grateful. You have several different options in terms of how you would like to play the game, do you want to be economically focused, do you want to focus on military, etc; this kind of choice makes the game strategically diverse and allows you to shape how you want to play the game, and I felt that this made the game far more enjoyable, especially if you play with friends and work together by taking up different roles.
Negatives: The game is a little buggy right now, and performance can vary. While trying to use the windowed mode feature I found my game crashing very frequently, and I ultimately had to disable that option. I also got stuck in one of the tutorials while trying to access the menu. So the game is definitely in need of some polish. Combat could also do with some work; the current system gets the job done but is quite clunky and very messy. You send your units in and then sit back and hope for the best. Of course the graphics are quite basic but they are bearable, a slight overhaul would be a nice quality of life improvement. A little more direction for players completely new to the genre would also be very useful.
Overall, from my gameplay experience and from the masses of reading I've done about the game, I think it's great and absolutely worth a try. The developers are keen on improving the game and are asking for feedback whenever possible, which really tells me they have their head in the right place.

It's worth a buy now and I've seen enough to have faith in the developers' ability to further improve upon the experience.
Pros:
+Multiplayer progression system doesn't lock equipment behind a grind like similar games.
+Land and space maps add quite a bit of variety to gameplay (it's like 2 good games in one).
+Map designs are very good (and I've seen/heard teases of more)
+Great deal of customization for infantry and vehicles to suit your playstyle.
+Developers have a very strong opinion against microtransactions and bad business practices like DLC map packs that split playerbase.
+Gameplay is fun and there are some novel elements like boarding capital ships in space.
+Well designed Bots allow you to play singleplayer or to fill an online match with only a few humans.
Cons:
-Low player base. There's no getting around this. At current state the servers are usually empty with only a few peaks where the populations rises. You can have enjoyable online experiences, but you can't always pick when they are available. If you are only interested in online play, I recommend bookmarking the game and seeing what happens.
-Balance issues. There are some weapon and vehicle imbalances that benefit one side over the other in certain areas. These issues are well known by the devs, but you will have to live with them until resolved.
-The learning curve is higher than usual (there is a lot going on in the game). Also the in-game tutorial is currently broken so you will need to use fan guides or ask other players to help you learn.
Mixed:
+-Developers are working on this as a labor of love rather than a full time job. The bad news is that production isn't full time (though they do work on it quite a bit). The good news is that this means the chances of progress stopping is extremely low.
+-Developers are intentionally holding off advertising the game until it is closer to release and they are sure new players will get the propper eperience (above negatives resolved). This means the player base will likely remain low for a while, but it also means there is a chance that a decent player base will arive later.

For such a simplistic concept that's been done a hundred times before AFF is surprisingly addiciting to play. with still being in its early stages the Devs behind this beauty are turning it into something i look forward to pplaying for some years to come. the graphics are about mid range but in a game like this the scenery isn't all that important. With update 12 the guns now sound like you are actually hitting something with real force. The fast paced combat and changing map as the match progresses makes the game feel like an actual battle instead of a bunch of people shooting at eachother. Having to move up and take different objectives while a single person or computer AI commands you through the battle can be something a bit strange at times when you and several people want to take a certain objective but you're told to remain behind and defend a dropship. However the game makes up for this with such large maps the AI has multiple routes to attack from. As you progress through an Incursion mission the attackers have to take areas further ahead in order to land more dropships which can be destroyed by the defenders and push you further back from the objective. the game runs and feels smooth at most times and the space combat is certainly something of note. Changing from different styles of flight in a fast paced fighter makes for sharp turns and even drifting in space to give you an upper hand in combat while still staying true to the physics of space. having the ability to not only command different types of ships and land inside hangers and fight through stations but also having the ability to command capital ships and use the weapons and even repair them from the inside to give your ship a fighting chance sets this game apart from many games that focus specificly on space combat. AFF if worth every bit of money you spend on it. I've enjoyed the game personally and I'm excited to see where it goes in the future.

AFF is the answer to the question "What if we took Unreal Tournament's Assault mode and mixed it with Starwars Battlefront?". Fans of the latter game, as well as those of Battlefield (Esp. 2142), and Wolfenstien Enemy Territory/ET Quake Wars will probably find the most fun out of this, as there are lots of parallels.
So, you got your ground battles. They play out like something between UT's Assault and SWBF - There are both objectives and cap points, shifting the battles across the map.
There are several vehicles to put to use in these scenarios - A jeep, APC, Tank and Gunship for each side, standard fare though lacking some archetypes, particularly air transports as well as anything particularly novel
Then you got the space battles - they have elements of the ground maps in that there is infantry combat in some space stations, but the meat of it is capital ship combat, with players able to take bombers and fighters to attack and defend theirs respectively. But wait, there's more - If you can get a dropship to an enemy capital ship, you can board it, allowing you to destroy its subsystems from the inside and generally disrupting its performance by killing its crew, if not outright destroying it.
What else? Plenty of customisation options allowing you to fulfil pretty much any infantry role you want, good bot support and a great overall look and feel to the game
The game still has a long way to come though. Unfortunately, its biggest shortcoming is a small playerbase, which is a vicious cycle - People aren't playing, so people who might otherwise want to play don't. Furthermore, the UI is pretty terrible, amounting to information overload. I'd bet that's the easiest part to change though. Last, optimisation is poor. My computer's a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥by this point so it's not really representative, but it ran pretty much fine when I played it as a UT3 mod. Now I'm lucky to get a framerate in the double-digits, and refunded the first time around as a consequence. Such is the nature of early access though, and I'm sure these will be addressed by the time it's fully released (They're currently overhauling the UI, what I've seen so far looks great). Hopefully the team will be able to get it some attention when that comes.

NOTE: I recommend this game at $9.99 - any additional "special edition" upgrades or whatever are a total waste of money and should NOT be where your money goes.
What this is not:
- an online replacement/playtesting tool for paper magic players who don't want to pay hundreds, if not thousands to maintain an online collection.
- worth investing more than $9.99 in
- designed for PC
- a challenge for real, competitve magic players
If you can accept these things, then you are not going to be disappointed by DOTPW 2015.
It is a short campaign with a decent amount of replay value, it is better executed in "most" regards vs. the previous iterations of this game. The AI is generally not challenging at all, even at the hardest levels, so if you are a good magic player, and you concede games quickly to poor RNG, you can easily finish this entire campaign in about 3-4 hours (you will note I have 7.2 hours on record, and that includes a reasonable amount of messing around and farming the post-campaign content)
Duels was clearly designed for tablets, so with that said, you may well just want to buy it on a tablet :), as the menus ask you to "swipe" the screen with your mouse, which is inaccurate to say the least, and infuriating in more cases than not.
What duels of the planeswalkers 2015 has improved on...
The overall game UI is solid, and is an excellent educational tool for those not necessarily too familiar with the game's rules. The mana-tapping complaints I have seen are really not a concern if you pay attention and use mana-cycling. Not being able to target your opponent's cards by default is something you MUST turn off. No spoilers, but there is a specific opponent where your life is a ton easier if you can target their cards. I would also turn off the handicap of allowing the AI to order your blocks for you - but do so understanding that assigning blocks is a bit of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥so you may well order incorrectly anyway.
The presentation of cutscenes, videos and even some voice acting is new to DOTPW with this edition, advancing on "motion images" of the previous incarnation. The underlying story of Garruk and his obsession with being a hunter is nicely realized and while the transitions from plane to plane are a touch, weird, it's all good and nothing that detracts from the overall story experience.
The collection management has decent filtering, the packs you get after each victory generally have at least a couple of good upgrades for your current deck, and by about plane 4 or so, you do get to have some real flexibility in adjusting your deck to handle the current task at hand (i.e. sideboarding in artifact or enchantment removal, etc)
The whole deck building interface is quite basic, however. So don't expect it to make it easy for you to see your deck at a glance.
Who is Duels of the Planeswalkers 2015 for?
anyone who is generally speaking a fan of Magic the Gathering, but is on the more beginner to intermediate side. The tutorial is good, the tool tips are accurate and useful, and the overall experience is very much intended to hand-hold the player with less experience. If you pay attention well enough, you will get a good introduction to core concepts such as the stack, correctly timing your instants and abilities and attacking before playing cards (something the AI does, and the game correctly (for the most part) recommends to you).
Anyone who is a bit more skilled who feels that $10 is a decent value for 7-10 hours (or more if you really get in to the multiplayer aspect) of magic-based entertainment.
It is sad to note the loss of the puzzle/challenge mode. This might have been a mistake to exclude since such things are generally speaking one diversion which entertains the more advanced player.
Keep your expectations low, and this game will be pretty much everything you want - and it's a heck of a lot more fun to play than full fledged Magic the Gathering in the recently launched v4 online client!

As opposed to what most people say about this game, I actually really enjoyed it.
Having the opportunity to play the colours I like, and build the deck I want to play from humble beginnings to wiping-the-floor-with-Garruk powerful was a lot of fun, and it added another scale of challenge to the game.
As a fan of previous Duels of the Planeswalkers titles, I didn't feel it was too much a stretch from them at all, and though only starting with one deck can be frustrating, you have the opportunity to create more as you play. By the time I finished the main campaign, I had 3 decks, and had turned the Blue/Black deck I started with into a Blue/Green one that I was more comfortable with.
It can feel a bit slow at the start, and your deck may seem woefully underpowered compared to your opponents, but isn't that the point of a game? Start small and work your way up? If they just gave you a powerful deck at the start and said "Go punch this guy", would you be as satisfied as you would be when you nurture your deck into a well oiled machine of destruction?
The duels themselves are no slower than the previous games, and in fact many of them felt a lot faster overall. I had to stop the timer repeatedly to drop in spells, which to me, felt more realistic than having your opponent wait extensively after every single trigger.
Finally, the money aspect. I found it wasn't too prevalent at all, and while yes, you can buy more cards, it is in no way a necessity, and it doesn't garuntee that you will win in any case. There are more than enough cards available in the regular sets that put the premium ones to shame, and anyone who thinks "There's no way to beat a premium deck Q.Q" is kidding themselves, and needs to take a better look at the cards they're given.
For casual players, it can seem a bit daunting, but the tutorials provided give a very thorough understanding of everything you need to know, and while they may seem frustrating for experienced players, they are a necessity as with most games.
Overall, I highly recommend this game, it's fun, engaging, and overall more challenging that previous DotP games.

Everglow Interactive went for the hail mary of a potentially good thing here, but they really have to get their crap together. There's a fan-made version of this game called "Maniac Mansion Deluxe".  It's far better than either version in this release, and it's free.  The NES version however is still the best of all current Maniac Mansion versions available.  It just isn't the same without Dave's theme.
This release holds no value beyond archiving, which isn't going to be a reason for most people to buy (who will want an actual good gaming experience), which is why I can't recommend this release.
In fullscreen, the mouse tracking is wildly inaccurate, and jumps all over the place.  *IF* you get this, hit alt+enter to put it in a very small (640x480) windowed mode, where mouse tracking is actually accurate.  F5 brings up the in-game menu.
Being stuck to the very small 640x480 window to play the game properly is a huge negative, though when I disable fullscreen stretch through my GPU so it's only vertstretch in fullscreen instead of widescreen stretch as well (something this game was not intended to display at), the image is quite blurry.  This game needed a remaster or a remake, not a re-release.
This is the worst audio presentation of the MM releases - the NES version had the best audio.  This actually has virtually *no* audio, and the audio it does have is highly annoying (even in the "Enhanced" version, which I'm pretty sure is the Amiga release).  This game needed a remaster or a remake, not a re-release.
Needs contextual interactions, annoying these days to have to click every specific action first before interacting with something, every single time.  Or at least keybinds for interactions to speed things up.  This game needed a remaster or a remake, not a re-release.
Has multiple "dead ends", which was common in old-school adventure games.  A "dead end" is when you use an item in the wrong way as it's meant to solve a later puzzle, but rather than give you a contextual error message and leave the item, it consumes that item and when you encounter the puzzle that correctly required that same item, you don't have it and that game no longer has it to be found anywhere, so you need to start over.  All interactable items blend is so well with the rest of the art that you don't know what's what unless you click on absolutely everything.  Two of the characters have "unwinnable" games.  Save yourself a headache, use a walkthrough.  This game needed a remaster or a remake, not a re-release.
This version doesn't have the censorship the NES version does (this becomes apparent very quickly), but regardless, this game needed a *lot* of work to really hold up to the legacy of its memory.  It doesn't need a re-release, not even of the NES version.  This game needed a remaster or a remake, not a re-release.

The audio is emulatred PC Speaker with modulated square-wave, so don't expect Amiga style music. Also, if your monitor is set up for 1:1, you're going to be playing this in a TINY rectangle. Because the ScummVM UI is supressed, you can't adjust that before launching. You have to launch the menu with F5, then return to launcher. Additionally, if you're into GPL, you'll note the lack of required GPL verbiage in the Disney EULA. It's way better to play this within Day of the Tentacle.

Kingdom Wars, previously known as Dawn of Fantasy, is a controversial game.
On the one hand, it offers some unique features well-made and set on a balanced way for the player to enjoy, when you could be expecting grinding. Despite being a FPS (free to play game) and, surprisingly, it offers very few advantages for players who decide to spend their money on it. Namely, you can buy singleplayer, a handful of skins for buildings, banners and heroes, some treasures (basically a 1 push economic boost that will give you a lot of resources) and the premium mode, that gives you better drops of Wealth (an ingame resource that is obtained through fighting), being only the premium mode timed. Excluding the treasures and the premium mode, everything else put together doesn't reach 5€ euros. One of the most non-greedy FPS MMOs I've seen in my gaming life.
Gameplay wise, it has its ups and downs. The player freedom is absolute and there are no restrictions to what you may or may not do, at all. There are 2 stances in the game: PvE (Player vs Environment, the AI) and PvP (Player vs Player). Each player has his own game bubble and therefore is own environment, allowing him to fully refuse any player interaction and stick to the questline (which works as a tutorial and introduces you to open field and siege battles to prepare you for multiplayer, as well as offering a grinding option to obtain crowns and loot. Completely skipable but enjoyable). Each player bubble is connected to the rest through the server. In order for 2 players to fight, one of them must select the PvP option always available, and a search engine will find you the nearest fair opponent. The term "fair" refers to a strenght value that every army has got attached, avoiding this way imbalanced fights in terms of army size and quality. You may also choose to play cooperative the same way to take over a town, defeat the AI or complete a quest.
As every MMO, there's a grinding component: obtaining Wealth. This is the most precious resource in the game that will allow you to upgrade buildings, recruit heroes and some other functions. However, you're free to choose your own way. You may earn as much gold as you can and trade it for Wealth. Raiding the countryside, taking over AI cities, player cities, armies, quests, unlocking achievements. Your own path and style all along.
The looting, construction and squad/formation system, as well as the training and siege mechanics are very peculiar and enjoyable, actually making you feel like you're fighting in the harsh mediaval age and adding a very important and heavy strategy factor. There's a wide variet of units and strategies for each one of the 3 races (Humans, orcs and elfs), being the player able to hire troops from other races at any given time. The art style and looking is quite colourful and lively, your town shines with activity from the very beginning.
On the other hand, not everything could possibly be good. The game has some unpolished factors and plain issues. Graphical glitches aren't hard to see, minor bugs (units getting stuck, happens very rarely) and a general feel of non polished textures and wierd motion when zooming in the battlefield. The beginning is quite slow and can make new players hesitate about playing the game any longer. The general perfomance FPS wise isn't the best either, making the less powerful PCs sluggish in large sieges and battles.
Only time can tell if the game is going to fix these minor issues and become a high quality, popular game.
Time has passed. I, as a beta tester who played the game almost 2 years ago now, can tell the development team has only improved in their work. New features are added almost every month, patches are released regularly and in good amount to fix both bigger and minor issues reported by the players. The community as a whole has a generally positive and friendly attitude. Mods and admins attend to every request the players make, include multiple (viable) suggestions and interact with the playerbase. There's almost everytime at least a set of mods in the chat in order to help players who have issues or don't know how to play the game, get started, etc. Refunds for minor losses, glitches or disconnects are instantaneous in-game and take a timelapse of (usually) less than 12 hours to happen. The support team also solves non gameplay related issues single- handed. (This is my own experience: I bought the game 2 years ago, and now that the system has changed, I've been given all the content that my original purchase included and some extras. For free). The playerbase grows in daily basis, the game is always in constant development and there's not such a thing as end-game.
All in all, the gameplay after a few hours become very enjoyable. It's by no means a fast paced game: you may take your time to take decisions, reconsiderate the ones you've taken and scratch the ones that didn't pay off.
There's a long-term plan. Even if you don't know. You're not going to build your castle overnight: it will take weeks, maybe even a month, as mentioned previously, the beginning is slow. The sieges are highly challenging and PvP is never easy, but the rewards are great. You'll lose entire armies that you'll have to rebuild from scratch, and you'll crush cities, kingdoms and races. The vassal system will allow you to eventually take over every AI center, and be attacked by players who desire such influence.
The game is good, it's going to get better, and it's free. It's nothing like you've tried before. You should give it a chance, go ahead and have fun with it. The entire community and support team will be available for you at every point of your Kingdom Wars experience.

The meta for this game is a fat japanese man grabbing you and killing you immediately regardless of health.
Every class in this game relies on one gimmick that deals massive damage. Combat is extremely repetetive: blocking and hitting and parrying fill up the beginning, while a few hours in every raider, warlord, valkyrie, lawbringer, the entire japanese hero list, conquerer, and peacekeeper has mastered their unblockable attack, which hits for 1/4 most character's health. Furthermore, the instakill environmental mechanic reduces most - if not all -  fights to a position and reaction check.
Few classes take actual skill, but even then the majority of them have some abilities such as the kunai and bow for the japenese, the artillery for the warden, the hand grenade for the peacekeeper, that vastly reduce the health that a character has before the fight even really starts.
The game itself has flaws, the peer to peer networking and lack of servers lead to some awkard encounters, and the "skill" filtering does absolutely nothing: even when given a metric of class level or class item level, the matchmaking puts your team of level 10 friends against prestige 2 players. Still too, the microtransactions present are worrying.
This game does have its high points, but they are few and far between, and only come whenever you're winning. Losing in this game doesn't feel like it is based on player skill, more often than not. Even in 1v1 duals, where player item level is neglected, the presence of abilities and environmental hazards puts a dampener on the fun. Further still, the gimmicky moveset of some heroes, including those which can apply damage over time attacks on top of an already healthy damage per regular attack or those that instakill full health heroes and heal the attacker, also reduce the fun in losing. Losing can be fun, but only whenever you can learn from your mistakes.
The practice mode, which is supposed to teach you how to play heroes, doesn't allow the player to choose what hero they are playing against, only the skill level of their opponant.
The campaign isn't great either. The story is lackluster, and the combat suffers from problems here too. The player's character is displayed as extremely powerful, able to cut through the rank and file with ease. Their sword that could cut through a shield and kill the man behind it in one swing suddenly is reduced to a rubber whacker when faced with anyone blessed with horizontal bars over their heads.
Still too, the writing can be criticized. Character movitivations are weak: the Warden is a harbinger of justice and protector of the weak, but serves an organization without real complaint whenever they slaughter prisoners.
Graphics are good. Sometimes buggy, especially when AOE buffs are used.
Despite everything I've said, the multiplayer has some redeeming qualities:
Every hero has a diverse moveset
Usually combat against a particular character is unique
Sometimes players forget that they have abilities
Visually, the heroes and combat themselves are well designed:
Unblockable attacks are telegraphed with a unique orange tint
Line of sight is irrelevent whenever surrounded: there is a wheel to easily block oncoming attacks
The ranged abilities have some telegraph, however it is extremely short.
In conclusion, I would not recommend buying this game based on its repetetive combat, lack of balance, microtransactions, terrible netcode and peer to peer networking system. Furthermore, I would invite you to read the first letter of the last two paragraphs.

Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic 2 takes place 5 years after the events of the first. We now play as “The Exile”, a jedi cast out of the order for going to war without the councils permission. As luck would have it he/she is one of the last jedi after the Sith's successful purge and has a huge bounty on his/her head. The situation really shows in game as a good amount of people will try to kill you or deceive you for that huge bounty. It does become a tad tiresome when the same assassin droids show up time and time again spouting the same dialogue each time.  As for the game itself it plays it very safe and only improves upon a few things while keeping everything from the original intact. It is not made by the same developers as the original.
Companions are far improved in this game and now feature a influence system in which they either disprove of you or like you  depending on the actions you take.  This time around there is a much better balance between Light Side and Dark Side companions unlike the original where near everyone had a holier than thou attitude. You never trust any of them either which I found very neat as I half expected the people that have my back to turn on me any moment. Some will flat out refuse to talk to you ever again if you annoy them enough. I still would like the option to kick teammates out of my ship. Which brings me to the ship, it is the same exact ship from the first game. They reuse a lot of material from the first game including planets that are ruin down but the same exact places as the original and much smaller.
They really took a huge step back when it comes to environments. Where as the first game had huge unique environments this one has small gray corridor after small gray corridor. Your choices in the last game doesn't really make a lick of difference and they even get the gender of the 1st game's protagonist wrong and they will default to being female. Not a big deal at all but slightly annoying.  This sequel is far more prone to glitches and crashes. I actually had to cheat to get past a game breaking bug.  It has this incomplete feel as if they either rushed the game out or just didn't care.  It does have a few improvements like your teammate AI is much better at following you around, a small improvement to inventory menus though they are still awful and regenerating health which is neither a good or bad feature.
Gameplay is pretty much the same as the original but with a few different force powers. I don't think they reused any music and it sounds just as amazing as the first.  You now seem to level up much faster and when I was done with the tutorial I was already half the level of the lasts game's character which I had at level 20 by the end of the game. Same abilities, same skills  and same stats as the first, they didn't really do anything to enhance character building. Story is pretty cool and feels much more mysterious than the first. There is no clear good and evil side in this game which is a huge improvement from the first. You never receive a lightsaber either, you have to build it if you want one. Overall I enjoyed the story more than the originals even though I saw the ending coming from a mile away unlike the first.
I mentioned the first a lot in this review but it cant be helped. This sequel is pretty much a carbon copy of the first with a new story and a few highly uninteresting new worlds. It felt like an unnecessary sequel since the last game ended so well and this  game does nothing to enhance the  last game's overall story or makes any improvements to gameplay. Though if you enjoyed the last game and wanted more then it is nearly guaranteed you will love this.  It is definitely more of the same but if that is what you want than this would be a great purchase.

This has potential.
I haven't played a huge amount so far, partly due to the fact that it's a struggle to get working at the moment; the client frequently screws up the update process, there are crashes and lag and the UI needs work. Also the movement is a little jerky and flickery.
And yet I'm glad I bought it. The setting is nice and bleak like a survival horror should be, the monsters are beautifully designed and far more interesting than the generic zombies you find in other games, the city is suitably huge, and the verticality of a map where you can enter half of the buildings, climb 20 stories and look down on the surrounding blocks sniping at golems is a great new twist on the genre.
As always, the most dangerous threats are other players. A great deal of the survival horror is because you simply can't trust other players not to stab you in the back and steal your gear. The rare instances where you and others end up trusting each other and cooperate to clear out safe zones are immensely satisfying. Whether such trust lasts after you all leave the safe zone is another matter.
So yeah, it's still in beta, so everything is rough around the edges and there's obviously still work required. But Nether is a game you'll want to keep an eye on, because I think it's going to do some very interesting things with the horror survival genre.

As someone who absolutely loved Shadow Warrior 2013 I was hugely let down by Shadow Warrior 2.
Shadow Warrior 2 is honestly a slog to get through from start to end. I played it by myself on the highest difficulty, and by the time I got to end credits I let out an honest sigh of relief (before getting angry at the ending)
The game starts with some potential as I was pretty excited to see how many different weapons were in the game but as that initial wonder wears off it's replaced by boredom and frustration.
This game is not at all difficult. I played on the highest difficulty which means that normal enemies could at times take literally hundreds of bullets to kill. This is by far the best way to make your game boring, let me sink clip after clip into a standard enemy before letting me move on without providing any actual challenge. If you die, even on the highest difficulty nothing much happens, your enemies get there health back (annoying) you lose your chi (mana) and a percentage of your total money, other than that you just spawn maybe five seconds away from where you were to jump straight back into the fight so you can hold that left mouse button for another ten minutes. The game sacrifices any actual challenge for bullet sponge enemies. If you invest in chi regen and your healing spell (which you should) you will have almost infinite health, at this point every battle is a battle of attrition as you dash from side to side holding the left mouse button until everything dies and you hear a repeated quip from your favourite murderer Lo Wang.
This game has very clearly taken inspiration from the Borderlands series (take from that what you will) meaning that its progression system revolves around boring upgrades that are based soley on small percentage upgrades that don't make a lick of difference to the way you play the game. Playing on the highest difficulty promises to give you the best upgrades however what I found was I got the upgrades that I was going to use around 8 hours into the game and never found an upgrade even up until the end credits. This effectively make the upgrade system useless given that even when I unlocked the ability to craft my own gems I still couldn't make anything better than what I had found earlier.
By the time I got to the last 5-6 hours of the game my experience was as follows.
Enter level
Run past every enemy to the objective
Run wherever I was told to run
Fight whatever I'm told to fight for upwards of ten minutes
Run around looking for ammo because enemies take hundreds of bullets to kill
Return to the fight
Repeat until end credits

So I have seen a lot of reviews for this game. Most negative. Very negative. Then I saw a few reviews that were good enough for me to try this game out anyways. Plus it is only $9.99 which is barley anything. So after 10 hours of play I have this to say about the game. The negative reviews are overstated... buy quite a lot.
Getting cards is now easier than ever. Whenever you win a match you get 10+ cards of all rarities each time (just like an actual booster). I have not stopped to count the exact number of cards, but you get quite a few. Even more so when compared to the past versions which would unlock one card every game you win which sucked.
You can skip the turtorial by pressing the button "skip" at the bottom right of the scree before you start it. So yeah if you have problems reading buttons like the people who complained about not being able to skip it I assure you it is there.
At the start of the game you pick 2 colors and from those 2 colors a deck. You can go back before you select a deck in order to choose different color combos and so that you can see the diff decks. I read that black red sucked at the start so I went with black green. It was not amazing, but it got the job done rather well for a starter deck.
Those who said things about not being able to change their color are also wrong here again. After you beat Avacin you are given the option of being able to change your color combination. YOU CAN CHANGE YOUR COLORS. And Avacin is only a few matches away. How people missed this I do not know at all.
As for how hard the game is with the starting deck, I had no problems at all getting to Avacin and I was able to beat her eventually after a few bad draws. Manages to somehow be even worse than the lackluster Magic 2014 by removing features that have become a series staple (such as Two-Headed Giant, both local and online) and restricting access to cards behind a paywall of microtransactions. The best cards in the game are blocked off behind $2 a pop for premium boosters, so players who have dished out cash for these will always win online matches. Deck building is something fans have wanted for a while, and while it works in itself, it is extremely limited, almost as much as the atrocious sealed play in the last instalment. Once you choose a colour you are locked down to it, and you must build a deck focused around that and one more colour. This cannot be changed. You can create a new deck using unique colours, but with the small amount of useful cards you pick up from random boosters (one per victory) these decks will inevitably lose every time.
Besides these drawbacks, the user interface is slow and clearly designed around a tablet device. Transitions and loading times are appaling and the game is bland and dull to look at. Swiping through icons for every menu choice should never be a feature in ANY PC game. There are also significant problems with the AI - some blatantly cheat and use cards that are unavailable in the game. When a loss comes from a lack of fairness the game becomes incredibly frustrating and even less fun to play.
This is a joke of a game - a truly pathetic, lazy attempt to please fans who have demanded full deck customisation for years. Well, they gave it to us, but they also took away everything else. With Hearthstone being as popular and well received as it is, this game needed to be great to compete, and it is not.

Maniac Mansion is unlike almost any other adventure game (except for Zak McKracken). The reason is that the NPCs in the game are alive. They have their own goals (get food, get mail, check out suspicious events), they can catch you, you can die or lose important items. Actions have real consequences, and there's even choice and different endings. The trailer above is very adequate and demonstrates some of that.
The reason this game is so alive is the scripter David Fox, the same designer who did Zak McKracken and was heavily involved in the recently released Thimbleweed Park. Even though he's not the official game designer, he's the one who loves to make NPCs have their own virtual theater with daily routines, reactions to your actions, etc.
This is also the first game that introduced mouse based interface and cut-scenes (in 1988). Sadly, the later games of Ron Gilbert and LucasFilm Games ended up being way more static, lifeless and fake, with NPCs that don't move, and player actions that never punish you, but at least kept the exploration and meaningful puzzles we can find here.
The modern port of Maniac Mansion is very good. It supports mouse, multiple saves, and different graphical versions of the game. Of course, it's the fan made ScummVM, but it's great nevertheless.
